p.seg: Someone said:
The rhapsody
is a lineage of the ancient Odes.
In the past, after Chéng and Kāng passed away, the sounds of the Eulogies ceased;
when the kingly favor was exhausted, the Odes were no longer produced.
At the beginning of the Great Hàn's stabilization,
there was no leisure time.
Until the eras of Wǔ and Xuān,
ritual officials were then honored,
and literary writings were examined.
Internally, the offices of Jīnmǎ and Shíqú were established;
externally, the matters of the Yuèfǔ and Xiélǜ were promoted,
to revive what had been discarded and continue what had been cut off,
and to embellish the grand enterprise.
Therefore, the common people were joyful and content,
and the responses of good fortune were particularly abundant.
The songs of the White Unicorn, Red Goose, Fungus Chamber, and Precious Tripod
were presented in the suburban temples.
The auspicious omens of the Divine Sparrow, Five Phoenixes, Sweet Dew, and Yellow Dragon
were used to mark the years.
Therefore, the ministers of speech and attendants,
such as Sīmǎ Xiāngrú, Yúqiū Shòuwáng, Dōngfāng Shuò, Méi Gāo, Wáng Bāo, and Liú Xiàng,
deliberated and reflected morning and night,
and made offerings and contributions daily and monthly.
Meanwhile, the high officials and great ministers,
Censor-in-Chief Ní Kuān,
Grand Ritualist Kǒng Zāng,
Grand Palace Grandee Dǒng Zhòngshū,
Minister of the Imperial Clan Liú Dé,
and Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince Xiāo Wàngzhī,
would also compose from time to time.
Some used it to express the feelings of those below and convey subtle admonitions;
others used it to proclaim the virtues of those above and exhaust loyalty and filial piety.
With elegant and expansive praise,
they recorded it for posterity;
it was indeed second only to the Elegantiae and Eulogies.
Thus, in the era of Xiào Chéng,
they were discussed and recorded.
There were over a thousand pieces presented to the throne,
and thereafter the literary grace of the Great Hàn
shone brilliantly, sharing the same spirit as the Three Dynasties.
Furthermore, the Way has its declines and peaks,
and learning has its coarse and refined aspects.
Those who establish virtue according to the times
do not change the principles based on distance.
Thus, Gāoyáo sang in Yú,
and Xīsī praised Lǔ;
both were collected by Master Kǒng
and listed in the Odes and Documents.
Their meaning is the same.
Investigating high antiquity reveals it was like that;
examining the Hàn house shows it is like this.
Although this matter is small,
it is the old model of former ministers
and the remaining beauty of the state,
which cannot be omitted.
I have humbly seen that the world within the seas is clear and peaceful,
the court is without affairs,
the capital is repairing its palaces,
dredging its moats,
and building parks
to complete the institutional systems.
The elders of the western lands
all harbor feelings of resentment and longing,
hoping for the Emperor's favorable gaze,
and grandly praising the old systems of Cháng’ān,
with discussions that disparage Luòyì.
Therefore, I have composed the Liǎng Dū Fù,
to exhaustively portray what dazzles the common people,
and then correct it with the standards of today.
The text says:
A Guest from the Western Capital asked a Host of the Eastern Capital, saying:
"I have heard that at the beginning of the Great Hàn's planning,
there was an intention to make the capital at Héluò.
But they stopped and were not at ease there,
so they actually moved west
to build our Superior Capital.
Has the Host heard the reason for this and seen its system?"
The Host said:
"Not yet.
I wish for the Guest to express his cherished thoughts of the past
and give vent to his deep feelings of antiquity.
Broaden my knowledge with the Imperial Way,
and enlighten me with the Hàn capital."
The Guest said:
"Indeed."
"The Western Capital of Hàn
is located in Yōngzhōu,
and is truly called Cháng’ān.
To the left, it relies on the barriers of Hángǔ and the two Xiáo mountains;
to the front, it is marked by the peaks of Tàihuá and Zhōngnán.
To the right, it is bordered by the hazards of Bāoxié and Lǒngshǒu;
it is girdled by the rivers of the Hónghé, Jīng, and Wèi.
At the bend of many streams,
the Qiān surges to its west.
Regarding the abundance of flora and fruit,
it is the most fertile land of the Nine Provinces;
regarding the natural defenses of its barriers,
it is a secluded region of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, it extensively covers the six directions
and has thrice become the imperial domain.
The Zhōu rose like a dragon from here,
and the Qín glared like a tiger from here.
When the Great Hàn received the mandate and made it the capital,
above they were enlightened by the essence of the Dōngjǐng constellation,
and below they harmonized with the spirit of the Hétú.
Fèngchūn proposed the plan,
and Liúhóu elaborated its completion.
Heaven and man responded in harmony
to radiate the imperial brilliance.
Looking back toward the west with favor,
they truly established the capital.
Thereupon, they gazed toward the Qín Mountains
and looked upon the Northern Heights.
Embracing the Fèng and Bà rivers,
and occupying the Lǒngshǒu ridge.
They planned the imperial foundation for a hundred million years,
and measured grand designs to rise on a large scale.
Starting from Gāozǔ and ending with Píngdì,
generations added decorations to enhance its magnificence.
Passing through twelve reigns of extended blessings,
it reached the heights of prosperity and the extremes of luxury.
They built a golden city with ten thousand battlements,
and opened a surrounding moat that became a deep pool.
They opened three wide thoroughfares
and established twelve connecting gates.
Inside, the streets and avenues were interconnected,
and the neighborhoods numbered nearly a thousand.
Nine markets opened their grounds,
with goods separated and alleys divided.
People could not look back,
and carriages could not turn around.
They filled the city and overflowed the suburbs,
spreading out into a hundred residential blocks.
Red dust converged from four sides,
and smoke and clouds were continuous.
Thus, being both populous and wealthy,
their entertainment was boundless.
The gentlemen and ladies of the capital
were distinct from those of the five regions.
Traveling scholars were likened to dukes and marquises,
and the rows of shops were more extravagant than the ladies of the Jī and Jiāng clans.
Local powerful figures
and heroes of the wandering knights,
in their integrity they admired Yuán and Cháng,
and their fame was second only to Chūnlíng.
They connected with associates and gathered crowds,
galloping and racing within it.
If one observes its four suburbs
and wanders through the nearby counties,
then to the south one looks toward Dù and Bà,
and to the north one views the Five Tombs.
Famous cities face the outer walls,
and settlements follow one after another.
It is a region of the eminent and talented,
where official sashes and caps arise.
Caps and canopies are like clouds,
with seven chancellors and five dukes.
Together with the heroes of the provinces and commanderies,
and the merchants of the five great cities.
Through the three selections and seven migrations,
they filled and served the funerary towns.
This was to strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches,
exalting the Superior Capital while overlooking the ten thousand states.
Within the capital domain,
its territory spans a thousand lǐ.
Excelling far beyond all the Zhūxià,
it incorporates all that they possess.
To its south, lofty mountains hide the heavens,
with deep forests and vaulted valleys.
A sea of land with precious hoards,
and the fine jade of Lántián.
Shāng and Luò follow its winding recesses,
Hù and Dù border its foothills.
Springs and sources pour and irrigate,
dams and ponds connect one to another.
Bamboo groves and fruit orchards,
fragrant herbs and sweet trees.
The wealth of its countryside
is reputed to be akin to Shǔ.
To its north, it is crowned by Jiǔzōng,
accompanied by Gānquán,
where numinous palaces rise up in their midst.
The grandest sights of Qín and Hàn,
praised in song by Yuān and Yún,
are preserved right here.
Below lie the fertile lands of Zhèng and Bái,
the source of clothing and food.
The total area is fifty thousand qǐng,
with borders and boundaries divided like fine silk.
Ditches and ridges are as if carved and engraved,
plains and marshes arranged like dragon scales.
Opening the channels is like falling rain,
shouldering the spades, they gather like clouds.
The five grains hang their heavy heads,
mulberry and hemp spread in abundance.
In the eastern suburbs, there are connecting canals and great waterways,
surging through the Wèi and piercing into the Hé.
Floating boats to Shāndōng,
pulling and leading from the Huái and the lakes,
sharing waves with the sea.
In the western suburbs, there are the superior parks and forbidden gardens,
forest foothills, marshes, and wetlands,
with ponds and pools stretching toward Shǔ and Hàn.
Encircled by a surrounding wall,
of over four hundred lǐ.
Detached palaces and separate lodges,
numbering thirty-six.
Divine ponds and numinous pools
are found everywhere.
Within them are the qílín of Jiǔzhēn,
and the horses of Dàyuān.
The rhinoceroses of Huángzhī,
and the birds of Tiáozhī.
Crossing Kūnlún,
traversing the great seas.
Strange regions and exotic species
coming from as far as thirty thousand lǐ.
As for the palaces and halls,
their forms and images resemble Heaven and Earth,
and their warp and woof follow Yīn and Yáng.
They occupy the correct position of the spirit of Kūnlíng,
and imitate the round and square of Tàizǐ.
They raise the magnificent watchtowers of Zhòngtiān,
and the vermilion halls that crown the mountains.
Rare materials are used to exhaust all wonders,
raising rainbow-like beams of Yìnglóng.
Rafters and laths are arranged like spreading wings,
while ridgepoles and beams soar high.
Carved jade plugs reside in the pillars,
and cut gold discs decorate the eaves.
They emit the rich brilliance of five colors,
their light flaming and bright, displaying a vivid scene.
Thereupon, the steps on the left are tiered and on the right are smooth,
with double railings and three flights of stairs.
Inner chambers are interconnected,
and palace gates are wide open.
Bell stands are arranged in the central courtyard,
and bronze statues are erected at the main gate.
Following the increased slopes to level the thresholds,
they overlook steep roads and open the doors.
They are followed by detached palaces and private chambers,
and supported by lofty terraces and quiet lodges.
Brilliant like the arrayed constellations,
they surround the Zǐgōng.
Qīngliáng, Xuānwēn,
Shénxiān, and Chángnián;
Jīnhuā, Yùtáng,
Báihǔ, and Qílín.
Buildings such as these
cannot be fully described.
Tiered platforms are towering and majestic,
and the ascent and descent are dazzling and bright.
Unique shapes and strange designs,
each offers a different view.
Riding on cushions or walking in litters,
one rests and feasts at will.
In the rear palace, there are the Yètíng and Jiāofáng,
the chambers for the Empresses and Consorts.
Héhuān and Zēngchéng,
Ānchù and Chángníng.
Zhǐruò and Jiāofēng,
Pīxiāng spreads its fragrance.
Lánlín and Huìcǎo,
where the ranks of Yuān and Luán fly and soar.
Zhāoyáng is particularly grand,
flourishing under Emperor Xiàochéng.
The woodwork does not show its material,
and the walls do not reveal their form.
They are covered with patterned silks,
and entwined with silken cords.
The pearls of Suíhóu and the Bright Moon
are scattered in between.
Golden lamps hold jade discs,
resembling strings of coins.
Kingfisher feathers and fire-rubies
flow with radiance and contain brilliance.
Xuánlí and Chuíjì gems,
the night-shining pearls are there.
Thus, the black courtyard and inlaid masonry,
jade steps and the vermilion court.
The patterned stones are finely textured,
and the blue gems are shimmering green.
Coral and green trees
grow around the corners.
Red silks flutter and stream,
and patterned ribbons are in colorful profusion.
The refined brilliance and flowery candles
make those looking up and down feel as if they are among the gods.
The titles of the rear palace
consist of fourteen ranks.
Graceful and flourishing,
they take turns in favor and nobility.
Those who occupy these ranks
are numbered by the hundreds.
In the courtyards to the left and right,
are the positions for the hundred officials of the court hall.
Xiāo, Cáo, Wèi, and Bǐng
deliberated and planned above.
Those who assisted the mandate handed down the tradition,
and those who aided the wings completed the transformation.
They spread the gentleness of the Great Hàn,
and washed away the poisonous stings of the fallen Qín.
Thus, they caused the people to raise the voice of joy and harmony,
and compose the song of uniformity;
their merit and virtue are manifest in the Ancestors,
and their bounty reaches the common people.
There are also Tiānlù and Shíqú,
the repositories of archives and books.
Commissioned are the earnest and instructional elders,
and famous Confucian masters and tutors.
They lecture and discuss the Liùyì,
and examine and reconcile similarities and differences.
There are also Chéngmíng and Jīnmǎ,
the courts of literary creation.
Men of great refinement and grand reach
gather here in crowds.
They trace the origins and follow the roots,
exhausting their sight and saturating their hearing.
They clarify chapters and sections,
and proofread and organize the secret texts.
Surrounded by the positions of the Gōuchén,
and guarded by the offices of the night watch.
They gather the first class of ritual officials,
and assemble the incorrupt and filial from the hundred commanderies.
The Hǔbèn guards and wardrobe attendants,
the eunuchs and gatekeepers.
Halberds on the steps in a hundred layers,
each has its own director and office.
Guard houses in a thousand rows,
and patrol paths crisscrossing like patterns.
Carriage roads are laid out,
with long steps and flying galleries.
From Wèiyāng they connect to Guìgōng,
extending north to Míngguāng and reaching Chánglè.
Crossing step-paths and surpassing the western wall,
they merge with Jiànzhāng and connect to the outer annexes.
They establish the Phoenix Watchtowers of the Bìmén,
with corner ridges above where golden sparrows perch.
Inside stands the towering Biéfēng,
subtly beautiful and skillfully soaring.
They set up a thousand gates and ten thousand doorways,
opening and closing in accordance with Yīn and Yáng.
Thus, the main hall is towering and majestic,
its layered structure reaching high,
overlooking Wèiyāng.
Passing through Tàidàng and coming out of Sàsuō,
it connects Yìjì with Tiānliáng.
Above, the upturned eaves act as a canopy,
reflecting the sunlight and taking in the radiance.
Shénmíng Pavilion rises uniquely and densely,
then proudly climbs upward.
It surpasses the clouds and rain by more than half,
and rainbows wind like belts around its rafters and lintels.
Although one might be swift and agile,
one still looks in amazement and cannot reach its steps.
Climbing the Jǐnggàn tower, before reaching halfway,
the eyes become dizzy and the mind becomes confused.
Leaving the lattice and leaning back,
it is as if one is falling but then held back.
The soul is dazed and loses its measure,
following the winding path to descend.
Having been terrified by the climb and view,
one descends and wanders around.
Walking the covered walkways in a winding manner,
they are dark and deep, and the sun cannot be seen.
Pushing open the flying gates and coming out above,
it is like letting the eyes wander beyond the heavens,
appearing to have no support, vast and boundless.
Before it is Tángzhōng and behind it is Tàiyè,
viewing the surging waters of the vast ocean.
Raising waves at Jiéshí,
and striking the divine peaks with a resounding roar.
Flowing into Yíngzhōu and Fānghú,
with Pénglái rising in the center.
Thereupon, spiritual herbs flourish in winter,
and divine trees grow in clusters.
The cliffs are steep and towering,
and the metal and stone are craggy.
Raising the immortal's palm to receive the dew,
the twin golden stems stand tall.
Surpassing the turbidity of dust and grime,
fresh is the purity of the bright air.
Giving rein to the great falsehoods of Wénchéng,
and galloping toward what Wǔlì enacted.
Hoping that the likes of Sōng and Qiáo,
would sometimes wander in this courtyard.
It is truly a lodging for the arrayed immortals,
not a place for us common people to find rest.
"Then you enjoy the magnificent spectacle of grand entertainment,
rousing the great martial spirit in the Upper Park.
By this means, you overawe the Róng and boast to the Dí,
displaying divine majesty and practicing military affairs.
You command the envoy of Jīngzhōu to flush the birds,
and decree the wilds of Liángyě to drive the beasts.
Hordes of furred creatures crowd within,
while feathered wings cover the sky above.
Wing to wing and foot by foot,
they gather and huddle in the Imperial Woods.
The Shuǐhéng officials and foresters
set up their encampment markers.
Species are separated and herds divided,
each unit with its assigned station.
Nets are linked by their cords,
encircling the mountains and enmeshing the wilds.
Ranks of soldiers surround the area,
scattered like stars and spread like clouds.
Thereupon, riding the imperial carriage,
equipped with the ritual regalia,
leading the various ministers,
clothed in Fēilián patterns,
you enter the park gates.
Thus, you circle Fèng and Hào,
and pass through Shànglán.
The six armies set out in pursuit;
the hundred beasts are terrified and exhausted.
Thunderous and flashing,
rushing like thunder and racing like lightning.
Plants and trees are leveled to the ground;
mountains and deeps are overturned.
When twenty or thirty percent have been trampled,
the fierce fury slightly abates.
Then the Qīmén and Cìfēi guards,
with blades drawn and arrows ready,
block the paths and follow the tracks.
Birds in fright fly into the silk nets;
beasts in terror meet the sharp blades.
The mechanisms are never triggered in vain,
nor are strings drawn a second time.
Arrows never kill but one creature;
every hit must fell a pair.
Whirling and chaotic,
tethered arrows are entangled.
Wind-blown fur and rain-like blood
sprinkle the fields and obscure the sky.
The plains turn red,
the brave warriors grow fierce.
Gibbons and monkeys lose their trees;
jackals and wolves hide in terror.
Then the army moves to rugged terrain,
treading through hidden and foul places.
Cornered tigers lunge and rush;
frenzied rhinoceroses gore and kick.
Xǔ Shǎo displays his skill;
Qín Chéng breaks them with force.
They seize the swift and cunning
and throttle the fierce and biting.
Tearing off horns and snapping necks,
wrestling and killing with bare hands.
Tucking leopards under their arms,
dragging bears and chī-dragons.
Hauling rhinoceroses and yaks,
felling elephants and brown bears.
Leaping over deep ravines,
scaling steep cliffs.
Trampling craggy peaks,
great rocks come tumbling down.
Pines and cypresses are toppled,
thickets and forests are destroyed.
Not a plant or tree remains;
birds and beasts are utterly annihilated.
Then the Son of Heaven ascends the Shǔyù Mansion
and visits the terrace of Chángyáng.
He surveys the forms of mountains and rivers
and observes the kills and captures of the three armies.
The wilderness is desolate,
his gaze extending to the four horizons.
Birds press upon one another;
beasts lie pillowed on each other.
Afterward, the game is collected and the masses assembled,
merits are discussed and sacrificial meat is bestowed.
Light cavalry are deployed to roast the meat;
wine wagons gallop forward to pour the drinks.
Carving fresh meat for a feast in the wilds,
beacons are lit to signal the draining of cups.
The banquet and rewards completed,
labor and leisure are balanced.
The grand carriage sounds its bells,
moving leisurely to and fro.
Gathering at the Yùzhāng Mansion,
overlooking the Kūnmíng Pond.
With Qiānniú to the left and Zhīnǚ to the right,
it seems like the shoreless Cloud River.
Lush trees provide dense shade,
fragrant grasses cover the embankments.
Orchids and angelica display their colors,
brilliant and graceful.
As if spreading brocade and embroidery,
shining upon the slopes.
As for birds, there are black cranes and white egrets,
yellow swans and spoonbills.
Grey cranes, bustards, and hawks,
wild ducks, cormorants, and geese.
Departing from rivers and seas in the morning,
roosting by the Jiāng and Hàn at night.
Sinking and floating, coming and going,
gathering like clouds and dispersing like mist.
Then the ladies of the palace board the carriages,
ascend the dragon boats,
unfurl phoenix parasols,
and raise flowered banners.
Drawing back the embroidered curtains,
mirroring themselves in the clear current.
A gentle breeze blows lightly,
drifting calmly on the water.
The boat-girls sing songs,
drums and flutes shake the air.
The sound is sharp and high,
reverberating to the heavens.
Flocks of birds soar;
fish peer from the depths.
Beckoning the silver pheasants,
bringing down a pair of swans.
Lifting the patterned fishing rods,
pulling out flatfish.
Tending to the great nets,
managing the silk lines.
Boats race side by side,
looking up and down in supreme joy.
Then, rising with the wind and swaying with the clouds,
they float and wander to take a broad view.
Ahead they cross the Qínlǐng mountains,
behind they pass over Jiǔzōng.
To the east they reach the River and Mount Huà;
to the west they traverse Qí and Yōng.
The palaces and lodges they pass through
number more than a hundred.
Wherever they travel, morning or night,
provisions are supplied without end.
Performing rites to Heaven and Earth and connecting with mountains and rivers,
exhaustively receiving the blessings and boons bestowed.
Gathering the joyful songs of playing children,
ranking the beautiful odes of the attending ministers.
At this time,
capitals gaze upon one another,
towns and villages are linked together.
The state relies on the foundation of ten generations;
families inherit the legacy of a hundred years.
Scholars live by the virtue and names of their ancestors;
farmers work the furrows of their ancestral fields.
Merchants follow the trade of their clans;
artisans use the rules and measures of their forefathers.
Brilliant and magnificent,
each person finds their proper place.
"As for a servant like me,
I have only observed the traces at the old ruins
and heard of them from the elders.
Out of ten parts, I have not grasped even one,
so I cannot list them all."
The Host of the Eastern Capital sighed and said:
"How painful it is that customs can change people!
You are indeed a man of Qín,
boasting of mansions and chambers,
guarding the boundaries of rivers and mountains.
Truly you know Zhāo Xiāng and are familiar with Shǐ Huáng,
but what do you know of the achievements of the Great Hàn?
When the Great Hàn began its era,
rising from commoner status to ascend the imperial throne,
within a few years it established a foundation for ten thousand generations.
This is something the Six Classics cannot describe,
and the former sages could not speak of.
At that time,
their achievements were vast and matched Heaven;
their punishments were for the rebellious and followed the people's will.
Thus Lóu Jìng assessed the situation and offered his counsel,
and Master Xiāo took expedient measures to expand the system.
Was it a time of peace and security?
It was a calculation they could not avoid.
You have not seen this,
looking only at the later creations of descendants.
Is that not being dim-sighted?
Now I shall tell you of the governance of Jiànwǔ
and the events of Yǒngpíng.
Look to the Tàiqīng
to change your confused mind."
In the past, Wáng Mǎng committed treason,
and the mandate of the Hàn was interrupted.
Heaven and man brought about his execution,
and within the Liùhé, mutual destruction ensued.
In the chaos of that time,
the living were nearly all gone,
and the spirits of the dead were cut off.
In the ravines, there were no intact coffins,
and in the outer cities, no houses remained.
The plains were glutted with human flesh,
and the rivers and valleys flowed with human blood.
Even the disasters of Qín and Xiàng
were not half as bad;
since the invention of writing,
nothing of the kind had been recorded.
Therefore, the people below wailed and appealed to the heavens,
and Shàngdì took pity and looked down.
He then bestowed the mandate upon the Shèng Huáng.
Thereupon, the Shèng Huáng grasped the celestial tally
and expanded the earthly treasures.
He opened the imperial charts
and examined the sovereign records.
Awe-inspiringly, he roused his resolve,
responding like the rising clouds.
He struck like a thunderbolt at Kūnyáng,
wielding his wrath like a crashing thunderclap.
He then crossed the Dàhé
and bestrode the Běiyuè.
He established his title at Gāoyì
and founded the capital in the Héluò region.
He inherited the desolation left by a hundred kings
and followed the cleansing of creation.
Embodying the origin, he established systems,
acting in succession to Heaven.
He connected to the lineage of Táng
and continued the thread of Hàn.
He flourished and nourished the masses of living things,
and restored the borders and territory.
His achievements surpassed those of the past,
and his labors were more diligent than those of the Sān and Wǔ.
How could he merely follow the same tracks and footsteps
as the numerous other rulers,
attending only to the concerns of recent antiquity,
or treading the easy or difficult paths of a single sage?
Furthermore, in the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Heaven and Earth renewed the mandate.
Within the four seas,
the roles of husband and wife were re-established,
and the relationship of father and son was begun anew.
Ruler and subject were first established,
and human relations truly commenced.
This was how Fúxī Shì laid the foundation for imperial virtue.
He divided the provinces and lands,
established markets and courts,
made boats and carriages,
and created tools and weapons;
this was how Xuānyuán Shì opened the path of sovereign achievement.
Respectfully carrying out Heaven's punishment
and responding to Heaven while obeying the people,
this was how Tāng and Wǔ manifested the royal enterprise.
In moving the capital and changing the cities,
there was the model of the restoration of Yīn Zōng;
in occupying the center of the land,
there was the system of prosperous peace under Zhōu Chéng.
Without relying on the handle of a single foot of land or a single person’s power,
he matched the tally of Gāozǔ.
Disciplining himself and returning to ritual
to uphold matters from beginning to end,
he was truly as reverent as Xiàowén.
Following the statutes and examining antiquity,
performing the sacrifices at Dài and inscribing his success,
his ceremonies were as brilliant as those of Shìzōng.
He consulted the Liù Jīng to examine virtue
and looked far into the past to weigh achievements;
when the matters of benevolence and sagacity were complete,
the Way of Emperors and Kings was fulfilled.
Arriving at the era of Yǒngpíng,

Magnificent were the supreme ceremonies of the Sān Yōng,

They spread vast literary elegance,

They extolled the ancestral temples

The harmony between humans and gods was perfectly attuned,

Then the Great Chariot was set in motion,

To inspect the regions and make tours of the borders,

Afterward, he extended the old legacies of Zhōu

He fanned the lofty grandeur

Thereupon, within the Imperial City,

Such luxury could not be surpassed,

Outside, the plains and wilds were used to create parks,

The regulations were like those of Liángzōu,

Then, following the seasons for the royal hunts,

The ritual officials arranged the ceremonies,

The phoenix canopy was lush and beautiful,

The celestial officials followed like shadows,

Spirits of the mountains guarded the wilds,

A thousand chariots rose like thunder,

Breathing flames and generating wind,

Then they gathered in the central park,

They aligned the battalions

They restrained the three armies

Light chariots dashed like thunderclaps,

Yóujī released his arrows,

The bowstring did not wait for the bird to look,

The flying ones had no time to soar,

In a mere glance and wave of the hand,

Pleasure did not reach the point of excessive revelry,

The horses still had energy in their hooves,

The vanguard returned to the road,

Then the three sacrificial victims were offered

Distant regions and different areas,

Internally comforting the Zhūxià

At this, the Shèngshàng observed the joy of the myriad regions,
and while bathed in bountiful favors,

causing neglect of the spring agricultural labors.
Thus, he reaffirmed the old regulations
and issued brilliant edicts.
He commanded the officials
to distribute the constitutional laws.
He manifested frugality
and demonstrated the primal simplicity.
He removed the beautiful adornments of the inner palace
and reduced the imperial equipage and attire.
He suppressed the wasteful industries of craftsmen and merchants
and promoted the flourishing tasks of farming and sericulture.
Consequently, he led the people within the seas to abandon the superficial and return to the fundamental,
to turn away from the false and return to the true.
Women applied themselves to weaving,
and men devoted themselves to plowing.
Utensils were made of pottery and gourds,
and clothing favored plain and dark fabrics.
They felt ashamed of delicate finery and did not wear it;
they held the strange and beautiful in low esteem and did not treasure it.
Gold was cast away in the mountains,
and pearls were submerged in the deep abysses.
Thereupon, the common people washed away their flaws and cleansed their filth,
becoming as clear as a mirror.
Form and spirit became tranquil,
and the ears and eyes were not distracted.
The source of desires was extinguished,
and a heart of integrity and shame was born.
None were not leisurely and self-satisfied,
possessing the luster of jade and the resonance of gold.
For this reason, within the four seas,
schools were as numerous as forests,
and local academies filled every gate.
Cups of toast were exchanged,
and ritual vessels were abundant.
Below they danced and above they sang,
treading in virtue and chanting of benevolence.
When the rites of ascending, descending, and feasting were completed,
they together sighed in admiration of the profound virtue,
offering upright words and grand discourses.
All harbored harmony and breathed forth its spirit,

"How magnificent is this age!"
"Nowadays, commentators only know how to recite the books of Yú and Xià,
and chant the poems of Yīn and Zhōu.
They lecture on the *Yì* of Fúxī and Wén,
and discuss the *Chūnqiū* of the Kǒng clan.
Rarely can they master the clarity and turbidity of ancient and modern times,
or investigate the origins of the Hàn virtue.
Only you possess some knowledge of the old classics,
yet you merely gallop through the superficial trends.
To review the old and know the new is already difficult,
but those who truly know virtue are few indeed!
Furthermore, to be in a remote border region of the Xīróng,
with obstacles and barriers on all four sides,
maintaining its defenses—
how can that compare to residing in the center of the land,
where it is level and interconnected,
and the myriad regions converge like spokes at a hub?
The Qín Ridge and Jiǔzōng,
the rivers of the Jīng and Wèi—
how can they compare to the Four Great Rivers and Five Sacred Peaks,
girded by the Hé and tracing back to the Luò,
the abyss of the Charts and Books?
Jiànzhāng and Gānquán,
where the various immortals were hosted—
how can they compare to the Língtái and Míngtáng,
which unify and harmonize Heaven and Man?
Tàiyè and Kūnmíng,
the preserves for birds and beasts—
how can they compare to the flow of the Pìyōng,
the richness of Dao and virtue?
The wandering gallants were excessively extravagant,
violating righteousness and encroaching upon ritual.
How can that compare to walking together within the laws and measures,
in a cautious and dignified manner?
You only study the way the Āfáng of Qín reached the heavens,
but you do not know that Jīng Luò has its proper systems;
you recognize that Hángǔ can be a pass,
but you do not know that a true King has nothing 'outside' his realm."
Before the host's words were finished,

He hesitated and descended the steps,
his spirit humbled and his mind lowered,
clasping his hands as if to take his leave.
The host said:
"Return to your place;
I shall now grant you the poems in five pieces."
After the guest finished studying them,

"How beautiful are these poems!
Their meaning is as correct as Yáng Xióng's,
and their facts are as substantial as Xiāngrú's.
It is not only that the host loves learning,
but also that he has encountered such a time as this.
I am simple and unrestrained,
not knowing how to judge.
Having now heard the correct path,
I request to recite them for the rest of my life."

There was a Píngxū Gōngzǐ,

He spoke to Ānchǔ Xiānshēng, saying:

Being somber leads to a lack of joy;

Those who can deviate from this are few.
This must be true for the small,
and so it should be for the great.
Therefore, emperors rely on Heaven and Earth to achieve transformation,

The root of transforming customs

How can we verify this?
Qín relied on Yōng and became strong;

Gāozǔ made his capital in the west and prospered;

The rise and fall of governance
always arises from this.
Have you alone, Sir, not seen the matters of the Xījīng?

On the plains of Màolíng
and the Zhū of Yánglíng.
Agile, fierce, and roaring,
like tigers and like leopards.
For a single glare or a tiny grudge,
corpses lie stiff in the corners of the road.
The Chancellor wished to ransom his son's crime,
but Yángshí was defiled and Gōngsūn was executed.
As for the wandering, elegant, and eloquent scholars of the five counties,
with street talk and alley gossip,
they criticize and judge good and bad.
Analyzing down to the smallest detail,
dissecting the flesh and separating the veins.
What they like grows feathers,
what they hate becomes a wound.
Within the suburbs and outskirts,
the villages and towns are prosperous and crowded.
The trade and wealth of the five capitals
have been transferred and drawn here.
Merchant caravans have their yokes linked,
thundering and spreading out.
Caps and sashes intermingle,
parallel shafts and connecting wheel-hubs.
The royal domain spans a thousand lǐ,
governed by the Jīngyǐn.
The palaces and lodges of the commanderies and kingdoms,
number one hundred and forty-five.
To the right they reach Zhōuzhì,
encompassing Fēng and Hù.
To the left they reach the Hé and Huà,
eventually reaching the land of Guó.
The Shànglín Forbidden Park
spans valleys and covers hills.
To the east it reaches Dǐnghú,
and it diagonally borders Xìliǔ.
It encompasses Chángyáng and connects to Wǔzhà,
encircles Huángshān and reaches to Niúshǒu.
Its encircling walls stretch continuously
for over four hundred lǐ.
Plants grow there,
and animals dwell there.
Flocks of birds flutter about,
and herds of beasts frolic.
They scatter like surging waves,
and gather like towering peaks.
Bóyì could not name them all,
and Lìshǒu could not record them all.
With such abundance in the woods and foothills,
what is there that it does not possess?
As for trees, there are the fir, juniper, palm, and phoebe,
the catalpa, oak, pián, and maple.
Fine plants and thickets
are as lush as the Dènglín forest.
They are dense and shadowy,
lofty and towering.
Flowers bloom and display their glory,
while leaves spread and cast shade.
As for grasses, there are the zhēn, shā, jiān, and kuài,
the vetch, fern, litchi-grass, and fāng.
The royal grass and fritillary,
the mallow and huáiyáng.
Luxuriant and thick,
they cover the marshes and hills.
Small and large bamboo spread out,
forming dense groves along the paths.
Mountains, valleys, plains, and marshes
are vast and boundless.
Then there is the Kūnmíng Imperial Pond,
with its deep waters and dark foundations.
It is surrounded by golden embankments
and planted with willows and medlars.
The Yùzhāng Treasure Hall
stands loftily in its midst.
The Qiānniú statue stands to its left,
and the Zhīnǚ statue stays to its right.
The sun and moon rise and set within it,
resembling the mythical Fúsāng and Méngsì.
Within it are giant soft-shelled turtles and alligators,
sturgeons, carp, silver carp, and snakeheads.
Snoutfish, salamanders, yellow-head catfish, and sharks,
with long foreheads and short necks.
With large mouths and crooked noses,
they are of strange and diverse species.
As for birds, there are the Sùshuāng, cranes, and bustards,
wild geese, swans, and giant cranes.
They arrive in early spring
and seek warmth in late autumn.
Flying south to Héngyáng,
and nesting north at Yànmén.
Soaring falcons and returning ducks
make a tumultuous clamor.
Their many forms and various sounds
cannot be fully described.
"Thus, when Mèngdōng brings its gloom,
and the cold wind is harsh and biting.
Snow falls in flurries,
and the ice and frost are severe.
All the plants wither,
and fierce beasts begin their hunt.
Then, the cords of heaven are shaken,
and the nets of earth are spread wide.
Rivers and streams are scoured,
and forests and thickets are searched.
All the birds are startled,
and all the beasts are roused.
Those hiding in the grass or roosting in trees,
those dwelling in holes or taking refuge in caves.
Rising from here and gathering there,
they flee in a confused swarm.
In that Língyòu park,
there are no bounds before or behind.
The Yúrén are in charge of it,
and they lay out the hunting grounds.
They burn the weeds to level the fields,
and cut down the oaks and thorns.
Nets are set for a hundred lǐ,
and animal trails and paths are blocked.
Does and stags are numerous,
crowded together in the fields.
The Tiānzǐ then mounts his carved carriage,
drawn by six piebald steeds.
He wears a kingfisher-feathered cap
and leans against the golden handrail.
With a jade cap and jade chin-straps,
he radiates a shimmering light.
He sets up the Xuányì banner,
and erects the Zhāoyáo standard.
He displays the crying kite
and trails cloud-like streamers.
There are bow-shaped flags and curved-arrow banners,
rainbow-colored flags and feathered standards.
The Huágài canopy aligns with the stars,
and the Tiānbì constellation leads the way.
A thousand chariots move like thunder,
and ten thousand cavalry gallop like dragons.
Among the attendant carriages,
are those carrying the hunting dogs Xiǎn, Qiè, and Xiāo.
It is not only for pleasure,
for there are also secret books.
Nine hundred Xiǎoshuō,
originating from the time of Yúchū.
For the purpose of leisurely inquiry,
they are truly awaited and stored.
Then Chīyóu holds the battle-axe,
with a bristling mane and striped skin.
He controls the unruly
to recognize the divine and the demonic.
The Chīmèi and Wǎngliǎng spirits
dare not encounter him.
He arrays the tiger-like troops at the Fēilián Palace,
and stations the ramparts at Shànglán.
He organizes the units
and puts the ranks in order.
They light great piles of firewood
and beat the thunder-drums.
They release the hunters
into the vast wilderness.
The guards clear the way,
and the warriors are filled with fury.
Dressed in tí robes and leather mèigé,
they look fierce and domineering.
Their radiance blazes to the heavenly court,
and the clamor shakes the seashores.
The Hé and Wèi rivers surge,
and Mount Wúyuè trembles and crumbles.
A hundred types of birds are terrified,
and beasts run and collide in panic.
Losing their spirits and souls,
they forget where to return or flee.
They throw themselves into wheels and spokes,
and are caught without being sought.
Flying nets whistle through the air,
and stray arrows strike.
No arrow is shot in vain,
and no spear leaps without purpose.
Those underfoot are crushed,
and those hit by wheels are run over.
Dead birds and beasts
are as thick as gravel on a beach.
One only sees the entanglement of the nets,
and the strikes of the poles and staves.
The stabbing of forks
and the blows of hand-to-hand combat.
Before the sun has even moved its shadow,
seventy or eighty percent of the prey have been killed.
"As for the high-flying pheasants,
crossing pits and leaping over salt flats.
The wily hares leaping together,
crossing peaks and jumping over ravines.
Even compared to the swiftest of Dōngguō,
none can escape capture.
Then there are those with swift wings and light feet,
chasing shadows to seize them.
Birds have no time to take flight,
and beasts are unable to flee.
Blue-legged hawks strike from the gauntlet,
and Hánlú bites at the end of the leash.
When it comes to those fierce and resolute with bristling manes,
with deep-set eyes and high brows.
Their majesty terrifies rhinos and tigers,
and none dare oppose them.
Then the men like Zhōnghuáng
and the likes of Yù and Huò,
with red headbands and topknots,
their hair standing up like poles.
Baring their chests and pointing their fingers like halbsrds,
they stride and pace about.
They pull the noses of red elephants
and corral giant apes.
They grab baboons and hedgehogs,
and slap at mythical beasts like the Yǔ and the Suān.
They push through thorn hedges
and break through prickly fences.
Thorny forests are flattened by them,
and thickets are destroyed.
The agile, nimble, and quick,
dive into caves
to pull out Fēnghú.
They climb multi-layered peaks
to hunt the Kūntú.
At the very tips of the treetops,
they capture the Chánhú monkeys.
Leaping over dense bushes,
they snatch the flying squirrels.
At this time, among the favorites of the inner palace and the ranks of the Zhāo-yí,
they were often secondary only to the imperial carriage.
They admired the Lady of Jiǎ at Rú-gāo,
and took pleasure in the "North Wind" shared carriage.
They reveled in the excursions and hunts;
their joy was truly great.
Thereupon, the birds and beasts were exhausted,
and the sights were seen to their limit.
Lingering and glancing sideways,
they gathered at the Cháng-yáng Palace.
They rested the attendants
and arrayed the horses and carriages.
They collected the game and lifted the carcasses,
counting and assessing the numbers.
They set up the barriers and laid out the sacrificial animals,
distributing and bestowing the captured spoils.
Carving fresh meat for a feast in the wilds,
they rewarded the diligent and honored merit.
The Five Armies and Six Divisions,
in a thousand ranks and a hundred layers.
Wine carts poured sweet spirits,
and side-by-side carriages provided the meals.
They raised their cups and lit the signal fires;
after drinking, the bells were rung.
The cooks galloped on horseback,
inspecting the leftovers and checking for vacancies.
Roasted and grilled meats were abundant;
clear wine was plentiful.
The Imperial favor was vast,
and great virtue was bestowed.
The followers and attendants were pleased;
the soldiers forgot their weariness.
The carriage master ordered the harness,
and turning the banners, they moved to the right.
They strolled about the Wǔ-zuò Pavilion
and rested by the Kūn-míng Pool.
Ascending the Yù-zhāng Tower,
they selected the red-feathered arrows.
Pǔ-qiě-like marksmen shot,
bringing down the high wild geese.
They snagged white swans
and connected with the flying dragons.
The weighted strings did not just catch one;
every shot necessarily added a pair.
"Then, the Master of Boats was commanded
to prepare water games.
They floated vessels with cormorant prows,
shaded by cloud-patterned canopies.
They hung pheasant-feathered tassels
and erected feathered banners.
Rows of rowing maidens
let loose their oar songs.
The lead singer set the harmony,
joined by the sounding reeds.
They played the music of Huái-nán
and moved to the rhythm of Yáng-ē.
Moving Hé-fēng the river god,
and evoking the Xiāng-é goddesses.
Startling the Wǎng-liǎng demons,
and frightening the dragons and snakes.
Then they fished for bream and tench,
and caught catfish and gobies in strings.
They gathered purple cowries
and seized aged tortoises.
They throttled water leopards
and bound the submerged cattle.
The Warden of the Marshes was excessive;
what concern was there for spring or autumn?
They dredged the deep pools
and searched the rivers and streams.
They spread nine-layered nets
and set up fish traps.
They scooped up the fry and small fish,
exterminating the aquatic tribes.
The lotus and water lilies were uprooted,
and the mussels and clams were peeled open.
To satisfy their desire to hunt the Wén-fish,
they vied to capture the fawns of the elaphure.
Churning the muddy waves and surges,
they drained the ponds and scoured the marshes.
Above, there were no birds escaping in flight;
below, there were no beasts left running.
They took the fetuses and gathered the eggs;
even the ant pupae and locust larvae were all taken.
Taking pleasure in today,
why worry for what comes after us?
Already settled and at peace,
how could one know of a future collapse?
"The Imperial procession graced the Píng-lè Palace,
where Jiǎ and Yǐ tents were pitched, draped in kingfisher-feathered covers.
They amassed treasures and precious toys,
a profusion of magnificent and extravagant things.
Looking out over the vast and distant plaza,
they watched the marvelous games of Jiǎo-dǐ.
Wū-huò lifted tripods;
the Dū-lú people climbed poles.
They burst through narrow gaps like swallows bathing,
and pressed their chests against sharp spearpoints.
The juggling of balls and swords was as swift as a flash,
as they met while walking upon a rope.
Mount Huá-yuè rose high and lofty,
its peaks and ridges uneven.
Divine trees and spiritual herbs grew there,
with vermilion fruits hanging in clusters.
There gathered the immortal entertainers,
with performing leopards and dancing bears.
A white tiger played the zither,
and a cerulean dragon blew the flute.
The maiden Nǚ-é sat and sang a long song,
her voice clear, fluid, and winding.
Hóng-yá stood and directed,
clad in a garment of trailing feathers.
Before the melody had ended,
clouds arose and snow began to fly.
At first it was light and drifting,
then it became thick and heavy.
Across the layered lands and multiple towers,
rolling stones sounded like thunder.
Thunderclaps struck with increasing echoes,
the crashing sound resembling Heaven's majesty.
A giant beast a hundred fathoms long
was known as the Màn-yán.
A divine mountain, towering and steep,
suddenly appeared from its back.
Bears and tigers climbed and clawed,
while apes and monkeys leaped and swung high.
Strange beasts pranced about;
Great Birds moved with a slow gait.
A white elephant, pregnant,
moved with its trunk coiled.
Sea scales transformed and became a dragon,
winding and writhing in form.
The Hán-lì beast exhaled a mist
and transformed into an immortal carriage.
It was drawn by four black deer,
with a mushroom canopy of nine petals.
Toads and tortoises appeared,
and water-men played with snakes.
Strange illusions appeared in an instant,
changing features and dividing forms.
Swallowing swords and spitting fire,
clouds and mist made the scene dim and obscure.
Drawing on the ground, they created a river,
letting the Wèi flow into the Jīng.
Old Man Huáng of Dōng-hǎi,
with his red knife and Yuè spells,
hoped to subdue the white tiger,
but in the end, he could not save himself.
Practicing evil and creating enchantments
was thus ineffective.
Thereupon, they constructed performance chariots
and erected tall banners.
Sturdy youths displayed their talents,
fluttering up and down.
Suddenly plunging headlong and catching themselves by the heels,
appearing as if falling to their deaths yet recovering.
A hundred horses with the same reins
galloped with their hooves in unison.
With the skills at the tip of the pole,
their forms and postures were inexhaustible.
They bent their bows to shoot at the Xī-qiāng,
then turned to fire at the Xiān-bēi.
At this point, the various performances come to an end,
and hearts are intoxicated as if with wine.
Feasting and music reach their peak,
while a melancholy mood gathers in the breast.
Secret orders are given to the Qīmén guards,
as the ruler prepares for an incognito stroll through winding ways.
Descending from his high status to join the lowly,
he carries the imperial seal and hides his sash of office.
He meanders through the neighborhoods and gates,
observing the suburban lands and distant roads.
Like a divine dragon transforming its shape,
he displays the nobility of the August Sovereign.
Afterward, he passes through the Yètíng,
and arrives at the Huānguǎn.
Casting aside those whose beauty has faded,
he yields to the charms of the young and graceful.
They sit closely together on narrow seats in the central hall,
and feather-cups of wine circulate without limit.
Secret dances are performed in turn,
as talented artists display their skills.
There are those as seductive and beautiful as Xià Jī,
whose lovely voices are as clear as those of the Yú clan.
At first, they step forward slowly with slender forms,
appearing as if they cannot bear the weight of their silks and satins.
Humming the notes of the Qīngshāng mode, they turn back,
their grace and beauty enhanced by these lithe movements.
Then, they give full play to their bodies in a swift rush,
like a flock of startled cranes scattering.
They shake their vermilion slippers among the trays and wine jars,
and wave their long sleeves with a rustling sound.
With slender waists and elegant postures,
their beautiful garments flutter brilliantly.
With a subtle gaze and flowing glances,
a single look could topple a city.
Even the likes of Zhǎn Jì or a recluse of the Sāngmén—
who could not be stirred by this?
Among the fourteen ranks of noble ladies,
they compete in charm to win honor.
Prosperity and decline are not constant,
for it depends entirely on where the ruler's love falls.
Empress Wèi rose to favor because of her thick black hair;
Fēiyàn was cherished for the lightness of her body.
Thus, he indulges his will and exhausts his desires,
pushing his body to the limit of pleasure.
He ignores the warnings in the Odes of Táng,
where "others will enjoy" what one leaves behind.
Since the lord himself sets the precedent,
what ritual restraint can hold him back?
He elevates a Zhāoyí above a Jiéyú,
and her relatives become Dukes and Marquises.
He promised the Zhào clan a position second to none,
and thought of making Dǒng like the sovereign of Yǒu Yú.
Though Wáng Hóng argued by his side,
the records of Hàn remained secure and unchanged.
"Gāozǔ began the great undertaking,
and his successors took up the foundation.
After a period of toil came eternal ease,
governing through non-action.
They followed the path of indulgence and pleasure;
what need was there for worry or thought?
Many years have passed,
more than two hundred cycles.
This was simply because the land was fertile and the fields abundant,
and all things were prosperous and plentiful.
Surrounded by secure rocky barriers,
the region was as easy to defend as a sash or collar.
Those who gained it became strong;
those who held it lasted long.
When the stream is long, it is hard to exhaust;
when the roots are deep, it is hard to rot.
Therefore, though they indulged in luxury and followed their whims,
their fragrant reputation grew ever more lush.
I, a humble man, was born three hundred years later,
and have heard what those before me had not heard.
It is almost like a dream,
of which I have not seen even a corner.
How does this compare to the people of Yīn who moved so often,
eight times before the capital was settled and five times after?
They resided in Xiāng, Pǐ, and Gěng,
never staying long in their lands.
Pán Gēng composed his 'Admonition,'
leading his people through hardship.
Now, our Sage Sovereign,
shares the title of Heavenly Emperor,
taking all within the four seas as his home.
In the enterprise of great wealth,
none is greater than ours.
Yet it is a pity that he cannot use magnificence as the flower of the state,
but instead remains solitary, frugal, and petty.
Has he forgotten what the poem 'The Cricket' says?
Is it that he desires it but cannot achieve it,
or is it that he could achieve it but does not desire it?
I am secretly confused by this,
and wish to hear the explanation that clarifies it."
Ānchǔ Xiānshēng then appeared as if unable to speak.
After a stunned silence,
he smiled faintly and said:
"What you, my guest, have said,
is the superficial learning of a late-comer,
who values what he hears but despises what he sees!
If one has a chest but no mind,
and cannot regulate himself with ritual,
it is only natural that he would look down on the present and glorify the past!
Even Yóu Yú, as a lone official from the Western Róng,
could criticize the palaces of Duke Mù.
How is it that you, who should understand the new by reviewing the old
and investigate the truth of right and wrong,
are so confused by this?
"At the end of the Zhōu dynasty of the Jī clan,
they could not manage their administration,
and their governance was full of errors.
It began with the influence of palace favorites,
and ended with the Metal Tiger of the west.
The Yíng clan spread their wings,
preying upon the western lands.
At that time,
the Seven Heroes struggled together,
competing with each other in luxury and splendor.
Chǔ built the Zhānghuá Terrace before,
and Zhào established the Cóngtái after.
Qín Zhèng, with his sharp beak and long talons,
finally dominated the field.
He thought only of monopolizing extravagance,
so that none could equal him.
Thus he constructed Ēpáng Palace,
raised the Gānquán Palace,
connected the Yúngé Pavilion,
and topped the Nánshān mountains.
Tax revenues were exhausted,
and human labor was spent.
Then he collected taxes amounting to more than half of the harvest,
and terrified the people with the punishment of exterminating three generations.
In his treatment of the people,
he was like a mower cutting grass:
after piling it up,
he set fire to it!
The trembling commoners,
were they merely 'crouching under the high heavens'
and 'treading carefully on the thick earth'?
They were trying to save their very necks from death!
Driven into forced labor,
their value was judged only by their strength.
The hundred surnames could not endure it,
so they rested their shoulders under the Great Hàn and joyfully supported Gāozǔ.
"Gāozǔ received the mandate and the charts of prophecy,
following the will of Heaven to carry out punishment.
Wielding the vermilion banner, he established the great title.
Those he opposed were sure to perish;
those he preserved were sure to be secure.
He swept away Xiàng's army at Gāixià,
and bound Zǐyīng at Zhǐtú.
He took over the Qín palaces,
and occupied their treasuries.
As for the regulations for building at Luò,
he had no time for them then.
Therefore, the craftsmen of the west built the palaces
with their eyes fixed on the model of Ēpáng.
Their plans were excessive and overflowing,
without measure or goodness.
Although the ruler reduced it again and again,
it still surpassed the Zhōu Hall.
Observers might think it small and call it crude,
but the Emperor already criticized its extravagance and felt uneasy.
"Furthermore, after Gāozǔ received the mandate and founded the house,
creating our domain of Xià,
Wén personally practiced frugality,
and his governance achieved the virtue of a peaceful era.
Wǔ greatly expanded the territory
and recorded his solemn achievements in the Shàn sacrifice.
Xuān exerted great majesty to pacify the Róng and Dí,
and Shānyú Hūhán came to offer tribute.
All these emperors recorded their ancestry and preserved the line,
their sacrifices continuing without end.
Their merits are inscribed on ritual vessels,
shining ever more brightly through the generations.
Now, you cast aside pure excellence to discuss flawed virtue,
turning what the Chūnqiū avoids into a fine topic of conversation.
It should not be suspicious that in the beginning
goodness was hidden and evil was promoted—
it is simply that you, my friend, do not understand the proper way to speak.
If you must consider indulgence in luxury as wise,
then the Hégōng of Huángdì
and the Zǒngqī of Yǒu Yú
would certainly not be as good as the Jasper Terrace of Xià Guǐ
or the Jade Chamber of Yīn Xīn.
Why then did Tāng and Wǔ overthrow them by force?
Why not look at the affairs of the Dōngjīng and awaken to the truth yourself?"
Moreover, when the Tiānzǐ possesses the Way,
his defense resides beyond the four seas.
He maintains his position through benevolence,
and does not rely on narrow passes or strategic hazards.
If the sincerity of the people’s will is lacking,
what use are craggy heights or the protection of mountains and rivers?
Qín relied on the obstructions of its two passes,
yet in the end, it opened them to Xiàng and submitted to Pèi.
That was a partial base with small designs;
how can it compare to dwelling in the center and planning for greatness?
In antiquity, when the former kings planned their capitals,
they surveyed the nine regions,
leaving no land unexamined.
They used the gnomon to measure the sun's shadow,
ensuring it was neither too short nor too long.
Finding the point where the winds and rains converge,
they then established the royal city.
Examining the contours and facing the favorable terrains,
they followed the Luò River and backed onto the Hé,
with the Yī River on the left and the Chán River on the right.
To the west, it is obstructed by Jiǔ'ā;
to the east, it is gated at Yúxuán.
Méngjīn reaches its rear,
and Tàigǔ connects to its front.
The winding road passes through Yīqué;
the shortcut hastens through Huànyuán.
Dàshì serves as its guardian,
and Xióng'ěr rises high.
Dǐzhù stems the current,
while Dàpī acts as its sword-hilt.
Warm fluids and boiling springs,
black cinnabar and dark stones.
Royal sturgeons dwell in the caves,
and three-toed soft-shell turtles are found there.
Fùfēi has her dwelling there;
divine spirits manifest their laws.
The Dragon Chart was granted to Xī;
the Tortoise Script was given to Sì.
Zhàobó surveyed the site;
the divination favored the Luò settlement.
Zhōugōng laid the first foundations;
his marking lines were perfectly straight.
Cháng Hóng and Wèi Shū
expanded and perfected it.
The main roads have nine carriage-lanes;
the city corners are nine zhì in measure.
The hall is measured by bamboo mats;
the chamber is measured by small tables.
The capital is magnificent and orderly,
the focus of all four quarters.
In the beginning, the Hàn did not dwell here,
and thus the dynastic line collapsed midway.
A great villain took advantage of the rift
and stealthily toyed with the Divine Vessel.
For a period of eighteen years,
he illicitly occupied the Heavenly Seat.
At that time, the common people
did not dare to be of two minds.
His hold on power was indeed heavy!
Our Shìzǔ was indignant at this,
so he rose like a dragon from Báishuǐ
and soared like a phoenix in the Shēnxū region.
Granting battle-axes to the twenty-eight generals,
he eliminated the Gònggōng-like rebels.
The baleful comets and omens of disorder
left no remnants of the villains.
The realm was pacified and settled;
he sought harmony and the Middle Path.
With sagely wisdom and profound insight,
he made his capital here at the Luò Palace.
"Here we stay, and this is the time," he said;
his bright glory was flourishing.
Having glorified his martial prowess,
his benevolence was pervasive and his Way abundant.
He ascended Mount Dài to perform the fēng sacrifice,
rivaling the majesty of the Yellow Emperor.
When it came to Xiǎnzōng,
the six directions were prosperous and flourishing.
He then renovated the Chóngdé Hall
and proceeded to build the Déyáng Hall.
He opened the singular gate at the southern end
and erected the majestic Yìngmén gate.
He displayed benevolence and kindness at the Chóngxián Gate
and raised the voice of righteousness at the Jīnshāng Gate.
He let the Yúnlóng fly on the spring path
and stationed the Shénhǔ in the autumn direction.
He established the twin towers of the Xiàngwèi gate,
displaying the old statutes of the Six Codes.
Within there are the Hándé and Zhāngtái halls,
as well as Tiānlù and Xuānmíng.
Wēnshì and Yíngchūn halls,
Shòu'ān and Yǒngníng.
The elevated corridors seem to move by divine power;
no one can fully describe them.
Zhuólóng and Fānglín parks,
with nine valleys and eight streams.
Lotus flowers cover the water,
and autumn orchids clothe the banks.
Fish leap in the islet shallows,
while turtles and soft-shell turtles swim in the deep pools.
In the Yǒng'ān detached palace,
tall bamboos remain green in winter.
Shady ponds have hidden currents,
and dark springs are pure and cold.
Beījuū birds roost in the autumn;
gǔzhōu birds sing in the spring.

At this time,

leading to total peace,

“As for drifting away and forgetting to return,

O, how glorious is the joyful capital,

*Sōngzǐ* at the divine pool,

Tigers, leopards, and yellow bears roam beneath them;
