Phoenixes and *wānyuán* soar above,
leaping monkeys and flying squirrels nest within.
As for the bamboo, there are *zhōnglóng*, *pǔ*, and *miè*,
small bamboo, arrow bamboo, and various canes.
They follow the banks and slopes,
spreading out in colorful variety.
Graceful and lush,
swaying in the wind like clouds unfolding.
As for its rivers and streams,
there are the *Zhì*, *Lǐ*, *Yǐ*, and *Jìn*,
originating from rocky caves.
Emerging from subterranean passages,
they submerge and gush forth.
Spreading out over a vast expanse,
wide and overflowing.
Gathering and rushing together,
swift as an arrow and fast as the wind.
Torrential flows clash,
with the sound of crashing and grinding waves.
Long-reaching and distant-flowing,
clear and surging.
For aquatic creatures, there are the *yīng* turtle and the crying snake,
hidden dragons and crouching *chī* dragons.
Sturgeon, sturgeon, *yú* and *yōng* fish,
soft-shell turtles, crocodiles, sharks, and *jīng* fish.
Giant clams containing pearls,
and variegated gems winding about.
Regarding its ponds and marshes,
there are *Qiánlú* and *Yùchí*,
and the *Zhěyáng* East Pond.
Stored water rests in stagnant pools,
stretching as far as the eye can see without end.
For grasses, there are *biāo*, *zhù*, *fán*, and *guǎn*,
wild rice, reeds, sedge, and rushes.
Algae, water-shield, water-caltrop, and gorgon-fruit,
lotuses holding their blossoms.
Flowering with the wind,
their fragrance spreads in a beautiful array.
For birds, there are mandarin ducks, swans, and gulls,
wild geese, bustards, and geese,
egrets and grebes,
*sùshuāng* and *kūnlú*.
Chirping in harmonious song,
floating peacefully along the waves.
As for the water, it is channeled through sluices and sprayed in flows,
to irrigate those rice fields.
Ditches and channels are connected like veins,
embankments and ridges follow one another.
Even if morning clouds do not rise,
the pooled waters arrive on their own.
When drained, the land dries;
it serves as both irrigated field and dry land.
Winter rice and summer grain,
ripen according to the seasons.
For the plains and wilds, there are mulberry, lacquer, hemp, and ramie,
beans, wheat, millet, and sorghum.
The hundred grains grow in abundance,
orderly and lush.
As for the gardens and orchards,
there are smartweed, *jí*, and wild ginger,
sweet potatoes, sugarcane, ginger, and garlic,
shepherd's purse, taro, and melons.
There are cherries, plums, and mountain persimmons,
peaches, pears, and chestnuts.
*Yǐng* dates and pomegranates,
*Ráng* oranges and *Dèng* mandarins.
For fragrant herbs, there are *bìlì* and *huìruò*,
*wēiwú*, *sūn*, and *cháng*.
Obscured and lush,
they hold their scent and breathe forth fragrance.
Regarding the kitchen and meals,
there are fragrant and heavy black millets,
and the aromatic non-glutinous rice of the *Zhìgāo*.
Returning geese and crying quails,
yellow rice and fresh fish,
used as seasonings.
Sour and sweet flavors,
of a hundred types and a thousand names.
Spring eggs and summer bamboo shoots,
autumn chives and winter turnips.
Perilla, prickly ash, and purple ginger,
to sweep away the gamey and fishy smells.
For wine, there are nine-times fermented sweet spirits,
and clear wines aged for ten decads.
The dregs spread an inch thick,
with floating yeast like duckweed.
Its sweetness does not cloy,
one gets drunk but does not suffer a hangover.
When gathering the clan and pacifying the kin,
for the seasonal sacrifices of *yuè*, *cí*, *zhēng*, and *cháng*.
To invite distant friends,
and welcome distinguished guests.
Bowing and yielding, they ascend,
to feast in the *Lán* Hall.
Rare delicacies and fine gems,
fill the round and square vessels.
Carved and engraved in layers,
gold and silver clinking like jade.
The attendants are charming and seductive,
their caps and robes bright and fresh.
Their clothing is of various patterns,
their shoes are of exquisite beauty.
Talented, clever, and quick,
they receive the cups and pass the goblets.
After the exchange of toasts is complete,
they follow ritual without fail.
Playing the zither and pressing the flute,
the flowing style lingers.
The *Qīngjué* and *Zhēng* notes are played,
making the listeners more sorrowful.
The guests compose poems about being drunk and returning,
the host claims the dew is not yet dry.
Continuing the joyful feast day and night,
concluding the merrymaking with dignified demeanor.
At this time, for the purification rites of late spring,
on the day of the first sì,
carriages line up axle to axle
to perform the ritual washing on the sunny banks.
Red curtains and interlaced nets
shine across the fields and reflect against the clouds.
Men and women in beautiful attire
move in an endless, colorful stream.
They adorn themselves with seductive elegance,
slender, graceful, and charming.
With subtle glances and darting eyes,
their delicate eyebrows are finely curved.
Then, the youths of Qí sing while the maidens of Zhào are arrayed.
They sit to sing southern songs and rise to perform the dances of Zhèng.
Like white cranes taking flight or silk threads being drawn from a cocoon,
long sleeves swirl and fill the courtyard,
while silk-clad feet step lightly and leisurely.
Fluttering continuously as if about to break,
dizzying as if falling, yet rising again.
Soaring and lingering,
tripping and whirling.
They weave the deepening sorrows of the nine autumn months
and the resentment of the circling dances of Xī Jīng.
They pluck the zither and blow the pipes,
creating new melodies.
Widows sing mournfully,
and the Kūn Jī birds cry in sorrow.
Those seated sigh with grief,
their souls stirred and their spirits pained.
At this point, the many gentlemen set out,
galloping across the sandy fields.
Fine steeds like Lù and Jì run bridle to bridle,
as the triggers of the Huángjiān crossbows are set.
Their feet outrun the startling whirlwind;
the arrowheads can split a tiny hair.
Looking down, they pierce bream and tench;
looking up, they bring down pairs of cranes.
The fish have no time to hide;
the birds have no leisure to soar.
Then, they man light boats and float upon clear ponds,
crossing the northern islets and reaching the southern shores.
Through splashing waves, the boats glide gracefully;
even as the god Yáng Hóu stirs the waters, the wild ducks are overtaken.
They chase water leopards and whip the Wǎngliǎng spirits;
they intimidate the Kuí dragons and terrify the Jiāo-Chī monsters.
As the sun approaches dusk,
the revelers have not yet grown weary.
Gathering their joy, they call for their carriages
and depart from the winding embankments.
The carriages rumble like thunder and speed like the wind;
the horses leap like deer and soar like dragons.
Returning as evening falls,
the pleasure is hard to forget.
This is the delight of touring and sight-seeing,
the amusement of the ears and eyes.
Those who have not witnessed this beauty
how can they be fit to praise it?
Now, Nányáng
is truly what is called the Old Capital of the Hàn.
In ancient times, the Lord of Liú relished the dragon mincemeat,
and seeing Lǔ County, he moved there.
He served the former emperors and practiced filial piety,
establishing the Táng sacrifices at Yáo Shān.
His divine roots were established in the Xià dynasty,
and throughout the Three Eras, they began to flourish.
Without a grand plan of pure virtue,
who could have designed and settled it there?
In more recent times, Kǎo Hóu longed for his origins,
finding neither rest nor peace.
Disdaining the lack of joy in Chángshā,
he crossed the Jiāng and Xiāng rivers on a northward journey.
A vermilion light shone at Báishuǐ,
meeting the ninth generation to bring soaring glory.
Observing the divine greatness of this land,
it opened the heart of Heaven and awakened the spirit.
As for its palaces,
there are gardens, huts, and old residences,
lofty and majestic.
The imperial chambers are solemn and magnificent;
the connected pavilions are brilliant in their mutual splendor.
It is where the Shèng Huáng roams at ease,
and where the spirits provide protection and peace.
Zhānglíng is lush and verdant;
the Ancestral Temple is solemn and ethereal.
The Imperial Ancestors accept the offerings and bestow blessings,
lasting through ten thousand generations without decline.
Emperors treasure its unique beauty,
singing southern tunes as they reflect upon it.
Furthermore, the gentlemen there
are magnanimous, excellent, wise, and perceptive,
truly respectful, gentle, and good.
Their bearing is a model to follow;
their speech is refined and orderly.
Advancing or retreating, yielding or expanding,
they rise and fall with the times.
In the present time, when heaven and earth are in discord,
and the ruler has disordered the government,
jackals and tigers run rampant;
it is the season for the Zhēnrén to receive the Mandate.
Thereupon, there are strategic ministers and martial generals,
all able to seize the rebellious and capture the fierce,
breaking the solid and crushing the strong.
They thrust aside the gate-bars and break through the locks,
treading upon Xiányáng.
Gāozǔ paved the way;
Guāngwǔ gathered the elite.
Thus, the gates of the passes were secured,
and the virtue of Hàn has lasted long.
When they left danger behind and rode upon peace,
they moved according to the people's needs.
Men like Zhōu and Shào
stood like the legs of a tripod,
to fulfill the royal duties.
The class of scholars and officials
organized the teachings and records,
and offered their words as tribute.
Thus, the court has no flaws in its administration,
and its noble influence is clearly proclaimed.
Thereupon, those with infant teeth and long eyebrows,
the elders with skin like a mackerel’s back,
those with white hair and yellowish locks,
sighed and sang together, saying:
“We gaze at the Cuìhuá banners, so luxuriant;
the Tàicháng standard is raised, fluttering beautifully.
Four flying dragons pull the carriage, sturdy and strong;
the bells ring out from the capital.
Leading ten thousand chariots, they linger;
following the level road, they return.”
Is this not a song of longing for the Son of Heaven’s southern tour?
Then, the eulogy was composed:
The Imperial Ancestor stayed here;
Guāngwǔ rose here.
Occupying Hé and Luò,
he unified the Four Seas.
The root and branches shall last a hundred generations;
he holds the position of the Son of Heaven.
For all ages, he can be filial,
cherishing his hometown.
The Zhēnrén tours the south
to see his old neighborhood.
Now, the Shī has six principles;
the second is called Fù.
Yáng Xióng said:
“The rhapsody of a poet is beautiful yet follows the rules.”
Bān Gù said:
“The rhapsody
is a derivative of ancient poetry.”
The former kings collected them
to observe the local customs.
Seeing
“green bamboo, so lush,”
one knows it is a product of Qí-ào in the land of Wèi;
seeing
“within their houses of planks,”
one knows it is the dwelling of the Western Róng in the wilds of Qín.
Thus, one can remain at home and distinguish the eight directions.
However, when Sīmǎ Xiāngrú composed the Shànglín Fù, he cited
“the loquat ripening in summer”;
when Yáng Xióng composed the Gānquán Fù, he displayed
“jade trees, lush and green”;
when Bān Gù composed the Xīdū Fù, he marveled at the appearance of flatfish;
and when Zhāng Héng composed the Xījīng Fù, he described traveling with Hǎi Ruò.
They falsely mention rare and strange things
to serve as embellishments.
Instances of this kind
are not limited to these.
Examining the fruits and trees,
they do not grow in those soils;
checking the divine creatures,
they do not originate in those places.
In terms of language, they are easily adorned,
but in terms of meaning, they are empty and without evidence.
Furthermore, a jade cup without a bottom,
though a treasure, is of no use;
extravagant words without proof,
though beautiful, are not a standard.
Yet critics all praise their meticulous refinement,
and authors mostly hold them up as models.
Long-standing habits become the norm;
this has been so for a long time.
I have thought of imitating the "Èr Jīng" and composing rhapsodies on the "Sān Dū."
As for their mountains, rivers, cities, and towns,
I have verified them through maps.
As for their birds, beasts, grasses, and trees,
I have confirmed them through local gazetteers.
Folk songs, music, and dances
are each attached to their local customs;
eminent figures and elders
are none other than those of old.
Why is this?
Those who speak to create poetry
chant what is in their hearts;
those who ascend heights and are able to compose rhapsodies
praise what they have seen.
When beautifying objects, it is important to rely on their origin;
when commending events, one should base it on the reality.
If it is not based on origin or reality,
how can the reader believe it?
Furthermore, paying tribute according to the resources of the land
is recorded in the *Yú Shū*;
distinguishing objects according to their regions
is what the *Zhōu Yì* cautions.
I shall briefly raise one corner,
grasp its essential system,
and refer it to ancient commentaries.
There was a young gentleman of Xī Shǔ
who spoke to a royal grandson of Dōng Wú,
saying:
"I have heard that Heaven takes the sun and moon as its principles,
and Earth takes the four seas as its boundaries.
The nine regions are divided like stars,
and ten thousand states stand interspersed.
Xiáo and Hán contain the dwellings of emperors,
Hé and Luò are the neighborhoods of kings.
Have you, my friend, also heard of the matters of Shǔ Dū?
Pray let me briefly outline and present them for you.
"Now, as for Shǔ Dū,
its foundations were laid in high antiquity,
and its state was established in the middle ages.
It expanded Líng Guān to serve as its gate
and enclosed Yù Lěi to serve as its eaves.
It is girded by the twin streams of the Èr Jiāng
and faces the layered barriers of Éméi.
Where water and land meet,
it converges with the six directions;
where abundance and luxuriance flourish,
it surpasses the eight regions in its verdant density.
"To the front, it strides across Jiān and Zāng
and leans against Jiāozhǐ.
The extent of its paths
spans over five thousand lǐ.
Hillocks and mounds follow one another,
containing brooks and embracing valleys.
Ridges and peaks are intricately entwined,
striking against rocks to breathe out clouds.
Lush and fragrant in the emerald mist,
lofty and towering in their grandeur.
They pierce the blue empyrean with their exquisite height
and spread vermilion vapors to become rosy clouds.
Lóng Chí's waterfalls gush in its recesses,
Lòu Jiāng's underground streams burst forth on its slopes.
Surging like the billows of Tāng Gǔ,
rushing like the swelling waves of Méng Sì.
Thereupon, Qióng bamboo lines the ridges
and Jùn cinnamon overlooks the cliffs.
To the sides sprout lóngmù,
and on the flanks grow lìzhī.
They spread green leaves in lush profusion
and bear vermilion fruits in dangling clusters.
They face the deep winter without withering,
always radiant and flourishing.
Peacocks and kingfishers fly in flocks,
rhinoceroses and elephants race together.
White pheasants crow in the morning,
and xīngxīng wail at night.
Jīn Mǎ gallops with light, outstripping its shadow,
and Bì Jī appears suddenly, flashing its splendor.
Fire wells glimmer deep in the hidden springs,
their high flames fanned toward the edge of heaven.
In between, there are amber, cinnabar, and azurite,
river pearls and xiáyīng jade.
Golden sands and silver gravel,
their patterns and colors are brilliant,
radiating beauty and shimmering splendor.
"To the rear, it turns its back on Huáróng
and points north toward Kūnlún.
It is bordered by Jiàngé
and obstructed by Shímén.
The swirling waters of the Hàn flow,
startling waves rushing like thunder.
Looking at it, the heavens seem to revolve;
approaching it, the clouds become dark.
Aquatic creatures are of distinct varieties,
scaled and shelled creatures are of different tribes.
Some hide jiāo and chī,
some conceal jasper and jade.
Fine fish emerge from Bǐng Xué,
and excellent timber gathers in Bāo Gǔ.
Its trees include magnolia, qǐn, and cinnamon,
qǐ, xiāo, catalpa, and paulownia,
palm, yá, xiē, and fir.
Pián and nán grow dark and dense at the valley floor,
pines and cypresses flourish luxuriantly on the mountain peaks.
They lift high their long trunks
and raise aloft their lengthy branches.
They fan the flying clouds
and brush against the light empyrean.
Xīhé borrows a path through the steep crags,
and the Yáng Bird turns its wings at the high peaks.
Those that nest and those that soar
surpass even the Dèng Lín.
Caverns house strange beasts,
and nests harbor unusual birds.
Brown and black bears roar on the sunny slopes,
eagles and ospreys swoop on the shaded sides.
Yuán and yòu leap through the sparse branches, competing in agility,
while tigers and leopards howl long and moan endlessly.
"To the east, it flanks Bāzhōng on the left,
where the Bǎi Pú people dwell in abundance.
Outside, it leans on Tóngliáng and Dàngqú;
inside, it contains strategic passes within fertile lands.
Within them are bāshū and bājǐ,
língshòu and táozhī bamboo.
Enclosed by gardens of sedges,
bordered by salt ponds.
Lizards and geckos dwell in the mountains,
soft-shell turtles and tortoises reside in the waters.
Hidden dragons coil in the marshes,
responding to the beating of drums to summon rain.
Cinnabar glows like fire coming from its slopes,
and honeycombs are clustered thick covering its mounds.
Shān Tú gathered them and attained the Way,
Chì Fǔ consumed them and became immortal.
As for the stout-hearted and fierce born in that region,
their customs and folk songs prize martial valor.
When roused, they are the Cóng troops;
when at leisure, they perform the Yú dance.
Their keen spirit was fearsome in middle ages,
and their agile movements are celebrated for generations in the Yuèfǔ.
To the west, it is flanked on the right by Mín Shān,
where bubbling streams and gushing rivers originate.
It is supported by the Bái Láng tribes,
whose barbarian songs form rhythmic verses.
The wilderness is untamed and primordial,
the forest foothills are dark and dense.
Trees with interlocking branches are planted there,
and "crouching owl" tubers lie hidden.
A hundred medicinal herbs grow in thickets,
and cold-weather flora stays fragrant through winter.
Of the many diverse species,
which one does not flourish there?
Within are blue pearls and yellow rings,
green stone arrowheads and Glauber's salt.
Some places are lush with green sprouts,
others abound with cinnabar peppers.
Míwú covers the mountain slopes,
and Fēnglián creeps along the orchid banks.
Red blossoms and purple adornments,
branches and leaves gradually budding.
Spreading stamen in profusion,
falling petals drifting in the wind.
Shénnóng once tasted them,
and Lú Fù examined them.
Their fragrance chases away evil qi,
and their flavor dispels pestilence and wasting diseases.
Within its boundaries,
there are plains, marshes, highlands, and lowlands,
providing a vast and panoramic view.
It is moistened by the Qián and Mèi rivers,
and soaked by the Mián and Luò rivers.
Irrigation ditches spread like veins,
and field boundaries are patterned like embroidery.
Millet and sorghum are lush and green,
glutinous and non-glutinous rice are thick and abundant.
The canal head is likened to the Yúnmén,
and the flowing pools are used for land irrigation.
Even the torrential rains of the Bié star,
could not equal the richness of this moisture.
Thus the settlements are dense and prosperous,
flanking the rivers and bordering the mountains.
Rooftops face one another,
mulberry and catalpa trees connect in a line.
Every household has a well of salt springs,
and every home has a garden of oranges and pomelos.
In the orchards, there are crabapples and loquats,
oranges, persimmons, and black dates.
Wild peaches are arranged in rows,
plums and apricots grow in order.
A hundred fruits start their growth,
different in color but sharing the same glory.
Red cherries ripen in spring,
white crabapples mature in summer.
When the Great Fire star sets,
and the cool wind becomes sharp.
White dew congeals,
and light frost freezes.
Purple pears become juicy and moist,
hazelnuts and chestnuts split open.
Grapes scatter in clusters and pomegranates compete to burst.
Sweetness arrives as they fall on their own,
their fragrance rich and intense.
In the gardens, there are konjac and medicinal cornel,
melon patches and taro plots.
Sweet sugarcane and pungent ginger,
thriving in the sun and spreading in the shade.
As days pass, they grow lush,
as months go by, they branch out.
Beautiful things according to the soil,
presented as various offerings and stored away.
In the fertile waters, there are clusters of wild rice and clumps of rushes,
green water-chestnuts and red lotuses.
Mixed with pondweed and algae,
blended with duckweed and mugwort.
Stems gathered together in tenderness,
damp leaves in thick luxinerance.
Abundant fruits are seasonal delicacies,
served to princes and dukes.
Among them are companions of wild geese and mates of swans,
egrets, herons, and pelicans.
Morning ducks arrive at dawn,
and seasonal geese carry reeds in their beaks.
When leaves fall, they fly south;
when ice thaws, they go north.
They fly through the clouds and sleep on the water,
singing in the clear canals.
In the depths, there are white soft-shelled turtles calling to their kind,
and black otters offering their catch in sacrifice.
Sturgeon, tuna, trout, and bream,
catfish, snakeheads, sharks, and yellowheads.
Varying in scales and ordered by color,
their brocade-like bodies showing patterns.
Leaping in the waves and playing in the shallows,

Thus, the golden walls and stone enclosures
surround the central district.
Both beautiful and majestic,
it is truly called Chéngdū.
Eighteen gateways are opened,
and wide roads for two-track carriages are laid out.
A new palace was built on high, dry ground,
modeled after Chéngmíng with its halls.
Connected to the elevated galleries of Yángchéng,
with soaring towers and pavilions in the clouds.
High balconies open to face the mountains,

Inside are the Deliberation Hall and the Rank Hall,
the Wǔyì and the Hǔwēi.
The Gate of Propagating Transformation,
and the Portal of Exalted Ritual.
Magnificent gate-towers stand distant and paired,

Golden door-knockers reflect one another,
and jade rafters shine in response.
Outside, tracks extend in eight directions,

Houses are joined at the eaves,

There are also grand mansions,
facing the thoroughfares and streets.
Their courtyards are prominent and spacious,

Bells and chimes are struck in the courtyards,

If not for the wealth of the Gě or Jiāng families,

Next is Shào Chéng,
connected to the west.
Where the market stalls gather,
a deep pool for ten thousand merchants.
A hundred layers of tunnels,

Goods are piled high as mountains,

The men and women of the capital

Merchants buy and sell,

Exotic items, extraordinary and strange,

There is cloth made from Tóng flowers,

Qióng canes carry their prestige to the cities of Dàxià,

Carriages and palanquins are crowded together,

The clamor is like a boiling cauldron,

Within the market neighborhoods

In a hundred chambers and separate rooms,

Shell-patterned brocade is beautifully made,

Yellow-silk cloth is compared in rolls,

Extravagant and immensely wealthy,

They control the mountains and rivers,

Storing tens of millions in cash,

Also using their financial might,

The magnates of Sān Shǔ,
come and go from time to time.
Cultivating friendships in the capital,
forming groups and attaching themselves to factions.
They engage in intense talk and witty debate,

When they go out, their horses follow in line;

As for their old customs,
from the end of winter to the start of spring,

Golden wine jars sit in the center,

Cups are filled with clear, settled wine,

Feathered cups are passed in competition,

Women of Bā pluck the strings,

They start the western music on tightened bridge-pins,

Twirling long sleeves, they dance repeatedly,

Bringing jars together and narrowing seats,

Joyfully drinking through this night,

As for those of the rank of Wáng Sūn,
and those of the class of Xì Gōng.
They pursue game in the wilds,

Side by side they ride fine steeds,

Dark and yellow, their varied trappings,

To the west they cross Jīn Dī,

From the new moon until the last day of the month,

Hawks and hounds flash by in an instant,

Furred creatures in colorful variety,

With a sudden rushing sound,

Their ambition is not yet sated,

Emerging from the gates of Péng Mén,

Passing through the towering Sān Xiá,

and twist off rhinoceros horns.
Birds lose their flight feathers,
and beasts are crippled in their feet.
Then they return,
together proceeding to Diān Chí,
and gathering at Jiāng Zhōu.
They test the boatmen,
and moor their light vessels.
They court the Jiāng Fēi,
and wander with the spirits.
They catch kingfishers in nets,
and angle for catfish and dace.
They bring down the high-flying swans,
and pull out the submerged dragons.
They blow the Dòng Xiāo flutes,
and raise the songs of the oarsmen.
Stirring the sturgeon,
and moving Yáng Hóu.
Billowing waves surge and boil,
pearls and shells float on the surface.
Like the Milky Way containing the stars,
their radiance illuminates the great flood.
Preparing to feast the hunters,
they spread out curtains and tents,
and assemble on the plains.
They pour clear wine,
and carve fragrant, fresh meat.
When the drinking is merry and full,
the guests and travelers return.
Chariots and horses thunder like a storm,
rumbling and clamoring.
Like the wind blowing and rain dispersing,
they scatter across hundreds of miles.
This is surely what the land provides for joy,
and what brings excitement to the eyes and ears.
How can only Sān Chuān
be the center of the world's court and market?
As for those of extraordinary brilliance and singular talent,
their unrestrained spirit is unending.
They are threaded by the divine and the supernatural,
and woven by the principles of humanity.
Afar, there is the essence of Mín Shān,
which above becomes the Jǐng constellation.
The Heavenly Emperor moves the cycles to bring prosperity,
and great fortune manifests in response.
Green jade arises from the blood of Cháng Hóng,
and birds are born from the soul of Dù Yǔ.
Transformations are marvelous and unusual,
truly seen as wonders in times of old.
Nearby, the Jiāng and Hàn rivers shine with spiritual power,
and for generations have produced heroes.
Splendid like Xiāngrú,
pure like Jūnpíng.
Wáng Bāo is radiant and outstanding,
Yáng Xióng is refined and born with talent.
Their deep thoughts adorn virtue and the way,
their literary brilliance illuminates the heavenly court.
Evaluated throughout the four seas as the most talented,
they achieved fame in the middle era.
Therefore, wandering talkers use them for praise,
and writers use them as a standard.
Reaching the point where valleys are made into passes,
and mountains are used as barriers.
Steep obstacles are like the Great Wall,
and vast perils are like a huge defense.
With one man guarding the pass,
ten thousand men cannot face him.
Gōngsūn spurred his horse and declared himself emperor,
and the Liú Zōng descended from their carriages to rule as kings.
Judging from this,
what in the world is superior?
Thus, even if one possessed the wealth of all the Huàxià states,
it would still not equal the boundlessness of this capital.
The Wáng Sūn of Dōng Wú smiled broadly and laughed,
saying:
"Indeed, looking up at the celestial bodies,
one distinguishes the patterns of heaven.
Looking down at the products of the soil,
one analyzes the geography of the earth.
In the eras of ancient emperors,
they once surveyed the great thread of the eight reaches.
They unified the six directions and dwelled in light,
soaring and gathering in distant lands.
The records of bird-track scripts on silk,
the jade tablets and stone inscriptions.
When has anyone heard that Liáng and Mín possessed a lodge for imperial tours,
or the foundations of a traveling palace?
Yet you, sir, speak of the wealth of the capital of Shǔ,
and the possessions of Yú Tóng.
You praise its territory,
and beautify its forests and thickets.
You boast of the obstacles of Bā and Hàn,
considering them the pinnacle of strategic peril.
You follow the richness of the crouching-taro soil,
yet think it can cross through ages of calamity.
Narrow-minded and immature,
this is merely what a person of limited vision sighs at.
To speak of a capital in such a fragmented way
is certainly not the grand vision of a great man.
Why is this?
Its soil is not sufficient to sustain life,
and its mountains and rivers are not sufficient for a complete defense.
Gōngsūn made it a state and was destroyed,
Zhūgě made it a home and was extinguished.
This is but a mound of ruin and disorder,
a track leading to downfall.
How can it be compared to the lords and kings, or display grand character?
One who toys with gravel and does not peer into the jade abyss,
does not know where the black dragon coils.
One who is accustomed to a flawed town and does not see the superior state,
does not know where heroes walk.
Have you alone not heard of the immense beauty of great Wú?
Furthermore, the founding of Wú
began with Tài Bó,
and was made manifest by Yán Líng.
This is where the ceremonial robes were displayed,
and where high integrity arose.
Establishing supreme virtue to initiate the enterprise,
the world could find no words to praise it.
Through yielding, they established customs,
treating the rule of a thousand chariots as lightly as a straw sandal.
If one discusses capitals throughout the land,
then Shǔ is not what the other states look up to.
Therefore, its strategic plan
corresponds above to the Xīng Jì constellation.
Expanding territory and drawing borders,
it surpassed others in its annexations.
It encompasses Gān Yuè,
and strides across Mán Jīng.
The Wù Nǚ star imparts its radiance there,
and the Yì Zhěn stars lodge their essence there.
It points to Héng Yuè to stabilize the wilderness,
and looks toward Lóng Chuān to girdle the outskirts.
As for its mountains and marshes,
they are towering, jagged, and lofty,
dark, misty, and densely clustered.
Vast and overflowing,
deep and boundless.
Some surge as rivers to open up canals;
some swallow the Jiāng and receive the Hàn.
Stony and craggy,
gushing and surging.
They wind through several provinces
and irrigate half of the world.
A hundred rivers branch off,
returning to the sea to meet.
Controlling the clear and leading the turbid,
mixing waves and merging rapids.
Bubbling and boiling,
solitary and traveling afar.
Bellowing with a great roar,
hidden with a thunderous crashing.
Emerging from the midst of the Great Wilderness,
traveling beyond the eastern limit.
Passing through the central forests of Fúsāng,
encompassing the surging waters of Tānggǔ.
Tidal waves rise abruptly,
returning and repeating for ten thousand miles.
Steaming mists billow,
clouds rise in murky darkness.
Deep, clear, and vast,
swirling and shimmering.
None can fathom its depth;
none can investigate its breadth.
Calm and tranquil without shores,
all streams unite to become long.
Where rare and strange things gather and grow,
where scaled and armored creatures assemble and go.
There, the great whales swallow ships,
and long salamanders spit out waves.
Leaping dragons and soaring snakes,
sharks, mullets, and rays.
King sturgeons and pufferfish,
remoras, turtles, and sawfish.
Cuttlefish clutching swords,
hawksbill turtles, mackerels, and crocodiles,
all swim and dive within.
With layered scales and carved shells,
strange species are mixed together.
Going against the current or following the flow,
gasping at the surface or sinking below.
As for birds, there are Kūnjī and Zhúyù,
frost-cranes, swans, egrets, and wild geese.
The Yuányú bird avoids the wind;
migratory geese reach the Jiāng.
Mergansers and cormorants,
water-hens, cranes, and storks.
Herons, gulls, hawks, and pelicans,
float and drift upon the waters.
They display their plumage in leisure,
rising and falling with the waves.
Preening their feathers and tidying their wings,
they move with grace and enjoy themselves.
Pecking at the creeping algae,
brushing through the rippling waves.
Fish and birds make a clamor,
ten thousand things come to life.
Vast and dark,
hazy and sudden,
divine transformations occur in an instant,
harboring the hidden and nurturing the bright.
Exhausting their natures and perfecting their forms,
waxing and waning according to nature.
Clams and oysters harbor pearls,
waning and waxing with the moon.
Great turtles exert their strength,
their heads bearing spiritual mountains.
The Great Péng bird flutters its wings,
wings like clouds hanging from heaven.
Shaking the vast currents,
clapping like thunder in the deep abyss.
Shaking the entire universe—
how can one fully trace its source!
The islands are distant and remote,
the islets are high and prominent.
Looking far into the distance,
gazing afar into the hazy mists.
Rare treasures are beautiful,
strange crevices are filled.
Paths are cut off,
but wind and clouds pass through.
Great peaches coil and bend,
cinnabar cinnamon grows in thickets.
Jasper branches raise their stems and put forth blossoms,
coral grows in hidden luxuriance, translucent and elegant.
Rising ridges and multiple barriers,
the abodes of the Lièzhēn.
Jade halls face the eaves,
stone chambers are adjacent to each other.
Lush are the emerald curtains,
slender are the maidens of Sùnǚ.
Jiāng Fěi comes and goes here,
and Hǎitóng feasts and talks here.
This is truly a divine and wondrous sight,
alas, it is difficult to describe in detail!
Thus the terrain is vast and expansive,
herbs and trees grow long and trailing.
Encountering a marsh, it becomes a garden;
meeting a forest, it becomes a park.
Strange blossoms are lush and abundant,
brilliant in summer and verdant in winter.
Noted in regional gazetteers,
and envied by the Central Provinces.
As for grasses, there are Huònà and cardamom,
and ginger of many kinds.
Species such as Jiānglí,
and types of sea moss.
Purple and crimson ribbons of seaweed,
edible kudzu and fragrant lemongrass.
Shífān and Shuǐsōng,
Dōngfēng and Fúliú.
Spreading across the marshes,
linked together over the hills.
Following the slopes of the mountains,
covering the flow of rivers and seas.
Bearing white stems,
holding red blossoms.
How lush and dense they are!
How bright and fragrant!
Their colors are dazzling,
their fragrance spreads far.
Their tributes are packed in boxes,
and the Lí Sāo sings of their "everlasting excellence."
As for trees, there are maple, Xiá, and camphor,
palm and Gǒuláng.
Miànyuán, Chūn, and Lú,
grain-oak, Zhēn, and Jiāng.
Píngzhòng and Jūnxī,
pine, catalpa, and Gǔdù.
The wood of Nánliú,
and the tree of Xiāngsī.
Growing together on high ridges,
flourishing in groups on hidden mounds.
Raising trunks a thousand fathoms high,
casting shade over ten thousand acres.
Crowded branches and tangled stems,
layered blossoms and thick leaves.
Gnarled and coiling like dragons,
their scales overlapping.
Flourishing colors are mixed together,
densely woven like rich embroidery.
Night dew is heavy and thick,
the morning sun is dim and obscured.
Swaying with the wind,
whistling and soughing.
The rustling branches follow the melody,
the flying sounds are resonant and clear.
It is as if the qín and zhù were played together,
and the sheng and yú flutes sang in unison.
Above, there is the mournful cry of the male gibbon,
and the long whistle of the Juézi monkey.
Yòu, flying squirrels, and Guǒrán monkeys
leap and soar through the air.
Competing to catch hanging vines,
vying to roam on distant branches.
Startled and jumping in chaotic flight,
scattered and disappearing like birds.
Below, there are the Xiāoyáng and Zhèláng,
the Yàyǔ, the Chū leopard, and the elephant.
The tribe of the Wūtù tiger,
and the kin of the rhinoceros.
With hooked claws and serrated teeth,
they naturally form sharp points.
Their eyes are like shining stars,
their voices like crashing thunder.
Their names are recorded in the Shānjīng,
and their forms are carved upon the Xià tripods.
As for its bamboos, there are the Yúndāng and the Lánshē,
the Guìjiàn and the Shètǒng.
Among the pummelo and parasol trees are bamboo groves,
and the Piǎoláo grow in thickets.
Luxuriant shoots sprout from the joints,
often twisting and entining together.
With green leaves and emerald stems,
they brave the frost and hold the snow.
Tall, upright, and densely clustered,
they are lush, verdant, and soughing in the wind.
Elegant, graceful, and undulating,
they are moist as jade and fresh as green kingfisher feathers.
The "Cloud-tipping" bamboo cannot surpass them,
nor can those of the Xiègǔ Valley compare.
The Yuèzhuó phoenixes eat their fruit,
and the Yuānchú chicks frolic among them.
As for its fruits, there are vermilion oranges and Yúgān,
and forests of Lìzhī.
The Bīnláng palm has no branches,
and the Yé coconut leaves provide no shade.
There are Lóngyǎn and Gǎnlǎn,
and Chánliú that resist the frost.
They take root in the shade of Bǐjǐng,
and stand in rows on the sunny slopes of Héngshān.
Their white blossoms are elegant,
and their red flowers are fragrant.
They overlook green cliffs,
and hang from purple chambers.
Partridges fly southward and linger among them,
and peacocks with variegated plumage soar and wheel.
Golden pheasants fly back to roost,
and kingfishers build their nests in multiple rows.
As for its rare treasures, there are mounds of Kūn and Yáo jades,
and banks of copper and iron.
There are treasures of "fire-tempered" stones,
and the "chicken-startling" gems.
Crimson cinnabar and bright pearls,
golden blossoms and silver ores.
Purple cowries and sulfur,
light blue jade and white jade.
Abundant and piled high,
they are interspersed in secluded corners.
Their refined brilliance is hidden in their shoots,
scattered throughout the mountains and valleys.
Because of them, the rocky banks never wither,
and the forest trees are kept moist and lush.
Thus, Suí Hóu would despise his "Night-shining" pearl,
and the Sòng Wáng would look down upon his "Jiélǜ" jade.
In its remote and strange corners,
there are Dragon Caves where internal vapors rise,
and where clouds and rain are stored.
The scaly pangolin is like a beast,
and floating stones are like rafts.
In pairs, there are the "parallel-eyes" flatfish,
and in pieces, the "King's Leftover" fish.
On the far reaches of land, creatures drink from trees;
in the deepest depths, they dwell in water.
In the spring-chambers, they secretly weave and roll up silk;
the guests of the abyss are moved to weep tears that turn to pearls.
Opening northern doors to face the sun,
the Nánmíng is made equal to the Yōudū.
In the surrounding countryside, the field paths are countless,
and the soil's fertility is doubled.
Highlands and lowlands have distinct products,
hollows and ridges are of different grades.
Elephants plow and birds weed,
this happens naturally.
Early-ripening rice and wild rice ears
are found right there.
They boil the sea to make salt,
and mine the mountains to mint coins.
The state taxes rice that ripens twice a year,
and the villages offer silk from eight-generation silkworms as tribute.
Merely observe the inner depths of its suburbs and roads,
and the organization of its capital cities.
It is the root and source of hegemons and kings,
the foundation upon which the state was founded.
Outer walls encircle it,
with layered cities forming corners.
There are sixteen main gates,
waterways, and land routes.
Thus it was first planned,
to last for a thousand generations.
Modeling it after the Zǐgōng to build the chambers,
they broadened the vast courtyards.
Cold and heat are kept out by the deep eaves,
while rainbows encircle the cloud-reaching halls.
Thus it stands majestic and brilliant for ten thousand miles.
They built the high terrace of Gūsū,
standing unique and overlooking the four distances,
girded by the deep moats of dawn and dusk,
and adorned with the lush gardens of Chángzhōu.
Peering into the storehouses of the Eastern Mountain,
marvelous treasures dazzle the eyes;
looking at the granaries of Hǎilíng,
red grain overflows.
They raised ancestral temples in Wǔchāng,
and built detached palaces in Jiànyè.
They expanded upon what Hélǘ had established,
and adopted the legacy of Fūchāi.
They raised the magnificent Hall of the Divine Dragon,
with decorated eaves and interlocking beams.
They elevated the towering heights of Línhǎi,
and adorned the splendor of Chìwū.
East and west, the structures are intricate,
north and south, they are lofty.
Room windows face each other,
and connecting galleries cross one another.
The gates are wondrous and strange,
given extraordinary names.
The left is called "Curved Bank,"
the right is named "Overlooking the Cliff."
Carved beams and engraved rafters,
blue lattice windows and red pillars.
They are illustrated with cloud vapors,
and painted with celestial immortals.
Although this residence is boastfully beautiful,
it was still not enough for a moment's peace.
They thought of making every house like a magnificent palace,
all adorned with jade and constructed of jasper.
The high gates are wide and tall,
the gatehouses allow carriages to pass side-by-side.
Vermilion watchtowers stand in pairs,
and the imperial roads are smooth as whetstones.
They are lined with green locust trees,
and spanned by green waters.
The dark shade is deep and vast,
the clear currents flow ceaselessly.
Rows of offices extend for seven miles,
flanking the central road with their ridges.
Garrison camps are as thick as the teeth of a comb,
and administrative offices are spread like pieces on a chessboard.
Below the embankment of Hèngtáng,
the houses of the town are grand and boastful.
Chánggàn extends continuously,
with flying eaves crisscrossing one another.
As for those who dwell there, they are the noble families of high gates,
the eminent and heroic.
The descendants of Yú and Wèi,
the progeny of Gù and Lù.
Exceptional youths inherit the lineage,
and the mature and wise succeed through generations.
Their galloping horses leave overlapping tracks,
and their red-wheeled carriages leave many ruts.
When they return from leading troops,
their weapon racks are set up inside.
Their caps and canopies cast shadows like clouds,
and the alleys are crowded and blocked.
Among their neighbors are the extravagant men of chivalry,
and the nimble-witted guests.
They form friendships with elegance,
followed by a grand retinue.
When they go out, they wear pearl-studded shoes,
moving in groups of hundreds or thousands.
Feasting in the neighborhoods and drinking in the alleys,
they pass the wine cups and drain them to the bottom.
They lift heavy gate-bars and carry tripods,
and engage in archery, pitch-pot, and board games.
Like the boisterous banter of Póyáng,
they become inspired while tipsy with wine.
Thus their joy is serene and their banquets are inexhaustible,
the capital is prosperous and people from the four corners arrive.
Some float on water, others travel by land,
in lashed-together boats or hitched teams of four.
With the singing of oars and the turning of wheels,
from early dawn throughout the long day.
They open the markets and courts to admit everyone,
and the market squares overflow.
All kinds of goods are mixed in the same shops,
and the city and countryside become one.
Men and women stand and gaze,
and merchants are crowded together.
Clad in fine ramie and thin linen,
they gather in a dense and bustling throng.
Light carriages press their reins through the paths,
and tower-ships hoist sails to pass the market stalls.
Fruits and cloth converge like spokes of a wheel as a matter of course,
and from afar come glass and mother-of-pearl.
Wealth and goods are multifarious,
and utensils are of ten thousand kinds.
Gold pieces are piled high like boulders,
and strings of pearls hang in abundance.
Peach-wood mats and ivory mats
are encased in tubes;
banana-fiber cloth and fine linen
are softer than silk gauze.
In a clamor of voices and a blur of activity,
they compete in trade.
The noise is a deafening roar,
while the splendor is dazzling.
When they wave their sleeves, a wind is stirred,
and the red dust darkens the day.
Sweat flows like fine rain,
making the central roads muddy.
The commoners in the midst of wealth,
the pick of the merchant class.
Seizing opportunities to seek profit,
their riches abundant to tens of millions.
Competing for dwellings and domains,
they annex borders and take over whole alleys;
boasting of their leisure living,
they wear pearl-adorned robes and dine on jade-like delicacies.
Agile, fierce, and strong men
live here in rows of houses.
As swift as Qìng Jì,
as brave as Zhuān Zhū.
Wearing tall hats they go out,
with swords held high they rush forth.
Wrapped in sharkskin armor,
carrying the Zhǔlòu sword at their waists.
Hiding spears among the people,
they drive the bold away from the village gates.
Every house has "crane-knee" spears,
every home has rhinoceros-hide shields.
Military equipment is stored for use,
weapons and gear are kept in abundance.
Wú hooks and Yuè halberds,
Chúnjūn and Zhànlú swords.
War chariots fill Shíchéng,
spear-laden boats cover the rivers and lakes.
"Dew departs and frost arrives,
as the sun and moon pass away.
Vegetation sheds its joints,
birds and beasts grow fat.
Watching the hawks and falcons,
one commands the hunters.
Arraying the silk-bound armor,
erecting the Sìgū flag.
Ordering officers to sound the bells,
they prepare for a grand hunt at Jùqū.
Wūhǔ and Lánghuāng,
Fúnán and Xītú.
Chiefs of Dān’ěr and Hēichǐ,
leaders from Jīnlín and Xiàngjùn.
Horses galloping like wind and clouds,
swift and sudden,
they lead the way on the path ahead.
Brave riders gallop on the road,
following the south-pointing chariot to determine direction.
Chariots roll out with a rumble,
armored riders clank and clatter.
The King of Wú then mounts his jade chariot,
drawn by Sùshuāng steeds.
Banners decorated with fish whiskers,
the imperial standard shining with double light.
Holding the Wūhào bow,
girded with the Gānjiàng sword.
Feathered banners wave their tassels,
mighty halberds flash their blades.
Shell-decorated helmets and ivory bow-tips,
woven patterns and bird insignias.
The six armies are in uniform,
the four steeds prance like dragons.
High fences are placed all around,
nets and snares are spread everywhere.
Hand-nets and cages are intricately knotted,
traps and foot-snares are linked by ropes.
Driving game toward Jiǔyí,
blocking them at Yuán and Xiāng.
Light carriages bustle about,
archers on horseback are brilliant and bright.
Baring their chests for hand-to-hand combat,
troops for leaping far and throwing stones.
Those with ape-like arms and joined ribs,
rushing wildly and fiercely.
Glaring like hawks and ospreys,
leaping and flying about.
Appearing now separate, now together,
they leap and bound across the vast wilderness.
Shields, spears, clubs, and javelins—
the troops of Yángyí and Bólú.
Long tassels and short weapons,
their hair standing on end as they gallop.
Nimble and light, they gather in crowds,
gagged with wooden bits to remain silent.
The long, trailing banners
drift together in the distant, misty borders.
Gongs and drums echo through the mountains,
fierce fires blaze through the forests.
Flying flames and floating smoke
carry the colors of sunset and shadow.
With a crashing like thunder,
peaks collapse and ridges give way.
Birds do not choose which tree to land on,
beasts do not distinguish sounds.
They seize white tigers and black tigers,
they bind elks and large deer.
Leaping over the Liùbó beasts,
chasing the flying squirrels.
Pelting the Luán and Qīng birds,
shooting the macaques and monkeys.
White pheasants fall,
black poisonous birds drop down.
Scaling high peaks,
they cross steep precipices.
Leaping over bamboo and cypress,
dashing through medlar and cedar.
Great boars are captured,
divine Chī-dragons are caught.
Steel arrowheads are moistened,
frost-bright blades are stained with blood.
"Then they slow their pace and pull the reins,
halting the horses and clearing the road.
Lingering and wandering,
they gaze upon the dense, secluded greenery.
Observing the prowess of the generals
and the high spirits of the soldiers.
The feathered tribes use beaks and spurs as knives and tongs,
the furred herds use teeth and horns as spears and blades,
all have these weapons attached to their bodies to meet sudden needs.
Thus they scratch and tear to cause wounds,
crashing and colliding to break sinews and bones.
None fail to have their sharpness blunted or their points broken,
their bodies torn apart and their internal organs crushed.
Though there are craggy cliffs in the stone forest,
they roll up their sleeves and level them;
though there are nine-headed giant serpents,
they raise their feet and trample them.
Overturning those that dwell in nests,
breaking open those that live in dens.
Reaching up to grab the Jùnyí pheasants,
stepping down to kick the jackals and tapirs.
Raiding the chambers of bears and brown bears,
plundering the haunts of tigers and leopards.
The Xīngxīng apes wail as they are captured,
the Xièxiè monkeys laugh as they are struck down.
Butchering the Bā snakes,
pulling out the bones of elephants.
Cutting off the wings of the Péng bird,
covering the vast marshes.
Light birds and cunning beasts
are flustered and hesitant.
Stumbling about within the boundaries,
they forget how to glare or look,
losing their sense of where to go or stay.
Souls stripped and spirits terrified, they kick and struggle;
those struck by arrows that 'drink the feathers' at the sound of the bowstring,
those whose bodies fall and whose shadows go stiff
are piled up in increasing numbers,
tangled and jumbled together.
Overturning the marshes and thickets,
toppling the capes and caves.
The rocky caverns are left without boars,
the dense undergrowth without deer or pipits.
Thinking to borrow a path from Fēnglóng,
they part the heavy clouds to hunt on high.
Ensnaring the Crow and the Rabbit from the sun and moon,
exhausting every nesting and lodging place of the flying and the walking.
The ravines in the valleys are silent,
and the hills and ridges are bare.
The fishing nets are full,
and the harvest from the fields is abundant.
Turning the reins to glance sideways while traveling,
one observes the fish in the Sānjiāng.
Floating boats on the Pénglǐ,
ten thousand vessels gather as one.
Great ships have their sterns connected,
and giant vessels have their bows touching.
Like flying clouds covering the sea,
their design is beyond ordinary patterns.
Tiered ornate towers stand like islands,
resembling the legendary Fānghú.
Compared to the Yìshǒu boats, they are more spacious,
surpassing the Yúhuáng of ancient times.
They unroll silk curtains
and set up tassels.
Opening the windows and screens,
they reflect the expanse of the water.
Pole-handlers and oarsmen
are selected from Mǐn and Yú.
Skilled at riding the long winds,
they are familiar with the spirit of Língxū.
Demanding a thousand miles in a brief moment,
they arrive in an instant, ahead of schedule.
Oar-songs are sung,
and the sounds of flutes and pipes ring out.
The great current echoes,
and the birds on the islets are startled.
Cords and arrows are released,
bringing down the Jiāopéng.
The traps of the foresters are sprung,
capturing the Jiāojīng.
Hooks and baits are cast everywhere,
and nets are linked together in succession.
Their skills surpass those of Zhāngōng,
and their ingenuity exceeds that of Rènfù.

"Indeed, loss and gain follow the times;
the principles have their constant nature.
The high takes the low as its foundation;
the people take food as their heaven.
To rectify the end, one must align the root;
to ensure a good outcome, one must be cautious at the start.
If the suitability of the nine lands is not utilized,
and the tasks of the four classes of people are not unified,
then the wilds will show the color of weeds,
and the court will lack the order of substituted labor.
Without reserves to prepare for disaster,
one merely looks to the harvest with empty certainty.
The decline of the three late periods
was entirely due to this.
Now the Sage Sovereign awakens before dawn to show his great brilliance,
and is vigilant and fearful in the evening.
He plans for scarcity during times of plenty,
and guards against lack during times of ease.
How reverent, how reverent!
His only concern is for grain.
He develops the great tasks of the three seasons,
and brings the granaries to overflowing.
This is truly the intent of Yáo and Tāng,
and the essential art of preservation and salvation.
When there are rituals in the ancestral temples,
and the Zhùzōng consult the auspicious days,
the fǔ and guǐ vessels are filled with soft grains;
it is from here that they are filled.
The strained aromatic wine and the xiāo and máo grasses
also come from here.
The millet and grain are fragrant,
and the fine wine is excellent and pleasing.
It is fitting that the people are harmonious and the year is bountiful,
and the spirits descend with good fortune.
The ancients had a saying:
'The virtue of the Sage
can be added to by nothing more than filial piety!'
Now, filial piety
is the nature of Heaven and Earth,
and the source of human spirit.
Formerly, the Ming Wang governed the world with filial piety,
but those who have succeeded them
are few and rare indeed!
Reaching our Imperial Jìn,
this Way is truly glorified.
The model and pattern are trusted by the myriad states;
love and respect are fully rendered to the ancestors.
Thus, he personally farms to provide the sacrificial grains,
which is the means to achieve filial piety.
He encourages agriculture to satisfy the hundred surnames,
which is the means to strengthen the foundation.
Being able to attend to the foundation and be filial,
such magnificent virtue and great achievement are supreme indeed!
From this one endeavor,
two beauties are both present.
Is it not far-reaching?
Is it not weighty?
I dare to compose a song of praise:
Joyfully thinking of the royal domains,
where we gather the máo grass.
The Great Lord has arrived,
to personally attend to his farming.
With his three pushes of the plow,
the myriad quarters show reverence.
We weed the public fields,
which extends even to our private ones.
Our fǔ vessels are thus filled,
our guǐ vessels are thus prepared.
Our granaries are like hills,
our stacks are like mounds.
Thinking of this, being in this,
forever harboring filial thoughts.
Human strength is universally preserved;
the invocators offer correct words.
The spirits find pleasure in this,
and ease and joy have no end.
When the One Man has cause for celebration,
the millions of people rely upon it.
Chǔ sent Zǐxū as an envoy to Qí.
The King dispatched all his chariots and horsemen to go hunting with the envoy.
When the hunt was over,
Zǐxū went to visit Wūyǒu Xiānsheng.
Wángshì Gōng was also present.
Once they were seated,
Wūyǒu Xiānsheng asked:
"Was today's hunt enjoyable?"
Zǐxū said:
"It was."
"Was the catch large?"
He said:
"Small."
"Then what was the joy?"
He replied:
"I enjoyed that the King of Qí wished to boast to me of the number of his chariots and horsemen,
and I replied with the matters of Yúnmèng."
He said:
"May I hear of it?"
Zǐxū said:
"You may.
The King's carriage had a thousand chariots,
and ten thousand selected horsemen,
hunting by the seashore.
Rows of soldiers filled the marshes,
and nets covered the mountains.
They ran over rabbits and crushed deer,
shot elks and trampled lín.
Racing across the salt flats,
they cut fresh meat and stained their wheels.
Their shots hit true and their catch was large,
and boasting of his own achievements,
he looked at me and said:
'Does Chǔ also have such plains and wide marshes for hunting,
as abundant and joyful as these?
How does the hunting of the King of Chǔ
compare to mine?'
I stepped down from the carriage and replied:
your servant, am a rustic man from the state of Chǔ.
Fortunately, I have served in the guards for more than ten years,
occasionally following him on outings.
We toured the back gardens,
viewing what was there and what was not,
yet I have still not been able to see everything.
How then could I be qualified to speak of the marshes outside?'
The King of Qí said:
'Even so,
tell me briefly of what you have heard and seen.'
I replied:
'Yes, yes.
Your servant has heard that Chǔ has seven marshes;
I have once seen one of them,
but have not seen the rest.
What your servant saw
was merely a very small one.
Its name is Yúnmèng.
As for Yúnmèng,
it is nine hundred lǐ square.
Within it, there are mountains.
These mountains wind and curve in dense clusters,
towering high and steep.
Their peaks are jagged and uneven,
obscuring the sun and moon.
They entwine and tangle,
reaching up to the blue clouds.
Sloping and undulating,
they connect below to the rivers.
Its earth has dān, qīng, ochre, and chalk,
cīhuáng, báifù,
tin, bì, gold, and silver.
The many colors dazzle,
shining like dragon scales.
Its stones include red jade and rose gems,
lín, mín, and kūnwú.
Jiǎn, lù, and dark whetstones,
ruǎn and wǔfū.
To its east, there are gardens of orchids,
héng, lán, zhǐ, and ruò,
qióng and chāngpú.
Jiānglí and mǐwú,
various sugarcanes and bājǔ.
To its south, there are plains and wide marshes,
rising and falling in gentle slopes,
spreading out in vast levels.
It is bordered by the Great River,
and bounded by the Wù Mountains.
In the high and dry areas grow zhēn, xī, bāo, and lì,
xuè, suō, and green fán.
In the low and wet areas grow cáng, liáng, jiān, and jiā,
dōngqiáng and wild rice.
Lotus, lotus root, gū, and lú,
ānlǘ and xuānyú.
A multitude of things dwell there,
too many to be fully described.
To its west, there are gushing springs and clear pools,
where the surging waters shift and move.
On the surface, lotuses and water chestnuts bloom;
beneath, great rocks and white sands are hidden.
Within them are divine turtles, dragons, and alligators,
hawksbill turtles, soft-shell turtles, and giant tortoises.
To its north, there are shaded forests,
with trees such as pián, nán, yù, and zhāng.
Cinnamon, pepper, and magnolia,
bò, lí, zhū, and willow.
Hawthorn, pear, ying, and chestnut,
orange and pomelo, all fragrant.
Above them are yuānchú, peacocks, and luán,
far-soaring shèyàn.
Below them are white tigers and black leopards,
wànyán, chū, and àn.
"Then he sends men of the caliber of Zhuān Zhū,
to grapple with these beasts by hand.
The King of Chǔ then hitches a team of four tamed piebald horses,
and rides in a carriage of carved jade.
He waves a pennant of fish-whisker streamers,
and trails a flag of bright-moon pearls.
He sets up the mighty halberd of Gān Jiàng,
holds the carved bow of Wū Hào in his left hand,
and the strong arrows of Xià Fú in his right.
Yáng Zǐ acts as his attendant,
and Xiān Ā serves as his driver.
Before the pace has even fully relaxed,
he is already overrunning the cunning beasts.
He tramples the Qióngqióng,
and runs down the Jùxū.
He overtakes the wild horses,
and the wheel-hubs strike the Táotú.
Riding on the lingering wind,
he shoots at the roaming Qí.
Swift and flashing, fast and flowing,
like moving thunder and arriving whirlwinds,
like falling stars and striking bolts.
No arrow is fired in vain,
and every hit must pierce the eye.
Penetrating the chest and reaching the armpit,
severing the veins of the heart.
The fallen beasts fall like rain,
covering the grass and blanketing the ground.
Thereupon, the King of Chǔ slows his pace and wanders about,
soaring and taking his ease.
He surveys the shaded forests,
observing the fierce anger of the warriors
and the terror of the wild beasts.
Capturing those who tried to escape and receiving those who submitted,
he fully observes the changing states of all things.
"Then the women of Zhèng and the graceful maidens,
clad in fine-spun silk,
trailing hemp and white silk.
Mixing fine gauze,
and draped in misty crepes.
With pleated folds and gathered wrinkles,
winding slowly and gracefully,
like the twisting curves of valleys.
Trailing and fluttering,
raising their sleeves and slender robes,
their sashes flying and streamers drooping.
Floating and elegant,
rustling and swishing.
Below they brush against the orchids and irises,
above they touch the feathered canopies.
Intermixed with the brilliance of kingfisher feathers,
and wound with jade tassels.
Remote and fleeting,
like the appearance of divine immortals.
"Then they join together to hunt in the orchid gardens,
moving gracefully and lightly,
ascending the golden embankment.
They catch the kingfishers,
and shoot the Jùnyí.
Fine arrows fly out,
and slender cords are cast.
They tether the white swans,
and snag the wild geese.
A pair of cranes falls,
and the black crane is struck.
Only after they are weary do they set off,
to wander upon the clear ponds.
They float on painted bird-boats,
and raise pennanted oars.
They stretch out kingfisher curtains,
and erect feathered canopies.
They net the tortoises,
and hook the purple shells.
They strike the metal drums,
and blow the resonant pipes.
The boatmen sing,
their voices flowing and hoarse.
The water creatures are startled,
and the waves surge like boiling water.
Fountains gush up,
rushing and clashing together.
Boulders strike one another,
with a clattering and crashing sound.
Like the sound of thunder,
heard several hundred lǐ away.
"When those who have been hunting are about to rest,
they strike the sacred drums,
and light the beacons.
The carriages move in order,
and the cavalry join their ranks.
Stretching out in a long line,
moving in an orderly procession.
Then the King of Chǔ ascends the Terrace of Yún Yáng,
calm and doing nothing,
serene and self-possessed.
Once the seasonings of the Sháoyào are prepared,
only then does he partake.
It is not like Your Majesty, who gallops all day long,
and never descends from your carriage.
Tearing flesh and scorching wheels,
considering this your pleasure.
From my humble observation,
Qí is likely not as good.
Thereupon, the King of Qí had nothing with which to answer me."
Master Wūyǒu said:
"What excessive words are these!
You have come from a thousand lǐ away
to bestow a visit upon the state of Qí.
The King called out all the warriors within his borders,
prepared a multitude of carriages and riders,
and went out to hunt with the envoy,
desiring to strive for a great catch
to entertain those around him.
How can this be called boasting!
When he asked whether such things existed in Chǔ,
he wished to hear of the grand customs of a great state,
and the further discourse of a gentleman.
Now you do not praise the King of Chǔ's deep virtue,
but instead greatly extol Yúnmèng as superior,
speaking extravagantly of excessive pleasures and displaying wasteful luxury,
which I humbly believe was not the right course for you.
If it is truly as you say,
it is certainly not the beauty of the state of Chǔ.
To speak of what is not there
is to harm your own credibility.
To highlight the faults of your ruler
and wound personal righteousness—
neither of these two is acceptable,
yet you, sir, have done them.
You will surely be looked down upon by Qí and be a burden to Chǔ.
Furthermore, Qí borders the Great Sea to the east,
and has Lángyá to the south.
We view things from Chéngshān,
and hunt at Zhīfú.
We float on the Bǒxiè,
and wander in Mèngzhū.
On our left we neighbor the Sùshèn,
and on our right Tāng Gǔ is our boundary.
We hunt in autumn on Qīngqiū,
and wander beyond the seas.
It could swallow eight or nine such places as Yúnmèng,
yet in its breast, they would not even be a grain of sand.
As for the extraordinary and magnificent,
the rare species from distant lands,
precious curiosities, birds, and beasts,
in ten thousand varieties, gathered like scales.
They fill the place to capacity,
beyond the power of recording.
Yǔ could not name them all,
and Xiè could not count them.
Yet, being in the position of a feudal lord,
he does not dare to speak of the joy of amusement
or the size of his parks.
You, sir, are a guest,
and that is why the King declined to respond,
not because he had nothing to say!"
Lord Wángshì laughed heartily and said:
"Chǔ was indeed in error,
but Qí has not exactly gotten it right either.
Now, the reason the feudal lords pay tribute
is not for the sake of wealth or coins,
but to report on their duties.
The reason borders are drawn and boundaries fixed
is not for the sake of defense,
but to restrain excess.
Now Qí is ranked as a vassal of the east,
yet it maintains private relations with the Sùshèn,
abandons the state and exceeds its limits,
crossing the sea to hunt.
Regarding righteousness, this is certainly not permissible.
Furthermore, in the discourse of you two gentlemen,
you do not strive to clarify the righteousness between ruler and subject,
or correct the rituals of the feudal lords,
but merely engage in a contest over the joy of amusement
and the size of parks,
desiring to surpass each other in extravagance
and outdo each other in profligacy.
This cannot enhance your name or spread your reputation;
it is only enough to degrade your rulers and damage yourselves."
"Moreover, how are the affairs of Qí and Chǔ even worth mentioning?
You have not yet beheld true grandeur and beauty.
Have you alone not heard of the Son of Heaven's Shànglín Park?
To its left is Cāngwú,
and to its right is Xījì.
The Dān Shuǐ flows across its south,
and the Zǐ Yuān passes through its north.
It encompasses the Bà and Chǎn,
and receives the Jīng and Wèi.
The Fēng, Gào, Lǎo, and Jué
meander and wind,
circulating within its boundaries.
Majestically, the eight rivers branch out,
flowing in opposite directions with diverse forms.
To the east, west, south, and north,
they race and gallop to and fro.
Emerging from the gaps of Jiāo Qiū,
they traverse the banks of sandbars and silt.
Passing through the midst of Guì Lín,
they cross the vast and boundless wilderness.
Rushing along in a turbid torrent,
following the slopes downward,
they plunge into narrow gorges.
Striking against vaulted rocks,
splashing against heaps of stones and riverbanks,
they boil with violent rage,
surging and crashing with thunderous roars.
Gushing and rushing,
they are crowded and surge in narrow passages.
Flowing crosswise and bending back,
they leap, turn, and spray.
Vast, overflowing, and drenching,
they vault high like gathering clouds,
coiling and twisting in whirlpools.
Leaping over waves and rushing into hollows,
with a whistling sound, they descend the rapids.
Striking rocks and surging against barriers,
they rush upward and gather in abundance.
Approaching islets and pouring into chasms,
they splash and fall with a heavy sound.
Deep and muffled,
they make a thunderous, booming roar.
Gurgling and bubbling,
they boil over like a cauldron.
With racing waves and leaping foam,
whirling and drifting swiftly,
they extend far into the distance.
Suddenly silent and still,
they spread out in a long return.
Then, vast and shimmering,
they glide calmly and slowly circle.
Glistening with bright whiteness,
they pour east into the Tài Hú,
overflowing into dikes and ponds.
Thereupon, scaled dragons and red hornless dragons,
wáng-měng and jiàn-lí fish,
yú, yóng, qián, and tuō fish,
yú-yú, qū, and sole,
raise their fins and lash their tails,
shaking their scales and flapping their fin-wings,
while hiding in deep rocky grottos.
The clamor of fish and turtles
and a multitude of all living things.
Bright-moon pearls
sparkle along the riverbanks;
Shǔ stones and yellow soft-jades,
and rock crystals lie in heaps.
Luminous and brilliant,
glistening with vibrant colors,
they are accumulated within.
Geese, sù-shuàng, swans, and bustards,
wild geese and zhǔ-yù,
jiāo-jīng and xuán-mù,
fán-wù and yōng-qú,
zhēn-cī and jiāo-lú
float in flocks upon the surface.
Drifting and spreading far and wide,
they glide gently with the wind.
Swaying and tossing with the waves,
they suddenly gather at the water's edge.
They nibble at duckweed and algae,
and chew on water chestnuts and lotus roots.
"Thereupon, the lofty mountains stand tall,
with towering and precipitous peaks.
Deep forests and giant trees,
steep crags and jagged heights.
Jiǔ Zōng with its high summits,
and the towering Nán Shān.
Rocky slopes and steep inclines,
high, uneven, and rugged.
Surging through streams and crossing valleys,
winding through ditches and channels.
With gaping mouths and wide openings,
there are mounds, hills, and isolated islands.
Rugged, craggy, and steep,
mounds and hollows, uneven and lumpy.
In great numbers and densely packed,
rising and falling in a continuous sweep,
they connect dikes and ponds in a long line.
Flowing, seeping, and welling up,
they disperse across the level plains.
The marshy shores extend for a thousand lǐ,
and nowhere is not leveled and built upon.
Covered with green orchid-grass,
clothed in jiāng-lí,
mixed with mí-wú,
intermingled with liú-yí.
Spreading knotgrass,
gathering clusters of sedge,
jiē-chē and hèng-lán,
gǎo-běn and shè-gān.
Purple ginger and ráng-hé,
zhēn-chí and fragrant iris.
Xiān-zhī and huáng-lì,
jiǎng-zhù and green fán.
Spreading throughout the vast marshes,
they stretch across the great plains.
Intertwining and widely expanding,
they sway as they yield to the wind.
Exhaling fragrance and sending forth scents,
rich and sweet-smelling.
A multitude of perfumes waft out,
spreading and diffusing in all directions,
dense, fragrant, and overpowering.
"Thereupon, looking all around and gazing far,
all is confused, crowded, and indistinct,
vast, hazy, and shimmering.
One looks and sees no beginning;
one observes and sees no end.
The sun rises from the eastern marsh,
and sets into the western embankment.
In its south, things grow even in deep winter,
where waters well up and waves leap.
Its beasts include the mǎ-tú, the yak, the tapir, and the grunting ox,
the water buffalo, the elk, and the Père David's deer.
Red-heads and round-foreheads,
the qióng-qí, elephants, and rhinoceroses.
In its north, even in midsummer there is ice and the earth cracks,
where one crosses ice and wades through rivers.
Its beasts include the qí-lín and the jiǎo-duān,
the táo-tú and the camel.
The qióng-qióng and the wild horse,
the mule, the donkey, and the hinny.
"Thereupon, detached palaces and separate villas
fill the mountains and span the valleys.
High corridors spread in four directions,
with multi-storied chambers and winding pavilions.
Flower-patterned rafters and jade eaves-tiles,
the imperial carriage paths are linked together.
Elevated walkways circle around,
so long that one may stay the night halfway.
Leveling hilltops to build halls,
stacking terraces to increase the heights,
with deep chambers carved into cliffs.
Looking down, all is dim and nothing is seen;
looking up, one touches the rafters and brushes the sky.
Shooting stars pass through the palace gates,
and winding rainbows trail from the railings.
The Azure Dragon wriggles in the eastern wing,
the ivory carriage glides in the western court.
Spirits and immortals banquet in the quiet rooms,
and the likes of Wò Quán sun themselves on the southern eaves.
Sweet springs well up in the pure rooms,
and flowing streams pass through the central courtyard.
Flat rocks bolster the banks,
craggy rocks lean and tilt,
lofty and towering,
chiseled and steep.
Rose-gems and green jades,
corals grow in clusters.
Stones resembling jade spread everywhere,
with veined and mottled patterns.
Red-spotted gems and variegated stones
are interspersed among them,
with morning-glow gems and fine jade pieces;
the likes of the Hè Shì jade are found there.
In this place, the lú jú ripens in summer,
along with the huáng gān, the chéng, and the zòu.
There are the pípá, the niǎn, and the persimmon,
the tíng, the nài, and the hòupò.
The black date and the yángméi,
the cherry and the grape.
The yǐnfū, the wild plum, and the cherry-plum,
the dātā and the lìzhī.
They are spread throughout the Hòugōng
and lined within the Běiyuán.
They extend across the hills
and descend to the plains.
Raising their emerald leaves
and swaying their purple stems,
they bloom with red flowers
and hang with vermilion blossoms.
Radiant and magnificent,
they illuminate the vast wilderness.
There are the shātáng, the oak, and the chǔ,
the maple, the píng, and the lú.
The liúluò and the xūxié,
the rénpín and the palm tree.
The sandalwood and the magnolia,
the camphor and the privet.
They stand a thousand rèn tall
and are many arm-spans in girth.
Their branches stretch out straight and smooth,
their fruit and leaves are lush and thick.
Standing together in clusters or leaning in groves,
they curve and intertwine like rafters.
Jagged and uneven,
gnarled and magnificent.
Their hanging branches spread out,
and their falling blossoms flutter like ribbons.
Dense, luxuriant, and tapering high,
they sway gracefully in the wind.
The rustling and whistling of the vegetation
resembles the sounds of metal and stone instruments,
or the melodies of pipes and flutes.
Rising and falling in irregular patterns,
they encircle the Hòugōng.
Layered and accumulated in abundance,
they cover the mountains and border the valleys,
following the slopes down to the wetlands.
Looking at them, there is no end;
searching through them, they are inexhaustible.
Here, the black gibbons and white females,
the wěi, the jué, and the flying squirrels,
the zhì, the tiáo, the qú, and the nǎo monkeys,
the zhānhú, the hù, and the guǐ,
all rest and dwell among the branches.
They let out long howls and mournful cries,
leaping and crossing over one another.
They coil among the limbs
and recline upon the very tips of the trees.
They leap across broken bridges
and bound over distant thickets.
Agilely seizing the hanging branches,
they move through the sparse gaps.
Scattered and far apart,
they wander freely to distant places.
Places like this number in the hundreds and thousands;
here one may wander for pleasure,
staying in the various palaces and lodges.
The kitchens need not be moved,
the Hòugōng need not shift,
and the hundred officials are all fully provided for.
At this time, as autumn turns to winter,
the Tiānzǐ holds the grand hunt.
He rides in a carriage of carved ivory
drawn by six jade dragon-steeds.
Trailing rainbow banners
and waving cloud-patterned flags.
In front is the Píxuān chariot,
and behind follows the Dàoyóu retinue.
Sūn Shū holds the reins,
and Wèi Gōng serves as the attendant on the right.
The retinue and guards march in formation,
emerging from the four enclosures.
They beat the drums for the stern vanguard
and unleash the hunters.
They use the Rivers as a corral
and Mount Tài as a lookout.
Chariots and cavalry rise like thunder,
shaking the heavens and moving the earth.
Moving ahead and behind in a brilliant array,
they scatter to pursue the prey separately.
Surging and flowing,
following the hills and streaming through the marshes,
they spread like clouds and fall like rain.
They capture live pí and leopards
and strike down jackals and wolves.
They seize bears and brown bears with their hands
and trample wild sheep with their feet.
Wearing caps adorned with hé feathers
and trousers made of white tiger skin.
Clad in patterned furs,
they straddle wild horses.
They ascend the heights of Sānzōng
and descend the stony slopes.
Taking shortcuts through steep paths and rushing into danger,
they cross ravines and wade through waters.
They strike down the Fēilián
and sport with the Xièzhì.
They wrestle with the xiāhá
and spear the měngshì.
They snare the Yàoniǎo
and shoot the monstrous boars.
Their arrows do not strike at random;
they sever necks and pierce through brains.
The bows are never drawn in vain;
at the sound of the string, the prey falls.
Then the Imperial Carriage slows its pace and lingers,
soaring and wandering to and fro.
The Tiānzǐ watches the advance and retreat of his ranks
and observes the maneuvers of his generals.
Afterward, he quickens the pace
and suddenly vanishes into the distance.
He scatters the light birds
and tramples the cunning beasts.
His wheels crush the white deer
and he swiftly catches the clever hare.
Outstripping the red lightning,
he leaves the light and radiance behind.
Chasing strange monsters,
he travels beyond the universe.
He draws the Fánruò bow
to its full extent with a white-feathered arrow.
He shoots the wandering xiāo
and strikes the Fēijù.
He selects the meat before releasing the arrow,
and where he commands it to hit, it strikes.
As the string and arrow part,
the target is killed and falls.
Then, raising his staff, he floats upward,
braving the startled winds
and passing through the terrifying whirlwinds.
He rides upon the void,
becoming one with the spirits.
He tramples the dark crane
and disrupts the kūn chicken.
He overtakes the peacock and the lúan
and presses the jùnyí.
He brushes against the yì bird
and strikes the phoenix.
He seizes the yuānchú
and captures the jiāomíng.
When the path is exhausted and the way is done,
he turns the carriage and returns.
He wanders leisurely at Xiāngyáng
and descends to gather at Běihóng.
He leads the way directly
and suddenly returns to his home territory.
He reaches the Shíquè gate
and passes over Fēngluán.
He passes Zhīquè
and gazes at Lùhán.
He descends at Tánglí
and rests at Yíchūn.
He gallops west to Xuānqū
and washes the boats at Niúshǒu.
He ascends Lóngtái
and takes cover at Xìliǔ.
He observes the diligent efforts of his officials
and balances the gains of the hunters.
The places crushed by the wheels and carts,
trampled by the foot soldiers and cavalry,
and trodden upon by the ministers and servants.
Together with those beasts driven to the point of exhaustion,
terrified and cowering in submission.
Those who died without being wounded by blades
lie scattered and piled in heaps.
They fill the pits and valleys
and cover the plains and marshes.
Thereupon he wandered and took his ease,
setting out wine on the Hào Tiān Terrace
and performing music in the vast and boundless spaces.
He struck bells of a thousand dàn
and erected stands of ten thousand dàn.
He hoisted banners of kingfisher plumes
and set up drums of spirit-alligator skin.
He performed the dances of Táo Táng Shì
and listened to the songs of Gě Tiān Shì.
A thousand people sang
and ten thousand people joined in harmony.
The mountains and hills shook because of it,
and the rivers and valleys surged with waves.
Songs of Bā, Yú, Sòng, and Cài,
the Gān Zhē of Huái Nán,
and the Diān Gē of Wén Chéng.
Grouped together, they played in turn;
bells and drums rose alternately.
The clanging and booming
pierced the heart and startled the ears.
The sounds of Jīng, Wú, Zhèng, and Wèi,
the music of Sháo, Huò, Wǔ, and Xiàng,
and tones that were decadent, overflowing, and unrestrained.
The fluttering movements of Yān and Yǐng,
the Jī Chǔ and the Jié Fēng melodies.
Jesters and dwarves,
the entertainers of Dí Dī,
things used to please the eyes and ears and delight the heart and mind,
beautiful and lavish, they overflowed before him,
delicate and graceful beauties.
“As for those like Qīng Qín and Mì Fēi,
they are extraordinary and apart from the common,
seductive, charming, refined, and elegant.
With fresh makeup and carved ornaments,
they are lithe, graceful, and slender.
Supple and yielding, soft and slow,
enchanting, delicate, and petite.
Trailing robes of single-thread silk,
they are elegant, light, and diaphanous.
Moving with a light and airy gait,
they dress differently from the common folk.
Their fragrance is thick and rich,
intense, pure, and sweet.
Their white teeth are bright and sparkling,
their smiles are fitting and brilliant.
Their long eyebrows are delicately arched,
their sidelong glances are deep and far-reaching.
Their beauty captivates the soul,
making the heart feel joy at their side.
“Then, amidst the wine and at the height of the music's joy,
the Son of Heaven became dazed and fell into thought,
as if he had lost something,
and said:
‘Alas!
This is great extravagance!
I have used my leisure time from state affairs
to waste days in idleness.
