Following the Way of Heaven in hunting and culling,
I have rested here from time to time.
I fear that future generations will be addicted to this splendor,
and will go on without returning,
which is not the way to continue the legacy and hand down the tradition for my successors.’
Thereupon, he stopped the wine and ended the hunt,
and commanded the officials, saying:
‘The land that can be cultivated
shall all be made into agricultural fields
to provide for the common people.
Tear down the walls and fill the moats,
so that the people of the mountains and marshes may come here.
Stock the ponds and pools but do not forbid their use;
empty the palaces and lodges and do not fill them.
Open the granaries to aid the poor
and supplement those who lack.
Show compassion to the widowed and orphaned,
and care for the lonely and childless.
Issue decrees of virtue,
and reduce punishments.
Reform the systems,
and change the colors of vestments.
Revise the calendar
and begin anew with the whole world.’
“Then, choosing an auspicious day and fasting,
he put on his court robes,
rode in his ceremonial carriage,
hoisted the flowered banners,
and rang the jade bells,
to wander in the garden of the Six Arts
and gallop along the path of Benevolence and Righteousness.
He observed the forest of the Chūn Qiū,
shot the Lí Shǒu,
and captured the Zōu Yú.
He hunted the dark crane
and danced with shield and axe.
Carrying the cloud-net,
he captured the many refinements.
He lamented the Fá Tán,
and took joy in the Lè Xū.
He cultivated his demeanor in the garden of Lǐ,
and soared in the park of Shū.
He expounded the way of the Yì,
and released the strange beasts.
He ascended the Míng Táng,
and sat in the Qīng Miào.
He ranked his ministers
and discussed successes and failures.
Within the Four Seas,
none failed to receive the benefits.
At this time,
the world was greatly pleased,
turning toward his influence and listening,
being transformed by the flow,
flourishing in the Way and moving toward Righteousness.
Punishments were set aside and not used,
his virtue was loftier than that of the Sān Wáng,
and his achievements exceeded those of the Wǔ Dì.
If it is like this,
then the hunt is indeed something to be pleased with.
“But as for galloping all day long,
exhausting the spirit and fatiguing the body,
wearing out the use of chariariots and horses,
and wasting the energy of the soldiers,
squandering the wealth of the treasuries
without providing the grace of thick virtue,
striving only for one's own pleasure
while ignoring the common masses,
forgetting the government of the state
and being greedy for the capture of pheasants and hares—
this is not what a benevolent person would do.
Looking at it from this perspective,
the affairs of Qí and Chǔ,
are they not lamentable!
Their territory does not exceed a thousand lǐ,
yet their parks occupy nine hundred;
thus the vegetation cannot be cleared for cultivation,
and the people have nothing to eat.
For those with the smallness of feudal lords
to enjoy the extravagance of ten thousand chariots—
I fear the common people will suffer the consequences.”
Thereupon, the two gentlemen looked solemn and changed their expressions,
appearing lost as if they had failed themselves.
They withdrew and left their mats,
saying:
“We commoners are ignorant and narrow-minded,
not knowing what was forbidden;
having received your teaching today,
we respectfully obey your command.”
At the time of Emperor Xiào Chéng’s feathered hunt,
Yáng Xióng followed.
He believed that in the past, under the Two Emperors and Three Kings,
the palaces, halls, terraces, and pavilions,
the ponds, lakes, parks, and enclosures,
and the woods, foothills, marshes, and wetlands,
were only just sufficient to serve the ancestral temples and altars,
to entertain guests,
and to supply the kitchens;
they did not seize the fertile and productive lands for grain, mulberry, and jujube from the common people.
Thus, women had surplus cloth,
men had surplus grain,
the state was prosperous and wealthy,
and those above and below were mutually satisfied.
Therefore, sweet dew fell in their courtyards,
sweet springs flowed in their halls,
phoenixes nested in their trees,
yellow dragons swam in their ponds,
qílín arrived in their enclosures,
and divine birds perched in their forests.
Formerly, when Yǔ employed Yì as the Forester, those above and below were in harmony
and the plants and trees flourished.
Chéng Tāng was fond of hunting, yet the needs of the world were sufficient.
King Wén’s park was a hundred lǐ,
yet the people still considered it small;
King Xuān of Qí’s park was forty lǐ,
yet the people considered it large:
this is the difference between enriching the people and taking from them.
Emperor Wǔ greatly expanded the Shàng Lín Park,
extending southeast to Yí Chūn and Dǐng Hú,
through Yù Sù and Kūn Wú,
bordering Nán Shān,
reaching west to Cháng Yáng and Wǔ Zuò,
circling Huáng Shān to the north,
and running east along the banks of the Wèi River,
covering a circumference of several hundred lǐ.
He excavated Kūnmíng Lake,
modeling it after the Diān River,
and constructed the Jiàn Zhāng Palace and the Phoenix Towers,
the Shén Míng and Sà Suō halls,
the Jiàn Tái terrace and Tài Yè pond,
to resemble the oceans and the circulation around Fāng Zhàng, Yíng Zhōu, and Péng Lái.
The spectacles were extravagant,
reaching the peak of refinement and the height of beauty.
Although he eventually cut away its three borders
to provide for the common people,
yet regarding the feathered hunt, the armored chariots, the war horses, the equipment, the provisions, and the restricted enclosures,
they were still excessively lavish and boastful,
not reflecting the spirit of the "three-sided drive" of Yáo, Shùn, Chéng Tāng, and King Wén.
Fearing that later generations would again pursue these former preferences
without the moderation shown at Quán Tái,
he took the occasion of the hunt
to compose a rhapsody to offer an admonition.
The words say:
Some praise Fú Xī and Shén Nóng;
is it because the institutions of emperors and kings have become increasingly ornate?
Commentators say no;
each was appropriate for its own time,
so why must they follow the same rules or the same lineage?
As for the sacrifices on Mount Tài Shān,
how could there have been seventy-two different ceremonies?
Thus, those who founded dynasties and handed down traditions
all saw no error in their ways;
from the Five Emperors and Three Kings, far and near,
who can know what was right or wrong?
Then he composed a song of praise, saying:
How magnificent and divine is the Sage,
dwelling in the Mysterious Palace.
His wealth is equal to the measure of the earth,
and his nobility is as lofty as the heavens.
Duke Huán of Qí was not even worthy to support his chariot wheels,
and King Zhuāng of Chǔ was not fit to be his companion rider.
Considering the limitations of the Three Kings as narrow,
he rises high and prospers greatly.
He traverses the vastness of the Five Emperors,
and treads upon the grand heights of the Three Sovereigns.
He establishes Virtue and the Way as his teachers,
and befriends Benevolence and Righteousness.
In the last month of winter,
when the heaven and earth are bitingly cold,
all things are beginning to stir within
but have withered and fallen without.
The Emperor intends to hunt in the Spirit Park;
he opens the northern borders,
following the regulations of Bù Zhōu,
to honor the winter lineage of Zhuān Xù and Xuán Míng.
He then commands the Foresters and Marsh Wardens
to extend to Kūn Lín in the east
and gallop to Chāng Hé in the west.
Provisions are prepared and gathered,
and garrison soldiers line the roads.
They cut down thickets of thorns
and level the wild grasses.
They defend the lands from Qiān and Wèi,
and manage the regions of Fèng and Hào.
The imperial majesty flows everywhere,
matching the coming and going of the sun and moon,
as if heaven and earth were meeting.
Then, with Hǔ Lù and Sān Zōng as markers,
they encircle a perimeter of a hundred lǐ,
serving as the palace gate.
Outwardly, it directly meets the southern sea
and obliquely borders the Yú Abyss.
Vast and boundless,
it is held up by lofty mountains.
They organize the assembly for the hunt,
first stationing themselves south of the white poplars
and east of the Kūnmíng Spirit Pond.
Men of the likes of Měng Bèn and Xià Yù,
bearing shields and carrying feathered arrows,
clutching Mò Xié swords, are arranged by the tens of thousands.
Others carry nets that reach the sky
and spread traps that cover the wilderness.
They raise vermilion poles that dim the sun and moon
and trail flying banners like comets.
Blue clouds serve as tassels,
and red rainbows as loops,
stretching to the slopes of Kūnlún.
Scattered like the stars in the sky,
vast as the waves of the surging sea.
Moving in a slow and steady flow,
they intercept the prey from front and back.
The Chán Qiāng star serves as the gate,
and the bright moon as the watchtower.
Mars commands their fate,
and the Heavenly Bow fires its shots.
Vivid and brilliant in their variety,
they spread out along the paths.
Light and swift war chariots
move in a continuous, interlocking stream.
Rumbling and crowded,
they cover the hills and climb the slopes.
Those from the most distant regions
are arrayed together upon the high plateaus.
Feathered riders swarm about,
each with distinct duties.
Moving to and fro in great numbers,
an unending succession.
Flickering as if light or shadow,
they are spread beneath the green forests.
Then, at the break of dawn, the Son of Heaven
first emerges from the Mysterious Palace.
He strikes the great bell,
raises the nine-tasseled banners,
harnesses six white tigers,
and rides in the divine carriage.
Chī Yóu rides alongside his wheels,
and Měng Gōng acts as the vanguard.
They raise flags that pierce the sky
and trail banners that sweep the stars.
Amidst thunder and lightning,
they spit fire and apply the whip.
Gathering and surging like a flood,
dripping and vast,
they frolic through the Eight Garrisons and open the gates.
Fēi Lián and the Master of Clouds
breathe deeply and move swiftly;
like fish scales or stars, they are spread out,
clustered like dragon feathers.
With the sounds of jingling and harmonious movement,
they enter the West Garden,
pass by Shén Guāng,
look toward Píng Lè,
and cross through the Bamboo Grove.
They trample the clover gardens
and tread upon the orchid paths.
They raise great beacon fires;
the charioteers display their skills,
driving a thousand teams of four horses abreast,
with ten thousand leaders of the cunning cavalry.
Like a formation of roaring tigers,
they weave and crisscross.
Fast as a whirlwind, fierce as thunder,
with a deafening and clattering roar.
Turbulent and surging,
heaven shakes and the earth quakes.
Overflowing and scattered,
stretching into the desolate distance for thousands of lǐ.
As for the vigorous men, full of high spirits,
they come from different lands and possess various inclinations.
From the east, west, south, and north,
they gallop to follow their tastes and race after their desires.
They drag the blue boars,
tread over rhinoceroses and yaks,
and kick the floating elks.
They cleave the giant monkeys
and wrestle with black gibbons.
They leap into the empty void
and ward off curling creatures.
They spring over writhing beasts
and sport amidst the mountain streams.
In obscure and numerous masses,
the mountains and valleys whirl with wind because of them,
and the forests and thickets raise dust because of them.
When it comes to the likes of Huò and the Yí,
they trample pines and cypresses
and strike down the caltrops.
They hunt through the dense foliage
and rumble over the light and flying.
They wear tiger-heads as shoes
and long serpents as belts.
They hook red leopards
and strike elephants and rhinoceroses.
They stride over ridges and pits
and leap across Tángpēi.
Chariots and horsemen gather like clouds,
ascending and descending in dark density.
Mt. Tàihuá is used as a banner-streamer,
and Mt. Xióng'ěr as a pendant.
Trees fall and mountains revolve,
spreading boundlessly as if beyond the heavens.
They linger by the great shores
and roam freely within the universe.
Thereupon, the sky is clear and the sun is peaceful;
Féng Méng lines up his sight,
and the Yì clan draws the bowstring.
The Imperial chariot rumbles deeply,
its light filling Heaven and Earth;
Wàngshū holds the reins,
and like wings, they slowly arrive at Shànglán.
Shifting the enclosure and moving the formations,
they spread out and trample in divisions.
The curved units are firm and heavy,
each keeping to its rank and file.
The ramparts turn like the heavens;
with divine lashes and lightning strikes,
whatever they meet is crushed,
and whatever they approach is broken.
Birds have no time to fly;
beasts cannot pass.
The army alarms and the hosts startle,
scraping the wilds and sweeping the ground.
When the net-chariots fly high
and the martial cavalry gallops swiftly,
they trample flying leopards
and snare the xiāoyáng.
They chase the Tiānbǎo
and emerge from one direction.
Responding to the thundering sound,
they strike at the flowing light.
The wilds are exhausted and the mountains reached to their ends;
they bag all, both male and female.
Flowing and surging,
they laugh afar within the four boundaries.
The Three Armies are dazed,
wandering to the limits of the barriers.
Truly behold the swift birds breaking their leashes,
and the rhinoceroses and wild oxen goring each other.
The brown and white bears claw and grab,
while tigers and leopards are in a frantic rush.
With only horns goring and heads butting,
they are focused, cramped, and trembling in fear.
Their souls are terrified and their spirits lost;
they strike the wheel-spokes and catch their necks in the shafts.
Random shots all find their mark;
whether advancing or retreating, the hunters tread upon the captured.
Wounds soak the wheels,
and bodies pile up like hills and gather like mounds.
Thereupon, when the prey is exhausted and strength declines,
they gather together at the Jìngmíng Zhī Guǎn
to overlook the precious pond.
It is filled from Qí and Liáng
and overflows with the waters of the Jiāng and the Hé.
To the east, the gaze reaches its limit;
to the west, it stretches without shore.
The pearls of Suí and the jade of Hé Shì
shine brilliantly on its banks.
Jade and stones are high and jagged,
dazzling with blue and shimmering light.
The Maidens of the Hàn dive in the water,
and strange creatures are hidden in the darkness,
their forms too many to be fully described.
Black phoenixes and peacocks,
and kingfishers trailing their glory.
The wángjū cry "guān guān,"
and the wild geese call "yīng yīng."
Flocks enjoy themselves therein,
chirping and calling in unison.
Wild ducks, gulls, and egrets
move up and down with crashing sounds,
a noise like thunder.
Then the tattooed experts are sent
to battle scaled creatures in the water.
They brave the solid ice,
enter the stern deeps,
explore caves and push through reefs,
hunting for flood-dragons and hornless dragons.
They trample otters,
seize soft-shelled turtles and alligators,
and grab spiritual tortoises.
They enter the cavernous holes
and emerge from Cāngwú.
They ride giant scaled fish
and mount the whale-like Jīngyú.
They float on Pénglí
and look toward Yǒuyú.
They smash the colored glass of the night-glow,
cut open the pearl-embryos of the bright moon,
whip the Consort Fú of the Luò River,
and offer food to Qū Yuán and Péng Xū.
At this time, great scholars and eminent literati,
with high caps and official robes,
in varied ceremonial dress,
cultivate the records of Táng,
rectify the Odes and Hymns,
and bow and yield to one another in front.
Their illuminating light shines brightly,
sudden and swift as spirits.
The sound of benevolence reaches the Běidí,
and martial righteousness moves the southern neighbors.
Thus the kings of felt and fur,
and the leaders of the Hú and Mò,
bring rare treasures to offer,
raising their hands to declare themselves subjects.
The former enter the enclosure’s mouth,
while the latter are arrayed at Lúshān.
The lords, the attendants, and the followers of Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí
sigh in unison and say:
"How lofty is this virtue!
Even with the prosperity of Táng, Yú, Dà Xià, and Chéng Zhōu,
how could they surpass this!
In ancient times, those who visited the Dōngyuè
and performed the Shàn sacrifice at the base of Mt. Liáng,
if they were to leave this age,
whom else would they choose?"
The Emperor still modestly declines and has not yet consented;
he is about to hunt the currents of the three spirits above,
and release the nourishment of the Sweet Spring below.
He opens the cave of the Huánglóng,
peers into the nest of the Fènghuáng,
visits the park of the Qílín,
and favors the forest of the Shénquè.
He considers Yúnmèng as extravagant
and Mèngzhū as wasteful.
He rejects Zhānghuá
and endorses the Língtái.
He rarely goes to detached palaces
and has ceased his sightseeing tours.
Earthworks are not decorated,
woodwork is not carved,
he assists the people in farming and sericulture,
encouraging them not to be idle;
he pairs men and women,
ensuring they do not miss their time.
Fearing that the poor might not fully receive the overflowing bounty,
he opens the forbidden parks,
distributes public stores,
creates a park of Way and Virtue,
and expands the preserves of Benevolence and Grace.
He gallops and shoots in the Park of Spiritual Brilliance,
observing whether his officials have what they need.
He releases the pheasants and rabbits,
and gathers in the nets.
Elks, deer, and fuel-gatherers are shared with the common people;
this is how he achieved this state.
Thereupon he purifies his great and penetrating virtue,
and enriches the regulations for a flourishing age.
Exerting more effort than the Sānhuáng,
and working harder than the Wǔdì—
is this not the ultimate?
Thus the respectful, solemn, harmonious, and majestic ones
establish the principles between ruler and subject,
honor the works of the wise and holy,
having no leisure for the beauty of parks
or the extravagance of the hunt.
Consequently, he turns his carriage and reverses the harness,
turns his back on Āfáng,
and returns to Wèiyāng.
Next year,
the Emperor intended to boast to the Hú people of the abundance of birds and beasts.
In autumn, he ordered the Yòu Fúfēng to mobilize the people to enter the Nánshān,
from Bāoxié in the west
to Hóngnóng in the east,
and driving from Hànzhōng in the south,
to spread nets and snares
to capture bears, brown bears, porcupines, tigers, leopards, monkeys, apes, foxes, rabbits, elks, and deer,
loading them into caged carts
and transporting them to the Shèxióng Guǎn at Chángyáng.
Using nets to form a circular enclosure,
they released the birds and beasts within,
ordering the Hú people to fight them with their bare hands
and take the catches for themselves,
while the Emperor personally oversaw the spectacle.
At this time,
the farmers were unable to harvest their crops.
Yáng Xióng followed the entourage to the Shèxióng Guǎn,
and upon his return, he presented the "Chángyáng Fù,"
taking the opportunity to compose an essay with brush and ink,
thus using Hànlín as the host
and Zǐmò as the guest-official to offer indirect criticism.
Its text says:
The guest-official Zǐmò asked the host Hànlín, saying:
“I have heard that when a sage ruler nurtures the people,
benevolence is pervasive and kindness is profound,
and his actions are not for himself.
This year, for the hunt at Chángyáng,
you first ordered the Yòu Fúfēng,
with Tàihuà on the left and Bāoxié on the right,
to hammer stakes into the steep cliffs for hunting posts
and to wind through Nánshān to set up nets.
A thousand chariots are arrayed in the thickets,
and ten thousand cavalry are stationed at the corners of the mountains.
Leading the army to drive animals into the enclosure,
rewarding the soldiers and capturing the Hú.
They strangle bears and brown bears,
and drag porcupines.
Trees are piled up and spears are stacked
to serve as fences.
This is the ultimate spectacle and grandest sight in the world.
Even so,
it has also greatly disturbed the farmers.
For more than thirty days,
their hardship has reached its peak,
yet their labor is not considered;
I fear that those who do not understand will externally view it as a pleasure trip of amusement,
and internally will not view it as a matter of sacrificial offerings;
how can this be for the sake of the people?
Furthermore, a ruler takes mysterious silence as his spirit
and detachment as his virtue.
Now you delight in traveling far to display your awe-inspiring power,
frequently mobilizing and exhausting the chariots and armor;
this was not originally the urgent task of a ruler of men,
and I am secretly confused by it.”
The host Hànlín said:
“Alas,
what are you saying, Guest!
What you have said is knowing one side but not having seen the other,
seeing the exterior but not recognizing the interior.
I have often been weary of speaking
and cannot detail everything point by point,
so please let me briefly mention the general outline,
and you, Guest, may observe for yourself what is pertinent.”
The guest said:
“Yes, yes.”
The host said:
“In the past, there was the powerful Qín,
which acted like a giant boar in its territory
and devoured its people like the Yàyǔ;
beings like the Záochǐ ground their teeth and fought over it.
Heroes surged like boiling water and swarmed like clouds,
and the masses were not at peace.
Then the Emperor on High looked with favor upon Gāozǔ;
Gāozǔ received the mandate,
following the Dipper and the Pole Star,
and turning the celestial gate.
He crossed the great seas
and flooded the Kūnlún.
Lifting his sword and shouting,
wherever he passed, he commanded cities and leveled towns,
and the generals below lowered their banners in surrender.
The battles of a single day
cannot be fully recorded.
During such labor,
his hair was disheveled with no time to comb
and he was hungry with no time to eat.
Lice grew in his helmet,
and his armor was soaked with sweat.
In this way, he pleaded for the lives of the myriad people before Huángtiān.
Then he expanded what had been constricted
and relieved what had been lacking.
He planned for a hundred million years
and expanded the imperial enterprise.
Within seven years, the world was at peace.
“Coming down to the Shèng Wén,
he followed the wind and rode the current,
turning his attention to ultimate tranquility.
He personally practiced frugality,
his coarse silk robes were not worn out
and his leather shoes were not punctured.
He did not live in great mansions,
and his wooden vessels had no ornamentation.
Thus, the inner palace devalued tortoiseshell and distanced itself from pearls,
rejecting kingfisher ornaments
and eliminating the skill of carving and polishing.
He detested extravagance and did not approach it,
rejected fragrances and did not use them,
suppressed the music of strings and flutes and banqueting,
and loathed hearing the delicate sounds of Zhèng and Wèi;
consequently, the Yùhéng was aligned and the Tàijiē was level.
“Thereafter, the Xūnyù committed atrocities
and the Dōngyí were in rampant rebellion.
The Qiāng Róng glared in anger,
and the Mǐnyuè caused chaos among themselves.
The distant fields were uneasy because of this,
and Zhōngguó suffered from these calamities.
Then the Shèng Wǔ erupted in fury
and set his troops in order.
He then ordered Piào and Wèi;
surging like billowing water,
gathering like clouds and striking like lightning.
Whirling like a windstorm and flowing like waves,
frightening as a trap and swarming like bees.
As swift as a falling star,
striking like a crashing thunderclap.
They crushed the armored carts
and broke the felt tents.
Brains were scattered on the Shāmù,
and marrow flowed in the Yúwú.
They then trampled over the royal court of the nomads.
Driving away camels
and burning the Mìlǐ.
Wounding the Chányú
and dismembering the dependent states.
Leveling pits and valleys,
uprooting the wilderness,
and carving inscriptions into mountain rocks.
Trampling corpses and transporting servants,
binding the old and the weak.
Those with spear wounds and scars
and those excessively wounded by metal arrowheads numbered in the hundreds of thousands,
all prostrating themselves with heads to the ground
and crawling on their bellies like ants.
It has been more than twenty years now,
and they still do not dare to breathe a sigh of alarm.
The heavenly troops approached from all sides,
reaching Yōudū first.
Turning their halberds to point slantwise,
the Nányuè were exterminated.
Displaying the imperial tallies on a western campaign,
the Qiāng and Bó fled eastward.
Thus, the distant regions with strange customs
and the areas of distinct neighbors and isolated tribes,
from those not transformed by supreme benevolence
to those not pacified by flourishing virtue,
none failed to stand on tiptoe and lift their heads,
asking to present their treasures.
They made the land within the seas peaceful,
forever free from the disasters of border cities
and the worries of war.
Today, the court is purely benevolent;
it follows the *Dào* and manifests righteousness.
It encompasses the *Shūlín*,
and the *Shèngfēng* spreads like clouds.
The essence of brilliance rises and falls,
overflowing across the eight regions.
Everything covered by the vast heavens
is moistened by this grace.
If there is a scholar who does not discuss the *Wángdào*, even the woodcutters laugh at him.
It is believed that no matter how flourishing an affair is, it will not fail to decline,
and no matter how prosperous a thing is, it will not fail to diminish.
Therefore, in times of peace, one does not disregard danger;
in times of stability, one does not forget peril.
Thus, during seasons of abundance, troops are sent out
to arrange the chariots and rouse the army.
They drill the troops at *Wǔzuò*
and train the horses at *Chángyáng*.
They select the strong to hunt cunning beasts
and test their prowess against swift birds.
Then, they gather to ascend *Nánshān*
and gaze toward *Wūyì*.
To the west, they appease the *Yuèzhī*;
to the east, they shake the *Rìyù*.
Furthermore, there is a fear that later generations might be confused by the events of a single moment,
thinking this is the primary concern of the state,
and indulge excessively in hunting,
declining without restraint.
For this reason, before the chariot wheels have even settled,
and before the sun has set the banners low,
the followers seem to vanish,
and the procession winds back to return.
This is also to uphold the achievements of *Tàizūn*
and follow the measures of *Wén* and *Wǔ*.
It restores the hunting fields of the *Sānwáng*
and returns to the stewardship of the *Wǔdì*.
It ensures that farmers do not cease their plowing
and weavers do not leave their looms.
Marriages take place at the proper time,
and men and women do not miss their seasons.
They go out with joy and ease,
and act with simplicity.
They take pity on the toil of the people
and give rest to the laborers.
They honor those a hundred years old
and care for the orphaned and weak.
The leader shares with them,
experiencing both hardship and joy together.
Then, the music of bells and drums is arranged,
the harmony of hand-drums and lithophones resounds,
and the tall frames for the bells are erected.
They strike the sounding stones
and perform the dances in eight rows.
They pour the "Brilliant Wine,"
and the feast is full of joy.
They listen to the harmonious sounds in the temple
and receive the blessings of gods and men.
Songs are performed as *Sòng*,
and the flutes harmonize with the *Yǎ*.
Their diligence is such as this,
so the true spirits reward their labor.
They are about to await the *Yuánfú*
to perform the *Shàn* sacrifice at the base of *Liángfǔ*
and increase the height of *Tàishān*.
They extend glory to the future
and match the fame of former titles.
How could it be merely for the sake of excessive viewing and superficial observation,
galloping through fields of rice,
or wandering through forests of pears and chestnuts,
trampling upon the fodder and fuel of the people,
boasting to the common masses,
maximizing the catch of monkeys,
or increasing the harvest of elaphures and deer?
Moreover, a blind man cannot see what is a foot away,
but *Lílóu* can illuminate a corner a thousand miles off.
The guest only cares that the foreigners might capture our birds and beasts,
but does not yet know that we have already captured their kings and lords.
Before the speech was finished,
the *Mòkè* descended from his seat,
bowed twice, touched his head to the ground, and said:
"How grand is this embodiment of virtue!
Truly, it is not something a lesser man could reach.
Today my ignorance has been dispelled,
and all is clearly revealed!"
I cross the *Qīnglín* to wander and gaze,
enjoying the flocking flight of the feathered tribes.
Behold the brilliant beauty of their plumage,
the famed five-colored pheasant.
It maintains a focused and upright mind,
showing off its grand and beautiful posture.
I patrol the hills to manage the land,
mapping the mounds and plains to divide the boundaries.
At this time, the *Qīngyáng* bids farewell,
and the *Zhūmíng* begins.
No tree is without growth,
no grass is without luxuriance.
The new stalks are lush and shine with freshness,
while the old branches wither and shed their past.
The sky is vast with hanging clouds,
and the springs trickle and pour forth.
The wheat gradually puts forth its awns,
and the pheasants cry out at the morning.
Looking at the bamboo cages and baskets held high,
I observe the shifting moods of the brave decoy bird.
It rouses its strong legs like clashing branches,
and glares with fierce eyes, looking from side to side.
Its wings are beautifully patterned and it strikes with reddish hues,
its neck is bright as embroidery and its back like royal robes.
It rises up with lingering anger,
longing to cry out and show its prowess.
Then, the hunting ground is prepared and the screen is set up,
under the lush and green trees.
The green cypresses are of varying heights,
and the feathered wings are arranged like scales.
Dense and flourishing,
winding and light.
Inside, it is clear and transparent;
outside, it is tightly knit and dense.
I fear my outing has started late,
and worry that the wild birds will seldom come.
I am willing to weary my heart with anticipation,
and focus my tired eyes on the view.
How tall and heroic are the adjusted feathers,
surpassing their kind with extraordinary talent.
Waiting for the signal to be raised, it gives a clear call;
the wilderness hears the sound and responds to the decoy.
Lifting the fine net to look afar,
a bird has already come stumbling slowly.
It displays its bright red crest,
and spreads its ornate feathers around its neck.
Its head is adorned with green and white,
its body trails patterns like fine embroidery.
Its green tail-feathers sway like grass,
its red breast is mixed with orchid hues.
Or kicking or pecking,
sometimes walking, sometimes stopping.
Its variegated tail is raised high,
and its double horns stand up uniquely.
The good decoy bird makes a clucking sound,
drawing it into range.
In response to a sharp cry, the bird stands still,
stretching its body and standing tall.
Holding the *Huángjiān* with a tight draw,
aiming through the strong net in secret.
The bird falls in a flurry,
the sound of the mechanism vibrates without end.
The wild *Shānbì* is fierce and harmful,
and is exceedingly swift.
It crosses ravines and clears peaks,
flying and crying near the granary.
The whale-tooth arrow-tip is lowered,
the heart is calm and the aim is steady.
Feathers and body are broken and fall,
suddenly like shredded silk.
The most outstanding of the flock
dominates the field and holds its ground.
It pecks at the female, jealous of anything different,
coming and going in a flash.
It avoids the biting wind from upwind,
and fears the bright reflection of the sun.
I hide behind the cloth and hold my breath,
my heart is anxious and my skills are itching to be used.
As the *Yìniǎo* meets the enemy,
it screeches upon the ground with a piercing sound.
The other bird hears the sound and advances directly,
suddenly their spurs cross as they engage.
Red fills the field of vision with beautiful feathers,
the heads fall in confusion and the breasts turn upward.
Or perhaps they are high mounds and uncultivated wastes,
where farmers do not easily till the ridges.
Weeds and pulse grow in tangled clusters,
thickets are lush and overgrown.
The crowing male shakes its feathers,
resting upon its mound.
One descends the hill to gallop toward the foe;
though the form is hidden, the grass moves.
Observing the tilting and swaying of the upright ears of grain,
one’s intent stirs and leaps with excitement.
As the sun rises, the bird leaves the sprouts to enter the field,
making one’s heart increasingly startled and spirit awed.
Looking as the black shadows merge and the white light is obscured,
the pheasant draws in its shoulders and turns its heels.
Delighted by the keenness of my resolve,
I aim for the green head and strike the neck.
There are also those whose eyes do not follow the body,
glancing sideways and peering askance.
Startled without hearing anything,
and fluttering without seeing anything.
Circling and returning,
winding about and pivoting.
Suddenly turning into cover,
entangled wherever they go.
Walking haltingly and stopping midway,
they are suddenly struck by an arrow.
The front row takes it in the breast,
and from the side, the overlapping wings are cut.
As for those with many doubts and little resolve,
whose courage is weak and hearts are irritable,
internally they have no steadfastness,
and when coming out, they do not join the fray.
They come like a maiden,
and depart like a flash of lightning.
Peering through the dense leaves,
they are suddenly seen in the thickets.
Thereupon, one calculates the smallest fractions
and judges the distance.
Raising the suspended blade,
one displays peerless skill.
Like the tilting of a carriage,
neither too high nor too low.
Striking the beak and hitting the chest,
splitting the crop and breaking the bill.
Level ground and treacherous terrain are different,
and the tame and the wild change differently.
At noon there is no time to eat,
and at evening one does not report fatigue.
In the past, when Jiǎ Shì went to Rúgāo,
she only began to smile after a single arrow was shot.
The ugly man changed his appearance because of it,
and the resentful wife released her grudge because of it.
Those who hunt for sport and obtain a catch,
all ride through danger and gallop in haste.
How is it that this art is so leisurely and at ease,
yet the birds are already prepared for capture?
One walks along a cleared path,
and chooses a place to stay.
Tail feathers adorn the bits of the harness,
and the meat is placed on the sacrificial vessel for eternal use.
Is it only for the lowly servants?
This is what a ruler performs!
If one indulges in pleasure and wanders aimlessly,
with a heart that does not return,
forgetting care for oneself,
and only monitoring the males and females;
experiencing joy without restraint,
one’s upright conduct may be compromised.
This is what the venerable Lǎo Shì cautioned against,
and what a gentleman does not do.
I encountered the upheaval of the world,
and suffered the distress of blockades and disasters.
My old home was destroyed and turned to ruins,
and I could not stay for even a short while.
Thus, I shook my sleeves and journeyed north,
traveling far to remote tracks.
In the morning, I started my journey from Chángdū,
and in the evening, I lodged in the dark palace of Hùgǔ.
Passing through Yúnmén and looking back,
I gazed at the towering height of Tōngtiān.
Crossing over ridges and hills, ascending and descending,
I rested in the townships of Xún and Bīn.
Admiring the lingering virtue of Gōng Liú,
reaching the point where even the walking reeds were not harmed.
Why was his life so abundant and rich,
while I alone suffer these hundred calamities?
Therefore, the changes in the meeting of the times
are not because the mandate of heaven is inconstant.
Ascending the long slope of Chìxū,
I entered the old city of Yìqú.
Resenting the excess and cunning of the King of Róng,
and the foulness of Empress Dowager Xuān's loss of chastity.
I praise Qín Zhāo for punishing the rebel,
flashing his anger in a northern expedition.
As I left this old capital in confusion,
my horses moved slowly through this place.
Thus, I traveled far at a relaxed pace,
setting Āndìng as my destination.
Crossing the long and winding road,
far and circuitous, twisting and turning.
Passing Níyáng and sighing deeply,
grieving that the ancestral temple was not repaired.
I released my horses at Péngyáng,
and for a while, I slowed my pace and reflected.
The sun grew dim as evening approached,
and I saw the cattle and sheep coming down.
Realizing how the resentment of the wilderness wounds the heart,
I mourned the poet’s lament of the times.
Passing Āndìng with a leisurely air,
I followed the endless Great Wall.
Distressed by Méng Gōng's exhaustion of the people,
building resentment for the sake of powerful Qín.
Casting aside the urgent worries of Gāo Hài,
and attending to the distant troubles of the Mán and Dí.
He did not illustrate virtue to soothe those afar,
but looked to thick walls to repair the borders.
Head and body were separated without his realization,
yet he still counted his merits and excused his faults.
Why did the Master speak so wildly,
saying that the earth's veins were severed?
Ascending the border towers to gaze afar,
I danced about for a short while.
Pitying how the Xūnyù harassed the Huà,
I mourned Wèi Qióng at Cháonà.
Following the ability of the sagely Wén Dì to yield,
who did not toil the army but increased the gifts.
He showed kindness to the father and elder brother in Nányuè,
and caused Wèi Tuó to cast off the title of Emperor.
He bestowed a stool and staff upon the vassal state,
and broke the rebellion of Wú Pì.
How vast and grand was Tài Zōng!
Could the former Qín have ever planned such things?
Ascending Gāopíng and looking all around,
I gazed at the towering mountains and valleys.
The wilds were desolate and vast,
for a thousand lǐ there were no homes.
The wind gusted and billowed,
and the valley waters flooded and raised waves.
Flying clouds and mist were dark and distant,
as I crossed through the pure white snow.
The geese flew in harmonious flocks,
and the kūn birds cried out shrilly.
The traveler grieves for his old home,
his heart sorrowful and wounded with grief.
Patting my long sword and sighing with emotion,
tears fell in streams, wetting my clothes.
Drying my tears in my distress,
I mourned the many troubles of the people.
Why is the shadow so dark and without sunlight?
Alas, we have long lost the proper measure.
Truly, it is the work of time and fortune;
in my eternal gloom, to whom shall I complain?
The envoi says:
The Master remained steadfast in poverty,
wandering in the arts and literature,
finding joy and forgetting sorrow—
only the sages and worthies can do so!
The man of attainment performs his duties,
following the proper rules and models;
whether acting or stopping, bending or stretching,
he rests in accordance with the times.
The gentleman walks in faithfulness,
and there is no place he cannot dwell;
even if he goes to the Mán or Mò,
what worry or fear could he have?
It was in the seventh year of the Yǒngchū era,
that I followed my son on an eastern expedition.
In the auspicious days of the first month of spring,
we selected a lucky hour to set out.
Then we lifted our feet and boarded the carriage,
and in the evening, I stayed at Yǎnshī.
Thus leaving the old and moving toward the new,
my heart was sorrowful and filled with grief!
At dawn I rose without having slept,
my heart lingering and hesitant.
I poured a cup of wine to relax my thoughts,
sighing as I suppressed my feelings and corrected myself.
Truly, not climbing to a nest or knocking on a shell,
how could I not exert my strength to follow along?
For now, I follow the crowd and take my place,
listening to where the mandate of heaven leads.
Following the broad road of the thoroughfare,
whom would I seek to follow for a shortcut?
Thus, I proceeded and traveled away,
letting my eyes wander and my soul roam free!
Passing through seven towns to observe and view,
I encounter the many hardships of Gǒng Xiàn.
Gazing at the confluence of the Hé and Luò rivers,
I look upon the Xuán Mén Pass of Chéng Gāo.
Having escaped the steep and dangerous heights,
I traverse Xíng Yáng and pass through Juàn.
Eating at Yuán Wǔ to rest my weary feet,
I lodge among the mulberry trees of Yáng Wǔ.
Crossing Fēng Qiū to tread the road,
I yearn for the Jīng Shī and secretly sigh!
It is the nature of common men to cherish their soil;
This has been so since the records of books and traditions.
Then I advance on the path and move slightly forward,
Reaching the northern border of Píng Qiū.
Entering the walls of Kuāng to reflect on the distant past,
I think of the distress and hardships of Fū Zǐ.
In those decadent and chaotic times of lawlessness,
They even besieged and intimidated the Sage.
Despondent and hesitant, I linger for a long time,
Forgetting the sun is setting and it will soon be dark.
Reaching the boundary of Cháng Yuán,
I observe the residents of the rural fields.
Seeing the ruins of Pú Chéng,
Overgrown with dense thorns and thickets.
Startled into awareness, I look around and ask,
Recalling the awe-inspiring spirit of Zǐ Lù.
The people of Wèi praised his courage and righteousness;
They speak of him even until this day.
The Qú clan lived in the southeast of the city;
The people still honor their burial mounds.
Only excellent virtue is immortal;
Though the person has perished, the name endures.
It is what the classics and scriptures praise:
Valuing morality, benevolence, and worthiness.
Wú Zhá claimed there were many gentlemen here;
His words are trustworthy and have proof.
Later it declined and met with calamities,
Gradually deteriorating and failing to rise again.
Knowing that life and destiny are in the hands of Heaven,
One approaches benevolence through diligent practice.
Strive to look up at the high and follow the great,
Exhausting loyalty and empathy in dealing with others.
Loving uprightness without turning back,
Sincerity reaches the bright spirits.
May the spirits and deities look down and see,
Protecting the virtuous and assisting the faithful.
The Envoi says:
The thoughts of a gentleman
Must be formed into words.
Why not each speak of our will,
Admiring the men of old?
The conduct of former lords
Is recorded in their works.
Though I am not quick-witted,
How could I dare not follow their example?
Nobility, lowliness, poverty, and wealth
Cannot be sought by force.
Rectify oneself and walk the Way
To await the proper time.
The span of a long or short life
Is the same for the foolish and the wise.
Be tranquil, reverent, and entrust oneself to fate,
Whether it be good or ill fortune.
Be respectful and cautious without neglect,
Thinking of humility and restraint.
Be pure and quiet with few desires,
Taking Gōng Chuò as a teacher.
In the year when the star was in Xuán Xiāo,
In the month when the moon was in Ruí Bīn,
When Bǐng and Dīng governed the days,
And Yǐ Wèi presided over the celestial signs.
Pān Zǐ leaned on his carriage rail for a western journey,
Traveling from the capital to Qín.
Then with a deep sigh, he said:
From the past to the present,
How vast and eternal!
Immense and indistinct,
Transforming the one Breath to distinguish the Three Powers.
These Three Powers
Are the ways of Heaven, Earth, and Man.
Only life and status
Are called the Great Treasures.
Life has a destiny of long or short span,
Status has encounters of success or obstruction.
Neither ghosts nor spirits can demand them,
Neither sages nor the wise can foresee them.
Living in an age of prosperity and enlightenment,
I relied on my humble and meager nature.
Recruited by banners and bows to the Xuán Tái,
Assisting in the various achievements of the Imperial House.
Alas, the constant burden of a common man:
Once he has attained something, he fears losing it.
Without the upright way of Liǔ Jì,
I assisted the Shì Shī and was once dismissed.
Wǔ Huáng suddenly ascended to the heavens,
The eight musical sounds were silenced within the four seas.
The Son of Heaven stayed in the mourning chamber,
And the officials took orders from the Zhǒng Zǎi.
That burden was exceptionally heavy;
Even for Yī or Zhōu, it would have been perilous.
Observing the Seven Nobles in the court of Hàn,
How could one expect a single surname to endure?
Lacking the wisdom to avoid danger and secure their positions,
They only clung to power to show their exclusivity.
Falling into rebellion and facing execution,
Disaster did not descend upon them from Heaven.
Kǒng acted or withdrew according to the times;
Qú unrolled or rolled up with the state.
If one conceals the subtle and confuses the manifest,
One fears the calamity of transgression is not far off.
I realized the worth of the hermits hidden in mountains,
Who loftily depart and never return.
How petty is the entanglement of my own person,
Drifting like duckweed and rolling like tumbleweed.
The positions of officials rise and fall in ruin,
Reputation and integrity are shattered and fallen.
Precarious as white eggs piled on shells,
Worse than a black swallow nesting on a curtain.
My heart trembles with fear and trepidation,
As if facing a deep abyss or treading on thin ice.
In the evening I returned outside the capital;
Before midnight, disaster struck.
It is not that I failed to choose a tree to roost;
Rarely does the forest burn while the bird survives.
Encountering a grand assembly of a thousand years,
The Emperor aligns his virtue with Heaven and Earth.
Relaxing the harsh severity of autumn frost,
Spreading the moistening grace of spring marshes.
Distinguishing great righteousness to clarify responsibilities,
I returned to my original attire at my private home.
The Emperor, considering my loyalty and sincerity,
Soon appointed me to a lowly rank.
To shepherd the weary people in Xī Xià,
I lead the old and the young to enter the Pass.
Kǒng Qiū sighed as he looked back leaving Lǔ;
Jì shed tears when passing through Pèi.
Oh, how one's old home is to be yearned for!
This hidden emotion pained even the sages and worthies.
How much more so for a commoner who loves his soil,
As I cast myself far away to Hào Jīng?
Like a dog or horse longing for its master,
I secretly harbor an attachment to the Imperial Court.
Looking back at Gǒng and Luò, I wipe my tears;
My thoughts are entwined around the ancestral graves.
And so I cross Píng Lè,
And pass by the street post-stations.
Feeding the horses at Gāo Mén,
I unhitch the carriage in Xī Zhōu.
Distant indeed was the virtue of the Jī clan,
Which originated from Gāo Xīn.
The refined Hòu Jì,
Was the first to give birth to our people.
Leading them along the western riverbanks,
Their influence flowed through Qí and Bīn.
Fortune flourished with Chāng and Fā,
Making the old state altogether new.
From the Battle of Mù Yě to this day,
They guarded gentleness more firmly as they strove for power.
Staying awake from night until dawn,
Worried that the protection of Heaven was not yet settled.
Though as stable as Tài Shān, it still felt precarious;
They offered sacrifices for eight hundred years with lasting blessings.
Seeing the pride and debauchery of fallen kings,
Who fled to Nán Cháo to cast away their lives.
Sitting on a pile of firewood waiting for it to burn,
They were just comparing their prosperity to the sun.
How contradictory are the judgments of men;
How vastly they differ from one another!
The center of the earth was surveyed in this city,
and King Chéng established the capital and constructed it.
Once the tripods were fixed at Jiárǔ,
the tortoise shell was bored to reveal the oracles.
King Píng, having lost the Way, moved here,
relying on the two states of Guó and Zhèng for protection.
Could the kings of that time be without flaws?
They relied on the former sages for enduring excellence.
Looking toward the two gates of Yǔběi,
I am moved by the kindness shown by Guó and Zhèng.
Punishing Zǐtuí for delighting in disaster,
especially for his perverse conduct west of the city gate.
Again, Dài was executed to stabilize King Xiāng,
promoting great compliance to dominate the era.
King Líng dammed the river to stop the fighting;
Jìn expounded on righteousness to offer advice.
Sighing from the reigns of Kings Jǐng and Dào down to Gài,
governance declined and grew increasingly decadent.
This caused the court to plot rebellion,
passing through two kings who usurped the throne.
After ten generations reaching King Nǎn,
the state collapsed and was divided into two.
Finally it was devoured by the tiger's mouth,
surrendering the sacred vessels of Kings Wén and Wǔ.
Bathing in the Xiào River and washing my cap strings,
I praise the beautiful name found here.
An infant died young at Xīn'ān;
a pit was dug by the roadside to bury him.
The pavilion bears the name Qiānqiū,
but the child did not reach seventy days.
Though I strive to emulate Yán Wú,
I am truly grieving in my parental heart.
Gazing at the mountains and rivers to cherish the past,
I sorrowfully hold the reins mid-journey.
The cruelty of the Xiàng clan and their unbridled violence—
burying the surrendered soldiers who were innocent.
Provoking the people of Qín to return to virtue,
it led to the arrival of the Liú house to bring relief.
Events cycle and revolve in retribution;
finally his clan was exterminated and he himself was slaughtered.
Passing through Miǎnchí and thinking long,
I stop my carriage and do not proceed.
Qín, the powerful state of tigers and wolves;
Zhào, the remnant of a weak and encroached state.
Crossing into danger for a high meeting,
relying on the world-renowned hero Lìn.
Ashamed of the solo playing of the eastern zither,
he held the western clay pot while facing the blade.
Shaming the hollow offer of ten cities,
he suddenly took the lead at Xiányáng.
Going out to assert authority beyond the River,
how fierce and surging was his spirit!
Coming in to humble himself before Lord Lián,
as if his four limbs had no bones.
He resided in the depth and greatness of wisdom and courage,
compared to the narrow-minded anger of the petty.
Though days have changed and years have passed,
there are no ranks to express this.
When Guāngwǔ was in exile,
he carried out royal punishment on the Chìméi.
Different from declaring the crimes to punish,
he initially drooped his wings at Huíxī.
He did not let a minor fault obscure his virtue,
finally flapping his wings and soaring high.
Establishing the great merit of assisting the mandate,
he revitalized the imperial discipline and renewed the bonds.
Climbing the steep slopes of Xiáobǎn,
I look up at the towering peaks.
Gāo recorded the tomb at Nánlíng;
Wén went against the custom at Běi’ē.
Jiǎn wept for Mèng, discerning the defeat;
Xiāng donned black mourning clothes and took up the halberd.
Not a single chariot wheel returned,
capturing the three commanders to cross the River.
Encountering a mediocre ruler's arrogance and obstinacy,
he almost executed the uncle in the court or market.
Rènhào had ample magnanimity;
alone, he took the blame upon himself.
Wisely not dismissing them after three defeats,
he finally overwhelmed Jìn to wipe away the shame.
How could a hollow name be established?
Truly, there was a reason he achieved hegemony.
Descending from Qūxiáo and pitying Guó,
they entrusted the allied state to the doomed Yú.
Greedy for bribes and selling out a neighbor,
before the winter sacrifice he was captured.
The Chuíjí gems returned to the old treasury;
the Qūchǎn horses were harnessed to Jìn carriages.
When virtue is not established, the people have no support;
the sacrifices to Zhòngyōng suddenly ceased.
I go to Ānyáng,
ascending the walls of Shǎn.
Walking to the mouth of Màndú,
resting at the ruins of Cáoyáng.
How beautiful and vast!
The antiquity of this land—
indeed, it is where Zhōu and Shào divided their realms,
where the Two Nán intersect.
"Línzhǐ" is as faithful as "Guān jū";
"Zōuyú" responds to "Quècháo".
Pitying the decline and chaos of the Hàn dynasty,
the court fled and was scattered.
Zhuó committed crimes reaching the heavens and caused a great cleansing;
he hijacked the palaces and shrines and moved the capital.
Causing the supreme majesty of the Ten-Thousand Chariots
to descend to distant thoughts on a forced journey.
Looking back to request a return to the East,
having received permission but fearing in his heart.
Pursuing the imperial carriage with sudden battles,
aiming whistling arrows at the jade carriage.
Grieving for the officials who served the king,
they all exerted their full strength unto death.
Bodies and heads were severed by sharp blades;
stray arrows pierced chests and armpits.
Some lifted their robes to leap onto the shore;
some rolled up their sleeves and jumped into the water.
Pitying the small size of the rafts and oars—
severed fingers were gathered by the handful in the boat.
Ascending Qǔwò and feeling melancholy,
lamenting the signs of chaos and the displacement of the elder brother.
The branches grew large and the trunk split;
the capital rivaled the state, and disaster ensued.
Zāng and Zhá soared with high integrity,
abandoning Cáo and Wú to fulfill their virtue.
How shameless were Zhuāng and Wǔ,
only opening for profit and closing to righteousness!
Stepping onto the heavy defenses of Hángǔ Pass,
I observe the natural barrier like a sash and belt.
Tracing the courage and cowardice of the feudal lords,
I calculate the advantages and disadvantages of the Yíng clan.
Some opened the pass to invite the enemy;
they vied to flee and hide in a scramble.
Some kept the gates shut and did not open them,
not daring to look at the soldiers outside the mountains.
Like tethered chickens unable to roost,
small states combined to become large.
Is it the security or danger of the terrain?
Truly, it is the success or failure of human affairs!
After six generations, the Hàn expanded the capital territory,
establishing Hóngnóng and moving the pass afar.
Tired of the spaciousness of the Purple Palace,
he delighted in incognito travels and wandering.
He was an arrogant guest at Bǎigǔ;
the wife saw his appearance and offered a meal.
Who would have thought an ordinary woman could be so magnanimous?
Why was her husband such a foolish official?
When wise kings of old went on inspection tours,
they certainly cleared the way before proceeding.
Fearing the bit or the linchpin might fail,
they strictly regulated the followers with punishments and rewards.
Like the white dragon in the guise of a fish,
caught in the tight net of Yùqiě.
Treating the Emperor's weight lighter than the world—
how can such a trend be allowed to grow?
Lamenting at the Lì Park in Hú District,
truly he suffered from the witchcraft accusations of that era.
Investigating hidden matters that were hard to clarify,
they were entrusted to the slanderous villain, the Zhào captive.
Inflicting public execution on the heir apparent,
severing his own flesh and blood without regard.
Building the Terrace of Thinking-of-Return in sorrow;
but what use is longing and gazing in vain?
I have already passed through this entire section,
and I continue by lingering here.
Inquiring about the old forest where the oxen were rested,
I am moved by the name given to the Peach Garden.
Departing from Wénxiāng and spurring the horse,
I go up toward Huángxiàng to cross the Tóng River.
Gazing at the shaded cliffs of Mount Huà,
I see the traces of the Great Palm.
Remembering the messenger of the River returning the jade ring,
announcing the time of death to Zǔlóng.
I do not speak of ghosts to seek the strange;
I heard this from Master Kǒng.
Resenting the great villains Hán and Mǎ,
who blocked the passes and valleys to start a rebellion.
Wèiwǔ blazed like a thunderclap,
carrying out a righteous declaration to punish the rebels.
Though they were many, what use was it?
Victory was thus decided by the ancestral temple calculations.
Striking the drumsticks and raising the dust,
they suddenly collapsed like tiles and melted like ice.
Chāo then fled and escaped to the Dí people,
and the armored soldiers were turned into a mound of corpses.
Tired of the narrowness of the confined roads,
the wheels tilted and jolted up and down.
Only upon treading the outskirts of Qín did it first open up,
wide and spacious, grand and magnificent.
A thousand miles of yellow soil,
fertile fields as far as the eye can see.
Flowers and fruits bloom in profusion,
mulberry and hemp grow smooth and long.
It is bordered obliquely by Bāoxié,
and to the right by the Qiān and Lǒng regions.
Bǎojī crows in the front,
Gānquán gushes in the rear.
Facing Zhōngnán in the front and backed by Yúnyáng,
it straddles the plains and connects to Bōzhǒng.
Jiǔzōng is towering and jagged,
Tàiyī is lofty and grand.
It exhales the swirling clear breeze,
and takes in the dense returning clouds.
To the south are the dark Bà and the white Chǎn rivers,
the hot springs and the warm valleys.
To the north are the clear Wèi and the turbid Jīng rivers,
and the winding shores of Lánchí.
The waters are channeled into the Zhèng and Bái canals,
transporting grain from the Huái and the sea.
In the lush forests are the bamboos of Hù,
and the mountains yield the jade of Lántián.
Bān described its treasures of land and sea,
Zhāng recounted the secluded regions of the divine land.
This is why the guest from the west spoke to the host from the east,
and why Ānchǔ listened to Píngxū;
how can it not be so?
The sturdy pine is revealed in the cold of the year,
the loyal minister is seen when the state is in danger.
Entering the capital of Zhèng and clapping hands in agreement,
one honors the loyal standards of Huányǒu.
He exhausted his strength for a dim-witted lord,
rushing into misery without wavering.
His family held the office of Sītú for generations,
replacing their black robes only when they were worn out.
Treading upon the land invaded by the Quǎnróng,
one detests the deceptive delusions of King Yōu.
He raised false beacon fires to discourage the masses,
and indulged the favored Bàosì to give rein to wickedness.
The army was defeated by the waters,
and he himself died north of Mount Lí.
The majestic Zōngzhōu
was extinguished and became a fallen state.
Then there was one who succeeded this—
how strange indeed
was the conduct of Qín Shǐhuáng as a ruler!
He exhausted the empire for a lavish burial,
unheard of since the dawn of creation.
The craftsmen labored without a plan for themselves,
as he had them buried alive to repay their diligence.
Externally, it suffered the calamity of Xīchǔ,
and internally, it was burned by the shepherd boy.
As the saying goes:
"If one acts without propriety,
it will surely come back to oneself."
Is this not the proof of that?
Heaven and Earth endure through kinship,
and the gentleman carries all things with profound virtue.
Observe the rise of Hàn Gāozǔ;
he was not merely intelligent, divine, and martial,
or magnanimous and open-minded.
He was truly careful until the end and mindful of the old,
sincere, earnest, and deeply loving.
His bounty reached everywhere,
and his grace left none untouched.
He did not neglect even the farthest lands,
how much more so for his neighbors?
Or for his ministers?
At that time,
he modeled and copied the old town of Fēng,
and built a new town.
The old shrines were relocated,
and the elms of Fényú were replanted.
The streets and alleys were identical,
and the courtyards and halls followed the same pattern.
Chickens and dogs were mixed and released together,
yet each recognized its own home and vied to enter.
Xiàng Yǔ harbored anger at Hóngmén,
while the Lord of Pèi came to him in submission.
Fàn Zēng plotted harm but was not permitted,
secretly handing a sword to command Xiàng Zhuāng.
He brandished the naked blade in a dance,
as perilous as a winter leaf awaiting the frost.
Treading on the tiger's tail but not being bitten,
he truly owed his life to Zǐfáng.
Fàn Kuài resisted with indignation and a goblet of wine,
chewing a pork shoulder to rouse his spirit.
Suddenly the snake transformed and the dragon soared,
the hero took Bàshàng and rose high.
Zēng shifted his anger and struck across,
what harm was there in shattering the jade cups?
Zǐyīng was bound with a cord at Zhǐtú,
surrendering with a plain chariot and bared torso.
Shū drank a farewell toast at the eastern capital,
fearing the peak of high position.
The golden ramparts were dense with ten thousand battlements,
the steep walls as straight as a plumb line.
Arriving at the Yángqiáo bridge for watering horses,
and treading upon the pure threshold of Xuānpíng.
Within the capital, people were crowded together,
households by the thousands and millions.
Men and women of the Central Plains and the frontiers,
were packed closely side by side.
Displaying the initial ceremonies of the famous capital,
he went to the new hall to assume his duties.
Encouraging the weary and dull to attend court,
and exhorting them to strengthen themselves without ceasing.
Thereupon, the mid-autumn month passed,
and in the remaining days of leisure,
he inspected the agricultural work,
and traveled around the dwellings.
The streets and alleys were desolate,
the town's residences scattered and abandoned.
The barracks, offices, and bureaus,
the markets, shops, and storehouses,
those huddled in the corners of the city,
were not one in a hundred.
The so-called Shàngguān and Xiūchéng,
Huángjí and Xuānmíng,
Jiànyáng and Chāngyīn,
Běihuàn and Nánpíng,
were all leveled and washed away,
their locations gone, leaving only their names.
Then he ascended the steps of Chánglè,
and went up to Wèiyāng.
Boating on Tàiyè,
and crossing over to Jiànzhāng.
Winding through Sàsuō and visiting Dàidàng,
passing over Yìyì and crossing Chéngguāng.
Wandering through the Guì Palace,
and feeling melancholy at Bàiliáng.
The Reeve's Pheasant calls at the terrace pond,
and foxes and rabbits burrow beside the halls.
How the millet sprouts grow so lush,
while my thoughts are so vast and mournful!
The great bell lies fallen in the ruined temple,
its wind-borne sound gone, no longer hanging.
The forbidden palace is overgrown with thick grass,
and the Golden Statues have been moved to the Bà River.
Cherishing the ministers like Xiāo, Cáo, Wèi, and Bǐng,
and the generals like Xīn, Lǐ, Wèi, and Huò.
As an envoy, there was Sū Shǔguó;
to shake the distant lands, there was Zhāng Bówàng.
Teachings were spread and the social order was arranged,
armies were raised and the Imperial majesty flourished.
Faced with danger, their wisdom and courage were roused,
sacrificing their lives, their high integrity shone bright.
And the loyalty and filial piety of the Marquis of Tuó was pure and deep,
while Lù Jiǎ was leisurely and joyful.
The writings of Chángqīng and Yuānyún,
and the histories of Zǐcháng and Zhèngjùn.
Zhào, Zhāng, and the three Wángs governed the capital,
and Dìngguó and Shìzhī heard legal cases.
The uprightness of Jì Zhǎngrú,
and Zhèng Dāngshí who promoted worthy men.
Zhōng Tóng, the brilliant youth from Shāndōng,
and Jiǎ, the talented son of Luòyáng.
Flying kingfisher tassels,
and trailing tinkling jades,
those who entered and exited the forbidden gates were many indeed.
Some had disheveled hair and buttoned their robes on the left,
rising swiftly from the mud.
Some were composed and conformed to expectations,
looking at the surface to know the interior.
Some achieved illustrious deeds but suffered execution in their time,
some had great talent but held no noble office.
All of them spread a clear breeze of superior merit,
leaving behind a fine reputation that never ends.
Thinking of the lingering sound of their jade pendants,
it is as if the clinking is still in my ears.
When the likes of Wáng Yīn, Fèng, Gòng, and Xiǎn held power,
their influence scorched the four directions,
shaking and illuminating the capital and the countryside.
Yet on the day they died,
they could not even be ranked among the followers of those ten-odd gentlemen.
Talent is indeed hard to find,
is it not so?
Gazing at Jiàntái and choking with emotion,
having beheaded the great villain but with anger still remaining.
Bowing to Zhū Bùyí at the northern gate-tower,
saluting the carriage of Chūlǐ at the armory.
The wine pools served as a warning for Shāng Xīn,
yet they followed the overturned cart without waking.
Qǔyáng usurped authority at Báihǔ,
wallowing in luxury and excess without limit.
Life has a beginning and must have an end;
who can achieve eternal life and long sight?
Where is the grand strategy of Wǔ?
Recently deluded by Wénchéng and drowning in Wǔlì.
Rivaling creation with his constructions,
exhausting the secrets of mountains and seas.
Spirits seemed to soar to the divine islands,
while whales in the waves lost their water.
Bones and scales parched on the shifting sands,
as a pair of bright moons fell together.
Raising the Immortal's Palm to receive the dew,
it reaches up to the Cloudy River.
How hard was it to obtain the Qióng betel?
It was only to indulge his every desire.
Indulging in leisurely games of wrestling,
adorning the Jiǎ and Yǐ with pearls and kingfisher feathers.
Bearing to see the common people reduced by half,
he carved empty beauty upon the Eastern Peak.
Overcome by long-harbored thoughts and distant memories,
like a cycle with nothing bestowed.
Comparing the brilliance of the morning court,
followed by the delicate grace of the rear palace.
The brave loyalty of the one who faced the bear,
the deep wisdom of the one who declined the carriage.
Wèi's dark hair shone like a mirror,
Zhào's light body was slender and beautiful.
All were well-established and their fame spread,
but extreme favor led to lavish disaster.
Passing Biàn Gate and turning to the right,
I reach the boundary of my territory.
Passing Xìliǔ and grasping the sword,
I delight in Xiàowén's appointment of the general.
Zhōu accepted the mandate and forgot his own life,
manifesting the resolute courage of military governance.
Blocking the imperial canopy at the camp gate,
he halted the horses of the sovereign's carriage.
Solemnly facing the majesty of Heaven,
he followed military etiquette with a long bow.
Scorning the child's play at Jí and Bà,
I honor the haughty dignity of the Marquis of Tiáo.
Searching for where Dùyóu is,
it is said to be the former name of Xiàolǐ.
Sadly I halt the carriage and linger,
mourning the Marquis of Wǔ'ān with rising grief.
He vied to attack Zhào to serve the state,
determining victory and defeat in temple calculations.
Stubborn words were offered but not accepted,
instead, resentment was pushed back and blame assigned.
Not even ten miles on the road to exile,
soon a sword was granted for him to slit his throat.
Alas! When the lord is dark and ministers are jealous,
where does disaster not arise?
Looking at the ruins of Qín at Wèichéng,
the gate-towers are distant and buried.
Seeking the remaining foundations of the halls,
seeing only the faint, undulating outlines.
Recalling the Zhào envoy clutching the jade,
staring at the pillar with defiant anger.
The map of Yàn ended and Jīng's dagger appeared;
with a torn sleeve, he pulled himself away.
The sound of the lute was stern and high-spirited;
he aimed the lead-filled lute but missed, having lost his kneecaps.
To hold the Heavenly position in such a manner—
how distressed and pitiable it was!
Selecting good men to assist himself,
he called Sī loyal and Shāng Yǎng virtuous.
Entrusting harsh laws to the disposal of ashes,
he exiled Fúsū to the northern frontier.
The forest of scholars was filled into pits,
the Poetry and History were burned to smoke.
The state was destroyed and the lineage cut;
his own body was torn by chariots, following the precedent.
How could Shāng’s laws provide a place to stay?
How could the yellow dog ever be led again?
Wild rushes were changed into dried meat;
the deer in the park were turned into horses.
Usurping the power of Heaven through slander,
they gagged the mouths of the masses while sitting in power.
With the blade at his neck, he looked back and asked:
"Why did you not tell me sooner?"
He wished to be a commoner, but who would listen?
Only his request for death was granted.
Brave was the decisiveness of Zǐyīng,
who dared to punish the traitor to alleviate the disaster.
The situation collapsed like earth and could not be restored;
he became a surrendered king by the side of the road.
Xiāo collected the maps to aid Liú,
calculating the terrain and the number of people.
Yǔ did not take what Heaven offered,
but wearing a monkey's cap, he set the fires.
This penetrates the three lights and pierces the nine springs;
it is not enough to illustrate the difference between them.
Moved by the gathered wells in the marketplace,
I sigh at the former site of Hán's corpse.
Subordinates wailed while guarding the gate;
people offered their lives to ransom him.
It was not that life was easily thrown away,
but that his kindness and love were truly profound.
Slandering Wàngzhī to seek uprightness
is something my heart truly loathes.
Thinking of that person's political methods,
they were truly a fine tool for managing the times.
If laws were only clarified to vent personal grudges,
and talent was not cherished to accomplish tasks,
then great character and noble dignity
were not what I expected from Tutor Xiāo.
Reaching Chángshān with a heart full of emotion,
I admire the heroic lord with the dragon's face.
His chest was wide and open,
all good things gathered and were surely uplifted.
His majesty reached the celestial regions while he lived,
but his grave was dug up after he died, and none could stop it.
Facing the pit and clapping many times,
I walk by the ruined walls and linger long.
Passing Ānlíng without a word of criticism,
for surely the reputation for kindness is silent.
Mourning the righteousness of Yuán Sī,
who fell to the sword of Liáng in the eastern suburbs.
Questioning Emperor Jǐng at Yángqiū:
Why believe slanders and act with pride and mockery?
Killing the heir of Wú at the game board,
he erupted in anger over a single match of Bo.
This led to the rebellion of the Seven States,
and he turned to help the rebels by executing Cuò.
I regret he listened wrongly without investigation;
this discouraged the good and encouraged the evil.
Criticizing Emperor Xiàoyuán at the Wèi tomb,
I hold the eunuch official responsible to clarify the blame.
Praising the good deeds of that lord,
who abolished the funerary park to promote frugality.
Passing Yán Gate and demanding results,
what crime did the loyal commit to be slaughtered?
Wáng Zhāng, a pillar of the state, was framed,
and made to die in prison without a trial.
Accustomed to the cruelty of the favored concubines,
they cut off the pregnancy of the imperial line.
The treachery of the Zhāng uncles began to grow,
leaving the Han lineage to be overturned.
Criticizing Emperor Āi at the Yì territory,
for usurping the heavenly rank at Gāo’ān.
Desiring to model after Yáo but bringing shame,
which will remain forever and never be erased.
Looking down at the solitary grave of Kāngyuán,
mourning the exclusive purity of Empress Píng.
Suffering from her father's usurpation and rebellion,
she bore the shame of Han without it being cleansed.
Stirring her righteous sincerity to resolve her life,
she rushed into the red flames to manifest her virtue.
Thrown into the palace fire and scorched to ruin,
vanishing together with the flying ashes.
Galloping across Héng Bridge and turning the carriage,
I pass the southern border of the ruined city.
Gates of lodestone and beams of magnolia,
constructing the eccentric wonders of Āfáng.
Opening Nánshān to mark the gates,
clearing Fánchuān to make a lake.
Could even ghosts or servants do this?
Much less the work of human power.
While the craftsmen's carving had not yet ceased,
the righteous armies were already galloping in confusion.
The ancestral temples were polluted and became ponds;
how could this building alone fall to ruin?
Passing the Nine Temples of the false Xīn,
they boasted of being descendants of Yú and ancestors of Huáng.
Driving the cries of "Alas!" as an evil omen,
they sought out flatterers to appoint as officials.
Reciting the Six Arts to disguise their treachery,
they burned the Poetry and History while facing the wall.
Their hearts did not follow virtue or righteousness;
though their methods differed, their destruction was the same.
We honor Emperor Xiào Xuān at Lèyóu,
who restored the declining lineage to a middle revival.
Unable to serve his mother in respectful nurturance,
he lavished every honor upon her tomb park.
The tomb site is only Fèngmíng,
and the town is named Qiānrén.
Inquiring of the elders,
they say it was built by Emperor Xún.
Grieving for his mother’s untimely death,
he let loose music to entertain her spirit.
Though it did not follow the old canons,
one may observe his faults and know his benevolence.
Leaning on the high ridge's sunny slope,
he observed the rise and fall of the rivers and lands.
Opening his robe at the Qīngshǔ Pavilion,
casting his gaze upon the Wǔzuò Palace.
Canals intersect to draw the grain transport,
surging rapids generate the wind,
and there is the Kūnmíng Lake in their midst.
That lake is vast and overflowing,
deep and boundless,
as immense as the Héhàn.
The sun and moon, the beauties of heaven,
emerge and enter from east to west,
appearing like Tānggǔ at dawn,
and resembling Yúyuān at dusk.
Formerly, the famous structure of Yùzhāng
rose uniquely from the dark flow.
It mirrored the auspicious stars in the sky,
and stood between the Ox and the Weaver stars.
It was intended to last ten thousand years without tilting,
yet suddenly it collapsed after twelve decades.
Where once a layered tower of a hundred fathoms rose,
now only a few cubits of remaining foundations exist.
Egrets rise in flight,
wild ducks leap and geese land.
Rising and falling with the clouds,
bobbing peacefully with the waves.
Splashing in the startled waves,
pecking at water chestnuts and gorgon nuts.
Splendid lotuses bloom in the clear pond,
green vegetation flourishes on the emerald ripples.
When this lake was first excavated,
it was to practice naval warfare against the remote regions.
The ambition was to diligently reach afar with military might,
truly not seeking future blessings.
Yet vegetables and fruits are gathered,
and aquatic products are varied,
thus providing for the plains and highlands.
In this imperial era, the land is assessed according to its nature,
so what was destroyed has been restored.
All the various officials,
having become wealthy, are now taught.
They lead the poor and the lazy,
together readying the oars and rudders.
Gathering nets and calculating the catch,
drawing the strings to show their success.
Widowers find households,
and the sorrowful find joy.
One merely observes the beating of oars and turning of wheels,
the casting of hooks and throwing of nets,
bait dangling as they go in and out,
spears raised as they come and go.
Fine lines connect the white fish,
sounding poles emit sharp noises.
Strung through the gills and dragging the tails,
pulling them in threes and dragging them in twos.
Then, the giant blue fish is released from the great net,
and the red carp is freed from the sticky trap.
Splendid bream leap with scales,
white dace raise their fins.
The cooks slice them into fine threads,
the phoenix-decorated knives seem to fly.
Following the blade, they fall onto the trays,
rustling and fluttering like falling rain.
The fresh red meat is piled high,
guests and travelers stand in awe, waiting to be served.
Once they have eaten their fill,
they are tranquil and without desire.
Turning the belly of a small-minded man
into the concerns of a gentleman.
Then, one straightens the whip and brushes the mat,
flicks the cap and shakes the clothes.
Lingering about Fèng and Hào,
as if thirsty and hungry for virtue.
The heart looks up with diligence and respect,
not adding reverence, yet naturally pious.
How would one dare to dream of the Three Sages,
but secretly hope for one of the Ten Ministers.
Building of the Spiritual Tower began,
and it was completed in no time.
Only Fèng and Hào
remain the capital of the house.
The common people came like children,
and the gods bestowed good fortune.
Accumulating virtue to extend the mandate,
none can compare to this.
Forever contemplating this land,
who truly knows it?
It can be heard in brief,
but it is hard to reach its ultimate depth.
A son lending a hoe to his father
was a lesson of the Qín laws, showing resentment in his countenance.
Plowing while yielding the borders of the fields
was the influence of the Jī family, now overgrown with thorns.
Sū and Zhāng took pleasure in galloping with deceit,
while the people of Yú and Ruì felt ashamed and ended their disputes.
From this we can see,
the land has no permanent customs,
but education has a fixed pattern.
The transformation of those below by those above
is like the molding of clay.
People from five directions gather together,
and customs become jumbled.
Lazy farmers love profit,
and do not work from dawn to dusk.
Being close to the Xiǎnyǔn,
war horses appear in the suburbs.
But those who govern must be decisive;
it truly depends on holding the knife.
The rise and fall of the people
follows the prosperity and decline of governance.
If one relies on trust, then everyone acts with sincerity;
if there is no desire, people will not steal even if rewarded.
Although wisdom cannot manage it,
and brightness cannot discern it;
trust in this heart,
and one may avoid transgressions.
As for rituals and music,
wait for the sages of the future.
Climbing this tower to look out in four directions,
I use this leisure day to dispel my sorrow.
Observing the location of this structure,
it is truly grand and without peer.
Flanked by the clear Zhāng River’s broad banks,
leaning on the long marshes of the winding Jǔ.
Behind it lie the vast and fertile plains,
before it is the rich flow of the marshes.
To the north it reaches Táo Mù,
to the west it connects to Zhāo Qiū.
Flowers and fruits cover the wilderness,
grains and millet fill the fields.
Though it is truly beautiful, it is not my land;
how could it be enough to stay for a while?
Having encountered turmoil and moved away,
more than a decade has passed until now.
My heart is full of longing as I think of returning;
who can bear such heavy sorrow?
Leaning on the railing to look into the distance,
I open my robe to the north wind.
The plains are vast as far as the eye can see,
obscured by the high peaks of Jīng Shān.
The road is winding and long,
the river is vast and deep.
Grieving that my old home is blocked and separated,
tears fall uncontrollably.
Formerly, when Nífù was in Chén,
he sighed with the sound of "Shall we return?"
Zhōng Yí was imprisoned yet played Chǔ music;
Zhuāng Xì was successful yet sang Yuè songs.
Human nature is the same in cherishing one's land;
how can success or failure change the heart?
I see the sun and moon passing by,
waiting for the Yellow River to run clear, which has no end.
Hoping for the King's Way to become smooth once more,
to gallop with my strength upon the high road.
Fearing to hang uselessly like a bitter gourd,
fearing to be a clean well from which no one drinks.
Walking aimlessly and pacing about,
the bright sun suddenly begins to hide.
The whistling wind rises from all sides,
the sky is gloomy and colorless.
Beasts look around wildly for their herds,
birds cry to one another and take flight.
The wilderness is silent and without people,
the traveler walks without rest.
My heart is pained and moved,
my mind is sorrowful and distressed.
Following the steps as I descend,
indignation fills my chest.
