At midnight I still cannot sleep,
lingering in disappointment, tossing and turning.
Mount Tiāntái
is the divine and elegant peak among mountains.
Crossing the sea, there are Fāngzhàng and Pénglái;
traveling by land, there are Sìmíng and Tiāntái.
Both are where mysterious sages wander and transform,
and where spiritual immortals make their dwellings.
As for its lofty and extreme form,
and the beauty of its auspicious omens,
it exhausts the magnificent riches of mountains and seas
and reaches the limit of the splendor of gods and men.
The reason it is not listed among the Wǔyuè
and is omitted from the standard classics,
is it not because its location is dark and profound,
and its paths are secluded and remote?
Sometimes its reflection hangs in the deep seas;
sometimes its peaks are hidden among a thousand ridges.
One first passes through the paths of demons
and finally treads upon uninhabited realms.
Rarely can the world's people climb it,
and kings have no means to offer sacrifices.
Thus its stories are absent from common chapters,
and its name is recorded in extraordinary chronicles.
Yet the emergence of its depictions,
how could it be in vain?
Were it not for those who leave the world to contemplate the Way,
abstaining from grains and eating fungus,
how could they lightly ascend and dwell there?
Were it not for those who far-reachingly send their spirits to seek the profound,
and who possess sincere faith and communicate with the divine,
how would they be willing to imagine and preserve it from afar?
Therefore, I let my spirit gallop and my thoughts move;
chanting by day and rising by night,
in the brief moment of a glance,
it is as if I have already ascended it twice.
Now I loosen my silk tassels
and forever entrust myself to these ridges.
Unable to bear the intensity of my chanting and contemplation,
I briefly exert my literary skills to express my feelings.
The Tàixū is vast and without obstruction;
it moves with the subtle existence of nature.
It flows to become rivers and streams,
and gathers to become mountains and hills.
Alas, the extraordinary height of Mount Tiāntái
is indeed supported by divine spirits.
It shades the Niú constellation to illuminate its peaks
and rests in spiritual Yuè to establish its base.
Its roots spread to Huá and Dài,
and its straight point is higher than Jiǔyí.
It should match Heaven in the Táng records
and equal the lofty heights in the Zhōu poems.
Distant is that remote region,
secluded, deep, and elegant.
Those of narrow wisdom hold to their views and do not go;
those who go find the roads cut off and cannot understand.
Mocking the summer insect's doubt of ice,
I prepare my light wings and think of soaring.
Principle has nothing hidden that is not revealed,
and it opens two wonders to show the signs.
Chìchéng's clouds rise to establish a beacon;
the Waterfall's flying flow marks the boundary of the path.
Having seen the spiritual evidence, I proceed;
suddenly, I am about to set out.
Following the winged men of Dānqiū,
I seek the blessed court of immortality.
If the ridges of Tiāntái can be climbed,
what need is there to envy Céngchéng?
Releasing the common attachments of the worldly realm,
I give vent to transcendent and high feelings.
Clad in thick garments of fur and hemp,
I shake the ringing bells of my golden staff.
Parting the tangled wild thickets,
I ascend the towering and jagged cliffs.
Crossing Yóuxī, I advance directly;
descending into Wǔjiè, I travel swiftly.
Striding over the vaulted hanging steps,
I overlook the ten-thousand-fathom dark abyss.
Treading upon the slippery stones of moss,
I grasp the sheer green screens of the walls.
Grasping the long vines of the winding trees,
I hold the flying stems of the creepers.
Though once risking the danger of the hall's eaves,
I shall forever abide in long life.
One must match sincerity with the dark and obscure,
then treading over repeated dangers becomes even flatter.
Having overcome the ascent of the nine bends,
the road becomes level and long.
I let my heart and eyes be vast and clear,
and allow my slow steps to be leisurely.
Resting on the lush and delicate grass,
I am shaded by the tall and lofty pines.
I see the soaring Luan birds in their flight,
and hear the harmonious cries of the Phoenixes.
Passing through Língxī, I wash once,
clearing the vexing thoughts from my heart.
Washing away the remaining dust in the swirling current,
I dispel the drifting mists of the Five Obscurations.
I trace the peerless tracks of Xī and Nóng,
and follow the mysterious footprints of the Two Elders.
Ascending and descending for several nights,
I finally reach Xiāndū.
Twin gates tower like clouds to flank the road,
and Jasper Terraces hang in the middle of the sky.
Vermilion gates are exquisite among the trees;
Jade halls are shaded in the high corners.
Red clouds shimmer to wing the windows;
the bright sun shines brilliantly through the lattice.
Eight cinnamon trees stand tall against the frost;
the five-colored fungus holds its beauty, blooming in the morning.
A gentle wind lingers with fragrance in the sunny forest;
sweet springs bubble and flow in the shaded channels.
The Jiànmù tree loses its shadow at a thousand fathoms;
the Qí trees are brilliant with hanging pearls.
Wáng Qiáo controls his crane to soar to heaven;
Yìngzhēn fly with their staffs to tread upon the void.
Galloping through spiritual transformations in an instant,
they suddenly emerge from being and enter non-being.
Thus, after the tour is complete,
the body is quiet and the mind is at leisure.
The harmful horses have been removed,
and worldly affairs are all discarded.
The blade is applied where it is empty;
the eye sees no whole ox.
Concentrating thought in the secluded cavern,
I chant clearly by the long river.
Then Xīhé is at high noon,
and the drifting mists are high and clear.
Dharma drums resonate with a clear sound,
and various incenses are fragrant, raising smoke.
I pay homage to Tiānzōng,
and there assemble the immortals.
I drink the cream of mysterious jade
and rinse with the spring of the Huáchí pool.
I am dispersed by the discourse beyond images,
and comforted by the chapter on non-birth.
I realize that discarding being is not exhaustive,
and perceive that wading into non-being has gaps.
Merging form and void to unite their traces,
suddenly through being, I attain the mysterious.
I explain how the two names come from the same source,
and dissolve the one non-being into the three banners.
I indulge in the joy of speech all day long,
which is equal to the silence of not speaking.
Merging the ten thousand phenomena into a dark vision,
I am one with nature in the same body.
Spreading across the level plains,
to the south it gallops toward Cāngwú and the Zhànghǎi,
and to the north it runs toward the Zǐsài and Yànmén.
It is towed by the transport canals
and pivoted by Kūngāng.
In the depths of repeated rivers and multiple passes,
it is a crossroads of four meetings and five reaches.
In the past, during its full prosperity,
chariot hubs were hooked together,
and people rode shoulder to shoulder.
Households covered the earth,
and songs and flutes boiled in the sky.
They multiplied wealth in the salt fields
and carved out profit from the copper mountains.
Their talent and strength were heroic and rich,
and their soldiers and horses were fine and elegant.
Thus they could surpass the Qín laws
and exceed the Zhōu orders.
They raised high walls,
hollowed out deep moats,
and planned for a long age to celebrate their mandate.
Therefore, the labor of building walls and battlements was abundant,
and the toil of well-frames and beacon towers was diligent.
Their heights matched the Wǔyuè,
and their breadth was as wide as the Sānfèn.
Looming like a severed cliff,
they stood tall like long clouds.
They fashioned magnets to resist rams
and smeared red earth to fly with patterns.
Observing the solid protection of the foundations and gates,
they expected one king for ten thousand generations.
Passing through three eras for over five hundred years,
it was finally split like a melon and divided like beans!
Marsh mallows lean against the well;
wild vines entangle the path.
The altars are filled with snakes and lizards;
the stairs are fought over by deer and martens.
Wood spirits and mountain ghosts,
field rats and city foxes,
howl in the wind and whistle in the rain,
appearing at dusk and rushing in the morning.
Hungry hawks sharpen their beaks;
cold owls frighten their chicks.
Lurking beasts and hidden tigers
suck blood and feast on flesh.
Fallen hazel trees block the road,
the towering ancient paths.
White poplars shed leaves early,
the grasses of the frontier wither first.
Severe is the frosty air,
whistling is the wind's might.
A solitary tumbleweed shakes itself,
startled sand starts to fly.
Overgrown weeds stretch vast and boundless,
dense thickets cluster together.
Connected moats are already leveled,
steep corners have already collapsed.
Looking straight for a thousand lǐ,
one sees only rising yellow dust.
Deep in thought, listening in silence,
the heart is grieved and broken.
As for the foundations of the painted doors and patterned curtains,
the halls of song and pavilions of dance.
The jade-like pools and emerald trees,
the lodges for hunting woods and fishing shores.
The sounds of Wú, Cài, Qí, and Qín,
the entertainments of fish-dragons and bird-horses.
All fragrance has dissipated and embers have died out,
the light has sunk and the echoes have ceased.
Exquisite maidens of the Dōngdū,
beautiful ladies of the Nánguó.
With hearts of orchid and bodies of fine silk,
jade-like faces and crimson lips.
All have their souls buried beneath dark stones,
and commit their bones to the deep dust.
How could they recall the joy of sharing the same carriage,
or the hardships of the detached palaces?
What of the Way of Heaven?
Those who swallow their resentment are many!
I draw my qín and command a tune,
to make a song of Wúchéng.
The song says:
The frontier wind is sharp and the city wall is cold,
the well-paths are obliterated and the hill-mounds are ruined.
Through a thousand ages and ten thousand generations,
all come to an end; what more is there to say!
The Lǔ Língguāng Diàn was built by Gōng Wáng Yú, the son of Chéng Jī of Jǐng Dì.
Initially, when Gōng Wáng first established his capital in the lower state,
he loved to build palaces and chambers,
so he constructed it upon the foundations and sites of Lǔ Xǐ Gōng.
Encountering the decline of the Hàn dynasty,
when bandits and rebels rushed forth,
from the Wèiyāng and Jiànzhāng palaces of the Xījīng,
all were seen to be destroyed and ruined,
yet the Língguāng alone remained towering.
I suspect, was it not that the spirits leaned upon and supported it to preserve the House of Hàn?
Thus its proportions and systems
correspond above to the constellations,
which is also why it has long remained secure.
I, a traveler from the southern borders,
went to observe the arts in Lǔ,
and seeing this, I was struck with awe.
Saying: Alas!
The inspiration of poets
arises from being moved by things.
Therefore Xī Sī praised Xǐ Gōng,
singing of his grand chambers,
so that his achievements were preserved in words,
and his virtuous reputation was clarified in sound.
Things are made manifest through rhapsodies,
events are proclaimed through praises;
without rhapsodies or praises,
how could they be transmitted?
Thereupon I composed this rhapsody:
Looking back to the ancient Emperors of Hàn,
the ancestors were profound, wise, reverent, and enlightened.
They inherited the pure brightness of the Five Dynasties,
and continued the fiery essence of Yí Táng.
Bearing the Heavenly Way with great prosperity,
they expanded the universe and established the capital.
Spreading the Imperial Ultimate to start the enterprise,
they harmonized with the Divine Way for great peace.
Thereupon the common people were illustrious,
and the nine branches of the clan were in cordial order.
Then they commanded the filial grandson,
to be enfeoffed as a lord in Lǔ.
Bestowing the jièguī as a token of authority,
he resided in the dependency and opened the territory.
Then he built the secret hall of Língguāng,
to match Zǐwēi and serve as its support.
It receives the Míngtáng at Shǎoyáng,
and shines illustriously in the field of the Kuí constellation.
Observing the form of that Língguāng,
it is craggy and towering,
lofty and majestic.
Ah! How fearsome and startling it is to people.
Soaring high and unconventional,
abundant, beautiful, vast, and spacious,
it is a cavernous maze without end.
Distant and rare in the world, it stands out uniquely,
indeed, it is wondrous, strange, and grandly diverse.
It stands tall like a mountain, twisting and dense,
rising abruptly into the blue clouds.
Thickly massed and towering high,
layered and pleated like dragon scales.
Bright and sparkling with brilliant luster,
dazzling and radiant, it illuminates the earth.
Its shape is like the clanging of piled stones,
and also seems like the majestic spirit of the Emperor's dwelling.
High walls connect like ridges and follow like mountain ranges,
cinnabar gates are lofty and stand in pairs.
The high gates are modeled after Chānghé,
wide enough for two carriages to enter side by side.
Thereupon one ascends the grand stairs,
to reach its hall.
Looking up and down, glancing around,
wandering to the east and west.
The decorations of red colors—
for what purpose are they?
Vast and gleaming,
flowing and brilliant.
White walls shine brightly like moonlight,
red pillars glow intensely like flashing lightning.
Like variegated clouds or mist,
appearing now dark, now bright.
Shimmering and flickering in confusion,
splendid and magnificent.
The hidden depths of the cool summer chambers are in the center,
deep, vast, and looming.
Grand and bright in their spaciousness,
the wind whistles through, cold and clear.
Moving droplets make a sound,
like the rumble of thunder responding in alarm.
The ears ring so that one loses hearing,
the eyes stare so that one loses focus.
Piles of dense stones and lánggān,
arranged with jade pendants and bi-jades.
Then pushing open the golden doors and entering from the north,
the mist is thick and dim.
The winding rooms are graceful and secluded,
the inner chambers are deep and mysterious.
In the west wing, one lingers in leisurely repose;
the eastern corridor is layered, deep, and occult.
Towering and dark, as if blurred,
shadowy and obscured in a vast expanse.
The soul is awestruck and startled,
the heart trembles and feels palpitation.
Then, examining its beams and roof in detail,
observing its structure.
The proportions correspond to Heaven,
modeled above on the Zīzōu constellation.
Extraordinary forms rise like clouds,
craggy and separated yet intertwined.
Three bays and four facades,
eight directions and nine corners.
Ten thousand pillars lean together in clusters,
piled up and supporting one another.
Floating pillars are high and lofty like hanging stars,
drifting and towering, supported by branches.
Flying beams are arched like pointing rainbows,
held high and soaring together.
Layered brackets are piled high and steep,
curved lintels are slender and encircling.
Mushroom-shaped short pillars are clustered and packed,
supporting branches are forked and leaning.
Sideways they twist and emerge horizontally,
mutually entwining and bearing the weight.
Below, they are dense and brilliantly variegated,
above, they are rugged and repeatedly layered.
Rapidly gathered like scales,
branching out and separating.
Crisscrossing and following in succession,
each having its own direction.
Thereupon, beams are suspended and eaves joined,
with patterned lattice in the celestial windows.
Round pools and square ceiling-wells,
where lotuses are planted upside down.
They put forth beauty and bloom in splendor,
lotus blossoms unfolding.
Green seed-pods and purple seeds,
dangling like clusters of pearls.
Cloud-patterned brackets and algae-decorated joists,
dragon-shaped rafters finely carved.
Flying birds and running beasts,
take on lifelike forms within the wood.
Leaping tigers clutch and grab as they lean against the beams,
vigorously bristling their manes.
Qiūlóng 虯龍 dragons soar and writhe,
their jaws seeming to move as they crawl.
The Zhūniǎo 朱鳥 (Vermilion Bird) spreads its wings to perch on the crossbar,
while Téngshé 騰虵 (Soaring Snakes) coil and wind around the rafters.
A Báilù 白鹿 (White Deer) stands solitary on a bracket,
and a coiled Chī 螭 dragon winds around to support the lintel.
Cunning rabbits crouch beside the pedestals,
and apes climb the rafters in pursuit of one another.
Black bears bare their teeth and gums,
crouching low as if bearing a heavy load.
With heads aligned and eyes staring,
they look on silently and fiercely.
Húrén 胡人 (Barbarians) gather from afar atop the upper pillars,
solemnly kneeling in pairs facing each other.
Fierce and brave with eagle-like gazes,
they stare with wide, protruding eyes.
Appearing as if grieving in their perilous heights,
they frown and look distressed.
Shénxiān 神仙 (Immortals) stand tall among the beams,
and Yùnǚ 玉女 (Jade Maidens) peer through windows looking downward.
Suddenly indistinct and phantom-like,
as if they were ghosts or spirits.
Painted there are Heaven and Earth,
and all categories of living beings.
Strange and wondrous things of every sort,
spirits of the mountains and spirits of the seas.
Their forms are depicted and recorded,
entrusted to the cinnabar and azure pigments.
Through a thousand shifts and ten thousand changes,
each matter is given its distinct shape.
Following colors to resemble their kind,
capturing their true essence in every detail.
Above, the record begins with the Creation,
at the very dawn of high antiquity.
The Wǔlóng 五龍 (Five Dragons) with joined wings,
and Rén Huáng 人皇 (Sovereign of Men) with nine heads.
Fúxī 伏羲 with a scaly body,
and Nǚwā 女媧 with a serpentine torso.
In the vast and simple primordial wilderness,
their appearances were strange and wide-eyed.
Brilliant and magnificent to behold
are Huángdì 黃帝, Táng 唐 (Yáo), and Yú 虞 (Shùn).
Carriage-top canopies and ceremonial caps were used to honor the worthy,
and robes were distinguished by rank.
Below these come the Three Sovereigns of later ages,
as well as licentious consorts and chaotic lords.
Loyal ministers and filial sons,
heroic men and chaste women.
The wise and the foolish, success and failure,
none are not recorded and narrated.
Evil is shown to warn the world,
and good is shown to instruct posterity.
Thereupon, connected galleries join the palaces,
and imperial roads encircle them.
From the sunlit kiosks one looks outward,
at the soaring towers and flying observatories.
Long pathways rise and descend,
and balustrades wind on continuously.
The Jiàntái 漸臺 (Graduated Terrace) overlooks the pond,
rising in nine curved tiers.
Towering and standing alone,
it is clearly of a unique form.
Rising as high as the Huágài 華蓋 (Flowery Canopy star),
one looks up to see the Celestial Court.
The flying stairs are lofty and steep,
following the clouds on an upward journey.
Sitting in the middle, one sees the hanging light of the sun,
and looking down, one sees the flowing stars.
A thousand gates resemble each other,
and ten thousand doors are as one.
Crags jut out and caverns emerge,
winding and twisting in intricate turns.
Walking around for several lǐ 里,
one looks up and cannot see the sun.
How magnificent and grand is this splendor,
alas, how wondrous the labor expended!
Were it not for a man of divinely inspired talent,
who could have accomplished such a feat?
Occupying the precious site of Kūnlíng 坤靈 (Earth Spirit),
receiving the pure abundance of Cānghào 蒼昊 (Vast Heaven).
Encompassing the transformations of Yīn 陰 and Yáng 陽,
and containing the misty vapors of the original Qi.
Sweet springs well up in the hidden drains,
and sweet dew covers the eaves, arriving from above.
Red cinnamon trees shimmer in the north and south,
while orchids and magic fungi sway in the east and west.
Auspicious winds gather and blow softly,
stirring up fragrances that remain forever sweet.
Divine spirits support these beams and eaves,
so that they grow firmer through a thousand years.
May it enjoy eternal peace and blessed fortune,
coexisting forever with the Great Hàn 漢.
Truly it is the dwelling of the Supreme Sovereign,
ensuring long life and blessing for descendants.
If it can be as precious as this,
who could speak of it and not treasure it?
The Envoi says:
The crimson, divine palace,
lofty, towering, and grand,
vast and multitudinous!
Steep and rugged,
high and craggy,
rising in clusters!
Curving and majestic,
coiling and massed together,
leaning and tilting to the sides!
Suddenly grand and then obscure,
covered by dense clouds,
deep and mysterious!
Verdant green and lush purple,
piled up in magnificent splendor,
capturing the light of the sun!
Having reached the peak of wonder and beauty,
since the beginning of architecture,
there has never been its like!
Divinely planned and constructed,
an auspicious omen for our Hàn 漢 house,
never to decay!
Great indeed is the Wèi 魏!
Generations have seen wise sages.
Wǔ 武 created the foundational basis,
Wén 文 gathered the Great Mandate.
Both embodied Heaven to establish systems,
and followed the seasons to set up governance.
Coming to the current Emperor,
he has redoubled the brightness and accumulated prosperity.
From afar, he inherits the natural order of Yīn 陰 and Yáng 陽,
and near at hand, he roots himself in the true feelings of humanity.
Above, he honors the grand way of investigating antiquity,
and below, he elaborates the good scriptures for an enduring reign.
All affairs are now at peace,
and the celestial order is most clear.
Thus, after only a few years,
the state is wealthy and punishments are light.
In the third month of the year,
he made an inspection tour to the East,
arriving at Xǔchāng 許昌.
He performed sacrifices to the mountains and rivers from afar,
and examined the seasons and measured the regions.
He inquired after the elderly,
and led the people in farming and sericulture.
Passing the full moon of the sixth month,
when the pitch-pipe Línzhōng 林鍾 sets the rhythm,
and the star Dàhuǒ 大火 is at its zenith at dusk.
The mulberry and catalpa trees were lush and thick,
and heavy rains fell in due season.
The Three Excellencies and Nine Ministers,
grand scholars and eminent students,
felt the oppressive sultriness of the humid summer,
and considered the equilibrium of life.
Seeing that the regions of Mín 岷 and Yuè 越 were not yet tranquil,
they realized the military expeditions had not yet brought peace.
Then he spoke openly, saying:
"In the past, there was Xiāo Gōng,
and later Sūn Qīng.
Both possessed foresight and extensive learning,
and were brilliant, fair, sincere, and earnest.
None of them believed that without grandeur and beauty,
one could unify the people or emphasize majestic awe.
Without adornment and elegance,
one could not instruct posterity or perpetuate their success.
Thus, in their time, they enjoyed the benefits of their achievements,
and later generations relied on their glorious reputation.
Furthermore, Xǔchāng
is where the great destiny resides
and what the prophetic charts signal.
If virtue and righteousness are as such,
why should palace halls not be constructed?"
The Emperor said:
"Indeed!"
The dark carriage was harnessed,
and light furs were worn.
Then he commanded the officials
to prepare the rites and ceremonies.
They assessed the daily labor
and calculated the expenses and tasks in detail.
They gathered the common people to begin the work,
collecting them during the leisure of the farming season.
Drawing from the spoils of the eastern army's victory,
and the tributes from the maritime rebels.
They erected the secret hall of Jǐngfú,
providing the systems for the imperial residence.
Thereupon, the double-layered roofs were made deep and grand,
and the high foundations were built majestic and imposing.
Sparse pillars were arranged in sequence,
and the embankments and stairs were solemn and resonant.
The flying eaves soared like wings,
and the curved roofs rose high like galloping steeds.
Floating feather decorations were lush and vibrant,
and hanging pearls and gems chimed like jade.
Nine streamers of the Cān flag
fluttered and flew in the wind.
Bright and dazzling,
the vermilion colors shone brilliantly.
Thus, its decorative pillars were gleaming and lustrous,
radiant and burning with light,
like the sun and moon gracing the heavens.
Its inner recesses were shaded and obscure,
seemingly withdrawing into themselves,
like a string of hidden stars.
Already arranged like the teeth of a comb and clustered together,
they were also vast, grand, and spacious.
Encompassing a wide variety of forms,
they did not follow a single pattern.
Looking at it from afar,
it seemed like spreading red clouds reflecting the celestial patterns;
observing it closely,
it seemed like gazing up at a lofty mountain wearing trailing clouds.
How magnificent and grandly beautiful!
So richly textured it is hard to distinguish,
this is its general appearance.
As for the high ridges being towering and steep,
the flying eaves catch the rainbow.
Dense and dark,
they move and dissolve with the clouds.
Like birds perching or mountains standing,
as if soaring or staying still.
Lofty and precarious,
one knows not where they end.
Even with the extreme vision of Lì Zhū,
one would still be dazzled and unable to see clearly.
Thereupon, the broad expanse of the southern end was opened,
and the massive bell-frames were displayed.
Magnificent bells were hung high,
and fierce beasts stood tall in pairs.
Embodying great strength and fierce resolve,
their sound rumbled like thunder.
There were also the Xiá Dí statues,
their silver bodies rounded and full.
Sitting in the side halls of the high gates,
they manifest the majestic spirit of the Sage Sovereign.
Fragrant herbs filled the courtyard,
and Sophora and Maple trees covered the palace.
Adorned with Evergreen trees,
and mixed with Purple Hazel.
Some gained favor for their auspicious names,
others were prized for their beautiful wood.
They bear fruit in the autumn
and spread flowers in the spring.
Lush and luxuriant,
fragrant and sweet-smelling.
As for its structure,
long beams were colorfully fashioned,
lower ones curving and upper ones unique.
Rafters and supports were layered,
their momentum united though their forms were separate.
Red like a winding rainbow,
bright like a galloping hornless dragon.
To the south, they reached the Yang side,
to the north, they reached the dark cliffs.
Carrying heavy weight for a long distance,
their merit is exceedingly great.
Then, rows of lacquered and vermilion embroidered rafters were set,
and jade-like patterned tiles were hung.
Curving like divine dragons ascending and descending,
shining like the flowing light of the bright moon.
There were the crossbeams,
carved and spreading like wings.
Supported by corner-rafters,
connecting the round and the square.
White patterns interspersed,
sparse and dense with order.
Flying brackets leapt like birds,
bearing the double shafts.
Crossing perils and braving the void,
they were swiftly joined together.
Gleaming white spaces,
and rows of coin-like patterns.
The morning light shines inward,
and the reflected radiance glows outward.
Intense as the Hooked Stars in the Milky Way,
brilliant as cloud-beams supporting the sky.
Brackets were intricately interlaced,
turning and suspended like city walls.
Lotus stems were planted upside down,
spitting out and covering the lotus flowers.
Surrounded by coffers,
woven with multicolored patterns;
red flowers in full bloom,
vermilion silks intricately woven.
Lotus blossoms bright and vivid,
fine embroidery spread about.
Numerous decorations and accumulated craftsmanship,
beyond the power of writing to describe.
Then, Orchid-wood pillars were stacked,
and supports were set in square patterns.
Brackets and blocks were arranged to support each other,
and curved arms intertwined.
Golden pillars were lined up,
with jade bases supporting the ends.
Green lattice windows and silver door-knockers,
these made the inner chambers.
The double door-frames were long,
and the heavy rafters were decorated.
Eaves and ledges lined the edges,
flowing around to the four poles.
The ranks of the guards,
and the duties of the vassal states.
Warm rooms occupied the eastern wing,
and cool rooms were located in the western side.
Opening the Jiànyáng gate brought the brilliance of the red flame,
opening the Jīnguāng gate brought the cool breeze.
Thus, in winter there is no piercing cold,
and in summer no scorching heat.
Harmoniously adjusted and moderate,
one can live for many years.
The walls and foundations
shone brightly.
The Zhōu system used white plaster,
but now only light blue is used.
Adorned with golden rings,
here there were two grades.
Bright pearls and kingfisher feathers
were found everywhere.
Admiring the sincerity of the former kings,
and delighting in the non-action of Zhòng Huá.
He commanded the Gòng Gōng to make paintings,
manifesting the application of the five colors.
Images were drawn of the past,
to serve as admonitions and regulations.
The ranks of the Pepper Chambers,
took these as their standard and model.
Observing the demeanor of Yú Jī,
one knows the sycophantic ministers who govern the state.
Seeing Jiāng Hòu remove her hairpins,
one realizes what former generations followed.
Honoring the honest words of Zhòng Lí,
and the virtue of Fán Jī of Chǔ in withdrawing herself.
Praising the refusal of Bān Qiè to share the carriage,
and the greatness of Mèng Mǔ in choosing her neighborhood.
Therefore, if one wishes to broaden wisdom,
one must first hear much.
If one hears much, there will be much complexity,
and complexity can obscure the truth.
Where lies the absence of confusion?
It lies in choosing the right people.
Therefore, if one wishes to establish virtue,
one must first be close to the benevolent.
Desiring that these rites do not fail,
one thus exhausts the ways of the ancient people who walked the path.
Viewing them morning and evening,
how could it just be like writing on one's sash?
When we come to the steps and porches extending continuously,
like drifting clouds traveling away.
The window-lattices and railings are wide and expansive,
hooks interlocking and squares perfectly formed.
The balustrades resemble leaping snakes,
the doorposts are like flowery jade.
Curled like a *Chī* dragon,
stayed like a *Qiú* dragon.
Dark verandas ascend in intersection,
their radiant patterns shining brightly.
The *Zōu Yú* is presented in offering,
with its white essence and benevolent form.
It manifests the excellence of Heaven’s auspicious signs,
and reflects the arrival of distant tribes to the court.
The *Yīn Táng* sits in the north,
with its square verandas and nine doors.
The right chamber is for quiet banquets,
with its eaves spanning west and east.
It is linked to the *Yǒng Níng* Hall,
while *Ān Chāng* overlooks the garden.
Then one reaches the *Bǎi Zǐ* Hall,
where the ladies of the inner palace reside.
Who are those who dwell there?
Elegant and virtuous ladies.
Emulating the fine reputation of *Sī Qí*,
they seek many blessings.
What are those blessings?
May they be fitting for your descendants.
May they be wise and discerning,
may they be acute and clever.
May they be forever granted longevity,
so that the millions of people may rely upon them.
To the south, there is the *Chéng Guāng* Front Hall,
the palace for administering government.
Receiving the worthy and employing the capable,
inquiring into the Way and seeking the golden mean.
Governing the boundaries of the universe,
molding the customs of the nation.
Like clouds moving and rain falling,
all categories of things are harmonized.
To its west are the "Left Steps and Right Leveling,"
the grounds for practice and study.
Two rows of six stand in opposition,
with the palace wings facing each other.
Agile movements seize the advantage,
modeled after military troops.
Discerning and explaining, they return to the essence,
likened to the administration of laws and punishments.
These are used to execute commands,
not merely for the pleasure of the emotions.
Anchored by a majestic terrace,
it is indeed called *Yǒng Shǐ*.
With double galleries and multiple gates,
it awaits the reckless and wild.
The stores of the capital's granaries
have nothing that is not present.
Precautions against the unforeseen
are taken from here.
Then one constructs the tiered basin of *Líng Yún*,
and dredges the numinous pond of *Yú Yuān*.
The pure dew is heavy and thick,
the clear waters are vast and deep.
It is planted with fine trees,
and set with fragrant herbs.
Leisurely are the dark fish,
gleaming are the white birds.
Sinking, floating, soaring, and wheeling,
they rejoice in our Imperial Way.
Then as the *Qiú* dragons pour forth,
the irrigation ditches flow into one another.
On land, halls and pavilions are established;
on the water, light boats are squared.
Bamboo groves house the *Kūn* and egrets;
in the shallows play the *Yǎn* and *Yóu* fish.
Its abundance equals the *Huái* and the Sea;
its wealth enriches the mountains and hills.
The gathered and accumulated stores
how can they be fully counted?
Even the grand spectacle of *Xián Chí*,
how could it be a worthy rival?
Thereupon, it is marked by the *Gāo Chāng* Lofty Lookout,
and indicated by the *Jiàn Chéng* Steep Lodge.
Loftily they stand like mountain peaks,
towering as if dwelling upon ridges.
Flying galleries touch the clouds,
floating stairs mount the void.
Gazing afar at the nine fields,
viewing from a distance the long plans.
Looking down upon the three markets,
seeing who has what and who lacks.
Seeing the farmers weeding and hilling,
one understands the hardships of sowing and reaping.
Considering whether the harvest years are bountiful or meager,
one reflects on the sighs within the *Wú Yì*.
Moved by the many things, thoughts become deep;
because of dwelling on high, one worries about peril.
Realizing the virtue of Heaven is not easily maintained,
fearing that worldly customs are difficult to know.
Observing the quality of tools and weapons,
examining the sincerity or falsity of social transformation.
Beholding where the noble and lowly reside,
realizing the smooth or uneven state of governance and punishment.
This is also how to examine customs and assist education;
how could it be merely for wandering pleasure and the exaltation of extravagance?
The walled wards and various offices
number thirty and two.
Arranged like stars in their dwellings,
elegant like patterns and scales in a row.
*Xīn*, *Rén*, *Guǐ*, and *Jiǎ*
serve as their names and ranks.
The rooms are uniform and even,
halls and courtyards are as one.
Exiting this and entering that,
one wishes to return but forgets the way.
Truly the methods of the craftsmen are manifold,
surely the ten thousand changes are inexhaustible.
Nothing is so difficult that it is not understood;
thus they are equal in loftiness to Creation itself.
Rivaling Heaven and Earth to establish the foundation,
aligned with the constellations to create the system.
No detail is so small that it does not harmonize with the sundial's shadow;
no work is so minute that it deviates from the water level.
Therefore, the added structures are like piles,
and the planted trees are like forests.
Districts are connected yet regions are distinct;
leaves are close together yet branches are divided.
Diverging and turning in different directions,
aligned like fields and joined together.
Lengthwise and crosswise they extend,
each having its own direction.
*Gōng Shū* would find his compass and square confused;
*Jiàng Shí* would not know where to apply his chisel.
Having exhausted the skill of the designs,
how could the colorful patterns ever be depleted?
Then it is patterned with vermilion and green,
and decorated with kingfisher-blue and cinnabar.
Dotted with silver and gold,
glistening like *Láng Gān* jade.
The brilliance is flashing and sparkling,
the elegant colors are variegated and bright.
Clear winds gather to create a sound;
the morning sun shines to increase the freshness.
Even the numinous palace of *Kūnlún*,
how could it be more extravagant than this?
Since the compass and square correspond to Heaven and Earth,
and actions and measures follow the four seasons,
thus the Six Directions are great and prosperous,
and the Nine Provinces are harmonious and bright.
Every household cherishes the custom of yielding,
and every person chants the poem of *Kāng Zāi*.
None are not leisurely and self-contented,
thus they are placid and have no worries.
Looking back at the successive rulers and discussing their achievements,
none had the supreme governance of today.
The extinction of those states of *Wú* and *Shǔ*
can surely be expected while standing on tiptoe.
Yet the Holy Sovereign still works diligently without error,
seeking how the world may realize itself.
He summons loyal and upright scholars,
and opens the path for the public and straightforward.
He remembers the past warnings of *Zhōu Gōng*,
and admires the statutes and plans of *Jiù Yáo*.
He eliminates useless offices,
and reduces the causes of creating trouble.
He cuts off the complex rituals of the drifting and dissolute,
returning the people's feelings to the Great Simplicity.
Thus, he can make the singing phoenix soar at *Qí Yáng*,
and receive the white jade ring of the Clan of *Yú*.
The Azure Dragon appears in the embanked ponds;
the Tortoise Script emerges from the source of the River.
Sweet springs gush forth in the pools and gardens;
numinous fungi grow in the hills and groves.
Gathering the blessings and protection of the spirits,
collecting the supreme joy of the *Huáxià*.
He equals the Three Sovereigns and surpasses the Five Emperors;
how could the *Zhōu* and *Xià* even be worth mentioning!
In the past, during the eras of Dì Guī and Jù Táng,
the heavenly net was in turmoil,
causing ruin and disease.
Great billows overflowed and surged,
for ten thousand lǐ without end.
Endless waves rolled and tumbled,
spreading out to the eight frontiers.
Thereupon, Yǔ
leveled the hills and plains that bordered cliffs,
and drained the marshes and pools to meet one another.
He opened the jagged heights of Lóngmén,
and cleared the ridges and peaks by hewing and chiseling.
Once the many mountains were managed,
the hundred rivers secretly flowed and were dredged.
Vast and boundless, calm and clear,
the leaping waves followed the terrain.
Once the Jiāng and Hé were channeled,
ten thousand hollows flowed together.
Pulling and uprooting the Wǔyuè,
draining dry the Jiǔzhōu.
Every drop and trickle seeped through,
gathered like dense clouds and mist.
Trickles and vast flows alike,
all came to pour in.
In the vast and numinous sea,
they became a perpetual receptacle.
For its breadth,
for its strangeness,
it is truly fitting that it be called great.
As for its appearance,
it is flowing and shimmering, glistening and surging,
floating to the sky without a shore.
Vast and deep, expansive and limitless,
misty and boundless, spreading far and wide.
Waves are like a chain of mountains,
suddenly joining, suddenly scattering.
It inhales and exhales the hundred rivers,
washing clean the Huái and Hàn.
Submerging hills and flooding wide lands,
its waters are vast and overflowing.
When the Dà Míng gathers its reins at the cave of Jīnshū,
and the soaring sun gallops in fright from the ford of Fúsāng.
Swirling sands and crashing stones,
winds buffet the shores of the islands.
Thereupon it rouses its fury,
overflowing waves toss and float.
Striking and clashing against one another,
flying foam gives rise to billows.
Shaped like the wheel of heaven,
twisting and violently rotating,
and like the axis of the earth,
standing tall and competing to spin.
High peaks fly and soar, turning over and over,
the Wǔyuè dance and pound against each other.
Gushing in whirlpools and accumulating,
surging and alternating in rising and falling.
Swirling and churning to form caverns,
rising up to become towering mounds.
Drifting and lingering, spreading and soaring,
piled up in layers and massed together.
Startled waves rush like thunder,
terrified waters burst and gather,
opening and closing, dissolving and meeting,
flowing copiously and damply.
Blossoms and flowers of foam are trampled and twisted,
thick and turbid, bubbling and seething.
When the haze and darkness secretly dissipate,
nothing quivers or trembles.
Light dust does not fly,
slender vines do not move.
Yet it still gapes and pants,
remaining waves surge alone.
Crashing and billowing, roaring and surging,
piled up like mountain ridges.
Its branched forks and deep pools,
surging and swelling to form backwaters.
Separating the Mán and isolating the Yí,
winding and interlocking for ten thousand lǐ.
When the remote frontiers send urgent word,
and the King's commands must be swiftly proclaimed.
Swift steeds and beating oars,
sailing the sea and surmounting the mountains.
Then they wait for a strong wind,
and hoist a hundred-foot mast.
Tying long silks,
they hang the sail mats.
Looking at the waves rushing far away,
they vanish brightly like birds.
Swift as a startled teal that has lost its mate,
sudden as if pulled by the Liù Lóng.
In one leap, three thousand lǐ,
reaching the destination before the morning is through.
If one who bears filth approaches the deep,
with hollow oaths and errant prayers.
Then there is the Hǎitóng to block the way,
and the Mǎxián to stand in the path.
Tiānwú suddenly appears in a glimmer,
the Wǎngxiàng is briefly revealed and flashes its corpse.
A host of demons meet and clash,
glancing with seductive and alluring eyes.
Sails are torn and masts are broken,
injurious winds give rise to evil.
Vast as numinous transformations,
blurred and indistinct in the deep twilight.
The atmosphere is like the heavenly vault,
dense clouds are spread out.
Clouds gather and lightning flashes,
a hundred colors of demonic light are revealed.
Panting and sighing, stifled and brooding,
flashing and gleaming without measure.
Flying floods grind against each other,
surging forces wash against one another.
Clouds collapse and rain is pulverized,
roaring and rushing.
Leaping and sinking,
boiling over and overflowing.
Splashing and churning,
shaking the clouds and drenching the sun.
Thereupon the sailors and fishermen,
traveling to the south and the far east.
Some are ground and submerged in the caves of giant turtles and gators,
or caught and hung on the peaks of high ridges.
Some are dragged or carried to the land of the Luǒrén,
or drift leisurely to the country of the Hēichǐ.
Some drift like duckweed and turn about,
or return by means of a following wind.
They only know that viewing wonders is full of fright,
but do not realize the distance of where they have been.
As for its great capacity,
to the south it drenches Zhūyá,
to the north it splashes Tiānxū.
To the east it reaches Xīmù,
to the west it borders Qīng and Xú.
The path across is vast and dark,
more than a hundred million lǐ.
It exhales clouds and rainbows,
and contains dragons and fish.
It hides the scales of the Kūn,
and is the dwelling of numinous beings.
Not only does it accumulate the treasures of Tàidiān,
and the bright pearls of Suíhóu.
Those things gathered by the world are often heard of,
while those not yet named are as if they do not exist.
Moreover, for those things rarely heard of in the world,
how can one examine their names?
Thus one can only describe their colors,
and cloudily portray their forms.
Inside its watery mansions,
in the courts of its greatest depths.
There are lofty islands atop giant áo tortoises,
towering and standing like solitary pavilions.
They cleave the great billows,
and point toward the Tàiqīng.
Resting on massive rocks,
they are home to a hundred spirits.
They soar with the Kǎifēng to depart south,
and when the Guǎngmò comes, they travel north.
On its shores there are heavenly treasures and sea monsters,
and the chambers of the Jiāorén.
Flawless stones with strange radiance,
scales and shells of extraordinary substances.
Like cloud-brocade scattering patterns at the edge of the sand,
or silk damask draped with light over the joints of snails and clams.
Myriad colors display their splendor,
ten thousand hues hide their brilliance.
Sun-ice does not melt,
and yin-fire secretly burns.
Bright charcoal burns again,
blowing its light through the Jiǔquán.
Red flames and green smoke,
subtle and shimmering, graceful and moving.
As for fish, there is the whale that spans the sea,
suddenly lunging and wandering alone.
Brushing against rocky ridges,
and lying down in the high billows.
It eats scaled and shelled creatures,
and swallows dragon boats.
When it inhales the waves, the great ripples contract,
when it blows out the flood, the hundred rivers flow backward.
Sometimes it falters in the ebbing waves,
and dies on land in the salt fields.
Its giant scales pierce the clouds,
its dorsal fins prick the sky.
Its skull becomes a mountain peak,
and its flowing fat becomes a deep pool.
As for the nooks of the rocky embankments,
and the crags of sand and stone.
Feathered wings produce fledglings,
and breaking eggs becomes birds.
Ducklings are bedraggled,
and crane chicks are sparse of feather.
They fly in flocks and bathe in pairs,
playing in the vastness and floating on the deep.
Soaring through the mist in continuous lines,
leisurely and at ease.
Their fluttering wings sound like thunder,
their chaotic plumage like a forest.
Calling and whistling to one another,
with strange colors and diverse sounds.
When the three luminaries are clear,
and heaven and earth are bright and harmonious.
One does not merely drift with Yáng Hóu,
but mounts the clouds to travel far away.
Encountering Ān Qí at Pénglái,
and seeing the imperial image at Qiáo Shān.
The myriad immortals are ethereal,
consuming jade on the shores of purity.
Stepping in the discarded sandals at Fù Xiāng,
draped in feathered garments that trail behind.
Soaring over the Heavenly Pond,
and playing in the furthest reaches of the sea.
Molding form within desirelessness,
and living forever in the eternal expanse.
Furthermore, as for its nature as a vessel,
it contains the mysteries of Qián,
and encompasses the regions of Kūn.
Only the spirits find their dwelling here,
and the deities their home.
What marvel is not present?
What wonder is not stored?
The vast, accumulated flow
contains form while remaining empty within.
How expansive is the virtue of Kǎn,
occupying a low position for itself.
Broadly sending out and receiving in,
serving as the ancestor and the capital.
All kinds of creatures come to life;
what is there that is not found?
Consider how the five elements are used together,
but the virtue of water is truly divine and enduring.
It is from Mín Shān that the river is guided,
its source first welling up in a cup.
Its beginning is marked at Luò and Mò,
gathering the myriad streams of Bā and Liáng.
Rushing through the Wū Xiá with swift fury,
ascending the Jiāng Jīn and rising in flood.
Exhausting the capacity of deep waters to move like the sea,
appearing to touch the sky in its boundless expanse.
It collects the Hàn and the Sì,
and encompasses the Huái and the Xiāng.
It swallows up the Yuán and the Lǐ,
and draws in the Jǔ and the Zhāng.
Its source branches into two at Jū Lái,
and its flow splits into nine at Xún Yáng.
Drumming great waves at Chì Àn,
and its lingering ripples settle at Chái Sāng.
It networks all the streams,
and weighs the merits of every brook and ditch.
Manifesting its divine commission at Jiāng Dū,
mixing the ancestral flows to meet in the east.
Pouring into the Wǔ Hú in a vast spread,
and irrigating the Sān Jiāng with a crashing surge.
Drenching the regions of the six provinces,
and operating beyond the burning sun.
Thus it serves as a boundary between the Huá and the Yì,
a majestic and perilous barrier of heaven and earth.
Breathing in and out across ten thousand miles,
inhaling and exhaling the divine tides.
Naturally coming and going,
sometimes in the evening, sometimes in the morning.
Stirring up a swift momentum to charge ahead,
it drums its fury to create waves.
Éméi serves as the high peak of Yuán Yáng,
and Yù Lěi acts as the marker of the eastern diversion.
Héng and Huò are grand in their continuous garrison,
Wū and Lú are towering in their adjacent peaks.
Harmonizing spirits and communicating vital breath,
gushing and surging, they mold one another.
Drifting winds and steaming thunder,
soaring rainbows and rising into the skies.
Emerging from Xìn Yáng on a long journey,
gurgling into the Great Abyss and Wò Jiāo.
As for the gorges of Bā Dōng,
which Xià Hòu carved and channeled.
The sheer banks are ten thousand fathoms high,
the walls standing straight and mottled with red.
Hǔ Yá stands loftily and sheer,
and Jīng Mén towers high and stable.
Round whirlpools revolve nine times as they hang and soar,
the gushing flow roars like thunder and strikes like lightning.
Terrifying billows spray violently,
and startling waves fly and thin out.
Swift whirlpools add to the churning,
and surging rapids leap repeatedly.
Battering the rocks with a drumming sound,
crashing and splashing in the light.
Roaring, rushing, and gurgling,
overflowing, pouring, and surging.
Bubbling, swirling, and vast,
shimmering, glistening, and boiling.
Spiraling, whirling, and circling,
swelling, churning, and cascading.
Surging, rushing, and overflowing,
like dragon scales interlaced together.
Green sands meander as they come and go,
and giant rocks lurch as they advance and retreat.
Where hidden currents gurgle and boil,
and rushing streams grind and collide.
The banks are eroded into ridges,
and the mountain capes are worn into crags.
Dark valleys accumulate obstructions,
and the sound of clashing stones rings out.
As for the palace of the layered pools,
and the abyss of the spirit lakes.
Clear, calm, and vast,
deep, wide, and shimmering.
Profound, surging, and swirling,
glittering, shimmering, and clear.
Mixing and washing in bright diffusion,
the flowing reflections shine and glow.
Boundless, vast, and limitless,
overflowing and expansive.
To observe it is to find no image,
to seek it is to find no border.
Its breath surges like a dark mist,
at times swirling like smoke.
Resembling the primordial chaos before it congealed,
like the Tài Jí forming the heavens.
Long waves spread and flow,
and steep rapids tower high.
Whirling vortices turn like valleys,
and towering billows collapse like mountains.
Yáng Hóu rises like the shore,
and great waves swirl and return like clouds.
Sinking and swirling,
now receding, now piling up.
Gaping as if the earth were splitting,
wide as if the sky were opening.
Touching the winding cliffs to coil around,
and startling the collapsing waves to crash together.
Drumming in the hollows with a booming sound,
it gushes forth and rides the bends.
As for fish, there are the Jiāng Tún and the sea pigs,
the Shū tuna and the king sturgeon.
The Hú, Liàn, Téng, and Yóu,
the Líng, Yáo, Lún, and Lián.
Some have deer antlers or elephant trunks,
some have tiger shapes or dragon faces.
Their scales and armor are dazzlingly diverse,
brilliant and patterned like brocade.
Raising fins and flicking tails,
spraying waves and flying foam.
Breaking through the flow with gasping sounds,
they swim and linger with the waves.
Some burst with color to brighten the deep,
some gape their gills among the rocks.
Giant whales ride the billows as they enter and exit,
while shad and anchovies come and go according to the seasons.
As for the strange and varied creatures of the water,
there are the diving swan and the fish-bull,
the tiger-crocodile and the hooked snake.
The Lún, Zhèn, horseshoe crab, and Mèi,
the rays, the Bèi, the Pèng, and the Zhū.
The giant clam and the sea-moon,
the earth-flesh and the stone-flower.
The three-braided snail and the cowry of the river,
the nautilus and the spiral snail.
The pea crab in the belly of the Suǒ clam,
and the jellyfish with the shrimp as its eyes.
Purple mussels as large as drains,
and great cockles that could fill a carriage.
Jasper clams dry in the sunlight to brighten their pearls,
and stone barnacles respond to the seasons by spreading their blossoms.
The Jū Zhū spider-crabs are dense and bristly with trailing plumes,
and black oysters are jagged and piled up in uneven masses.
Some float on the surging tides,
while others are buried in the mud and sand.
As for the dragon-carp with a single horn,
and the strange nine-headed *qíqiāng* birds.
There are soft-shell turtles with three legs,
and tortoises with six eyes.
Red *chēngbiē* leap from the depths and spit out pearls;
patterned *wénpí* sound like chimes and gestate fine jade.
The *tiáoyán* brushes its wings and emits flashes of light;
the divine *shénlì* curls and coils as it swims in the depths.
*Bó* horses gallop through the waves, snorting and treading;
water *sì* roar like thunder at *Yánghóu*.
The *Yuānkè* builds his house at the bottom of the crags;
the *Jiāorén* constructs his dwelling within the hanging torrents.
Like hail scattered is the remnant grain;
like stars dispersed are the sand-mirrors.
Green silk-threads tangle together;
ornate ribbons vie in their brilliance.
Purple seaweed glows brightly, covering in clusters;
green moss grows shaggily upon the whetstones.
Stone-sails grow densely to cover the islets;
*píng* fruits occasionally emerge and drift about.
Beneath are gold ores and cinnabar pebbles,
cloud-essences and candle-silver.
*Lì*, *liǔ*, *xuán*, and *guī* gems;
water-jasper and hidden *mín* stones.
Resonating stones are lined up on the sunny banks;
floating chimes are spread out on the shaded shores.
Some shimmer with color in the light ripples;
some glow brilliantly beside the cliffs.
Not a forest that is not moist;
not a bank that is not damp.
As for the feathered tribes,
there are the dawn-swans and the heavenly chickens,
the *yǎo*, *áo*, gulls, and *lù*.
Solar birds soar there,
during the dark months of the year.
A thousand kinds with ten thousand sounds,
clamoring and chirping among themselves.
They wash their feathers in the thinning breeze,
and beat their wings in rapid flight.
Flapping and playing, they sprinkle pearls;
brushing and stroking, they scatter foam.
Alighting, they are like clouds of gauze spread out;
dispersing, they are like clouds breaking apart.
They molt and pile up their feathers,
coming and going between *Bó* and *Jié*.
Willow and medlar grow thick on the banks;
*lì* and *lián* trees stand tall on the ridges and line the peaks.
Peach-branch bamboo and *yúndāng* bamboo
produce fruit in abundant clusters.
Reeds and rushes spread like clouds,
interwoven with the red of orchids.
They raise white plumes
and sprout purple buds.
They shade the deep pools and bends,
and cover the long River.
Lush and fragrant are the hedge-vines;
hidden and dark are the water-pines.
The bank-side thickets are verdant;
the submerged vegetation is lush and green.
The *líng* and *lù* huddle at the edges of the banks;
the civet and otter peer out from the hollows.
Swift *wěi* monkeys lean into the void to show their skill;
solitary *jué* apes climb the heights with composure.
The *kuí* and *niú* prance in the evening sun;
the *yuānchú* chick plays with its feathers east of the mountain.
Dividing currents form islets;
meeting ravines open into channels.
Rushing into hollows, they create shores;
partitioned off, they become lakes.
Steeped in overflowing waters,
drained through the *Wěilǘ*.
Marked by kingfisher-green canopies;
floating with drifting wild rice.
Sowing seeds not planted by man;
growing natural fine vegetables.
Scales of water-chestnuts and lotus leaves;
gathered and spread are the aquatic fruits.
Rising stems spray pollen;
washing sprouts scatter their casings.
Swaying gracefully with the wind;
undulating with the waves.
Flowing light is hidden and reflected;
the scene blazes like misty fires.
Beside it are *Yúnmèng* and *Léichí*,
*Pénglǐ* and *Qīngcǎo*,
*Jùqū*, *Táogé*,
*Zhūchǎn* and *Dānchǎo*.
Gazing as far as the eye can see for hundreds of miles,
the vast waters are white and boundless.
There are *Bāoshān* and *Dòngtíng*,
and the subterranean passages of *Bālíng*.
Hidden paths communicate laterally;
obscure caverns are deep and winding.
Gold essences and jade blossoms are set within;
jasper pearls and strange stones are inlaid on the surface.
Black dragons entwine at the base;
clouds brushing the tips crown the summits.
Where the *Hǎitóng* wanders,
and where *Qíngāo* miraculously ascends.
*Bīngyí* leans on the waves with a haughty look;
the *Jiāngfēi* goddesses frown with distant gazes.
Treading the soaring waves like leaping ducks,
inhaling the kingfisher mists in graceful movements.
When the universe is clear and silent,
and the eight winds do not blow.
Boatmen then grasp their oars;
travelers then push their poles.
Drifting like flying clouds,
they move the great *yúhuáng* ships.
Stern and bow follow one another;
for ten thousand miles, masts are linked.
Going against or with the current,
some for fishing, some for trade.
Reaching *Jiāo* and *Yì*,
venturing into the remote waves.
Exhausting the southern extremes;
reaching the eastern wastes.
Then they observe the vapors in the clear dawn,
watching the movement of the *wǔliǎng* wind vane.
A strong wind blows to add its fan;
the *Guǎngmò* wind whisks and its air is orderly.
Gentle but not slackening;
swift but not violent.
With sails drummed out, they cross quickly,
galloping over the swells and cutting through the depths.
Braving the waves and releasing the rudder,
they go like lightning into the vast gloom.
Towering like a morning cloud on a solitary journey;
distant as a winged cloud crossing a peak.
Suddenly hundreds of miles are covered;
a thousand miles in an instant.
*Fēilián* cannot keep up with their tracks;
*Qūhuáng* cannot catch their shadow.
Thus the reed-dwellers and fishermen,
abandoned to the rivers and mountains.
Their clothes are made of feathers and coarse wool;
their food is only vegetables and fresh fish.
They stack weirs to form pools;
they set traps across the confluences.
Bamboo tubes are cast in succession;
nets of all kinds fill the boats.
Sometimes they swing the wheel-line at the overhanging bank;
sometimes they spin across the middle of the rapids.
Suddenly forgetting the evening and returning at night,
singing "Picking Water Chestnuts" while tapping the gunwale.
Proud and self-sufficient with a single song,
following the winds and waves until the end of their years.
Thus it is bordered by winding crags,
and opened by cavernous ravines.
Branched by the *Tuó* and *Sì* rivers,
and pulsed by the morning and evening tides.
Where the river currents converge,
where clouds and mists turn into liquid.
Where rare and strange things are transformed and produced;
where monstrous and wondrous creatures have their dens.
It takes in the ranks of perfected hermits,
and gives birth to the spirits of extraordinary men.
It spreads its spiritual moisture for a thousand miles,
surpassing the clouds of *Dàizōng* hitting the rocks.
When its transformations are sudden and illusory,
the auspicious signs are not just one.
Its movements respond without a fixed way;
it emerges in response to events.
It manages Heaven and Earth,
and interweaves the arts of man.
Its mystery cannot be exhausted in words;
its affairs cannot be fully captured by the pen.
As the essence of *Mín* sheds its light upon the *Dōngjǐng*,
*Yánghóu* hides his form in the great waves.
*Qíxiàng* attained the Way and made it her divine residence,
then joined her spiritual brilliance with the *Xiāng'é*.
One marvels at the yellow dragon carrying the boat,
and remembers *Bóyǔ* sighing in respect.
Brave was *Jīngfēi* in capturing the *jiāo* dragon,
finally manifesting his spirit through the *Tài'ē* sword.
Fierce was *Yàolí* in plotting against *Qìng*,
thrusting his spear in the midst of the stream.
One grieves for *Língjūn* entrusting himself to the stone,
and sighs at the fisherman's rowing song.
One imagines King *Zhōumù* crossing with his army,
driving his eight steeds over turtles and alligators.
One is moved by *Jiāofù* losing his jade pendant,
and pities the divine messenger caught in the net.
Resplendent is the fluid form of the Great Bulk,
blending ten thousand endings into a single category.
Preserving without lack and eternally solid,
it receives original *qi* from the spiritual harmony.
When examining the rivers and waterways for a marvelous view,
indeed none are more prominent than the Yangtze and the Yellow River.
Chǔ Xiāng Wáng was wandering at the Palace of Lán Tái,
with Sòng Yù and Jǐng Chāi in attendance.
A gust of wind suddenly arrived with a rustle,
and the King opened his robes to face it,
saying:
"How pleasant is this wind!
Is it something I share with the common people?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"This is only the Great King's wind;
how could the common people share it?"
The King said:
"Wind
is the breath of heaven and earth,
reaching everywhere in its flow,
without choosing between the noble and the base, the high or the low.
Now you alone think it is my wind;
is there an explanation for this?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"I have heard from my teacher
that curved branches invite nests,
and hollow caves invite the wind.
Where it rests determines its nature,
and thus the quality of the wind differs."
The King asked:
"Where then does the wind first arise?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"The wind is born from the earth
and rises from the tips of the green duckweed.
It gradually spreads through the valleys
and rages at the mouth of the earthen hollows.
It skirts the slopes of Tài Shān
and dances beneath the pines and cypresses.
It billows and surges,
surging with fierce anger.
It resounds like the roll of thunder,
swirling and clashing in confusion.
It overthrows rocks and fells trees,
striking down the forest undergrowth.
As it begins to wane,
it scatters and disperses,
rushing through holes and shaking door-bars.
Shimmering and brilliant,
it drifts and shifts away.
Therefore, its clear, cool, and masculine wind
rises and falls as it floats.
It scales the high city walls
and enters the deep palace.
It brushes against flowers and leaves to shake out their fragrance,
lingers among the cinnamon and pepper trees,
soars over the surging waters,
and strikes the essence of the lotus.
It brushes the fragrant herbs,
scatters the Qín Héng,
brushes the magnolias,
and covers the budding poplars.
Swirling through hollows and rushing over mounds,
it wilts the various fragrances.
Then it wanders through the central courtyard
and moves north up to the Yù Táng.
It climbs the silken curtains
and passes through the inner chambers.
Only then does it become the Great King's wind.
Thus, when this wind strikes a person,
it feels sharp, cool, and bracing,
its refreshing chill bringing a sigh of relief.
Clear and cool,
it cures illness and dispels the effects of wine.
It sharpens the hearing and sight
and brings comfort and ease to the body.
This is what is called the Great King's masculine wind."
The King said:
"Well reasoned!
As for the wind of the common people,
may I hear of it?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"The wind of the common people
rises in a swirl from the narrow alleys,
churning up clouds of dust.
Pent up and agitated,
it strikes through holes and assaults doors.
It stirs up sand and grit
and blows upon dead ashes.
It churns up filth and turbid waters
and raises the stench of rot.
It slants into windows made of jars
and reaches into their hovels.
Thus, when this wind strikes a person,
it feels stifling, murky, and depressing,
driving in heat and bringing on dampness.
It fills the heart with distress
and breeds illness and fever.
Striking the lips, it causes sores;
hitting the eyes, it causes redness.
It makes one gasp and struggle,
caught between life and death.
This is what is called the common people's feminine wind."
In the fourteenth year of the Jìn dynasty,
I was thirty-two years of age
and first saw gray hairs.
Serving as a subordinate to the Grand Marshal and concurrently as the Palace Guard Commander,
I was stationed in the Secretariat.
High pavilions reached the clouds,
where the sunlight rarely shone;
there, scholars wearing cicada-adorned caps and fine silks
spent their time.
I am a man of the fields,
whose rest was never more than beneath thatched roofs and lush forests,
and whose conversation was never more than with farmers and elders.
Taking up office to fill a vacancy,
I was humbly placed among the court ranks.
Rising early and retiring late,
I had no leisure to find peace.
Like a fish in a pond or a bird in a cage,
I yearned for the rivers, lakes, mountains, and marshes.
Thereupon, I dipped my brush and took up paper
to write this rhapsody with deep emotion.
As it was then autumn,
I titled the piece 'Autumn Sentiments.'
Its words say:
The four seasons follow their sequence in haste,
and the myriad things swirl and turn in profusion.
I look upon the timely growth of planted flowers
and observe the source of their flourishing and decay.
I am moved by the desolation of winter and the blossoming of spring,
and sigh at the luxuriance of summer and the falling of autumn.
Though the prosperity or decline of a lowly official
is like the beauty or ugliness of human nature.
Well were the words of Sòng Yù when he said:
"How sorrowful is the air of autumn!
Desolate indeed, as the grass and trees shake, wither, and decay.
Mournful as if setting out on a long journey,
climbing mountains and looking over waters to see one off on a return."
Sending one back brings the longing of those left behind;
a long journey holds the bitterness of a traveler.
Facing the river, one is moved by the flow and laments the passing of time;
climbing a mountain, one yearns for the far-off and grieves for what is near.
These four sorrows distress the heart;
meeting them all on one path is hard to endure.
Alas, how lamentable are the days of autumn;
truly there is no sorrow that does not reach its end.
Swallows return across the fields,
and hawks soar over the marshes.
Wandering mists rise in the morning,
and withered leaves fall in the evening.
Thereupon I set aside the light fan
and take off the fine linen.
I lay out mats of rushes
and put on lined robes.
The trees in the courtyard are bare and desolate,
and a stiff wind rages, blowing against the curtains.
Cicadas chirp shrilly in the cold,
and geese drift southward in flight.
The sky is bright and exceedingly high,
while the sun is distant and its warmth gradually fades.
How short the duration of that faint sunlight;
I sense the cold nights are becoming long.
The moon is hazy and holds its light,
and the dew is cold and congealed in its chill.
Fireflies shine brilliantly at the steps and doors,
and crickets chirp by the porch and screen.
I listen to the morning cry of the solitary goose
and gaze at the remaining light of the fading Fire Star.
Throughout the night I am upright and sleepless,
tossing and turning alone in the grand office.
I realize the year is coming to its end
and sigh as I bow my head in self-reflection.
Speckled sideburns grow thin beneath my cap,
and white hair falls sparsely over my collar.
I look up at the soaring paths of the many talents
who climb the Milky Way to gallop and roam.
They ascend the Spring Terrace in joyous spirits,
with gold and sable ornaments shining brightly.
Since the paths of seeking and abandoning are different,
how can one know whether one is restless or still?
I have heard of the fine influence of the ultimate man,
who equates heaven and earth with a single finger.
They know peace and forget danger,
thus passing out of life and into death.
One walks by placing his feet in existing tracks,
yet almost fails to find a place to stand without treading upon them.
Fearing to step sideways and fall into the spring,
even monkeys and apes would not tread there.
The tortoise has its bones offered in the ancestral temple,
yet it longs to return its body to the green waters.
And so, I tidy my robes to return home,
and suddenly cast off my official ribbons to soar high.
I till the fertile soil of the Dōng Gāo,
and pay the remaining taxes of millet and grain.
Springs gush in rapids among the rocks,
and chrysanthemums spread their fragrance by the cliff shores.
I wash in the trickling autumn waters,
and watch the darting minnows splash.
I wander leisurely in the bends of mountains and rivers,
and live freely in the world of men.
In ease and leisure,
I shall thus pass my years.
The year is drawing to a close,
and the hour has grown dark.
Cold winds gather,
and sorrowful clouds thicken.
Liáng Wáng was displeased,
and went for a stroll in Tù Yuán.
Thereupon he set out fine wine,
and summoned his guests and friends.
He called for Zōu Shēng,
and invited Méi Sǒu.
Xiāngrú arrived last,
and was seated to the right of the guests.
Soon, a light sleet fell,
followed by dense snow.
The King then sang "Běi Fēng" from the "Wèi Shī",
and chanted "Nán Shān" from the "Zhōu Yǎ".
He handed a tablet to Grandee Sīmǎ,
saying:
"Draw forth your hidden thoughts,
and give rein to your beautiful words;
match the colors and weigh the descriptions,
to compose a rhapsody for me."
Xiāngrú then left his mat and rose,
hesitated a moment, and bowed.
He said: "I have heard that Xuě Gōng was built in the eastern states,
and Xuě Shān tower in the western regions.
Qí Chāng composed a song on 'coming back',
and Jī Mǎn offered a song at Huáng Zhú.
The "Cáo Fēng" compared its color to hempen robes,
and the Chǔ ballads paired their melodies with "Yōu Lán".
When it reaches a foot deep, it presents an omen of a bountiful year;
when it spans a zhang, it signals a disturbance in the dark virtues.
Far-reaching indeed is the significance of the season of snow!
Pray let me speak of its beginning.
When the dark pitch-pipe reaches its end,
and the harsh qi rises.
Jiāo Xī dries up,
and Tāng Gǔ congeals.
Huǒ Jǐng are extinguished,
and the Wēn Quán turn to ice.
The boiling pools no longer surge,
and the fiery winds do not rise.
The northern doors are plastered shut,
and the people of the naked lands hang up silks.
Then, clouds arise from the rivers and seas,
and sand flies in the Shuò Mò.
Mists and vapors layer upon each other,
obscuring the sun and hiding the dawn-glow.
Sleet patters and gathers first,
then snow falls in confusion and grows heavy.
As for its appearance:
it is scattered and interlaced,
misty and desolate.
Abundant and floating,
falling fast and fluttering.
Flying and sprinkling in succession,
lingering and piling up.
At first, it follows the eaves and covers the ridgepoles,
and finally, it opens the curtains and enters the gaps.
First it gracefully swirls in the courtyards and corridors,
then it drifts and fills the curtains and mats.
Following a square shape, it becomes a jade tablet,
and meeting a circular one, it forms a jade disc.
Gazing at the marshes, ten thousand acres are all as white silk;
looking at the mountains, a thousand crags are all white.
Thus the terraces are like layered jade,
and the roads like strings of precious gems.
The courtyards are lined with stairs of carnelian,
and the forests stand with trees of jasper.
The white crane loses its freshness,
and the white pheasant loses its purity.
White silk sleeves are ashamed of their luster,
and jade faces are eclipsed in their beauty.
When the accumulated purity is not yet diminished,
and the white sun shines fresh,
it is as brilliant as the Zhú Lóng,

Then there are the dripping icicles,
hanging from the eaves at every corner,

who opens clams to display bright pearls.
As for the appearance of its swirling profusion,
and the manner of its bright and pure luster;

and the wonder of its flying clusters and condensed radiance.
Truly it is ever-changing and infinite,
and alas, difficult to fully comprehend!
If one seeks to extend the joy of appreciation without end,
the night is deep and quiet, full of many thoughts.
The wind strikes the pillars and changes its sound,
and the moon meets the curtains and passes through its light.
Pouring the fine wine of Xiāng and Wú,
and wearing double robes of fox and raccoon.
Facing the pair of cranes dancing in the courtyard,
and watching the solitary flight of the geese in the clouds.
Treading on the intermingled frost and snow,
pitying the parting of branches and leaves.
Sending distant thoughts across a thousand miles,
wishing to join hands and return together.
Zōu Yáng heard this,
and was filled with admiration.
Cherishing his own beautiful song,
he respectfully added a final verse.
Thereupon he rose and composed the "Song of Accumulated Snow."
The song said:
Taking the hand of a beautiful lady, we draw the heavy curtains;
reaching for the patterned quilts, we sit on fragrant cushions.
Lighting the incense brazier, the bright candles glow;
pouring cinnamon wine, we raise a clear melody.
Then he continued with the "Song of White Snow."
The song said:
The melody has been raised and the wine set out,
flushed faces turn toward each other in intimacy.
I wish to lower the curtains and nestle against the pillow,
thinking of unfastening the jade pendant and loosening the sash.
Resenting that the years so easily turn to dusk,
grieving that there is no cause for a future meeting.
Do you not see the white snow upon the stairs?
How could it shine so brightly in the sunny spring?
The song ended.
The King then contemplated and savored it,
stroking the text and clasping his wrists in admiration.
He looked to Méi Shù,
and asked him to rise and provide the envoi.
The envoi said:
White feathers may be white,
but their substance is light.
White jade may be white,
but it vainly guards its constancy.
None are like this snow,
which rises and falls with the seasons.
Though the dark Yin congeals, it does not obscure its purity;
though the great Sun shines, it does not hold fast its integrity.
How could "constancy" be my name?
How could "purity" be my virtue?
Relying on clouds to ascend and descend,
following the wind to drift and fall.
Taking shape according to the things it meets,
and distributing its form according to the ground.
Its whiteness is established by chance,
and its stain is formed by what dyes it.
Letting the heart be pure and bright,
what is there to worry about or strive for?
When Chén Wáng had just lost Yìng Zhēn and Liú Zhēn,
he was filled with sorrow and had much leisure.
Green moss grew in the pavilions,
and fragrant dust gathered on the terraces.
Quietly his heart was pained,
and he found no joy in the middle of the night.
Then he cleared the Lán Lù,
and walked through the Guì Yuàn.
He let the pipes sound over the cold mountains,
and rested his carriage on the autumn slopes.
Facing the deep ravines, he resented the distance;
climbing the high peaks, he grieved at the remoteness.
At that time, the Xié Hàn bordered the left,
and the sun's path moved from the Běi Lù to the south.
White dew dimmed the sky,
and the plain moon flowed across the heavens.
He pondered the chapters of Qí,
and attentively read the scrolls of Chén.
He drew his brush and brought forth a tablet,
to command Zhòng Xuān.
Zhòngxuān knelt and said:
"Your servant is a person from the remote eastern borders,
raised among hills and woods.
Ignorant of the Way and lacking in learning,
I have alone received your enlightened favor.
I have heard that 'sinking and submerging' constitutes righteousness,
and 'high and bright' constitutes the constant law.
The sun represents the Yáng virtue;
the moon represents the Yīn spirit.
It holds the Fúguāng over the Eastern Marsh
and succeeds the Ruòyīng in the Western Abyss.
It leads the Xuántù at the Emperor's Terrace
and gathers Sù'é in the Rear Palace.
Its waxing and waning warn of deficiencies;
its first light and the dark of the moon show humility.
Following the seasons, it spreads its illumination;
following the stars, it moistens with wind.
It adds splendor to the Táishì
and spreads its brilliance through the Xuāngōng.
By bestowing its radiance, the Wú enterprise flourished;
by sinking its essence, the Hàn Way harmonized.
As for when the atmosphere clears over the earth's surface
and clouds recede to the sky's edge;
when Dòngtíng Lake begins to ripple
and tree leaves slightly fall;
when chrysanthemums scatter their fragrance on the mountain peaks
and wild geese send their mournful cries along the riverbanks;
then its pure substance rises distantly
and its clear brilliance descends in abundance.
The numerous constellations are obscured by its richness;
the Chánghé is enveloped by its reflection.
The Róuqí is like congealed snow;
the Yuánlíng is like a water-mirror.
The connected towers are white as silk;
the surrounding courtyards are clean as ice.
The Prince then tires of the morning's joys
and finds pleasure in the night banquet.
He withdraws the wonderful dancers
and loosens the clear chimes.
Leaving the candlelit rooms,
he goes to the Moon Pavilion.
Fragrant wine is served,
and the singing zither is presented.
Now when the cool night turns chilly
and the wind in the bamboos creates a rhythm,
although kinsmen do not follow,
the lonely travelers are invited in turn.
Listening to the evening cries of the marsh birds,
hearing the autumn melodies of the northern flutes,
then the strings of the paulownia zither are refined in sound,
and music and appearance are chosen for harmony.
Lingering amidst the Fánglù,
sorrowfully at Yáng Ā.
The sounds of the forest are like hollow pipes;
the ripples on the sunken pond vanish.
With feelings so tangled, where can they be placed?
I appeal to the bright moon and sing a long song.
The song goes:
'The beauty has departed, and news is cut off;
separated by a thousand miles, we share the bright moon.
Facing the wind I sigh—when will it cease?
The river path is long and cannot be crossed.'
Before the song's echoes ended,
the remaining light was nearly gone.
Everyone in the hall changed their expression,

Again he sang a song:
'The moon has set and the dew is about to dry;

Chén Wáng said:
'Excellent!'
Thereupon he ordered the attendants
to offer toasts and present jades.
Respectfully cherishing these 'jade sounds,'

Yì served as Grand Tutor to the King of Chángshā.
In the third year,
an owl flew into Yì's residence
and stopped in the corner of his seat.
The owl resembles a screech-owl;
it is a bird of ill omen.
Since Yì was living in exile in Chángshā,
and Chángshā was low and damp,
Yì felt self-pity and grief,
believing his life would not be long.
Therefore, he composed a rhapsody to console himself.
Its words said:
'In the year of Dānyuè,
in the fourth month of early summer,
on the day of Gēngzǐ when the sun was low,
an owl alighted in my house.
It stopped in the corner of my seat,
appearing quite calm and leisurely.
When a strange creature thus gathered,
I privately wondered at the cause.
Opening books to divine it,
the omens spoke of its portents.
It said: "When a wild bird enters the room,
the master of the house is about to depart."
I asked the owl:
"Where am I to go?
If it be good, tell me;
if bad, speak of its disaster.
As for the measure of delay or speed,
tell me the time."
The owl then sighed,
raised its head and flapped its wings.
Its mouth could not speak,
so it requested to respond with its heart.
The myriad things transform and change;
indeed, there is no rest.
Revolving and shifting,
some are pushed and return.
Form and Qì alternate and continue,
transforming like the molting of a cicada.
Profound and boundless,
how can it be fully told?
Fortune is what misfortune leans upon;
misfortune is where fortune hides.
Sorrow and joy gather at the same gate;
auspicious and inauspicious signs dwell in the same region.
That state of Wú was strong and great,
yet Fūchāi met with defeat.
Yuè was sheltered at Huìjī,
yet Gōujiàn became hegemon of the world.
Sī's travels were finally successful,
yet in the end he suffered the five punishments.
Fù Yuè was a convict laborer,
