yet he became the minister to Wǔ Dīng.
As for misfortune and fortune,
how are they different from a twisted rope?
Fate cannot be explained;
who knows its limit?
When water is struck, it surges;
when an arrow is struck, it goes far.
All things revolve and clash,
shaking and transforming each other.
Clouds steam and rain falls,
entangled and confused with one another.
The Dàjūn casts out things,
vast and boundless without end.
Heaven cannot be anticipated;
the Way cannot be plotted.
Late or early, there is fate;
how can one know its time?
Furthermore, Heaven and Earth are the furnace,
and Zàohuà is the smith.
Yīn and Yáng are the charcoal,
and the myriad things are the copper.
Combining and dispersing, waxing and waning,
how can there be a constant rule?
A thousand changes and ten thousand transformations
have no beginning or end.
Suddenly one becomes a human,
why should that be held onto tightly?
Transforming into something different,
why should that be a cause for worry?
Those of small wisdom are selfish,
devaluing others and exalting themselves.
The person of attainment has a broad view,
and for them, no thing is unacceptable.
The greedy man dies for wealth;
the heroic man dies for fame.
The boastful man dies for power;
the common people long for life.
Those driven by fear and pressure
rush east or west.
The Great Man is not biased;
myriad changes are all the same to him.
The foolish man is bound by custom,
confined like a prisoner.
The Zhìrén disregards things
and dwells alone with the Way.
The multitude are confused,
their likes and dislikes accumulating by the millions.
The Zhēnrén is calm and indifferent,
resting alone with the Way.
Casting off wisdom and abandoning form,
he transcendently loses himself.
In the vast and boundless emptiness,
he soars with the Way.
He flows with the current and goes;
he stops when he finds a bank.
Giving himself up to fate,
he does not treat his life as his own possession.'
Its birth is like floating,
its death is like resting.
Placid as the stillness of a deep spring,
drifting like an unmoored boat.
Not treasuring itself because of life,
it nurtures emptiness and floats.
The virtuous man is without burdens;
knowing fate, he does not worry.
Petty matters and trifles
are not enough to cause doubt.
At that time, Huáng Zǔ’s eldest son, Shè, held a great gathering for guests.
Someone presented a parrot,
and raising a cup of wine before Héng, he said:
“Scholar Niè,
today there is nothing to entertain the guests.
I venture that since this bird has come from afar,
and is bright, wise, clever, and good,
being the most precious of the feathered tribes,
I wish for you, Sir, to compose a rhapsody for it,
so that all those seated around may together enjoy the sight—
would that not be well?”
Héng then composed the rhapsody;
his brush did not stop its composition,
and he added no corrections to the text.
The words said:
Oh, the divine bird of the Xīyù,
manifesting a marvelous form of nature.
It embodies the wondrous essence of Metal
and joins with the bright radiance of the virtue of Fire.
Its nature is eloquent and wise, capable of speech;
its talent is clever and bright, discerning the subtle signs.
Thus it plays among the high and steep,
and perches within the secluded and deep.
It does not land at random when flying;
it must choose its forest when soaring.
Dark purple feet and vermilion beak;
a green coat and kingfisher-blue collar.
Brilliantly colorful and beautiful appearance;
chirping and pleasant sounds.
Though of the same clan as other feathered creatures,
it is truly distinct in wisdom and different in mind.
It matches the Luán and Huáng in equal beauty;
how could its virtue be compared to the common birds?
Thereupon, envying the far-reaching spread of its fragrant reputation,
and admiring its laudable divine appearance,
they commanded the foresters at Lǒngdǐ
and ordered Bóyì to the Liúshā.
Crossing over Kūnlún to cast their hunting arrows;
topping the clouds and rainbows to spread their nets.
Although the nets were fully prepared,
it was ultimately caught by a single mesh.
Furthermore, its bearing is leisurely;
it remains steadfast and calm.
It is not afraid when approached,
nor startled when stroked.
It would rather be submissive to stay far from harm
than be defiant and lose its life.
Therefore, those who presented it whole were rewarded,
while those who injured its flesh were punished.
Thereupon, it resigned itself to its fate in extremity,
leaving its flock and losing its mates.
Enclosed in a carved cage,
its wing feathers were clipped.
Drifting for ten thousand lǐ,
through rugged and repeated obstacles.
Crossing the Mín mountains and passing through barriers,
repeatedly suffering through cold and heat.
Like a woman leaving home to marry,
or a minister leaving his person to serve a lord.
Even when the wise and sagacious meet with calamity,
they still linger as sojourners.
How much more so for a tiny thing like a bird,
to be tamed and live in peace.
Looking back at the western road with long-held thoughts;
gazing toward its old home, standing for a long time.
Thinking of its humble body’s rank smell,
why should it trouble the cauldron or sacrificial stand?
Alas, that its fortune and fate are so meager;
why has it encountered such treacherous times?
Is it that speech is the stepping stone to disorder?
Or that a lack of secrecy leads to danger?
Pained by the eternal separation of mother and child;
mourning the living parting of husband and wife.
It is not that its remaining years are worth regretting,
but it pities the ignorance of its many chicks.
Leaving behind the lower lands of the barbarians,
to attend upon the radiant bearing of a gentleman.
Fearing that its reputation and reality do not match;
ashamed that its talents have nothing extraordinary.
Envying the fertile soil of the Xīdū;
knowing the different suitability of bitterness and joy.
Cherishing the distant thoughts of Dài and Yuè;
therefore, every time it speaks, it mentions these things.
Now when Shǎohào takes charge of the season,
and Rùshōu readies the reins.
Severe frost begins to fall;
the cool wind is soughing.
Chanting longingly for the distant;
its mournful cries affect its kind.
Its voice is sorrowful and resonant;
its appearance is wretched and haggard.
Those who hear it are grieved;
those who see it shed tears.
Banished ministers sigh repeatedly for it;
abandoned wives sob for it.
Sensing the companionship of its whole life,
like the Xūn and Chí flutes needing each other.
Why today are the two severed,
like the different regions of Hú and Yuè?
Submitting to the cage and bars, looking up and down;
peering through the door and window, hesitating and pacing.
Recalling the high peaks of Kūnlún;
thinking of the spreading branches of Dènglín.
Looking back at its ruined wing feathers;
though it may struggle and speed, where can it go?
Its heart longs to return but cannot;
it only harbors resentment in a single corner.
If it exhausts its heart in what it serves,
how would it dare turn its back on kindness or forget its origins?
Entrusting its light and lowly tiny life;
resigning its humble and base meager body.
Expecting to maintain death to repay virtue;
willing to exhaust its words to offer its folly.
Relying on the great favor of the past;
hoping that as time passes, it will not change.
The Jiāoliáo
is a small bird,
born among the mugwort and weeds,
growing up beneath fences and hedges,
soaring and landing within a small space,
and the principles of living are sufficient for it.
Its color is plain and its body humble;
it is not used by people.
Its form is tiny and its position low;
nothing harms it.
It multiplies its kind,
perching in groups and swimming in pairs,
fluttering about and finding joy for itself.
Those vultures, ospreys, Kūnhóng, and swans,
peacocks and kingfishers—
some soar to the edge of the red empyrean,
some dwell beyond the farthest reaches.
Their wings are enough to pierce the sky,
and their beaks and talons are enough to defend themselves.
Yet all bear the hunting arrows and are entangled by the strings;
their feathers are sent as tribute.
Why?
Because they are useful to humans.
Words may be shallow yet can convey the profound;
things may be small yet can symbolize the great.
Therefore, I have composed this rhapsody.
How manifold are the ways of creation!
Sowing many forms among ten thousand kinds.
Oh, the tiny bird of the Jiāoliáo!
It too maintains its life and receives its vital breath.
It nurtures its fluttering humble body,
having no black or yellow colors to make itself precious.
Its feathers are not applied to utensils;
its meat does not ascend the sacrificial stand for flavor.
When hawks and falcons pass, they even tuck their wings;
what fear should it have of bird-nets?
In the thickets and dense undergrowth,
there it plays and gathers.
It flies without soaring high;
its soaring is not rapid.
Its dwelling is easily accommodated;
its needs are easily supplied.
Nesting in the forest, it takes no more than one branch;
for every meal, it takes no more than a few grains.
It perches without lingering;
it plays without loitering.
It does not find thorns and brambles humble,
nor does it find the Chǎi and Lán glorious.
Moving its wings, it is at ease;
setting its feet, it is at peace.
Entrusting its life to follow reason;
together with all things, it has no troubles.
Consider these birds in their ignorance,
yet how they carry themselves seems like wisdom.
They do not harbor treasures to invite harm,
nor do they adorn their appearance to attract trouble.
In stillness, they maintain simplicity without pride;
in movement, they follow nature with ease.
Relying on nature as their resource,
they have no desire for the deceptions of the world.
The eagle and the hégé bird rely on their beaks and talons;
the swan and the heron soar beyond the clouds.
The kūnjī fowl hides in dark and perilous places;
the peacock and kingfisher are born in remote regions.
Those morning ducks and returning geese,
also lift their wings and fly ever further.
All have beautiful feathers and rich flesh;
thus, though guiltless, they all meet their end.
In vain they hold reeds in their beaks to avoid arrows,
for in the end, they are slaughtered in this world.
The goshawk is fierce yet is tethered;
the parrot is clever yet enters a cage.
They subdue their wild wills to be tamed and fed,
confined in isolation within the ninefold palace.
They change their voices to suit the ruler's will,
thinking of breaking their wings to be of use.
They long for the forests and fields of Zhōng Dài,
and yearn for the tall pines on the slopes of Lǒngdǐ.
Although they receive favor today,
it is not like the leisure of former days.
The sea bird Yuánjū,
arrived to escape the wind.
The giant birds of Tiǎozhī,
brought themselves across the mountains.
Carried for ten thousand lǐ,
fluttering in fear and awe.
It is only because their large bodies obstruct things,
and their magnificent forms are so extraordinary.
As Yīn and Yáng transform and steam,
the myriad species occupy one realm.
The great and the small are mixed and varied,
many in species and diverse in kind.
The jiāomíng nests on a gnat's eyelash,
while the great Péng spans the corners of heaven.
Looking upward, it is never enough;
comparing downward, there is always plenty.
Gazing afar across the whole earth,
how can I know where greatness or smallness leads?
A Jì horse is not praised for its strength alone;
horses are named after dragons.
Is it not because the state values majestic appearance,
and the army values agility and speed?
Truly, there are those with soaring light who reveal diagrams,
possessing the virtue of auspicious signs for a Sage.
Therefore, words exalt their spirit,
and the world honors their arrival.
When our Gāozǔ founded the Sòng dynasty,
the five regions performed their duties,
and the four corners brought tribute.
Secret treasures filled the Jade Storehouse;
patterned teams of four lined the Splendid Stables.
Then there was the Imperial Zhěbái,
who possessed a particularly extraordinary form.
Exquisitely selected by the Emperor's heart,
it was granted to the imperial stable.
Its service followed the Emperor's will;
its galloping was always in measure.
Though its years have declined with age,
its beautiful skills have not faltered.
Nurtured over many years,
the imperial favor was profound and all-encompassing.
As its years grew old and its spirit exhausted,
it died in the inner stable.
Having spent its strength in youth,
the Sovereign's benevolence was moved with pity.
Thus he commanded his attendants
to convey his inner intentions.
I, your humble servant, mediocre and obscured,
venture to join in presenting this rhapsody.
Its words say:
In the twenty-second year of the Sòng,
the magnificent achievements shine through successive generations.
Military righteousness has been solemnly deployed;
civil education has reached full harmony.
The level of the Grand Staircase can be ascended;
the tracks of rising kings can be followed.
Seeking the beauties of the state in old histories,
examining the records of the regions in ancient documents.
Of old, when Emperor Xuānyuán ascended the throne,
the Fēihuáng horse served in his stable.
When the Sovereign of Táng received the Mandate,
the Red-Writ horse appeared at the sun.
When the Way of Hàn flourished, Heavenly Horses displayed their talent;
when the Virtue of Wèi prospered, Marsh Horses showed their substance.
Those extraordinary and peerless feet,
have appeared intermittently since ancient times.
All are glorified in the auspicious records,
and recorded in the suburban songs of the Music Masters.
They are used to exalt and guard the majestic spirit,
and to protect the imperial processions.
Their essence and brilliance harmonize,
and all spiritual creatures are ranked in order.
Since the foundation of the Bright Mandate,
the nine regions have all been submissive.
Some ventured through perils to receive the calendar;
others crossed great distances to offer tribute.
Hearing of the prosperity of the King's assembly,
knowing that the land of Xià was filled to overflowing.
Gathering the wise from the six zones,
and obtaining fine steeds from the seven tribes.
This horse is of the fine kind that rides the wind,
truly the great descendant of the Sun's shadow.
Thus it could replace the side-horses of the Elephant Chariot,
and be paired with the stars of Gōuchén.
Its years were long and extended;
its reputation was high and resounding.
Truly a gift from the Holy Ancestor,
it remained in the Imperial favor and advanced frequently.
Just observe its tendons and bones,
its trailing tail and erect mane.
Its two eyes are like mirrors;
its two cheekbones are like the crescent moon.
Its unusual body has peaks like mountains;
its extraordinary appearance is full of vigor.
It leaps beyond the tracks of dust,
its galloping faster than a disappearing shadow.
Selected as great at the fortress gates,
its form was presented at the Crimson Palace.
At dawn it brushed through Yōuyān;
at noon it grazed in Jīngyuè.
Teaching reverence is an unchangeable canon;
instructing the people is an act that must be recorded.
The Emperor and the Ancestor,
here they traveled and took pleasure.
Flying light carriages to clear the way,
surrounding archers and cavalry to purify the road.
Ordering the five camps to inspect their divisions,
sounding the eight bells to pace the steps.
Fully equipped with golden silks,
and adorned with vermilion and cinnabar.
Precious bits like stars entwined,
carved patterns spread like clouds.
Advancing close to the guards,
following behind the imperial carriage.
Suddenly it rears up like a startled wild goose,
then it soars gracefully like a dragon.
Subduing its majestic posture to lead the way,
with a gentle heart it waits to be ridden.
When the dew is moist and the moon is clear,
when the frost is sharp and autumn harvests are in.
The King sets out on a journey,
to display his majestic power.
Looking out from the heights,
seated on a hundred-layered terrace.
Evaluating martial skills,
ranking the galloping steeds.
Flowing patterns are spread all around,
and harmonious bells are set in place.
Looking at its shadow and neighing loudly,
it is about to leap across the middle of the field.
Racing across the distant grounds,
competing in strength on the long track.
Surpassing its companions and leaving the herd,
its colorful harness trailing far behind.
Spurred by the agile hands of the riders,
urged by the rapid beats of the flower-drums.
Passing like dark hooves scattering hail,
crossing like white limbs cracking ice.
Its chest is stained with ocher foam;
its sweat-grooves run with blood.
Though its tracks wind back and forth,
its pent-up fury is not yet spent.
The Emperor's heart descends with a slight joy;
the people of the capital look up with collective delight.
Once the displays of beauty and transformation are finished,
its soaring and hasty spirit remains.
Though constrained by the bit and bridle,
and confined by the enclosures of the great city.
It looks toward the far west and raises its head,
gazes at the northern clouds and stomps its feet.
It could be paired with the Zǐyàn at the yoke,
or the Lǜshé to guard the wheels.
Following the heels of the Xiānlí horse,
and standing alongside the Xiùqí.
To see the Wángmǔ at the ruins of Kūnxū,
and meet at the Emperor's Terrace at Xuānyuè.
Crossing the tracks of the Central Realm,
exhausting the paths of divine travel.
However, indulging in pleasure and hunting,
serving as a mirror to previous kings.
Acting willfully over the people,
bringing regret to the path of righteousness.
The Tiānzǐ then halted his carriage and turned his thoughts,
resting his followers and unpacking the gear.
Taking Wǔmù as a reflection,
and modeling himself after Wénguāng.
Relieving the hidden hardships of the people,
and cultivating the state statutes.
Warning against the failed driving caused by a bolting pig,
and being wary of birds perching on the yoke.
Thus, being scrupulously careful about what is usually neglected,
and respectfully preparing for what has not been guarded against.
The carriage has the stability of double wheels,
and the horse is free from the idleness of overturning the coach.
Placed in the inner chambers of Zhuólóng,
and entrusted with an official rank of red grain.
Submitting to care and knowing benevolence,
following old age to reach the end of life.
Covered with a worn curtain,
his fallen remains were collected.
The Heavenly sentiment was comprehensive,
and the Imperial grace was complete.
The Luàn says:
Only virtue moves Heaven;
a divine creature is the model.
At this time, grand steeds
fill the steps and streets.
Endowed with the spirit of the Yuèsì constellation,
they are descended from the Yúnchī.
Their heroic will is free and easy,
their spirit extraordinary and unique.
Being both strong and virtuous,
they submit to the bridle and halter.
Rendering service at Zhōnghuáng,
they are devoted to galloping and racing.
Wishing to finish in kind care,
sheltering the original branches.
Yet preceding the morning dew,
they are forever discarded and gone.
Examining the mysterious classics to verify things,
I marvel at the immortal bird born of the womb.
Concentrating a buoyant and vast refined essence,
it embraces a clear and distant bright mind.
Pointing toward Pénghú and fluttering its wings,
it looks toward Kūnlàng and raises its cry.
Circling the solar realm with a turning gallop,
exhausting the celestial steps in high pursuit.
Having trodden far into the divine regions,
spiritual sacrifices have accumulated for many years.
Its essence contains cinnabar, shining like stars;
its crown congeals purple, flowering like mist.
Stretching the slender elegance of its round throat,
it bends the grand beauty of its long legs.
Folding its frost-white feathers and playing with its shadow,
it shakes its jade-like wings and approaches the clouds.
In the morning, it plays in the Zhītián;
in the evening, it drinks at the Yáochí.
Tired of rivers and seas, it wanders the marshes,
but is caught in the cloudy net and restrained.
Leaving the solitude of the Emperor's realm,
it returns to the clamor and baseness of the human world.
The year is aging and grieving for its end,
and the heart is melancholy, mourning the separation.
At this time of extreme Yīn and the killing season,
the fleeting light marks the dying year.
Cold sands shake the wilderness,
and the Jī wind moves the heavens.
Severe, bitter fogs,
white, sorrowful springs.
Ice blocks the Chánghé,
and snow fills the many mountains.
Soon the murky night rests,
and the scenery becomes clear and vast.
Stars overturn and the Hàn galaxy turns,
the dawn moon is about to set.
Moved by the early morning of the cold rooster,
pitying the frost-covered geese leaving the desert.
Facing the desolation of the startling wind,
opposite the brilliance of the flowing light.
It cries out a clear sound on the Dānchí,
and dances with a flying form at the Jīngé.
Beginning with a soaring Phoenix-like stride,
it ends with a graceful Dragon-like leap.
Pacing back and forth,
shaking swiftly and rising high.
Startling its body like tumbling tumbleweeds,
it raises its wings like flying snow.
Breaking from the ranks and departing separately,
joining the threads and leaning on one another.
About to rise but stopping midway,
as if going but then returning.
Swiftly descending with proud looks,
it lingers until the late evening.
Its swift wings leave dust behind,
soaring and flying ahead on the path.
Pointing to the gathering and soaring in circles,
it faces the crossroads with measured steps.
Its posture has lingering beauty,
its appearance has unending charm.
Rushing like a machine following the rhythm,
its eyes glance and forms separate.
Swaying long and galloping slowly,
with wings paired and voices joined.
Light tracks are scattered,
and floating shadows cross one another.
Many changes in complex poses,
uneven yet dense in succession.
Smoke mingles and mist congeals,
as if it has no physical plumage.
Wind departs and rain returns,
it cannot be fully described.
Having scattered the soul and dazzled the eyes,
one is confused and knows not where it goes.
Suddenly stars disperse and clouds dissipate,
it adjusts its divine appearance and holds its poise.
Looking up at the loftiness of the Heavenly dwelling,
feeling more melancholy with startling thoughts.
At this time,
the beauties of Yàn lose their color,
and the boys of Bā feel ashamed in their hearts.
The scarf and whisk both stop,
and the balls and swords both cease.
Though Hándān might dare to compare,
how could Yáng’ā possibly emulate?
Entering the state of Wèi and riding in a carriage,
leaving the capital of Wú and captivating the city.
Keeping tame through a thousand years,
it knots long sorrow across ten thousand miles.
Descended from the dark lineage of Gāoxù,
a clan of brilliant spirits from the middle generations.
Riding the southern wind and molting like a cicada,
heroic in the northern wilderness, spreading its fame.
Through ten imperial cycles, progressing like a swan,
possessing wings and decorum in the Shàngjīng.
Great floods reached the heavens and extinguished Xià,
the father met with sorrow and composed songs.
Finally preserving oneself and leaving a model,
residing in the neighborhood of supreme benevolence.
How beautiful the pure virtue of former ancestors,
whether in poverty or success, they always crossed through.
Alas, this lonely and ignorant one is so small,
facing ruin and disconnection without a ladder to climb.
Is it my body that is worth sacrificing,
or the abandonment of the ancestral legacy that I cherish?
Quietly dwelling in seclusion to meditate forever,
as days and months pass, the distance grows.
Not that I dare to associate with those people,
I hope these words will not bring disgrace.
The soul, lonely and solitary, communes with the spirit,
sincerity arises from the nightly sleep.
Dreaming of climbing a mountain and looking far off,
I glimpse the faint likeness of a recluse.
He grabs the creepers and hands them to me,
looking at the steep valley and saying, "Do not fall!"
Waking at dawn and thinking upward,
the heart is murky and has not yet perceived.
The Huángshén is distant and without form,
consulting the remaining omens to match my thoughts.
It says: Ascending high and meeting the spirit,
the way leads far and clear without confusion.
The creepers stretch long on the drooping trees,
chanting "Nánfēng" to bring peace.
Apprehensively approaching the deep,
is what the two Yǎ respect.
Having informed you with auspicious signs,
and again with bright caution.
Why not strive forward to catch up with the crowd?
The time is fleeting and will not come again.
Serene and slow, I receive the divine teachings,
Lingering and waiting as I stand.
Only Heaven and Earth are infinite,
Rare is the clarity among living people in their darkness.
Tangled in difficulties and stumbling in succession,
How numerous are the hardships, yet how meager is wisdom!
Even the highest sages meet opposition before being raised up,
Though they are resisted by the common masses.
In the past, when Wèi Shū drove for his brother,
The brother became a bandit and I was lost.
Guǎn drew his bow, wishing to kill his enemy,
But the enemy became the sovereign and fulfilled him.
Changes in circumstances are so deceptive,
Who can predict the end or the beginning!
Yōng built up resentment yet was first rewarded,
Dīng was favored but then executed.
Lì met with mourning where there should have been luck,
The King received celebration in what he grieved.
Fate turns and twists like this,
The Běi Sǒu somewhat understood its lurking fortunes and misfortunes.
Shàn managed the inner but withered on the outside,
Zhāng refined the outer but was pressured within.
Seeking the Middle Way and harmony as a goal,
Even Yán and Rǎn did not achieve it.
Nì beckoned Lù to join him,
Claiming that the way of Kǒng was still not right.
Peacefully idling without flourishing,
In the end, they fell victim to the world's calamities.
Wandering in the gate of the Sage yet finding no rescue,
Though one be minced into meat, what does it mend?
To be obstinate and forceful surely leads to disaster;
To escape robbery and chaos, one relies on the Way.
Form and Qi emerge from the roots;
Branches and leaves gather, withering or flourishing.
I fear the Wǎngliǎng shadow-monsters reproaching the shadow;
Alas, I have not yet reached the end of it.
The Lí clan shone brightly during the time of Gāoxīn,
The Mi clan grew powerful by the southern waters of Sì.
The Yíng took their majesty from Bóyí,
The Jiāng family branched out from Sānzhǐ.
Since benevolence is truly attained,
Look up to the heavenly path and follow the same track.
The eastern neighbor was cruel and destroyed the benevolent,
The King joined the ranks of the Three and Five.
The Róng woman was fierce and lost her filial piety;
The Count went and returned to the dragons and tigers.
Fā turned back the army to fulfill the mandate,
Zhòng walked as if drunk and found his mate.
The dragon's scales dripped foam in the courtyard of Xià;
Passing through three cycles, it destroyed the Jī clan.
The phoenix feather transformed in the palace of Xuān,
Spanning five monarchs and becoming a disaster.
The Way is long and the generation is short;
Distant, dark, and silent, it is not comprehensive.
Waiting upon things and consulting with spirits,
Thus exhausting the universe and reaching the profound.
The Guī clan nested with the Jiāng at the child's divination,
Dàn calculated the sacrifices using the scorched tortoise shell.
The rise and fall of Xuān and Cáo were in a dream,
The names and posthumous titles of Lǔ and Wèi were in inscriptions and ballads.
The Ancestress heard the cry and condemned the stone;
Xǔ examined the principles and investigated the details.
The Way is formed from chaos and is natural,
Methods share the same source but branch out.
The spirit precedes the heart to determine fate,
Fate follows action to grow or diminish.
The turning currents shift and do not settle;
Thus one encounters gain or loss.
The three Luán were of one body;
Though they changed, they did not stray.
Vast is the unevenness and tangled confusion,
This is what the many omens find confusing.
Zhōu and Jiǎ were tossed about and offered their indignation,
Equating life and death with fortune and misfortune.
Lifting bold words to correct the feelings,
Indeed fearing the sacrificial ox and dreading the owl.
What is valued is the ultimate discourse of the Sage,
To follow natural disposition and decide on righteousness.
Things have desires but do not dwell in them;
They also have aversions but do not avoid them.
Guarding the simple constraints without wavering,
Then virtue is light and without burden.
The Three Benevolent Men differed in their path to one goal,
Yí and Huì were different but shared the same reputation.
Mù rested to make Wèi flourish;
Shēn traveled with heavy callouses to save Jīng.
Jì burned his own body to protect his superior;
Hào nurtured his will and did not falter.
Look at the distinctions among grasses and trees;
If they can bear fruit, they will surely flourish.
To seek immortality after death—
That is the standard set by the people of old.
Observe the vast covering of Heaven's net;
It truly assists the faithful and provides instruction.
Planning the great path of the former sages,
It also neighbors virtue and aids sincerity.
The Sháo music of Yú was beautiful and invited the phoenix;
Kǒng forgot the taste of food even after a thousand years.
The Plain King's writing was trusted and reached the Qílín;
Hàn receives the mandate in a different age.
The essence communicates with the divine and moves things,
The spirit moves the breath and enters the subtle.
Yǎng cast his gaze and the apes wailed;
Lǐ shot at a tiger and the stone split.
Without absolute sincerity, how could one communicate?
If there is no substance, who would believe?
Even in practicing minor skills it is so,
How much more so for one devoted to the truth of the Way!
Climbing the great expanse of Heaven, ascending and descending,
Traversing the paths of the many dragons.
Seeing the truth in the morning and transforming by evening,
Still forgetting oneself and leaving the physical form behind.
If one could grow old like the descendants of Yìn Péng,
One would appeal to future sages and share these feelings.
The Envoi says:
Heaven created the primordial chaos,
And established nature and fate.
Restore the heart and broaden the Way,
Only the sages and worthies can do this.
The Primal Origin moves all things,
Flowing without rest.
Preserve the self and leave a name behind,
As a model for the people.
To give up life to choose righteousness,
Is to be used by the Way.
Grief and sorrow wither things prematurely,
There is no pain more disgraceful.
Pure and bright is the Great Simplicity,
How could its color change?
Still surpassing its subtle signs,
One sinks into the divine realm.
Looking up at the profound teachings of former sages,
Though they are ever higher, I do not stray from them.
If not in the neighborhood of benevolence, where should I dwell?
If not the tracks of righteousness, what should I follow?
Secretly taking it to heart to remain forever still,
Stretching through days and months without decline.
Indeed my inner feelings are truly cultivated,
I admire the upright integrity of the ancients.
I straighten my body and act in accordance,
Following the plumb line and ink without stumbling.
My will is concentrated to respond to what is suspended,
My sincere heart is as firm as a knot.
I flag my nature and conduct to make a pendant,
Wearing the night-shining pearl and the jade branch.
I bind the autumn flowers of the dark orchid,
And adorn them with river-parsley.
The beauty of the layers is intense and pure,
Truly distant from the dust and hard to diminish.
Already beautiful and rare without peer,
It is not what this age treasures.
I display my splendor but no one sees,
I spread my fragrance but no one hears.
In solitude, I guard this narrow and humble place,
How would I dare be idle or abandon my diligence?
The sixteen worthies luckily met with Yú,
I admire how Fù Yuè lived in the time of Yīn.
I still cherish the remaining style of the former good men,
Sorrowing that I was born later and cannot reach them.
Why must I walk alone so desolately,
Solitary, not of the crowd, standing firm?
Moved by the simurgh and the widgeon perching alone,
I grieve that virtuous people rarely find their match.
What harm is there in having no match?
The worry is that the many falsehoods pass for the truth.
Dàn received slanders from his younger brothers,
Only after opening the Jīnténg was he believed.
Observing that the common people have many biases,
I fear establishing a bias that would endanger myself.
Increasing irritation and poison in my confusion,
Alas, to whom can I speak?
Privately sinking into grief and deep reflection,
My thoughts are tangled and cannot be unraveled.
I wish to exert my strength to guard righteousness,
Though I be poor, I will not change.
To grab a carved tiger or test an elephant,
To stand on the edge of the Jiāoyuán on tiptoe.
I hope to offer this and carry it through,
I will only stop after I have died.
Customs shift and affairs change,
The round and square of the compass and square are lost.
They treasure mugwort in layered boxes,
While saying that the orchids are not fragrant.
They reject Xī Shī and do not employ her,
They tether the Yǎoniǎo steed to pull a cart.
Those whose conduct is biased and crooked achieve their aims,
While those who follow the laws and standards meet with disaster.
Only Heaven and Earth are infinite,
How inconsistent are the encounters of life!
Not suppressing my integrity to seek base favor,
is like coming to a river without a boat.
To desire artful smiles to win affection,
is not what my heart has ever practiced.
I wear the ceremonial robes of gentleness and respect,
and put on the embroidered skirts of ritual and righteousness.
I braid integrity and brightness into a belt,
and mix diverse arts into a pendant gem.
Illustrious with colorful patterns and carved jade,
the sound of the jade huáng reaches far and lingers long.
Lingering and resting to indulge my whims,
the Radiant Spirit suddenly hides in the west.
Relying on my own knowledge to make myself flourish,
the shrike cries and the fragrance is lost.
I hoped for the triple blooming within a year,
but soon the white dew becomes frost.
The seasons move tirelessly in their succession,
who is there that can be my match?
Alas, beauty and excellence are hard to find together,
I think of following Hán and going into exile.
Fearing that I will gradually age without achievement,
staying would mean being obscured and not manifest.
My heart hesitates with fox-like doubts,
I go to the slopes of Qí Zhǐ to express my feelings.
Wén Jūn consults the milfoil for me,
it is beneficial to fly away and hide to preserve my name.
I pass through various mountains in a wide circuit,
borne by the swift wind to spread my voice.
Two women were moved at the high mountain,
some break like ice and do not seek worldly gain.
Heaven is indeed high and forms the marshes,
who says the road is not level!
I strive for self-strengthening without rest,
treading the towering heights of the jade steps.
Fearing the length or shortness of the diviner's stalks,
I drill the eastern tortoise shell to observe the omen.
I encounter the solitary bird of the Jiǔ Gāo marshes,
lamenting that my original intent is not fulfilled.
Roaming beyond the dust, I glimpse at heaven,
dwelling in the dark shade, I cry mournfully.
Eagles and ospreys compete in their greed,
while I cultivate purity to increase my glory.
You have an old bond with the Xuán Niǎo bird,
return to your mother's clan to find peace.
The divination is auspicious and brings no regret,
I select an auspicious day and prepare my baggage.
At dawn, I bathe in the Qīng Yuán spring,
and dry my hair in the morning sun.
I rinse my mouth with the spray of a flying fountain,
and chew the flowing petals of the stone fungus.
Light birds rise and fish leap,
I am about to set out for the Bā Huāng.
Passing through the remote wilds of Shǎo hào,
I inquire about the Sān Qiū from Gù máng.
How pure and simple is the True Way,
casting off filth and burdens to float lightly.
Ascending Péng lái to wander at ease,
though the giant turtles clap their fins, it does not tilt.
Staying at Yíng zhōu to gather magic fungi,
merely to achieve long life.
Riding the returning clouds to journey far,
at evening, I lodge at Fú sāng.
Drinking the jade wine of the Qīng Cén peak,
and eating the evening mist as my rations.
Realizing the old dream of the Mù Hé grain,
I harvest on the high ridges of Kūn lún.
In the morning, I travel through the Tāng Gǔ valley,
following Bó Yǔ to Jī Shān.
I admire the assembly of gods holding jade,
but despise Fáng fēng for breaking his word.
Pointing toward the winding paths of Cháng shā,
I remember Zhòng huá in the southern neighborhood.
Lamenting that the two consorts have not followed,
they flutter and dwell on the Xiāng Bīn banks.
I cast my gaze toward the slopes of Héng Ā,
seeing the ruined tomb of the Yǒu lí clan.
Grieving that the Huǒ Zhèng master had no comfort,
his lonely soul is entrusted to the mountain slope.
Melancholy and longing for the distant,
I cross over Áng zhōu to roam.
I reach the midday sun at Kūn wú,
resting where the blazing fires forge.
Raising brilliant flames to redden the sky,
the waters swirl and billow in waves.
The warm wind gathers and increases the heat,
my distress and sadness are hard to endure.
Lonely and a traveler without friends,
how can I remain here?
Looking toward Jīn Tiān and sighing,
I wish to go and play in the West.
Sending Zhù róng ahead to raise the signal,
stringing the Zhū Niǎo bird to support the flag.
Treading on the Jiàn Mù tree in Guǎng dū,
I gather Ruò Huá flowers and hesitate.
Surpassing Xuān yuán at the Xī Hǎi sea,
striding over the dragon-fish of the Wāng Shì.
Hearing that this land lives for a thousand years,
how could it suffice to amuse me?
Thinking of the different customs of the Jiǔ Tǔ,
I follow Rù shōu and proceed.
Suddenly undergoing a divine transformation like a cicada,
joining with the pure and refined as companions.
Kicking open the Bái Mén gate and racing east,
the Yún Tái moves through the central wilderness.
Crossing the murmuring Ruò Shuǐ,
I stop at the turbulent islet of Huà yīn.
Calling for Féng yí to clear the ferry,
rowing the dragon boat to carry me across.
It happened that Dì Xuān had not yet returned,
disappointedly wandering and standing for a long time.
Sighing at the lushness of the river forests,
I marvel at the Guān jū that warns women.
Huáng líng divines to inquire about fate,
where does the winding Way of Heaven lead?
It is said that what is near is believed and what is far is doubted,
the Liù Jí are incomplete and do not record it.
The divine paths are dark and hard to investigate,
who can plan and follow them?
Niú āi fell ill and became a tiger,
though he met his brother, he would surely bite.
Biē lìng was killed and his body vanished,
he took the abdication of Shǔ and led the world.
Death and life are mixed and uneven,
even the Sī mìng cannot distinguish them.
Dòu was a crying beggar on the roads of Dài,
later he received the mandate and his house flourished.
Wáng was recklessly extravagant in the Hàn court,
in the end he bore sorrow and his line was cut off.
Wèi had shaggy eyebrows and remained a lowly official,
until the third generation when he met Wǔ.
Dǒng held high office in his youth,
he prepared the royal tomb but did not dwell in it.
Fortune and misfortune follow each other,
constantly turning over without a fixed place.
Mù reached Heaven and pleased the ox,
the page Shù threw Shū into chaos and imprisoned the lord.
Wén cut his sleeve and avoided the elder brother,
the eunuch served the traitor and brought peace to the empress.
Men of understanding are dark about likes and dislikes,
how could the confused analyze them?
Yíng picked a prophecy and guarded against the Hú,
preparing against the outside while the trouble arose within.
Some pull bribes and avoid the carriage,
pregnant on the way and giving birth as a response.
Shèn zào became prominent by speaking of Heaven,
divining by water and fire with reckless inquiries.
Liáng Sǒu was troubled by the Lí qiū ghosts,
he encountered his son and used the blade.
Even what is seen is not recognized,
how much less can the dark and mysterious be trusted?
Do not be tied down and hope for luck,
thinking of a hundred worries will only make one sick.
That heavenly gaze is very bright,
it aids the sincere and protects the benevolent.
Tāng purified his body to pray,
receiving great blessings to save the people.
Jǐng had three considerations to manage the state,
and Yíng huò moved to another station.
Wèi Kē was faithful in following the command,
and the ghost tripped up the enemy to defeat Qín.
Jiù yáo went forth and planted virtue,
establishing virtue that flourished in Yīng and Liù.
The mulberry tips depend on the roots,
even when plants wither, they have been nurtured.
No word goes without an answer,
and where can one go without a return?
Why not distance one's tracks to spread one's fame?
Who says that time can be stored up?
I lift my head and gaze into the distance,
my soul despondent and without a companion.
Pressed by the cramped pettiness of the world,
I shall journey north to roam and vent my feelings.
I travel over the grinding, piled-up ice;
the clear springs are frozen and do not flow.
The cold wind arrives in its piercing permanence,
brushing against the whistling, lofty peaks.
Xuánwǔ shrinks into his shell,
while the Téngshé serpent coils and twists upon itself.
Fish pride themselves on their scales yet are caught in the ice;
birds climb the trees but lose their branches.
Sitting in the dark chamber of Tàiyīn,
I sigh with lamentation, my sorrow increasing.
I resent that Gāoyáng lodged me here,
and that Zhuānxū resided in this dark place.
Why open a path to the four remote regions,
if there is no remedy for this or that?
I gaze toward the endless horizon of Hánmén,
and loose my reins at Bùzhōu.
Swift gusts moisten and escort me;
I gallop fluttering and soaring, unrestrained.
I cross through the deep, hollow caves,
and float over the rushing, resonant rivers.
Passing through layered enclosures in the silence,
I pity the deep-diving Fènyáng.
I chase the blurred shadows beneath the earth,
then pass beyond the formless and float upward.
Emerging from the dark wilds of Shìmì,
I know not which path to follow.
I urge Zhùlóng to hold his torch,
and pause for rest at Zhōngshān.
I look down upon the red banks of Yáoxī,
and mourn where the Zǔjiāng was slain.
I visit Wángmǔ at the Yíntái,
and she offers jade lichen to satisfy my hunger.
She wears her crown of victory, and though she is pleased,
she also chides me for my slow progress.
I take on board the Jade Maiden of Tàihuà,
and summon Mìfēi from the banks of the Luòpǔ.
Both are beautiful and enchanting,
with lovely eyes and moth-like brows.
They stretch their slender, graceful waists,
and toss their variegated robes and ribbons.
Their vermilion lips part in a slight smile,
their radiant countenances shedding light.
They offer rings of jade and precious silken sashes,
extending their favor with black and yellow silks.
Though their colors are brilliant and their gifts beautiful,
my mind is pure and vast, and I find no joy in them.
The two beauties grieve that they are not accepted,
and together they chant poems and sing clear songs.
The song says:
Heaven and earth are in misty union;
a hundred plants hold their buds.
Singing cranes cross their necks;
ospreys call in harmony.
The maiden harbors spring longings,
her spirit swaying and shifting.
Why is the virtuous and bright one
so truly forgetful of me?
I have no time to compose a reply,
so I prepare my carriage and depart in haste.
I behold the towering heights of Kūnlún,
and approach the vast, winding River.
Spiritual turtles lie prostrate to support the banks;
flying bridges of hornless dragons span across.
I ascend the tiered city of Làngfēng,
and construct a couch of immortality.
I grind jade stamens for my provisions,
and ladle white water for my drink.
I urge Wūxián to divine my dreams,
and it is a primary omen of auspiciousness.
I cultivate my fine virtues in the center,
and harbor excellent blooms as my display.
Having hung my blossoms and looked back to my roots,
I also yearn for my old dwelling.
At peace and tranquil, I follow the times,
for the dwelling place of pure excellence is here.
I command my many officials to meet early,
and they all attend to their duties, surprised together.
Fénglóng rumbles with crashing thunder;
Lièquē flashes, illuminating the night.
The Cloud Masters gather in profusion;
the heavy rain pours down, drenching the path.
I harness my carved carriage and plant flowers upon it;
I tame the Yìnglóng to serve on the road.
A hundred gods stand in dense attendance;
the throng of riders is spread out like stars.
I shake my sleeves and take to the carriage,
my long sword rising and falling at my side.
My lofty cap reflects the canopy;
my pendants hang in brilliant splendor.
The groom solemnly readies his whip;
the eight steeds leap and gallop forward.
The atmospheric banners dissolve like the turning sky;
the rainbow flags flutter and fly upward.
I lean on the carriage rail and look back,
my heart churning like boiling water.
I admire the brilliant light of the Shàngdū,
but how could I be so lost as to forget my home?
To the left, Qīngdiāo holds the magic herbs;
to the right, Sùwēi manages the gongs.
In front, Chánglí brushes its feathers;
in the rear, the balance is entrusted to Xuánmíng.
I charge Jībó to contain the winds,
to purge the impurities and make all clear.
I trail the cloud-banners in their fluttering,
as the jade phoenix-bells tinkle in harmony.
I cross the clear empyrean and ascend far away,
floating like a tiny gnat as I journey upward.
In many-layered order, I slowly arrive;
the winds whirl and circle, manifesting my spirit.
I call to the Gatekeeper of the Emperor to open the doors,
and behold the Tiānhuáng in his Jasper Palace.
I listen to the Nine Variations of the Great Music,
spreading out in leisurely abundance.
I examine order and chaos through the musical pitch,
intending to establish the beginning and consider the end.
Seeing that indulgence and ease are never-ending,
I fear that joy will pass and sorrow will come.
Sùnǚ touches the strings, leaving a lingering sound;
Tàiróng intones, saying, "Be mindful!"
Having guarded against excess and quieted my will,
I take advantage of my leisure to soar.
I emerge from the solemn Purple Palace,
and gather at the vast Tàiwēi.
I order Wángliáng to hold the reins of the four-horse team,
as we pass the towering heights of the High Pavilion.
Setting up the expansive hunting nets,
we hunt in the boundless Azure Forest.
Drawing the Mighty Bow with a snapping sound,
I shoot the great wolf of Bāzhǒng.
I observe the fortifications at the Northern Gate,
and strike the River Drum with a thundering boom.
I ride upon the floating celestial waters,
and drift upon the surging Milky Way.
Leaning on Chāoyáo and Shèti, I wander and drift,
observing the intricate and brilliant movements of the two nodes and five planets.
Towering and twisting,
curling and winding they go;
a dense and crowded throng,
galloping together in a gust.
Rapidly and whistling they pass,
surging like formless spirits;
brilliant, beautiful, and fine,
distant and retreating in turn.
I ride over the crashing of startled thunder,
and play with the far-reaching flash of wild lightning.
Crossing the vast chaos in the dark void,
I pierce through the inverted reflections and soar high.
Vast and wide, without limit,
I now peer beyond the heavens.
Resting on Kāiyáng, I look down,
and approach my old home in its dim shadows.
I grieve that living apart wearies the heart,
my feelings anxious as I think of returning.
My soul yearns and I look back repeatedly;
my horses lean against the chariot pole and hesitate.
Though I roam for amusement and seek temporary joy,
how can I bear this sorrowful longing?
I exit the Chānghé gate and descend the heavenly path,
riding the swift moment through the void.
Clouds gather thickly around my wheels;
the wind blows gently, shaking my banners.
In a chaotic flutter, all becomes dim and dark;
suddenly dazed, I return to my common gate.
I withdraw from my past ease and pleasure,
and pull back my far-reaching heart of indulgence.
I cultivate my original attire in its flowing grace,
lengthening my pendants in their dangling splendor.
My patterns are elegant and brilliant;
my beauty is abundant, following the wind.
I drive the precious carriage of the Six Arts,
and roam in the level forest of Virtue and the Way.
I knot the classics to make a net,
and drive the followers of Confucius and Mozi as my prey.
I toy with the transformations of Yin and Yang,
and chant the fine sounds of the Odes and Hymns.
I admire the return to farming of Master Zèngshì,
and yearn for the steep heights of Lìbǎn.
Revering morning and night without duplicity,
I remain firm in what I have practiced from beginning to end.
Vigilant at evening as if in peril, I examine my errors;
I fear that my person is not yet disciplined.
If my inner feelings are upright and straight,
even if no one knows me, I shall not feel ashamed.
Silent and without action, I concentrate my will,
wandering freely with Benevolence and Righteousness.
Without leaving the door, one knows the world;
why must one travel far and toil in exhaustion?
The envoi says:
Heaven and Earth endure forever, but the years do not stay;
to wait for the Yellow River to run clear brings only sorrow.
I wish to travel far to amuse myself,
wandering up and down through the six regions.
Leaping and soaring, I shall break from the common world,
floating freely with a divine spirit to fulfill my desires.
Heaven cannot be climbed, and immortals are rare;
like the "cypress boat," I am anxious and cannot fly.
Since Sōng and Qiáo stand so high, who can leave them behind?
Consolidating my essence to travel afar makes my heart wander.
Turning my will to follow profound schemes,
I obtain what I sought—what more is there to think about!
I have lived in the capital for a long time,
yet I have no brilliant strategies to assist the age.
In vain I stand by the river envying the fish;
waiting for the river to clear is without a set date.
Moved by the indignation of Cài Zǐ,
I followed Táng Shēng to resolve my doubts.
Understanding that the Way of Heaven is subtle and obscure,
I shall follow the fisherman to play together.
Rising above the dust to depart for distant places,
I bid a long farewell to the affairs of the world.
At this time, in the auspicious month of mid-spring,
the weather is harmonious and the air is clear.
The plains and marshes are lush and flourishing;
the hundred grasses grow in abundance.
The ospreys flap their wings;
the orioles chirp mournfully.
Necks entwined, they fly up and down,
calling out "guān guān" and "yīng yīng."
Therein I wander at ease,
briefly amusing my feelings.
Then the dragons roar in the square marshes,
and the tigers howl upon the hills.
Looking up, I shoot thin silk-lined arrows;
looking down, I fish in the long streams.
Hit by arrows, birds perish;
greedy for bait, fish swallow the hook.
Thus I bring down the wandering birds from among the clouds,
and pull up the deep-dwelling sharks and minnows from the abyss.
At this time, the sun's light suddenly fades,
followed by the moon goddess Wàngshū.
Having reached the ultimate joy of wandering,
though it is evening, I forget my fatigue.
Mindful of the legacy and admonitions of Lǎo Shì,
I shall turn my carriage back to my thatched hut.
Plucking the five strings with subtle fingers,
I chant the books of Zhōu and Kǒng.
Brandishing brush and ink to flourish my literary style,
I lay out the models of the Sān Huáng.
If I let my heart wander beyond material things,
how should I know where honor or disgrace leads?
I, Yuè, once read the *Jì Àn Zhuàn*;
when it came to the part where Sīmǎ Ān reached the position of one of the nine ministers four times,
and the good historian recorded it,
labeling it under the heading of "Clever Officialdom,"
I never failed to close the book with a sigh of indignation.
I said: "Alas!
If there truly is cleverness,
then clumsiness must also have its place."
I have always believed that for a scholar's life,
unless one is a supreme sage with no fixed tracks, subtle, profound, and all-penetrating,
then one must establish merit and conduct affairs,
proving one's utility to the current age.
Therefore, one relies on loyalty and practices sincerity to advance in virtue;
one refines speech and establishes integrity to dwell in one's profession.
In my youth, I privately gained a reputation in my local village
and was honored with appointments from the Sīkōng and the Tàiwèi.
The lord I served
was none other than the Tàizǎi Lǔ Wǔ Gōng.
I was recommended as a Xiùcái and became a Láng.
I served under the Emperor Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì
as the Magistrate of Héyáng and Huái,
as a Shàngshū Láng,
and as a Tíngwèi Píng.
During the mourning period of the current Son of Heaven,
I held the post of Zhǔbù to the Tàifù.
When the head of the office was executed,
my name was removed from the rolls and I became a commoner.
Soon after, I returned to office
and was appointed Magistrate of Cháng'ān.
I was promoted to Bóshì,
but before I was summoned and formally appointed,
my parent fell ill,
so I left my post and was dismissed.
From the age of twenty until reaching fifty,
I moved between offices eight times and advanced in rank once;
I was dismissed twice,
removed from the rolls once,
and once did not take up a post;
I was promoted only three times.
Although success and failure depend on fortune,
this is surely the result of being a "clumsy" man.
Formerly, when the man of penetration Hé Zhǎngyú evaluated me,
he certainly said I was clumsy at using my many talents.
As for "many talents," how would I dare claim that?
But as for being "clumsy," it is truly proven by evidence.
Now that talented men are in office
and all officials are in their proper places,
a clumsy man can give up all thoughts of favor and glory.
My mother is in the hall,
suffering from the infirmities of old age;
how could I still neglect the duty of serving her personally
and bother myself with the petty tasks of a minor official?
Therefore, recognizing the share of contentment and knowing when to stop,
I aspire to the will of the floating clouds.
I build a house and plant trees,
wandering at ease and self-contented.
My ponds and marshes are sufficient for fishing;
the grain from the mortar is enough to replace plowing.
Watering the garden and selling vegetables
provides for my morning and evening meals;
herding sheep and selling milk products
covers the expenses for the seasonal festivals.
Filial piety is truly filial piety,
and being friendly to one's brothers,
this is also a clumsy man's way of governing.
Thus I have composed this *Xiánjū Fù*,
to sing of my successes and express my feelings.
Its words are as follows:
Proudly I wander through the fields of ancient texts,
walking the high paths of the former sages.
Though the skin of my face is said to be thick,
I still feel inward shame before Níng and Qú.
When the Way prevails, I do not serve;
when the Way is absent, I am not "foolish."
Why is my clever wisdom so insufficient,
while my clumsy hardships are so abundant?
Thus I have retired to live in idleness
on the banks of the Luò River.
My person is ranked among the recluses,
and my name is listed among the lower scholars.
Adjacent to the capital and upstream from the Yī River,
I face the suburbs and have the market behind me.
Floating bridges cross darkly over the water;
the Língtái stands heroically and high.
I observe the secret mysteries of the celestial patterns;
I investigate the beginnings and ends of human affairs.
To the west, there are the forbidden camps of the grand army,
with black curtains and green banners.
Crossbows like the Xīzǐ and Jùshǔ,
with different bows but the same mechanism.
Stone catapults crash like thunder;
flying arrows buzz like gadflies.
They lead the way for the procession,
displaying our imperial majesty.
To the east, there are the Míngtáng and Bìyōng,
pure, solemn, spacious, and serene.
Circular forests cast entwining shadows;
the Circular Moat flows with swirling waters.
There we follow filial piety by honoring our fathers,
and revere the ancestral Wén Kǎo to match Heaven.
We observe sacred reverence to demonstrate obedience,
and nourish the elderly to honor long life.
When winter is left behind and spring arrives,
the Yin wanes and the Yang is bestowed.
The Son of Heaven performs the fire sacrifice,
carrying out righteousness at the suburban altar.
He performs the "Great Music" of the Jūntiān,
accompanied by a myriad of riders in a thousand chariots.
Dressed in majestic black ritual robes,
pipes and flutes wail as they blow together.
How brilliant!
How magnificent!
Such is the grand spectacle of ritual decorum,
and the immense splendor of the king's system.
Two schools stand in equal rows,
their twin buildings looking as one.
To the right, they invite the noble scions;
to the left, they admit the talented and retired.
Countless students gather,
a grand assembly of Confucian learning.
Some ascend to the hall,
some enter the inner room.
In teaching, there is no fixed master;
wherever the Way resides, there is the teacher.
Thus eminent men cast off their official ribbons,
and famous kings embrace their seals of office.
Instruction spreads like the wind,
and response is like the grass bending.
This is why living among the virtuous is beautiful,
and why the mother of Mèng moved her home three times.
Thus I established my residence,
building a house and digging a pond.
Tall poplars are reflected in the pool;
fragrant trifoliate oranges are planted as a hedge.
Swimming fish splash in the water;
lotus flowers bloom and spread.
Bamboos and trees are lush and dense;
auspicious fruits grow in varying heights.
The pears of Zhāng Gōng from Dàgǔ,
the black persimmons of Liáng Hóu,
the weak-branch dates of Zhōu Wén,
the plums of Zhū Zhòng from Fánglíng—
none are not fully planted.
Three types of peaches distinguish the Yīng and Hú varieties;
two types of crabapples display their red and white colors.
Treasures like pomegranates and grapes
hang in clusters or trail along the sides.
Species like plums, apricots, and bush cherries
provide a flourish of beautiful decoration.
Flowers and fruits shine brilliantly,
beyond what words can fully describe.
As for vegetables, there are scallions, leeks, garlic, and taro,
green bamboo shoots and purple ginger.
Violets and shepherd's purse are sweet and delicious;
water pepper and coriander are fragrant.
Wild ginger leans toward the shade;
seasonal bean leaves face the sun.
Green mallows hold the dew;
white shallots bear the frost.
Thus, when the heat recedes in chilly autumn,
and the cold departs in bright spring,
the slight rain has just cleared,
and the six realms are clear and bright.
The Tài Fūrén then rides in a hand-carried carriage
or mounts a light chariot,
gazing afar at the Wángjī and
touring the family garden nearby.
The body is harmonized through movement;
the effects of medicine are spread through exertion.
Her regular appetite increases,
and her old ailments are cured.
Setting out long mats,
she lines up her grandsons.
Willows cast their shade;
carriages are parked in rows.
On land, they pluck purple seedpods;
from the water, they pull up red carp.
Some feast in the woods;
others perform the purification ritual by the stream.
Brothers with hair turning gray,
and children with milk teeth—
they toast wishing her ten thousand years of long life,
all feeling both awe and joy.
The longevity cup is raised;
her kind face is serene.
Floating cups for joyful drinking;
strings and flutes are arranged together.
Stamping feet to rise and dance;
lifting voices in high song.
When life is peaceful and happy,
who knows of anything else?
Retiring to seek within and reflect on myself,
I truly have little integrity and inferior talent.
Following the maxim of Zhōu Rèn,
I dared to display my strength and join the ranks of officials.
I nearly failed to protect my humble self;
how could I ever compare to the wise and discerning?
I look up to the manifold wonders and cease my worries,
ultimately roaming at leisure to nurture my clumsiness.
During the time of Xiàowǔ Huángdì, Chén Huánghòu enjoyed his favor,
but she was quite jealous.
Sent to live separately in the Chángmén Gōng,
she was filled with sorrow, depression, and mournful thoughts.
Hearing that Sīmǎ Xiāngrú of Chéngdū in Shǔ Jùn was the most skilled writer in the world,
she offered one hundred pounds of gold
to Xiāngrú and Wénjūn to buy wine,
so as to request a composition to alleviate her sorrow.
Xiāngrú wrote a piece to enlighten the Sovereign,
and Chén Huánghòu again received his favor.
The text says:
Oh, what a beautiful lady,
walking at leisure to amuse herself.
Her soul has wandered far and does not return;
her form is withered as she dwells alone.
It was said that "I go in the morning and return in the evening";
"in food and drink, we find joy and forget others."
But his heart is dissatisfied and has shifted, no longer remembering the old;
finding new favor, he is close with another.
It is because my own mind was slow and foolish,
though I harbored a joyful heart of chastity and sincerity.
I wished to be granted an inquiry to present myself,
that I might once more value your jade-like voice.
Holding onto empty words while hoping for sincerity,
I waited at the detached palace south of the city.
I prepared humble arrangements and set them out,
yet you were never willing to favor me with a visit.
In the vastness, I hide alone and focus my thoughts;
the sky is vast and the wind is swift.
I climb the Lántái Terrace to gaze afar;
my spirit is dazed and wanders away.
Floating clouds gather and block the four directions;
the sky is deep and dark, though it is day.
Thunder rumbles and rises;
the sound resembles the noise of your carriage.
A whirlwind swirls and rises in my chamber,
lifting the curtains and making them flutter.
Cassia trees intertwine in confusion;
their fragrance is sharp, strong, and pervasive.
Peacocks gather and look after each other;
black gibbons howl and utter long cries.
Kingfishers fold their wings and come to rest;
Luan and Phoenix birds soar north and south.
My heart is stifled with sighs and not at ease;
a baneful vapor grows strong and attacks my core.
I descend from Lántái and look all around,
walking slowly through the deep palace.
The main hall stands massive as if reaching the sky,
rising up grandly and loftily.
In between, I lean against the eastern wing,
gazing at the exquisite and endless sights.
I push the jade doors and shake the golden ring-knockers;
the clanging sound is like that of a bell.
Magnolias are carved to make the rafters;
patterned apricots are decorated to serve as beams.
Lush and wandering trees are arranged;
the Lóuwú trees support one another.
Brackets of rare wood are installed,
placed in uneven rows upon the crossbeams.
Sometimes they resemble various creatures,
like the Jīshí Mountains, grand and imposing.
Five colors dazzle and shine upon each other,
brilliantly glittering and forming light.
Finely laid are the variegated stone tiles,
resembling the patterns on hawksbill turtle shells.
Gauze and silk curtains are hung;
cords of Chǔ weave the connecting nets.
I touch the pillars and lintels with leisure,
viewing the vastness of the Qǔtái Terrace.
White cranes cry out in mournful wails;
a lone female perches on a withered poplar.
At twilight, my hopes are exhausted;
despondent, I entrust myself alone to the empty hall.
I hang the "Bright Moon" pearls to light my way,
passing the clear night in my inner chamber.
I take up the elegant zither and change the tune,
playing of a sorrowful longing that cannot be endured.
I play the flowing Zhǐ mode with subtle turns;
the sound is delicate and then rises again.
I go through the movements of the music;
my mood is fervent and elevated.
Attendants on both sides are saddened and shed tears;
their weeping flows crisscross and unrestrained.
I heave a heavy sigh and sob more;
putting on my shoes, I rise and pace about.
I lift my long sleeves to hide my face,
counting the misfortunes of past days.
I have no face to show;
thus, with dejected thoughts, I go to bed.
I bundle fragrant pollia to make a pillow;
I lie on a mat of fragrant herbs and orchids, scented with angelica.
Suddenly I fall into a slumber and dream;
your spirit seems to be by my side.
Startled, I wake but see nothing;
my soul is bewildered as if something were lost.
The many roosters crow, saddening me;
I rise and look at the brilliant light of the moon.
I observe the alignment of the various stars;
Bì and Mǎo have emerged from the east.
Looking at the misty courtyard,
it seems as if the frost of late autumn has fallen.
The night is long and drawn out as if it were a year;
my heart is so gloomy it cannot bear more.
Quietly I tarry, waiting for the dawn;
the vast sky gradually brightens again.
Your handmaiden secretly grieves for herself;
even as the years come to an end, I dare not forget.
I lived close to Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān;
both men possessed unrestrained talent.
However, Jī’s aspirations were lofty and detached,
while Lǚ’s mind was expansive and free.
Later, they were each executed due to certain incidents.
Jī was broadly accomplished in the arts and techniques,
and was particularly masterful with string and wind instruments.
When he was about to face his end,
he looked back at the shadow of the sun,
asked for a zither, and played it.
As I was about to journey westward,
I passed by his old cottage.
At that time, the sun was sinking into Yúyuān,
and the cold ice felt desolate!
There was a neighbor playing the flute,
its sound resonating clearly.
Recalling the joys of our past excursions and banquets,
I was moved by the sound and sighed;
therefore, I composed this rhapsody:
Fulfilling a command to go to the distant capital,
I then turned back and journeyed north.
Crossing the Huánghé by boat,
I passed the old residence in Shānyáng.
Gazing at the desolation of the vast wilderness,
I halted my carriage at a corner of the city walls.
Walking upon the traces left by these two men,
I passed through the empty cottages in the secluded lanes.
Sighing for the sorrow of Zhōu in "The Luxuriant Broomcorn Millet,"
grieving for the ruins of Yīn in "The Wheat in Flower."
Contemplating the past to reflect on the present,
my heart wavered and hesitated.
The buildings remain and are not destroyed,
but where have their forms and spirits gone?
Of old, when Lǐ Sī was punished,
he sighed for the yellow hound and chanted long.
Lamenting Master Jī’s eternal departure,
he looked back at the sun’s shadow and played the zither.
Entrusting his fate to his inner understanding,
he placed his remaining life in the final moments.
Listening to the impassioned sound of the flute,
its wondrous notes fade and then are sought again.
Halting my carriage, about to move on,
I take up my brush to express my heart.
In the past, I often heard elders recounting their lifelong friends and relatives;
some had all withered away,
and some were the only ones left.
I am now just forty years old,
yet among my close kin and relations,
many are dead and few remain;
of my intimate companions and close friends,
not even half are still here.
Some with whom I once traveled the same path
or feasted in the same room,
after ten years,
have all utterly vanished.
Thinking of this brings sorrow;
the sorrow is plain to see!
Thus I compose this rhapsody:
Oh, the flowing cycles of Heaven and Earth,
rising and falling in succession.
The sun races across the empty void,
the seasons follow the vacuum and stand in warning.
Alas, for the short span of human life,
who can hold onto long years?
Time flits away and does not return,
and old age draws near in the twilight.
Resenting that the jade blossoms leave no sign,
regretting that the morning clouds are hard to grasp.
I gaze toward Tānggǔ and stand on tiptoe,
lamenting that this light is so often eclipsed.
How tragic!
The river experiences the water to become a river,
the water surges on, passing day by day.
The generation experiences people to become a generation,
people drift slowly toward their evening.
What generation of people is not new?
What person of a generation can endure as of old?
The fields must bloom every spring,
and the grass never misses the morning dew.
This has been so throughout antiquity;
all things follow their original nature.
Like the hibiscus on the branch,
though its days end, it does not realize.
Although its lack of realization is pitiable,
my heart is despondent and self-pitying!
Clearly, creation is like this;
how can I obtain longevity?
Grieving that the divine roots withered early,
resenting that so many kinsmen are lost.
Mourning the collapse of the family foundation,
pitying the city gates turned to wild mounds.
The closer the kin, the more are gone;
of what friend is the sorrow not remembered?
Alas, I am now in peril;
how vast and hazy the heavens appear.
My wounded heart is sorrowful with many thoughts,
my face is haggard with little joy.
Hidden feelings arise and form a thread,
stagnant thoughts are struck and find a beginning.
Distressed by the lack of joy in this world,
I chant of the past to find words.
Residents filled the halls and expanded the eaves,
travelers joined carriages and stood carriage-to-carriage.
How many years and seasons have passed?
Where can one go that is not ruined?
Some are far away in the darkness and gone,
some are in the vast void and barely half remain.
True it is that the pine’s luxuriance gladdens the cypress,
alas, when the mushrooms burn, the orchids sigh.
If their lives were not different,
how could they be on the same wave but have different ripples?
Seeing that the tracks ahead have overturned,
I know this road is truly difficult.
Exposing my limbs, I deeply mourn,
fearing that this body will also become so.
Suffering from the lack of ways to amuse my feelings,
resenting the many faces that meet my eyes.
Truly, many faces meet the eye,
but where can the spirit go to find joy?
Seeking my past life in echoes and images,
I look at former things and cherish them.
Walking through the cold woods with sorrow,
admiring the spring blossoms with reflection.
Touching all things brings forth grief,
sighing that the seasons are the same but the times are different.
As years pass, my thoughts broaden;
as the path reaches twilight, my mind narrows.
Relatives scatter and become fewer daily;
friends drift away and become more distant.
Looking at old friends among the survivors,
finding only ten or one out of a thousand or hundred.
Joy crumbles in my heart as if forgotten,
sorrow follows my feelings and comes to dwell.
Entrusting final bonds to the younger generation,
I am about to grow old and become a guest.
Then I slow my pace and calm my mind,
reflecting on the wondrous creation of Heaven.
The essence floats and the spirit sinks,
suddenly beyond the world.
Awakened to the fact that the Great Night is the same sleep,
why boast of lateness or resent earliness?
Pointing to that day which is about to end,
how could these feelings be enough to disturb?
Moved by autumn flowers on a withered tree,
distressed by the falling dew on lush grass.
Amid deep sorrow, one does not stray;
how can it be said that one knows the Way?
I shall nourish the great virtue of Heaven and Earth,
and leave behind the vast treasures of the Sages.
Untying the heart’s burdens from superficial traces,
I shall wander freely to amuse my old age.
At twelve, I met my father’s friend, Yáng Jūn, the Marquis of Dài of Dōngwǔ;
when I first met him, I became known,
and subsequently, we were joined by marriage;
and Dàoyuán and Gōngsì
also shared the deep love of family friends.
Unfortunately, their lives were short,
and father and sons withered and died.
Since I have had my own private hardships,
and have been serving abroad,
I have not visited the mountains of Sōngqiū
for nine years now.
Now that I am passing through,
I feel deeply moved by memories and compose this rhapsody:
Departing from Kāiyáng in the morning,
I cross the clear Luò River directly.
The morning wind is desolate and piercingly cold,
the evening snow is white and covers the road.
The ruts contain ice and obscure the tracks,
the water wets the wheel-blocks and freezes solid.
The road is difficult and hard to traverse,
the sun is waning and it will soon be evening.
Looking up at the returning clouds,
looking down at the reflection in the spring water.
Before me, I gaze at Tàishì,
beside me, I look toward Sōngqiū.
The Marquis of Dōngwǔ is buried there,
his tomb built and fields laid out.
Tall and towering are the twin pillars,
orderly are the rows of catalpa trees.
Gazing at those catalpas,
I am moved by my thoughts.
I feel admiration for the Marquis of Dài,
and also mourn Yuán and grieve for Sì.
The graves are piled up, mound after mound,
the cypresses are dense, planted together.
How the departed follow one another,
even the old grass has not yet changed.
I was granted a meeting when I was still a child with my hair in tufts,
and I received the pure dust of Dài Hóu.
He honored me as a scholar of the state,
and favored me with a fine marriage.
From the time of our grandfathers and fathers, our friendship flourished,
reaching us two sons, making us family for generations.
We rejoiced in holding hands to grow old together,
hoping that neighborly virtue would find its reward.
Now, after nine years, I come but once,
and the empty hall is silent and without people.
Withered roots cover the steps of the hall,
and the old garden has turned into firewood.
I pace to and fro through the courtyards and corridors,
as my tears flow and soak my handkerchief.
At night, I toss and turn without sleep,
letting out frequent long sighs until dawn.
In my solitary depression, to whom can I speak?
I merely stitch my thoughts into this writing.
Rèn Zǐxián of Lè'ān had the capacity to encompass the world,
and we were happy together since our youth!
Even the love between brothers
could not exceed it.
Unfortunately, he died at the age of twenty;
now that my good friend is gone,
what pain could equal this!
His wife is also my maternal aunt,
who lost her parents in youth;
after she married, her "Heaven" has also died.
Their orphaned daughter is tiny, just an infant;
this is indeed the greatest hardship for a living soul,
and the ultimate sorrow of bitter suffering.
In the past, after Ruǎn Yǔ died,
Wèi Wén mourned him
and ordered his old acquaintances to compose rhapsodies on a widow.
I have therefore imitated this
to describe her heart in its solitude and widowhood.
Its words say:
Alas, my life has been unfortunate,
I mourn that Heaven's hardships are heartless.
In youth, I was lonely and orphaned of one parent,
the pain and distress crush my heart.
Looking at the lingering sighs of "The Cold Spring,"
I recite the remaining notes of *Lù É*.
My feelings are of eternal grief and everlasting longing,
my thoughts grow more distant yet even deeper.
That a woman should marry,
and thus serve as a wife in a noble clan.
Receiving the light and cover of auspicious clouds,
I bore the rich kindness of my gentleman.
Looking at the spreading kudzu vines,
I entrusted my tiny stem to the drooping trees.
I feared my person was light while his favors were heavy,
as if treading on ice or overlooking a valley.
I followed the clear instructions of righteous methods,
and took the canonical warnings of the Female Scribes as my model.
I offered the seasonal sacrifices to show my obedience,
and provided sweeping and cleaning for many years.
What the poets sighed about
was merely speaking their wishes while their hearts were sick.
How strangely thin is the fate I encountered,
meeting a heavenly disaster that has not relented.
Just as the glory and splendor began to flourish,
my good man suddenly departed and turned his back.
Silently I close the door to live in desolation,
a solitary clod, alone with nothing to rely on.
I replace brocade mats with straw mats,
and substitute silk bed-curtains with plain white hangings.
I order the nursemaids to take their places,
and look upon his kerchief and fan to ease my grief.
My mouth sobs until I lose my voice,
and tears burst forth and soak my clothes.
To whom can I tell my melancholy and resentment?
I hold my orphaned child by my side.
The time grows dim as dusk approaches,
the sun fades away and hides in the west.
Sparrows fly in flocks toward the pillars,
and chickens climb to their roosts and fold their wings.
I return to the empty hall and pity myself,
touching the quilts and blankets with a sigh.
Thoughts are entangled and confused,
my heart is shattered and sorrowful.
The sun shines and moves quickly,
the four seasons revolve and shift.
The heavens congeal dew and drop down frost,
trees drop their leaves and shed their branches.
I look up at the vast emptiness of the divine hall,
and gaze at the spirit-robes hanging down.
Retiring with secret sorrow to the corner of the hall,
I advance alone to bow by the bedside.
My ears lean to listen for the past,
my eyes see what seems to be his usual self.
Though all is dark and I see nothing,
I still linger as if leaning on him.
I grieve that the living and the dead have different laws,
his spirit will be moved and laid to rest.
The dragon hearse is solemn in its starry harness,
and the flying banners flutter to open the way.
The wheels follow the track as they advance slowly,
and the horses neigh mournfully and look back hesitantly.
The hidden spirit is far away and will not return,
deep sorrow is knotted and there is no one to tell.
I gaze at his form and shadow upon the ritual table,
and my soul races toward the burial mound.
Since mid-autumn I have been in mourning,
passing from treading on frost to stepping on ice.
Snow falls heavily in thick flakes,
and the wind soughs as I rise early.
Rain drips coldly through the night,
and the water is still and slightly frozen.
My mind is dazed and wanders away,
my spirit rises nine times in a single night.
I hoped that as time passed, grief would diminish,
but the sorrowful feelings only grow more intense.
I wish to use dreams to communicate with his spirit,
but my eyes are bright and I do not sleep.
The night is endless and long,
and the cold is bleak and shivering.
Anguish presses and fills my chest,
and tears cross and flow onto the pillow.
The departed soul has gone forever,
and the year suddenly comes to an end.
My appearance is withered and exhausted,
those around me are pained and pity me.
Moved by the Three Worthies who followed the ruler of Qín,
I would gladly give up my life and take my own.
But cradling the young child in my arms,
I hesitate and cannot bear to do so.
Alone I point to the sun and swear in my heart,
that though my body survives, my will has perished.
Again it is said:
I look up to the Great Vault and sigh,
to what end can my self-pity go!
I examine my humble person, solitary and weak,
and look at the young child who knows nothing.
As if crossing a river without a bridge,
as if climbing the void and losing my wings.
Looking up, I see his remaining image,
looking down, I face the springs and soil.
Dark and deep, he is hidden away,
my heart remembers and my eyes imagine.
I serve the empty seat in solemn silence,
and cry out to the empty halls, vast and bright.
Vast and standing alone, I look at my shadow,
a solitary clod speaking alone, I listen to the echo.
