Looking at my shadow, I am broken,
and listening to the echo, my sorrow increases.
He has gone far away, more and more distant,
remote and vague, we are forever parted.
The four seasons flow and suddenly change their order,
the year is at its end and the sun sinks in the west.
Frost covers the courtyard and wind enters the room,
the night is half-over and the Milky Way has turned.
I dream of my good man coming to visit,
as if the Gate of Heaven were wide open.
Startled, I wake to find no sound,
lost in a daze, my heart is in mourning.
My heart is in mourning, what can be done?
I ascend the bend of the mountain.
The tomb gate is solemn and still,
and the long burial mound is high and towering.
A solitary bird chirps a mournful cry,
and the tall pines are lush, their branches shaking.
Sorrow and gloom gather together,
and tears flow across my face like a torrential downpour.
I follow Gōngjiāng in her clear vow,
and sing the clear song of *Bǎizhōu*.
In the end, my bones shall return to the foot of the mountain,
while I live, I rely on my remaining years.
I promise my lord we shall share the same grave,
until death I swear I shall have no other.
Looking out upon the level plain,
creeping weeds entwine the bones,
and great trees enfold the souls.
When human life comes to this,
how can we even discuss the Way of Heaven!
Thus, I am essentially a man of resentment,
and my heart startles without end.
I simply reflect on the ancients,
who died harboring resentment.
For example, the Qín Emperor grasped his sword,
as the feudal lords galloped westward.
He leveled all under heaven,
unifying the script and standardizing regulations.
Huà Shān served as his city wall,
and Zǐ Yuān as his moat.
His grand ambitions were already overflowing,
yet his military might was not exhausted.
He was just bridging the sea with giant turtles and crocodiles,
patrolling the western shores to escort the setting sun.
Suddenly his soul was severed,
and the imperial carriage departed late.
Then there was the King of Zhào, who having been captured,
was relocated to Fáng Líng.
At dusk his heart was moved,
at dawn his spirit was stirred.
He parted from radiant concubines and beautiful women,
and lost his golden carriages and jade chariots.
Setting out wine to drink,
sorrow came to fill his breast.
For a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
his resentment would be hard to overcome.
As for Lord Lǐ surrendering to the North,
his name disgraced and his person wronged,
he drew his sword to strike a pillar,
pitying his shadow and ashamed before his soul.
His feelings went to Shàng Jùn,
his heart remained at Yàn Mén.
Tearing silk to tie a letter,
he vowed to repay the Hàn kindness.
The morning dew suddenly arrived,
clasping hands, what could be said?
When Míng Fēi departed,
she looked up to heaven and sighed deeply.
The Purple Terrace grew distant,
the mountain passes were boundless.
Shifting winds suddenly arose,
the white sun hid in the west.
Few wild geese flew from Lǒng,
the clouds of Dài were devoid of color.
Looking toward the sovereign, when could she hope to return?
Destined to waste away and perish in a foreign land.
Then there was Jìng Tōng being rejected,
dismissed to return to his village fields.
He closed his gates and stopped sweeping,
blocking his door and no longer serving in office.
On his left facing his wife,
looking back to play with his young children.
He disregarded high officials,
and gave himself over to literature and history.
Harboring his ambitions till he entered the earth,
his eternal longing never ceased.
When the Zhōng Sǎn Counselor was cast into prison,
his spirit remained stirred and lofty.
Drawing thick wine in the evening,
stringing his plain zither in the morning.
The autumn sun was desolate,
the floating clouds lacked light.
Stifling his extraordinary aspirations for the blue mist,
he entered the long night that never dawns.
Some are orphaned ministers shedding tears of peril,
or sons of concubines with sinking hearts.
Banished travelers by the sea,
exiled soldiers in the shadows of Lǒng.
These people only hear the sorrowful wind rushing up,
their blood-tears wetting their collars.
They also harbor bitterness and swallow their sighs,
wasting away and sinking into oblivion.
Then there are riders in close formation,
and carriages crowding the tracks,
yellow dust covers the earth,
songs and flutes arise on all sides.
None escape having their smoke cut off and fire extinguished,
their bones enclosed within the underworld springs.
It is over!
Spring grass fades and the autumn wind startles,
the autumn wind ceases and the spring grass grows.
Silks and gauze come to an end, ponds and halls vanish;
zithers and lutes fall silent, and the burial mounds are leveled.
Since ancient times all must die,
none do not drink their resentment and swallow their voices.
That which desolately melts the soul,
is nothing but parting!
Especially between Qín and Wú, lands far apart,
or Yàn and Sòng, separated by a thousand lǐ.
Perhaps the spring moss has just begun to grow,
or the autumn wind suddenly arises for a while.
Therefore the traveler's heart is broken,
a hundred feelings are poignant and sad.
The wind soughs with a strange sound,
the clouds spread boundlessly with a peculiar color.
The boat lingers by the water's edge,
the carriage winds slowly along the mountainside.
Hesitating and dazed, how can one go forward?
The horses whinny in the cold without ceasing.
Covering the golden goblet, whom would one serve?
Laying down the jade zither bridges, tears wet the carriage rail.
The one who stays lies down in sorrow,
dazed as if something were lost.
The sun sinks below the wall, its colors fading;
the moon rises above the veranda, casting its light.
Seeing the red orchids receiving the dew,
gazing at the green catalpas beset by frost.
Walking past the layered pillars, the doors are closed in vain;
touching the brocade curtains, they feel empty and cold.
Knowing the dreams of parting are hesitant,
sensing the soul of separation is fluttering away.
Thus, though parting is but a single thread,
its circumstances are of ten thousand kinds.
As for dragon-horses with silver saddles,
and red carriages with embroidered axles.
Drinking in tents at the Eastern Capital,
seeing off guests at Jīn Gǔ.
Zither strings are tuned and flutes and drums arrayed,
songs of Yàn and Zhào sadden the beautiful women.
Pearls and jade are radiant in late autumn,
gauzes and silks are lovely in early spring.
Startling the team of four horses so they look up,
and alarming the red-scaled fish in the deep.
Reaching the moment of parting, they hold back tears,
moved by the silence and wounded in spirit.
Then there are swordsmen who feel ashamed of the kindness shown them,
and young men who would repay their patrons.
In the state of Hán, in the latrines of Zhào,
in the palaces of Wú, or the markets of Yàn.
Severing affection and enduring love,
they leave their states and depart from their villages.
Shedding tears as they say farewell,
wiping blood-tears as they gaze at each other.
They urge on their journey horses without looking back,
only seeing the dust of travel rising from time to time.
They are just harboring gratitude for a single sword,
not seeking a price within the underworld springs.
Even metal and stone tremble and change color,
kin are sorrowful and their hearts die.
Or perhaps the frontier commanderies are not at peace,
and men shoulder feathered arrows to join the army.
The Liáo River is boundless,
Yàn Shān reaches into the clouds.
In the lady's chamber, the wind is warm,
on the paths, the grass is fragrant.
The sun comes out in the sky and brightens the scene,
the dew falls on the ground and creates patterns.
Reflecting the brilliance of the cinnabar dust,
imbued with the mist of the green atmosphere.
Clinging to peach and plum branches, unable to bear parting,
seeing off a beloved one till her silk skirt is wet with tears.
As for once departing for a distant land,
when can there be a time to meet again?
Looking at the tall trees of the old village,
at the northern bridge, taking an eternal leave.
Attendants’ souls are stirred,
relatives and guests find their tears flowing.
They may spread thorns to sit and present their resentment,
with only a cup of wine to narrate their sorrow.
It is the day when the autumn geese fly,
at the time when the white dew falls.
Resentment upon resentment in the bends of distant mountains,
going and going along the banks of the long river.
Or again, if the lord dwells to the right of Zī,
and the lady’s home is in Hé Yáng,
they once shared the morning light on their jade pendants,
and together enjoyed the evening incense of the golden brazier.
The lord ties his official sash and goes a thousand lǐ,
pitying the precious grass that blooms in vain.
Ashamed of the zither and lute in the secluded chamber,
the yellow silks of the high terrace grow dim.
The spring palace shuts in this color of green moss,
the autumn curtains hold this light of the bright moon.
The summer mat is cool, but the day does not end;
the winter lamp is frozen, how long is the night!
Weaving the "Song of Brocade," her tears are already exhausted;
composing the "Palindrome Poem," her shadow is solitary and pained.
If there were a superior scholar of Huàyīn,
who, having consumed elixirs, returns to the mountains.
His arts are already marvelous, yet he continues to study;
the Way is already tranquil, but has not been transmitted.
He guards the cinnabar furnace without looking back,
refining the golden tripod with steadfast resolve.
Riding a crane up to the Milky Way,
yoking a simurgh to soar through the heavens.
Briefly roaming ten thousand miles,
parting for a mere thousand years.
Yet in the world of men, parting is held heavy;
bidding farewell to the host, he remains unchanged.
Below, there are poems of peonies,
and songs of beautiful ladies.
The women of Wèi among the mulberries,
the beauties of Chén in the upper palaces.
Spring grass is emerald green,
spring waters are clear waves.
Seeing you off at the southern bank,
how can one bear such grief!
Even when autumn dew is like pearls,
and the autumn moon is like a jade tablet.
Bright moon and white dew,
time comes and goes.
Parting with you,
the longing mind wavers and lingers.
Therefore, the places of parting are not fixed,
and the reasons for parting have a thousand names.
Where there is parting, there must be resentment;
where there is resentment, it must overflow.
It makes one's will vanish and spirit tremble,
the heart break and the bones shudder.
Even with the marvelous ink of Yuān and Yún,
the refined brushes of Yán and Yuè.
All the talents of the Golden Chamber,
the assembly of elites from the Lántái.
Though their rhapsodies are praised for reaching the clouds,
and their eloquence has the reputation of carving dragons.
Who can depict the state of a brief departure,
or portray the feelings of a final farewell?
Whenever I observe the works of talented scholars,
I privately gain insight into their intentions.
In setting forth words and dispatching phrases,
there are truly many variations;
beauty and ugliness, likes and dislikes,
can indeed be discussed.
Whenever I compose my own writings,
I particularly see the underlying emotions,
always worrying that the intent does not match the subject,
and the writing does not reach the intent.
For it is not the knowing that is difficult,
but the doing.
Therefore, I have composed the Wén Fù,
to describe the magnificent literary graces of former scholars,
and to discuss the reasons for success or failure in writing,
so that one day it might be said to have fully exhausted its subtleties.
As for holding an axe to cut a handle,
though the model is not far off,
yet the variations that come with the hand
are truly difficult to capture in words;
what can be said
is all contained herein.
Standing in the center of the world to take a mystical view,
nourishing my feelings and will in the ancient classics.
Following the four seasons to lament their passing,
beholding the myriad things as thoughts swarm.
Grieving over the falling leaves in the harsh autumn,
rejoicing in the tender branches in the fragrant spring.
The heart is awe-struck as if harboring frost,
the will is lofty as if reaching for the clouds.
Chanting of the great achievements of worldly virtue,
reciting the pure fragrance of ancestors.
Roaming through the forest and treasury of literature,
admiring the refined elegance of beautiful ornaments.
Moved to set aside the texts and reach for a brush,
I shall briefly express it through this writing.
In the beginning,
one withdraws the vision and turns back the hearing,
lost in thought and seeking far and wide.
The essence gallops to the eight poles,
the mind roams ten thousand fathoms high.
When the inspiration arrives,
emotions emerge from the gloom and become increasingly clear,
objects become distinct and present themselves one after another.
Pouring out the essence of all words,
rinsing with the fragrant moisture of the Six Arts.
Floating on the celestial abyss with a steady current,
washing in the lower springs while deeply submerged.
Then, submerged words emerge with joyful struggle,
若 like a swimming fish biting a hook,
coming out from the depths of the heavy abyss;
floating ornaments flutter together,
like a winged bird caught by a tethered arrow,
falling from the heights of the layered clouds.
Collecting the lost writings of a hundred generations,
gathering the lingering rhymes of a thousand years.
Discarding the morning blossoms that have already opened,
opening the evening beauties that have not yet flourished.
Observing past and present in an instant,
surveying the four seas in the blink of an eye.
Then, selecting meanings and arranging them into sections,
examining phrases to put them in order.
Everything that holds luster is struck for its sound,
everything that contains resonance is fully played.
Some follow the branch to shake the leaves,
some follow the waves to search for the source.
Some start from the hidden to reach the manifest,
some seek the easy but find the difficult.
Sometimes it is a tiger transformation that startles the beasts,
sometimes a dragon appearing that scatters the birds.
Sometimes it is harmonious and easy to apply,
sometimes it is jagged and ill at ease.
Exhausting the clear mind to condense one's thoughts,
narrowing the myriad concerns to form words.
Caging heaven and earth within a form,
mastering the myriad things at the tip of a brush.
Starting with hesitation on dry lips,
ending with smooth flow from a moistened brush.
Reason provides the substance to establish the trunk,
style hangs down like branches and forms a thicket.
Believing that emotion and appearance do not differ,
so every change shows upon the face.
Thoughts touching on joy will surely bring a smile,
about to speak of sorrow, one has already sighed.
Sometimes one takes the tablet with impulsive haste,
sometimes one holds the brush with distant contemplation.
How delightful this undertaking is!
Truly it is what sages and worthies respect.
Taxing the void to demand existence,
knocking on silence to seek for sound.
Enclosing the distant and vast on a foot of white silk,
pouring forth a torrential flow from a square-inch heart.
Words expand it and it becomes even wider,
thought probes it and it becomes ever deeper.
Spreading the fragrance of blossoming flowers,
sending forth the dense growth of green branches.
Bright as the wind blowing and the whirlwind rising,
dense as clouds rising from the Hànlín.
Forms have ten thousand variations,
objects have no single measure.
Swirling and flashing,
forms are difficult to describe.
Words display talent to show off skills,
intent holds the contract and acts as the craftsman.
Striving between being and non-being,
facing shallow and deep without yielding.
Though departing from the square and escaping the circle,
one aims to exhaust every form and fulfill every appearance.
Thus, those who dazzle the eye value luxury,
those who satisfy the heart prize appropriateness.
When words are exhausted, there is no confinement,
when discourse is lucid, it is only through vastness.
Poetry follows emotion and is fine and ornate;
the rhapsody describes objects and is clear and bright.
The stele displays writing to match the substance;
the elegy is lingering and mournful.
The inscription is broad yet concise, warm and smooth;
the admonition has pauses and transitions, and is clear and vigorous.
The eulogy is leisurely, elegant and lush;
the discourse is subtle and clear-flowing.
The memorial is balanced and thorough, calm and refined;
the persuasion is brilliant, deceptive, and cunning.
Though the distinctions lie here,
they also forbid wickedness and restrain excess.
The essential is that words be expressive and principles be upheld,
therefore, there is no value in verbosity.
As a thing, it has many guises;
as a form, it frequently changes.
In conceiving ideas, it values ingenuity;
in dispatching words, it prizes beauty.
And when sounds and tones alternate,
it is like the five colors enhancing each other.
Though their passing and stopping are without constancy,
they are indeed uneven and difficult to manage.
If one understands the changes and knows the order,
it is like opening a channel to receive a spring.
But if one misses the opportunity and tries to join later,
it is like always grasping the tail to mend the head.
If the order of black and yellow is confused,
it will be muddy and lack freshness.
Sometimes one is constrained by preceding lines,
or encroached upon by subsequent chapters.
Sometimes the diction is harmful though the reasoning is orderly,
or the words flow smoothly while the meaning is obstructed.
Separate them, and both are beautiful;
join them, and both are marred.
One weighs the merits to the smallest unit,
and decides what to keep or discard by a hair’s breadth.
If the scales of judgment have made their cut,
one must surely follow the standard with exactness.
Sometimes the writing is ornate and the reasoning rich,
yet the intent does not reach its goal.
The ultimate cannot have two versions;
the perfect cannot be further augmented.
Establishing a few words to hold the essential
becomes the striking passage of the whole piece.
Though the many words have their order,
they must rely on this to achieve success.
Truly, when the merits are many and the flaws few,
one settles for sufficiency and does not change it.
Sometimes ornate thoughts interweave like silk,
pure and lovely, shimmering and soft.
Brilliant as variegated embroidery,
mournful as the sound of many strings.
If what is imitated is not distinct,
it will secretly coincide with former works.
Though it was woven from my own heart,
I fear others have preceded me.
If it harms integrity or offends righteousness,
then despite one's love for it, it must be cast away.
Sometimes it sprouts like a reed or stands tall like a grain-ear,
detached from the crowd and of peerless refinement.
Its form cannot be pursued,
its echo is difficult to bind.
It stands solitary and singular,
not something common notes can weave.
The mind is desolate and without a peer,
the intent hesitates and cannot be discarded.
When a rock hides jade, the mountain glows;
when water contains pearls, the river becomes charming.
Though the hazel and thorn bushes are not pruned,
they share the glory of the gathered kingfishers.
Mixing the songs of *Xiàlǐ* with *Báixuě*,
I also make use of what is grand.
Sometimes one entrusts words to a short rhyme,
facing a dead end with solitary inspiration.
Looking down into silence, there are no friends;
looking up into the vastness, there is nothing to receive.
It is like a single string stretched alone,
holding a clear note but finding no response.
Sometimes one entrusts diction to a weary sound,
using extravagant words that lack brilliance.
Beauty and ugliness are mixed into one body,
marring the good quality and creating a flaw.
Like the lower pipes sounding out of rhythm,
they may respond but do not harmonize.
Sometimes one abandons reason to preserve eccentricity,
seeking only the empty and pursuing the minute.
The words lack emotion and have little love,
the diction drifts and does not return.
Like a thin string with a tight bridge,
it harmonizes but does not evoke sorrow.
Sometimes it is unrestrained to achieve harmony,
striving for clamor and seductive beauty.
Merely pleasing the eye and matching the vulgar,
the sound is high but the tune is low.
Awakening the songs of *Fánglù* and *Sāngjiān*,
it is mournful but not elegant.
Sometimes it is pure and void, subtle and reserved,
removing the troublesome and discarding the excessive.
Lacking the "leftover flavor" of the Great Sacrificial Soup,
it is like the clear sound of the zither's red strings.
Though one singer leads and three sigh in response,
it is indeed elegant but not ornate.
As for the tailoring of abundance and brevity,
and the shapes of rising and falling,
one should adapt to what is appropriate,
for every turn contains subtle feelings.
Sometimes the words are clumsy but the metaphors are clever;
sometimes the reasoning is plain but the diction is light.
Sometimes one follows the old and it becomes newer;
sometimes one follows the turbid and it becomes clearer.
Sometimes one looks and must examine it closely;
sometimes one polishes it and then it becomes exquisite.
It is like a dancer moving to the beat with waving sleeves,
or a singer responding to the strings with their voice.
This is something *Lúnbiǎn* could not express in words,
and thus it is not something flowery talk can master.
The universal branches of diction and laws of literature
are truly what I keep in my heart.
I have studied the common errors of the world,
and recognized the excellence of former masters.
Though it flows deeply from a clever heart,
it may be criticized by a clumsy eye.
Those flowery blossoms and jade-like ornaments
are like the beans on the central plains.
Like the inexhaustible bellows,
they are born together with Heaven and Earth.
Though they are abundant in this world,
alas, they do not fill my cupped hands.
I worry that my small vessel is often empty,
and grieve that eloquent words are hard to join.
Thus I hop along the short wall,
using mediocre sounds to complete the tune.
Always ending a piece with lingering regret,
how could I harbor fullness or be self-satisfied?
I fear the dust on the clay pot,
and look back with shame at the ringing jade.
As for the gathering of inspiration,
and the cycles of flow and blockage,
when it comes, it cannot be stopped;
when it leaves, it cannot be halted.
It hides like a shadow vanishing,
it moves like an echo rising.
When the Heavenly Mechanism is swift and sharp,
what confusion cannot be put in order?
Thoughts rise like wind from the breast,
words flow like a spring from the lips.
Abundant and luxuriant in their swift arrival,
they are captured by the brush and paper.
The writing is glorious and fills the eyes,
the sound is melodious and fills the ears.
But when the six emotions are stagnant,
the will wanders while the spirit remains.
Rigid as withered wood,
hollow as a dried stream.
One clutches the soul to explore the profound,
and exhausts the essence in self-seeking.
Logic is obscured and further hidden,
thought is labored as if being drawn out.
Therefore, sometimes one exhausts one's feelings yet has much regret,
and sometimes one follows one's whim with few errors.
Although this thing is within me,
it is not something my strength can force.
Thus I often pat my empty chest and lament;
I do not yet know the reason for this opening and closing.
For the use of literature
is indeed the basis of all principles.
It expands over ten thousand miles without obstruction,
and bridges a hundred million years.
Looking down, it leaves a model for future generations;
looking up, it observes the patterns of the ancients.
It saves the ways of *Wén* and *Wǔ* from falling,
and spreads their reputation so it does not perish.
No path is too distant for it to cover,
no principle too minute for it to encompass.
It matches the nourishing moisture of clouds and rain,
and mirrors the transformations of ghosts and gods.
Carved on metal and stone, its virtue is broad;
flowing through pipes and strings, it is daily renewed.
Regarding the birth of the flute's stalk,
it grew on the hills of *Jiāngnán*.
Its hollow stem was smooth with few nodes,
its spreading foliage was luxuriant and sparse.
Merely looking at the mountain side,
it is rugged, steep, and towering,
leaning against peaks and ridges.
Truly, its lack of stability is pitiable!
Looking as far as the eye can see across the vastness,
stretching continuously into the open distance,
it is also joyful in its spacious leisure.
Entrusting its body to the Earth,
it has passed ten thousand years without moving.
Absorbing the brilliance of the ultimate essence,
it receives the moist firmness of the azure color.
Feeling the changes of *Yīn* and *Yáng*,
it attaches its life to *Huángtiān*.
The soaring wind whistles through its tips,
and the winding river flows to irrigate its mountain.
Raising white waves and splashing continuous pearls,
the sound thunders and pours into the abyss.
Morning dew, clear and cold, falls by its side;
"jade liquid" soaks and sustains its roots.
Solitary females and lonely cranes
amuse themselves leisurely beneath it;
spring birds in flocks play,
soaring above its peaks.
Autumn cicadas do not eat,
embracing simplicity and chanting long;
black apes howl mournfully,
searching among the branches.
Dwelling in the deep, hidden, and secluded,
dense, silent, and solitary.
Only by carefully observing its plain substance
is it clear that it should be pure, quiet, and not noisy.
Fortunately, it was named the *Dòngxiāo*,
receiving the deep grace of the Sage Lord.
It can be called a benefit without expense,
following the natural disposition of its heavenly nature.
Thereupon, the master craftsman Bān applied his skill,
and the consort of Kuí established the standards.
Bound with ivory,
the joints were perfectly fused.
Engraved and carved in elaborate patterns,
crimson lips were interspersed within.
Spiraling and entwining like fungi,
scales were layered in swift succession.
Firmly glued and precisely aligned,
pressed and smoothed with care.
Then, one employs a man whose nature is immersed in the vast darkness,
who from birth has not seen the forms of heaven and earth,
and is blind to the shapes and colors of black and white.
His pent-up frustrations are deep and bitter,
lamenting the loss of clarity in his eyes.
Having few ways to express his thoughts,
he pours all his indignation into sounds.
Thus, when his lips meet the Gōng and Shāng notes,
a harmonious profusion overflows.
The form is graceful, following the breath,
full of suppressed and pent-up emotion.
The air surges sideways in flying bursts,
galloping and scattering in rhythm.
Its pace is leisurely yet beyond description,
racing in complex and marvelous clusters.
Sometimes murky and flowing like a stream,
snapping like broken twigs.
Sometimes spreading and continuous,
surging and competing in an overflow.
Chilly and dense in its rhythm,
it covers and then vanishes.
With a sudden, brilliant flash,
it leaps forth once again.
If one listens slowly to its melodies
and carefully observes its songs,
it chirps and warbles as if about to sigh,
moving in harmony and resonance.
The wind is vast and unending,
gentle and swaying in its movement.
Fluttering and continuous in its desolation,
drifting away and turning into something else.
It returns to block its previous paths,
harmonizing with folk songs and chants.
Therefore, listening to its great sounds,
they flow and overflow everywhere,
containing and releasing all at once,
like a compassionate father nurturing his son.
Its subtle sounds
are pure, quiet, and peaceful,
following in humble succession,
like a filial son serving his father.
Categorized and compared,
they truly accord with righteousness and principle;
surging and impassioned,
how like a brave warrior!
Gentle, soft, warm, and moist,
they are also like a gentleman.
Thus, its martial sounds
are like the crashing of thunder,
unrestrained and boiling with vigor.
Its benevolent sounds
are like the southern breeze scattering,
leisurely bestowing grace.
Sometimes gathered in a dense throng,
sometimes discarded in a sudden burst.
Sorrowful and dazed with grief,
sometimes tranquil and free.
Covered in a fine, mist-like drizzle,
sometimes bursting forth like sunshine.
A sorrow so deep it lingers in the mind,
truly rich and full of flavor.
Thus, the greedy hear it and become upright,
and the perverse hear it and cease their resentment.
The resolute and violent return to benevolence and grace,
while the idle and self-indulgent are warned of their errors.
Zhōng Qī, Yá, and Kuàng are lost in wonder, and Qǐ
Liáng's wife cannot match its spirit.
Shī Xiāng and Yán Chūn dare not hide their skill,
while Shū Zǐ's influence is far-reaching.
The stupid and stubborn Zhū and Jūn are startled back to kindness,
while Jié, Zhí, Yù, and Bó are left withered and exhausted.
Playing the cāncī enters into the Way and Virtue,
thus it is forever valued and precious.
When playing a playful tune,
it wanders and soars,
or stays without moving,
or moves without staying.
Disturbed and overflowing,
losing its mate and leaving its kind.
Scant yet clustered,
seeking the intangible.
Thus, those who know music rejoice and are saddened by it,
while those who do not know music find it strange and grand.
Therefore, hearing its sorrowful sounds,
none fail to be moved to heavy sighs,
wiping away tears and sobbing.
When it plays joyful tunes,
none fail to be relaxed and happy,
their graceful movements becoming supple.
Thus, crickets and inchworms,
crawling and breathing,
mole crickets, ants, and lizards,
buzzing and fluttering,
linger and move slowly,
with the gaze of a fish or a chicken.
Drooping their beaks and winding about,
staring in a daze and forgetting to eat.
How much more so does it affect the harmony of yīn and yáng,
and transform the customs of the people!
The Envoi says:
Its form is like a swift warrior,
leaping and soaring, trailing along,
rapid, drifting, and clever.
It is also like flowing waves,
bubbling and floating,
rushing along the mountain paths.
Roaring and shouting,
stumbling and then connecting,
murky and chaotic.
Stirring and splashing,
wandering and leaping,
like a collapsing mound.
Leisurely and drifting,
hesitating and reaching a destination,
it is also enough to indulge in.
Declining and then continuing,
taking a long leave and departing far away,
drifting and not returning.
Relying on the influence of sage transformation,
it calmly follows the Middle Way,
joyful without being excessive.
Flowing smoothly and penetrating deeply,
it accords with rhythm and integrity.
Ending the poem and finishing the melody,
there is still a lingering sound.
The chanting breath leaves a resonance,
continuous and drifting,
giving rise to a slight breeze.
Stretching out in succession,
its changes are infinite.
After Chǔ Xiāng Wáng had wandered through Yúnmèng,
he commanded Sòng Yù to compose a rhapsody on the events of Gāotáng.
As they were about to set out the wine for a banquet,
he said to Sòng Yù:
"I wish to offer wine to my ministers;
how shall I entertain them?"
Sòng Yù said:
"I have heard that songs are used to chant words,
and dances are used to express meaning.
Therefore, discussing the poetry is not as good as listening to its sound;
listening to its sound is not as good as observing its form.
The dances of Jī Chǔ, Jié Fēng, and Yáng Ā
are the ultimate sights for talented people,
the most marvelous things in the world.
Ah, may they be presented?"
The King said:
"What about the music of Zhèng?"
Sòng Yù said:
"Small and great have different uses;
the music of Zhèng and the Yǎ music each have their proper occasions.
The measure of loosening and tightening
is what sages and philosophers apply.
Thus, the Yuè records the appearance of shields and axes,
the Yǎ měi praises the graceful dances,
the Lǐ establishes the system of three cups of wine,
and the Sòng have songs of returning home drunk.
Now, Xiánchí and Liùyīng
are used to display in the pure temple
and to harmonize gods and men.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi
is used to entertain those in private gatherings
and to share joy.
In our leisure days of pleasure,
it is not used to influence the common people,
so what harm can it do?"
The King said:
"Try to compose a rhapsody about it for me."
Sòng Yù said:
"Yes, your majesty."
How bright and clear is this tranquil night,
The bright moon radiates its brilliant light.
Vermilion fires blaze and spread their glow,
Illuminating the grand hall and brightening the inner chambers.
Patterned curtains are drawn back and tied with cords,
The knocker-plates shine with a dazzling luster.
Mats and cushions are arranged for the seating,
Golden jars overflow and jade cups are lined up.
Beakers and chalices are raised in pouring,
All are tipsy, enjoying health and joy.
Stern countenances soften with pleasure,
Hidden feelings take shape and are revealed.
The man of letters cannot conceal his refinement,
The brave warrior cannot hide his strength.
The casual and carefree leap and dance,
In a colorful and bustling array.
The profound and steady become unrestrained,
Changing their usual habits.
Then the maidens of *Zhèng* come forward,
Sixteen of them slowly attending.
Their beautiful attire is exceptionally elegant,
Their gentle movements convey grace.
Their features are lovely and enchanting,
Their rosy faces shine with radiant bloom.
Their eyebrows are delicate and finely curved,
Their eyes cast sidelong glances like rippling waves.
Pearls and kingfisher feathers sparkle and shine,
Flowered robes with flying sashes are mixed with fine gauze.
They look at their own forms and shadows,
Straightening their own attire.
They move with the gentle breeze,
Waving their fragrance.
They move their vermilion lips,
And lift their clear gazes.
They raise their voices in high song as a way of joy.
The song says:
I express my thoughts to broaden my view,
To unravel what constrains the spirit.
Relax the tension of the tight strings,
Soften the trivial and crooked matters.
Expand the great capacity of the mind,
Broaden the petty and overly ornate details.
Admire the *Guānjū* for not being licentious,
Lament the *Xīshuài* for its narrow constraints.
Open the blockages of the supreme truth,
Transcend worldly things and cross beyond the mundane.
Raise the resonant *Zhǐ* note,
Perform the clear *Jué* note.
Accompany the dance movements,
Playing the harmonized tunes.
Appearance and form are in harmony,
Spirit and intent are in accord.
They achieve ease and composure,
Their will is not constrained.
Then, following the beat as the drums are laid out,
They relax their minds and broaden themselves.
Their hearts roam without limit,
Lost in far-reaching thoughts and long reflections.
When they first begin,
They seem to bow and then look up,
Seeming to come and then depart.
Composed yet melancholic,
They cannot be fixed in one image.
As they proceed a little further,
They seem to fly and then to walk,
Seeming to stand tall and then to lean.
Their movements match the rhythm perfectly,
Every gesture and look responds to the sound.
Their gauze robes follow the wind,
Long sleeves crisscross.
Spreading out in a continuous stream,
Then swiftly coming back together.
Hovering like swallows at rest,
Then dashing like startled swans.
Graceful, elegant, and soft,
Their bodies are quick and light.
Displaying peerless and wonderful postures,
Cherishing a sincere and pure spirit.
They refine their conduct to manifest their will,
Galloping in thought through the deep and distant.
Like mountains, lofty and high,
Like waters, vast and surging.
Transforming along with their will,
Their appearance is not created in vain.
Clarifying the poems and showing their intent,
Sighing with great emotion.
Their spirit is like floating clouds,
Their will is like autumn frost.
Onlookers sigh in admiration,
Even masters cannot rival them.
Then they gather on the floor and come forward in turn,
Waiting according to their order.
Matching their talents and competing in skill,
Their boastful beauty is well-ordered.
Extraordinary postures emerge in abundance,
Remarkable forms rise unexpectedly.
Looking at the decorated drums, they flash their clear eyes,
Singing delicate melodies, they reveal their white teeth.
Adjusting their ranks to be even,
Carefully planning their movements.
It seems as if spirits are moving,
Soaring, circling, and standing tall.
In striking the drums, they do not use sticks,
In treading the floor, they do not tire their feet.
Like wings, they move gracefully away,
And then suddenly come to a halt.
When they turn their bodies to return,
They are pressed by the rapid rhythm.
Leaping, soaring, and repeatedly kneeling,
Their feet tread and brush the ground.
Bending their forms to reach far,
Looking as fragile as if about to break.
Their fine gauze flies like moths,
Whirling like a sudden gust.
Leaping like birds gathering,
Relaxing and disappearing from view.
Moving like wriggling snakes, lithe and slender,
Turning like clouds, swift and sudden.
Their bodies are like swimming dragons,
Their sleeves are like white rainbows.
At the end, they gather and bow,
The melody and rhythm come to an end.
Lingering with a faint smile,
They retreat to their ranks.
Onlookers praise their beauty,
None are not delighted.
Thus the joy is full at the night feast,
And the guests are sent on their way.
In a bustle, they go to their carriages,
The grooms ready the whips.
Chariots and horses are crowded together,
Looming and pressing close.
Fine steeds with swift feet,
Galloping and leaping ahead.
Like dragons soaring, they rise up,
Tossing their bits and throwing foam.
The horses' abilities vary,
Each competing with the other.
Some rise above the dust to follow the track,
Like sudden thunder or flashing lightning.
Treading the earth, they outdistance the herd,
Leaping alone in the dark, peerless.
Some curl their feet in pent-up anger,
Lingering and not moving forward.
Those who started later arrive first,
Thus chasing the last.
Some take pride in their appearance and manner,
Grand and composed.
Moving slow or fast according to the rider's will,
Controlled with ease or urgency.
The sound of carriages is like thunder,
Galloping and racing to catch up.
Scattered, they return home,
Like clouds dispersing into the towns.
The *Tiānwáng* feasts in joy,
Happy but not licentious.
To delight the spirit and forget old age,
This is the art of longevity.
Leisurely and free,
Just to pass the long days.
Since I, *Róng*, have extensively read the classics and refined texts,
Thoroughly examined the arts and techniques,
And am also fond of music by nature,
Being able to play the *Qín* and blow the flute;
And while serving as a *Dūyóu*,
With no pending business,
I was lying alone in the *Wù* of *Píngyáng* in *Méi*.
There was a guest from *Luò* staying at the inn
Who played the flute,
Performing *Qìchū* and *Jīngliè* in harmony.
Since *Róng* has left the capital for over a year,
Hearing it suddenly,
I felt deeply moved and delighted by it.
Admiring *Wáng Zǐyuān*,
*Méi Chéng*,
*Liú Bókāng*,
*Fù Wǔzhòng*, and others for their panegyrics on the *Xiāo*, *Qín*, and *Shēng*,
But the flute alone had none.
Therefore, I have prepared this to fill the void,
Composing the *Cháng Dí Fù*.
Its words say:
Only the rare Zhōnglóng bamboo grows
on the shaded cliffs of Zhōngnán.
It rests upon the solitary peaks of Jiǔchéng,
overlooking stone ravines ten thousand fathoms deep.
Stout as arrows, its stalks stand upright,
alone listening to the wind at the utmost heights.
Autumn floods wash its lower roots;
winter snows seal its branches.
Rooted on the jagged crest of a precipice,
it feels the swirling gales and seems ready to fall.
Upon its flanks are layered peaks and heaped stones,
piled high and rugged.
Towering heights and jagged crests,
leaning against or crouching beneath the sky.
Deep hollows and arched spaces,
interconnected caves and valleys.
Ravines, gullies, and streams,
pits, crags, and dark recesses.
Winding depressions and sunken pools,
where ridges connect and ranges join.
Forests of bamboo and creeping vines,
dense thickets of oaks and shrubs.
Then the mountain waters arrive in mass,
stagnant pools and blocked dams burst.
Swelling currents flow in torrents,
plunging like pestles into cavernous holes.
Competing rapids swirl and eddy,
gurgling and splashing with a roaring surge.
Billows and waves ripple like scales,
sinking and rising in erratic ways.
Waterfalls spray their foam,
rushing and dashing, clashing and thrusting.
Swaying and shaking the mountain,
jolting and uprooting its base—
this happens five or six times a year.
Thus, the terrain is secluded without paths,
and human footprints rarely reach there.
Gibbon-apes howl by day,
and flying squirrels cry at night.
Cold bears shake their jaws,
and solitary stags bristle their coats in the dusk.
Mountain chickens gather in the morning,
and pheasants crow at dawn.
Seeking mates and calling to their young,
they utter sorrowful cries and long whistles.
Following the slopes, they find their paths,
chirping and chattering in a noisy din.
Passing to the left and right,
clamoring in front and behind—
they never cease, day or night.
Truly, it is a place pressed by peril and danger,
an accumulation of gathered grief and collected sorrow.
Therefore, when it responds to the clear breeze,
its slender tips flutter and wave,
ringing and echoing with a resonant sound.
Like a Sè with tightened bridges,
or the high-tuned melody of a Háozhōng.
Then, the exiled official and the banished son,
the deserted wife and the separated friend—
Péng Xū and Bó Qí,
Āi Jiāng and Xiào Jǐ—
gather downwind,
collecting their spirits and focusing their ears.
With thunderous sighs and heavy breaths,
they beat their breasts and wail.
Weeping blood and shedding tears,
which fall crisscrossing down.
Throughout the dawn, they forget sleep,
unable to restrain themselves.
Thereupon, they command Lǔ Bān and Sòng Zhái
to construct cloud-ladders
and raise floating pillars.
They tread over slender roots
and pull themselves up by thin fibers.
Pressing their chests against steep slopes,
and their bellies against narrow ridges.
Reaching the top,
they crawl forward to fell and take it.
They trim the base and the tip,
following designs and measurements.
Kuí and Xiāng match the pitches,
and Zǐ Yě harmonizes the tones.
All twelve notes are prepared,
with Huángzhōng as the principal.
Bending and straightening with tools,
carving and polishing to precise standards.
Hollowed through to the very bottom,
marked on the outside and lacquered within.
They name it the Dí,
to observe the character of worthy men.
Displayed upon the Eastern Steps,
the eight sounds rise together.
At the banquet's start and the ritual's end,
it encourages and assists the gentlemen.
Then it is brought back to the high corridors of the Huángmén.
Zhòng Qiū and Sòng Guàn,
the famous masters Guō and Zhāng,
craftsmen and skilled artists,
practice their trade and refine the sounds.
Then, the leisurely young lords
and the carefree royal grandsons,
their hearts delighting in the harmony of the five notes,
their ears attuned to the modulation of the eight sounds,
gather together in the courtyard.
They observe the dense assembly and variety of the melodies—
how rich they are!
Flourishing and brilliant,
truly delightful.
Spreading like waves, broad and vast,
truly extraordinary.
Clashing and colliding,
yet again wonderful.
Chirping and chattering, noisy and sharp,
like colorful feathers,
twisting and burning, intense and piercing.
Thundering with pent-up frustration and leaning on anger,
booming and shocking, bold and unrestrained.
Breath erupting to cover everything,
suddenly standing firm and erratic.
Like thunder striking an anvil on a high peak,
then clear and chilling as a biting wind.
Pressing together and overriding the rhythm,
racing toward the appointed time and plunging forward.
Then, hearing the sounds and imagining their forms,
they are like flowing water,
or like flying wild geese.
Overflowing and vast,
grand and expansive.
Long-stretching and far-reaching,
circling and returning.
Coiling and pent up,
swelling and grand.
Resonant and numerous,
layered and vast.
Giving and taking at the proper time,
moving and staying with purpose.
Loud and soft in orderly succession,
rare or frequent as required.
A gentle breeze, subtle and fine,
as if existing, yet as if gone.
Trapped and then breaking off,
pausing in the middle to start anew.
Suddenly vanishing,
then brilliantly rising again.
Sometimes lingering in careful protection,
devoted to beauty and skilled mastery.
Surpassing the strings and reeds,
overshadowing the drums and bells.
Sometimes held steady like taut ropes,
hesitant and broad-minded.
Flutes and pipes are all raised,
metal and stone instruments sound together.
Without disrupting the proper order,
to proclaim the Eight Winds.
Once the tones and pitches are harmonized,
the sorrowful sounds descend fivefold.
As the tune ends and the piece concludes,
the remaining strings rise again.
Rapid hands move repeatedly,
dense as the teeth of a comb, layering upon each other.
Crowded and squeezed together,
gathering like bees or ants.
Multitudinous sounds pile up
to see the end through.
Then, after a short rest and brief pause,
various melodies are played in between.
Changing what is heard to startle the ear,
swaying and performing.
Soaring peacefully and unrestrained,
leisurely and expansive.
Melancholy and resentful,
muffled and resonant.
Swiftly searching,
now near, now far.
Abandoning oneself at the edge of peril,
as if falling, yet returning.
Intertwined and convoluted,
winding and coiling.
Soft and subtle, suppressed and hidden,
entering into various transformations.
Intense and rushing like a flood,
the five notes take turns revolving.
Rubbing, grasping, pressing, and hiding,
they pass and follow one another.
Returning to Shāng and descending to Zhǐ,
each with its own unique excellence.
Therefore, those who listen to the main melodies,
observe the laws in the rhythm,
and examine the changes in the phrasing,
so as to know that the ritual system cannot be overstepped.
Those who listen to the interludes,
cast their thoughts back to ancient times,
and find repose for their wills in times of trepidation,
so as to know that enduring sorrow cannot be lived with in leisure.
Thus, they discuss and record its meanings,
and harmonize and compare its images:
Wandering and unrestrained,
vast and boundless—
such is the air of Lǎo Zhuāng.
Gentle, upright, mild, and resolute—
such is the method of Kǒng Mèng.
Piercing, bright, clear, and stern—
such is the integrity of Suí Guāng.
Stubborn, contrary, and defiant—
such is the spirit of Zhū Bèn.
Measured in joints and severed in phrases—
such is the system of Guǎn Shāng.
Branching out and complex—
such is the scrutiny of Shēn Hán.
Ornate and continuous—
such is the rhetoric of Fàn Cài.
Sharp, scraping, and piercing—
such is the cleverness of Xī Lóng.
Above, it imitates the laws of *Sháo Shuò* and *Nán Yuè*;
in the middle, it takes its measure from *Bái Xuě* and *Lù Shuǐ*;
below, it gathers its forms from *Yán Lù* and *Bā Rén*.
Thus, the noble and the lowly, the refined and the vulgar,
the wise and the foolish, the brave and the fearful,
and even the fish, turtles, birds, and beasts,
none who hear it fail to prick up their ears like startled deer.
They stretch like bears and extend like birds,
watch like owls and look back like wolves.
They clap, shout, and leap about,
each attaining their proper proportion.
People fulfill their desires,
and all return to the center of harmony,
thereby beautifying the customs.
Qū Píng departs for a happy land;
Jiè Tuī returns to receive his emolument.
Dàntái carries the corpse back;
Gāo Yú tempers his weeping.
Zhǎng Wàn halts his treasonous plot;
Qú Mí no longer harbors malice.
Kuài Kuì is able to repel the enemy;
Bù Zhàn achieves integrity and courage.
Kings and dukes preserve their positions;
recluses find peace in the thickets and woods.
Officials delight in their duties;
scholars make their homes through generations.
Sturgeon gasp at the water's edge;
the four carriage horses look up while the dark cranes dance.
At that time,
Mián Jū fell silent,
and Bó Yá destroyed his strings.
Hù Bā leaned against the tuning pegs;
Qìng Xiāng loosened his hanging stones.
They stared with wide-eyed wonder,
offering praise again and again.
They lost their composure and fell from their seats,
clapping their hands like rolls of thunder.
With narrowed eyes and searching gazes,
their tears flowed in profusion.
Therefore, it can communicate with the spirits and move all things,
express the spirit and convey intentions.
It brings forth sincerity and manifests the will,
leading the people to take up their tasks.
It washes away filth and impurity,
cleansing the soul of its grime.
In ancient times, Páoxī made the zither,
and Shénnóng created the se-zither.
Nǚwā fashioned the reed pipes,
and Bàoxīn made the ocarina.
Chuí harmonized the bells;
Shū separated the chimes.
Some smelted gold or ground stone,
making them radiant, cut, and polished.
They molded, carved, and burnished,
engraving and drilling with great effort.
Exhausting every subtle and ingenious skill,
they spent months and years in the task.
Only then were the instruments completed,
and their sounds were as they are.
Only the flute follows its natural disposition,
without changing its material.
Once cut and blown,
its sound is thus.
This, indeed, is the principle of simplicity,
the work of a worthy man.
If this is so,
then the six instruments
were still refined and improved by the two sage sovereigns.
How much more so the flute, born in the Great Hàn!
Yet scholars do not recognize that it can assist in achieving great beauty;
they neglect it and do not praise it—
how tragic!
There was the scholar Qiū Zhòng, who spoke of its origins
but did not know its vast profundity.
His song said:
"In recent times, the double flute arose from the Qiāng;
the Qiāng people never cease cutting the bamboo.
The dragon cries in the water, unseen;
they cut the bamboo and blow it, and the sound is similar.
They sharpen the upper holes to make them clear and piercing;
they trim it to the length of a horsewhip, making it easy to carry.
Yì Jīng Jūn Míng understood the musical scales,
so he took the original four holes and added one.
The hole added by Jūn Míng was the last to appear;
this is called the Shāng sound, completing the five notes."
When I was young, I was fond of musical sounds;
as I grew older, I delighted in them.
I believe that while things have their peak and decline,
this music never changes;
while flavors can bring satiety,
this never brings weariness.
To nourish the spirit and vital energy,
to harmonize the emotions and will,
and to dwell in solitude without distress—
nothing comes closer than musical sound.
Therefore, if repeating it is not enough,
then one chants and sings to give free rein to the will;
if chanting and singing are not enough,
then one entrusts words to expand the meaning.
However, regarding the instruments of the eight sounds
and the forms of song and dance,
talented men throughout the generations
have all composed rhapsodies and eulogies for them.
In their style and refinement,
they all follow one another.
When praising the quality of the material,
they regard peril and hardship as supreme;
when describing the sound,
they take sorrow and lamentation as the main theme;
when extolling its transformative power,
they value the shedding of tears.
Beautiful they may be,
yet they have not exhausted the true principles.
Judging from their origins,
it seems they fundamentally did not understand musical sound;
observing their intent,
they also failed to grasp the essence of ritual and music.
Among all the instruments,
the virtue of the zither is the most excellent.
Thus, I have set down my thoughts
and composed a rhapsody for it.
Its words say:
How the Paulownia trees grow!
They cling to the towering ridges of the high mountains.
Breaking through the deep soil, they are born;
they rise high to meet the stars and the celestial pole.
They contain the pure harmony of Heaven and Earth;
they inhale the auspicious light of the sun and moon.
Lush and dense, they flourish alone;
they spread their flowering branches into the vast azure.
In the evening, they receive the light at Yúyuān;
in the morning, they dry their trunks in the nine suns.
Passing through a thousand years to await their value,
they stand in divine stillness, eternally at peace.
Furthermore, the terrain of its mountains and rivers
is winding and deeply secluded,
towering and craggy.
Ranges intersect with jagged peaks,
steep and lofty.
Cinnabar cliffs are perilous,
and green walls reach ten thousand fathoms.
When overlapping peaks rise high,
they loom loftily, shrouded in clouds;
majestic and grand to the extreme,
towering and uniquely beautiful.
They exhale divine fluids to disperse as clouds,
and dwell upon sacred depths to pour forth streams.
Then the cresting waves rush forth,
wildly racing and competing in their flow.
They strike the rocks and hit the bends,
pent-up in fierce anger.
Surging and tossing,
they cast up foam and raise billows.
Splashing and pounding,
they wind and entwine like serpents.
Letting loose into the great rivers,
they cross through the central provinces.
Flowing back calmly and proceeding slowly,
they float silently in the distance.
Tranquil and vast,
they encircle and embrace the hills.
Carefully observe the products of this land,
the treasures nurtured in its hidden recesses.
Rare curiosities and Lánggān pearls,
Yáo and Jǐn jades shine with brilliance.
Clustered and accumulated,
they are spread in abundance along its sides.
Thus the Spring Orchids cover its eastern side,
and Shātáng trees grow on its western side.
Juānzǐ dwells on its sunny southern slope,
and Jade Wine wells up before it.
Dark clouds shade it from above,
and soaring Luan birds gather on its summit.
Clear dew moistens its surface,
and a gracious breeze flows through.
Standing solemn and quiet,
it is dense, subtle, and serene.
The reason for managing its surroundings
is that it is naturally divine and beautiful,
sufficient for one to desire and love it.
Thereupon, recluses of the world,
peers of Róng Qīqī and Qǐ Jì,
together they ascend the flying bridges,
cross deep ravines,
pull on branches of jasper,
and climb steep crags
to wander below.
Looking all around into the distance,
they feel as though they are soaring through the air.
They gaze toward Kūnlún
and look down upon the seashore.
They point to distant Cāngwú
and face the meandering curves of the river.
Realizing the many burdens of worldly customs,
they look up to the lingering radiance of Jīshān.
Envying the vast openness of this peak,
they are moved and forget to return.
With emotions released and views expanded,
they catch the lingering tones of Xuānyuán.
They admire Lǎotóng at the corner of Mount Guīyú
and respect the high chanting of Tàiróng.
Looking at this Wútóng tree, they are stirred with thought,
desiring to borrow an object to entrust their hearts.
So they cut its supple branches,
measuring them for the task.
The Perfected Man expresses his thoughts
and crafts the elegant Qin.
Then Lízǐ was made to oversee the ink,
and Master Jiàng Shí wielded the axe.
Kuí and Xiāng provided the methods,
and Bān and Chuí exerted their divine skill.
Carving the joints and inlaying the pieces,
making it clear yet dense, tuned and balanced.
Decorated with flowery paintings and carvings,
spreading patterns and trailing designs.
Inlaid with rhinoceros horn and ivory,
set against a kingfisher-green background.
Strung with the silk of Yuánkè,
and fretted with the jade of Zhōngshān.
There are images of dragons and phoenixes,
and the forms of ancient men.
Bó Yá waves his hands,
and Zhōng Qī listens to the sound.
Its brilliant appearance is dazzling,
radiating splendor and light.
How beautiful it is!
Líng Lún compares the pitches,
and Tián Lián stretches the strings.
Presented to the gentleman,
the new sounds are clear and resonant.
How magnificent it is!
When it is first tuned,
the Jiǎo and Yǔ notes rise together,
while Gōng and Zhǐ harmonize.
Various notes start in unison,
high and low responding repeatedly.
Rising and falling, uneven and craggy,
the beautiful sound is about to emerge.
It is truly harmonious and sufficient for one to be enthralled.
Then the correct sounds are refined
and marvelous melodies are played.
Raising Bái Xuě,
and sounding Qīng Jiǎo.
Copious and flowing in profusion,
abundant, overflowing, and rich.
Bright and shimmering, it rises high,
racing loftily in succession.
Surging and clashing as they compete,
suddenly brilliant and complex.
Its form is like towering mountains,
and its likeness like flowing waves.
Vast and surging!
Dense and majestic!
Agitated and troubled,
winding and dancing.
Rising and falling, wandering free,
shimmering and blossoming.
Controlling the posture and giving the rhythm,
responding to changes and fitting the measure.
Competing for fame and excelling in the art,
following the path with slow steps.
Vast and gentle,
the sound's fame spreads afar.
Containing a hidden charm until the end,
the lingering echoes drift into the Tàisù.
As for the high carriages and flying towers,
wide halls and quiet rooms;
on a clear, solemn winter night,
when the bright moon sheds its light.
New clothes are brilliant with kingfisher green,
and the hat-strings and emblems waft fragrance.
Thereupon the instrument is cool and the strings are tuned,
the mind is at ease and the hands are swift.
Every touch and stroke is as one wishes,
following only what the intent conceives.
First performing Lù Shuǐ,
then playing Qīng Zhǐ.
Chanting of the elegance of Táng Yáo,
and ending with the song of Wēizǐ.
Broad, bright, grand, and moist,
wandering at leisure and pausing.
Plucking the strings and singing calmly,
new sounds arise in succession.
The song says:
Riding the Fúyáo whirlwind to rest at Yíngzhōu,
I invite Lièzǐ to be my good companion.
Feasting on the morning mist and wearing the dawn clouds,
far away and light, I travel through the heavens.
Equalizing all things and transcending in self-attainment,
I entrust my life to the flow of coming and going.
Stirring clear echoes to join the gathering,
how intimate is the harmony of strings and song!
Then the melody draws to a close,
and the various sounds are about to cease.
Changing the rhyme and altering the mode,
a wondrous movement then begins.
The player brightens their harmonious countenance,
and rolls up their white sleeves.
Slender fingers fly and gallop across the strings,
in a flurry of rapid, overlapping sounds, flowing and spreading.
Sometimes lingering and longing,
sometimes suppressed and pressed down.
Circling and nurturing,
leisurely and secretly enjoying.
Suddenly it breaks forth in a vigorous gallop,
like a startling wind or chaotic clouds.
Lofty and piercing,
spreading out and partially dispersing.
Luxuriant and scattering,
elegant and brilliant.
Heroic sounds erupt and transcend,
colorful and radiant.
Sometimes intermediate sounds are intermingled,
appearing like a strange convergence.
Dual beauties advance together,
galloping side by side like wings.
At first they seem about to diverge,
but in the end they follow the same path.
Sometimes winding but not bending,
straight but not haughty.
Sometimes overlapping without confusion,
sometimes separating without becoming distinct.
Sometimes seizing and pulling with fervent spirit,
sometimes resentful and hesitant.
Suddenly fluttering and stepping lightly,
then lingering and spreading like foliage.
Sometimes rhythmic and rapid,
overlapping and densely packed.
Crisscrossing in a continuous stream,
chasing and pressing upon each other.
Sighing and praising repeatedly,
without a moment's breath between.
Exotic, gorgeous, strange, and grand;
it is impossible to fully comprehend.
As for the calm, relaxed, and elegant parts,
the grand and the subtle are each appropriate.
Clear, harmonious, and flowing;
smooth and variegated.
Solemn and gentle to please the heart,
graceful and orderly in its winding path.
Sometimes braving danger to find a meeting point,
seeking gaps and rushing toward peril.
The sound is like a lonely *kūn* bird calling over a clear pond;
its movement is like a traveling swan soaring over high cliffs.
Intricate patterns and elegant finishes,
fluttering and trailing in elegant succession.
Like a slight breeze's lingering echo,
delicate and beautiful.
Sometimes plucking, stroking, and sliding;
winding and clear.
Lightly moving and floating plucks,
bright, elegant, and intelligent.
Swift but not hurried,
lingering but not stagnant.
Fluttering and drifting into the distance,
subtle notes quickly vanishing.
Listening from afar,
it is like the harmonious cries of the *luán* and *fèng* playing amidst the clouds;
observing closely,
it is like various blossoms blooming and shining in the spring breeze.
Both abundant in its many forms,
and fine from beginning to end.
Alas, how beautiful and magnificently grand!
How endless are its transformations!
At the beginning of the three months of spring,
dressed in beautiful seasonal attire,
taking along friends,
to wander and play.
Wading through orchid gardens,
ascending high foundations.
With long forests at the back,
shaded by blossoming plants.
Overlooking clear streams,
composing new poems.
Admiring the leisure of fish and dragons,
rejoicing in the flourishing growth of a hundred plants.
Performing the legacy of *Zhònghuá*,
moved by distant admiration and long thoughts.
As for private banquets in grand halls,
with close friends and intimate guests,
orchid-scented delicacies served together,
delicious wines clear and pure.
Presenting *Nánjīng*,
performing *Xīqín*.
Following with *Língyáng*,
transitioning to *Bārén*.
Various transformations arise together,
startling the listeners and awing the spirit.
When comparing the extraordinary merits of these performances,
how could the reed pipes even be mentioned in the same breath?
If we list the suitable melodies,
there are *Guǎnglìng*, *Zhǐxī*,
*Dōngwǔ*, and *Tàishān*.
*Fēilóng*, *Lùmíng*,
and the floating strings of *Kūnjī*.
Alternating songs and successive performances,
the sounds seem natural.
The flowing *Chǔ* melodies are graceful,
calming agitation and clearing away vexation.
Reaching down to folk songs,
the *Cài Shì Wǔ Qū*.
*Wáng Zhāo*, *Chǔ Fēi*,
and *Qiānlǐ Biéhè*.
There are still others used temporarily to fill gaps,
which are also worth hearing.
Yet, if one is not broad-minded and far-reaching,
one cannot wander and play with it;
if one is not profoundly tranquil,
one cannot remain at leisure with it;
if one is not free and unconstrained,
one cannot be without regret with it;
if one is not of the highest refinement,
one cannot analyze its principles with it.
If we discuss its form and momentum,
and detail its style and sound:
the instrument is harmonious, so the resonance is transcendent;
the strings are tight, so the sound is clear.
The intervals are wide, so the notes are low;
the strings are long, so the markers ring out.
Its nature is pure and quiet, upright and orderly,
containing the harmony of supreme virtue.
It can truly move and stir the heart's will,
and release hidden emotions.
Therefore, when those harboring grief hear it,
they all feel sorrowful and distressed,
their hearts aching with melancholy.
Holding in their sorrow and moaning in distress,
they cannot restrain themselves.
When those who are healthy and happy hear it,
they are joyful and relieved,
clapping and dancing with overflowing spirit.
Lingering in boundless delight,
laughing heartily throughout the day.
When those who are balanced and peaceful listen to it,
they are nurtured with pleasure and joy,
reaching a state of virtuous, solemn, and profound truth.
Tranquil and empty, delighting in antiquity,
they cast aside affairs and forget themselves.
Thus, *Bóyí* used it to attain incorruptibility,
*Yán Huí* to attain benevolence,
*Bǐgān* to attain loyalty,
and *Wěi Shēng* to attain trustworthiness.
*Huì Shī* used it for eloquence,
and *Wànshí* for cautious reticence.
For the rest, it extends to all categories;
the results are not just one.
They reach the same goal by different paths,
some through refinement, some through substance.
Summing up central harmony to govern all things,
all utilize it daily without fail.
Its power to move people and touch things
is indeed great!
At that time,
metal and stone instruments fall silent,
gourd and bamboo instruments hold their breath.
*Wáng Bào* stops his singing,
*Dí Yá* loses his sense of taste.
*Tiānwú* leaps in the deep abyss,
*Wáng Qiáo* parts the clouds and descends.
The *yuèzhuó* phoenixes dance on the courtyard steps,
and the wandering spirits flutter and gather.
It moves Heaven and Earth to achieve harmony,
let alone the many kinds of crawling creatures.
Admiring the excellence and luxuriance of this instrument,
I chant this composition to console myself.
Forever serving and using it without wearying,
it is truly what has been valued from antiquity to the present.
The Envoi says:
The tranquil virtue of the *qín*,
it cannot be measured!
Its body is pure and its heart distant,
so remote it is hard to reach the end!
Fine substance and beautiful hands,
meet in this present age!
Vibrant and gathering sounds,
it stands at the head of all arts!
Those who understand its sound are rare;
who can truly treasure it?
Only the Ultimate Man
can fully realize the elegant *qín*!
The treasure of the Hé and the Fén,
is the hanging gourd of Qǔwò.
The rarity of Zōu and Lǔ,
is the solitary bamboo of Wènyáng.
As for the beauty of trailing vines spreading profusely,
the nourishment of soaking in divine fluids,
the terrain of corners and bends, level and steep,
and the play of birds soaring and gathering—
these are indeed detailed by many authors,
so I may omit them.
Merely observe the crafting of the instrument:
then one examines the thick and the thin,
and measures the short and the long.
The raw stalks are arranged,
and the cured reeds are cut.
Establishing the Gōng and dividing the Yǔ,
arranging the Zhǐ and lining up the Shāng.
Releasing air makes it quiet,
while pressing it makes it soar.
The pipes are clustered and displayed in rows,
the sound is subtle and contains clarity.
Each keeps to its one to oversee its response,
united by the large gourd to form the Shēng.
Rooted in Huángzhōng to raise the tone,
looking toward the Fènghuáng's posture to lift its shape.
Imitating the imperial wings to insert the pipes,
mimicking the Luán bird's notes to sharpen the voice.
Like a bird standing on tiptoe,
fluttering and soaring.
A bright pearl in its beak,
as if held or as if hanging.
Long stalks lean inward,
and the remaining pipes meander outward.
Side by side in dense array,
uneven like the scales of fish.
Thereupon, there is a beginning of abundance and an end of restraint,
former glory followed by later exhaustion.
Stirred by indignation at current lowliness,
ever longing for past nobility.
While the crowd fills the hall drinking wine,
one sits alone in a corner covering tears.
Holding the sounding Shēng and about to blow,
first clearing the throat to steady the breath.
At first easy and leisurely,
midway, it becomes stifled and distressed.
Finally high and abrupt,
then rushing and boiling over.
Surging and melancholy,
as if about to stop, yet breaking forth again.
Rapid and swift like a chase,
as if about to let go, yet failing in the middle.
Sorrowful and grieving,
bright and dazzling.
Flooding and overflowing,
shining and lofty.
Sometimes drifting and smooth,
sometimes leaping and swift.
Sometimes going and not returning,
sometimes leaving and re-entering.
Lingering and spreading,
dispersing and layering.
The dance begins then stops mid-way,
the rhythm is about to be struck but cannot be caught.
When joyful sounds erupt, the whole room rejoices;
when sorrowful notes play, all present weep.
Stirring the slender feathers to vibrate the hidden reeds,
passing through the upper tubes and connecting to the lower pipes.
Responding to blowing and inhaling to come and go,
following the rise and fall of emptiness and fullness.
Bursting with passion and clarity,
looking back with hesitation and slow ease.
Cease the mournful plucking of "Zhāng Nǚ",
let flow the famous melody of "Guǎnglíng".
Chanting the "Yuán Táo" of the blooming peach,
singing "Zǎo Xià" of the clustered fruit.
The song says:
Beneath the date tree, clusters hang,
red fruits in abundance.
Suddenly they fall,
and turn into withered branches.
If in life one cannot make merry,
what is the use of a hollow posthumous title after death!
Then drawing out "Fēilóng",
sounding "Kūnjī".
The "Shuāng Hóng" soar,
the "Bái Hè" fly.
Zǐqiáo rises lightly,
Míngjūn longs for home.
The King of Jīng sighs and chants long,
the Consort of Chǔ sighs with increased sorrow.
How mournful and poignant,
yīngyīng and guānguān,
like a separated goose calling to its young;
harmonious and gentle,
yōngyōng and jiējiē,
like a flock of chicks following their mother.
Intricate and sudden realizations,
deep, grand, and blending,
chattering and twittering—
how discernibly clever.
Sharp and quiet,
how like the bending of a chime stone.
As for when the spring sun first warms,
sending off a traveler by the river.
The wine is mellow and the guests are bustling,
the music ends and the sun moves.
Distant guests begin to leave,
the host is slightly weary.
Loosening strings and sheathing the flute,
removing the ocarina and putting away the bamboo flute.
Thereupon, moving closer to the central feast,
bringing along friends.
Relaxing the stern expression,
bringing forth hidden feelings.
Peeling the yellow skins to offer sweet citrus,
tilting the pale porcelain to pour the wine of Líng.
The rays of light are solemn as they align,
a pair of Fènghuáng chirp in harmony.
Jìn Yě was startled and threw away his qin,
to say nothing of the zither of Qí and the zheng of Qín.
New sounds change the tune,
strange rhythms flow freely.
Entwining with songs and drums,
encompassing all the musical bells and pipes.
Brilliantly glowing and releasing splendor,
vigorously the spirit emerges.
"Qiūfēng" is chanted on the road to Yān,
"Tiānguāng" is as grand as "Zhāorì".
The deep tones do not exceed Gōng,
the high tones do not surpass Yǔ.
Singing out "Zhāng" and "Xià",
guiding and raising "Sháo" and "Wǔ".
Harmonizing Chén and Sòng,
uniting Qí and Chǔ.
Near but not crowding, far but not detached,
the sounds form a pattern and the rhythm has order.
Since governance has its gains and losses,
and customs vary between the pure and the thin.
Music is that which shifts customs toward the good,
and also that which changes habits away from the bad.
Therefore, though the instruments of silk and bamboo have not changed,
the melodies of Sāng and Pú have already arisen.
Only the reed
can refine the clarity of all sounds;
only the Shēng
can aggregate the forest of all purities.
Wèi has no place to practice its deviance,
Zhèng has no room to contain its licentiousness.
If it were not the harmonious music of the world,
the unchangeable sound of virtue,
who else could attain to this!
The extraordinary young gentlemen,
are of singular nature and fond of the unusual.
They look down on the world and forget glory,
abandoning and cutting off human affairs.
Looking toward the heights and admiring the ancients,
longing with deep and distant thoughts.
Intending to climb Jīshān to maintain their integrity,
or float upon the vast sea to let their will roam.
Thereupon they invite friends,
gathering those of similar tastes.
They refine the ultimate mechanisms of life and nature,
and study the profound mysteries of virtue and the Way.
Pitying the common folk for their lack of realization,
they alone are transcendent and the first to awaken.
Cramped by the narrowness of the world's paths,
they look up to the celestial roads and stride high.
Distant and beautiful, transcending the vulgar and forgetting the self,
they then give a passionate and long whistle.
At that time, the sun casts its late shadows,
its flowing light reaching *Méngsì*.
Wandering hand in hand,
pacing with hesitant steps.
They emit marvelous sounds from cinnabar lips,
and stir mournful notes from pearly white teeth.
The echoes rise and fall, secretly shifting,
as the breath surges and sparks like fire.
Harmonizing *Huánggōng* with *Qīngjiǎo*,
mingling *Shāng* and *Yǔ* with the flowing *Zhǐ*.
Floating like drifting clouds in the *Tàiqīng* heavens,
gathering like a great wind across ten thousand miles.
When the song ends and the echoes cease,
the lingering pleasure does not fade.
Truly a supreme sound of nature,
it is beyond what silk and bamboo instruments can emulate.
Thus, the voice relies on no instrument,
and its use borrows from no external thing.
Drawing nearby from one’s own body,
the mind governs and the breath directs.
Moving the lips creates a tune;
opening the mouth forms a sound.
Touching upon categories and moved by things,
one sings or hums accordingly.
It is grand but not vulgar;
it is fine but not muffled.
Its clarity is sharper than the pipe or flute,
its gentle richness more harmonious than the zithers.
Its mystery is enough to communicate with spirits and divine the soul;
its subtlety is enough to exhaust the hidden and fathom the deep.
It gathers the mournful desolation of *Jīchǔ*,
and moderates the decadent excess of *Bèilǐ*.
It relieves the great disaster of scorching drought,
and returns extreme *Yáng* to layered *Yīn*.
Chanting and leading through ten thousand changes,
its melodic use is without limit.
It is peaceful, joyous, and pleasant;
it is sorrowful, tragic, and heart-rending.
At times faint and scattered as if about to cease,
then suddenly forceful, impassioned, and bold.
Sometimes slow, graceful, and leisurely,
then rushing, bustling, and soaring.
Emotions are pensive yet able to return;
the heart, though sorrowful, is not harmed.
Gathering the supreme harmony of the eight sounds,
it is truly the peak of joy without ruin.
When climbing a high terrace to overlook the distance,
or opening a decorated window to cast one’s gaze far.
Sighing and clapping, lifting the head high,
a long, loud, and resonant sound issues forth.
Sometimes stretching out and returning to itself,
sometimes lingering and then released again.
Sometimes weak, soft, and supple,
sometimes surging and vigorously rushing.
Transverse echoes resonate and overflow,
cold and distant, clear and bright.
Its extraordinary spirit gushes forth,
in a chaotic yet intertwining flurry.
Like a biting wind rising,
chirping echoes break out.
It performs the long longing of the horses of *Hú*,
facing the cold winds of *Běisuò*.
Or it is like a wild goose leading its chicks,
their flock crying out in the desert.
Thus it can create sound based on form,
and compose melodies according to events.
Responding to things without end,
the mechanism is triggered and the echo is swift.
Pent-up feelings surge and flow,
continuous as the connecting clouds.
As if separating, as if joining,
about to break, then continuing again.
*Fēilián* drums in the dark abyss;
a fierce tiger responds in the middle of the valley.
*Nánjī* moves in the vault of heaven;
a clear breeze shakes the tall trees.
Scattering stagnant accumulations and spreading them wide,
it cleanses the turbid filth of dust and haze.
It transforms the supreme harmony of *Yīn* and *Yáng*,
and shifts the corrupt customs of licentious ways.
When wandering on lofty ridges,
or ascending *Jǐngshān*.
Standing by the side of a cliff,
watching the flowing stream.
Sitting on a flat rock,
rinsing with clear spring water.
Reclining on the lush orchids of the banks,
shaded by the swaying tall bamboo.
Then one chants and whistles to express oneself,
the sounds following one another in a continuous echo.
Releasing the pent-up frustration of accumulated thoughts,
unfolding the long-entwined knots of the heart.
The mind is cleansed and free of burdens;
the will leaves the world, floating away.
If it takes the image of metal and leather,
or emulates the laws of pottery and gourd.
Many sounds play together,
like the pipe or the flute.
Booming and thundering,
crashing and echoing loudly.
When *Zhǐ* is sounded, mid-winter becomes warm and steaming;
when *Yǔ* is unleashed, severe frost makes summer wither.
When *Shāng* is moved, autumn rain falls in spring;
when *Jiǎo* is played, valley winds whistle through the branches.
The pitch and harmony are not constant;
the melody has no fixed system.
It moves without drifting away;
it stops without stagnating.
Expressed through the lips and mouth,
it takes the fragrant breath and travels afar.
The notes are exquisite and the echoes flow;
the sounds are sharp, clear, and piercing.
Truly the peak of natural beauty,
how extraordinary and unique in all the world.
It surpasses the *Shào*, *Xià*, and *Xiánchí*,
why merely distinguish it from the music of *Zhèng* and *Wèi*?
At this, *Miánjū* became tongue-tied and lost his spirit,
while *Wáng Bào* shut his mouth and turned pale.
*Yú Gōng* ceased his voice and stopped his song;
*Níng Zǐ* folded his hands and sighed.
*Zhōng Qī* abandoned his zither to listen instead;
*Kǒngfù* forgot the taste of food and did not eat.
The hundred beasts all dance and clap their feet;
the *Fènghuáng* comes with its graceful bearing and flaps its wings.
Thus one knows the wonder of Long Whistling;
it is indeed the ultimate of all sounds.
Long ago, Chǔ Xiāng Wáng and Sòng Yù were traveling at the Yúnmèng zhī Tái,
looking out toward the Gāotáng zhī Guàn.
Above it, there was a unique cloud vapor,
towering and rising straight up,
suddenly changing its appearance,
in just a brief moment,
transforming without limit.
Wáng asked Yù, saying:
“What vapor is this?”
Yù replied:
“It is what is called Zhāoyún.”
Wáng asked:
“What is meant by Zhāoyún?”
Yù said:
“In the past, Xiānwáng once traveled to Gāotáng.
Feeling weary, he took a nap during the day.
In a dream, he saw a woman who said:
‘I am the woman of Wūshān,
a guest at Gāotáng.
Hearing that you, my Lord, are traveling at Gāotáng,
I wish to offer you my pillow and mat.’
Wáng thereupon favored her.
When she left, she took her leave, saying:
‘I dwell on the sunny side of Wūshān,
by the slopes of the high hills.
At dawn I am Zhāoyún,
at dusk I am Xíngyǔ.
Morning after morning, evening after evening,
beneath Yángtái.’
The next morning he looked out for it,
and it was as she had said.
Therefore, he established a temple for her,
calling it
‘Zhāoyún’.
Wáng said:
“When Zhāoyún first emerges,
what is its form like?”
Yù replied:
“When it first emerges,
it is dense and lush like an upright pine.
When it advances a little,
it is bright and clear like a beautiful lady.
Raising her sleeves to shield the sun,
she gazes toward the one she longs for.
Suddenly its appearance changes;
swift as if driving a team of four horses,
and raising feathered banners.
It is cool like the wind,
and chilly like the rain.
When the wind stops and the rain clears,
the cloud is nowhere to be found.”
Wáng said:
“May I also travel there now?”
Yù said:
“You may.”
Wáng asked:
“What is it like there?”
Yù said:
“It is high and prominent;
the view from there is vast!
It is broad and pervasive;
it is the progenitor of the ten thousand things!
Above, it reaches to the heavens;
below, it is reflected in the deep.
Rare wonders and marvelous sights,
beyond description.”
Wáng said:
“Attempt to compose a rhapsody on it for me.”
Yù said:
“Yes, yes.”
“As for the overall form of Gāotáng,
it is utterly unique and incomparable to any other thing.
Wūshān is majestic and without equal,
