its paths twisting and winding in layers.
Climbing the craggy peaks and looking down,
one overlooks the pooled waters at the foot of the high slopes.
When the rain from the heavens has just cleared,
one sees the waters of a hundred valleys gathering together.
They rush and roar without sound,
overflowing and surging as they flow in together.
They spread out vast and wide in all directions,
billowing and deep, never ceasing.
When a long wind arrives, waves arise,
like the solitary ridges of Lì Shān.
Their momentum crashes against the banks and they strike each other,
drawn through narrow passes and then merging back.
In the center they swell in fury and rise particularly high,
as if floating on the sea and gazing at Jiéshí.
Gravel and boulders grind against each other,
with a thundering roar that shakes the heavens.
Huge stones are submerged in the splashing water,
and the foam surges up high and fierce.
The water ripples and swirls around,
while the great waves roll and overflow.
Rushing and leaping, they strike one another,
raising a sound like a torrential downpour from the clouds.
Fierce beasts are startled and leap in terror,
recklessly fleeing and racing away.
Tigers, leopards, jackals, and rhinoceroses,
lose their spirit and gasp in fear.
Eagles, ospreys, hawks, and falcons,
fly about or dive for cover,
with trembling legs and bated breath,
how would they dare to seize prey recklessly?
Then the water creatures are all exposed,
resting on the sunny side of the islets.
Soft-shell turtles, alligators, sturgeons, and tunas,
lie piled together in every direction.
Shaking their scales and flapping their fins,
they slither and coil about.
Gazing from halfway up the slope,
the dark trees bloom even in winter.
Brilliant and shimmering,
they dazzle the eyes.
They are splendid as the arrayed stars,
their forms cannot be fully described.
The hazel groves are lush and dense,
their blossoms forming a canopy.
Pairs of catalpa trees hang their clusters,
their intertwining branches meeting together.
Swaying and moving gently,
following the air like dark shadows.
Stretching their wings to the east and west,
they are graceful and abundant.
Green leaves wrap around purple flowers,
with red stems and white calyxes.
Slender branches moan sadly,
with a sound like reed pipes and flutes.
High and low notes harmonize,
with five variations and four reunions.
It moves the heart and stirs the ears,
twisting the bowels and wounding the spirit.
Orphans and widows,
feel a chilled heart and an aching nose.
High officials would neglect their offices,
and worthy men would lose their resolve.
Sorrowful thoughts would not cease,
as they sigh and shed tears.
Climbing high and looking into the distance,
makes the heart weary.
The winding banks are craggy and steep,
stacked and layered in massive piles.
The boulders are perilous and sharp,
leaning and precarious as if the cliffs might collapse.
Rugged peaks are uneven,
crisscrossing and chasing one another.
Corners clash and intersect,
back-to-back or crouching low.
They cross and accumulate,
layer upon layer, ever increasing.
Their shape is like the Dǐzhù Rock,
situated below Wū Shān.
Looking up at the mountaintops,
how solemn and loftily they tower,
dazzling like a rainbow.
Looking down into the abyss,
it is hollow, silent, deep, and dark.
One cannot see its bottom,
only the empty sound of the pines is heard.
The leaning banks are vast and wide;
standing there, one moves like a climbing bear.
Remaining there for long without leaving,
one's feet are exhausted and sweat breaks out.
In a daze and sudden trance,
one is sorrowful and loses oneself.
It makes the heart tremble,
and for no reason, one is struck by fear.
Even the decisiveness of Bèn and Yù
could not muster courage here.
Suddenly startled by strange things,
not knowing where they emerged.
Swarming and numerous,
as if born of ghosts,
or appearing from spirits.
Their shapes resemble running beasts,
or take the form of flying birds.
Deceptive, wondrous, and grand,
they cannot be fully described.
Ascending to the side of the lookout,
the ground is surprisingly level.
Spreading out like a winnowing fan,
fragrant grasses grow in rows.
Autumn orchids, Chǎi, and Huì,
Jiānglí is in full bloom.
Green Quán and Shègàn,
Jiéché grows in dense clusters.
The thin grass sways gently,
stretching far in lush beauty.
Fragrances from Yuè are subtle and hidden,
and many birds cry out.
Male and female lose each other,
calling out in mournful song.
Wángjū and Líhuáng,
Zhèngmíng and Chǔjiū.
Zǐguī and Sīfù,
Chuíjī in their high nests.
Their chirping is harmonious,
wandering in the prime of their years.
They sing in turn and harmonize together,
following the rhythm and the flow.
There are men of the Way,
Xiànmén and Gāoxī.
To the north is Yùlín,
where the Duke of Lè gathers grain.
They offer pure sacrificial animals
and pray in the jeweled chamber.
They sacrifice to the various gods
and pay homage to Tài Yī.
The prayers of the invocators are prepared,
and the ritual words are completed.
The King then rides a jade chariot,
drawn by four grey dragons.
Tassels hang from the banners,
and the pennants wave in harmony.
Large strings are plucked and elegant sounds flow;
a cold wind passes, increasing the sorrow.
Then the songs are tuned,
making one feel pained and distressed,
catching one's breath and sighing more deeply.
Then the hunters are unleashed,
their positions scattered like stars.
Orders are passed for the feather-hunt,
bits are held in mouths for silence.
Bows and crossbows are not yet fired,
nets and traps are not yet overturned.
They wade through the vastness,
and gallop over the lush greenery.
Before the flying birds can take wing,
and before the running beasts can flee,
how sudden was the strike,
as hooves and feet are splattered with blood?
Deeds are accomplished and the first prize taken,
the capture-wagons are already full.
When the King wishes to go and see,
he must first fast and abstain,
choosing the right time and selecting the day.
With a simple chariot and dark robes,
he raises cloud-pennants
and uses rainbows as banners,
with kingfisher feathers for the canopy.
The wind rises and the rain stops,
as he travels a thousand lǐ.
The canopy is raised as if to clear the fog,
as he goes to the meeting.
Thinking of all the ten thousand regions,
worrying about the state's harms.
He welcomes the wise and the sagely,
assisting where there is inadequacy.
The nine orifices are cleared of congestion,
and the spirit perceives what was stagnant.
May he extend his years and increase his longevity for ten thousand years.
Chǔ Xiāng Wáng and Sòng Yù were wandering at the shores of Yúnmèng,
and the King ordered Sòng Yù to compose a rhapsody on the events of Gāotáng.
That night, the King slept,
and indeed dreamed of meeting a goddess,
whose appearance was exceedingly beautiful.
The King was amazed by this,
and the next day,
he told Sòng Yù about it.
Sòng Yù said:
“What was the dream like?”
The King said:
“After dusk,
my spirit was in a trance,
as if I were experiencing some joy.
All was fluttering and restless,
and I knew not what it meant.
A blurred vision appeared before my eyes,
and suddenly it felt as if I remembered something.
I saw a woman,
whose form was most extraordinary.
I dreamed of her while sleeping,
but upon waking, I did not recognize myself.
I was bewildered and unhappy,
feeling dejected as if I had lost my purpose.
Then I calmed my heart and steadied my breath,
and saw the dream again.”
The King said:
“What was her appearance like?”
Sòng Yù said:
“How lush! How beautiful!
All perfections are prepared in her!
How magnificent! How lovely!
She is difficult to fathom or exhaustively describe!
In ancient times she did not exist,
and the world has never seen her like.
Her extraordinary posture and exquisite manner
cannot be praised enough.
When she first arrives,
she is as radiant as the morning sun first shining on the roof beams.
When she advances a little,
she is as bright as the clear moon spreading its light.
In a brief moment,
her beautiful features overflow.
Dazzling like a flower,
as gentle as a piece of jade.
The five colors race together,
her form cannot be fully depicted.
Looking at her closely,
she dazzles the essence of one's eyes.
When she is fully adorned,
then silks, gauzes, and brocades are rich in pattern.
Her ultimate attire and wonderful colors illuminate all directions.
Shaking her embroidered robes,
she is draped in fine skirts.
The thick parts are not short,
the thin parts are not long.
Her gait is elegant as she illuminates the palace hall.
Suddenly she changes her expression,
graceful as a wandering dragon soaring on the clouds.
Her clothing is beautiful,
her light makeup is refined.
She is bathed in orchid scents,
and breathes the fragrance of Ruò.
Her nature is harmonious and gentle,
suitable to serve by one's side.
She follows the order of the lowly,
and attunes her heart and mind.”
The King said:
“She is indeed this magnificent!
Try to compose a rhapsody on her for me.”
Sòng Yù said:
“I obey.”
Oh, how beautiful is the Shénnǚ!
She possesses the rich adornments of Yīn and Yáng.
Clad in floral patterns so lovely to behold,
like a kingfisher spreading its wings.
Her image is peerless,
her beauty is limitless.
Even if Máo Qiáng covered her face with her sleeves,
she would not be enough to set a standard for her.
Even if Xī Shī hid her face,
she would lose all color by comparison.
Near her, she is enchanting;
from afar, she has a commanding presence.
Her bone structure is full of wonders,
matching the physiognomy of a sovereign.
Looking at her fills the eyes;
who could ever surpass her?
My heart alone is delighted,
enjoying her without measure.
Our meeting was rare and the favor sparse,
so I could not fully express my feelings.
Others did not see her,
but the King viewed her form.
Her form was lofty and grand,
how can it be fully described?
Her appearance was full and dignifiedly beautiful,
embodying a warm and lustrous jade-like countenance.
Her pupils were bright and clear,
clear-eyed, most beautiful and admirable.
Her eyebrows were curved and arched like a moth's antennae,
her vermilion lips as vivid as cinnabar.
Her natural substance was robust and rich,
her will relaxed and her body at ease.
She was both graceful in quiet seclusion
and dancing among the world of men.
She is suited for high palaces to broaden the mind,
with wings relaxed and spacious.
Moving her misty gauze as she walked slowly,
the sound of her tinkling on the courtyard floor.
Gazing toward my curtain with a lingering look,
like flowing waves about to ripple.
Shaking her long sleeves to straighten her lapel,
standing hesitantly and restless.
Calm and quiet, tranquil and serene,
her nature deep and deliberate, not irritable.
At times moving slightly with composure,
her intentions could not yet be fathomed.
Her mind seemed near yet was already far,
as if about to come but turning back again.
Lifting my bed-curtain and asking to serve,
wishing to give her heart with total devotion.
Harboring a purity of integrity and brilliance,
in the end she remained aloof from me.
She offered fine words in response,
breathing a fragrance like that of orchids.
Our spirits intermingled in coming and going,
the heart joyful and full of happiness.
But the spirit alone enjoyed it without forming a bond,
the soul solitary and without purpose.
Containing promises but not clearly given,
I sighed aloud with a mournful sound.
Showing a flash of slight anger to maintain herself,
she could never be violated.
Then she shook her pendant ornaments,
making the jade bells chime.
She tidied her clothes,
and composed her expression.
She looked back at her female tutor,
and called for the Tàifù.
Before the joy of love could be joined,
she was about to say farewell and depart.
Hesitating and withdrawing her person,
she could not be closely approached.
Seemingly gone but not yet walked away,
in her heart she seemed to look back.
Her eyes glanced slightly,
spirit and brilliance exchanged.
Her moods and forms overflowed,
beyond what can be recorded.
Her intent to leave was not yet final,
but my spirit and heart were filled with fear and upheaval.
Rites were not finished in time,
the farewell could not be fully explored.
Wishing to borrow just a brief moment,
the Shénnǚ claimed she was in a hurry.
My intestines churned and my spirit was wounded,
upside down and losing my composure.
Darkly it became night,
and suddenly I knew not where I was.
With these feelings held privately in my heart,
to whom can they be told?
Melancholy and shedding tears,
seeking her until the dawn.
The Dàfū Dēngtú Zǐ was in attendance upon the Chǔ Wáng,
and slandered Sòng Yù saying:
“Yù is a man of graceful and beautiful appearance,
his speech is full of subtle words,
and he is by nature fond of sex.
I wish Your Majesty would not let him enter or leave the inner palace.”
The King asked Sòng Yù about Dēngtú Zǐ’s words,
Yù said:
“A graceful and beautiful appearance
is what I received from Heaven;
speech full of subtle words
is what I learned from my teachers;
as for being fond of sex,
I, your servant, have no such inclination.”
The King said:
“If you are not fond of sex,
do you have an explanation?
If there is an explanation, you may stay;
if not, you must withdraw.”
Yù said:
“Of the fine women in the world, none are like those of Chǔ Guó;
of the beauties of Chǔ Guó, none are like those of my neighborhood;
of the beauties of my neighborhood, none are like the daughter of my eastern neighbor.
The daughter of the eastern neighbor,
if increased by one inch she would be too tall,
if decreased by one inch she would be too short;
if she applied powder she would be too white,
if she applied rouge she would be too red.
Her eyebrows are like kingfisher feathers,
her skin like white snow,
her waist like bundled silk,
her teeth like held shells.
With a charming smile,
she would bewitch Yángchéng
and mesmerize Xiàcài.
Yet this woman has climbed the wall to peep at me for three years,
and until now I have not consented.
Dēngtú Zǐ is not like this.
His wife has disheveled hair and curled ears,
protruding lips and gapped teeth.
She walks sideways and is hunchbacked,
and moreover has scabies and hemorrhoids.
Dēngtú Zǐ delights in her,
and has had five sons by her.
May Your Majesty carefully examine this,
to see who is truly fond of sex.”
At that time, the Dàfū of Zhānghuá from Qín was at the King’s side,
and thus stepped forward and said:
“Now Sòng Yù grandly praises his neighbor’s daughter,
considering her a great beauty;
this is a source of folly and disorder!
I consider myself one who maintains virtue,
and I say I am not like him.
Furthermore, a concubine from a dead-end alley in southern Chǔ,
how is she worthy of being spoken of to the Great King?
As for my own lowly self,
of the things my eyes have seen,
I have not dared to speak.”
The King said:
“Try to speak of them for me.”
The Dàfū said:
“Yes, yes.”
“When I was young, I once traveled far,
observing all the lands,
and my feet traversed the five capitals.
I left Xiányáng,
and enjoyed myself in Hándān.
I wandered leisurely between the Zhēn and Wěi rivers of Zhèng and Wèi.
It was then at the end of spring,
welcoming the sun of summer.
The orioles chirped,
and many women went out to gather mulberries.
The beauties of these suburbs
had radiant complexions containing light.
Their bodies were beautiful and their faces seductive,
not needing any adornment.
I observed the beautiful ones among them,
and thus recited from the Book of Poetry:
‘Following the great road, I grasp your sleeve,’
gifting her fragrant flowers with most wonderful words.
Then the maiden seemed to have expectation but did not come,
suddenly seemed to come but was not seen;
our intentions were intimate but our bodies distant,
her movements provided different views;
containing joy and a slight smile,
she glanced secretly with flowing eyes.
Again I recited from the Book of Poetry:
‘Awakening in the spring breeze, fresh glory blooms.’
‘Purifying and fasting to wait for the kind voice.’
‘To give me such as this, it would be better not to have been born.’
Thus she hesitated and declined with excuses,
for it was only through subtle words that we moved each other,
and our spirits relied upon one another;
my eyes desired her face,
while my heart regarded her righteousness;
praising with poetry and maintaining the rites,
in the end there was no transgression;
therefore, it is worthy of praise.”
Thereupon the Chǔ Wáng praised it as good,
and Sòng Yù consequently did not have to withdraw.
In the third year of Huángchū,
I attended court in Jīngshī,
and on my return, I crossed the Luò River.
Ancient people had a saying
that the spirit of this water
is named Mìfēi.
Moved by Sòng Yù’s account of the goddess to Chǔ Wáng,
I composed this rhapsody.
Its words say:
I departed from Jīngyù to return to the eastern fief.
Leaving Yīquè behind,
I crossed Huányuán.
Passing through Tōnggǔ,
I ascended Jǐngshān.
The sun was already leaning to the west;
the carriage was weary and the horses tired.
Thus, I unhitched the carriage at Hèngāo
and grazed the team in Zhītián.
I lingered in Yánglín
and let my gaze wander over the Luò River.
At this, my essence shifted and my spirit was startled;
suddenly my thoughts were scattered.
Looking down, I saw nothing;
looking up, I beheld a different sight.
I saw a beautiful woman
at the side of the cliffs.
I reached for the driver and told him,
“Do you see someone over there?
Who is that person,
so exceedingly beautiful?”
The driver replied,
“I have heard that the spirit of the Hé and Luò
is named Mìfēi.
Could it be that what the Jūnwáng sees
is she?
What does she look like?
I wish to hear it.”
I told him,
“Her form —
she flutters like a startled swan,
and undulates like a swimming dragon.
Her radiance outshines the autumn chrysanthemum;
her luxuriance rivals the spring pine.
Dimly seen as the moon obscured by light clouds;
drifting like snow whirled by the flowing wind.
Gazing from afar,
she is as bright as the sun rising through morning mists;
observing from near,
she is as glowing as a lotus rising from clear ripples.
Neither too plump nor too thin,
her height is perfectly measured.
Her shoulders seem carved,
her waist is like bundled silk.
Her long, elegant neck
reveals her fair skin.
No fragrant oils are added,
no powder or rouge is applied.
Her cloud-like hair is piled high,
her long eyebrows are delicately arched.
Red lips glow on the outside,
white teeth shine within.
Her bright eyes glance skillfully;
dimples grace her cheeks.
Her bearing is magnificent and her beauty unrestrained,
her manner is quiet and her body composed.
Gentle in emotion and graceful in posture,
she is enchanting in her speech.
Her extraordinary attire is rare in this world,
her frame matches the paintings.
Clad in the brilliance of silk garments,
she wears earrings of jade and kingfisher feathers.
Wearing hair ornaments of gold and kingfisher,
she is adorned with bright pearls to illuminate her body.
She treads in patterned shoes for far travel,
trailing a light skirt of misty silk.
Exhaling the faint fragrance of orchids,
she paces hesitantly at the mountain’s corner.
“Then, she suddenly relaxes her body
to wander and play.
To the left, she leans on a multicolored banner;
to the right, she is shaded by a cassia flag.
She bared her white wrists at the divine bank,
plucking the black lichen from the rushing rapids.
My feelings were delighted by her virtue and beauty,
but my heart was agitated and uneasy.
Having no good matchmaker to join our joy,
I entrusted the ripples to convey my words.
Wishing my sincerity to reach her first,
I untied my jade pendant to invite her.
Alas! The beauty's cultivation is truly deep;
she is practiced in ritual and understands the Shī.
She held up a fine jade to harmonize with me,
and pointed to the deep pool as a meeting place.
Holding onto a persistent and sincere heart,
I yet feared this spirit would deceive me.
Moved by the broken promise to Jiāofǔ,
I was disappointed, hesitant, and suspicious.
I composed my countenance and quieted my will,
maintaining myself with the restraints of ritual.
“Then the Spirit of the Luò was moved;
she paced and hesitated.
Her divine light flickered and coalesced,
now dark, now bright.
She straightened her light body like a crane standing,
as if about to fly but not yet soaring.
She trod on the fragrant pepper path,
walking through the thicket of fragrant herbs, spreading fragrance.
Breaking into a long chant of eternal longing,
her voice was mournful and piercingly long.
“Then a host of spirits gathered in a crowd,
calling their companions and whistling for their peers.
Some played in the clear stream;
some soared over the divine isle.
Some gathered bright pearls;
some picked up kingfisher feathers.
They followed the two consorts of Nán Xiāng,
and took the hands of the wandering maidens of the Hànbīn.
Lamenting that the Páoguā has no mate,
singing of the Qiānniú living alone.
Raising her light robes in graceful motion,
she shaded herself with long sleeves and stood for a long time.
Her body moved as fast as a flying duck,
fleeting like a spirit.
Treading over the waves with tiny steps,
her silk stockings stirred up dust.
Her movements followed no constant rule,
appearing now precarious, now stable.
Her advances and stops were hard to predict,
as if going, yet returning.
Turning her eyes and letting her spirit flow,
radiance graced her jade-like face.
Words were held back but not yet spoken,
her breath like the fragrance of orchids.
Her beautiful appearance was graceful and supple,
making me forget to eat.
“Then Píngyì gathered the winds,
and Chuánhòu stilled the waves.
Féngyí beat the drums,
and Nǚwā sang clear songs.
Striped fish rose to alert the carriage,
and jade phoenix-bells rang as they departed together.
Six dragons solemnly held their heads level,
pulling the cloud-carriage in a stately manner.
Whales leapt to flank the wheels,
and water birds soared as guards.
“Then she crossed the northern isle
and passed the southern ridge.
Turning her white neck,
she looked back with clear eyes.
Moving her cinnabar lips to speak slowly,
she stated the principles of our meeting.
Regretting that the paths of humans and gods are different,
she lamented that our prime years could not coincide.
Raising her silk sleeve to hide her tears,
they fell onto her collar in a stream.
Grieving that this fine meeting is forever ended,
she mourned that once gone, they would be in different lands.
‘I have no small token to prove my love,
so I offer this bright earring from Jiāngnán.
Though I dwell in the depths of Tàiyīn,
my heart will long be sent to the Jūnwáng.’
Suddenly I did not realize where she went;
saddened that the spirit had vanished and her light was hidden.
“Then I left the lowlands and ascended the heights;
my feet moved but my spirit remained.
My lingering feelings imagined her;
looking back, I felt sorrow.
Hoping her divine form would reappear,
I took a light boat to row upstream.
Floating on the long river and forgetting to return,
my thoughts were continuous as my longing grew.
Through the long night, I was restless and could not sleep,
soaked by heavy frost until dawn.
I ordered the servants to prepare the carriage,
for I would return to the eastern road.
Grasping the reins and raising the whip,
I was melancholy and lingered, unable to leave.”
Nángāi
is where filial sons remind each other to provide nourishment.
Following that Nán Gāi hillside,
I gather those orchids.
Longing for the family halls,
my heart finds no rest.
The child dwelling there,
must not wander or play.
Make fragrant your evening meal,
make pure your morning food.
Following that Nán Gāi hillside,
its grass is lush and green.
The child dwelling there,
thinks of a gentle countenance.
Longing for the family halls,
my heart cannot stay.
Make fragrant your evening meal,
make pure your morning delicacies.
There is an otter, there is an otter,
by the banks of the river.
Riding the waves and plunging into the currents,
it bites the bream and catches the carp.
Crying are the forest crows,
receiving food from their young.
If care is great but respect is thin,
one is merely like the beasts.
Strive to increase your reverence,
to invite great blessings.
*Bái Huá*,
is the pure integrity of a filial son.
White flowers and red calyxes,
cover the dark thickets.
Resplendent is the son of the house,
as if polished and ground.
Throughout the morning, he examines himself three times,
never lazy in his devotion.
White flowers and crimson stems,
at the corner of the mound.
Elegant is the scholar-gentleman,
dyed but never changing.
Exhausting sincerity and fulfilling respect,
tirelessly forgetting his toil.
White flowers and dark roots,
at the curve of the hill.
Grand is the youth,
without schemes or desires.
Fresh as the morning blossoms,
none can stain or disgrace him.
*Huá Shǔ*,
is for times of harmony and years of plenty,
suited for the growth of millet and grain.
Dense are the heavy clouds,
gentle are the harmonious winds.
Millet flowers on the ridges,
wheat flourishes on the hills.
No field is left unsown,
the nine grains are thus abundant.
Grand is the dark sky,
misty is the sweet rain.
The millet sends forth thick blossoms,
standing tall in their beauty.
No field is left uncultivated,
the nine grains are thus lush.
No high ground is unsown,
no low ground is uncultivated.
Vast are the crops,
orderly is the harvest.
Storing up the royal reserves,
to fill the people's food.
The Jade Candle seasons are bright,
the glorious Way is majestic.
*Yóu Gēng*,
is for the myriad things following their proper path.
Vast is the level path,
all things follow it.
The myriad living things,
the King also treats them gently.
Since the path is followed,
and transformation is gentle.
Trees wither in the autumn,
grass sprouts in the spring.
Beasts remain in the grass,
fish leap following the flow.
The four seasons yield in turn,
the eight winds fan by turns.
Xiān Ā keeps to the schedule,
stars follow their orbits.
The five elements do not conflict,
the six energies do not change.
Tranquil is our King,
succeeding the traces of Wén.
*Chóng Qiū*,
is for the myriad things reaching their full height and greatness.
Look at that lofty hill,
its forests are dense and lush.
Plants grow tall,
moving creatures grow large.
The winds of Zhōu are pervasive,
the King's Way is truly great.
Vast is the square earth,
swirling is the great canopy of heaven.
What species does not multiply?
What life does not flourish?
Things fulfill their natures,
people prolong their lives.
Infinite is the great circle of heaven,
vast are the nine lands.
Relying on life and looking up to transformation,
what is not nurtured?
People do not die young against the Way,
things grow until they reach their limit.
*Yóu Yí*,
is for the life of the myriad things,
each obtaining its proper decorum.
Solemn is the gentleman,
following decorum and leading his nature.
Bright is the sovereign ruler,
taking benevolence as his governance.
Fish swim in the clear pond,
birds gather in the level forest.
Washing scales and flapping wings,
their sounds are resonant.
The guests offer their sincerity,
the host exhausts his heart.
The times are harmonious,
what need for anxious thought or cultivation?
Civil culture is gathered within,
military merit extends afar.
The realized man values self-reliance,
his high sentiments belong to the heavenly clouds.
He embraces the nature of saving things,
without being entangled in the dust and grime.
Duàn Shēng protected the Wèi Guó,
Zhǎn Jì saved the people of Lǔ.
Xián Gāo rewarded the Jìn army,
Zhòng Lián repelled the Qín army.
Facing the official ribbons, they did not suddenly bind themselves,
before the ritual jade, would they ever care for division?
Benefiting others, they declined rewards,
encouraging their will, thus surpassing common men.
Reaching across a thousand years,
from afar they spread their pure legacy.
Who shall succeed such pure legacy?
The wise and discerning who manage the times.
Abandoning lectures to join the discourse on the Way,
changing robes to soothe the world's hardships.
Once the hardships were soothed,
they honored the Lord and elevated the people.
Long ago there was chaos in the Central Plains,
how could such chaos be easily resolved?
Surging at the end of Yǒng Jiā,
pressing at the beginning of Tài Yuán.
Beyond the Hé, there was no return to order,
along the Jiāng, there was collapse.
The myriad states were all terrified,
the overflowing flood relied on the gentleman.
Saving the drowning came from his devotion to the Way,
quelling the violent relied on divine principles.
Qín and Zhào rejoiced in their revival,
Yān and Wèi awaited the civil order.
The worthy minister Xiè left the world's movements,
his far-reaching plans ceased due to circumstances.
Bowing high from beyond the seven provinces,
shaking his robes within the Five Lakes.
Following the mountains, he dredged deep pools,
beside the cliffs, he planted elms and catalpas.
Leaving behind his feelings, he cast off worldly things,
with pure vision, he saw the beauty of hills and valleys.
Mèng served as the Grand Tutor to Yuán Wáng;
the Tutor taught the son Yí Wáng and the grandson Wáng Wù.
Wù was dissolute and did not follow the Way;
Mèng composed poems to admonish him.
It said:
Majestically grand was my ancestor,
whose state began at Shǐ Wéi.
In robes embroidered with axes and red knee-covers,
with four stallions and dragon banners.
With the vermilion bow he went on campaign,
pacifying and settling the distant wilds.
He gathered and unified the various states,
to support the Great Shāng.
Succeeding those of Dà Péng,
his meritorious achievements were glorious.
Reaching the time of Zhōu,
through successive generations they attended the royal assemblies.
King Hǎo listened to slanders,
and indeed severed our state.
Once our state was severed,
its governance became negligent.
The exercise of rewards and punishments
no longer originated from the Royal House.
The many ministers and various lords
provided no support or defense.
The five zones of submission crumbled and fell apart,
and the House of Zhōu thereby collapsed.
My ancestors then became obscure,
and moved to Péngchéng.
Coming to me, this insignificant one,
I have labored over my life.
In the hardships of this arrogant Qín,
I took up the plow and shared in the tilling.
The long-lasting, arrogant Qín
gave Sovereign Heaven no peace.
Thus Heaven looked down toward the south,
and granted the Hàn at the capital Jīng.
How magnificent is the Hàn!
It has campaigned in the four directions.
There is nowhere it goes that is not cherished;
ten thousand states have been pacified.
Then the Emperor commanded his younger brother,
to be established as a noble in Chǔ.
Causing me, a minor official,
to serve and assist as a tutor.
Resolute and cautious was Yuán Wáng,
respectful, frugal, serene, and focused.
He showed kindness to the common people,
and accepted the guidance of his ministers.
He enjoyed the state through successive generations,
leaving a legacy of merit to his descendants.
Then it reached Yí Wáng,
who was able to uphold that succession.
Alas, the mandate was not long-lasting,
yet the King continued the ancestral sacrifices.
The attendant ministers on the left and right
were indeed august gentlemen.
Why is it that our current King
does not think of preservation?
He does not think of "treading on thin ice,"
so as to continue the work of his ancestors.
The affairs of the state are neglected,
and idle wandering is his pleasure.
Hounds and horses are his constant concern,
letting them loose and driving them on.
Devoted to these birds and beasts,
he neglects the crops and seedlings.
The common people are thus impoverished,
and our King is thus negligent.
What he promotes is not virtue,
and those he is close to are not the talented.
Only the hunting parks are expanded,
and only flattery is believed.
Fawning and sycophantic men
versus the blunt and honest elders.
Why is it that our King
does not examine this?
Having slighted his humble ministers,
he pursues desires and indulges in ease.
He treats his illustrious ancestors with contempt,
and makes light of the threat of being deposed.
Alas, oh my King,
the Hàn treats its kin with harmony.
Yet you do not labor day and night
to cultivate a fine reputation.
Majestic is the Son of Heaven,
shining upon the lands below.
Brilliant are the many officials,
upholding the laws without partiality.
Correcting the distant begins with the near;
perhaps you rely on this kinship.
Alas, oh my King,
why do you not think of this?
If you do not think or reflect,
the succession will have no standard.
Ever-increasing is the indulgence,
and ever-perilous is the state.
Reaching ice does not happen without frost;
falling does not happen without negligence.
Looking upon our King,
there is no moment he does not practice [neglect].
To revive the state and save it from collapse,
who can avoid repenting of errors?
Recalling the advice of the elders,
Qín Mù thereby achieved hegemony.
The months and years pass by,
and age approaches old man's years.
Oh, magnificent gentleman,
may you be manifest to posterity.
What is our King doing,
that he does not look into this?
If he does not keep the elders near,
why does he not reflect in time?
The Great Instrument revolves and turns,
Heaven rotates and the Earth wanders.
The four seasons follow in order like scales,
cold and heat circle around.
When the Fire Star has set in the evening,
suddenly it is the plain autumn.
The cool wind shakes the leaves loose,
and fireflies drift through the night.
The auspicious gentleman reflects in autumn,
truly moved by the transformation of things.
The days and months,
gradually replace one another.
What passes is like this,
never ceasing day or night.
Oh, you many gentlemen,
how can you be so at ease with yourselves?
The Way of Benevolence is not far off;
virtue is as light as a feather.
If sought, it is reached;
yet few among the many can uphold it.
The Great Way is profound and obscure;
one must draw out its threads.
The former people have made their works,
leaving me with high standards.
Although one may have a fine natural disposition,
if the mind is let go in indulgence,
hunting and wandering in pleasure,
dwelling in many days of leisure,
it is like that catalpa wood:
if one is not diligent with cinnabar and lacquer,
though there be the labor of rough carving,
it will ultimately betray its raw quality.
When Yǎng Yóu readied his arrow,
the beasts wailed in the forest.
When Pú Lú wound his silk lines,
his spirit moved the flying birds.
The wonder of these minor skills
was that animals responded to their hearts.
If one studies with refinement and dwells in the Way,
how can there be anything too deep or obscure?
Set the mind at ease in tranquility,
and let the will lodge among the floating clouds.
Embody it with substance,
and adorn it with patterns.
Like those southern fields,
once the labor of the plow is diligent,
and the ultimate work of weeding and hilling is done,
there must be a bountiful harvest.
Water accumulated becomes an abyss,
flowing with waves and becoming clear.
Earth accumulated becomes a mountain,
where mists and vapors rise in the dark.
The mountain does not reject a speck of dust,
and the river does not decline to be full.
Strive to be broad-minded and magnanimous,
so as to exalt the reputation of your virtue.
The high relies on the low as its foundation;
the great arises from the minute.
A broad river starts from its source;
a perfected person begins at the start.
Accumulating the minute to become manifest
is the principle of all things.
The length of a lead-rope
is truly accumulated over a thousand lǐ.
Returning to ritual for a single morning,
and the world returns to benevolence.
Like metal receiving the whetstone,
like clay on the potter's wheel.
Advance in virtue and cultivate your work,
your glorious light daily renewed.
Xí Péng looked up in admiration,
and what kind of man am I?
Your servant Zhí says:
Since I, your servant, returned to my fief bearing my offenses,
it has been etched into my skin and bone;
I have reflected deeply on my crimes and transgressions.
I eat only at midday,
and sleep only at midnight.
Truly, I felt that the net of Heaven must not be encountered again,
and that the Sagely grace could hardly be relied upon once more.
In secret, I was moved by the poem "Xiàng Shǔ,"
and the principle that those without propriety should quickly die.
My body and shadow console each other,
and my five emotions are filled with shame and fear.
To cast away my life because of my crimes
would be to go against the ancient sages' encouragement to change upon one's evening errors;
yet to endure disgrace and survive
would be to invite the poet's mockery of "what face does he have."
I prostrate myself before Your Majesty, whose virtue is like Heaven and Earth,
and whose kindness is as profound as that of parents.
Your favor flows like the spring breeze,
and your bounty is like timely rain.
Thus, that which makes no distinction even for thorns and brambles
is the grace of the Qìngyún;
the equal nurturing of the seven young
is the benevolence of the Shījiū.
To set aside guilt and demand merit
is the action of an enlightened ruler;
to pity the foolish and love the talented
is the grace of a compassionate father.
Therefore, your foolish servant lingers within your grace and bounty,
and does not dare to cast himself away.
Previously, I received an imperial edict
stating that I and others were cut off from court;
my heart was detached and my will severed.
I resigned myself to becoming an old man,
with no hope of ever holding the ceremonial guī again.
Unexpectedly, a sagely edict
has condescended to summon me.
On the day I arrived,
my heart raced toward the imperial carriage.
Residing in a secluded corner of the Western Hostel,
I have not yet attended the palace court.
With a leaping heart,
I look forward and toss in bed,
unable to bear my dog-and-horse-like longing for my master.
I respectfully submit this memorial and offer two poems;
their wording and meaning are shallow and meager,
and they are not worthy of your perusal.
I only value revealing my inner feelings
and risk your countenance to let them be heard.
Your servant Zhí is truly fearful and trembling,
bowing his head repeatedly,
for a capital offense, a capital offense.
Oh, how majestic was my late father,
who was none other than Wǔ Huáng.
He received his mandate from Heaven
to bring peace and relief to the four quarters.
Wherever his crimson banners brushed,
the nine lands were cleared and opened.
His mysterious transformation flowed everywhere,
and the wild regions came to pay homage.
Surpassing the Shāng and exceeding the Zhōu,
he matched the footsteps of Táng.
Then was born our Emperor,
possessing great wisdom for generations.
In martial matters, he is solemn and fierce;
in civil matters, he brings harmony to the times.
He received the abdication from the Hàn
and reigns over the myriad states.
Since the myriad states were transformed,
all have followed the old regulations.
He widely appointed his virtuous kin
to serve as princes of the frontier states.
The Emperor said: "You, Marquis,
shall rule this Qīngtǔ."
Possessing the entire seacoast,
it is comparable to the state of Lǔ in Zhōu times.
My carriage and robes had splendor;
my banners and insignia had order.
Numerous talented and virtuous men
were my assistants and advisors.
But I, this small child,
relied on favor and became arrogant and filled with pride.
I got caught in the net of the times
and disrupted the national laws.
Being a frontier prince and a screen for the state,
I was the first to destroy the established rules.
I was arrogant toward our Emperor's envoys
and violated our court etiquette.
The state has its penal laws,
so I was stripped of my rank and dismissed.
I was to be handed over to justice,
as the leader of the great culprits.
The bright and brilliant Son of Heaven
was nonetheless kind to his kin.
He could not bear to see me punished
or exposed in the marketplace of the court.
Going against those who uphold the law,
he took pity on me, his minor servant.
He changed my fief to Yǎnyì,
on the banks of the Hé.
My ministers and assistants were not appointed;
I had a ruler but no subordinates.
In my deficiencies of reckless indulgence,
who was there to assist my person?
I lived alone with a solitary servant
in the region of Jìfāng.
Alas, I, this small child,
encountered such misfortune.
The glorious Son of Heaven
does not leave any creature out of his grace.
He placed the black cap upon my head
and the crimson sash around my waist.
The magnificent Great Envoy arrived
to bring me glory and splendor.
Splitting the tally to receive land,
the rank of King was added to me.
Looking up, I was granted the golden seal;
looking down, I held the sagely mandate.
The Imperial grace was excessively grand;
I received it with reverence and fear.
Alas, I, this small child,
am entwined in stubbornness and evil.
In death, I would be ashamed before the ancestral tombs;
in life, I am ashamed before the palace court.
I do not dare to be arrogant toward your virtue,
but truly I rely upon your grace.
Your awesome spirit has been granted again,
enough to last me until the end of my days.
Great Heaven is boundless,
and I did not expect to survive.
I used to fear falling into ruin
and carrying my guilt to the Huánglú.
I wish to face arrows and stones,
to plant my banner on the Dōngyuè.
I hope to achieve even a tiny bit
of minor merit to redeem myself.
Risking my life and giving my life,
I would know satisfaction in being free from my transgressions.
I would gladly go to the Jiāng and Xiāng,
or brandish my spear in Wú and Yuè.
Heaven has opened my heart
to allow me to meet in the capital region.
I long to behold the sagely countenance
as if I were thirsty or hungry.
My heart's longing
is poignant and sorrowful.
Heaven is high but hears those below;
will the Emperor be willing to shine upon my insignificance?
Reverently I received the bright edict
to attend the meeting at the imperial capital.
I set out early under the stars,
foddering my horses and greasing my carriage.
I commanded the master of the attendants
to prepare my traveling party.
In the morning, I departed from Luántái;
in the evening, I stayed at Lánzhǔ.
Vast are the plains and marshes;
many are the men and women.
Passing by those public fields,
they enjoy our millet and sorghum.
There are drooping trees,
but I do not rest in their thick shade.
Though there are provisions of food,
being hungry, I have no time to eat.
I gaze at the cities but do not pass through;
I face the towns but do not wander there.
The groom alerts and urges the horses,
following the level road.
The four dark horses move gracefully,
their bits covered in foam.
The flowing wind assists the crossbar;
light clouds support the canopy.
Wading along the banks of mountain streams,
following the bends of the mountains.
Following the banks of the Hé,
I ascended the Huángbǎn.
Westward I crossed through the pass and valleys,
now descending, now ascending.
The side horses are weary from the road;
I sleep and wake again.
About to have an audience with the Sagely Emperor,
I do not dare to take ease or peace.
Slackening the pace yet galloping long,
I travel quickly toward the sun.
The vanguard raises torches;
the rear carriages fly banners.
The wheels do not stop turning;
the carriage bells never cease their sound.
Thus I arrived at the Imperial House,
and rested at this western wall.
The fine edict has not yet been granted;
I cannot yet follow the court audience.
Looking up at the city threshold,
looking down at the palace court.
My long-held thoughts are of eternal longing;
my troubled heart is as if intoxicated with sorrow.
Oh, how grand is the Jìn!
The Mandate it received is already firm.
The three ancestors are in Heaven;
The Sage Emperor continues the succession.
Virtue is broad and its transformation is brilliant;
Penalties are simple and wrongs are corrected.
A small fire was not guarded against,
And it spread to our precious treasury.
The foolish Róng and Dí,
Cunningly thought to run wild.
Taking advantage of our nation’s distress,
They spied upon our state's sharpest tools.
The regional governors had differing views;
Awe and conciliation are two separate principles.
The generals lacked a singular strategy;
The soldiers were not trained in advance.
The eminent Zhào Wáng,
Requested thirty thousand foot soldiers.
The court’s discussion was only of doubt,
And his wish was not fulfilled.
The valiant Liáng Zhēng,
Set up his high ivory standards.
Flags and canopies were visible to one another;
A secondary force acted as support.
Glaring like tigers,
They overawed those at Hàozhǐ.
Plain armor shone like the sun;
Dark tents rose like clouds.
Who followed him?
It was the official Xiàhóu Qīngshì.
Only waiting and staying put,
The camps were arrayed like pieces on a chessboard.
Was it that there was no plan?
The soldiers had grown accustomed to peace.
In defense, they had intact city walls;
In battle, they had no capable army.
When blades crossed, the troops fled;
Who could escape like Mèngmíng?
Flying dispatches were sent to the outskirts of Qín;
Defeat was announced at Shàngjīng.
Zhōu Chǔ died following military orders;
His body greased the axes of the Dǐ.
As for the death of such a man,
His upright integrity was clearly upheld.
Lú Bō disobeyed orders,
And was cast away to the northern lands.
Accepting the penalty for the sake of the law,
Who can call sowthistle bitter?
Alas for these common people,
Without sin or guilt.
Livers and brains smeared the ground;
White bones filled the crossroads.
The husband travels and the wife is widowed;
The father departs and the child is orphaned.
Causing our Jìn people
To be turned into captives of the Dí.
The distress of disorder and displacement,
Has ripened over months and years.
The Son of Heaven feels compassion for this;
He eats late and sleeps late.
When the lord worries, the ministers toil;
Who would not be reverent and fearful?
Ashamed to have nothing to contribute,
I am purely a useless official.
The Emperor, grand in his wrath,
Then reorganized his elite troops.
He commanded that man from Shànggǔ,
To depart quickly on the appointed day.
Personally receiving established plans,
His majestic power reached far and wide.
First, he captured Zhōngtíng,
Raising his fame by ten thousands.
Warfare is indeed a way of deception,
Putting reputation first and reality second.
Heard by the officials in charge,
They took ten thousand for one.
The wickedness of Zhòu,
I cannot be certain of it.
Vainly illuminating the virtue of Nǎn,
Falsely manifesting the luck of Jiǎ.
The Yōng gate was not opened;
Chén and Qiān were dangerously pressed.
Guān Suì rose like a tiger,
Grateful and exerting his strength.
The heavy siege was lifted;
The imperiled city regained its color.
How can it be said there were no faults?
But his merit was also beyond measure.
Circumstances are indeed of ten thousand kinds;
What could not happen?
The chaotic Qí Wàn,
Was also extremely hideous.
One said to accept his surrender;
Another said to behead him.
What truth can be concealed?
What falsehood can endure?
Having summoned your words,
Having concluded your lawsuit.
One should clarify the facts,
Otherwise, the testimony is empty.
Fine titles are already lost,
And public execution followed.
Have you not seen Dòu Lín,
Whose corpse lay in the land of Hàn?
The poems of the Zhōu people,
Are truly titled "Cǎi Wēi."
In the north, they suffered from the Xiǎnyǔn;
In the west, they were troubled by the Kūnyí.
Comparing the past with the present,
How is it enough to show off our power?
I only pity these people,
My heart is filled with sorrow.
What of these people?
They were poisoned in Qín.
After the armies arrived,
Famine followed them.
Pestilence spread rampantly;
Thorns and brambles became thickets.
The grain from Jiàngyáng,
Floated along the banks of the Wèi.
The brilliant Son of Heaven,
Looks upon the people as if they were wounded.
Repeatedly commanding the various officials,
To protect your borders.
Do not be tyrannical to the masses;
Do not let the strong bully others.
The fearful and the weak,
Are like those enjoying the spring sun.
The young gentleman respects and loves his guests;
The banquet ends without him feeling tired.
On a clear night, we wander in the Xīyuán;
Flying canopies follow one another.
The bright moon clarifies the scenery;
The stars are scattered in order.
Autumn orchids cover the long slopes;
Vermilion flowers bloom over the green pond.
Hidden fish leap in the clear waves;
Fine birds sing on high branches.
A divine breeze reaches the cinnabar wheels;
The light carriage moves with the wind.
Drifting and soaring, giving rein to our will;
May it be like this for a thousand years.
Great Heaven sends down abundant moisture;
A hundred plants grow lush and luxuriant.
A cool wind removes the steaming heat;
Clear clouds keep back the flaming sun.
A grand gathering in the hall of a gentleman;
Sitting together under the shade of the ornate rafters.
Fine dishes fill the round and square vessels;
Excellent wine fills the golden wine jars.
Pipes and strings produce beautiful sounds;
The melodies are clear and sorrowful.
All those seated share the same joy;
Only complaining that the cup circulates slowly.
I have often heard the words of the poet:
If not drunk, then do not go home.
If we do not reach the height of joy today,
For whom do we harbor our feelings?
Receiving such great favor is indeed substantial;
Keeping my station, how could I disobey?
The ancients had a saying:
The gentleman is where blessings reside.
May my worthy host
Enjoy greatness as long as Heaven.
Able to match the achievements of Zhōu Gōng;
For generations, he cannot be surpassed.
All day long we go on excursions;
The joy has not yet ended.
Remaining thoughts linger in the deep night;
Together we soar once again.
The carriages fly with white canopies;
Attendants fill the roadside.
The moon comes out and shines in the garden;
Rare trees are lush and dark green.
A clear stream passes through the stone channel;
Flowing waves serve as a pond for the fish.
The lotuses scatter their blossoms;
The buds overflow the golden pond.
Spiritual birds roost at the water's edge;
Benevolent beasts wander on the flying bridge.
The ornate lodge overlooks the flowing waves;
Spacious and open, the cool breeze comes.
In my life, I have never heard of such a place;
How can I sing of it in detail?
I put down my brush and sigh deeply;
Such beauty is impossible to forget.
Morning geese cry in the clouds,
how sorrowful is their sound!
I ask you, to which land do you travel?
Folding your wings, you linger in hesitation.
You say you come from a humble gate,
and will soon go to Héngyáng to roost.
Last spring you soared in the northern lands,
this winter you are a guest in Nánhuái.
Traveling far, you endure frost and snow,
your feathers wither day by day.
Ever fearful of harm to flesh and bone,
or that your body might perish and sink into the yellow mud.
When choice pearls fall among sand and stones,
how can they find harmony within?
You wish to use the gathering of clouds and rain,
to wash your wings and ascend the high ladder.
But a fine encounter is hard to meet;
to raise your brows, by what path shall you climb?
The Gōngzǐ respects and loves his guests,
joyfully drinking without knowing fatigue.
With a gentle countenance and easy spirit,
he is willing to look upon the small and lowly.
You presented a poem to offer comfort and care;
this humble one is not worthy of such grace.
For now, let us reach the height of joy,
and not return until we are drunk.
All you officials, respect your positions,
to satisfy this heart of hunger and thirst.
The Sānzhèng succeed one another in turn,
a great sage initiates the cycle of destiny.
Since the wise kings of old,
they preceded Heaven and acted in accord with it.
The various lords rose and fell,
descending to the recent past.
When the Huánghuī had already faded,
the Sùlíng received the divine blessing.
With a glance of favor and concern,
He granted them the central lands.
The Sānhòu established the foundation,
Shìwǔ grandly inherited the legacy.
Harmonious winds surged from the sides,
the celestial sun and moon shone clear above.
Pure radiance illuminated the six directions,
imperial blessings began to flourish.
From those regions of the Hé and Fén,
they suddenly united the seven celestial bodies.
Cultured and refined was the Jìn,
generation after generation, sincere in their sageliness.
Reverently following the Great Heaven,
they responded to and upheld the established mandate.
The nine regions were all brought to harmony,
feasts and songs were used to chant their praise.
The Emperor continues the flourishing line,
broadening the Way through classical teachings.
As the transformation became abundant,
the works of the craftsmen were examined.
Below, he regulates the various achievements,
above, he governs the great creation.
Modeling himself after the ancestors,
he secures and soothes the heavenly protection.
Truly born was our lord,
both brilliant and outstanding.
His person radiates double brilliance,
inheriting the standards and the great destiny.
His flourishing virtue is deep and serene,
his natural poise is like the abundance of jade.
A tiny, humble minister like me,
from those distant and desolate borders.
Relieved of my heavy burdens,
I shake my cap-strings and serve at the Chénghuá.
It was not my original wish,
but the excellence of the mandate.
Magnificent is the blessing of the August Heaven,
grandly bestowing the great mandate.
The Sìzǔ rectified the family,
the heavenly emoluments were preserved and settled.
Wise and sagacious was the Jìn,
every generation possessing enlightened sages.
Like the sun and the moon,
ten thousand lights are set right by them.
Towering are the enlightened sages,
their Way flourishes from Heaven itself.
Distinguishing the light and the dawn,
observing the images and penetrating the mystery.
Riding the wind to harmonize the records,
their peerless brilliance illuminates the depths.
Solemnity and harmony were spread in the past,
blessings and prosperity arrive now.
In former times, treacherous ministers
claimed rebellion within the Zǐwēi.
Divine winds were secretly stirred,
majestic was this awesome power.
Divine banners and pennons were raised,
wielded like flashes of lightning.
Reaching the boundaries of Heaven,
to the banks of the rivers.
The mandate gathered once again,
the imperial carriage returned in triumph.
The fallen principles were restored,
all categories of things were put in order.
The Way of the spirits revealed its simplicity,
discarding the flowery to return to the essential.
The stars and sun shine with renewed light,
harmonious winds respond to the pitch-pipes.
Within Hánxià there is no dust,
beyond the seas there is tranquility.
Throughout the boundless universe,
Heaven and Earth are in communion.
The King is in the Chénghuá Hall,
holding a banquet for a fine gathering.
The dark radiance is lofty and bright,
emerald clouds form dense mists.
Ceremonial caps and shaking tassels,
patterned robes and hanging sashes.
Numerous are the officials,
coming together in harmony.
Briefly they examine the works,
receiving his countenance from below.
Looking down upon the fine guests,
looking up at his jade-like face.
He treats himself with restraint,
but in ritual he is abundant.
May Heaven grant him longevity,
lofty as the mountain peaks.
Remote and vast is high antiquity,
the very beginning of the people.
The Huángjí was first established,
and the constant relations were spread.
The Five Virtues rotated in succession,
receiving the registers and accepting the tallies.
When Táotáng had already passed,
the celestial calendar rested with Yú.
At that time, Shàngdì
looked down with favor.
To glorify our Jìn destiny,
the abdication was accepted in accordance with the cycle.
The position was taken like a dragon flying;
the pattern was formed like a tiger changing.
Profound grace flowed abundantly;
the wind of benevolence was subtly fanned.
Within the realms, hearts found a home;
from every corner, faces turned toward him.
Heaven suspended its images;
Earth shone with its patterns.
A phoenix sang to the morning sun;
a dragon soared amid auspicious clouds.
The Jiāhé grain bore double ears;
the Míngjiá plants were fragrant once more.
Throughout the land, all were in order;
the people were filled with joy.
Vast was the imperial magnanimity;
solemn was the sage-like countenance.
In speech, he sought to be compliant;
in appearance, he sought to be respectful.
In seeing, he was perceptive;
in hearing, he was acute.
He promoted the worthy based on virtue;
he tested them clearly based on merit.
Of what did his respect consist?
He was grandly manifest at the break of dawn.
There was no principle he did not traverse;
there was no righteousness he did not practice.
In conduct, he discarded flashiness;
in speech, he removed rhetoric.
He allowed his mind to wander in the ultimate void,
following the same rules of simplicity as the Yì.
The Six Treasures were greatly cultivated;
the Jiǔyǒu were thereby pacified.
There was no place his grace did not reach;
there was no one his transformation did not touch.
His reputation and teachings reached the south,
and soaked the shifting sands of the west.
Recluses traversed the dangers;
distant countries forgot the distance.
The Yuèshāng people brought multiple translators
to fill our imperial house.
Lofty were the assembled lords;
illustrious were the tiger-like ministers.
Internally, they harmonized the five ranks;
externally, they overawed the four guests.
They offered their seasonal tributes and duties,
entering to have an audience with the heavenly person.
They were fully addressed with granted mandates,
with feathered canopies and red-wheeled carriages.
Bestowing banquets for pleasant gatherings,
their frequency was not fixed.
What the divine mind receives
is understood without words.
At that time, they practiced archery;
the bows and arrows were thus mastered.
Hitting those five targets,
they were satiated with wine.
The Way of Wén and Wǔ
has its path not yet fallen.
In the past, the former kings
used archery and charioteering as these tools.
They showed martial skill for fear of neglect;
yet going to excess was also an error.
All you various lords,
be not slothful in your positions.
When the wind arrives, winter clothes are granted;
when the frost falls, the various craftsmen rest.
The thick forests withdraw their sunny colors;
the dense gardens shed their flowering clusters.
No swallows remain in the nests under the eaves;
to the banks come the returning wild geese.
Light mists crown the autumn sun;
swift autumn winds press against the clear vault.
The sage’s heart favored the beautiful season;
raising the bells, he reached the traveling palace.
The four rows of mats were moistened with fragrant wine;
in the central hall, the silk and paulownia instruments were played.
The sunlight approached the western abyss;
the remaining joy of the banquet had its end.
Departing now, the returning guest
can achieve an end in cultivating simplicity.
Overlooking the stream, I grieve that I cannot follow;
with a joyful heart, I sigh like flying tumbleweed.
Grandeur returns to the gates of the court;
void and silence reside in the river peaks.
The pheasant on the mountain bridge accorded with the nature of Kǒng;
the yellow imperial carriage was not the heart of Yáo.
Before the imperial carriage was yet solemn,
he descended to shine upon the Wényòu park.
Floating clouds rose like a moving canopy;
the morning wind drew forth the sound of the carriage bells.
The plains and marshes were indeed level and lush;
the terraces and ravines were doubly deep.
The orchid pool cooled the summer air;
the long tents held the autumn shade.
Following the shore, I climbed through the dense growth;
following the mountain, I went up the craggy heights.
Looking out, there was a limitless view;
letting the feelings wander, there was no search for what was near.
Although hearing the Way has already accumulated,
years and strength have mutually declined.
Searching within myself, I decline the vermilion and black robes;
moved by events, I cherish the long forests.
In late autumn, the northern frontiers are bitter;
the traveling geese avoid the frost and snow.
Sadly the sunny plants wither;
brightly the cold pool is pure.
The fine season moved the sage's heart;
the cloud-patterned banners rose in the late season.
Sounding the reed pipes, he reached the Vermilion Palace;
orchid goblets were offered to the worthies of the time.
The farewell banquet shone with sincerity;
harmony and joy increased what was lacking.
In Zàiyòu, the world is governed;
the blowing of the myriad things makes all regions glad.
The returning guest reaches the corner of the sea,
taking off his cap to resign from the court ranks.
Stopping the oars, he rests at the crooked islet;
watching the shadows, he waits for the music to end.
The river flow has rapid surges;
the floating team of horses has no slow tracks.
How could it be only the thought of the river path?
My long-held heart is ashamed of this impending parting.
That beautiful way of the hills and gardens—
with a sigh, I grieve over my own weakness.
The Dào is hidden and has not yet taken shape,
governance is manifest once disorder has been quelled.
Imperial traces hang as a standard,
the sovereign flow is a consistent thread.
Only the King creates things,
forever bestowing great calculations.
Benevolence firmly established the Zhōu,
and righteousness rose high to ascend the Hàn.
Good fortune flourishes through generations of wise men,
and the legacy shines through the various sages.
The Supreme One occupies the correct position,
like the heavens looking down upon the sea-mirror.
He governs through transformation and regulation,
establishing form and nature.
Grace soaks the budding life,
and trust reaches those who fly and swim.
To honor emptiness is not the proof,
and to accumulate substance is unsurpassed.
Is it only the harmony of men?
Truly, it is what the spirits have bestowed.
The sun completes its new moon phase,
and the moon does not obscure the full moon.
Ships with treasures cross the waters,
and carriages with tribute surpass the barriers.
The Imperial body is beautiful and bright,
the Ritual Star acts as the second.
You rule that Dōng Cháo,
with the brilliance of gold and the purity of jade.
Virtue provides nourishment for the self,
and ritual does not err in its vessels.
Gentle and centered, reflecting like a deep pool,
your fragrant legacy is as secret as an orchid.
Formerly there was Wén Zhāo,
today there is only Wǔ Mù.
O magnificent Wáng Zǎi,
like Dàn, you occupy the position of the younger uncle.
With a bright and wise domain,
you thus tread and establish the pasturage.
Peace reaches the ultimate harmony,
acting as a screen for the capital and maintaining the service.
The crescent and the soul of the moon meet twice,
the lunar qi undergoes triple changes.
Opening glory and sprinkling moisture,
stretching rainbows and flashing lightning.
Transformation reaches everywhere without interval,
and the Imperial heart then shows its regard.
Thinking of the drinking at Gào,
always remembering the banquets at Luò.
For the farewell in the suburbs, there is an altar,
for the Lord's actions, there are rituals.
Tents and curtains in the Lán Diàn,
painted currents by the high steps.
Dividing the courtyard to present music,
parting the waves to float the sweet wine.
Joy is shared as in the Xià proverbs,
and affairs combine to bring forth relief.
Looking up at the abundant bestowals,
I look down at my own meager self.
Thrice I have hindered the service of the heir,
five times I have dusted the courtly robes.
The path is prosperous, but my fate is difficult,
grace is full, but my repayment is lacking.
There are regrets that can be mended,
but stagnant flaws are hard to brush away.
The nation honors the position of the teacher,
the family exalts the Rú gate.
Receiving the Dào and nurturing virtue,
lecturing on arts and establishing words.
Deep brilliance brightens the dawn,
understanding righteousness dispels this darkness.
Forever looking toward those who attained prior awakening,
and looking back at those of the later generations.
The Great Man leads all things,
succeeding Heaven and connecting with the sages.
When the times are difficult, they must become prosperous,
when the fortune is obscured, it shall be corrected.
Setting aside military arts,
and promoting the civil commands.
The many scholars lean toward your wind,
the myriad streams look up to the mirror.
The Yú Xiáng decorates its halls,
the wise plan shines with brilliance.
Those cherishing benevolence gather from afar,
those holding wisdom arrive in herds.
Following to the gate to present writings,
stepping in straw sandals to offer their talents.
Washing the body in the dark abyss,
housing the mind in the secrets of the Dào.
In the past, there was the Zhōu heir,
whose glory followed the ancient records.
Thinking of the August generation of the wise,
embodying the Primal to act as the successor.
Endowed with this early knowledge,
he descended to follow the canonical will.
Remote are those former writings,
following the compass of Zhōu and the square of the standard.
In the main hall, there are empty mats,
the officials choose a day.
Offering the seat and presenting the staff,
the assistant of doubts holds the scrolls.
Waiting for words with a formal refusal,
the diligent historian holds the brush.
Subtly discerning the sounds of the first signs,
the Royal Record has its descriptions.
Freely discussing the fragrant news,
the great teaching is made clear.
Respectfully performing the sacrificial rites,
announcing the offerings to the sacred spirits.
The ritual pertains to the observation of the washing,
the music presents the songs and pipes.
Serving the brilliance with solemnity,
the contents of the sacrificial platters are not merely for the aroma.
The offerings completed, auspicious robes are donned,
going to the palace for a grand feast.
In the hall, ivory mats are set,
in the courtyard, golden bells are hung.
The Three Ducal Ministers preserve their combined excellence,
the Imperial relatives are compared to the talented.
The dried meats are ready and the wine is clear,
with correct robes and tidy caps.
The Liù Guān watch for commands,
the Jiǔ Bīn assist in the ceremony.
Hat strings and tablets fill the ranks,
headscarves and scrolls fill the streets.
The capital's solemnity moves like clouds,
the wild paths are as fast as the wind.
Matching the Zhōu and equaling the Hàn,
how transcendent and far-reaching!
Clear radiance is in the sky,
and every shadow must be illuminated.
All things follow their nature and feelings,
and principles declare their depths.
I am rashly among the scions of the state,
listening from the side to the teachings of the land.
Vainly ashamed of my insignificance and obscurity,
I ultimately lack any wise contribution.
At early dawn, the Chāng Hé gates open,
on the imperial road, the phoenix flutes are heard.
Light sprouts support the jade carriage,
fine grass is trodden by the dragon-steeds.
The wind is slow, and the mountains still echo,
the rain ceases, and clouds still accumulate.
The nests are empty as birds first take flight,
the water-lilies are ruffled by the play of new fish.
Truly, the Běi Mén is of great importance,
if not to a relative, to whom would it be entrusted?
Various thoughts of parting arise,
as the solemn waves of grace cover all.
This small official is truly fortunate,
how could I risk my life to repay such righteousness?
Dān Pǔ does not delight in war,
bearing the heavy burden of ruling the people.
Our Emperor holds the utmost virtue,
forgetting himself to use the heart of Yáo.
Pitying those within the world,
where fish and birds had lost their flight and swim.
Pushing the chariot hubs through the two Xiáo ridges,
raising the banners by the shade of the Jiǔ Hé.
Those leaping onto the chariots are all of the three ranks,
the selected soldiers are all worth a hundred gold.
The war chariots set out from Xì Liǔ,
the farewell banquet is held at Shàng Lín.
Commanding the army to punish those who were late to submit,
giving orders to be lenient with the captured.
At Hán and Huàn, they are just loosening their belts,
at Yáo and Wǔ, they gradually open their lapels.
Punishing the guilty at the bend of Máng Shān,
comforting the people at the banks of the Yī Shuǐ.
I shall accompany the ceremony of announcing success,
waiting for this before I remove my hairpin.
Walking, I ascend the slope of Běi Máng,
looking afar at the mountains of Luò Yáng.
How desolate and lonely Luò Yáng is,
the palaces and chambers are all burnt to ashes.
The walls are all tumbled and broken,
thorns and brambles reach up to the sky.
I do not see the elders of old,
I only behold the new youths.
Treading carefully, there are no paths to walk,
the wild fields are no longer farmed.
The traveler has not returned for a long time,
and does not recognize the paths and lanes.
How desolate the middle of the fields is,
for a thousand lǐ there is no smoke of men.
Thinking of my usual place of dwelling,
my breath catches and I cannot speak.
Peaceful times are hard to come by frequently,
and a fine gathering cannot be constant.
Heaven and Earth have no ultimate end,
yet human life is like the morning frost.
I wish to express our tender affection,
as my friend departs for the Shuò fāng region.
Close kin and friends gather together to see him off,
setting out wine here in Hé yáng.
How could the food provided be meager?
Yet the guests do not drain their cups.
Love is so deep that the longing is bitter,
how can I not feel ashamed in my heart?
Mountains and rivers are obstructed and far,
the parting is hurried and the time until we meet will be long.
I wish to be a bird with shared wings,
spreading feathers to soar high together.
The morning wind blows at the fork in the road,
and falling rain covers the autumn grass.
The whole city follows far to see me off,
feasting me on my thousand-mile journey.
Life, destiny, and wealth all have their limits,
in a brief moment, how can anything be preserved?
No one is older than the child who dies young,
and even Péng Dān is considered to have died early.
Good and bad fortune are like a twisted rope,
sorrow and joy are entangled with one another.
Heaven and Earth serve as my furnace,
and how small the myriad things seem!
The attained man maintains a grand vision,
warning that it is not too early to be troubled by this.
Separation begins at the long highway,
and melancholy fills my breast.
Who can perceive my heart?
Let the azure Cāng hào be my witness.
Our pact is made this morning,
to be kept until we grow old together.
Wáng Shēng harmonizes the ingredients of the ritual cauldron,
while Shí Zǐ guards the regions of Hǎi yí.
Close friends each say they must depart,
and in my heart, I feel a sense of loss.
How to express these parting thoughts?
Hand in hand, we stroll through the outskirts of the capital.
In the morning we depart from the sunny side of Jìn Jīng Yáng,
and by evening we rest at the banks of Jīn Gǔ.
Winding streams coil through curved obstacles,
and the path up the steep slope is treacherous.
The green pond ripples gently,
how the green willows sway.
The overflowing spring has waves like dragon scales,
surging ripples scatter like strings of pearls.
In the front courtyard, Shātáng trees are planted,
in the back garden, black plums are set.
The divine orchard is lush with pomegranates,
and the dense forest is lined with fragrant pears.
We drink beside the flowering pond,
then move our seats to climb the high embankment.
Dark ale stains our crimson faces,
we only complain that the cups move too slowly.
Raising the drumsticks to strike the spirit drums,
the flutes and pipes sound clear and sad.
Who does not admire the spring blossoms?
Yet those who endure the year's cold are truly rare!
I entrust my devotion to my steadfast friend,
until our white heads return to the same place.
Receiving the summons, I return to Běi Jīng,
leaving my post to return from the southern regions.
On moored boats, new and old acquaintances meet,
facing a banquet, I miss the brilliant governor.
Raising cups, we toast at the farewell drink,
pointing to the road, I think of the journey ahead.
Tomorrow morning has no certain beginning,
the time of parting is rapidly approaching.
The setting sun shines on the busy ferry,
and evening shadows dim the level plains.
The boatman prepares the rowing oars,
and the light carriage orders the returning servants.
We part ways at the eastern city gate,
as the oars set out for the bend of the Western River.
Though parting and meeting bring us closer,
how can the flowing river return?
Who says feelings can be written down?
A short letter cannot say all there is to say.
On official duty, I depart from the imperial city,
planning to rest in Ōu Yuè.
I loosen the moorings and catch the flowing tide,
yet cherishing old memories, I cannot depart.
The whistling wind enters the decaying forest,
and the bright autumn moon shines purely.
Containing emotions, they easily overflow,
encountering things, it is hard for them to cease.
Long-standing illness has ended my worldly concerns,
and with few desires, I rarely lack anything.
Relying on this to live in seclusion forever,
how could it be a parting for only a year?
Let each of us strive with a daily renewed will,
and news from afar will comfort the lonely silence.
Dòngtíng is the place where music was spread,
and the Xiāo xiāng is where the emperor’s daughters roamed.
Clouds drift away to the wilds of Cāng wú,
and water returns to the flow of the Jiāng Hàn.
I stop my carriage and look out in melancholy,
while you pause your oars, hesitant.
Guǎng píng listens to the local records,
and Mào líng will soon be sought.
Our past aspirations are all over,
only the sorrow of parting remains upon the river.
In the youthful days of our lives,
it was easy to set a time to meet again after parting.
Now that I am in old age with you,
this is no longer a time for simple parting.
Do not speak of this one jar of wine,
for tomorrow it will be hard to hold it again.
In dreams, I do not know the way,
how then can I comfort our mutual longing?
Since ancient times, none should die to follow the dead,
as all enlightened people know.
Qín Mù killed the three virtuous men,
what a pity he did so in vain.
They served a brilliant lord since youth,
receiving truly immeasurable grace.
At the moment of his death, he required them to die,
how could they not follow him?
Wives and children weep at the door,
brothers cry by the roadside.
Facing the grave, they call out to the blue Heavens,
tears falling like a continuous rope.
Every person has their own will,
which in the end will not be moved for this.
Though they knew the agony of being buried,
their hearts also had something to offer.
In life, they were heroes among a hundred men,
in death, they were models for brave warriors.
Huáng Niǎo was composed as a song of grief,
and its voice has not diminished to this day.
Fame and merit cannot be forced,
I find my peace in loyalty and righteousness.
Qín Mù passed away first,
and the three ministers all destroyed themselves.
In life, they shared glory and joy,
after death, they share sorrow and hardship.
Who says it is easy to sacrifice one's life?
Killing oneself is truly the most difficult.
Wiping away tears, I climb your tomb,
facing the grave, I sigh to the Heavens.
How dark and deep is the long night?
Once gone, there is no return.
The yellow bird cries in sorrow,
how tragic, it wounds the lungs and liver!
At twenty, I toyed with the supple brush,
and with excellence, I surveyed various books.
I wrote treatises modeled on Guò Qín,
and composed rhapsodies imitating Zǐ Xū.
The border cities suffered from the whistling arrows,
and feathered dispatches flew to the capital.
Although I was not a soldier in armor,
in the past, I had studied Ráng Jū.
My long whistle stirred the clear wind,
my ambition was as if Dōng Wú did not exist.
Even a lead knife values its one cut,
and in dreams, I galloped toward grand plans.
To the left, I looked to clear the Jiāng Xiāng,
to the right, I gazed to pacify the Qiāng Hú.
When success was achieved, I would not accept a title,
but with a deep bow, return to my rural cottage.
Stately are the pines at the bottom of the ravine,
scattered are the sprouts atop the mountain.
With those stems only an inch in diameter,
they overshadow these hundred-foot branches.
Those of noble lineage step into high positions,
while the talented and heroic are submerged in low offices.
The terrain of their status makes it so,
and this has not been the case for just one day.
The Jīn and Zhāng families relied on their old estates,
for seven generations, they wore the marten furs of the Hàn court.
Was Féng Gōng not great?
Yet with a white head, he was never summoned.
I hope to emulate Duàn Gàn Mù,
who rested and protected the Lord of Wèi.
I admire Lǔ Zhòng Lián,
who with talk and laughter repelled the Qín army.
The world values being unconstrained,
and being able to resolve difficulties when encountering trouble.
When success is achieved, one does not accept rewards,
such noble integrity is outstanding and peerless.
Facing the official ribbon, he would not fasten it,
before the ritual jade, he would not take his share.
Linked seals may shine in the front courtyard,
but to him, they are like floating clouds.
Crowded is the capital city within,
resplendent are the dwellings of princes and marquises.
Official caps and carriages shade the four crossroads,
vermilion wheels race along the long thoroughfares.
In the morning they gather at the halls of Jīn and Zhāng,
at evening they lodge in the villas of Xǔ and Shǐ.
The southern neighbor strikes bells and chimes,
in the northern lane they play pipes and reeds.
Silent and still is the house of Master Yáng,
at his gate there are no carriages of ministers or chancellors.
Desolate within the empty halls,
what he discourses upon is the Dark Mystery.
His arguments are modeled after Xuāní,
his rhapsodies emulate Xiāngrú.
After many, many hundreds of generations,
his heroic name reigns supreme across the eight regions.
The bright sky unfolds the white sun,
its divine light shines upon Shénzhōu.
Rows of mansions are within the Purple Palace,
their flying eaves are as if floating clouds.
Within those towering high gates,
all the numerous residents are princes and marquises.
Unless one is a guest "clinging to the dragon,"
why would one suddenly come to wander here?
Wearing coarse hemp, I exit the Chánghé Gate,
with high strides I follow the path of Xǔ Yóu.
Shaking my robes on a thousand-fathom ridge,
washing my feet in a ten-thousand-mile stream.
Jīng Kē drinks in the marketplace of Yàn,
drunk with wine, his spirit grows ever more stirred.
Singing mournful songs in harmony with Jiànlí,
as if there were no one else around.
Although I lack the integrity of a true hero,
I too am of a different sort from the world.
Looking upward, gazing far across the four seas,
how are the powerful and wealthy worth mentioning?
Though the noble think themselves noble,
I view them as mere dust.
Though the lowly think themselves lowly,
I value them like a thousand tons.
Zhǔfù Yǎn’s official career did not prosper,
and even his own kin treated him coldly.
Zhū Mǎichén was distressed while gathering firewood,
and his wife could not bear to stay in their home.
Chén Píng had no property or livelihood,
returning home to a lean-to against the city wall.
When Chángqīng returned to Chéngdū,
only bare walls stood in the vast emptiness.
How were these four sages not great?
