Their legacy shines in the records and books.
When they had not yet met their opportunity,
their worry was ending up in a ditch or valley.
Heroes have their times of difficulty and hardship,
this has been so since ancient times.
In what age are there no extraordinary talents?
They are left to linger in the marshes and wilds.
Flapping, flapping, the bird in the cage,
lifts its wings only to strike the four corners.
Aloof and lonely, the scholar in the dead-end alley,
embraces his shadow and guards an empty hut.
Stepping out the door, there is no path forward,
thorns and brambles block the way.
His strategies are discarded and not taken up,
he is like a fish in a dried-up pond.
Looking outward, he has not an inch of stipend,
looking inward, he has not a peck of grain in store.
His relatives turn to despise him,
his friends grow distant day and night.
Sū Qín traveled north to persuade and lobby,
Lǐ Sī went west to submit his memorial.
In the blink of an eye, glory and splendor arise,
in a sudden gasp, they wither and decay again.
Drinking from the river, one seeks only a full belly,
valuing enough, one desires no surplus.
Nesting in the forest, the bird perches on a single branch,
this can serve as a model for the man of attainment.
Long ago, in the time of the Western Capital,
court and countryside shared much joy.
Crowded was the East Gate of the capital,
when the various lords held a farewell for the Èr Shū.
Vermilion carriages shone in the Golden City,
tents and feasts were set along the long thoroughfare.
Men of attainment know when to stop and be content,
casting off glory as if it were nothing.
Withdrawing the hairpin and loosening the court robes,
with hair loosened, they returned to the sea's edge.
Passersby shed tears for them:
"How worthy are these great men!"
They scattered their gold to enjoy their remaining years,
at the end of their lives, they kept no stores.
Looking back, they told the guests in the four seats:
"Much wealth only brings burden to the foolish."
Their pure wind inspires ten thousand generations,
their names endure as long as heaven and earth.
Alas, those guests with cicada-wing caps and crowns,
you gentlemen of the sash should see this written down.
The House of Zhào possessed the jade of Héshì,
there was no one in the world who had not heard of it.
The men of Qín came seeking to trade for it,
but the price they offered was merely empty words.
To give it would be to be cheated,
not to give it, they feared, would bring disaster.
They selected talent to prepare for the journey,
seeking to keep the nation’s fate whole.
Lìn Shēng was in a lowly position,
but Miù Zǐ praised his worthiness.
Bearing the message, he galloped across the border,
leaning on the carriage rail, he went straight into the Pass.
The King of Qín sat presiding in the hall,
the envoy of Zhào held his staff of office before him.
Waving his sleeve, he glared at the golden pillar,
ready to sacrifice both his body and the jade.
Since the "connected cities" were a false promise,
the jade of Jīng also truly returned.
Then at the meeting of Miǎnchí,
the two rulers managed to exchange courtesies.
Zhāoxiāng wished to rely on his might,
but Xiāngrú thwarted his designs at the start.
Blood from his glaring eyes soaked his collar,
his hair rose in anger, thrusting against his cap.
In the end, the western jar was struck by both,
while the eastern zither was not played alone.
Is it not easy to give up one's life?
But to face death rightly is truly difficult.
His imposing majesty atop the Zhāngtái Terrace,
even the powerful and oppressive could not infringe.
Yielding his status in the midst of Hándān,
he bowed his head and patiently turned his carriage.
What kind of man was Lián Gōng?
He carried thorns to apologize for his fault.
Their wisdom and courage surpassed their age,
their alternating yielding and firming makes me sigh in admiration.
The royal influence became mournful and pensive,
the Way of Zhōu was dissolved and without order.
Divining at Luò, prosperity and decline alternated,
what rose in chaos never failed to perish.
Governing by force, they swallowed the Nine Tripods,
harshness and evil were violent to the young.
Resting their shoulders, the people's thoughts were entwined,
divine scrutiny gathered the vermilion light.
That man felt the duty of the age,
and so he came to support the rising King.
Subtle and profound were the plans within the tent,
resplendent grew the flourishing celestial enterprise.
At Hóngmén, the partial eclipse was dispelled,
at Gāixià, the baleful comet fell.
He ennobled his enemy and established Xiāo Zǎi,
fixed the capital and protected the Crown Prince.
Truly he fulfilled the bond with the secluded elder,
then soared away, heading back to his divine home.
His benevolent heart inspires for a thousand years,
his pure dust is spread without bounds.
Divine martiality harmonizes the Three Primaries,
its transformations cover the eight wildernesses.
Double brightness illuminates the south of Héyīn,
auspicious clouds approach Fényáng.
The imperial phoenix banners pass the ancestral tomb,
adorning the image and offering fine sacrifices.
The sage's heart is not merely for distinction,
but because virtue lies in not forgetting.
If the departed could be raised again,
I would look to you and long for the Great Way.
Crowded and numerous are the attendants of the imperial carriage,
brilliant is the arena of brush and ink.
This blind man misses the grand spectacle,
but rises on tiptoe to gaze from afar.
Although the road in all directions is level and straight,
with my halting steps, I am ashamed of my lack of skill.
Feeding on harmony, I forget my lowly distance,
lifting my head to sing of the peace of Tàikāng.
The dryandra and paulownia trees lean toward the lofty phoenix,
The Hán gǔ valley awaits the sounding of the pitch-pipe.
How could shadow and echo not cherish one another?
From afar, they always seek their match.
Graceful is that secluded and quiet lady,
Who became a bride in a gentleman’s house.
Her lofty integrity pierces the autumn frost,
Her bright beauty rivals the morning sun.
Since a favorable destiny followed me,
My joyful wishes were fulfilled from then on.
Before the leisure of home life could be enjoyed,
My husband, alas, had duties that drew him away.
He cast off his commoner’s cap for a thousand miles away,
And fastened his official ribbon to enter the Royal Domain.
Preparing his followers at the break of dawn,
Attendants came to support him on either side.
Driving the carriage out beyond the city walls,
The road ahead was long and winding.
In life, it meant a long separation;
In death, it would mean never returning.
Alas, I resent the hardships of travel,
Climbing thrice until morning and evening were spent.
Sternly driving through wind and cold,
Unsaddling the horse amidst frost and dew.
The plains and marshes are full of sorrow and chill,
Whirling gusts coil around the tall trees.
Stray beasts rise from desolate paths,
Startled birds fly off in all directions.
How tragic for the traveling official,
Toiling along these mountain and river roads.
Far away, the traveler is distant,
As the years go turning and passing by.
A good season was lost to this parting,
Days and months were about to be cast away.
Who knew the cold and heat would accumulate?
With effort, one sees the blooming and the withering.
At year’s end, facing the empty room,
A cool wind rises from the corner of the seat.
Sleeping and waking, the days have grown cold,
White dew forms on the courtyard weeds.
Having served diligently, he follows his wish to return,
Taking the return path along mountains and rivers.
When he left, the autumn had not yet turned white;
Now, the year is in its flowering season.
In the month of silkworms, observing a moment of leisure,
He passes through many mulberry fields.
A beautiful lady is engaged in this work,
Slender and graceful, she reaches for the high branches.
Who would not gaze at such city-toppling beauty?
He slows his pace and stops in the valley.
Years have passed and he is weary from toil,
Affairs are distant, and her voice and form have faded from memory.
Though they have been parted for five years,
They have become strangers to each other's lives.
Leaving the carriage, he follows the path toward her,
His eyes fix upon her like ducks darting toward algae.
Is Southern gold not precious?
Yet he holds it lightly in his mind as an offering.
A righteous heart has many bitter tones,
Dense and firm as the sound of gold and jade.
Lofty integrity cannot be long delayed,
He quickly departs, his words in vain.
Slowly, the road ahead comes to an end,
Lingering, he reaches the threshold of his gate.
Entering the hall, he offers joyful greetings,
Entering the room, he asks where she has gone.
At dusk, she returns from her picking,
The scenery is that of the mulberry and elm hour.
The beauty arrives as twilight falls,
With shame and sighs, they face each other as before.
Who can end the feelings held within?
Let me use this to express my hardships.
We lived apart for many years and seasons,
One parting blocked by rivers and passes.
When spring came, there was no time for pleasure;
When autumn arrived, it was always early cold.
At dawn, my sorrowful heart is moved,
In the inner chamber, I let out a long sigh.
Miserable and chilly, as the year grows late,
The sun sets on the traveler's face.
High tension causes the string to break;
The urgent sound arises from the tuning.
Since long ago, I have humbled my light and dust for you,
Firmly bound by words from beginning to end.
How could you stay away so long,
Failing in all conduct through your own fault?
If a gentleman loses his clear righteousness,
With whom can I grow old until my teeth fall out?
I feel ashamed before the "Xíng lù" poem,
and would rather sink into the long river's waters.
Although Ruǎn Gōng obscured his tracks,
His knowledge was subtle and his insight profound.
His deep drunkenness was like burying his light,
His metaphors were akin to allegorical satire.
His long whistles were as if yearning for someone,
Transgressing rites, he naturally startled the masses.
The causes of things cannot be debated;
At the end of the road, how could he not wail?
Zhōng Sàn did not accord with the world;
He was originally a man who fed on the mists.
His "release from the form" proved him a silent immortal,
His discourses showed a concentrated spirit.
Standing apart from customs, he defied common opinion,
Seeking mountains to join the recluses.
Even the simurgh's wings are sometimes clipped,
Who could ever tame a dragon's nature?
Liú Líng was good at closing himself off,
Harboring feelings while extinguishing hearing and sight.
Drums and bells were not enough to please him,
How could glorious colors dazzle him?
Concealing his essence, he drank deeply every day;
Who could know it was not wild revelry?
Though the "Ode to Wine" is but a short piece,
His deep sincerity is revealed through it.
Zhòng Róng was a man of lofty talent,
Truly endowed with the refinement of the people.
Why need one be deep to understand music?
He discerned the subtle in the sounding of metals.
Guō Yì was already enchanted by him,
Shān Gōng’s high opinion was no empty encounter.
Often recommended, he did not enter office,
Until with one wave of the hand, he went out as a governor.
Xiàng Xiù was content with being simple and indifferent,
Entrusting his deep mind to brush and paper.
Exploring the Dào, he loved the profound and mysterious;
Reading books, he despised mere philological analysis.
His friendship with Lǚ was like the soaring of great birds,
His association with Jī was like the flight of a phoenix.
Lingering on journeys within the river region,
Sorrowfully composing the "Rhapsody on Shān yáng."
The Five Capitals boast of their vast wealth,
The Sān chuān region nurtures fame and profit.
A hundred pieces of gold cannot buy off death,
Yet mastery of the Classics brings high status.
In the capital's twelve thoroughfares,
Flying eaves are arranged like fish scales.
Officials wave their flowery tassels,
Travelers pull tight their light reins.
Before the morning stars have grown sparse,
Carriages and canopies have already arrived like clouds.
Guests and attendants are in a tumultuous throng,
Saddles and horses reflect light onto the ground.
Cold and heat exist within a single moment,
Prosperity is as lovely as the spring.
Jūn píng alone remains in solitude,
He and the world have mutually abandoned each other.
Holding the yak-tail banner as a Hàn general,
On a sweating horse, he goes out beyond the Cháng chéng.
The terrain of the Cháng chéng is perilous,
Stretching ten thousand miles, level with the clouds.
In the cool autumn of the eighth and ninth months,
Barbarian cavalry enter Yōu and Bìng.
At Fēi hú, the bright sun grows late,
Over the Hàn hǎi desert, sorrowful shadows arise.
Feathered dispatches are occasionally cut off,
The watch-drums startle by day and night.
Mounting the ramparts, he brandishes a precious sword;
Blocking the sun, he raises the high banners.
Like massing clouds are the soldiers of the Seven Guards,
In Yú lí formation are the troops of the Six Commanderies.
The Tartar flute brings longing below the pass,
The Qiāng flute wails atop Lǒng mountain.
The Gǔ dū lords are first struck with fear,
The Rì zhú kings then lose their spirit.
At Yù mén, the scouts are dismissed,
And grand mansions begin to be built.
His rank rises to the accumulation of ten thousand granaries,
His merit is established, and all conduct is perfected.
Heaven is eternal and Earth is lasting,
But the way of man has its waning and waxing.
Before the "Jī chǔ" music has ended,
One already sees the high terrace collapse.
It should be that upon the Lín gé Pavilion,
He shall have a heroic name for a thousand years!
The lowlands are not a place to stay;
a Jūnzǐ is cautious at his beginning.
High fame is not established overnight,
yet it is easily subjected to slander and encroachment.
Formerly, I cast off my office and left;
someone came to my village gate.
A farmer’s home has nothing to offer,
so I poured sweet wine and roasted dried fish.
They asked me what merit or virtue I had,
to be one of the three at the Chéngmíng Lú.
What I occupy in this land
is called a dwelling of the benevolent and the wise.
My writings are not of state-crafting quality;
my baskets and cases hold not a foot of letters.
On what basis are my talent and learning praised,
so that they are frequently met with acclaim?
Leaving my mat and kneeling, I explained:
this lowly person is truly empty.
Like a man of Sòng meeting a guest from Zhōu,
I am so ashamed I have nowhere to turn.
Green are the pines upon the mound,
tall are the cypresses upon the high mountain.
Their luster and color flourish in winter and summer;
their roots never wither or fall.
A virtuous man harbors a steadfast heart;
understanding things, he contemplates a distant refuge.
He raises his will to the edge of the dark clouds,
and lets his eyes gaze upon the crags and rocks.
I envy Wángzǐ Qiáo of old,
whose path of friendship began at the Yī and Luò.
Distant and far, he scaled the steep peaks,
sailing swiftly, riding a flying crane.
Leaving his footprints ten thousand lǐ behind,
how could he linger on the joys of the common people?
Long harboring a longing for the immortal kind,
the heart wanders far away in a dizzying haze.
The capital is a den of wandering knights;
the mountains and forests are dwellings for those in hiding.
How can vermilion gates be worth the glory?
They are not like entrusting oneself to Pénglái.
By the spring, I scoop up clear waves;
on the hills, I pluck cinnabar sprouts.
At the Língxī, one can dwell in seclusion;
why bother with the business of climbing the cloud-ladder?
Qīyuán had its proud official;
Lái-shì had his reclusive wife.
To advance is to maintain the visibility of the dragon;
to retreat is to be a ram caught in a hedge.
Stepping high outside the wind and dust,
I bow long to bid farewell to Yí and Qí.
Qīngxī is over a thousand rèn deep;
within it there is a Dàoshi.
Clouds arise between the beams and pillars;
wind issues from within the windows and doors.
May I ask who this is?
It is said to be Guǐgǔzi.
Standing on tiptoe to gaze at Yǐngyáng,
I think of washing my ears by the river.
The Chānghé wind comes from the southwest;
the hidden waves ripple like rising scales.
The Língfēi looks back and smiles at me,
brilliantly revealing her jade-like teeth.
Jiǎn Xiū is no longer of this time;
to make an agreement, whom shall I send?
The kingfisher plays on the orchid branches,
their colors brightening each other.
Green vines tie together the tall forest,
lushly covering the entire mountain.
Within there is a man of dark silence,
quietly whistling and plucking clear strings.
Letting his emotions soar beyond the clouds,
chewing on flower stamens and scooping from flying springs.
Chìsōng looks down from the upper reaches,
driving a swan and riding on purple smoke.
To the left, he tugs the sleeve of Fúqiū;
to the right, he pats the shoulder of Hóngyá.
May I ask the company of mayflies,
how could you know the years of the turtle and crane?
How can the six dragons be halted?
The cycles of fortune flow with succession.
The changing seasons stir human thoughts;
once it is autumn, one wishes for summer again.
In Huáihǎi, small birds undergo transformation,
but my life alone does not change.
Though I wish to leap over Dānxī,
cloud dragons are not mine to ride.
Ashamed I lack the virtue of Lǔyáng,
to turn back the sun by three stages.
Facing the river, I lament the passing years;
clutching my heart, I sigh in solitary grief.
Swift wings long to brush the sky;
fast feet envy a distant journey.
In clear springs, there are no rising billows;
how can one maneuver a ship-swallowing fish?
Though jade tablets are uniquely excellent,
it is hard to cast a bright moon pearl into the dark.
Hidden sprouts resent the Qīngyáng;
trumpet creepers mourn the Sùqiū.
Sorrow comes and pains my sincere heart;
falling tears flow along my hat-strings.
In various counties I stay at the Lǔ gate;
the warm wind is about to become a disaster.
The ship-swallowing fish surges from the sea floor;
high waves ride over Pénglái.
Immortals emerge by parting the clouds;
one sees only the terraces of gold and silver.
Língyáng scoops from the cinnabar stream;
Róngchéng brandishes a jade cup.
Héng'é raises a wondrous sound;
Hóngyá nods his chin in approval.
Rising and falling with the long smoke,
fluttering and playing through the nine realms.
A marvelous age exceeding the Five Dragons;
at a thousand years, they are but infants.
Yàn Zhāo had no spiritual aura;
Hàn Wǔ was not a talent for immortality.
The new and full moons follow a circle;
when the moon is full, the waning light is already seen.
Rùshōu clears the Xīlù;
the Zhūxī will yield to the white.
Cold dew brushes the trumpet creepers;
the dodder vines take leave of the pines and cypresses.
The hibiscus’s bloom does not last the morning;
how can the mayfly see the evening?
On Yuánqiū there is wondrous grass;
Zhōngshān produces numinous fluid.
Wángsūn arrays the eight delicacies;
Ānqī refines the five stones.
A long bow to those in power,
I come and go as a guest of the mountains and forests.
Leaning on a staff to summon the recluse,
the wild path lies across past and present.
In the rocky caves, there are no structures;
amidst the hills, there is the sound of a qín.
White snow lingers on the shady ridges;
red blossoms shine in the sunlit woods.
Rocky springs rinse fine jade;
tiny fish also float and sink.
It need not be strings and flutes;
mountains and waters have their own clear sounds.
Why wait for whistling and singing?
The dense shrubs moan sadly on their own.
Autumn chrysanthemums serve as provisions;
fragrant orchids fill the folds of my robes.
Hesitating, my feet feel the weariness;
I merely wish to cast off my hairpin.
Planning and starting my cottage on Dōngshān,
beneath the fruit trees, thickets naturally form.
Before it lies a well of cold spring water,
sufficient to polish the mind and spirit.
Amidst the steep and lush greenery,
bamboo and cypress retain their true nature.
Tender leaves harbor frost and snow;
flying blossoms flow on the remaining moisture.
Rank and robes are not for permanent enjoyment;
likes and dislikes have their bending and stretching.
Tying the seal-ribbon brings entanglements;
brushing the cap removes the dust.
Huìlián's compromise is not my subjection;
Shǒuyáng's way is not my benevolence.
Together let us observe what is esteemed;
roaming freely, choosing an auspicious time.
At dawn, my heart is not at peace;
shaking my robes, I pace back and forth.
Pacing back and forth, where should I go?
The man of seclusion is in the deep valley.
In the morning, gathering algae in the southern stream;
in the evening, resting at the foot of the western mountain.
Lithe branches resemble cloud-like structures;
dense leaves form a kingfisher-green canopy.
Lingering in the orchid forest to the tune of Jīchǔ;
swirling fragrances cling to the elegant trees.
How cool and clear the mountain trickles are;
flying springs rinse the ringing jade stones.
Plaintive notes drift upon the numinous waves;
falling echoes rush to the winding banks.
Ultimate joy is not something borrowed;
why bother with diluting pure simplicity?
If wealth and honor are difficult to plan for,
I shall unhitch my carriage and follow my heart’s desire.
Small hermits hide in the hills and marshes;
great hermits hide in the court and market.
Bó Yí fled to Shǒu Yáng;
Lǎo Dān served as an archivist.
Once, in times of great peace,
there were also those who lived in nests.
Although today is a flourishing and enlightened age,
could there be no scholars in the woods?
Releasing the spirit beyond the blue clouds,
leaving no trace within the remote mountains.
The crane-pheasants cry before dawn;
a mournful wind rises to meet the night.
Congealing frost withers the rosy face;
cold springs hurt the jade-like feet.
Comprehensive talent is indeed common to many;
partial wisdom is left to oneself.
Accepting one’s lot, one gains heavenly harmony;
forcing one’s nature, one loses the ultimate truth.
Upon returning, what is there to expect?
To be one with things in both end and beginning.
Riding a carriage on a night excursion,
wandering leisurely through the Xī Yuán.
Dual channels irrigate one another;
fine trees surround the flowing stream.
Low-hanging branches brush the feathered canopy;
long boughs touch the azure sky.
A startling wind assists the wheel hubs;
flying birds soar before me.
Rosy clouds flank the bright moon;
brilliant stars emerge from among the clouds.
The high heavens cast down their radiant luster;
how vivid are the five colors!
My lifespan is not that of Chì Sōng or Wáng Qiáo;
who can truly become a divine immortal?
Roaming freely to gladden the heart and mind,
I shall preserve myself until the end of a hundred years.
Although the four seasons follow in succession,
change and transformation each have their standard.
Only the clear days of autumn
can bring one’s high spirits to their peak.
The atmosphere is mostly bright and far-reaching;
the scenery is naturally chilly and brisk.
Crisp sounds from the pipes alert the hidden rhythms;
mournful ravines echo in the empty hollows.
In the year’s cold, there is no early blooming;
fleeting glory is willing to wither early.
How to distinguish the steadfast from the fragile?
I briefly entrust this thought to the pine and the mushroom.
The wise master is moved by the forlorn morning,
solemnly preparing his carriage for beyond the dust.
At the wide banquet, universal love is spread;
leisure cups invite distinguished guests.
As for me, I delight in loving benevolence;
delusions are removed and stinginess vanishes.
Humbly serving in the court of the Ā Héng,
I shall surely invite the ridicule of the Xiōng Nú.
Awakening to the chirp of that cricket,
I believe in this song of the laborers.
Does time not come swiftly?
Good outings are often missed.
Wandering leisurely beyond the city markets,
I wish to pass through here many times.
Winding paths cover the hills and gaps;
from a high terrace, I gaze at the flying clouds.
A kind wind stirs the dense gardens;
white clouds gather on the layered hills.
At sunset, the singing birds gather;
water and trees are steeped in clear brilliance.
Lifting my robes, I follow the orchid-covered islet;
lingering, I lean against the fragrant branches.
The fair one lets the months and years slip by;
in the twilight of life, what can be done alone?
Do not be pulled by your thoughts;
Nán Róng was cautioned against having too many.
At sunset, we float on the clear waters;
under the arrayed stars, we row light oars.
Resting in a pavilion facing the winding stream,
overlooking the current against the returning tide.
Stopping the horses and sharing mats together,
sitting side by side, we invite one another.
Mournful wild geese cry on the sandbars;
sorrowful apes echo on the mountain peaks.
Tall and upright, the moon is reflected in the river;
briskly, a wind emerges from the valley.
Streaking mists veil the peaks;
dripping dew fills the branches.
Looking nearby dispels hidden gloom;
gazing afar washes away the clamor.
Engaged in talk, we know no fatigue,
from evening until the clear morning.
The jade seal counsels sincerity and trust;
the yellow-roofed carriage displays loftiness.
Affairs are used for the sake of moral teachings;
the Way transcends through divine principles.
Long ago, I heard of the outing at Fén Shuǐ;
today I see horses beyond the dust.
Sounding pipes set out from the spring bank;
unhitching the bells, we climb the mountain peak.
Spreading the curtains to gaze at the inverted reflection;
arranging the mats to watch the returning tide.
Distant cliffs reflect the orchid thickets;
the bright sun beautifies the river marshes.
Plains and marshes sprout green willows;
ruins and gardens are scattered with red peaches.
The Emperor's heart praises the sun's bounty;
all phenomena are brightly illuminated.
Looking at myself, I am bound in vain;
considering my intent, I feel ashamed before the garden sprouts.
Skill and clumsiness each have their place;
in the end, I shall return to my forest nest.
As these old thoughts entwine me,
viewing things, I compose a long song.
Walking out of the west city gate,
I gaze afar at the peak west of the city.
Continuous barriers of stacked peaks and crags,
emerald green, distant and profound.
Morning frost turns maple leaves red;
evening twilight makes the mountain mist dark.
As the season passes, my sorrow is not shallow;
as feelings arise, my thoughts are already deep.
The captive female bird longs for her old mate;
the lost bird yearns for its former forest.
Full of emotion, still toiling for love;
how can one be separated from a kindred spirit?
Checking the mirror, my black sideburns have grayed;
clutching my belt, I loosen my tight collar.
Finding peace is but empty words;
in solitude, I rely on the sounding zither.
The submerged dragon charms with its hidden grace;
the flying goose echoes with a distant sound.
Approaching the sky, I feel ashamed before the floating clouds;
dwelling by the river, I feel sheepish before the deep abyss.
To advance in virtue, my wisdom is clumsy;
to retreat to farming, my strength is insufficient.
Seeking a salary, I returned to the distant sea;
lying ill, I face the empty forest.
Leaning my ear to listen to the waves,
lifting my eyes to gaze at the rugged peaks.
Early sunlight changes the lingering wind;
new warmth replaces the old cold.
In the pond, spring grass grows;
in the garden willows, the singing birds change.
The many crowds bring sorrow to the songs of Bīn;
the lush growth brings feeling to the chants of Chǔ.
Living alone, time seems to last forever;
separated from the herd, it is hard to settle the heart.
Maintaining one’s principles is not only for the ancients;
being without regret is evidenced today.
At the end of the day, it cleared at evening;
clouds return as the sun gallops west.
The dense forest holds a lingering clarity;
distant peaks hide half the sun’s disc.
Long afflicted by the misery of dampness,
from the inn, I gaze at the suburban crossroads.
Marsh orchids gradually cover the paths;
lotuses begin to bloom in the pond.
Not yet weary of the beauty of spring,
I already see the summer season shifting.
Mournfully, I sigh, moved by things;
scattered like stars, my white hair hangs down.
Medicine and food are where my feelings rest;
decline and illness are suddenly here.
I shall wait for the autumn waters,
resting my shadow and reclining on the old cliff.
With whom can I clarify my intent?
Only a true friend can appreciate my heart.
Early summer is still clear and mild;
fragrant grasses have not yet withered.
Lodging on the water through morning and evening;
cloudy mists frequently rise and vanish.
Weary of surveying the shores of the sea,
even more so of traversing the barren lands.
The River God occasionally lets the current flow peacefully;
Tiān Wú remains quiet and does not stir.
Raising sails to gather stone flowers;
hanging the mats to pick up sea moons.
The rising tide has no limit or edge;
an empty boat has its own transcendence.
Zhòng Lián made light of the seal of Qí;
Zǐ Móu longed for the towers of Wèi.
Boasting of fame, the Way is insufficient;
following oneself, things can be ignored.
I beg to follow the words of Rèn Gōng,
and ultimately decline the Heavenly Punishment.
At dusk and dawn, the weather changes;
the mountains and waters contain a pure radiance.
This pure radiance can delight a person;
the traveler is so content he forgets to return.
Leaving the valley, the sun was still early;
entering the boat, the sunlight is already faint.
Forest ravines gather the colors of twilight;
clouds and mists pull in the evening vapors.
Water lilies and lotuses shine in alternating lushness;
reeds and grasses lean upon one another.
Pushing through the brush, I hasten toward the southern path;
with joy, I rest by the eastern door.
When thoughts are detached, worldly things naturally become light;
when the mind is content, principles are not violated.
I send word to those who seek to preserve life:
try using this way to find the truth.
At dawn, with a staff, I seek the sheer cliffs;
at evening, I rest in a mountain dwelling.
Sparse peaks support the high hall;
facing the ridges, I overlook the winding stream.
Vast forests surround the doors and windows;
piled stones embrace the foundations and steps.
Connected crags make me feel the road is blocked;
dense bamboo makes me lose the path.
Newcomers forget the recent techniques;
those leaving are confused by the old paths.
Gurgling, the evening stream flows swiftly;
shrilly, the night apes cry.
Is deep seclusion any different from the true principle?
By guarding the Way, one naturally does not stray.
My heart is in harmony with the trunks of late autumn;
my eyes delight in the sprouts of the third month of spring.
I live in the ordinary to wait for the end;
I abide in compliance, thus I am at peace.
I regret I have no companion of like mind
to climb the ladder to the blue clouds together.
At dawn, I set out from Yáng Á;
as the sun falls, I rest at Yīn Fēng.
Leaving the boat, I gaze at the distant islet;
stopping my staff, I lean against a lush pine.
The side path is already secluded and deep;
the surrounding isle is also exquisite.
Looking down, I see the tips of tall trees;
looking up, I hear the splashing of the great ravine.
Rocks lie across, causing the water to divide;
the forest is dense, the path's traces are cut off.
What do I feel upon understanding this creation?
Everything that rises and grows is full of beauty.
The first bamboo is wrapped in green sheaths;
the new reeds contain purple down.
Sea gulls play on the spring banks;
the Tiān Jī bird sports in the gentle breeze.
Observing transformation, the heart is never weary;
viewing objects, my affection grows deeper.
I do not mind being far from people;
I only regret that no one is with me.
Traveling alone is not a cause for sighs of emotion;
but if appreciation is abandoned, who can understand the principle?
The ape's cry truly signals the dawn;
in the deep valley, the light has not yet appeared.
Below the crags, clouds are just gathering;
upon the flowers, dew still hangs.
Winding along the bends and corners;
distant and high, I climb the mountain passes.
Crossing the mountain stream is both steep and rapid;
climbing the plank road is also high and far.
River islets are repeatedly passed;
following the current, I enjoy the twists and turns.
Duckweed floats in the deep water;
wild rice and reeds cover the clear shallows.
Reaching from a rock, I scoop up a flying spring;
climbing the forest, I pick a curled leaf.
I imagine seeing the Shān Ā Rén;
the ivy and dodder seem to be before my eyes.
Holding orchids is a vain effort;
breaking hemp, my heart cannot unroll.
Emotion is made beautiful through appreciation;
if things are obscure, who can ultimately distinguish them?
Observing this, I discard worldly worries;
with one realization, I find what can be cast away.
Mù of Zhōu exhausted his wheel tracks;
Yǔ of Xià traveled through mountains and rivers.
How could hoarding one's carriage be considered brilliant?
Those good at traveling are all sages and immortals.
The Emperor's radiance follows the season's movement;
the cleared paths patrol the vast marketplace.
From the tower, one gazes at the abundant grain;
the golden carriage is reflected by Sōng Shān.
Flying speed and flowing connectivity;
the vermilion silk wraps in alternating cycles.
The divine progress matches the floating shadows;
competing in light, it fills the center of the sky.
At the start of winter, I look at the passing things;
withered and weary, they fill the change.
The sunny lands gather the pure essence;
the shaded valleys drag the cold mist.
Gathered whiteness is already dense and lush;
accumulated green is also verdant.
The end-of-year feast rewards the good year;
the communication of urgency warns of lean times.
Warm kindness reaches the servants;
harmony and grace belong to the rear banquet.
Observing the customs, I have long wanted to write;
presenting this poem, I am ashamed it is not beautiful.
Weak and weary, I decline the rapid pace;
taking on burdens is not a matter of ropes and chains.
The primordial heaven is high in the northern constellations;
Rì Guān overlooks the eastern sea.
Entering the river, the Yáng Xiá rises;
treading on Huá Shān because of its sheer cut.
Rocky dangers have left the lands of Hàn;
the strategic defense has moved to the capital of Wú.
The flowing ponds were created by nature;
the mountain passes were surely built by the spirits.
The park districts reach the limits of the horizon;
the towns and shrines gather the spirits of the earth.
The dwelling's path shines like the stars;
its birth and light correspond to the divine spirits.
Wise thoughts entwine the old village;
the patrolling carriage circles the former lands.
Climbing the peak, the imperial carriage road ascends;
seeking clouds, the jade eaves are raised high.
The spring river has grand winds and waves;
the orchid fields are lush with young sprouts.
Promoting travel broadens the reach to those below;
exploring the distance concentrates the sage's feelings.
On the shore of the Great Peak, there is a harmonious gathering;
the auspicious practice lies in the divination of the journey.
In Zhōu Nán, one grieves for the elders of old;
lingering here, one is moved by the remaining people.
Eating for free, I am weary of the court halls;
returning to taxes, I dedicate myself to mountain farming.
The winds of Yú record the Emperor's hunt;
the proverbs of Xià praise the King's travels.
In the spring direction, the imperial carriage moves;
hoping for the royal visit, the five provinces lean in.
Mountain spirits clear the mountain roads;
water spirits alert the blue currents.
The divine carriage sets out on jade wheels;
the heavenly presence descends on the decorated boat.
Ten thousand axles follow the escort;
a thousand wings float upon the water.
Carved clouds beautify the jade canopy;
auspicious breezes cover the colorful banners.
Jiāng Nán presents the beauty of Jīng;
the rushing river offers the songs of Zhào.
Golden silks shine on the sea shore;
pipes and drums shake the islands of the deep.
Gazing far, one sees the blue cliffs;
drifting along, one views the green fields.
Spirits and mortals soar through capital and wild;
fish and birds rise from abyss and hill.
Virtue and ritual are now universally pervasive;
rivers and peaks are everywhere pacified.
At the cock's crow, the pass officials rise;
beating the drums, they announce the morning.
The stern carriages approach the distant paths;
gazing out, they pass through the city gates.
Creeping grass climbs the high corners;
tall poplars line the broad crossing.
The swift wind begins at dawn;
the level road is blocked by flying dust.
Bustling are the office-seeking sons;
busy are the marketplace people.
Clutching gold, they stay near to profit;
grasping swords, they go far to leave their kin.
Racing to be first on the ten-thousand-mile road;
each serving their hundred-year life.
Flowers bloom during the youthful season;
holding their colors, they are wary of the startling spring.
Honoring the worthy is forever bright;
the lonely and humble are long hidden away.
Beauty and glory sit and fade away;
for whose sake is all this bitter toil?
Sorrowful and bitter, without any joy;
hand in hand, let us go and seek pleasure.
Seeking clouds, we climb the tiered towers;
following the mountain, we look toward the mushroom-shaped pavilion.
Distant trees are dark and lush;
rising mists are thick and boundless.
Fish play, and the new lotuses move;
birds scatter, and the remaining flowers fall.
If not facing the fragrant spring wine,
I would still look back at the city in the green mountains.
Guǎngchéng loved the sacred tripod,
Huáinán favored the elixir scriptures.
This mountain possesses simurghs and cranes,
those coming and going are all immortals.
Jade grasses are just now glowing brightly,
jade trees are truly verdant and lush.
Crimson vapors swirl below in the thickets,
white clouds reach up into the dark heights.
Sitting in the center, one overlooks the coiling rainbow,
bowing down, one watches the shooting stars.
If one does not seek the utmost of distant wonders,
then one knows how ears and eyes can be startled.
The sun sets over the banks of Chángshā,
layered shadows of ten thousand lǐ arise.
Resting on orchids, I have many reflections,
facing the wind, I silently harbor deep feelings.
I am just learning the reclusion of pines and cypresses,
ashamed to chase after the fame of marketplaces.
Fortunate to receive the end of your radiant recitation,
I humbly think of entrusting myself to your future banners.
Lìngshān records the virtues of the earth,
the dangerous terrain relies on the mountain spirits.
Zhōngnán stands as the lookout for Qín,
Shàoshì is near to the royal city.
Emerald phoenixes soar over Huáihǎi,
sashes and collars surround the divine outskirts.
How towering are the northern hills!
The dense forests are dark and verdant.
From the earth rise many strange ridges,
piercing the clouds in no single form.
Crowded together, they jointly hide the sky,
uneven and jagged, they look toward one another.
Looming and winding, they form cinnabar peaks,
steep and high, they raise blue precipices.
Their momentum follows the height of Jiǔyí,
their spirit is as grand as the Sānshān.
The immediate scenery is already full of beauty,
the distant view is even more extraordinary.
Gazing south at the Chǔxū Observatory,
looking west toward the Kūnmíng Lake.
Everything in the mountains is delightful,
appreciation follows the shift of the four seasons.
Spring light emanates from the ridges,
autumn wind rises among the cassia branches.
I often meet companions who have stilled their hearts,
building their shelters at the foot of the mountain.
The Eight Liberations sound in the mountain streams,
the Four Dhyanas are hidden in the bends of the crags.
Deep and obscure, they are never seen,
desolate and aloof, they have no desires.
My wish is to wander with them,
my heart would be satisfied with this.
The Prince possesses an extraordinary interest,
feathered banners approach the lofty foundations.
White clouds follow your jade steps,
blue mists mingle with the cassia banners.
Lingering to search for the five medicines,
pacing about to wait for the three fungi.
Thus I look up to your harness and carriage,
making the year's end our appointed time.
Chén Wáng’s cockfighting road,
Ānrén’s woodcutting path.
How could the eastern suburbs differ from the past?
For now, I can leisurely wander there.
The wild paths are already winding and twisted,
the desolate tracks also crisscross one another.
Hibiscus fences are sparse yet dense,
thorn gates are new yet old.
At the treetops, the wind-whirls cry,
at the grass roots, frost and dew accumulate.
Startled deer do not rest,
migrating birds occasionally look back at each other.
Under thatched eaves, sorrowful owls hoot,
on level mounds, cold rabbits run.
Evening shadows drape over the layered hills,
long smoke draws out light white silk.
Flying light suddenly presses upon me,
it will not stop just because the year is ending.
If I could receive the medicine of Xīshān,
my declining years might perhaps be sustained.
Qín Huáng governed the universe,
Hàn Dì expanded military achievements.
Their joys and human affairs were exhausted,
yet their natures were still not satisfied.
They fixed their minds on the Sānshān,
entrusting their longings to the nine heavens.
They already built the Qǐnián Observatory,
and further erected the Wàngxiān Palace.
It was not that their hearts truly loved the Way,
it was simply that their desires were limitless.
I say that I know when I have enough,
this wish need not be grand.
Where I encounter a place to linger,
I then wish to rest my weary frame.
Mountain peaks are distant and overlapping,
bamboo and trees are near and tangled.
Opening my collar to wash in the cold water,
loosening my belt to face the clear breeze.
What burdens me are not external things,
for my thoughts reside in the Profound Void.
When friends come, they hold stone marrow,
when guests arrive, they ride light swans.
All of them make the human paths vanish,
only allowing the cloud roads to open.
With one leap, rising above the reflected light,
with nothing to do, wandering to Huá and Sōng.
I send word to those with appreciative hearts:
come and join me at the year's end.
Gānquán warns with beacon fires,
Shànggǔ resists Lóulán.
This river is called vast and perilous,
this mountain is also densely coiled.
Inside and out, it exhausts the beauty of form,
its surroundings are all crags and peaks.
Tall bamboos flourish and connect below,
high towers loftily pierce the sky above.
Mounting the parapet to gaze into the distance,
turning my head, I see Cháng'ān.
Golden channels face the Bà and Chǎn rivers,
covered walkways lead to the Yuān and Luán.
Bright carriages race on ornate wheels,
sweating horses leap with silver saddles.
Young men rely on their vigorous spirit,
upright and bold, their hair lifting their caps.
They dream of recording deeds on the stones of Yànshān,
and think of opening the pass with a pellet from Hángǔ.
How could it be like the games at Bàshàng,
ashamed to be mere spectacles for roadside observers?
I send word to those seeking to be enfeoffed as lords:
such a twist of fate is truly to be lamented!
In the middle of the night, I cannot sleep,
I rise and sit to play the resonant zither.
The thin curtain reflects the bright moon,
the clear breeze blows against my collar.
A solitary swan cries in the outer wilds,
a bird of the north calls in the northern woods.
Pacing back and forth, what shall I see?
Sorrowful thoughts alone grieve the heart.
The two consorts wandered the riverbanks,
roaming freely, soaring with the wind.
Jiāofǔ held the ring pendants,
beautiful and charming, they possessed fragrance.
Graceful and soft were the feelings of joy and love,
for a thousand years, they would not forget each other.
Such city-toppling beauty dazed Xiàcài,
their lovely countenances tied to the inner heart.
Deeply moved, sorrowful thoughts arise,
planting daylilies in the orchid chamber.
For whom is the ointment and bathing applied?
Longing for rain, yet resentful of the morning sun.
How is it that a bond of metal and stone
would one day change to the pain of separation?
Fine trees form paths beneath them,
the peaches and plums of the eastern garden.
Autumn wind blows the flying bean leaves,
scattering and falling begins from here.
Luxuriance turns to withered exhaustion,
thorns and wolfberries grow in the hall.
Spurring my horse, I leave them behind,
going up to the foot of Xīshān.
I cannot even protect my own person,
much less long for wife and children?
Congealed frost covers the wild grass,
the year's end is also finished.
The flourishing youths of former days,
Ānlíng and Lóngyáng.
Delicate like peach and plum blossoms,
brilliant and glowing with radiance.
Joyful as if in the nine days of spring,
bowing as low as the autumn frost.
Their glancing eyes emit charm and beauty,
their speech and laughter breathe out fragrance.
Hand in hand, they shared joy and love,
day and night, they shared the same robes.
They wished to be a pair of flying birds,
soaring together wing to wing.
Their bright oaths were recorded in cinnabar and blue,
never to be forgotten through eternal ages.
Heavenly horses come from the northwest,
following the road from the east since olden times.
The spring and autumn seasons have nothing to rely on,
how can wealth and honor be permanently kept?
Clear dew covers the marsh orchids,
congealed frost wets the wild grass.
In the morning, one is a charming youth,
by evening, one becomes ugly and old.
Unless one is Wángzǐ Jìn,
who can remain beautiful forever?
Climbing high to gaze over the four fields,
I look north toward the ridges of Qīng Shān.
Pines and cypresses shade the mountain ridges,
flying birds call to one another as they pass.
Stirred by emotion, I harbor bitterness and pain;
resentment and malice are always too much to bear.
Lord Lǐ grieved at the East Gate;
Master Sū felt restricted within the Sān Hé region.
They sought benevolence and attained it;
why then should they sigh and lament once more!
The beginning of autumn heralds the cool air,
crickets chirp by the bed curtains.
Moved by things, I harbor deep sorrow;
quietude makes my heart mournful.
With many words, to whom should I speak?
With elaborate phrases, to whom shall I complain?
A light breeze blows my silken sleeves,
the bright moon shines with clear brilliance.
The morning cock crows from a high tree;
I order my carriage to rise and return home.
In the days of my youth,
I was frivolous and fond of strings and song.
I traveled west into Xiányáng,
where the Zhào and Lǐ families visited one another.
Before the pleasure reached its end,
the bright sun suddenly slipped away.
I spurred my horse to return once more,
looking back to gaze at Sān Hé.
A hundred measures of gold were all spent;
expenses were always a bitter burden.
Looking north toward the road of Tàiháng,
having lost my way, what shall I do?
Long ago I heard of the melons of Dōnglíng,
grown just outside the Qīng Mén.
Carts were lined up axle to axle along the paths,
large and small melons clinging to their vines.
Five colors shone in the morning sun;
honored guests gathered from all sides.
Fat in the lamp fries itself away;
great wealth becomes a source of harm.
Plain clothes may serve for a lifetime;
how can favor and salary be relied upon?
Walking out through the Shàngdōng Mén,
I look north toward the peak of Shǒuyáng.
Below are those who gathered ferns;
above is a forest of fine trees.
Where is the auspicious time to be found?
Thick frost dampens my lapel.
A cold wind shakes the mountain ridges;
dark clouds rise into heavy gloom.
Honking geese fly on their southern journey;
the nightjar gives forth a mournful sound.
Pure essence wanders in the Shāng note;
the sorrow wounds my heart.
In years past, at fourteen or fifteen,
my ambition was set on the *Shī* and *Shū*.
Clad in coarse cloth but harboring pearls and jade,
I hoped to be like Yán and Mǐn.
I opened the window to look over the four fields;
climbing high, I gazed toward what I longed for.
Graves and mounds cover the mountain ridges;
ten thousand generations become as one moment.
After a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
where will a glorious name go?
I was misled by Xiànmén Zǐ;
wailing now, I mock myself.
Wandering by the side of Péng Chí,
I look back to gaze at Dàliáng.
Green waters stir great waves;
the vast wild is a boundless blur.
Running beasts gallop back and forth;
flying birds soar in pursuit of one another.
At this time, the Quail Fire is at the zenith;
the sun and moon face each other directly.
The north wind brings severe cold;
Yin energy descends as light frost.
A traveler without a companion,
looking up and down, I harbor grief and sorrow.
The petty man calculates his achievements;
the gentleman follows his constant path.
Why should I regret ending in distress?
I chant these words to compose this chapter.
The burning heat belongs to this summer;
the thirty days are about to pass.
Fragrant trees hang their green leaves;
clear clouds drift languidly of their own accord.
The four seasons replace one another in turn;
the sun and moon pass by in succession.
Pacing to and fro in the empty hall,
I am filled with anguish that no one knows.
I wish to see the end in joy and love,
and not see the sorrow of parting.
Brilliant is the sun sinking in the west,
its remaining light shines upon my clothes.
A whirling wind blows against the four walls;
cold birds huddle together for warmth.
The Zhōuzhōu bird still carries feathers in its beak;
the Qióngqióng beast also thinks of its hunger.
Why is it that those in power
bend like chimes and forget where to return?
Is it for the sake of boastful fame
that they let distress make their hearts sad?
I would rather fly with the swallows and sparrows
than follow the flight of the great swan.
The great swan roams the four seas;
midway on its journey, where shall it return?
Sitting alone in the empty hall,
with whom can I share joy?
Going out the door to face the long road,
I see no carriages or horses passing.
Climbing high to gaze at the Nine Provinces,
far and wide stretch the vast wilds.
A solitary bird flies northwest;
a stray beast runs down to the southeast.
At sunset, I think of relatives and friends;
I speak to myself to express my feelings.
In the northern wards are many strange dances;
upon the Pú river are subtle notes.
Frivolous and idle wanderers
drift and sink in the blink of an eye.
They take shortcuts along narrow paths,
striving to hasten toward dissipation.
How can they see Wángzǐ Qiáo,
riding the clouds and soaring through Dènglín?
Only the art of prolonging years
can bring comfort to my heart.
Deep and clear are the waters of the Cháng Jiāng;
above them is a forest of maple trees.
Marsh orchids cover the paths;
the black horse gallops swiftly.
Looking into the distance makes one sad;
the spring air moves my heart.
In the Sān Chǔ regions are many talented men;
the morning clouds lead toward dissipation.
Vermilion flowers shake out their fragrance;
Gāo Cài follows in pursuit.
Once I feel the grief of the yellow sparrow,
who can stop the tears from falling?
Throughout my life I have lacked grand ambitions;
from my youth I have been entangled in worries.
How can I carry this bitter heart,
especially when encountering the late autumn?
Brightly the heavenly moon shines;
brilliantly the River stars glitter.
The cicada in the wind sounds desolate;
the goose among the clouds cries out in the distance.
The cold Shāng note moves through the pure chamber;
the solitary lamp dims within the dark curtains.
Upright and firm, my many worries accumulate;
I toss and turn through the middle of the long night.
Safety and danger are hard to plan for in advance;
fortune and misfortune are obscured from prior calculation.
Although I like the success of Xiāngrú,
I do not share the arrogance of Chángqīng.
I am quite pleased with Zhèng Shēng's retirement;
I have no desire for the officialdom of a commoner.
Not knowing the hearts of the ancients,
I shall follow the inclinations of my nature.
When guests arrive, I can order the wine cups;
when friends come, we should dip our brushes in ink.
Suddenly climbing and treading upon the high terrace,
the clear shallows are occasionally disturbed.
The waning moon will not be round again;
the setting sun has no second dawn.
Gold and stone will eventually crumble and perish;
red and blue pigments momentarily glow.
Let each strive before the sigh of black hair turning gray;
do not leave the joy of white heads to regret.
Thus I sing and complete this rhapsody,
to briefly share it with my close relatives.
Bóyáng went to the Western Róng;
the Master wished to dwell among the Jiǔmán.
If one harbors ambitions for the four directions,
any place can be a site for wandering.
How much more so when encountering hardship and obstruction,
stumbling upon disasters and calamities.
The ancients understood the subtle signs of things;
they whipped their horses and wandered near the passes.
Alas, I am young and ignorant,
burdened by responsibility while holding a lowly office.
Secret plots were already being constructed in the dark,
giving rise to this turn of fortune and misfortune.
Within the vastness of the six directions,
how broad indeed are the four seas!
Yet the heavenly net is spread wide with its cords,
and one cannot find peace in taking a single step.
Pines and cypresses wither in the height of winter;
only then does one know the cold of the year.
Without crossing the dangers of Tàiháng,
who would know the difficulty of this road?
Truth and falsehood are revealed through events;
human sentiments are difficult to foresee.
Failure and success have fixed portions;
in one's indignation, why sigh again?
Above, I have failed the kindness of my merciful mother;
the bitter pain destroys my heart and liver.
Below, I look upon the daughter I pity;
my inner heart is pained and sorrowful.
My two sons are abandoned as if cast away;
I think of how they have all met with cruelty.
I do not begrudge the death of my own body,
but only this cycle of thought.
Holding the paper, my five emotions are blocked;
wielding the brush, my tears flow in torrents.
Alas, my fortune is meager;
I encountered misfortune in my youth.
Pitiful and alone, without understanding,
I was still in swaddling clothes.
Reared by my mother and elder brother,
there was kindness but no severity.
Relying on love, I was willful and arrogant,
neither disciplined nor taught.
When I reached adulthood,
relying on favor, I let myself go.
I set my heart on the ancients,
following what I esteemed.
Entrusting my interests to Lǎo and Zhuāng,
I held things cheap and valued the self.
My will was to preserve simplicity,
nourishing purity to keep my nature whole.
It is said that I am not clever;
I love the good but am blind to people's nature.
The failure of Zǐyù
has repeatedly added to my burden.
A great man is magnanimous,
concealing filth and bearing insults.
The people have many deviations,
and government does not follow one's own will.
With this narrow mind of mine,
I clearly distinguished good and bad.
Realizing and thinking of my faults,
the pain is like a fresh wound.
Desiring to lessen my errors,
slanderous talk seethes and bubbles.
My nature is not to harm things,
yet I frequently cause resentment and hatred.
Formerly I was ashamed before Liǔhuì,
now I am embarrassed before Sūn Dēng.
Inwardly I have failed my long-held heart;
outwardly I am ashamed before my good friends.
I look up with admiration to Yán and Zhèng,
delighting in the Way and living in leisure.
Having no dealings with the world,
my spirit was calm and composed.
Alas, I was unlucky,
entangled in many worries.
It was not sent down from Heaven,
but truly came from my own stubbornness and negligence.
Reason failed and calamities knotted together,
finally landing me in prison.
Responding to vulgar interrogations,
I am fettered in this secluded, blocked place.
I am truly ashamed to litigate for release;
the time is not with me.
Though I may be right and upright,
my spirit is humiliated and my will dejected.
Washing the body in the Cānglàng river,
how could it be said to make amends?
Harmony of the crying geese,
spreading their wings to wander north.
Moving in accordance with the seasons,
attaining their desires and forgetting sorrow.
Alas, in my indignation and sighs,
I have never been their equal.
Events go against my wishes,
and I encounter this long detention.
Failure and success are fated,
so what else is there to seek?
The ancients had a saying:
For the sake of the good, do not get close to fame.
Serving the times with respect and silence,
blame and regret will not arise.
Wànshí was cautious and prudent,
bringing peace to his kin and preserving glory.
Worldly affairs are numerous and tangled,
only disturbing my feelings.
In times of peace and joy, one must be cautious;
only then will one find profit and perseverance in the end.
Brilliant is the spiritual língzhī mushroom,
blooming three times in one year.
Why am I alone,
having ambitions but failing to achieve them?
Chastened by hardship, I think of returning;
my heart is inwardly pained.
May I exert myself for the future,
with neither fragrance nor stench.
Gathering ferns on the mountain slope,
with hair loose among the rocky peaks.
Forever whistling and chanting long,
nourishing my nature and tending to my longevity.
The bright moon shines on the high tower;
its flowing light lingers and wavers.
Above is a woman full of sorrowful thoughts,
her heavy sighs filled with lingering grief.
May I ask who is the sigher?
She says she is the traveler's wife.
"My lord has been gone for more than ten years,
and I, your lonely handmaiden, always dwell alone.
If you are the dust of the clear road,
I am the mud of the turbid water.
Floating and sinking in different states,
when will we ever meet in harmony?
I wish to be the southwest wind,
drifting far away into your embrace.
But your embrace is truly not open to me;
on whom should I, your humble handmaiden, rely?"
In the Western Capital, all is in chaos and disorder;
jackals and tigers are causing calamity.
Again, I abandon the Central Kingdom and leave,
taking myself far away to the Jīngmán.
My relatives grieve before me;
my friends follow and cling to me.
Going out the gate, there is nothing to be seen
but white bones covering the level plains.
On the road is a starving woman,
clutching her child and abandoning it in the grass.
Looking back, she hears the sound of wailing and weeping;
she wipes her tears and alone does not return.
"I do not even know where I shall die,
how can I keep us both alive?"
I drive my horse and leave them behind,
unable to bear hearing these words.
Southward I climb the banks of Bàlíng,
turning my head to gaze back at Cháng'ān.
Thinking of the person who wrote "Xià Quán,"
I sigh deeply, my heart and liver pained.
Jīngmán is not my home;
why have I delayed here so long?
My boat is coupled, sailing up the Great River,
at sunset, my heart is filled with sorrow.
On the mountain ridges, there is lingering light,
but the rocky slopes are deepened with shadows.
Foxes and wild dogs race to their burrows;
birds fly circling to their old woods.
The flowing waves stir up clear sounds;
monkeys and apes wail along the banks.
A swift wind brushes my skirts and sleeves;
white dew wets my lapel.
Alone in the night, I cannot sleep;
gathering my clothes, I rise and play the qín.
The silk and tong-wood resonate with human feelings,
producing mournful notes for me.
My traveler's journey has no end;
my sorrowful thoughts are strong and hard to bear.
At Běimáng, how crowded are the mounds,
Large tombs number four or five.
I ask whose graves these are?
All say they are the Hàn lords of old.
Gòng and Wén gaze at each other from afar,
Yuánlíng is lush and fertile.
In the final ages, chaos and rebellion rose,
Thieves and bandits were like jackals and tigers.
They destroyed the earth more than a handful,
Opening the dark doors of the burial chambers.
The jade shroud left the jade body,
Precious treasures were seen by the looters.
The garden shrines turned to ruins,
Not a single wall of the surrounding enclosure remains.
Overgrown with thickets and thorns,
Paths are climbed by wood-gathering boys.
Foxes and rabbits burrow within,
Overgrown weeds are no longer swept.
The collapsed mounds are all plowed up,
Sprouts and shoots grow where farmers tend their plots.
Once they were lords of ten thousand chariots,
Now they are but soil of the hills.
Moved by those words of Yōngmén,
Pained and grieving for the ancient past.
The autumn wind breathes out the Shāng tone,
Soughing and sweeping through the front forest.
Sunny birds withdraw their harmonious sounds,
Cold cicadas have no remaining song.
White dew congeals at midnight,
Leaves fall and branches grow stark.
The vermilion light races to the northern lands,
The floating shadow suddenly sinks in the west.
I look around but see nothing,
Seeing only the shade of pines and cypresses.
Solemn and still are the high paulownia branches,
A lonely bird alights there, fluttering.
Looking up, I hear the cry of the departing wild goose,
Looking down, I hear the chirp of the cricket.
A grieving person is easily moved to sorrow,
Touching things only increases the heart's sadness.
The grave mounds grow distant day by day,
Lingering thoughts grow ever deeper.
Sorrow comes and turns my hair white,
Who says that grief can be endured?
Pacing to and fro against the long wind,
Tears fall and soak my robes.
Gradually winter and spring pass away,
Cold and heat suddenly flow and change.
You have returned to the Exhausted Springs,
Forever separated by layers of dark earth.
Who can fulfill my private wishes?
What is the benefit of lingering here?
Diligently I obey the court's command,
Turning my heart back to my initial service.
Looking at the house, I think of the person,
Entering the room, I recall where she had been.
Behind the curtain and screen, no resemblance remains,
But in brush and ink, there are traces left behind.
Her lingering fragrance has not yet faded,
Her remaining garment still hangs on the wall.
In a daze, as if she might still exist,
I wander about, anxious and startled.
Like those birds of the Hánlín forest,
Roosting as a pair, then one morning alone.
Like those fish swimming in the stream,
The Bìmù fish split mid-way.
The spring wind comes through the gaps,
Morning drips fall from the eaves.
When can I ever forget while resting?
Deep sorrow accumulates day by day.
I hope that it might one day diminish,
Yet I might still beat the basin like Zhuāng.
Bright is the moon in the window,
Shining on the southern end of my room.
The clear Shāng melody arrives with autumn,
Humid heat fades with the season.
A chilling cold wind rises,
I first realize my summer quilt is thin.
How can I say there is no heavy silk?
But with whom shall I share the year's cold?
There is no one to share the year's cold,
How hazy is the bright moon.
Tossing and turning, I look at the pillow and mat,
The long bamboo mat leaves the bed empty.
The empty bed is covered in fine dust,
The vacant room invites the sorrowful wind.
Only without the spirit of Lǐ Shì,
I cannot even faintly see your face.
Clutching my lapel, I sigh long,
Unaware that tears have soaked my breast.
Once they soak my breast, how can they stop?
Sorrowful thoughts arise from within.
Sleeping or waking, your form is before my eyes,
Your lingering voice is still in my ears.
Above, I am ashamed before Dōngmén Wú,
Below, I feel rebuked by Měng Zhuāngzǐ.
I compose a poem to express my will,
But this will is difficult to record in full.
It is fate—what can be done!
Constant grief only makes one base.
The sun moves the heavenly machine,
The four seasons take turns passing away.
Coldly the morning dew congeals,
Fiercely the evening wind blows.
Alas, mourning my virtuous wife,
Her form is forever hidden and obscured.
Thinking of this, it feels like yesterday,
Yet who knew a full year had already passed?
Changing robes to attend to court affairs,
My grieving heart is kept in private mourning.
Curtains and mats are set in the old room,
On the new and full moon, I attend your sacrifice.
How long can your sacrifices last?
New and full moons suddenly come to an end.
Once the quilts and clothes are removed,
They will not be brought out again for a thousand years.
Diligently the cycle of months is complete,
Sadly I pity you more and more.
Sorrowful thoughts are stirred by things,
Tears fall in response to my feelings.
I drive my carriage to climb the eastern hill,
Looking at the grave, my thoughts are knotted with pain.
Lingering among the ruins and tombs,
Wishing to leave but unable to bear it.
Lingering, unable to bear leaving,
I pace back and forth, hesitant.
Fallen leaves are piled by the tomb path,
Withered roots cling to the corners of the mound.
The lonely soul is all alone,
How can one know if the spirit exists or not?
Submitting my heart to obey the court's command,
I wipe away tears and force myself into the carriage.
Who says the imperial palace is far?
The road is short but grief remains in excess.
At dawn the moon rises over Yúnyáng,
At sunset I stop at Zhūfāng.
Filled with grief, I float on the broad river,
Shedding tears, I gaze at the continuous ridges.
Turning back, I think of the gentleman,
Deep pain knots within my bowels.
When the Way fails, indignation binds the heart,
When luck turns, one expresses sorrow and cold.
The spiritual bond seems always present,
His virtuous voice is never forgotten.
Passing away into the long distance is easy,
Pines and cypresses already stand in rows.
Like the Lord of Yánzhōu who kept his heart's promise,
Like the Old Man of Chǔ who cherished the orchid's fragrance.
What use is hanging the sword now?
Caressing the tomb, I only hurt myself in vain.
In life, I wondered about such a person,
Wisdom and blindness hindering each other.
Reason is moved by deep emotion's grief,
Surely it is not something knowledge can guide.
Fragility and brevity are truly pitiable,
Early death is especially unnatural.
Once following the transformation into nothingness,
What use is spreading a hollow name?
Raising my voice, my tears have already spilled,
A long sigh does not form a verse.
The virtue of Zhōu respected the bright sacrifices,
the way of Hàn honored the glorious spirits.
Sorrow and reverence flourished at the ancestral temple,
trees were planted and added to the garden tombs.
I served since the beginning of the auspicious mandate,
casting my footsteps upon the stairs of the royal court.
Attending as an escort, I received the Heavenly gaze;
at morning banquets, the Sagely emotions flowed.
Early on, I valued the duty of the self;
reaching success late, I treated life's warnings lightly.
When misfortune came, the King's bounty exhausted;
when prosperity departed, people showed signs of regret.
Disciplining myself, I feel ashamed of my accumulated simplicity,
yet again I join with the flourishing fortune.
Favors met not through gradual soaking,
but the meeting of glory lay in the reception.
At dawn, I managed the strict, pure regulations;
in the morning carriage, I guarded the Forbidden City.
Binding my sash, I entered the Xī Qǐn;
leaning on the carriage rail, I went out to the eastern outskirts.
Caps and robes end in the dark void;
the mausoleum towns turn lush and green.
Pine winds follow the road urgently;
mountain mists rise to cover the mounds.
The Imperial heart relied on accommodating all things,
the people's thoughts were covered by the sound of songs.
Ten thousand eras are recorded in strings and winds;
a thousand years are entrusted to the tasseled banners.
Not yet far from the era of the Emperors,
we are already like the sprouts of a sinking transformation.
A young bull is troubled by solitary uprightness;
in the late twilight, I decline secluded chastity.
Starting the journey, one loses the easy and level path;
returning the carriage, one is wary of steep tilts.
Thin silk curtains flutter on the Jǐng Gàn;
the jar of wine is as it was during life.
Lush are the trees of Xī Líng;
how could they hear the sound of songs and flutes?
Fragrant lapels are stained with tear tracks;
lingering affection is but a vain emotion.
The Jade Throne remains silent and desolate;
how much more so for this lowly concubine's body!
The ritual courtesies of life are severed;
I look upon the bulwark of the state.
One morning, the myriad transformations end;
yet there remains the feeling of my old friend.
Waiting for the time, one belongs to a rising fortune;
royal assistants wait for the heroes of the people.
Bound in joy for thirty years,
in life and death, a single friendship.
Hand in hand, we escaped the declining calamities;
following the light, we served the auspicious and bright.
When fortune was blocked, balanced words changed;
when times were prosperous, the Jade Stairs were level.
Jùn Chōng obtained a flourishing talent;
you, sir, encountered a wild scholar.
These people have their Jīng and Wèi;
it is not for me to distinguish the turbid from the clear.
About to part, I cannot bear to say goodbye;
I wish to use this to dispel the sorrow of parting.
The intent of a single morning that cannot be endured,
gives rise to ten thousand regrets for a thousand years.
It is over, the matters of a lifetime;
chants and songs fill the chests and boxes.
Also back to teasing each other,
always encountering an empty boat.
When shall I see Fàn Hóu again,
to once more recount our lifelong intentions?
How many days since I parted from you?
The journey has not yet lasted ten days.
Without seeing your vermilion face change,
I vainly think of the person I knew in life.
How could I know that on the day of peaceful songs,
it would be the morning you withdrew your zither?
It is over, why should I sigh?
I stop my pestle to mourn the loss of the state's balance.
Solemnly fly the luan-birds,
now flying, now going east.
My friend is said to be departing,
to go to his old country.
The boats flutter along,
heading up the Dà Jiāng.
Overgrown is the wild path;
at this time, there is no passage.
I am moved by my yearning,
shared by the gentleman.
Long is the road of the world;
chaos and separation bring many obstacles.
Crossing the Jì and Dài, traveling the river,
far away in different places.
Like wind-blown flow and scattered clouds,
once parted, it is like rain.
Life is truly difficult;
I wish not to be with it.
Gazing toward the distant road,
I truly stand on tiptoe waiting.
Fierce is the winter sun;
solemn is the chilling wind.
Hidden fish are in the abyss;
returning geese are in the porch of the sky.
If one were not a swan or eagle,
who could fly and soar?
Although I pursue my yearning,
my thoughts are not proclaimed.
Gazing toward the eastern road,
sorrow and distress increase my sighs.
Following that river flow,
you depart without a set time.
A gentleman is faithful to his oaths,
not changing with the times.
Being colleagues with you,
we are bound by life and death.
What shall I give as a parting gift?
I offer these poems.
My inner heart is greatly grieved;
tears flow in succession.
Alas, you gentleman,
how can I not think of you!
Heaven sent down death and disorder;
no state was not leveled.
I and my friend
came from that Jīng Shī.
Ancestral defenses were shaken and lost;
thus we fled and escaped.
We moved to Jīng Chǔ,
on the banks of the Zhāng River.
On the banks of the Zhāng River,
we were also able to live in peace.
In harmony like the chí and xūn flutes,
our virtues compared to the carriage and its wheel-aids.
Having measured ourselves by ritual and righteousness,
we finally attained laughter and conversation.
We hoped for these long days,
without any fault in our succession.
Although we say there was no fault,
time would not wait for me.
With the same heart, we separate for tasks;
thus there is departing and staying.
Crossing this Dà Jiāng,
you linger at that Nán Sì.
My thoughts cannot reach you;
I sit and then I rise.
Only that Nán Sì,
where the gentleman dwells.
Longing is my heart;
I quietly yearn for him.
People also have a saying:
not a day goes by without thinking of him.
How much more so for one so graceful,
how can one not be sorrowful?
The morning wind departs in the evening;
I entrust it with our meeting time.
Looking up at the Royal House,
I heave a long sigh.
The good man is outside;
who will assist the Heavenly officials?
The four states are currently obstructed;
you are sent to return to the frontier.
Your return to the frontier
will serve as a model for the lower states.
Do not say they are Mán or Yì;
do not be irreverent in your virtue.
Be careful of what you uphold;
follow the excellent rules.
Although the dragon is not used,
its will also has no error.
Distant and calm are the Dàn and Lǐ rivers;
lush is that Táng Lín.
Although we are in the same region,
it is distant and deep.
Bái Jū and Yuǎn Zhì
are what the ancients cautioned against.
Truly, you are a gentleman;
do not distance your heart.
Having gone and having come,
do not keep your news a secret.
The wild goose flies gracefully,
along the banks of the Jiāng.
A gentleman sets out on a journey,
to visit the Western Neighbor.
Coming to this great islet,
one thinks of Liáng and Mín.
Your journey is so far,
how could you not be diligent?
A gentleman respects the beginning,
be careful of whom you serve.
Your plans and words must be worthy,
like providing support through sound advice.
When the man of Yánlíng performed his duties,
he was in accord with Qiáo and Xì.
The traces left by former people
are the rules for coming generations.
Since you are careful of your master,
you must also be guided to know the subtle signs.
Probe the essence through the surface,
see what is manifest to know what is minute.
Be sharp of sight and keen of hearing,
let there be nothing you do not contemplate.
Dǒng Hè bore a great name,
why not take him as a teacher?
One cannot surpass the multitude,
do not overvalue my words.
Debate in the Wú Gōng
caused trouble between Qí and Chǔ.
Success has its essential point:
it lies in the joy of the multitude.
People have many taboos,
it is truly difficult to cover them all.
Look at that Hēishuǐ,
its flow is vast and surging.
The Jiāng and Hàn have their meanders,
surely peace and rest will come.
Whether the two states harmonize or not
will depend entirely on you.
Looking at that traveler far away,
few are able not to linger.
How noble is the gentleman,
different from other rivals.
Who among men is not diligent?
Do not deepen my sorrow.
I offer this poem as a gift,
daring to chant it while in the boat.
Formerly I followed the Yuánhòu,
preparing the carriage to go to the southern lands.
Passing through the capitals of Fēng and Pèi,
I soared and roamed together with you.
The four seasons push against each other,
in late winter the wind was cold.
Many guests gathered in the wide hall,
bright lamps shone with fiery light.
Clear songs produced marvelous sounds,
the myriad dances were in the central hall.
Golden vessels held sweet wine,
feathered cups were passed without limit.
Through the long night we forgot to return,
for a while making great merry.
Four stallions galloped toward the road,
sighs of joy were truly unending.
I was afflicted by a lingering illness,
taking refuge by the banks of the clear Zhāng.
From summer through the dark winter,
it lasted more than ten decades.
I often feared I would wander to Dàizōng,
and never see my old friend again.
How deep was your affection!
You walked here to comfort my person.
We had pure conversations day and night,
our glances expressed our sorrows and toils.
Then again came the words of parting,
your carriage returns to the Western Neighbor.
Pale leaves rise with the wind,
the wide road stirs up dust.
That which passes is like flowing water,
I grieve that we must now part.
I asked when we would meet again;
you promised it would be in the sunny spring.
My longing is a knot that cannot be untied,
I send you this new poem.
Strive to cultivate fine virtue,
facing north, you will be cherished.
Autumn days bring much sorrowful reflection,
I am moved to deep sighs.
All night I have no time for sleep,
expressing my thoughts with a moistened brush.
Bright lamps shine in the chamber,
the clear wind is chilly and cold.
White dew covers the front courtyard,
the gates are doubly barred.
The four seasons push against each other,
months and years are suddenly about to end.
A brave man goes far on a campaign,
military matters will be uniquely difficult.
Tears fall and soak my clothes,
how can I not cherish the one I love?
A cool wind blows the sand and gravel,
how white is the frosty air!
The bright moon shines on the red curtains,
flowery lamps scatter their fiery glow.
Composing poems, stanza after stanza,
in the deep night we knew not of returning.
The Lord has many grand thoughts,
his refined elegance flies in all directions.
This minor official is truly dull and slow,
how can I ever keep up?
Who says we are far apart?
Separated only by this Xīyè Yuán.
Constrained by the strict palace prohibitions,
there is no way to declare my inner feelings.
Thinking of you, my heart sinks,
I sigh long and cannot speak.
Rising and sitting out of order,
moving three or four times in a single day.
Walking out of the Běisì Mén,
I gaze toward the Xīyuàn Yuán.
Slender willows grow along the road,
the square pond contains a clear source.
Light leaves turn with the wind,
how the flying birds flutter!
One who is parted is easily moved,
tears fall and meet at the collar.
Looking up at the white sunlight,
bright and high it hangs.
It illuminates all within the eight directions,
without bias toward any creature.
I alone hold deep feelings,
and cannot be compared to them.
Drifting, drifting, the water flows east,
over the bright stones in the water.
Duckweed and pondweed grow on its banks,
how delicate and swaying are their blossoms!
Gather them to offer at the ancestral temple,
they can be served to fine guests.
Is it that there are no mallows in the garden?
Yet I admire these coming from the deep marshes.
Tall, tall stands the pine on the mountain,
soughing is the wind in the valley.
How powerful is the sound of the wind!
How sturdy are the branches of the pine!
While ice and frost are bleak and dismal,
throughout the year it remains upright.
Does it not encounter the freezing cold?
It is the inherent nature of the pine and cypress.
A phoenix alights on Nányuè,
lingering by the root of the Gūzhú.
In its heart there is something unsatisfied,
it spreads its wings to soar through the purple mist.
Does it not always work with diligence?
It is ashamed to be among the flock of sparrows.
When will it come to grace us?
It must wait for a sagely and brilliant ruler.
A sudden wind carries away the white sun,
which abruptly returns to the western mountains.
The round orb's light is not yet full,
the many stars are bright and numerous.
Men of ambition build the legacy of the age,
even the common folk are not idle.
For now, I take a night walk,
wandering between the Shuāngquè.
Wénchāng rises like dense clouds,
greeting the wind high in the heavens.
Spring pigeons cry on the flying eaves,
a swirling gale strikes the latticed windows.
I think of the scholar in his humble hut,
poverty and low station are truly piteous.
Wild greens do not fill his belly,
his leather and hemp clothes are incomplete.
Moved to a sorrowful heart,
I compose this piece.
Whom to blame for the discarded treasure?
Hèshì had his grievances.
Brushing off one's cap to wait for a soulmate,
who among soulmates would not be so?
