Climbing the wall, I overlook the clear pond.
A cool breeze gathers from afar,
My light lapels blow with the wind.
The divine garden shines with flowers and fruits,
The main thoroughfares are lined with tall catalpa trees.
Melon vines spread their long buds,
Ginger and taro are abundant in the broad plots.
Rice seedlings are solemnly lush,
How drooping are the millet sprouts!
Lacking in substance, I am of little use to the times,
My position is slight, and my name daily more humble.
Driven to serve as magistrate of two districts,
Administrative achievements have ultimately not been applied.
Since I left the capital's carriage,
Four years have passed until now.
My capacity is not of the stature for the court,
Frequent postings abroad are indeed appropriate.
In vain, I cherish the desire of the bird from Yuè,
Longing for the southern branches.
Springs and autumns pass in succession,
The four seasons are varied and pleasing.
Easily unstartled by favor or disgrace,
Yet longing for my roots makes my thoughts hard to bear.
When I arrived, the ice had not yet thawed,
Suddenly the seasonal heat is intense and blazing.
Moved by this, my return date is delayed,
Lamenting how the years speed away.
Climbing the wall to gaze at the outskirts,
My eyes roam over the court and temples.
A small state with few civil duties,
All day long, it is quiet with nothing to do.
White water splashes through the courtyard,
Green locust trees are planted flanking the gate.
Indeed beautiful, but it is not my land,
It only stirs my will to return home.
Anxiously I look back toward Gǒng and Luò,
Mountains and rivers are far and separated.
I wish to return to my old village,
But I fear the prohibitions of the official documents.
I merely respect the guardianship of the state,
And dwell reverently in my appointed post.
The South Mountain is lush and towering,
The Luò River is swift and rapid.
Green pines shade the long ridge,
Green artemisia covers the broad marsh.
In the morning sun, I follow the long road,
At evening, there is nowhere to rest.
Returning clouds float atop my carriage curtain,
Chilly winds find their way into the curtains.
On the road, I meet a man of deep knowledge,
He raises his hand and bows to me.
The world's troubles are not yet leveled,
Xiáo and Hán are currently dangerous and rugged.
Foxes and raccoon dogs flank both shafts of the cart,
Wolves and jackals stand in the middle of the road.
The soaring phoenix is entangled in a cage,
The fine steed is bound and tethered.
Of ritual vessels, I have heard in the past,
But in military affairs, I have never been trained.
Please stop your carriage for a while,
And wait slowly for the weapons to be stowed.
Seeking the world, I lack high credentials,
Pursuing the Way, I lack a fierce heart.
Quietly and uprightly, I received a solemn command,
Borrowing an oar to cross the river's deeps.
Relatives and friends see me off on my journey,
Shedding tears on the shady bank of the broad river.
Clutching my chest, we let go of hands,
A long sigh leaves a lingering sound.
Having no tracks, there is a place to hide,
In silence, the voice must sink away.
Gazing out, my eyes cannot reach,
Remote as if both were submerged.
Looking south, I weep at the dark islet,
Journeying north, I traverse the long forest.
The valley wind brushes the long thickets,
Dense clouds shade the high peaks.
Tirelessly, a solitary beast gallops,
Chirpingly, a longing bird sings.
Moved by things, I long for my home,
How deep is the sorrow of separation!
Standing still, I sigh with indignation,
Awake or asleep, tears fill my lapel.
I regret lacking the resolve to return,
Who knows the bitterness in my heart?
A traveler on a far-off official journey,
I entrust myself to the side of the Chénghuá Gate.
Grasping my sword, I follow the bronze carriage,
Shaking my hat-strings, I am fully reverent.
How easily the months and years pass!
Cold and heat have suddenly changed.
Carrying separation, I have much sorrow in my heart,
Moved by things, my feelings are pained.
Fervently, I leave behind peace and ease,
With long sighs, I give up my food.
Thinking of joy, joy is hard to entice,
Speaking of returning, I have not yet succeeded.
What can be done about this suffering?
It entwines within my breast and chest.
Looking up at the birds soaring to the heavens,
I envy your wings flying home.
Gathering the reins, I set out on the long road,
With sobs, I bid farewell to my close kin.
May I ask where you are going?
The net of the world entangles my body.
With long sighs, I follow the northern islet,
Lingering thoughts are tied to the southern ferry.
Walking on and on, I have gone far,
The wild paths are vast and empty of people.
Mountains and marshes are winding and sprawling,
The woods and thickets are dark and lush.
Tigers howl at the bottom of deep valleys,
Roosters crow at the tips of tall trees.
A mournful wind flows in the middle of the night,
A solitary beast passes before me.
Sorrowful feelings are moved by touching things,
Deep thoughts are gloomily entwined.
Standing still, I gaze toward my hometown,
Looking at my shadow, I feel pity for myself.
Traveling far, I cross mountains and rivers,
The mountains and rivers are long and wide.
I shake the whip to climb the high hills,
I check the reins to follow the level plains.
At evening I rest, embracing my shadow as I sleep;
In the morning I go, harboring my thoughts as I move on.
Halting my horse, I lean against the Sōng Yán,
Listening intently to the sound of the sorrowful wind.
Clear dew drops its pure radiance,
How brilliant the bright moon is!
Leaning against the table, I cannot sleep,
I shake my clothes and think long thoughts alone.
In the past, I enjoyed a favorable destiny,
Changing my tracks to enter the Chóng Xián.
Borrowing wings, I sang upon the branches for a male phoenix;
Washing my feet, I ascended to the abyss of the dragon.
Within a dark ceremonial cap, there is no ugly gentleman;
Elegant attire makes me look beautiful.
A light sword brushes against my sash-tassel,
A long hat-string is beautiful and fresh.
Who says the time of service is short?
My separation and toil have exceeded three years.
Briefly I respectfully attend to the later orders,
Changing my robes to serve as a vassal.
Setting out early, I seek the pure tracks;
Traveling far, I cross Liáng and Chén.
Moved by things, I have many distant thoughts;
Filled with passion, I cherish the people of old.
In my youth, I placed myself outside worldly affairs,
Entrusting my heart to the qín and books.
Wearing coarse hemp, I was happy and self-content;
Though often empty, I was always at peace.
When the time came, if it was suitable to meet,
I turned my reins to rest on the great thoroughfare.
I threw down my whip and ordered the morning journey,
Temporarily becoming distant from gardens and fields.
Far, far away, traveling in a lonely boat;
Endless and continuous, my thoughts of returning are tangled.
Has my journey not been long?
Climbing and descending for more than a thousand lǐ.
My eyes are weary of the different sights on the long road,
My heart longs for the dwelling in mountains and marshes.
Looking at the clouds, I feel ashamed before the high-flying birds;
Approaching the water, I feel embarrassed before the swimming fish.
True thoughts were originally in my bosom;
Who says I am constrained by physical traces?
For now, I rely on the transformations of nature,
In the end, I shall return to Bān Shēng’s hut.
Living in leisure for thirty years,
I eventually became obscure to worldly affairs.
Poetry and books strengthened my old loves,
Woods and gardens had no worldly sentiments.
How could I leave this place and go
Far away to Xī Jīng?
Knocking the oar under the new autumn moon,
By the stream, I part from my friends.
A cool wind rises as evening approaches,
The night scene is deep, empty, and bright.
Clear and bright, the heavens are wide;
Pure white and level is the surface of the river.
Mindful of my service, I have no time for sleep;
At midnight, I am still traveling alone.
Shāng songs are not my business;
My heart lingers on plowing together.
I shall cast off my cap and return to the old ruins,
Not for the glory of fine noble rank.
Nourishing my true self under a thatched roof,
I hope to distinguish myself through goodness.
My duty-report period is late summer,
Handling the oars, the season changes.
On the autumn banks, the evening shade is clear;
In the Huǒ Mín sky, the morning dew gathers.
For whom do I endure such hardship?
A traveler encountering the waning twilight.
Love is like Zhuāng thinking of the past;
Long-standing respect like Céng preserving old ties.
Why this heart that longs for its home soil?
Holding this to decline the distant journey.
Lǐ Mù was ashamed of his long sleeves;
Xì Kè was embarrassed by his limping gait.
A good time did not abandon me;
My ugly appearance did not become an evil.
I say I too am eccentric and detached;
Following the right way, I early had an admiration.
Born fortunately in a bright and peaceful age,
Personally receiving the care of the brilliant and talented.
In vain I am like the jade of the Zhào clan;
Uselessly I am like the gourd of King Wèi.
Since then, nearly twenty-four years have passed;
Only now do I get near the road home.
I will exhaust my tracks in mountains and seas,
Forever severing the realization of a joyful heart.
Since my hair was bound, I have cherished integrity,
Yet following things, I was eventually pushed and changed.
Going against my will seems like yesterday,
Twenty-four years have reached this year.
Black dye and grinding have faded my pure leisure;
Exhausted and weary, I am ashamed before the upright and firm.
Clumsiness and illness lean upon each other;
I finally obtain the convenience of being a quiet one.
Splitting the bamboo to guard the Cānghǎi;
Turning the sail to pass my old mountains.
Traveling through mountains, exhausting climbs and descents;
Wading through waters, following all the currents and eddies.
Crags are steep, ridges are layered;
Islets wind, shoals are continuous.
White clouds embrace the secluded rocks,
Green bamboo delights in the clear ripples.
I repair my house overlooking the winding river,
Building a pavilion on the foundation of the high peak.
Waving my hand, I bid farewell to my kinsmen,
Expecting to return after three years.
For now, I plant catalpa and walnut trees,
Do not let my lonely vow be in vain!
At night I cross the Yúpǔ pool;
At dawn I reach the Fùchūn city wall.
Dìng Shān is far away in the clouds and mist;
At Chì Tíng, I do not linger.
Going against the current, I encounter startling rapids;
Near the bank, I am hindered by jagged rocks.
I truly lack the composure of Bóhūn;
The danger exceeds the Lǚliáng gorge.
When one thing follows another, one should adapt;
Doubled mountains suggest the virtue of stopping and resting.
All my life I agreed with a secluded destiny,
But falling into hardship, I was exhausted by my weakness.
Long exposed to the requests of seeking office,
Only now is the promise of distant travel fulfilled.
My old heart is gradually expressed;
All the myriad things wither and fall together.
My heart is already clear and vast;
External things are but the hiding and emerging of dragons and cicadas.
A traveler's heart accumulates through autumn mornings;
Accumulated mornings unfold into distant views.
A lonely guest is grieved by the flowing torrent;
My companions suffer from the rushing rapids.
Stones are shallow where the water gurgles;
The sun sets as the mountains shine.
Desolate woods are thick and lush;
Sorrowful birds cry out to one another.
Encountering things, I lament my exile;
For the future, I have found the essential mystery.
Since I hold the heart of the Shànghuáng,
Why should I care for the scorn of this later age?
My eyes behold the rapids of Yán Zǐ;
My thoughts belong to Rèn Gōng’s fishing.
Who says the past and present are different?
Across different ages, we can be in the same harmony!
In Jiāngnán, I am weary of extensive sightseeing;
In Jiāngběi, I have lacked the chance to travel around.
My thoughts are tangled as the road turns far;
Seeking the unusual, the daylight does not linger.
Crossing the current, I head straight across the break;
A lonely islet looks lovely in the middle of the river.
Clouds and sun shine upon each other;
The sky and water together are clear and fresh.
Displaying divinity, yet no one appreciates the thing;
Harboring the truth, for whom shall it be passed on?
I imagine the appearance of Kūnlún Shān;
Far away are the ties of this worldly realm.
Now I begin to believe in the techniques of Ānqī;
One can live out the years of nourishing life.
Péng Xuān and Xuē Guāngdé only just knew the meaning of shame,
But Gòng Gōng had not yet abandoned his glory.
Perhaps they could excel over those driven by greed and competition,
But how could they be called masters of understanding life?
I, however, hold onto a slight noble aspiration,
Clumsy and slow, I decline superficial fame.
My cottage and garden shall be set among the crags,
A humble position replaces tilling the soil myself.
Looking at myself, though I am self-assured,
My mind and outward tracks are not yet aligned.
Lacking talent, I should not hinder Zhōu Rèn;
Ailing with illness, I resemble Sīmǎ Chángqīng.
Having completed marriages for my children like Shàng Zǐ,
I take a brief excursion like Bǐng Shēng.
Reverently following the intent of the ancients,
I pack my bags to return to my bramble gate.
My official service began in the Yuánxīng era,
My retirement took place in the Jǐngpíng era.
Having betrayed my heart for twenty years,
From now on, I cease the business of welcoming and seeing off.
Setting the oars, I hasten the date of return;
Following the banks, I race toward the distant fields.
Heading up the creek, finally wading through water;
Climbing the peaks, I begin my mountain journey.
The wilderness is vast, the sandy banks are clean;
The sky is high, the autumn moon is bright.
Resting on rocks, I scoop up flying spring water;
Climbing trees, I pick falling blossoms.
Having won the battle over desire, the lean man grows stout;
Stopping the reflection, the flowing water comes to rest.
This is the transformation of Fúxī and Táng Yáo;
I have attained the sound of the commoner's song!
White jade can still be polished,
But these words are easily stained black.
Though I hold the hexagram of Zhōngfú,
I am still troubled by the "Shell-patterned Brocade" poem.
If my inch of a heart is not understood,
My tiny life is as fragile as a thread.
The sun and moon cast down their light,
Granting me favor to continue until now.
Staying overnight near the capital outskirts,
In the morning, I pack and face the winds of Lǔ.
Once again passing through the place of life-long parting,
Once again saying farewell to friends and acquaintances.
My home mountains grow more distant by the day;
When will I ever return through these winds and waves?
A lonely sail traveling ten thousand lǐ—
Into the vastness, where will it eventually go?
My travels should go toward Luófú Mountain;
My rest must be destined for Lúshān and Huòshān.
Crossing the sea to reach the three immortal mountains,
Traveling the Xiāngjiāng and passing the Jiǔyí Mountains.
Admiring the sages as if from morning till evening;
Longing for the worthy also makes one mournful.
The bright and clear heart of the morning
Will not be deceived by the cold of the year.
The tune of "Picking Water Chestnuts" is easily hurried,
The song of "Jiāngnán" is not slow either.
The heart of the man of Chǔ was broken long ago;
The intestines of the guest from Yuè are severed today.
Though the reasons for the break are different,
Both are sincere in their thoughts of returning.
You accumulate thoughts of your home village;
I feel stifled and indignant remembering the mountains.
Seeking back to the time of resting and dwelling,
Lying down and giving way to wild abandon.
Finding one's nature is not an external quest;
From oneself, who else could compile it?
I do not complain that autumn evenings are long;
I always suffer because summer days are short.
Washing in the stream, I stir the floating rapids;
Resting in the shade, I lean against dense bamboo.
Cherishing the old makes new joys difficult;
Carrying sorrow, I forget the warmth of spring.
Mournful is the flute playing "Bright Moon";
Sad is the melody of "Guǎnglíng Sǎn".
Earnestly I plead with the high bridge of the zither;
With intense emotion, I command the hurried pipes!
The traveler is weary of sleeping on the water;
Wind and tides are difficult to describe fully.
Islands and shoals suddenly converge and part;
Banks and shores repeatedly crumble and rush.
Under the moon, I listen to the mournful gibbons;
Drenched in dew, the fragrant herbs are scented.
In late spring, the green fields are lush;
On high crags, white clouds gather.
A thousand thoughts collect day and night;
Ten thousand feelings fill morning and dusk.
Climbing cliffs to gaze at the Stone Mirror;
Pulling at leaves to enter the Pine Gate.
Many things of the Sānjiāng have passed;
The principles of the Jiǔpài exist in vain.
Hidden things are stingy with their rare wonders;
Extraordinary beings hide their refined spirits.
Golden elixirs extinguish their bright light;
Jasper stones are set in the flowing warmth.
In vain I compose a "Thousand Lǐ" song;
As the strings break, my thoughts become even more profound.
Nánzhōu truly possesses the Virtue of Fire;
Cinnamon trees brave the cold mountains.
Copper peaks reflect in the green streams;
Stone steps pour down red springs.
Having welcomed the guests who live in seclusion,
Also home to the worthy ones who have retired.
Dangerous paths are beyond measure;
The heavenly road is not a common path.
Thus I climb to the head of the various peaks,
Distant as if ascending into clouds and mist.
Feathered immortals are barely perceptible;
Dānqiū is but an empty fish-trap.
Maps and records have again been worn away;
Who has heard the traditions on the stone steles?
One cannot distinguish a hundred generations later;
How can one know a thousand years before?
For now, I shall express my intent of going alone;
Under the moon, I play with the murmuring water.
Always satisfying the needs of a brief moment;
Why worry about how things were in the past or future!
Changing clothes, I organize my followers;
Starting the journey, we are constrained by dangers.
Shaking the oars, we set out from Wúzhōu; spurring
horses over the mountains of Chǔ.
The path comes out through the outskirts of Liáng and Sòng;
The road goes through the lands of Zhōu and Zhèng.
Ahead, we climb the road to Yángchéng;
From dawn to dusk, we gaze at the Sānchuān.
In the past, the divine timing was interrupted;
Since the beginning, the distance from sages has been vast.
The Yī and Gǔ rivers have no ferries;
Palaces and halls lack even a foot of rafters.
Palace steps are full of nests and burrows;
From the city gates, clouds and smoke arise.
The King's Way ascends to the eight horizons;
Alas, this journey occurs in my later years.
A cold wind shakes the chilly wilderness;
Flying snow blurs the edge of the sky.
Facing the path, there is no time to guide the way;
Setting out wine, we are somber and speechless.
Pitying the sorrow of my followers and charioteers;
The horses are weary from the slow, difficult trek.
The traveling service leaves during the fragrant season;
Returning home, the time has often been delayed.
My mind, like tumbleweed, is already gone;
Flying and thin, it is truly so.
Distant and silent, the track of the road is long;
Haggard and worn by the toil of the campaign.
Formerly I went ahead of the departing army;
Now I come back after the returning troops.
Raising the whip, I look back at the eastern road;
Leaning over, I cannot keep up with the crowd.
Resting my followers as evening approaches;
Gazing far toward the borders of Liáng and Chén.
The old capital has many tall trees;
Over the empty city, cold clouds congeal.
Mounds and graves fill the outer city walls;
Inscriptions and records are worn away and wordless.
Wood and stone lock the dark gates;
Millet sprouts spread over the high tombs.
Think of that Yōngmén Zǐ,
And the sighs for Mèngcháng Jūn.
The foolish and the lowly are buried and forgotten alike;
Who among the noble and eminent is heard of alone?
Why remain a traveler for so long?
Sorrowful thoughts naturally become heavy.
The Jiāng and Hàn rivers divide the Chǔ region;
Héngshān and Wūshān settle the southern realm.
The three Xiāng rivers sink into Dòngtíng Lake;
The seven marshes are lush in Jīng and Mù.
Passing through paths, following old tracks;
Climbing the city walls to look at rivers and land.
The water country is surrounded by dangerous terrain;
Rivers and mountains are truly overlapping.
Looking back toward the Yúnmèng forest;
Looking forward toward the gardens of the Jīngtái.
Clear atmosphere clears over Yuèyáng;
Layered sunlight reaches the coves and inlets.
Mournful is the wind from afar;
Painful is the view from a thousand lǐ.
Throughout eternity, the coming and going are displayed;
For a hundred generations, the rise and fall have been wearying.
Who, in the end, are the living and the dead?
Brilliance and integrity lie in purity and goodness.
I beg to follow the people of high antiquity,
And return to plant mulberries and bamboo.
Last night I stayed in Nánlíng,
this morning I enter Lúzhōu.
A traveler treasures the days and months,
for the crashing waves cannot be stayed.
Braving the stars, I hasten on the early road,
throughout the day, I chase my former companions.
Scale-like clouds arise in the evening,
the whistling dawn wind grows fierce.
Soaring sand gathers into a thick yellow mist,
overturning waves toss the white gulls.
Climbing the prow, I gaze at the Huái region,
concealing tears, I look toward the Jīng stream.
As far as the eye can see are level plains,
where occasionally distant smoke floats.
Sudden sorrow sinks and then gathers again,
brief thoughts are heavier than many autumns.
Having never left my door or courtyard,
how could I travel a thousand lǐ?
Who made me lack the integrity of the ancients,
bequeathing me this sorrow of leaving my home?
The river road stretches long toward the southwest,
the returning current rushes to the northeast.
At the horizon, I recognize a returning boat,
amidst the clouds, I distinguish the river trees.
Traveler’s thoughts are weary and wavering,
a solitary journey has often been repeated before.
Having enjoyed the feeling of holding office,
I also harmonize with the charm of Cāngzhōu.
The clamor and dust are separated from here,
an appreciative heart is met at this place.
Though I lack the nature of the dark leopard,
I shall ultimately hide in the mist of Nánshān.
This mountain stretches for a hundred lǐ,
piling up to be level with the clouds.
Since the recluses have already entrusted themselves here,
the spiritual and strange all dwell within.
Above, it reaches the sky and obscures the white sun,
below, it connects to and girdles the winding creeks.
Intertwined vines are wild and spreading,
drooping branches are now high, then low.
A lone crane happens to cry at dawn,
a hungry flying squirrel wails this night.
Floating clouds are already vast and boundless,
much rain is also cold and dismal.
Although my journey is bound by official ribbons,
I can also seek out secluded paths.
Following the source, I have not yet reached the end,
the returning path is dark as if I were lost.
Wishing to pursue marvelous delights,
I now ascend these cinnabar stairs;
Imperial favor has ultimately come to an end,
this principle will hopefully not be at odds.
For this brief journey, I follow the order to report,
thinking of leisure, I wish to resign and return.
Returning to Qióng is like the rhapsodies and odes,
retiring to Rǔ is not about the carriages and riders.
Bà chí is hard to part with,
Yīchuán is difficult to leave again.
Reeds on the beach gradually sway,
rushes by the river are again lingering.
Field cranes call to each other from afar,
sand bustards suddenly fly in competition.
At the edge of the clouds, the mountains of Chǔ appear,
above the forest, the peaks of Wú are faint.
Attempting to look with my fellow travelers,
tears for home completely soak our robes.
I rely on this full goblet of wine,
to hold the scene and gaze at the fragrant flowers.
You ask me what I am toiling for?
To receive and look up to the pure brilliance.
With narrow ambitions, I slight carriages and crowns,
but with deep gratitude, I long for the palace gates.
In the prime of the year, there is wine in spring,
wearing my original clothes, I recline by the rustic gate.
From the banks of the Bà, I look toward Cháng’ān,
from Héyáng, I view the capital district.
The white sun beautifies the flying eaves,
unevenly arranged, they can all be seen.
Lingering clouds scatter to form silk,
the clear river is still as a bolt of white silk.
Noisy birds cover the spring islet,
various flowers fill the fragrant fields.
Leaving now, I shall linger long,
yearningly, I end the joyful feast.
Where is the beautiful rendezvous I mournfully seek?
Tears fall like drifting sleet.
Those with feelings know to yearn for home,
who can remain steadfast and unchanged?
In a bustle, I pack my evening bags,
solemnly, I prepare the traveling gear.
The morning star is just then lonely and sparse,
the dawn light is again vast and hazy.
Still moistened by the remaining dew drops,
I gradually see the morning clouds rise.
My hometown is already far and remote,
the mountains and rivers are long and wide.
Memorials and reports just now fill my front,
but I cherish the person and lack a heart for enjoyment.
Constraining my person, I am always apprehensive,
beholding favor, I only feel shaken.
I go on, weary of the long road,
with no way to unhitch my returning carriage.
Upholding duty, I reach Jiānghàn,
only then do I know the Chǔ border is long.
The southern pass winds around Tóngbǎi,
the western peak emerges from Lǔyáng.
On the cold outskirts, no shadow remains,
the autumn sun hangs with clear light.
A sorrowful wind shakes the heavy forest,
clouds and mist solemnize the river's rise.
The year draws to a close—how are you, my lord?
Falling tears soak my robes.
The jade bridge of the zither is covered in dew in vain,
the golden goblet sits containing frost.
Once I hear the music of "Bitter Cold,"
it makes the beautiful song even more sorrowful.
The mist on Yútán has not yet cleared,
the wind at Chìtíng has already risen.
Boat songs start in the middle of the stream,
the sounding drums echo through the layered barriers.
Village children suddenly gather together,
an old man of the wilds looks out from time to time.
Bizarre and strange are the unusual forms of the rocks,
towering and steep are the peculiar shapes of the peaks.
Dense and tall, the wild trees are level,
whistling and cold, the sands swell.
With hanging vines, the island is easy to climb,
with leaning cliffs, the islet is hard to approach.
Truly this is an eternal secluded dwelling,
how could it be merely a temporary clarity?
Whistling while seated was once assigned to me,
governing while reclining can now be admired.
From an early age, I loved distant ravines,
coming to office late, I see marvelous mountains.
Prominent peaks beyond the colorful rainbow,
ridges placed amidst the white clouds.
Slanting walls suddenly stand askew,
solitary summits are again lonely and round.
Flowing to the sea, the current is vast and boundless,
coming out of the mouth, the water is shallow and clear.
Wild crabapples have opened but not yet fallen,
mountain cherries are about to bloom like fire.
Forgetting to return, I belong with the Lán and Dù,
cherishing office, I entrust myself to the fragrant Quán.
Thoughtfully I gather the Sānxiù herbs,
lingering, I look toward the Jiǔxiān.
Thoughtfully I visit the travelers on the boat,
this river is truly to be treasured.
Thoroughly transparent regardless of depth,
bright as a mirror in winter or spring.
A thousand fathoms reflect the tall trees,
a hundred feet down, one sees the swimming fish.
Cānglàng is sometimes turbid,
the clear Jì dries up without a ford.
How can they compare to riding upon this,
looking down at the glistening stones?
Being separated from the clamor and dross,
why would I need to wash my robes and cap?
I wish to use this rippling water,
to moisten the dust on your hat strings.
There are hardships and joys in joining the army,
but I ask: whom are you following?
If the one you follow is divine and martial,
how could the troops be weary for long?
The Chancellor (*Xiànggōng*) campaigned to the west of the passes (*Guānyòu*),
his majestic anger shook the heavenly power.
With one strike he destroyed the *Xūnlǔ*,
with a second he subdued the *Qiāng* and *Yí*.
In the west he seized the bandits of the borderlands,
as effortlessly as picking up something dropped.
Rewards were piled higher than hills and mountains,
wine and meat surpassed the riverbanks.
The soldiers were satiated and wealthy,
men and horses were all overflowing with fat.
Those who went on foot returned with mounts,
they went out empty but came back with surplus wealth.
He expanded the territory by three thousand *lǐ*,
the round trip was as fast as flying.
With singing and dancing they entered *Yèchéng*,
all their wishes were fulfilled without fail.
All day spent in the great court,
at sunset one says they are returning home.
Outside, participating in the enlightened governance of the times;
inside, not neglecting one's private family matters.
Even birds and beasts fear becoming sacrificial victims,
while good sprouts have indeed been cast aside.
I cannot emulate *Jiǔ* and *Nì*,
following each other holding hoe and plow.
Who would read the Master's (*Fūzǐ*) poems,
and truly believe that what he said was wrong?
The cold wind sharpens the autumn season,
the Minister of Rites announces the detailed punishments.
Our lord sets out according to the season,
valiantly campaigning in the southeast.
Floating boats cover the long river,
arrayed troops blanket the marshy plains.
The campaigning soldiers long for their kin,
who can be without feelings of attachment?
Clutching my lapel, leaning against the mast,
with longing I think of *Yèchéng*.
Lamenting those people of *Dōngshān*,
sighing, I am moved by the crane's cry.
The sun and moon do not stay in one place,
what person can obtain constant peace?
Men of old followed *Gōngdàn*,
once they departed, it was always for three years.
Now our divine and martial army,
going briefly, will surely settle it quickly.
Setting aside the kindness of my kin and relations,
I give my strength and exhaust my loyalty and devotion.
Fearing I lack the use of even one man,
to repay my sincerity for receiving unearned pay.
Day and night I discipline my nature,
thinking of the departure like pulling a thread from a reel.
I shall hold the feathers of the first to climb,
how would I dare listen to the sound of the signal to retreat?
Joining the army to campaign on the distant road,
to punish those *Yí* of the southeast.
Coupled boats follow the wide river,
toward dusk, we have not yet rested on an islet.
The bright sun is halfway down the western mountains,
the mulberry and catalpa trees catch the remaining glow.
Crickets chirp along the banks,
a solitary bird flies gracefully.
The campaigning soldier's heart is full of thoughts,
the sorrow and grief make me sad.
Leaving the boat to climb the high embankment,
the dew on the grass soaks my clothes.
Turning back to lie on my bed to sleep,
to whom should I tell this sorrow?
My body is occupied with the affairs of shield and spear,
how can I think of private matters?
In military service there is the giving of one's life,
this principle must not be violated.
At dawn we depart from the bridge of *Yèdū*,
at dusk we cross the *Báimǎ* Ford.
Wandering leisurely upon the river dike,
looking left and right at our army.
Connected boats exceed ten thousand vessels,
armored soldiers are a thousand ten-thousands.
Leading them along that southeast road,
we will settle the merit of a single strike.
Strategies and plans are deployed in the command tent,
all directed by our Sage Lord.
I regret that I have no timely schemes,
like those officials who merely fill their posts.
Bowing respectfully within the main army,
I have no humble plans to present.
*Xǔ Lì* was a man of integrity,
his single word alone defeated *Qín*.
I have the burden of receiving unearned pay,
and truly feel ashamed before the man who "cut the sandalwood" (*Fátán*).
Though I lack the utility of a leaden knife,
I hope to exert my meager body.
Traveling long and far on the wild road,
slowly and steadily my heart grieves.
Looking in all directions, there is no smoke from fires,
only forests and hills are to be seen.
Brambles and thorns grow in the city walls,
the paths and trails offer no way through.
Reeds and rushes cover the wide marsh,
rushes and reeds line the long stream.
At evening the cool wind rises,
gracefully drifting my boat.
Cold cicadas chirp in the trees,
cranes and swans roam across the sky.
The traveler is full of grief and sorrow,
tears fall and cannot be stopped.
At dawn entering the borders of *Qiáojùn*,
expansively, my worries vanish.
The crowing of roosters reaches across the four borders,
millet and grain fill the plains and fields.
Hostels and houses fill the neighborhoods,
ladies and gentlemen crowd the village roads.
If it were not a land of Sages and Worthies,
who could enjoy such excellence?
The poets praised the happy land,
though a guest, I still wish to stay.
Reverently fearing the majestic precious mandate,
solemnly respecting the Imperial Ancestors.
Shining over the seas and manifesting at *Dài*,
descending from the lineage of *Táng* and the ancestry of *Chǔ*.
The spirit oversees the keen and refined,
the people belong to the keen and martial.
Suddenly receiving the widespread bestowals,
dwelling in the center and expanding the territory.
Spanning the earth, he is called Emperor,
exhausting the heavens, he acts as Lord.
From the moon-caverns guests arrive,
from the sun’s edge they offer their lands.
Opening the new era on the first day of the first month,
rituals are exchanged and music is performed.
The six departments coordinate their affairs,
the nine officials are arranged in order.
There are pure sacrificial beasts being cleansed,
there are pure offerings on the sacrificial platters.
Offerings are presented to the King’s heart,
to respond to the divine blessings.
The Sage offers sacrifices to the Emperor of Heaven,
the Filial Son offers sacrifices to his parents.
How magnificent and complete!
Affairs are held in the first month of spring.
Rituals are performed in the ancestral temple,
respect reaches the suburban sacrifices.
Golden branches are planted in the center,
grand music is displayed on all four sides.
Ascending to be paired in the capital,
descending virtue resides among the people.
Racing spirits illuminate the night,
high bonfires warm the dawn.
Yin and Ming float and sparkle,
deep sacrifices reach the sunken depths.
Announcing completion with the great report,
receiving blessings from the Primal Spirit.
The moon-charioteer keeps to the rhythm,
the stars race to support the wheels.
Arising from afar and driving from a distance,
shining brightly and moving valiantly.
Green, green, the grass by the riverbank,
long and continuous, my thoughts of the distant road.
The distant road is beyond my reach in thought,
but last night I saw him in a dream.
In the dream, he was by my side,
but suddenly I awoke in another land.
Another land, each in a different county,
tossing and turning, he cannot be seen.
The withered mulberry knows the wind from heaven,
the sea water knows the cold of heaven.
People enter their gates and each pleases their own,
who is willing to speak on another's behalf?
A traveler came from a far-off place,
and left me a pair of carp.
I called the boy to cook the carp,
inside there was a letter on a foot of white silk.
Kneeling long, I read the silk letter,
what was written in the letter after all?
Above, it said "Try to eat more,"
below, it said "I will always remember you."
The clear white moon shines bright,
its radiance illuminating my bed.
Worried and unable to sleep,
oh, how long and restless the night is!
A light breeze blows through the inner doors,
the silk curtains flutter on their own.
I gather my clothes and trail my long sash,
stepping into my shoes to descend from the high hall.
To the east or west, where shall I go?
Pacing back and forth in hesitation.
Spring birds turn and fly south,
fluttering and soaring alone.
With mournful voices they call for their mates,
their sorrowful cries wound my heart.
Moved by these things, I long for the one I love,
tears suddenly soak my clothes.
Standing still, I utter a loud chant,
releasing my indignation to appeal to the vast heavens.
Green, green are the mallows in the garden,
the morning dew waits for the sun to dry.
The bright spring spreads its virtuous grace;
all things grow in radiant splendor.
Always I fear the arrival of the autumn season,
when yellowed petals and stamens wither and fade.
A hundred rivers flow east to the sea;
when will they ever return to the west?
If one does not work hard in youth,
in old age one will only suffer sorrow.
Newly cut white silk from Qí,
pure and white as frost or snow.
Tailored into a "Joined-Joy" fan,
round and round like the bright moon.
Carried in and out of my lord's sleeves,
its movement generates a gentle breeze.
Always I fear the arrival of the autumn season,
when the cool wind displaces the summer heat.
Cast away and discarded in a bamboo box,
our affection cut short halfway through.
Facing wine, one should sing;
for how long does life last!
It is like the morning dew;
the days gone by are painfully many.
One should be vehement and resolute,
for sorrowful thoughts are hard to forget.
What can dispel my sorrow?
Only Dù Kāng.
Green is your collar,
long is my longing.
Only for your sake
have I been murmuring until now.
"Yōu yōu" cry the deer,
eating the artemisia in the wilds.
I have honored guests;
strike the zithers and blow the reed pipes.
Bright as the moon,
when can it be grasped?
Sorrow comes from within,
and it cannot be cut off.
Crossing the paths between fields,
you have gone out of your way to visit me.
We talk and feast after a long separation,
my heart remembers old kindnesses.
The moon is bright, the stars are few;
the crows and magpies fly south.
They circle the tree three times;
which branch can they rely on?
The mountain does not weary of height;
the sea does not weary of depth.
Zhōu Gōng spat out his food to receive guests;
the whole world turns its heart toward him.
Going north up the Tàiháng Shān,
how difficult and how towering it is!
Yángcháng Bǎn is winding and treacherous;
the cart wheels are broken by it.
How soughing are the trees,
the sound of the north wind is truly mournful.
Bears and grizzly bears squat facing me;
tigers and leopards howl on both sides of the road.
There are few people in the valleys;
how heavily the snow falls.
Stretching my neck, I sigh deeply;
on a long journey, there is much to miss.
How frustrated and depressed is my heart;
I long to return once to the east.
The water is deep and the bridges are gone;
midway, I am hesitating.
Confused, I have lost the old road;
at dusk, there is no place to lodge.
Traveling on and on, the days grow distant;
both man and horse are hungry.
Carrying bags, I go to gather firewood;
hacking ice, I make congee.
I grieve for that Dōng Shān poem;
its far-reaching thoughts make me mourn.
The autumn wind soughs and the weather turns cool;
the plants wither and fall, and dew becomes frost.
Flocks of swallows take their leave and geese fly south;
thinking of your travels as a guest makes my heart break.
Dissatisfied and longing to return, you love your hometown;
why do you linger and stay in a foreign land?
I, your humble concubine, am all alone guarding the empty room;
when sorrow comes, I think of you and dare not forget;
before I know it, tears soak my clothes.
I take up the qín and pluck the strings, playing the Qīng Shāng mode;
I chant a short song softly, unable to make it long.
The bright moon is brilliant, shining on my bed;
the Starry River flows west, and the night is not yet ended.
Qiānniú and Zhīnǚ gaze at each other from afar;
for what crime are you alone restricted by the Héliáng bridge.
Ascending the mountain to gather vetch,
at dusk I suffer from hunger.
The valleys are very windy;
frost and dew soak my clothes.
Wild pheasants crow in groups;
monkeys and apes chase each other.
Looking back toward my hometown,
how crowded and clustered are my gloomy thoughts.
High mountains have cliffs;
forest trees have branches.
Sorrow comes without a fixed direction;
no one knows of it.
Human life is like a temporary sojourn;
what is the use of so much sorrow?
If I am not happy now,
the years and months will gallop away.
The rushing river flows;
in it, there is a traveling boat.
Turning with the waves,
it is like a traveler's journey.
I whip my fine horse
and put on my light furs.
Driving and galloping along,
just to forget my sorrow.
Wine is set out in the high hall;
relatives and friends follow me in my travels.
The kitchen prepares a bountiful feast;
boiling sheep and slaughtering fat oxen.
How stirring is the Qín zither;
the Qí zither is harmonious and soft.
Yáng’ā music accompanies a marvelous dance;
from Jīng Luò come famous songs.
Happily drinking more than three cups,
we loosen our sashes and enjoy various delicacies.
The host offers a toast for a thousand-gold lifespan;
the guests offer a return toast for ten thousand years.
Old commitments must not be forgotten;
a poor ending is what righteousness reproaches.
Modest and humble is the virtue of a gentleman;
bowing like a lithophone, what does he seek?
A sudden wind blows the bright sun;
the light and shadows race toward the west.
The prime of life cannot come again;
a hundred years suddenly press upon me.
Born living in a magnificent house,
one eventually withers and returns to the hills.
Among the people of old, who did not die?
Knowing one’s fate, why then feel sorrow?
The beautiful lady is enchanting and poised,
gathering mulberry leaves at the fork in the road.
The tender branches are many and swaying;
how gracefully the leaves fall.
Rolling up her sleeves, her plain hands are seen;
her white wrists are adorned with gold rings.
On her head is a gold sparrow hairpin;
at her waist, she wears emerald jade.
Bright pearls cover her jade-like body;
coral is interspersed with precious gems.
How her silk clothes flutter;
her light skirts turn with the wind.
A glance from her leaves a radiant glow;
her long whistle has a fragrance like orchids.
Travelers stop their carriages because of her;
those resting forget to eat.
May I ask where the lady lives?
She is at the southern end of the city.
A blue building overlooks the main road;
high gates are secured with multiple latches.
Her appearance shines like the morning sun;
who does not admire her beautiful face?
What are the matchmakers doing?
Jade and silk gifts are not presented in time.
The beautiful lady admires high righteousness;
seeking a worthy man is truly difficult.
Why do the common people clamor so?
How could they know what she looks for?
Spending her prime years in her chamber,
in the middle of the night she rises and sighs deeply.
The white horse is adorned with a golden bridle,
Galloping swiftly toward the northwest.
May I ask whose son is this?
A roaming knight-errant from Yōu and Bìng.
He left his home village in his youth,
Spreading his fame to the desert's edge.
Always he holds a fine bow,
With arrows of bitterwood of varying lengths.
Drawing the string, he pierces the left target,
Releasing to the right, he destroys the Yuèzhī target.
Raising his hand, he catches a flying gibbon,
Leaning down, he hits the horse-hoof target.
His agility surpasses monkeys and apes,
His fierce prowess is like a leopard or dragon.
The border towns have many alarms,
The Hú barbarians frequently shift their positions.
Feathered dispatches arrive from the north,
He spurs his horse to climb the high embankments.
Driving far, he tramples the Xiōngnú,
Glancing left, he overawes the Xiānbēi.
Risking his life at the edge of blades,
How could he cherish his own existence?
He does not even care for his parents,
Much less mention his children and wife.
His name is recorded on the roster of heroes,
He cannot look back on private concerns.
Sacrificing his life for the nation's peril,
He views death as simply returning home.
Famous capitals abound with alluring women,
Jīngluò produces fine young men.
A precious sword is worth a thousand pieces of gold,
Their clothing is bright and fresh.
They hold cockfights on the eastern suburb road,
And race horses among the tall catalpa trees.
Before they have galloped half the way,
A pair of rabbits cross before me.
Reaching for his bow, he takes a whistling arrow,
Riding far up the Nánshān.
Drawing to the left then releasing to the right,
With one shot, both animals are struck together.
Before his remaining skill is fully displayed,
Raising his hand, he catches a flying kite.
All the spectators praise his excellence,
And the masters of craft acknowledge my beauty.
I return to feast at Pínglè,
Fine wine at ten thousand per peck.
Minced carp and stewed baby shrimp,
Cold turtle and roasted bear paws.
Calling to companions and whistling to peers,
They sit in rows along the long banquet mats.
In quick succession, they play ball and toss stones,
Their skill and agility take ten thousand forms.
The white sun gallops toward the southwest,
The passing light cannot be held back.
Like clouds dispersing, they return to the city,
To return again the next morning.
Wáng Míngjūn,
was originally Wáng Zhāojūn,
but her name was changed to avoid the taboo of Emperor Wéndì.
When the Xiōngnú were powerful,
they requested a marriage alliance with Hàn.
Emperor Yuándì took Zhāojūn, a daughter of a good family in the rear palace, to match with them.
Formerly, when the Princess was married to Wūsūn,
she was ordered to play the pípá on horseback
to soothe her thoughts of the journey.
When sending off Míngjūn,
it must have been the same;
when she composed new songs,
they were mostly sounds of sorrow and resentment,
thus they are recorded on paper.
I was originally a child of a Hàn house,
Now I must go to the Chányú's court.
Before the final farewell could end,
The vanguard already raised the banners.
Attendants and drivers shed streaming tears,
The carriage horses mourn and whinny.
Sorrow and gloom wound my internal organs,
Weeping tears soak my crimson chin-strap.
Traveling on and on, the days grow distant,
Until arriving at the Xiōngnú city.
They invited me into a yurt,
And gave me the title of Yánzhī.
A different kind is not where I find peace,
Though noble, it is not what I honor.
Seeing father and son being humiliated,
Facing it, I am ashamed and startled.
Taking one's own life is truly not easy,
So I silently live on for now.
Living on for now, what is there to enjoy?
Accumulated thoughts are always full of indignation.
I wish to borrow the wings of a flying wild goose,
To ride upon them and travel far.
The flying goose does not look back at me,
I stand still in anxiety and fear.
Formerly I was jade in a casket,
Now I am a flower upon dung.
Morning blossoms are not enough for joy,
I am content to be one with the autumn grass.
Pass this word to people of later generations,
Marrying far away makes it hard to bear one's feelings.
When thirsty, do not drink from Dàoquán water;
When hot, do not rest in the shade of a wicked tree.
Does the wicked tree not have branches?
A man of ambition has many bitter thoughts.
Preparing the carriage to respect the timely command,
Holding a staff, I shall seek far away.
Hungry, I eat at the fierce tiger's den,
Cold, I roost in the wild sparrow's woods.
As the sun sets, my merit is not yet built,
Time passes, and the year turns dark.
Towering clouds are startled by the shore,
Singing branches moan with the wind.
Thinking quietly at the bottom of a dark valley,
Chanting loudly at the peak of a high mountain.
Tense strings have no weak sounds,
Bright integrity is difficult to set to music.
Human life is truly not easy,
How can one say this heart is opened?
Cherishing my upright and unyielding heart,
Looking up and down, I feel ashamed before the past and present.
The Way of Heaven is level and simple,
The Way of Man is perilous and difficult.
Good and bad fortune follow upon each other,
Turning over like waves.
Disease and suffering are not far away,
Doubt and suspicion truly produce trouble.
Being near fire, one should naturally be hot,
Treading on ice, how could one dislike the cold?
Plucking the bees destroyed the Way of Heaven,
Picking up dust deluded Kǒng and Yán.
What more can an exiled official have?
Why sigh over an abandoned friend?
When blessings gather, there are always signs,
When disasters collect, it is not without cause.
Heavenly loss is not easy to decline,
Human gain is still something to rejoice in.
Why look far for a clear mirror?
Find it in the tilting of one's cap.
In intimate matters, one is pained by trusting oneself too much,
A gentleman guards against what has not yet happened.
How bitter it is, the man on a distant campaign,
Drifting and wandering to the four extremities.
To the south, climbing the peaks of Wǔlǐng,
To the north, guarding the bends of the Chángchéng.
Deep valleys are distant and bottomless,
Lofty mountains are dark and jagged.
Exerting arms to climb tall trees,
Shaking off tracks to cross the shifting sands.
The intense heat of summer is already miserable,
The cool winds of autumn are severe and harsh.
Summer branches gather fresh foliage,
Winter ice freezes the surging waves.
Hú horses are like gathered clouds,
Yuè banners are spread like stars.
Flying blades leave no shadow,
Whistling arrows echo each other.
At the morning meal, one does not remove the helmet,
For the evening rest, one always carries a halberd.
How bitter it is, the man on a distant campaign,
Patting his heart, how can he not be sorrowful!
Floating a boat by the islet of a clear stream,
Looking afar at the shade of a high mountain.
River and land take different paths,
I shall seek my dear kin from afar.
The three thorn trees rejoiced on the same trunk,
The four birds are saddened by being in different woods.
Joy in meeting is truly from of old,
Is mourning at parting only for today?
How long will one remain in this world?
As the sun sinks, the shadow does not stop.
The road ahead is already long,
The path behind is encroached upon by age.
Hurriedly, the evening light fades,
Diligently, few can restrain it.
Why do I return to this again?
It is because I harbor a bitter heart.
Distant integrity is entangled with worldly things lightly,
Can intimate feelings not be deep?
Go now, and preserve your good fortune,
When the sight of you ends, let it be followed by news.
I travel north to the city of Yōu Shuò,
where the chilly wilderness has many dangerous passes.
Looking down, I enter the depths of hollow valleys;
looking up, I climb the winding high mountains.
Solid ice freezes in the deep ravines,
and accumulated snow covers the long ridges.
Dark clouds rise from the sides of the crags,
and a mournful wind howls through the treetops.
I do not see the light of the white sun;
I only hear the clamor of cold birds.
Fierce tigers roar from the woods,
and black gibbons sigh by the cliffs.
At evening, I lodge beneath tall trees,
sorrowful and distressed, I have little joy.
Thirsty, I drink the liquid of hard ice;
hungry, I wait for a meal of fallen dew.
The longing of separation has surely lasted long,
and waking or sleeping, I have no one to talk to.
How arduous it is for the man on labor service,
discontented, he constantly suffers from the cold.
Spurring the horse, I climb Yīn Shān;
the mountain is high, and the horse will not go forward.
I go to ask the scout of Yīn Shān,
who says the fierce enemies are at Yān rán.
The war chariots' tracks never stop,
and banners and pennons frequently shift and move.
Looking up, I lean against crags of accumulated snow;
looking down, I cross rivers of solid ice.
Winter has come, but the autumn traveler has not returned;
I am far from home, a vast distance away.
The Xiǎn yǔn truly have not been pacified;
how can the campaigning soldier return in vain?
Those of lesser virtue compete to speak first,
but weapons of slaughter allow no two to survive.
If the army conquers, a meager reward is given;
if the army is lost, one's small life is sacrificed.
I shall follow the traces of Gān and Chén,
and achieve merit at the banner of the Chán yú.
Bringing the army back, I will toil for the returning soldiers,
receiving a title at the Gǎo jiē relay station.
At the gate, there is a guest with horse and carriage,
setting out, he says, from my old hometown.
Thinking of how you have not returned for long,
your tracks have soaked through as you crossed the Jiāng and Xiāng.
I throw back my sleeves and rush to the gate's path,
grabbing my clothes, not even pausing for my skirt.
Beating my breast, I hold the guest and weep;
wiping tears, we talk of health and well-being.
I ask about those in our home district,
and with sorrow, we discuss those living and dead.
Most kinsmen and friends have scattered and fallen,
and the elders have all withered and passed away.
The marketplace and court have changed places,
and the city gates and palaces are now mounds and wastes.
The days and months on the grave mounds increase,
and the pines and cypresses are lush and vast.
The Way of Heaven truly values rise and fall;
how can human life be long?
Moved by the memories of my whole life,
looking up and down, I am alone in my grief.
I order my carriage to climb Běi Shān,
standing long to gaze at the city walls.
How flourishing the market neighborhoods are,
and the streets and alleys are bustling and dense.
Grand mansions have lofty gates,
and inner chambers connect to towering pavilions.
How deep and clear the winding ponds are;
pure streams encircle flowery thickets.
Deep halls are lined with patterned windows,
and orchid rooms are joined with silk curtains.
Beautiful faces appear with grace,
and mournful sounds are made in response to their countenances.
Human life is truly a journey,
and beauty fades with the years.
Excellent are the gentlemen of wealthy families;
their ways of living are profound and broad.
Seeking ease consumes the spiritual root;
one cannot indulge in poisonous wine.
Do not use the resources of meat-eaters
to be mocked by those who eat mallows and pulse.
Yíng Qiū leans against the curve of the sea,
where the fertile fields are bright and level.
Great rivers control the Hé and Jì,
and high mountains enter the lofty dark sky.
To the east, it reaches the side of Gū and Yóu;
to the south, it borders the city of Liáo shè.
Sea products comprise ten thousand species,
and land products number a thousand names.
Mèng zhū swallows the Chǔ mèng,
and the "hundred-to-two" advantage equals the capital of Qín.
Only the Great Preceptor expanded the eastern borders,
and Lord Huán stabilized the decline of Zhōu.
The Way of Heaven has its successions;
the Way of Man has no lasting fullness.
How lowly was the sigh on Niú Shān;
it did not reach the feelings of the Perfect Man.
If the Shuǎng jiū have already passed away,
how could you, my friend, remain?
Going on and on, I shall depart again;
living forever is not what I seek.
At Yī and Luò, there are diverging paths;
the diverging paths are crowded with red-wheeled carriages.
Light canopies catch the flowery sunlight,
and galloping steps tread upon the flying dust.
Are those with tinkling jades merely simple scholars?
Those leaning on the carriage rails are all outstanding people.
Their fierce hearts are sharpened by the biting autumn;
their beautiful robes are fresh as the fragrant spring.
I was originally a weary traveler,
and among the heroic and talented, many are old kin.
Lowering the carriage canopy to receive fragrant news,
I know that if one wishes to cry out, it should be at dawn.
Keeping to the One is not enough to be proud of;
the diverging paths are truly worth following.
Following rules leaves no vast tracks;
how can measured steps catch up to others?
Once my feet are set on this course,
there is no need to follow the four seasons.
I shall follow a different track and path,
inviting you to join me at the same ferry.
Passing away are the suns that traverse the sky;
mournful are the rivers that gird the earth.
An inch of shadow never stops its dial;
a foot of wave does not return in vain.
Past years are faster than a swift arrow;
coming time is truly like a tight string.
Distant goals are seldom reached;
the full number of years is surely rare to complete.
Beauty fades from morning to night;
physical luster is abandoned as one sits.
If these things are truly hard to keep,
how could my life be extended?
In the blink of an eye, it will pass;
how long is that fleeting moment?
In my fervor, where can I lodge my plea?
The Way of Heaven is truly natural.
I only regret that my fame is thin,
with nothing to be proclaimed on bamboo and silk.
Before the year reaches its evening,
I sing a long song to pass my leisure.
A traveler wanders in the fragrant spring woods,
and the spring fragrance wounds the traveler's heart.
A gentle breeze sends forth clear sounds;
bright clouds cast a thin shade.
Orchid grass is rich with lovely scent;
seasonal birds have many fine songs.
Lightly fluttering are the wings of the calling doves;
chirping and singing are the orioles' cries.
Hidden orchids fill the entire valley;
their long stalks cover the high peaks.
The parasitic vine also has something to cling to;
the creeping kudzu also has its support.
How sorrowful is the traveling scholar;
how deep is his anxious thought!
His eyes are moved by the grass that follows the seasons;
his ears are saddened by the birds that sing of the time.
Waking or sleeping, he has many distant thoughts,
remote as if soaring or sinking.
I wish to rely on the sound of the returning wind,
to send a word to the one I admire.
Consort of Chǔ, please cease your sighing;
maiden of Qí, please stop your singing.
Let all in the four seats listen clearly
to my rendition of the Song of Wú.
The Song of Wú has its own origin;
let it begin from Chāng Mén.
How lofty and grand is Chāng Mén,
with soaring galleries spanning the flowing waves.
Tiered beams support the high roof;
winding balconies open toward the curved bank.
Dense and vast, the auspicious clouds cover it;
cool and refreshing, the propitious winds pass by.
The mountains and marshes store and nurture much;
the local customs are pure and fine.
Tài Bó initiated the benevolent influence;
Zhòng Yōng spread its ripples.
August was the Master of Yán Líng,
brilliantly shining upon the various Zhū Huá states.
When the royal traces declined in the time of calamity,
the imperial merit rose in the four distant reaches.
The Great Emperor Dà Huáng came from Fù Chūn;
raising his hand, he cast off the worldly net.
The talents of the state rose in response to the turn of fate,
as radiant as the blossoms of a spring forest.
All subordinate cities possess scholars,
but the city of Wú has the most.
The Eight Clans are not even worth boasting of,
for the Four Surnames are truly the eminent houses.
Their civil virtue is brilliant, pure, and admirable;
their military achievements equal the mountains and rivers.
How dignified are the rituals and deference;
the civilizing influence flows like a torrential rain.
Such goodness and beauty are hard to record in full;
I offer this song as a brief assessment.
Setting out wine in the high hall,
singing a sad song before the goblets.
How long is a person’s life?
It passes like the morning frost.
Time never comes a second time;
flowers do not bloom twice in the sun.
Duckweed relies on the spring radiance;
orchids rely on the autumn fragrance.
The days to come are bitterly short;
the days gone by are bitterly long.
If I do not enjoy myself now,
the crickets will soon be in the room.
Joy arises from the gathering;
sorrow is the mark of parting.
How can I say I have no feelings?
My worries are forgotten because of you.
My wine is already delicious;
my meats are already fine.
This short song has its chant;
let the long night not be wasted in idleness.
Some call this the Beautiful Song of Luó Fū.
The Fú Sāng tree rises with the morning radiance,
shining upon the edge of this high terrace.
On the high terrace are many bewitching beauties;
from deep chambers come pure countenances.
Their fair looks outshine the bright sun;
their wise hearts are pure and serene.
Beautiful eyes radiate a jade-like luster;
moth-eyebrows resemble kingfisher feathers.
How moist and fresh is their skin;
their exquisite beauty seems almost edible.
Graceful and elegant in their many postures,
charming and seductive in their clever smiles and speech.
In late spring, the spring garments are completed,
radiant with fine silks and gauzes.
Golden phoenix hairpins dangle ornate tips;
jade pendants are strung with precious gems.
Side by side, their carriages stir up the clear dust;
they wash their feet in the ripples of the Luò Shuǐ.
Dense as the meeting of wind and clouds,
how numerous are the beautiful ladies!
The southern cliffs are filled with silk curtains;
the northern islets are crowded with screened carriages.
The clear stream holds the reflected scenery;
the high cliffs are covered in floral red.
Fragrant, fragrant, their scented sleeves wave;
cool and crisp, their slender fingers pluck the strings.
Sad songs pour forth clear sounds;
elegant dances broadcast the Secluded Orchid.
Vermilion lips contain the spirit of the nine autumns;
their beautiful steps surpass the Seven Disks.
Moving to the music as swiftly as a startled swan;
treading the rhythm like a gathering of phoenixes.
Their fine expressions change with their faces;
their profound grace has an inexhaustible source.
Bending and rising in a flurry of elegance;
every glance and step is delightful.
Lingering fragrance gathers in the flying whirlwind;
floating light reflects in the clear rapids.
A seductive appearance is not enough to praise;
a spring outing is truly worthy of a sigh.
Roaming immortals gather the divine race;
a grand assembly at the slope of Céng Chéng.
The long wind rises for ten thousand miles;
auspicious clouds are dense and towering.
Mì Fēi rises from the Luò Pǔ banks;
Wáng and Hán emerge from Tài Huá.
To the north, they summon the maiden of Yáo Tái;
to the south, they invite the maidens of the Xiāng River.
Solemnly, the night chariots set out;
lightly, the kingfisher canopies are arrayed.
Feathered banners perch jade phoenixes;
jade crossbars chime in harmony.
Tài Róng plucks the high strings;
Hóng Yá sends forth clear songs.
When the toasting is completed,
they rise lightly, riding the purple clouds.
Gathering the reins at the branches of Fú Sāng;
washing their feet in the waves of Tāng Gǔ.
Clear radiance overflows the Gates of Heaven,
bestowing blessings upon the Imperial House.
The Jiāng Lí grows on the secluded islet;
its faint fragrance is not enough to be known.
Favored by the meeting of wind and clouds,
it was moved to the side of a flowery pond.
It displayed its beauty beneath the Jade Terrace;
it cast its shadow in the Cāng Láng spring.
Having already been soaked in rich moisture,
its roots are deep and firm.
The four seasons pass and do not stay;
many flowers find it hard to stay fresh for long.
The fair spirit perishes with the season;
the remaining fragrance is abandoned to the wind.
The Way of Heaven has its changes;
human affairs are never permanently whole.
A man's favor shifts with his wisdom and folly;
a woman's love fades to avoid the loss of beauty.
I do not begrudge the withdrawal of my humble person,
but I only fear the "bluebottles" coming forward.
I wish you would broaden your remaining light
to shine upon me in my twilight years.
The Liù Yǐn slow the clear singing;
the Sān Diào wait for the complex notes.
The arrayed banquet is all quiet and still;
everyone together listens to the Huì Yín.
The Huì Yín has its own beginning;
let it start from the spread of Wén Mìng's work.
He began his achievements at Hú and Jì,
clearing the woods to the banks of the Jiāng and Sì.
The constellations brighten the celestial patterns;
bordering the sea lies the terrestrial geography.
Linked peaks compete in their thousand-fathom heights;
back-to-back streams each flow for a hundred miles.
The flowing ponds irrigate the nonglutinous rice;
light clouds shroud the pines and wolfberries.
The Two Capitals Liǎng Jīng should feel ashamed of this beauty;
how could the Three Capitals Sān Dū ever be like this?
Tiered terraces point toward the middle of the sky;
high walls are built of many layers.
Flying swallows leap over the broad paths;
boats with heron-head prows play on the clear islets.
They freely display their graceful forms;
the roads are brightened by charming youngsters.
From the past through many generations,
the worthy and accomplished cannot all be recorded.
Gōu Jiàn was good at managing rise and fall;
the Yuè Sǒu understood when to act and when to stop.
Fàn Lǐ went out into the rivers and lakes;
Méi Fú entered the city markets.
Dōng Fāng sought leisure in travel;
Liáng Hóng left his home village.
I have linked together these writings on local customs;
my words are exhausted, but my thoughts have not ended.
Host, please do not be noisy;
let this humble person sing a few words:
I was originally a scholar from a cold village,
but I went out to serve, favored by Hàn grace.
At first, I followed Zhāng Xiào Wèi,
recruited to go to the source of the river.
Later, I followed Lǐ Qīng Chē,
pursuing the captives to the end of the frontier walls.
The secret paths stretched for ten thousand miles;
in a year of peace, there were still seven rushes.
My muscle and strength were exhausted on the saddle and armor;
my mind and thoughts experienced cold and warmth.
Since the general has passed away,
his subordinates are also rarely seen.
Worldly affairs changed in a single morning;
who will again discuss my solitary deeds?
I left home in my youth and prime;
in poor old age, I return through the door.
With a sickle at my waist, I reap mallow and pulse;
leaning on a staff, I tend to chickens and piglets.
Once like a hawk upon a gauntlet,
now like a monkey within a cage.
I only harbor a thousand years of regret,
and carry a hundred years of bitterness in vain.
Leaving the mat, I think of your tent,
the weary horse yearns for your carriage.
I wish to receive the grace of the Jìn Lord,
and not be ashamed before the soul of Tián Zǐ.
Feathered dispatches rise from the border posts,
beacon fires enter Xiányáng.
Conscripted cavalry station at Guǎngwǔ,
divided troops go to rescue Shuòfāng.
In the harsh autumn, bowstrings and bamboo are strong,
the enemy ranks are elite and powerful.
The Son of Heaven grips his sword in anger,
envoys gaze at each other from afar.
In goose formation, they follow the stone paths,
in fish file, they cross the flying bridges.
Flutes and drums pour forth thoughts of Hàn,
banners and armor are covered in Hú frost.
Swift winds rise, rushing against the pass,
sand and pebbles fly of their own accord.
Horse hair bristles like a hedgehog's,
horn bows cannot be drawn.
In times of peril, a minister's integrity is seen,
in an age of chaos, the loyal and good are recognized.
I cast my body to repay the brilliant lord,
even in death, I will be a martyr for the state.
A piebald horse with a golden bridle,
a brocade belt bearing a Wú blade.
Losing one's way amidst cups of wine,
naked blades rise in mutual enmity.
Once the pursuing soldiers arrive,
carrying a sword, I travel far away.
Thirty years since leaving my hometown,
once again, I return to my old hills.
Climbing high to overlook the four passes,
looking inside and out toward Huángzhōu.
The nine roads are as level as water,
the double gate-towers seem to float on clouds.
Flanking the palace are ranked generals and ministers,
along the roads stand princes and marquises.
At midday, the markets and courts are full,
carriages and horses flow like a river.
Striking bells and setting out feasts in tripods,
side-by-side carriages seek one another.
Now, what am I doing alone?
Despondent, harboring a hundred sorrows.
A wounded bird dreads the sound of the string,
a weary traveler dreads the sound of parting.
The sound of parting breaks the traveler's heart,
guests and attendants all shed tears.
Tears fall, and the heart is shattered,
about to leave, then returning to say farewell again.
Even for a moment, we do not know each other,
how much more so when parting for a distant land.
Far, far away, the traveler's carriage goes,
deep and dim, the setting sun grows late.
Those who stay close their doors and sleep,
the traveler eats his meal in the middle of the night.
Wild winds blow through the autumn trees,
the traveler's heart and soul are broken.
Eating plums, one always suffers from sourness,
wearing kudzu cloth, one always suffers from cold.
Strings and flutes fill the seats in vain,
the sorrowful man does not show a smile.
I wish to console myself with a long song,
but it only gives rise to more ends of long regret.
Chìbǎn stretches across the western barrier,
Huǒshān blazes with southern might.
The body is hot and the head aches,
birds fall, and the soul returns home.
Hot springs erupt from cloudy pools,
scorching smoke rises from rocky shores.
Sun and moon are constantly dimmed,
rain and dew have never dried.
Cinnabar snakes exceed a hundred feet,
dark bees are ten spans in girth.
Holding sand to shoot at shadows,
blowing poison, hurting the traveler's light.
Miasmic vapors steam the body by day,
mang-grass dew soaks the clothes by night.
Hungry apes do not come down to eat,
morning birds do not dare to fly.
In the poisonous Jīng River, many still die,
crossing the Lú River, how could one remain unharmed?
A living body treads on ground of death,
a flourishing will climbs upon the mechanism of disaster.
The glory of the Gēchuán warships is thin,
the rewards for General Fúbō are also slight.
Even if the wealth is small, the lord still begrudges it,
how then can scholars be expected?
Straight as a vermilion silk string,
clear as ice in a jade pot.
Why be ashamed of my past intentions?
Suspicion and resentment follow one after another.
Human nature scorns old kindness,
public opinion follows rise and fall.
Once there is a flaw as small as a hair,
it becomes as insurmountable as a mountain.
Those who eat the sprouts are truly giant rats,
those who stain the white are truly blue flies.
Wild ducks and swans are beautiful from afar,
firewood and hay are trampled upon before one's eyes.
Shēn was dismissed while Bāo was brought in,
Bān left while Zhào Jī rose.
The Zhōu King daily sank into delusion,
the Hàn Emperor sighed and praised more and more.
Appreciation from the heart is still hard to rely on,
respectful appearances are hardly easy to trust.
It has been thus since ancient times,
you are not the only one to beat your breast.
The smartweed insect avoids mallows and violets,
accustomed to bitterness, it does not say it is wrong.
Small men are naturally petty,
how could they know the heart of a broad-minded scholar?
Roosters crow within Luòchéng,
the forbidden gates open at dawn.
Caps and canopies arrive from all directions,
carriages and riders come from the four quarters.
Plain belts trail in the long wind,
splendid tassels gather the distant dust.
At midday, how can they stop?
Even when the bells chime, they have yet to return.
A peaceful age cannot be encountered,
a virtuous lord truly loves talent.
His brilliant insight is decided by Heaven,
he is not subject to external suspicions.
With one word, he distributes jade batons and noble ranks,
with a single merit, one leaves the weeds and wilds.
It is not merely the gift of white jade,
he is about to build the Huángjīn Tái.
Now what ailment do you have,
that you alone hesitate and linger by the road?
My family has resided in Guānfǔ for generations,
with high sashes, we served as officials in the royal city.
I have heard fully of the deeds of ten emperors,
and know the intricate details of the two capitals.
I am weary of seeing the rise and fall of things,
having often witnessed the world's troubles and peace.
It flutters and flips like the turning of a palm,
ephemeral like the morning glory.
At the end of the road, I regret my short-sighted plans,
in my late years, my will values long life.
Following a master into the distant peaks,
making friends to serve the immortals and spirits.
The Wǔtú reveal golden records,
the Jiǔyuè hide the Dānjīng.
Dining on wind and entrusting my sleep to the pines,
sleeping on clouds, wandering as I please under heaven.
Crowning with rosy clouds, I ascend the colorful pavilion,
unfastening my jade, I drink in the Jiāotíng.
A brief journey traverses ten thousand miles,
a short parting lasts several thousand years.
From the Fèngtái, no carriage returns,
only the sounds of flutes and pipes remain.
When shall I, like you all,
peck at rot and swallow the stench together?
Jiāngnán is a place of beauty,
Jīnlíng is the capital of emperors.
Winding paths are girdled by green waters,
distant and tall, vermilion towers rise.
Flying eaves flank the imperial road,
weeping willows shade the royal moat.
Resonant pipes flank the high carriage canopies,
repeating drums escort the splendid chariots.
Submitting memorials to the Yúntái,
fame and merit can truly be achieved.
In life, one wanders the capital,
in death, one is abandoned in the middle of the wilds.
In the morning, setting out from the high hall,
in the evening, lodging beneath the Huángquán.
The bright sun enters the Yúyuān,
the carriage is hung up, the four horses rest.
Though Creation is divine and brilliant,
how can it preserve me forever?
My appearance gradually fades and perishes,
teeth and hair are about to fall out.
Since ancient times, it has always been so,
who can escape this?
Divining and choosing to find an auspicious omen,
the excellent decree all resides here.
Starting early, startling the attendants and drivers,
tying the reins, pausing at the heavy foundation.
The dragon-shroud covers the large funeral carriage,
the vanguard raises light banners.
How noisy is the funeral hall!
Mournful sounds boil within the inner chambers.
Inner chambers, please do not be clamorous;
listen to my “Xiè Lù Shī.”
Life and death follow different principles,
the departure sacrifice must have its time.
Setting down the wine cups between the two pillars,
opening the funeral hall, the spirit-hearse advances.
At the farewell drink, the goblet is not raised;
setting out to stay, with no date for return.
Curtains and mats are empty of the shadow left behind;
the pillars and eaves bid you farewell.
Close relatives all rush together,
friends come from afar.
Swiftly fly the light carriages,
galloping, they whip the white steeds.
Holding the reins, following the long thicket,
sending you to the Terrace of Eternal Night.
I call you, but you do not hear;
I weep for you, but you do not know.
Sighing beside the heavy coffin,
thinking of our days in the past.
Three autumns can still be gathered;
how can ten thousand generations be contemplated?
Following in death, the body is easily lost;
to save you is not within my power.
Holding back words, the speech is choked;
brushing away tears, the tears flow and scatter.
How towering are the layered mounds!
The dark dwelling is hidden among them.
Spreading out, it stands at the four extremities,
arched high like the vast blue heavens.
Listening closely to the gushing of the hidden conduits,
lying down to view the suspended celestial well.
How vast and empty is the wide sky!
How can the Great Night ever see morning?
When people go, there are years of return;
but for this journey, there is no year of return.
Formerly dwelling in the houses of the four peoples,
now entrusting oneself as a neighbor to ten thousand ghosts.
Formerly a body of seven feet,
now turned to ash and dust.
Gold and jade were what you once wore;
now even a goose feather cannot be lifted.
Plump flesh feasts the mole crickets and ants;
beautiful features are forever extinguished.
The longevity hall invites demons and spirits;
in nothingness, they treat each other as guests.
Mole crickets and ants, what grudge do I have against you?
Demons and spirits, what kinship do I have with you?
Beating my breast, I ache with bitter poison;
long sighs cannot express it all.
Wandering thoughts of relatives and friends,
melancholy, the spirit is not at ease.
White horses wait by the funeral carriage,
dark steeds race with the flying canopy.
Mournful cries arise from the funeral hall,
lingering sadly in the wilds.
The soul-carriage is silent without a sound;
one only sees the cap and the belt.
The funerary objects resemble those of life;
for whom does the long banner flutter?
A sad wind marks the wheel tracks,
slanting clouds form drifting mists.
Raising the whip, pointing toward Líng Qiū,
the carriage departs from here forever.
How vast the wild grass!
The white poplars also rustle in the wind.
Bitter frost in the middle of the ninth month,
sending me out to the distant suburbs.
No one lives on any side;
high mounds are truly steep.
Horses neigh toward the sky,
the wind is desolate of its own accord.
Once the dark chamber is closed,
for a thousand years, it will never see morning.
For a thousand years, it will never see morning;
even the wise and reaching can do nothing.
Those who just now came to see me off
have each already returned to their homes.
Relatives may have some lingering grief;
but others have already begun to sing.
What is there to say of dying?
Entrusting the body to be one with the mountain slope.
Yàn Tàizǐ Dān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the Qín Wáng,
Dān performed the departure sacrifice and saw him off by the Yì Shuǐ.
Gāo Jiànlí struck the zhù,
Jīng Kē sang,
Sòng Rúyì joined in harmony,
saying:
The wind soughs, the Yì Shuǐ is cold!
The brave warrior goes away and shall never return!
Gāozǔ returned,
passing through Pèi,
he stayed. He set out wine in the Pèi Gōng,
summoning all his old friends, elders, and youths to assist with the wine.
He selected one hundred and twenty children of Pèi
and taught them to sing.
When the drinking was at its height,
the Emperor struck the zhù and sang himself, saying:
A great wind rises, the clouds fly and spread!
Might is felt within the seas, I return to my old home!
How can I find brave warriors to guard the four directions!
In the morning, I depart from the Guǎngmò Mén,
at evening, I lodge at Dānshuǐ Shān.
My left hand draws the Fánruò bow,
my right hand wields the Lóngyuān sword.
I look back toward the palace towers,
looking up and down, I drive the flying carriage.
Leaning on the saddle, I give a long sigh;
tears fall like a flowing spring.
Tying the horse beneath a tall pine,
removing the saddle at the peak of a high mountain.
A fierce and mournful wind rises,
chilly and clear, the mountain stream flows.
I wave my hand in long farewell,
choked with sobs, I cannot speak.
Floating clouds gather for me;
returning birds circle for me.
Having left home, the days grow distant;
how can one know of survival or death?
Resolute and impassioned in the deep forest,
I clasp my knees, alone and broken-hearted.
Elks and deer roam before me,
apes and monkeys play by my side.
Provisions and grain are already exhausted;
how can ferns and vetch be enough to eat?
Gathering the reins, I call to my companions,
chanting and whistling among the sheer cliffs.
The path of the gentleman is diminished;
the Master indeed faced extremity.
Thinking of Lǐ Qiānqī in the past,
marooned in the court of the Xiōngnú.
Loyalty and trustworthiness instead brought guilt;
