Hàn Wǔ was not clear-sighted.
I wish to finish this song,
this song is mournful and long.
Put it aside and do not speak of it again;
to speak of it again makes the heart grieve.
Rú Jī in the sleeping chamber,
Bān Jié sitting in the same carriage.
Hóng Bō accompanied in the drinking tent,
Lín Guāng feasted on the remains of Qín.
At the year's end, the cold gale arrives,
autumn waters drop the lotus blossoms.
Zǐxiá feigned the King's carriage,
Ānlíng wept over the first fish.
Your humble servant's time is finished,
where will the gentleman go!
Traveling on and on, then on and on again,
parting from you while still alive.
Separated by more than ten thousand lǐ,
each at a different edge of the sky.
The road is obstructed and long;
how can we know when we shall meet? Hú horses lean into the north wind,
Yuè birds nest on southern branches.
Since our parting, the days grow distant;
my robes and belt grow looser every day.
Floating clouds obscure the bright sun;
the traveler does not think of returning.
Longing for you makes one grow old;
years and months have suddenly grown late.
Cast it aside, speak of it no more;
strive to eat more food.
Green, green is the grass by the riverbank,
lush, lush are the willows in the garden.
Lovely, lovely is the lady upstairs,
bright and radiant, she stands by the window.
Beautifully, beautifully she is powdered and rouged,
slenderly, slenderly she extends a white hand.
Formerly a singing girl,
now the wife of a wandering man.
The wandering man has gone and does not return;
it is hard to keep a lonely bed alone.
Green, green the cypress on the mound,
Piled high, the rocks within the stream.
Man's life between heaven and earth
Is fleeting, like a traveler from afar.
With a measure of wine let us enjoy one another,
To be generous, not meager.
Drive the carriage, whip the slow horse,
Wandering for pleasure in Wǎn and Luò.
How bustling it is within Luò,
Where caps and sashes seek one another.
Long thoroughfares are lined with side alleys,
Where princes and nobles have many mansions.
The two palaces face each other from afar,
The double towers rise over a hundred feet.
Feasting to the full to gladden the heart,
Why should one be pressed by sorrow?
Today is a fine banquet,
The joy and delight are hard to fully describe.
Plucking the zither, sending forth elegant sounds,
New melodies so wonderful they reach the divine.
Those of high virtue voice noble words,
Those who know music listen to the truth.
With one heart we share the same wish,
Yet the meanings held within are not fully expressed.
Man's life is lodged in a single generation,
Passing swiftly like a whirlwind of dust.
Why not whip the fleet-footed steed
And be the first to occupy the essential roads and fords?
Do not remain in poverty and low station,
Enduring long hardships and frustrations.
In the northwest there is a high tower,
Reaching up to level with the floating clouds.
Lattice windows are hung with silken curtains,
The terraced pavilion has three tiers of stairs.
From above comes the sound of singing to strings,
How sorrowful the music!
Who could perform such a tune?
Surely it is the wife of Qǐ Liáng.
The Qīngshāng melody rises with the wind,
In the middle of the song, it lingers and hesitates.
For every pluck, there are two or three sighs,
Full of passionate and lingering grief.
I do not pity the singer’s bitterness,
But grieve that those who understand the music are rare.
I wish we were a pair of calling cranes,
Spreading wings to rise and fly high!
Crossing the river to pluck lotus flowers,
In the orchid marsh are many fragrant herbs.
I pluck them, but to whom shall I give them?
The one I think of is on a distant road.
I look back toward my old home,
The long road stretches on and on.
With hearts as one, yet living apart,
We grow old in sorrow.
The bright moon shines its night light,
Crickets chirp by the eastern wall.
The Yùhéng points to Mèngdōng,
How clearly the many stars shine.
White dew moistens the wild grass,
The season has suddenly changed again.
Autumn cicadas buzz among the trees,
Where have the swallows gone?
Once my friends from the same school
Soared high, beating their great wings.
They do not remember our friendship hand-in-hand,
But cast me aside like a footprint.
In the south is the Winnowing Basket, in the north the Dipper,
The Qiāniú does not bear a yoke.
Truly they are not firm like a solid rock,
What use then is an empty name?
Slowly the lonely-growing bamboo
Takes root on the slopes of Tài Shān.
To be newly wedded to you,
Like the dodder clinging to the lichens.
The dodder has its season to grow,
Husband and wife have their proper time to meet.
Married from a thousand lǐ away,
Separated by far-stretching mountains and hills.
Longing for you makes one grow old,
Why does your carriage arrive so late?
I grieve for those orchid flowers,
Holding their buds and radiating brilliance.
If they are not plucked when the time passes,
They will wither along with the autumn grass.
If you truly maintain your high integrity,
What should I, your humble wife, do?
In the courtyard there is a wondrous tree,
Its green leaves putting forth lush blossoms.
I pull down a branch and pluck its flower,
Intending to send it to the one I long for.
The fragrance fills my breast and sleeves,
But the road is far, and it cannot be sent.
How could this thing be worth offering?
It is just that I am moved by how long it has been since we parted.
Far away, the Qiāniú star,
Bright and white, the lady of the Héhàn.
Slenderly she stretches out her white hands,
Click-clack goes the movement of her shuttle.
All day long she fails to finish the pattern,
Her tears falling like rain.
The Héhàn is clear and shallow,
How far apart can they be?
Between them is only a stretch of full water,
Gazing at each other, unable to speak.
Turning my carriage, I drive away,
On and on, I travel the long road.
Looking around, how boundless it is,
The east wind sways the hundred grasses.
Nothing I meet is as it used to be,
How could I not age so quickly?
Prosperity and decline each have their time,
I regret not establishing myself earlier.
Man's life is not made of metal or stone,
How can he live a long and enduring life?
Suddenly he follows the transformation of things,
A glorious name is what he should treasure.
The eastern city wall is high and long,
Winding and stretching in succession.
A whirling wind rises from the ground,
The autumn grass is thick and no longer green.
The four seasons change in turn,
How quickly the year draws to its close!
The Morning Wind hawk harbors a bitter heart,
The cricket grieves for its narrow space.
Let go and give free rein to your will,
Why bind yourself so tightly?
In Yān and Zhào there are many beauties,
The fair ones have faces like jade.
Dressed in silk and gauze garments,
They sit by the door performing clear melodies.
How sorrowful the sound! The strings are tight,
I know the bridges have been shortened.
My feelings race as I straighten my sash,
Pondering and hesitating for a while.
I wish to be a pair of flying swallows,
Carrying mud to nest in your house.
I drive my carriage up to the East Gate,
Looking far off toward the tombs north of the city.
How the white poplars rustle,
Pines and cypresses line the broad road.
Below are those long dead,
In the deep darkness of eternal night.
Sleeping deeply beneath the Huángquán,
For a thousand years, never to awaken.
Boundlessly the Yīn and Yáng shift,
A man's life span is like morning dew.
Man's life is fleeting as a guest's stay,
His years have not the firmness of metal or stone.
Ten thousand years pass in succession,
Neither sages nor worthies can transcend this.
Those who take elixirs seeking immortality
Are mostly deceived by the drugs.
It is better to drink fine wine
And clothe oneself in fine silks and satins.
Those who go are daily more distant,
Those who live are daily more intimate.
I walk out of the city gate and look straight ahead,
Seeing only mounds and graves.
Old tombs are plowed into fields,
Pines and cypresses are chopped into firewood.
Among the white poplars is much mournful wind,
The rustling sound fills a person with sorrow.
I think of returning to my home village,
But wishing to go back, there is no way.
A life span does not reach a hundred,
Yet it often harbors a thousand years of worry.
The day is short and the night distressingly long,
Why not take a candle and wander?
Make merry while there is time,
Why wait for the year to come?
Fools are stingy with their expenses,
Only to be laughed at by later generations.
The immortal Wángzǐ Qiáo,
Is someone with whom it is hard to expect to be equal.
Piercing cold, the year draws to its close,
The mole crickets chirp sadly in the evening.
The cool wind has already become harsh,
The traveler has no clothes for the cold.
My brocade quilt I left at Luòpǔ,
He who shared my robe has departed from me.
I sleep alone through the long nights,
Dreaming and longing to see his countenance.
My husband thinks only of our old joys,
Turning his carriage to favor me with his presence.
I wish for his constant charming smiles,
To return in the same carriage, hand in hand.
Having come, he stays not a moment,
Nor does he dwell within the inner chambers.
Truly, without the wings of the Chénfēng hawk,
How could I fly, soaring upon the wind?
I look around to soothe my heart,
Straining my neck to gaze into the distance.
Pacing back and forth, filled with grief,
Tears fall, wetting the double doors.
In early winter, the cold air arrives,
How bitter and shivering is the north wind!
With many sorrows, I know the night is long,
Looking up, I watch the ranks of stars.
On the fifteenth, the bright moon is full,
On the twentieth, the toad in the moon wanes.
A traveler came from afar,
And gave me a letter.
In the beginning, it spoke of "everlasting longing,"
At the end, it spoke of "long separation."
I placed the letter in my sleeve,
For three years the ink has not faded.
With a single heart, I hold my humble devotion,
Fearing that you, my lord, might not perceive it.
A traveler came from afar,
And gave me a bolt of fine silk.
We are separated by more than ten thousand lǐ,
Yet my old friend’s heart remains thus.
The pattern is of a pair of mandarin ducks,
I cut it to make a quilt of shared joy.
I stuff it with "everlasting longing,"
And edge it with "knots that never untie."
Like glue cast into lacquer,
Who could ever separate them?
How bright, how white is the bright moon,
Shining upon my silken bed-curtains.
Worried and sad, I cannot sleep,
I gather my robes and rise to pace.
Although a traveler’s journey is said to be joyful,
It is not as good as returning early.
Out the door, I wander alone in hesitation,
To whom should I tell my sorrowful thoughts?
Straining my neck, I return to my room,
Tears fall and wet my robes.
The good time will not come again,
Parting occurs in an instant.
Pacing anxiously by the side of the crossroads,
Holding hands in the wilds, hesitating to leave.
Looking up at the floating clouds racing by,
Suddenly, they pass over one another.
Once the wind and waves lose their place,
Each is at a different corner of the sky.
We must part forever from this moment,
Let us stand together just a moment longer.
I wish to follow the Chénfēng hawk as it takes flight,
To see you off with my humble person.
A joyful meeting is hard to encounter again,
Three years seem like a thousand autumns.
By the river, I wash my long hat-strings,
Thinking of you, I am filled with melancholy.
Looking afar, a sorrowful wind arrives,
Facing the wine, I cannot raise a toast.
The traveler is mindful of the path ahead,
With what can I comfort my sorrow?
There is only the wine that fills the goblet,
To bind my deep affections with you.
Hand in hand, we go onto the river bridge,
Where does the traveler go at dusk?
Lingering by the side of the path,
Deeply aggrieved, unable to say farewell.
The traveler cannot stay for long,
Each speaks of everlasting longing.
How can one know it is not like the sun and moon,
Which have their set times for waning and fullness.
Strive to exalt your bright virtue,
Let our promise be until our hair is white.
Flesh and blood are like branches and leaves,
Friendships also follow such connections.
Within the four seas, all are brothers,
Who should be treated as a mere passerby?
How much more so for us, like trees with intertwined branches,
You and I share the same body.
Formerly we were like a pair of mandarin ducks,
Now we are like the stars Shēn and Chén.
In the past, we were always close,
Now we are as remote as the Hú and the Qín.
Only when thinking of our parting,
Does our affection grow newer by the day.
The Lù Míng poem speaks of longing for wild grass,
Which serves as a metaphor for honored guests.
I have a jar of wine,
Wishing to gift it to the one going far away.
I hope you will stay to drink a little,
To recount the intimacy of our lives.
Once the yellow swan makes its long parting,
It looks back after a thousand lǐ, lingering.
When a Hú horse loses its herd,
Its longing heart is always pining.
How much more so for a pair of flying dragons,
Whose wings are about to be separated.
Fortunately, there are songs on the strings,
Which can express the feelings of the heart.
I ask to sing "The Traveler’s Song" for you,
How clear and how sad it is!
The silk and bamboo instruments raise a pure sound,
Passionate and filled with lingering grief.
The long song is at its most intense,
My heart is broken with sorrow.
I wish to perform a song in the Qīngshāng mode,
But thinking that you cannot return.
Looking down and then up, I am grieved within,
Tears fall and cannot be brushed away.
I wish we were a pair of yellow swans,
Flying far away together to see you off.
Tying our hair, we became husband and wife,
Our love was never in doubt.
Joy and delight are for this night,
Let us be tender while the time is good.
The soldier is mindful of the path ahead,
He rises to see how late the night is.
The stars Shēn and Chén have both set,
"I must go, I must go," and from here we part.
Going on duty to the battlefield,
There is no set date for us to meet again.
Holding hands with a long sigh,
Tears flow for this parting in life.
Strive to cherish the blossoms of spring,
Do not forget the times of joy.
If I live, I shall surely return,
If I die, I shall think of you forever.
Brightly shines the morning moon,
Fragrantly smells my orchid scent.
The fragrance blooms on this fine night,
And follows the wind into my hall.
The soldier is mindful of the long road,
The traveler yearns for his old home.
In the twelfth month of midwinter,
I rise at dawn to tread upon the severe frost.
Looking down, I watch the flow of the Jiāng and the Hàn,
Looking up, I see the floating clouds soaring.
Good friends are parted far away,
Each at a different side of the heavens.
Mountains and seas separate them from Zhōngzhōu,
The distance is vast and long.
A joyful meeting is hard to encounter twice,
Our happiness is far from reaching its end.
I wish for you to exalt your fine virtue,
And cherish the sunlight as the seasons pass.
Zhāng Héng was unhappy with remaining in confidential positions for a long time.
During the Yángjiā era,
he went out to serve as the Chancellor of Héjiān.
At that time, the King of the state was arrogant and extravagant,
not following laws and regulations,
and there were many powerful and noble families who were annexing land.
When Zhāng Héng arrived at his post,
he governed with dignity and severity,
and was able to privately investigate the subordinate counties.
Those who were treacherous and cunning, or who practiced clever robbery,
were all secretly known to him by name.
He ordered the officials to arrest them,
and they all confessed and were captured.
The various powerful gallants and transient guests
were all terrified and fled the borders.
The commandery was well-governed,
litigation ceased,
and the prisons held no captives.
At that time, the world was gradually declining;
he felt frustrated and unable to fulfill his ambitions,
so he wrote the Sì Chóu Shī.
Qū Yuán used beautiful women as a metaphor for the gentleman,
precious treasures for benevolence and righteousness,
and deep water and heavy snow for the petty man.
He thought of repaying with the Way and its arts,
to present them to the ruler of the time,
but feared that slander and evil would prevent him from reaching him.
The lyrics say:
The First Sorrow:
The one I long for is at Tàishān,
I wish to go and follow them, but Liángfù is difficult.
Turning my body to look east, tears moisten the brush.
The beautiful one gifted me a gold-inlaid knife,
How shall I repay it? With fine Qióngyáo jade.
The road is far and unreachable, I lean and wander,
Why harbor sorrow, my heart troubled and weary?
The Second Sorrow:
The one I long for is at Guìlín,
I wish to go and follow them, but the Xiāng Shuǐ is deep.
Turning my body to look south, tears dampen my lapel.
The beautiful one gifted me golden Lánggān,
How shall I repay it? With a pair of jade plates.
The road is far and unreachable, I lean in melancholy,
Why harbor sorrow, my heart troubled and pained?
The Third Sorrow:
The one I long for is at Hànyáng,
I wish to go and follow them, but the Lǒngbǎn slopes are long.
Turning my body to look west, tears dampen my clothes.
The beautiful one gifted me a sable robe,
How shall I repay it? With a bright moon pearl.
The road is far and unreachable, I lean and hesitate,
Why harbor sorrow, my heart troubled and tangled?
The Fourth Sorrow:
The one I long for is at Yànmén,
I wish to go and follow them, but the snow falls thick.
Turning my body to look north, tears dampen my kerchief.
The beautiful one gifted me a piece of silk brocade,
How shall I repay it? With a blue jade table.
The road is far and unreachable, I lean and sigh more,
Why harbor sorrow, my heart troubled and grieved?
At sunset I wander in the West Garden,
Hoping to express my sorrowful feelings.
The winding pond tosses up white waves,
Rows of trees display their red blossoms.
Above there is a bird nesting alone,
Yearning for spring, it cries toward me.
Lifting my robes, I wish to follow it,
But the road is steep and I cannot travel.
Lingering, I cannot bear to leave,
Standing still, I gaze at your form.
A fierce gale stirs up the dust,
The bright sun suddenly grows dark.
Turning back, I enter my empty room,
Entrusting a dream to convey my sincerity.
When man desires it, Heaven does not refuse,
Why fear that we shall not be united?
Official duties pile up and weigh me down,
Writing and ink are scattered in confusion.
Racing the brush without leisure to eat,
The sun sets without my knowing it is late.
Immersed in registers and documents,
Dazed and dizzy, I am naturally muddled.
Leaving this behind, I exit the West City,
Climbing high to wander and look.
Square ponds hold clear water,
Within are wild ducks and geese.
How can I obtain swift wings,
To follow you and float upon the waves?
Boundless and long is the autumn night,
Fierce and cold is the north wind.
Tossing and turning, I cannot sleep,
Putting on clothes, I rise and pace about.
Pacing for a long time,
White dew dampens my clothes.
Looking down at the ripples of clear water,
Looking up at the light of the bright moon.
The Tiānhàn turns toward the west,
The stars are scattered across the sky.
How mournfully the crickets chirp,
A solitary goose flies south alone.
Melancholy and filled with many sad thoughts,
Unceasingly I think of my hometown.
I wish to fly but have no wings,
I wish to cross but the river has no bridge.
Facing the wind, I heave a long sigh,
My inner heart feels broken.
In the northwest there are floating clouds,
Towering like the canopy of a carriage.
Alas, that the time is not favorable,
Just meeting with a drifting wind.
It blows me toward the southeast,
Traveling south until reaching Wúhuì.
Wúhuì is not my home,
How can I stay and linger here for long?
Cast it aside and speak no more of it,
A traveler is always fearful of others.
Looking up at that north wind,
I cherish thoughts of Wèidū.
I wish to gallop on a Dài horse,
Suddenly heading toward the north.
The gentle southern breeze arrives forever,
I think of those southern regions.
I wish to follow the Yuè birds,
To soar and fly southward.
The four seasons alternate,
The hanging sun and moon move in cycles.
Parting is like a brief moment,
Yet it feels like three autumns have passed.
When I first moved away,
The red flowers were not yet sparse.
Now as I return and stop,
White snow flies like clouds.
Looking down a thousand fathoms,
Looking up to climb the obstacles of heaven.
Like tumbleweed in the wind,
I have been separated through winters and summers.
A thousand fathoms are easy to climb,
The obstacles of heaven can be crossed.
Once we shared the same robe,
Now we are eternally separated.
You are fond of fragrant herbs,
How could I forget your gift?
The lush blossoms were about to flourish,
But the autumn frost withered them.
If you do not show favor,
How can my sincerity be expressed?
The autumn orchid can be a metaphor,
The cassia tree flourishes in winter.
Music and song stir my thoughts,
With whom can I dispel my sorrow?
Thinking at the river at dusk,
Why am I drifting in a boat?
Is there no harmony and joy?
My companions are not my neighbors.
Who has forgotten the drifting boat?
I am ashamed to have no boatman.
Upon the high tower there is much mournful wind,
The morning sun shines on the northern forest.
That person is ten thousand lǐ away,
Rivers and lakes are distant and deep.
How can a boat reach the end?
The sorrow of separation is truly hard to bear.
A solitary goose flies toward the south,
Passing the courtyard with a long, mournful cry.
Looking up with longing for the distant one,
Wishing to entrust my lingering message.
Suddenly the form and shadow vanish,
Soaring away, it wounds my heart.
Tumbleweed separated from its root,
Drifting and swaying with the long wind.
Why does the whirlwind rise, blowing me into the clouds?
Higher and higher without limit,
How can the path of heaven be exhausted?
Like this wandering traveler,
Giving up his life to join the army far away.
Coarse wool does not cover the body,
Ferns and beans never fill the belly.
Go, go, say no more,
Deep sorrow makes one grow old.
In the northwest there is a weaving woman,
Her fine silks and satins are so numerous.
At dawn she takes up the loom and shuttle,
But by sunset she has not completed a pattern.
Sighing deeply through the long night,
Her mournful whistle reaches the blue clouds. I keep to the empty bedroom,
While my husband has gone to the army.
He promised to return in three years,
But now nine springs have passed. Flying birds circle the trees,
Calling clearly, seeking their flock.
I wish to be the light flowing south,
Casting my light to see my lord.
In the southern lands
there is
a beautiful woman, whose face is like
peach and plum.
At dawn she wanders the northern bank of the River,
at sunset she rests on an islet of the Xiāng Shuǐ.
Modern customs slight a rosy face,
for whom shall she show her pearly teeth?
In the blink of an eye the year draws to a close,
glory and splendor are hard to rely on for long.
The groom early on prepares the carriage,
I am about to travel far.
Where do I wish to go?
Wú Guó is my enemy.
I shall gallop along a ten-thousand-lǐ path,
but how can I take the eastern road?
Along the river is much mournful wind,
in the Huái and Sì rivers the rapid currents race.
I wish to make a light crossing,
but alas, there is no boat.
Living in leisure is not my ambition,
I am willing to go and serve the state's worries.
The soaring tower reaches over a hundred feet,
I lean by the window and the latticed railing.
Looking far, I survey a thousand lǐ,
from morning to evening, I see the level plains.
Men of noble spirit have many sorrowful hearts,
while the base man is lazily at ease.
The national grievance is truly not redressed,
I would willingly give up my life.
Grasping my sword, I look toward the southwest,
wishing to hasten to Tài Shān.
The strings are urgent, a mournful sound breaks forth,
listen to my impassioned words.
A slight gloom veils the sunlight,
a cool breeze flutters my clothes.
Wandering fish dive into the clear water,
soaring birds fly close to the sky.
Far, far away is the traveler,
on a distant mission, unable to return.
When he first set out, the harsh frost had set,
now that he returns, the white dew has dried.
The wanderer sighs at Shǔ Lí,
the one at home sings Shì Wēi.
With impassioned heart, I face the fine guests,
yet inwardly, I am wounded by grief.
A gentle breeze provides a cool fan,
the clouds are cleared away on all sides.
The bright, clear moon
is beautiful in the high corner of the sky.
I invite the noble Gōngzǐ,
and hand in hand, we share a carriage.
The dragon-steeds are majestic,
tossing their bits as they hesitate.
Solemnly we travel by night,
reaching the hut of my friend.
Bright lamps cast their glow,
flowered curtains are draped long.
Phoenix goblets pour the sweet wine,
divine cauldrons cook the fish.
The strings surpass those of Zǐ Yě,
the singing exceeds that of Mián Jū.
We chant of the Tài Sù,
and look down to praise the Xuán Xū.
Who can match the heroic and worthy,
to share the tallies of office with you?
The man of ambition regrets that the days are short,
the sorrowful man knows that the nights are long.
Lifting my robes, I walk in the front courtyard,
looking up to see the southern geese soaring.
The dark shadow moves with the body,
the flowing echoes return to the empty room.
How the cool breeze sways and flutters,
the crescent moon emerges from the west.
Numerous stars lean against the blue sky,
the constellations form their own ranks.
Cicadas chirp among the tall trees,
wild birds cry in the eastern wing.
Thin clouds appear now and then,
heavy dew dampens my skirt.
The good time has no lingering light,
the Běi Dǒu suddenly rises and falls.
I always fear the arrival of the cold season,
when the congealed air turns to frost.
Falling leaves are destroyed by the wind,
once severed, they are like fleeting light.
The movement of time follows the celestial cycles,
the four seasons succeed one another.
The Dōng Bì constellation is exactly in the middle of the dusk,
solid Yin and the cold season rise.
Heavy frost falls this very evening,
a mournful wind rises at midnight.
The red fire turns blue and loses its light,
the orchid oil congeals of its own accord.
Layered quilts have no warmth,
clutching the silk wadding is like holding ice.
Leaning on my pillow, I endure the whole night,
I wake and speak, but no one answers.
Long I ponder the rise and fall of things,
and with a sigh, I alone clutch my breast.
A cool breeze stirs the curtains,
the morning moon shines on the secluded room.
The beautiful one is in a far-off place,
the orchid chamber has no radiant light.
My heart embraces the spiritual light,
light quilts cover the empty bed.
In joy, one begrudges that the night is short,
in sorrow, one resents that the evening is long.
Patting the pillow, I whistle and sigh alone,
with an impassioned heart, I am wounded within.
I let my gaze wander beyond the four fields,
and stroll alone, lingering long.
Orchids and thoroughworts grow along the clear canal,
their lush flowers shade the green islets.
The beautiful one is not here,
to whom should I give these picked flowers?
Those who live in nests know the wind and cold,
those who live in caves recognize the cloudy rain.
If one does not experience far separation,
how can one know the longing for a companion?
I planted sunflowers in the northern garden,
the sunflowers grew lush and green.
In the morning, their blossoms lean toward the northeast,
in the evening, their tips dry in the southwest.
Falling dew hangs fresh and moist,
the bright moon shines its light.
Time passes, the gentle breeze ceases,
at the year's end, the autumn gale flies.
Layered clouds have no warm moisture,
harsh frost has a congealing power.
Fortunately, they receive the virtue of the high wall,
and the dark light shades the white blossoms.
Their thick branches flourished together in spring,
their falling leaves will wither after autumn.
I celebrate their fortune of late withering,
and forget the sorrow of this solitary life.
Dense clouds veil the sunlight,
heavy rains flood the courtyard.
Harsh frost withers the emerald grass,
cold winds shake the slender, dry branches.
Brisk and cold, the weather is clear,
scattered and sparse, the plants and trees are thin.
Moved by the season, I sing Xī Shuài,
thinking of the worthy, I chant Bái Jū.
My emotions stagnate with the dark Yin,
my heart moves with the whirling gale.
What does my longing heart cherish?
I cherish my friend Ōuyáng Zǐ.
His refined insights fathom divine mysteries,
his clear intellect brings forth subtle truths.
Since I parted from him for a month,
his subtle words have been cut off from my ears.
Lifting my skirts is not difficult,
but the clear sunlight cannot yet be awaited.
I crane my neck from the eaves of the steps,
standing for a long time, my yearning grows.
Wealth and honor bring others together,
poverty and lowliness drive relatives apart.
Lián and Lìn's gates easily changed paths,
Tián and Dòu shifted their favor.
The morning wind gathers in the lush forest,
roosting birds leave the dry branches.
Now I am only in distress and ignorance,
the scholars of the commandery turn away from me.
The people of my village esteem fine righteousness,
in great numbers, they shade my radiant bearing.
Facing the guests, I laud Yǒu Kè,
raising the goblet, I chant Lù Sī.
Faced with music, why do I sigh?
Over the white silk and the fork in the road.
The autumn wind rises with the evening,
the bright moon shines on the tall trees.
A clear air enters the quiet room,
the wide courtyard gives off a white glow.
In the stillness, I sigh with sorrow,
melancholic, I go out to wander and look around.
Looking up, I see the grass atop the wall,
looking down, I observe the dew beneath the steps.
With an empty heart, the body feels naturally light,
fluttering as if on an immortal's path.
Looking at the immortal Wò upon the mound,
I imagine meeting with divine beings.
The Dao is deep and hard to reach,
its essence and subtlety are not what I can aspire to.
Diligently thinking through the whole night,
I use long words to express my feelings and thoughts.
The north wind stirs the autumn grass,
the border horses have hearts that wish to return.
How can we be separated for so long?
Imperceptibly, we have suddenly reached today.
Royal affairs have separated me from my will,
we are further apart than Shāng and Shēn.
When I went away, the Cāng Gēng was singing,
now that I return, the Xī Shuài chirps.
Human feelings cherish the old home,
the traveler bird longs for its native forest.
Shī Juān has not played for a long time,
who can express my heart?
The Wú invaders have not yet been destroyed,
and signs of chaos encroach upon the frontier.
The Tiānzǐ ordered the Shàngzǎi
to act as a protector at Hànyáng.
The eminent scholar who founded the state
used jade and silk to recruit the worthy and virtuous.
I am not the unpolished jade of Jīngshān,
but mistakenly I ascended the arena of Héshì.
A sheep’s nature but a tiger’s stripes,
relying on swallow’s wings to fly like a phoenix.
Fearing that I am not fit for the appointment,
I resent the length of that southern road.
A thousand lǐ is far and distant,
and the route is constrained by passes and bridges.
The servant is exhausted from the long journey,
and the horses and carriage are worn out by the mountain ridges.
The deep valleys reach down without bottom,
and the high cliffs touch the Qióngcāng.
Lush grass halts its moistening,
and mist and dew drench my garments.
The dark forest gathers yin energy;
even without wind, it is naturally cold and chilly.
Looking back, my emotions are poignant;
sorrowful and pained, my heart is grieved.
When a man is born, a bow is hung;
his duties lie in the four directions.
How can he always wander at leisure,
sitting upright guarding the inner chambers?
I draw on righteousness to sever external feelings,
yet the inner emotions are truly hard to forget.
How biting is the autumn wind;
the white dew becomes morning frost.
Tender branches grow stiff morning and evening;
green leaves turn yellow day and night.
The bright moon emerges from the cloud-cliffs,
brilliantly flowing with pure light.
Opening the window to overlook the front courtyard,
the wailing morning geese fly.
High ambitions are confined by the four seas;
solitary, I guard the empty hall.
Vigorous years do not stay forever;
at the year’s end, I am always filled with emotion.
In late spring, the harmonious qi responds;
the bright sun shines upon the gardens and forests.
Green branches are like gathered emeralds;
yellow flowers are like scattered gold.
Beautiful plants are truly worth beholding,
but looking at this, it is hard to indulge for long.
Stretching my neck, there is no good path;
stomping my feet, I entrust myself to the deep seclusion.
Glory departs together with vigor;
lowliness and old age seek each other out.
Joy does not shine upon my face;
sadness and pain give rise to chants and songs.
What is the use of sighing in song?
The ancients can comfort the heart.
The cool wind of an autumn night rises;
pure air clears away the muggy heat.
Crickets chirp beneath the steps;
moths brush against the bright candle.
The nobleman follows a distant service;
the beautiful lady keeps her lonely solitude.
How long has it been since we lived apart?
The wood for drilling fire has suddenly changed.
No footprints are found by the windows;
the courtyard grass is lush and green.
Green moss clings to empty walls;
spiders weave webs throughout the rooms.
Touched by things, many thoughts arise;
deep sorrow knots in the heart's core.
The Great Fire star flows toward the southwest;
the white sun races toward the west land.
Floating sunlight reflects on the emerald forest;
whirling gales fan the green bamboo.
Flying rain sprinkles morning orchids;
light dew rests on clusters of chrysanthemums.
Dragons hibernate as the warm air congeals;
the sky is high and all things are solemn.
Weak branches do not bloom again;
how could fragrant blossoms be fragrant twice?
A person's life within the vast seas
is as sudden as a bird passing before the eyes.
The lament over the flowing river;
the former worthies used it to encourage themselves.
The metal wind fans the plain season;
crimson clouds open the period of shade.
Rising clouds are like surging smoke;
dense rain is like scattered silk.
Cold flowers bring forth yellow colors;
autumn grass holds green moisture.
Living in leisure, I enjoy all things;
away from the crowd, I long for the one I think of.
On the table, there are no tablets of the Xiāo family;
in the courtyard, no shoes of Gòng Gōng.
High-mindedness leaves behind kings and marquises;

This region

extraordinary troops.

Far away from the world's common feelings.

Not for the masses to speak of,

It is the yearning for your virtue and voice.
Your voice and virtue depart day and night,
remote and distant as if one had flown or sunk.
The *Wángwěi* fish longs for the *Héxiù* caves,
and the *Chénfēng* bird yearns for the *Běilín* woods.
The traveler is far off at the end of the sky,
and the distant date of return cannot be sought.
A sudden gale pulls back the returning message,
though returning clouds might carry a word.
Standing still, I think of ten thousand miles,
as heavy sorrow gathers in my heart.
Pulling my clothes, there is excess belt,
and checking my form, it does not fill the lapels.
Away, away! Leave behind the burden of emotion,
and in a peaceful place, stroke the clear zither.
On a quiet night, I summon joyful friends,
and set out wine at the Wind-Welcoming Hall.
A youth of *Qí* sings the *Liángfǔ yín*,
and a maiden of *Qín* plays like the *Zhāng* girl.
Mournful sounds wrap around the pillars and eaves,
and the lingering echoes enter the *Yúnhàn*.
Those in the four seats are all of one mind,
and the feathered wine cups are beyond counting.
How elegant is the lofty talk!
Resplendent as the brilliant morning clouds.
Human life does not last for long,
and to make merry, one always fears it is too late.
Like those birds that watch for the dawn,
one should raise one's voice when morning comes.
Why always suffer in sorrow and bitterness,
guarding this poverty and low station?
Bright is the glow of the clear *Qīnghàn*,
and resplendent is the light on the celestial path.
*Qiānniú* turns toward the northwest,
and *Zhīnvǔ* gazes toward the southeast.
How alluring is her beautiful countenance!
She waves her hand as if shaking white silk.
She resents that the River has no bridge,
and grieves that the year is drawing to its close.
Standing on tiptoe, she lacks a good connection,
staring blankly, she cannot cross over.
Stretching her neck to gaze at the great river,
her double tracks of tears are like soaking dew.
Going up the mountain to pluck jade stamens,
the deep valleys are rich with fragrant orchids.
Plucking and plucking, they do not fill my handfuls,
and far away, I cherish my beloved.
How vast is my old hometown!
The mountains and rivers are obstructed and difficult.
Deep thoughts are concentrated ten thousand miles away,
and hesitating, I sigh and chant alone.
Delicately trailing is the *Jiānglí* grass,
sparkling as it grows by the riverbank.
Bright and clear is that beautiful lady,
gracefully weaving by the window.
Resplendent is her enchanting form,
and brilliant is her lovely complexion.
Her husband has traveled and not returned,
and she lodges alone, like a single wing.
Into the empty room comes a sorrowful wind,
and in the middle of the night, she rises and sighs.
Resting peacefully in the *Běitáng*,
the bright moon enters my window.
It shines with a surplus of light,
but grasping it, it does not fill my hand.
A cool breeze winds through the inner chambers,
and cold cicadas chirp in the tall willows.
Hesitating, I am moved by the seasonal things,
as my journeying has lasted for so very long.
Seeking office will surely come to nothing,
and the sorrow of separation is hard to constantly bear.
A fine tree grows in the morning sun,
and thick frost encases its branches.
With a steadfast heart, it keeps faith with the season,
and in the cold of the year, it never withers.
How distant is the beautiful one?
Resplendent up in the clouds and sky.
High thoughts last through months and years,
as a long whistle enters the flying winds.
Stretching my neck to gaze at the edge of the sky,
like a bird preening toward the sun.
Slowly rising is the duckweed on the high mounds,
gently following the wind-borne feathers.
How long should a human life last?
Like the ripples on turbid water.
Sorrowful, with many lingering thoughts,
I set out wine to feast with my beloved.
Aligning carriages, we shake the flying reins,
on a long journey into *Cháng’ān*.
How elegant is the famous capital!
The city gates and towers are grand and winding.
Flying pavilions are girded with rainbow belts,
and tiered terraces are capped with cloud crowns.
High gates are lined up at the *Běiquè*,
and first-class mansions are scented with pepper and orchid.
Gallant knights control their swift steeds,
and people of the capital ride in jade carriages.
Wandering about, indulging every wish,
with such passion, for whom do I sigh?
How steep is the *Xīshān*!
Its tiered peaks are dark and towering.
Falling dew drops from the whole sky,
and orchid leaves wither against the woods.
Cold and heat follow one another in succession,
and time passes suddenly, like a collapse.
The *Sānlǘ* official tied his flying reins,
and an old man sighs at the setting sun.
Why be pulled by worldly affairs,
when the heart feels as if it goes against them?
In *Jīngluò*, there are many alluring beauties,
whose jade-like faces equal the jade blossoms.
On a quiet night, they stroke the sounding zithers,
and the gracious notes are clear and sad.
A long song follows the quickening tempo,
as mournful echoes follow the high bridges.
With one song, ten thousand men sigh,
and with a second song, the dust on the rafters flies.
I wish to be a bird of the river bend,
swimming in a pair on the banks of the *Fēngshuǐ*.
How steep is the high tower!
Soaring high, yet secure.
Patterned windows emerge from the dusty gloom,
and flying stairs tread upon the edge of the clouds.
A beautiful lady strokes the zither and lute,
her weaving hands are clear and idle.
Fragrant air knots together with the wind,
and mournful echoes are fragrant as orchids.
Who can gaze upon her jade countenance?
A city is toppled in a single strum.
Standing still, watching the sun set,
and hesitating, I sigh again and again.
I do not resent standing still for so long,
I only wish the singer to be happy.
I wish to ride the wings of a returning swan,
with pinions joined, flying in a pair.
My joyful friend departed in the orchid season,
far away, their voice and virtue are hidden.
*Yúyuān* draws in the setting sun,
and the four seasons pass as if flying.
The fragrant grass has long been lush,
yet the beautiful one never returns.
Hesitating, I follow the woods and shores,
as a kind breeze enters my breast.
Moved by things, I long for my beloved;
plucking this, to whom should I give it?
As the year ends, a cool wind rises,
and the Great Heaven is solemn and bright.
*Zhāoyáo* points to the northwest,
and the Heavenly River tilts toward the southeast.
The bright moon shines on the quiet room,
and crickets chirp in the courtyard.
Fluttering, the returning geese gather,
and shrilly, the cold cicadas cry.
Friends from the banquets of former days,
have flown like birds to the high heavens.
With fine clothes, they changed their voices and ways,
and living in pleasure, they abandoned old feelings.
*Zhīnvǔ* has no loom or shuttle,
and *Dàliáng* does not support any pillars.
The one I long for is in Yíngzhōu,
I wish to go and follow them, but the road is blocked and long.
Climbing the cliff to gaze into the distance, my tears and snivel flow,
My yearnings bring sorrow and grief to my heart.
The fair one left me a Lǜqǐ zither,
With what shall I repay them? A pair of southern gold pieces.
I wish to follow the flowing waves across the deep layers of water,
But in the end, I cannot reach them, only adding to my eternal sighing.
At sunset, the sky has no clouds,
The spring breeze fans a gentle harmony.
The fair one appreciates the clear night,
Drinking deeply and singing until the dawn.
When the song ends, there is a long sigh,
Holding onto this, many emotions are stirred.
Bright is the moon among the clouds,
Brilliant are the flowers among the leaves.
Is there not a moment of beauty?
But what of it when it does not last long?
At the end of the Jiàn'ān era,
I was then in the palace at Yè,
Wandering by morning and feasting by evening,
Seeking the utmost limit of pleasure.
Under heaven, a fine time and a beautiful scene,
A delighted heart and a joyful event,
These four things are difficult to bring together.
Now brothers and friends,
These few eminent scholars,
Have exhausted them all together.
Since ancient times, this kind of amusement
Has not been seen in the records.
Why is this?
In the time of Chǔ Xiāng Wáng, there were Sòng Yù and
Táng Jǐng;
In the time of Liáng Xiào Wáng, there were Zōu,
Méi, Yán, and
Mǎ; the guests were indeed brilliant,
But their lords were not literary.
In the time of Hàn Wǔdì, Xú Lè and other talents
Possessed the ability for clever responses,
But the Emperor was ambitious, suspicious, and full of jealousy;
How could they achieve the comfort of heart-to-heart conversation?
Without deceiving future generations,
Perhaps they must be even more virtuous than those of today.
Time flows like a stream,
Scattered and almost exhausted.
I compose these writings to remember those people,
Feeling the past and increasing my sorrow.
The text says:
A hundred rivers rush to the great sea,
A multitude of stars encircle the North Star.
Radiating brilliantly, they light up the Milky Way,
Stretching far from the long ford.
In the midst of heaven and earth, there was a great collapse,
The King of our house saved the living people.
Once the realm was cleansed and swept,
All the heroes were bound to arrive.
Unworthily, I possess a nature that admires the worthy,
And from the start, I have always cherished benevolence.
Moreover, I have met many gentlemen,
Giving my whole heart to their ever-renewing glory.
In discussing things, there is no empty talk,
In analyzing principles, they truly expound and set them forth.
How could there be a lack of words in their detailed threads?
Deeply and subtly, they investigate the divine and the human.
Clear wine cups fill the golden jars,
Joined couches are spread with magnificent mats.
Urgent strings stir the soaring listeners,
Clear songs brush the dust from the rafters.
Who says it is easy to meet one another?
This joy is truly to be treasured.
My home was originally in Qínchuān,
A descendant of a noble family.
Encountering chaos, I drifted as a refugee,
Pitying myself for having so many emotions.
Yōu and Lì presided over collapse and chaos in the past,
Huán and Líng have brought about upheaval today.
The Yī and Luò rivers are already covered in smoke from fires,
Hángǔ and Xiáo passes have vanished without a trace.
Packing my gear, I bid farewell to Qínchuān,
Goading my horse toward the land of Chǔ.
The Jǔ and Zhāng rivers are inherently beautiful,
But a traveler's heart is not moved by external praise.
I often sigh at the words of the poets:
"It is declining; why not go home?"
The High Minister receives the imperial spirit,
All the feudal lords look to him as their leader.
Cloud-like cavalry swept through the south of the Hàn River,
Jǐ and Yǐng were all cleared of rebels.
Pushing through the fog, I joined this flourishing brightness,
Parting the clouds, I faced the clear light.
Blessings and peace were about to pile up,
And the Young Lord especially appreciated me first.
I did not expect my wish to rest my shoulders
Would suddenly encounter the "Double Radiance."
Together we rode to visit the capital Yè,
Mooring boats side by side, we floated on the wide Yellow River.
Bound together in the joy of clear feasts,
In the silence, the beams and pillars echoed.
Having already turned it into an all-night drinking session,
Why would we care about following the sun's cycle!
A scribe under Yuán Běnchū,
He therefore described many matters of death and chaos.
The August Hàn encountered difficulty and hardship,
The world met with evil vapors.
The Dǒng clan brought ruin to Guānxī,
The Yuán family held sway over Héběi.
Solitary people were easily thrown into panic,
My distressed body submitted to the bridle and reins.
Who would have thought things would go against my wishes,
Forever cherishing the memory of my old country.
The Xiànggōng truly served the King,
And could surely pacify the destructive pests.
Once again, I see the radiance of the Eastern Capital,
Once again, I see the standards of the Hàn court.
In my remaining life, I have been fortunate enough,
Even more so to have encountered such brilliant virtue.
He loves guests and never speaks of fatigue,
Drinking and feasting, we forget the passing moments.
Listening at night until the stars fade,
Wandering by day until the darkness falls.
Sorrowful tunes stir the dust on the beams,
Rapid wine cups wash away the silent depths.
Let us exhaust the joy of a single day,
And know nothing of the confusion of old times.
Since youth, I had no desire for officialdom,
My heart was set on Jī and Yǐng,
So my service to the world was full of plain words.
In the past, my home was in Línzī,
Carrying and playing the Qí zither.
Setting out wine, I drank in Jiāodōng,
Staying and resting in Gāomì.
I thought this joy could last to the end,
But external things began to be difficult to conclude.
My feelings for Jī and Pú were shaken,
As the year ended, I was pressed by anxiety and fear.
Fortunately, the end of the road met with peace and light,
I settled down and established my humble self.
Having escaped the toil of carrying firewood,
I still wander in the chambers of pepper and orchids.
In clear discussions, we investigate ten thousand matters,
Fine talk is truly not limited to one topic.
Passing the wine cups, we play sorrowful songs,
Linking the eternal night to the white sun.
A magnificent house is not a thatched hut,
How could the fashionable ones be my peers?
In the midst of drinking, I look back at my former heart,
Feeling a sense of loss and melancholy.
A person of outstanding and extraordinary talent,
Whose writing has the most spirit,
What he attained was quite extraordinary.
Living in poverty in the Yàn neighborhood,
I grew up in Dōngpíng from my youth.
Hé and Yǎn were at the strategic crossroads,
I drifted and arrived at the capital Xǔjīng.
The wide river has no reverse current,
Recruiting and admitting me among the many heroes.
Crossing the Líyáng Ford to the north,
Climbing the city of Jǐ and Yǐng to the south.
Having observed the affairs of past and present,
I somewhat understand the circumstances of order and chaos.
Joyful friends understand each other,
Presenting and expounding on their whole lives.
Even more so, I receive the care of the wise and bright,
With such deep recognition, I feel my life is of little weight.
Wandering in the morning as the oxen and sheep descend,
Sitting in the evening while the cicadas chirp.
Throughout the year, not just for a day,
We pass the goblet and play new tunes.
Since the affairs of the time are hard to harmonize,
Joyful wishes are now brought together.
I only envy the solemn wings,
Flying in abundance toward the high heavens.
The scholars of Rǔ and Yǐng,
Displaced by the ways of the world,
Often have sighs of drifting and wandering.
The wailing geese in the clouds
spread their wings after shedding feathers.
Seeking coolness by the banks of the Ruòshuǐ,
avoiding the cold on the islets of Chángshā.
Looking back on my time at Liángchuán,
I walked slowly to gather at Yǐng and Xǔ.
Once I encountered the hardships of the age,
I was cast low, forever a traveler.
In the past, when the world was not yet settled,
I early on found a place to entrust myself.
At Guāndù, I was ranked among the common soldiers;
at Wūlín, I partook in the hardships and obstacles.
In my later years, I met with many worthies;
together we gathered under the shelter of the heavens.
Sitting in rows under the shade of ornate rafters,
golden goblets were filled with clear wine.
First we played the "Yánlù" melody,
followed by conversation into the late evening.
Jests were always answered with laughter;
teasing brought no shame or dejection.
I gave of myself without lingering worry;
what was in my heart has indeed been expressed.
Holding the office of Shūjì,
there were words of great favor.
The river islands are full of sand and dust;
the wind wails as yellow clouds rise.
Riders with golden bridles race one another;
following in quick succession, how could it end?
The Qìngyún bestows abundant favor;
though humble, I associate with many scholars.
Thinking of the former time at Bóhǎi,
we played by the clear waters of Nánpí.
Now once more touring the river bend,
blowing on reeds and floating on the fragrant waters.
Stepping lightly up the cinnabar stairs,
sitting together in attendance of the gentleman.
Elegant talk gladdens the heart;
mournful music truly harmonizes with the ear.
Pouring out the fragrant wine,
how can our drinking and talking ever reach an end?
Ever since the time of eating duckweed,
I have only seen the beauty of today.
The young master does not concern himself with worldly affairs,
but only delights in wandering;
yet he has many sighs about the sorrows of life.
In the morning, he tours and ascends the Fènggé;
at dusk, he gathers by the ornate pond.
Bending branches to pull down the weak twigs,
climbing limbs to pluck huì grass.
Lingering to look as far as the eye can see,
he gazes to the limit of all he can explore.
Looking west toward the Tàiháng Mountains,
gazing north toward the Hándān Road.
The level road is long and straight;
the poplars are indeed rustling.
The Fùjūn commands a banquet;
joy and pleasure express the feelings of the heart.
A fine outing knows no day or night;
why speak of late or early?
The guests are all refined and subtle;
their pure words are scattered like orchid patterns.
Mournful sounds bring down the circling swans;
the lingering notes reach the clear heavens.
Like one at Zhōngshān, he knows no drunkenness;
drinking in virtue, only then does he feel satisfied.
I wish for a life long until the time of hoary hair,
cultivating life while mindful of approaching old age.
How dashing are the sword-bearing riders!
Among the Wǔlíng of Cháng'ān.
The land of Qín is the pivot of the world;
from all eight directions, talents and worthies gather.
Jīng and Wèi have many brave men;
Wǎn and Luò are rich with spirited youths.
With high spirits and deep self-confidence,
would they deign to serve local authorities?
In crowds they come from beyond the Passes;
their chariots and followers fill the markets of the capital.
The Wǔhóu compete to send letters and gifts;
the various lords frequently speak on their behalf.
Their sense of duty is clearer than frost;
their conduct is as straight as a string.
Joyfully befriending one another below Chíyáng,
lingering at banquets west of Fényīn.
Once a promise is given to another,
how could they sit by and abandon them?
Swinging their tassels, they leave Hángǔ;
casting off their pendants, they depart Gānquán.
Sighing at these grand far-reaching plans,
their hearts are hung upon the four seas.
They only strive for their intentions to be fulfilled;
why bother with what is before their eyes and ears?
Heroic chivalry is truly renowned;
it has been known so since ancient times.
Inquiring of this weary traveler,
whose original home is in Liáodōng.
Formerly serving under General Lǐ,
for ten years he dealt with the Xīróng.
Stopping the chariots below Gāoquè,
looking far to see Yúnzhōng.
In all four directions, each a thousand li;
harsh winds rise from every side.
How can cold and heat follow the seasons?
Frost and rain differ greatly.
Sleeping at night on the north bank of the Běihé,
he dreams of returning to the Gānquán Palace.
Hard service has not yet ended;
his prime years are wasted in vain.
Thus one knows why people of ancient times
grieved over the rolling tumbleweed.
Gazing far along the long road,
traveling distantly to a remote place.
Turning the chariot, turning one's back on the capital districts;
waving hands and bidding farewell from here.
On the hall, drifting dust arises;
in the courtyard, green grass flourishes.
Cold cicadas hover by the river bend;
autumn hares huddle at the foot of the mountain.
The fragrant years have their flowery months,
but the beautiful one has no date of return.
At sunset, the cool wind rises;
facing the wine, I long for you.
Sorrow is expressed in the tunes of Jiāngnán;
grief is entrusted to the "Zǐjīn" poem.
Lying down, I feel the bright lamp grow dim;
sitting up, I see my light silk gown turn dark.
The tear-stained face cannot be adorned;
the dark mirror is difficult to use again.
I wish for the light of dusk to descend
and shine upon me in my waning years.
Fading stars hang halfway over the distant city;
floating clouds obscure the high towers.
A clear breeze comes to the jade halls;
silken curtains invite the autumn moon.
My thoughts are bound, thinking of that person;
deep sorrow lasts until the dawn.
Who has been a traveler for so long,
repeatedly seeing the flowing fragrance wither?
The river is wide and the stream has no bridge;
the mountains are high and the road is hard to cross.
In youth, I loved galloping and chivalry;
traveling as an official, I wandered the Guānyuán.
Having trodden upon ancient ruins,
I briefly inquire into the tales of rise and fall.
Great Zhōu has become a marshy thicket;
Imperial Hàn has become mountain forests.
Long submerged are the sites of the detached palaces;
how can one recognize the Shòulíng Gardens?
In mid-autumn, the border winds rise;
a solitary tumbleweed rolls with frost on its roots.
The bright sun has no brilliant light;
yellow sands darken for a thousand li.
On the manifest path, there are no different tracks;
on the hidden road, how could souls be different?
The sages and worthies are indeed gone;
holding to my fate, what more should I complain!
Yōu and Bìng value horse-riding and archery;
the youths love racing and chasing.
Felt belts carry double quivers;
ivory bows are placed in carved cases.
Beasts are fat and spring grass is short;
flying bridles cross the level plains.
In the morning, touring atop Yànmén;
at dusk, returning to Lóufán to lodge.
The Shíliáng bow has leftover strength;
the startled birds are left with no whole eyes.
Hàn and the barbarians are not yet at peace;
border towns have repeatedly changed hands.
Leaving me a single white feather,
intending to share the Hǔzhú.
A guest from Lǔ serves the King of Chǔ,
carrying gold and wearing red and white silks.
Having received the master's favor,
and also enjoying the Língyǐn's regard.
When the day is late and the court dismissed,
saddles and horses clog the thoroughfares.
Clan and kinsmen glow with splendor;
guests and servants admire from afar.
Wealth and honor are what people desire;
why should one fear morality?
In the southern lands, there is a scholar,
lost in direction and sunk in error.
Cutting wood by the banks of the blue river,
setting traps to wait for the crafty hare.
At fifteen I chanted the *Shījīng* and *Shàngshū*,
there was no writing I did not master.
Upon reaching my majority I joined the ranks of scholars,
walking with swift steps through the Qín Gōng.
I observed from the side the discussions of gentlemen,
and witnessed beforehand the character of the ancients.
My eloquence exhausted both sides of an argument,
and my brush-tip could defeat five carts of books.
I would be ashamed to receive a gift of a white jade disk,
and I would feel disgraced to accept the merit of Liáochéng.
In my later years, I followed worldly affairs,
guarding the barriers and harmonizing with the Rong far away.
I unfastened my sash-pendants to don rhinoceros armor,
and rolled up my scrolls to attend to the black bow.
My initial aspirations were beyond my strength;
how could I have known where I would end up today?
Hú winds blow the northern snows,
for a thousand miles, they cross Lóng Shān.
They gather within the Yáo Tái,
dancing and flying before the two pillars.
This time of year is beautiful in itself;
one should avoid the season of flamboyant sun.
The sunlit season of peaches and plums,
in its brilliant purity, cannot achieve such grace.
Westward I go out and climb the Què Tái,
eastward I look down upon the Yún Què.
Tiered pavilions stand solemn in the celestial dwelling,
the imperial road is as straight as a hair.
Embroidered roof-ridges join with flying clouds,
and jade eaves-tiles take in the moving moon.
Artificial mountains are built to mimic Péng hú,
and ponds are dug to resemble the Mǐng bó.
Beauties are selected from throughout Qí and Dài,
and music is summoned from all across Qiōng and Yuè.
Bells are arranged to accompany the evening banquet,
with songs and pipes awaiting the dawn.
One’s years and appearance cannot be brought back,
and the fortunes of the body must eventually wax and wane.
Ant-holes cause leaks that ruin mountains and rivers,
and tears like silk threads destroy the golden bones.
A vessel loathes the tipping that comes from being full,
and things avoid the demise that follows a surplus of life.
How wise are the many scholars,
who follow reason and distinguish between clarity and obscurity.
Cold sands are level on all four sides,
flying snow startles for a thousand miles.
The wind breaks the trees of Yīn Shān,
and mist obscures the city of Jiāohé.
At dawn I galloped toward the Zuǒ Xián array,
at night I drew near the Xiūtú camp.
In the past, I served in the front army's tent,
today I follow the Piáoyáo soldiers.
The penalty for losing one's way is heavy,
and the law for delaying is by no means light.
What we rely on is the current Son of Heaven,
for the way of Hàn grows more beautiful and bright each day.
I went far to bid you farewell,
all the way to Yànmén Guān.
Yellow clouds obscure a thousand miles;
when will the traveler return?
Sending you off seems like only yesterday,
yet before the eaves, the dew has already gathered.
I do not regret that the orchids are fading late,
what I grieve for is the coldness of the journey.
You are at the edge of the sky,
while I am forever separated from you.
I wish to see your face just once,
and that you are no different from a branch of the Qióng tree.
Like the dodder and the water lentil,
that which they lean upon never shifts.
With a vessel of wine, I see off the traveler,
hesitating during our final banquet.
At dusk, the floating clouds increase,
as I clasp your hand, my tears fall like sleet.
Long and far flows the water of the Qīng Chuān,
where the fine bream finds its place.
But I am ten thousand miles away,
since the binding of our hair, we have not seen each other.
Inside my sleeve, there is a short letter,
which I wish to send by a pair of flying swallows.
A silk fan like the round moon,
comes from the plain white cloth of the loom.
On it is painted the daughter of the King of Qín,
riding a luan bird toward the mist and clouds.
Its colors are prized by the world,
but though it is new, it should not replace the old.
I secretly worry that the cool breeze will arrive,
blowing upon the trees by my jade steps.
The gentleman’s favor has not yet ended,
yet I wither and fall mid-way.
Setting out wine, we sit in the flying pavilion,
wandering at leisure beside the Huá Chí.
A divine gale arrives from afar,
and the lotuses on either side unfurl.
Green bamboos line the clear water,
and autumn orchids cover the secluded banks.
The moon comes out to shine upon the garden,
as caps and pendants follow one another.
A guest comes from southern Chǔ,
playing the panpipes for me.
Even the fish in the depths remain submerged to listen,
and the listeners do not speak of weariness.
How elegant is this lofty literature!
How can a minor scholar hope to achieve it?
Solemn are the shadows of the wide hall,
the sound of sparrows brings sorrow to the northern woods.
The many guests return to their cities;
what then shall comfort my heart?
The King treats the talented with ritual,
not begrudging disks of a thousand gold pieces.
The twin towers point toward the imperial road,
and red palaces are arranged among the residences.
We take our ease at the Bīngjǐng Tái,
where the clear pond reflects the flowery thickets.
A cool breeze stirs the fragrant air,
and the green trees are the first to fall before autumn.
At dawn, I had an appointment with a beautiful one,
and from dawn to dusk, I look toward the blue pavilion.
Lifting my skirts, I pluck bright pearls,
pacing back and forth, I gather orchids and sweet grass.
He looks upon us few men with favor;
our words and meanings are as beautiful as gold and vermillion.
Yánlíng held his precious sword lightly,
and Jì Bù held his promises heavily.
Though in a position of wealth, one does not forget the poor;
the Way lies in following like the sunflower.
Green and lush is the cinnamon of Zhōng Shān,
round and full with the color of frost and dew.
How biting are the frost and dew!
Yet the cinnamon branches grow straight of their own accord.
Oranges and pumelos are in the southern land,
relying on you to serve as their wings.
By mistake, I received the favor of the Sage Lord,
entrusting myself to a literary office.
Now that my prime has already passed,
how could I dare not to adorn myself?
The magnificent moon shines upon the square pond,
as we sit in rows beside the Golden Hall.
This humble minister has indeed received gifts,
and this grand grace is truly immeasurable.
Once, encountering a world in disorder, I urged
my horse to leave the Dì jīng.
Already wounded by the separation of the creeping grass,
I then came to know the sorrow of the solitary pear tree.
Xiáo and Hán had become ruins,
and the Jì Què was far away in chaos.
Leaning on my oar, I drifted on the Jīng and Wèi,
at dusk, the mountains and rivers were clear.
Crickets clung to the mulberry fields,
and a harsh wind blew against the stalks.
Storks and herons were among the hidden grasses,
and the traveler’s tears had already fallen.
Having left my home for thirty years,
I was fortunate to encounter a peaceful world.
A wise lord bestowed fine rewards,
and I wore the golden marten and the black tassel.
Attending banquets, I went out to Héqū,
with flying canopies, I traveled through Yè Chéng.
How long, after all, does the morning dew last?
Suddenly it is like duckweed upon the water.
A gentleman is earnest in kindness and righteousness;
his branches and leaves shall never wither.
Since his blessings and prosperity are secure,
his fine name will be passed down for a thousand years.
I say that I did not follow traditional teachings,
but hid my will and left the dust of the world.
My distant thoughts went out to vast realms,
and my high steps transcended the common sort.
The Spirit Phoenix shakes its plumage,
folding its wings by the shore of the Xī hǎi.
At dawn, it eats the fruit of the Lánggān,
at night, it drinks from the Jade Pond.
Dwelling in accord with nature, one is free from burdens;
nurturing virtue, one enters the realm of the divine.
How vast is the grace of the universe!
The clouds and nets are spread out in the four directions.
A wise man prizes the knowledge of righteousness,
and the great man is clear about protecting his person.
Zhuāng Shēng understood non-action,
and Lǎo Shì maintained his true nature.
All under heaven attained the One,
and name and reality have long been guests to each other.
The Xiánhí music was offered to the Yuánjū bird,
but the bells and drums perhaps brought it sorrow.
Liǔhuì was good at following the straight path,
and Sūn Dēng nearly understood the nature of men.
Expressing my feelings is truly not a distant matter;
I record this sentiment upon my sash as a gift.
The Qīngniǎo wanders over the sea,
The Yùsī flies beneath the wormwood.
Sinking and floating are not suited to each other,
Wings and feathers each have their own destination.
Drifting and fluttering, one can pass the years;
In the vast expanse of water, how can there be right or wrong?
Morning clouds ride upon transformations,
Their radiance is rare in the world.
Jīngwèi carries wood and stones in her beak;
Who can fathom her subtle and hidden purpose?
The autumn moon shines through the window screens,
Its suspended light enters the Dānchí.
A beautiful lady strums the sounding qín,
In the clear night, she keeps watch over empty curtains.
Upon the orchid path, footprints are few;
On the jade terrace, spiderwebs grow.
Garden trees burst with red colors,
Boudoir grasses hold emerald moisture.
Waiting long, she tidies the patterned silks,
To send across ten thousand lǐ to her beloved.
May you bestow the favor of heavy dew,
Trust in my pledge, clear as the sun.
Verdant spring hastens the heavenly mechanism,
Plain autumn gallops the white sun.
The beautiful one has returned to Zhòngquán,
Sorrow and grief have no end.
The funerary hall is already solemn and still,
Pines and cypresses turn more desolate.
Bowing and looking up, my pain cannot be eased;
My recurring thoughts are not just of one thing.
Clutching my lapel, I mourn in loneliness,
Dazed, as if I have lost something.
The bright moon enters the patterned window;
Faintly, I imagine her orchid-like character.
It is not the daylily that dispels grief;
How could long-lasting yearning be settled in sleep?
Sleeping and dreaming are dark and obscure again;
How can I see your form?
I am ashamed of my lack of Běihǎi arts,
You do not have the spirit of the Dìnǚ.
I drive my carriage out to the distant mountains,
Lingering, I weep before the pine-shaded inscription.
Rain ceases, and no clouds return;
When blossoms fall, how can the petals remain?
Sun and moon follow their order of succession;
When will my sleeping and waking find peace?
The Chǔhòu sent down a gracious command,
Grace and favor covered my humble person.
At dawn, I looked back at my Sāngzǐ homeland,
Sighing long, I thought of my close kin.
Wandering thoughts bid farewell to the southern bank,
Carrying resentment, I departed from the western ferry.
Galloping my horse along the Huái and the Sì,
From morning to evening, I saw Liáng and Chén.
Following righteousness, I pursued the upper ranks;
Elevating my conduct, I joined the palace officials.
Those in vermilion robes were all eminent scholars,
Those with long tassels were all men of talent.
Sharing hardships within the Chénghuá,
Bound in close service for more than a year.
At sunset, I briefly hitched my carriage,
Wandering at ease to view the Luòchuán.
Among the departed, there are many large trees,
Old graves' grass braves the cold mist.
A traveler is easily moved to sighs,
Pacing back and forth, I pity myself.
I wish to send word via the Sānniǎo,
The longing of separation is not in vain.
Hán Gōng was reduced to selling medicine,
Méi Shēng hid by the market gate.
A hundred years truly pass in a flash;
Why should one distress their heart and soul?
One should learn from Generals Wèi and Huò,
To establish merit at the Héyuán.
Scepter and seal draw the gaze of a worthy ruler,
Blue and purple robes are the grace of a brilliant lord.
Zhōng Jūn's talent has only just been recognized,
Jiǎ Yì's position is just becoming honorable.
The Jīn and Zhāng families wear sable caps,
The Xǔ and Shǐ families ride in ornate carriages.
Princes and marquises value a brief discussion,
High officials prize a single word.
In times of great peace, there is much joy,
Flying canopies pass through the gates of Dōngdū.
Looking back, I think of Zhāng Zhòngwèi,
Whose garden was filled with weeds and mugwort.
Cinnabar clouds hide the sunlight,
Green springs well up on the shaded islet.
Water storks nest on the layered roof-tiles,
Mountain clouds moisten the pillar bases.
Dark clouds rise in the spring season,
Sorrowful rains persist through the autumn sequence.
Rustling, the cool leaves are stripped away,
Fiercely, the whistling wind rises.
In lofty talk, I enjoy the four seasons;
Living in isolation, I long for my former companions.
Green moss turns yellow day and night,
Fragrant blossoms become old brushwood.
At the year's end, a hundred anxieties intersect;
There is nothing to comfort my long waiting.
Imperial Jìn encountered the Yángjiǔ calamities,
Across the realm, mists and fogs spread.
Qín and Zhào faced eclipses,
Yōu and Bìng provinces were occupied by tigers.
I, too, received favor and grace,
Moved, I devoted myself to the rush of service.
Although I lack the tactics of the Six Wonders,
I hoped to meet with such as Zhāng and Hán.
Nìng Qī sang while beating his ox horn,
Huán Gōng met and then promoted him.
Xún Xī braved dangers and difficulties,
Truly for the sake of loyalty and integrity.
In vain I let the days and months pass,
Ashamed that I lack the measure of the ancients.
Watering my horse, I go out of the city moat,
Looking north toward the desert road.
How desolate are the thousand lǐ,
The white sun is hidden behind cold trees.
Tossing my sleeves, I am filled with indignation;
Clutching my pillow, I harbor a hundred thoughts.
I regret that fame and merit are not yet established,
While my black hair has already turned white.
If one happens to meet with the right time,
Order and chaos are determined by mysterious fate.
A great mansion requires exceptional timber,
The imperial court is no place for mediocre vessels.
The brilliant and talented display worldly merit,
Many scholars assist in these positions.
Your kind regard has become an enduring bond,
Thus I am paired with the elite of the age.
Our alliance has long been substantial,
Our shared hardships are not just one.
Since we have faced adversity together,
Being in danger is not what we worry about.
Always admiring the bearing of the former worthies,
Observing the ancients to discuss gains and losses.
Mǎfú served as a general for Zhào,
The borders achieved peace and tranquility.
Xìnlíng wore the seal of Wèi,
The Qín troops dared not come out.
I lament that I have no strategy for the commander's tent,
Vainly I am ashamed of my plain silk nature.
A sojourner leaving my old home,
Moved by our meeting, compared to the harmony of qín and sè.
Considering myself, I am no fine Qǐzǐ timber,
My efforts lie in avoiding idleness.
Even more, I stand in awe of my friends,
Falsely playing the flute violates name and reality.
Yǎnshān has many spiritual herbs,
The seashore abounds in strange rocks.
Lofty and proud, I seek the blue clouds;
Living in seclusion, I settle my vital spirit.
The man of the Dào reads the cinnabar scriptures,
The alchemist refines the jade elixir.
Vermilion clouds enter the windows,
Yàolíng shines into the crevices.
Looking around proudly, I pick tree-mushrooms;
Treading the waves, I gather water-jade.
Gazing far on a ten-thousand lǐ journey,
Raising my palm, I look toward the "Guest of the Mists."
If I could forever attain the arts of Ānqī,
Why worry about the approach of Méngsì?
When the Tàisù was first divided,
The myriad breathings manifested in forms and omens.
If stillness and motion have a source,
Why say a young child died prematurely?
The Dào has been lost for a thousand years,
Who can understand the crossing and the bridge?
I think of riding on the wings of the whirlwind,
Rising prominently, soaring against the wind.
Quietly observing the meaning of the "one-foot pole,"
Its logic is sufficient and never lacking.
Brightly, the autumn moon shines;
Leaning on the railing, I chant of Yáo and Lǎo.
Wandering without concern for ugly or beautiful;
Only then is it the way of the Jūnzǐ.
To grasp and return to the One;
On Nánshān, there is the elder Qǐhào.
Folding the arms, transformations have long occurred;
The passing of the flame depends on the firewood and grass.
Unceasingly, the mysterious thoughts are clear;
Within the breast, clever schemes are removed.
Both the world and the self are forgotten;
Then one can be intimate with the gulls.
Zhāng-zǐ was inward-focused,
Shàn-shēng was obscured by external forms.
At once discarding the snare of the dark,
Coolly appreciating within the void.
Dispelling this feeling of one lost in weakness,
Providing for the spirit to wander alone.
Gathering herbs at the edge of the white clouds,
For a while indulging in what I cultivate.
Cinnabar blossoms shine with fragrant clusters,
Green bamboos shade the quiet and open space.
Loftily entrusting my superior intent,
Unaware of ascending into the void.
Curved lattices stir fresh breezes,
The stone chamber has subtle echoes.
Go then, following what you desire,
Gain and loss are not awarded from without.
How supreme is the guest who wields the axe,
Double brilliance is inherently bright.
The five difficulties are already washed away,
Transcending tracks and cutting off the worldly net.
Morning wandering, wherever things gather,
Leisurely harboring true interest.
The clouds and sky are also clear and bright,
Sometimes meeting with an appreciative heart.
Green pines put forth elegant calyxes,
Beautiful colors emerge from the tall trees.
Gazing to the limit where clear waves are deep,
Remotely reflecting the plain stone walls.
Lustrous feelings without remaining dross,
Brushing my clothes, I release worldly affairs.
Since seeking benevolence comes from within myself,
How could the dark mystery be sought from without?
Directly placing and forgetting what governs,
Carefree and relaxed, I obtain forgotten worries.
Truly, one is weary of physical transformations,
The sorrowful bosom cannot yet be straightened.
Briefly following the suburban roads,
Gathering the reins to leave the Tái shěng.
Chilly, the seasonal sequence is high,
Lonesome, the heart's awakening is eternal.
Seasonal chrysanthemums shine on the rocky slopes,
Clouds and mist crown the autumn peaks.
Looking back, cherishing the good hour,
Lingering, I walk upon the fading light.
Though rolling and unrolling have ten thousand threads,
Movement always returns to stillness.
Already approaching the mulberry and elm,
At the year's end, I follow what I hold.
The boat in the ravine cannot be climbed,
Forgetting cares, I entrust myself to the Master of Yǐng.
Sowing sprouts in the Dōng gāo,
Sprouts grow, filling the paths between fields.
Although I have the weariness of carrying a hoe,
Turbid wine allows me to suit myself.
At sunset, I cover the firewood cart,
The road is dark, and the light is already evening.
Returning people gaze at the cooking fires,
Young children wait at the eaves' gap.
I ask you, what are you doing?
In a hundred years, there must be labor.
I only wish for the mulberry and hemp to grow,
In the silkworm months, to be able to spin and weave.
The simple heart is just like this,
Opening a path to look for the Three Friends.
Rivers and seas pass through twists and turns,
Mountain peaks provide fullness and lack.
The spiritual realm truly detains one,
A heart of appreciation is not established in vain.
At dawn, I climb the cloud peaks,
Far away and cut off from Lú and Huò.
Green barriers circulate long,
Golden pools are always clear.
Paulownia forests are girded with morning mist,
Stone walls reflect the first light.
Stalactites are already dripping,
The Cinnabar Well is again vast and deep.
Rocky crags turn increasingly strange and elegant,
Lofty peaks still hide one another.
Red jade is hidden in the Jasper Stream,
Cloud-brocade covers the sandy river bend.
At night I hear the orangutans crying,
In the morning I see the flying squirrels departing.
The climate in Nán zhōng is warm,
Vermilion flowers transcend the white snow.
Fortunately wandering to the Village of Jiàn dé,
Observing wonders, I pass through the Cave of Yǔ.
Who can distinguish between body and name?
Maps and histories eventually wear away.
I shall float on the tide of the Guì River,
Reflecting the moon, I wander the seashore.
Preserving life values following nature,
This shall be told to the wise.
Tài wēi congeals in the Emperor's abode,
Yáo guāng aligns with the Divine Prefecture.
Observing the sun, brilliant are the records and histories,
Assessing the capital, beautiful are what is heard and seen.
Lined with the Milky Way, they construct celestial palaces,
Opening the heavens, they fashion precious halls.
Cinnamon pillars retain the summer breezes,
Orchid rafters stop the winter sleet.
Green forests form a dark mist,
Vermilion peaks are covered in lush green.
Mountain clouds provide auspicious mists,
Pond plants possess spiritual transformations.
On the Double Ninth, clear qi gathers,
Descending from the carriage for a dark banquet.
Gazing afar, dividing the world's regions,
Surveying with the eyes, reaching the capital's suburbs.
Qi arises in the shade of rivers and mountains,
Smoke vanishes and Huái hǎi appears.
Middle seats overflow with vermilion ribbons,
Walking along the eaves, among jade caps.
Rites performed, awaiting the sage's sentiment,
Music ends, inviting the imperial gaze.
Measuring favor, I ascend beyond ease,
Following the records, I am confused by my floating lowliness.
Honor is heavy, gifting double gold,
Patrolling splendor passes the full ear-plugs.
I dare to adorn the commoner's song,
Ashamed to present the Lǜ shuǐ.
Yesterday I set out from the islet of Chì tíng,
Tonight I lodge at the bend of Pǔ yáng.
Just experiencing the marvels of cloud-peaks,
How is it merely a thousand-mile separation?
Fragrant dust has not left the mat,
Streaming tears are still on the sleeves.
Stopping the boat to gaze at the far shore,
Resting the oars, blocked by wind and snow.
Wind and snow having lasted for some time,
In the long night, longing thoughts arise.
Wandering on the Běi hú,
An appointment at the Lofty South Tower.
