Applying the brush to sing of new appreciation,
Opening the scrolls to clarify doubts.
Plucking flowers, loving their fragrant air,
Gathering stamens, pitying their moist color.
Color's moisture fears withering,
Human affairs also melt away.
The "Zǐ jīn" resents not going,
The "Gǔ fēng" rebukes fickleness.
Together holding the faith of Yán zhōu,
Without shame before the promise of Zhòng lù.
Spiritual Ganoderma, hoping for three blossoms,
A solitary bamboo, where my feelings are entrusted.
Entrustment is already sincere,
Sufficient to stir the person of my heart.
Now traveling beyond Cū and Shèng,
Holding thoughts until the seashore.
Seeing you is far and not yet achieved,
On what day will we look at each other?
Though miscellaneous pendants could be gifted,
Sparse flowers ultimately have no presentation.
Without presentation, the heart is weary,
How can a traveler just wander?
Fortunately catching the clearing of wind and snow,
The green of spring fills the riverbanks.
Casting off the lines to wait for companions ahead,
Looking back, I am full of melancholy.
The misty landscape seems far away,
Final echoes are sent on jasper and jade.
Deep and dark is the void of Xiāo and Xiāng,
The emerald stream is calm without moisture.
Quietly, the hundred grasses are dark,
Suddenly, the Kūn-jī cries in sorrow.
Clear shadows come and go from afar,
Moonlight scatters on the front steps.
Refining medicine, gazing at the empty curtain,
Playing the zither while lying by the remote drapes.
The water's blue proves it is not defiled,
The golden paste is divine, how could it blacken?
On the northern islet is the Emperor's Child,
Drifting and flowing, she cannot be expected.
Disappointed at evening in the mountains,
Nursing illness, I compose this poem.
The rites of the ancestral temples show sorrow and reverence;
the way of the village of Fényì is solemn and profound.
Respectful purity arises from the bright sacrifices;
the solemn carriage is for the Qínián prayers.
The decree for the followers is issued in the final month of the season;
the phoenix-patterned oars are prepared to travel the river.
Cloud-banners resemble the shifting of the Milky Way;
the imperial net is like the stars suspended in the sky.
Vermillion oars are beautiful by the cold islets;
golden bridles reflect the autumn mountains.
Feathered guards obscure the flowing light;
colorful wind instruments shake the deep abyss.
Evaluating poems to gauge the capital and the state;
consulting records to survey the city marketplaces.
Peasant songs resonate with the jade pitch-pipes;
town praises are played on cinnabar strings.
Cultural influence reaches the Guìhǎi;
teachings and fame illuminate the Bīngtiān.
Harmony and kindness are bestowed from the upper tablets;
gracious favor saturates the lower banquets.
Fortunate to attend after the viewing of the Luò River;
why should one envy the former tours of the Hé?
Adhering to righteousness without end;
this song of praise is yet to be fully proclaimed.
Solemnly rowing the boat to the outskirts;
shifting the music, we linger at Jiāngyīn.
The emerald mountains are lush and misty;
the green banks are deep and serene.
Cool leaves reflect upon the sandy islets;
autumn blossoms cover the water's edge.
Wind scatters where pines hang over the precipice;
clouds gather where the stone path runs deep.
Quietness mirrors the vast fields;
looking in four directions, the peaks appear in disarray.
The air is clear, knowing the geese are leading;
the brilliance of the dew recognizes the cry of the apes.
Cloud-like robes truly loosen the official ribbons;
riding the mist, one can renounce gold.
First, I prepare the arts of the Dānquán;
finally, I behold the purple fragrant heart.
The moving light flows leisurely by itself;
let not weak thoughts invade.
Noble men treat a foot-long jade as trivial;
common men value favor and light.
Sacrificing for righteousness is not for profit;
holding the reins, one leaves home lightly.
In the first month of winter, the month of suburban sacrifice;
a killing aura rises with the harsh frost.
The war horses' grain is not warm;
the soldiers take ice as their broth.
At dawn, ascending the slopes of Chénggāo;
the gravel and rocks are all like winding sheep's intestines.
Cold shadows shroud the white sun;
Tàigǔ is dim and vast.
Resting the troops and unyoking the carriages;
leaning on a sword, overlooking the eight wildernesses.
The Jīngpéng bird cannot fly;
the Xuánwǔ hides by the river bridge.
Broken wings are caused by the season;
moved by things, I briefly grieve for myself.
Simple scholars cling to a single classic;
not enough to understand whether to serve or withdraw.
The northwest autumn wind arrives;
the traveler from Chǔ feels a long-lasting sorrow.
At sunset, the green clouds gather;
the fair one has not come at all.
The colors of the dew are floating and brilliant;
the moonlight begins to linger.
The precious book is closed for you;
how could the jade lute be played?
Longing for each other by the shores of Wùshān;
looking regretfully toward the Yángyún Terrace.
The incense burner has ceased its deep burning;
dust rises on the beautiful mat.
The Guì River flows a thousand miles a day;
entrusting to it the feelings of a lifetime.
Scion of the High God Gāoyáng;
my late august father was called Bóyōng.
When Shètí pointed to the first month of Mèngzōu;
on the day of Gēngyín, I was born.
My father, observing my first movements;
conferring on me an auspicious name.
He named me Zhèngzé;
and gave me the style name Língjūn.
Abundant was the inner beauty I possessed;
to which I added cultivated talents.
I wore Jiānglí and Bìzhǐ;
and wove Qiūlán for my girdle.
Hurrying as if I could not keep up;
fearing that the years would not wait for me.
In the morning I plucked the magnolia of the Bǐ hills;
in the evening I gathered the winter-grass of the islets.
Sun and moon hurry on without staying;
spring and autumn follow in succession.
Thinking of how the plants and trees wither;
I fear the Fair One will also grow old.
Why not use your prime and cast off impurities?
Why not change these ways?
Mount the fine steed Qíjì and gallop!
Come, I shall lead you on the path ahead!
Of old, the Three Sovereigns were pure;
truly, they were where all fragrances gathered.
Mixing Shēnjiāo and Jùnguì;
it was not only weaving Huì and Chǎi.
Those kings Yáo and Shùn were upright and great;
they followed the Way and found the path.
How reckless were Jié and Zhòu!
They took shortcuts and stumbled!
Those partisans seek only easy pleasure;
their path is dark, dangerous, and narrow.
It is not that I fear personal calamity;
I fear the royal carriage will be wrecked.
I hurried here and there, before and behind;
to follow the footsteps of former kings.
The Quán does not see my loyalty;
he listens to slander and turns his anger on me.
I know well that plain speaking brings trouble;
yet I cannot refrain from it.
I point to the Nine Heavens to witness;
it is all for the sake of the Língxiū.
At first he gave me his word;
but later he regretted and went another way.
It is not hard for me to leave;
but it grieves me that the Língxiū is so fickle.
I had planted nine fields of Lán;
and a hundred acres of Huì.
I planted Liúyí and Jiēchē in rows;
mixing Dùhéng with fragrant Bìzhǐ.
I hoped for their branches and leaves to flourish;
wishing to wait for the time to harvest.
Even if they wither and die, what does it matter?
I mourn that the many fragrances have turned to weeds.
The crowd all competes for advancement with greed;
insatiable in their seeking.
They excuse themselves and judge others;
each harboring jealousy in their heart.
Suddenly they race and chase;
but these are not what my heart seeks.
Old age is gradually approaching;
I fear that a fine name will not be established.
In the morning I drink the fallen dew of the magnolias;
in the evening I eat the fallen petals of the Qiūjú.
If my feelings are truly beautiful and firm;
what does it matter if I am thin and hungry?
I take tree roots to bind the Chǎi;
and string the fallen blossoms of the Bìlì.
I straighten the Jùnguì to weave with the Huì;
twining the Húshéng into long strands.
Indeed, I follow the model of the former sages;
it is not what the current world wears.
Although I do not fit in with the people of today;
I wish to follow the legacy of Péng Xián.
I heave a long sigh and hide my tears;
grieving for the many hardships of human life.
Although I love cultivation and have restrained myself;
I am rebuked in the morning and cast aside by evening.
They cast me aside for my sash of Huì;
and further for my gathering of Chǎi.
But this is what my heart approves of;
even if I die nine deaths, I shall not regret it.
I resent the Língxiū for being so aloof;
to the end, he does not examine people's hearts.
The many women envy my Éméi;
slandering me, saying I am wanton.
Truly, it is the skill of the current age;
to ignore the square and compass and change the measure.
Turning from the plumb-line to pursue the crooked;
competing to make flattery the rule.
Troubled and dejected, I am lost;
I alone am in distress at this time!
I would rather die suddenly and pass away;
than endure to take such a shape!
The bird of prey does not flock;
it has been so since former times.
How can the square and the circle fit together?
Who can live in peace following different ways?
Bowing the heart and suppressing the will;
bearing blame and enduring insults.
Holding to purity and dying for uprightness;
this is truly what the former sages valued.
Regretting that I did not observe the path I chose,
I linger and stand, about to turn back.
I turn my carriage to return to the road,
before my straying has led me too far.
I walk my horse along the orchid-covered bank,
and gallop to the pepper hill to take my rest.
Advancing, I found no entry and met with blame,
so I withdraw to mend again my former garments.
I tailor water chestnuts and lotus leaves for my coat,
and gather hibiscus petals for my skirt.
If no one understands me, let it be,
so long as my heart is truly fragrant.
I wear my cap high and towering,
and my pendants long and shimmering.
Fragrance and luster are mingled together,
yet my bright inner quality is not yet diminished.
Suddenly I look back and let my eyes wander,
intending to travel and observe the four wild frontiers.
My pendants are magnificent with many ornaments,
their fragrance is rich and ever more apparent.
Every person has what they enjoy in life,
I alone love cultivation as my constant rule.
Though my body be torn apart, I would not change,
how could my heart be made to repent?
Nǚ Xū in her distress
repeatedly rebuked me, saying:
"Gǔn was obstinate and upright and so lost his life,
in the end he died young in the wilds of Yǔ."
"Why are you so outspoken and fond of cultivation,
possessing alone these beautiful qualities?"
"Caltrops, green-briars, and cockleburs fill the room,
yet you keep apart and will not wear them."
"One cannot go from door to door to explain to the crowd,
who will ever examine our inner feelings?"
"The world acts together and loves cliques,
why are you so solitary and will not listen to me?"
Following the moderation of the former sages,
I sigh, having endured this with a heavy heart.
Crossing the Yuán and Xiāng rivers, I travel south,
to approach Chóng Huá and state my case.
Qǐ performed the Jiǔ Biàn and Jiǔ Gē,
and the Xià kings indulged in pleasure and gave themselves up to license.
Not considering difficulties or planning for the future,
the five brothers thus lost their home and lane.
Yì wandered excessively and lived for the hunt,
he loved to shoot the great foxes.
Chaos and excess surely seldom have a good end,
and Zhuó then coveted his household.
Āo put on his strong armor,
he indulged his lusts and would not restrain himself.
Daily he enjoyed himself and forgot his duties,
and so his head fell to the ground.
Xià Jié constantly went against what was right,
and thus he met with disaster.
Sovereign Xīn pickled and minced his subjects,
so the lineage of Yīn did not endure.
Tāng and Yǔ were solemn and reverent,
the Zhōu kings followed the Way without error.
They promoted the worthy and gave office to the capable,
they followed the plumb line and were not biased.
August Heaven has no favorites,
it observes people's virtue and grants them help.
Only the sages with their splendid deeds
could thus possess this land below.
Looking before and glancing behind,
I observe the ultimate plans of men.
Who that is not righteous can be employed?
What that is not good can be followed?
I risk my life and face death,
yet looking back at my beginning, I still have no regret.
To force a square peg into a round hole without measuring,
is why the former worthies were pickled and minced.
I sigh and sob in my distress,
lamenting that I live in an improper time.
I take up the soft orchids to wipe my tears,
which wet my lapel in a stream.
I kneel and spread my robes to state my case,
clearly I have attained this centered uprightness.
I harness a team of jade hornless dragons to pull my phoenix-chariot,
suddenly, amidst dust and wind, I begin my ascent.
In the morning I set off from Cāng Wú,
in the evening I arrive at Xuán Pǔ.
I wish to linger a while at these divine gates,
but the sun is hurried and about to set.
I order Xī Hé to slow the pace,
to look toward Yān Zī and not draw near.
The way is long and far-reaching,
I will go up and down to seek my goal.
I water my horses at the Xián Chí,
I tie my reins to the Fú Sāng tree.
I break a branch of the Ruò tree to brush against the sun,
for a while I wander and linger.
I send Wàng Shū ahead as my precursor,
I send Fēi Lián behind to follow in haste.
Lúan and Phoenixes clear the way before me,
the Master of Thunder tells me that things are not yet ready.
I order the phoenixes to fly aloft,
and continue through day and night.
Whirlwinds gather and separate,
leading the clouds and rainbows to welcome me.
They flock and crowd together, parting and joining,
in shimmering colors they move up and down.
I order the Heavenly Porter to open the gates,
but he leans against the Chāng Hé gates and stares at me.
The light grows dim as the day is about to end,
I tie together dark orchids and linger there.
The world is turbid and does not distinguish,
it loves to hide beauty out of jealousy.
In the morning I will cross the Bái Shuǐ,
I climb Làng Fēng and tether my horses.
Suddenly I look back and shed tears,
mourning that on the high hill there is no lady.
Suddenly I wander to this Spring Palace,
I break off a jade branch to add to my pendants.
Before its blossoms have fallen,
I look for a lady below to whom I may give them.
I order Fēng Lóng to ride the clouds,
to search for the dwelling of Fù Fēi.
I unfasten my sash-pendant as a token of my word,
I order Jiǎn Xiū to be my intermediary.
Things shift and change in a flurry,
suddenly she is headstrong and difficult to move.
In the evening she returns to stay at Qióng Shí,
in the morning she washes her hair in the Wěi Pán.
She guards her beauty with arrogance,
daily she enjoys herself in excessive wandering.
Though she is truly beautiful, she lacks propriety,
so I turn away from her and seek elsewhere.
I look and observe the four extremes,
I travel all through the heavens and then descend.
I gaze at the towering Yáo Tái,
and see the beautiful lady of Yǒu Sōng.
I order the Zhèn bird to be my matchmaker,
but the Zhèn tells me she is not good.
The male pigeon flies away crying,
but I still dislike its craftiness.
My heart wavers and is full of doubt,
I wish to go myself but it is not proper.
The Phoenix has already received the betrothal gifts,
I fear that Gāo Xīn has preceded me.
I wish to find a distant resting place but have nowhere to settle,
for a while I drift and wander.
While Shǎo Kāng is not yet married,
there remain the two girls of the Yáo clan from Yǒu Yú.
The intermediary is weak and the matchmaker is clumsy,
I fear that the words of introduction will not be firm.
The times are turbid and envious of the worthy,
people love to hide beauty and speak of evil.
The inner chambers are deep and far away,
and the wise king does not awaken.
I harbor my feelings and cannot express them,
how can I bear to live with this until the end of time!
I seek the jasper grass and bamboo splints,
and order Líng Fēn to perform a divination for me.
He said: "Two beauties must surely join together,
who that is truly cultivated would not desire it?"
"Think of the vastness of the Jiǔ Zhōu,
is it only here that there are ladies?"
He said: "Strive to go far away and have no doubt,
who that seeks beauty would let you go?"
"In what place is there no fragrant grass?
Why must you cling to your old home?"
"The times are dark and dazzlingly confused,
who will examine our beauty or ugliness?"
"People's likes and dislikes differ,
but this faction is uniquely strange."
"Every house wears mugwort to fill their waist,
they say that dark orchids should not be worn as pendants."
"They look at plants and trees but fail to distinguish,
how could they appreciate the beauty of a fine gem?"
"They take dung and soil to fill their sachets,
they say that the pepper plant is not fragrant.
I wished to follow the auspicious divination of Líng Fēn,
but my heart hesitated and was full of doubt.
Wū Xián was to descend in the evening;
I prepared pepper and rice grains to invite him.
A hundred spirits descended in a vast shadow,
the crowds from Jiǔ Yí came to welcome them.
Their divine light flashed with brilliant splendor,
and they told me of auspicious portents.
They said: "Strive to ascend and descend,
seeking those who share the same standards."
Tāng and Yǔ sought their matches with reverence,
and Zhì and Gāo Yáo achieved harmony with them.
If one's inner heart truly loves cultivation,
why must one rely on a matchmaker?
Yuè worked as a laborer at Fù Yán,
but Wǔ Dīng employed him without hesitation.
Lǚ Wàng wielded a butcher’s knife,
until he met Zhōu Wén and was raised to power.
Nìng Qì sang his songs of labor,
and Qí Huán heard them and made him an advisor.
Before the years have grown too late,
and while the season is not yet over,
I fear the shrike will sing too early,
causing all the flowers to lose their fragrance.
How magnificent is this jade pendant!
Yet the crowd gathers to obscure its light.
These partisans are truly untrustworthy;
I fear that out of jealousy they will break it.
The times are chaotic and ever-changing;
how can I linger here any longer?
The orchid and angelica have changed and are no longer fragrant;
the sweet flag and melilot have turned to weeds.
Why is it that the fragrant herbs of the past
have now become nothing more than mugwort?
Could there be any other reason
than the neglect of self-cultivation?
I thought the orchid could be relied upon,
but it has no substance and only a fair appearance.
It cast away its beauty to follow the vulgar,
just to be counted among the common crowd.
Pepper is purely sycophantic and insolent,
and dogwood wishes to fill the perfume bags.
Since they focus only on gaining entry and advancement,
how could they ever respect true fragrance?
Truly the worldly customs follow the current;
who then can remain unchanged?
Seeing that even pepper and orchid are like this,
what then of the jiēchē and jiānglí?
Only this pendant of mine is worthy of esteem;
I have cherished its beauty through all these years.
Its fragrance is rich and hard to diminish,
its scent has not faded to this day.
I regulate my conduct to amuse myself,
and roam about to seek a lady.
While my adornments are still in their prime,
I shall travel and observe all above and below.
Since Líng Fēn has given me an auspicious omen,
I choose a propitious day to set out.
I break a branch of jasper for my meat,
and grind fine jade for my grain.
Harnessing flying dragons to my chariot,
I decorate it with jasper and ivory.
How can hearts that have drifted apart be united?
I shall travel far to distance myself.
I turn my path toward Kūnlún,
the road is long and I wander far and wide.
I raise the cloudy banners to darken the light,
and the jade bells on the harness tinkle.
In the morning I depart from Tiānjīn,
and by evening I reach the western limits.
Phoenixes bear the flags on their wings,
soaring high with orderly grace.
Suddenly I cross these shifting sands,
and follow the Chì Shuǐ, wandering at ease.
I command the water dragons to bridge the ford,
and bid Xī Huáng to ferry me across.
The road is long and full of hardships;
I send my many chariots ahead by side paths.
I pass by Bùzhōu and turn to the left,
pointing toward the Xī Hǎi for our rendezvous.
I marshal my chariots by the thousand,
their jade hubs aligned as they gallop together.
I drive eight dragons that wind and coil,
bearing cloud-banners that stream in the wind.
I curb my will and slow my pace,
but my spirit soars into the far distance.
I play the Jiǔ Gē and dance the Sháo,
borrowing the day for a moment’s pleasure.
I ascend the brilliant splendor of the heavens,
and suddenly look down upon my old home.
My groom is sad and my horses yearn for home,
they look back and will not go on.
Envoi:
It is over!
There is no one in the kingdom, no one knows me;
why then should I pine for the old capital?
Since no one is worthy of building a beautiful government with me,
I shall follow Péng Xián to where he dwells.
On an auspicious day and a propitious hour,
reverently I shall please the Shàng Huáng.
I grasp my long sword by its jade hilt,
and the jade pendants tinkle and chime.
Upon the jasper mats and jade weights,
will you not take up the jade-like blossoms?
Meats with melilot are steamed on orchid leaves,
I offer cassia wine and pepper broth.
Raise the drumsticks and strike the drums;
with slow rhythms and peaceful songs,
set out the flutes and zithers for a grand chorus.
The spirit moves with grace in beautiful attire,
the fragrance fills the hall.
The five notes blend in rich harmony,
may the Lord be joyful and serene.
Bathing in orchid water and washing with fragrance,
wearing clothes of many colors like blossoms.
The spirit coils and remains,
shining with a brilliance that never ends.
Residing in the Shòu Gōng,
shining with the sun and moon.
Riding a dragon chariot in imperial robes,
roaming and wandering for a while.
The spirit descends in majesty,
then rises like a whirlwind into the clouds.
Looking over Jì Zhōu and beyond,
traversing the four seas without end.
Thinking of the Lord, I sigh deeply;
my heart is heavy with distress.
The Lord does not come, but hesitates;
for whom do you linger on the middle isle?
Beautiful and delicate, well-adorned,
I ride swiftly in my cassia boat.
Let the Yuán and Xiāng have no waves,
let the waters of the Jiāng flow peacefully.
I watch for the Lord to return,
for whom do I play the pipes in longing?
I drive flying dragons on a journey north,
turning my path toward Dòngtíng.
Fig-leaves form the roof and melilot the curtains,
sweet flags are the oars and orchids the banners.
Gazing at the distant shores of Cènyáng,
I cross the Great River, manifesting my spirit.
My spirit is manifested but has not reached its goal,
Chàn Yuàn sighs deeply for my sake.
My tears flow in a stream,
secretly pining for the Lord in sorrow.
With cassia oars and orchid sweeps,
breaking the ice and through the piled snow.
Gathering fig-leaves in the water,
plucking lotuses from the treetops.
When hearts are not in accord, the matchmaker labors in vain;
if love is not deep, it is easily severed!
The water flows shallow over the stones,
flying dragons soar and flutter.
Disloyalty in friendship leads to long resentment;
breaking a promise, you tell me you have no time.
In the morning I gallop along the river banks,
in the evening I rest on the northern islet.
Birds nest on the roof,
water circles the hall below.
I cast my jade ring into the river,
and leave my pendant on the shores of the Lǐ.
I gather pollia on the fragrant isle,
to give to the lady below.
Time once gone cannot be regained,
I shall wander and roam at ease.
The Dì Zǐ descends to the Běi Zhǔ,
eyes gazing afar, filling me with sorrow.
Gently blows the autumn wind,
Dòngtíng's waves swell and the leaves fall.
Treading on white duckweed, I gaze into the distance,
making a tryst with the beauty to spread the mats at dusk.
Birds flock among the duckweed,
why is the fishing net up in the trees?
The Yuán has angelica, the Lǐ has orchids,
I think of the lord but dare not speak.
Dazed and lost, I look afar,
watching the flowing water murmur along.
Why is the deer in the courtyard?
Why is the dragon at the water's edge?
In the morning, I gallop my horse along the Jiāng bank,
in the evening, I cross to the western shore.
I hear the beauty calling me,
I will drive my chariot and we shall depart together.
I will build a house in the water,
thatching it with a roof of lotus leaves.
Walls of iris and a courtyard of purple,
scattering fragrant pepper to make the hall.
Cassia for the pillars, orchids for the rafters,
magnolia for the lintels, angelica for the rooms.
Weaving creeping fig to make the curtains,
splitting orchids for the screens already set.
White jade for the weights,
scattering stone orchids for fragrance.
Thatching the lotus house with angelica,
binding it with sweet basil.
Gathering a hundred herbs to fill the courtyard,
setting fragrances at the gate.
The spirits of Jiǔyí come in a crowd to welcome,
the divine ones arrive like clouds.
I toss my sleeve into the Jiāng,
I leave my garment at the Lǐ shore.
I pluck sweet flag from the islet,
to give to the one far away.
Time cannot be easily grasped,
for now, I wander and linger in leisure!
Autumn orchids and clover
grow in rows below the hall.
Green leaves and white blossoms,
their fragrance strikes me.
People have their own beautiful children,
why does the Sūn suffer in sorrow?
Autumn orchids so lush and green,
green leaves and purple stems.
The hall is full of beauties,
but suddenly our eyes meet alone.
Coming in without a word, leaving without a goodbye,
riding the whirlwind and carrying cloud banners.
No sorrow is greater than parting in life,
no joy is greater than a new acquaintance.
Wearing lotus clothes and an orchid belt,
coming suddenly and departing quickly.
Staying the night at the Dì's outskirts,
whom do you wait for at the edge of the clouds?
Wandering with you across the Jiǔhé,
a storm rises and the water waves.
Bathing with you in the Xiánchí,
drying your hair at Yáng zhī Ā.
Looking for the beauty who has not come,
facing the wind, I sing a loud song in a daze.
Peacock canopy and kingfisher banners,
ascending the Nine Heavens to stroke the comet.
Grasping a long sword and protecting the young,
you alone are fit to be the judge of the people.
There seems to be someone in the mountain fold,
clad in creeping fig and belted with dodder.
With a look in the eye and a lovely smile,
you admire me for my grace.
Riding a red leopard, followed by a striped lynx,
a magnolia chariot and cassia banners.
Clad in stone orchid and belted with sweet basil,
plucking fragrances to give to the beloved.
I live in the dark bamboo, never seeing the sky,
the road is hard and dangerous, I come late.
Standing alone on the mountaintop,
clouds surge and gather below.
Dark and gloomy, the day is like night,
the east wind blows and the spirits send rain.
Lingering for the Líng Xiū, I forget to return,
the year is late, who will make me bloom?
Gathering the Sān Xiù in the mountains,
rocks are piled and vines are tangled.
Resenting the lord, sadly forgetting to return,
you think of me but have no time.
The person in the mountain is like sweet flag,
drinking from rock springs, shaded by pines and cedars.
You think of me, but doubt arises.
Thunder rumbles and the rain is dark,
monkeys chirp and apes howl at night.
The wind soughs and the trees rustle,
thinking of the lord, I suffer in vain.
In my youth, I loved this strange dress,
even in old age, this has not faded.
Wearing a long sword, bright and tall,
a Qièyún cap, towering high.
Clad in bright pearls and wearing precious gems.
The world is turbid and knows me not,
I soar high without looking back.
Driving green dragons and pulled by white hornless dragons,
I wander with Chónghuá in the Yáo zhī Pǔ.
Ascending Kūnlún and eating jade blossoms,
with a lifespan equal to Heaven and Earth,
and light matching the Sun and Moon.
Pitying that the Nán Yí know me not,
at dawn, I cross the Jiāng and Xiāng.
Climbing Èzhǔ and looking back,
sighing at the lingering wind of autumn and winter.
Walking my horse on the mountain bank,
resting my carriage at Fānglín.
Taking a boat up the Yuán,
keeping pace with the Wú oars to strike the waves.
The boat lingers and does not advance,
caught in the swirling water, stalled.
At dawn, I set out from Wǎngzhǔ,
at evening, I stay at Chényáng.
If my heart is upright and straight,
what harm is there in being remote?
Entering Xùpǔ, I hesitate and wander,
lost, not knowing where to go.
Deep forests are dark and gloomy,
the dwelling place of monkeys and apes.
Mountains are steep and high, blocking the sun,
below is dark and rainy.
Sleet and snow fall without bound,
clouds are thick and touch the eaves.
Pitying my life of no joy,
dwelling alone in the mountains.
I cannot change my heart to follow the custom,
I will surely end in sorrow and poverty.
Jiēyú shaved his head,
Sānghù walked naked.
The loyal are not necessarily employed,
the worthy are not necessarily used.
Wǔ Zǐ met with disaster,
Bǐ Gān was minced into meat.
It was the same in previous generations,
why should I resent the people of today?
I will follow the straight path without hesitation,
I will surely remain in darkness all my life.
Qū Yuán had been in exile for three years,
and was unable to see the King again.
Though he exhausted his wisdom and fulfilled his loyalty,
he was obstructed and obscured by slander.
His heart was troubled and his mind in turmoil,
not knowing which path to follow.
Thus he went to see the Great Diviner Zhèng Zhānyǐn
and said:
"I have a doubt,
and I wish for you, Master, to resolve it."
Zhānyǐn then straightened the stalks and brushed the tortoise shell,
saying:
"What do you wish to instruct me with?"
Qū Yuán said:
"Should I be sincere and earnest,
simple and loyal?
Or should I be busy with social greetings and laboring to welcome guests,
so as to be without end?
Should I weed the brush and weeds
to labor at farming?
Or should I associate with great men
to establish my name?
Should I speak directly without concealment,
thereby endangering myself?
Or should I follow the vulgar in wealth and honor
to live stealthily?
Should I be transcendent and soar high
to preserve my true nature?
Or should I be sycophantic and cowering,
forcedly smiling and fawning,
to serve a woman?
Should I be incorruptible, pure, and upright
to keep myself clean?
Or should I be slippery and glib,
as smooth as grease or soft leather,
to polish the pillars?
Should I be high-spirited like a thousand-li colt?
Or should I float aimlessly like a duck on the water,
rising and falling with the waves,
stealthily preserving my body?
Should I match the yoke with the Qíjì?
Or should I follow in the tracks of a hack?
Should I spread my wings beside the Huánghú?
Or should I compete for food with chickens and ducks?
Which of these is auspicious and which is ominous?
What should be discarded and what followed?
The world is turbid and not pure;
a cicada's wing is considered heavy,
while thirty thousand catties are considered light.
The Huángzhōng is discarded and destroyed,
while clay pots thunder like drums.
Slanderers are in high favor,
while worthy men have no name.
Alas, I remain silent!
Who knows my integrity and purity?"
Zhānyǐn then set down the stalks and excused himself,
saying:
"A foot has its shortcomings,
an inch has its strengths.
Things have their insufficiencies,
wisdom has its obscurities.
Divination has its limits,
spirits have what they cannot penetrate.
Use your own heart,
follow your own intent.
Truly, the tortoise and stalks cannot know this matter."
After Qū Yuán was exiled,
he wandered among the pools of the river,
chanting as he walked along the marsh bank.
His complexion was haggard
and his form was withered.
A fisherman saw him and asked,
saying:
"Are you not the Sānlǘ Dàfu?
For what reason have you come to this?"
Qū Yuán said:
"The whole world is turbid and I alone am pure;
everyone is drunk and I alone am sober;
therefore I was exiled."
The fisherman said:
"The Sage does not stagnate in things,
but is able to shift with the world.
If the whole world is turbid,
why not churn up its mud and raise its waves?
If everyone is drunk,
why not eat the dregs
and drink the thin wine?
Why think so deeply and soar so high,
only to bring exile upon yourself?"
Qū Yuán said:
"I have heard that
one who has just washed his hair must flick his cap;
one who has just bathed must shake his clothes.
How can one, with a body so pure,
receive the filth of things!
I would rather leap into the Xiāng current
and be buried in the bellies of the river fish;
how could I, with such brilliant whiteness,
be covered by the dust of the vulgar world!"
The fisherman smiled faintly,
beat his oar, and departed.
Then he sang:
"If the waters of the Cānglàng are clear,
they can wash my hat strings;
if the waters of the Cānglàng are turbid,
they can wash my feet."
Then he left
and spoke no more with him.
How sorrowful is the spirit of autumn!
Desolate, as the plants and trees shake, shed their leaves, and wither.
Forlorn, as if on a long journey,
climbing mountains and looking over waters to see someone off on their return.
Vast and empty, the sky is high and the air is clear;
quiet and deep, the floodwaters recede and the streams turn clear.
Sadness and sighs increase as the slight chill strikes a person;
distraught and dejected, I leave the old and approach the new.
Disheartened, the poor scholar loses his position and his mind is restless.
Abandoned, the traveler is without friends.
Melancholy, I pity myself in private.
Swallows flutter as they bid farewell and return;
cicadas are lonely and without sound.
Wild geese cry in unison as they travel south;
the Kūnjī chirps and cries in sorrow.
Alone, I stay awake until dawn,
grieving for the cricket's nightly journey.
Time flows on and has passed its midpoint,
yet I linger on with nothing achieved.
Sorrowful and distressed, I dwell alone in the vastness;
there is a beautiful person whose heart is not at ease.
Having left my village and home to become a distant guest,
soaring and wandering, where do I alight now?
My thoughts are devoted to the Lord and cannot be changed;
the Lord does not know, so what can be done!
Harboring resentment and accumulating thoughts,
my heart is so troubled that I forget to eat.
I wish for one meeting to speak my intent,
but the Lord's heart is different from mine.
The carriage is prepared and suddenly goes away;
unable to see him, my heart is grieved.
I lean against the carriage rail and sigh deeply;
my tears flow steadily and drench the crossbar.
My high spirits are exhausted and I have gained nothing;
within, I am confused and bewildered.
When will this private self-pity ever end?
My heart beats with sincerity and uprightness.
Huángtiān divides the four seasons equally,
yet I alone secretly grieve for this freezing autumn.
Since the white dew has fallen upon the hundred grasses,
the sterculia and catalpa trees have suddenly withered and scattered.
Leaving the brilliance of the white sun,
I enter the endlessness of the long night.
Leaving the fragrant lushness in its prime,
I am withered and bowed by sorrow and grief.
Since autumn first warned with white dew,
winter further commands with severe frost.
I recall the grand warmth of Mèngxià,
yet now I am frustrated and hidden away.
The leaves are withered and colorless;
the branches are tangled and crisscrossed.
My countenance is overflowing with weariness;
the stems seem to wither and turn yellow.
The falling leaves are so pitiful;
my form is wasted away and bruised.
Seeing how they are jumbled and about to fall,
I regret that they have lost their time and are out of place.
I take up the reins and slacken the pace,
wandering for a while to linger.
The year passes hurriedly toward its end;
I fear my life will not last.
I lament that my life is ill-timed,
encountering this world of turmoil.
Quiet and leisurely, I lean alone;
the cricket chirps in this western hall.
My heart is fearful and trembling;
why are my worries so multifaceted?
I look up at the bright moon and sigh deeply,
walking among the stars until the utmost light of dawn.
I secretly grieve that the Huì flowers once blossomed,
in profusion and beauty within the capital chambers.
Why did the blossoms bear no fruit,
following the wind and rain to be blown away?
I thought the Lord alone would wear this Huì,
but alas, it is no different from the common flowers.
Lamenting that my singular thoughts cannot reach you,
I shall leave the Lord and soar on high.
My heart pities the wretched sorrow;
I wish for one meeting to have clarity.
I dread a parting in life when there is no cause for resentment,
while within my heart is knotted with grief and increasing pain.
How could I not be full of anxious longing for the Lord?
But the Lord's gates are ninefold.
Fierce dogs bark and snarl to meet me;
the passes and bridges are closed and impassable.
Huáng Tiān overflows with autumn rains;
when will Hòu Tǔ ever be dry?
Alone and desolate I stay in this waterless land,
looking up at the floating clouds and sighing forever.
Why are the customs of the age so clever and crafty,
turning their backs on the plumb line to change their ways?
They cast aside the Qí jì and do not ride it,
but whip the Nú dài to take the road.
Is it that the present age has no Qí jì?
Truly, there is no one who can drive them well.
Seeing that those who hold the reins are not the right men,
the colts leap and gallop far away.
Wild ducks and geese all peck at the grain and algae,
while the Fèng soars ever higher and drifts away.
Like a round peg in a square hole,
I surely know they are discordant and difficult to fit together.
All the birds have a place to perch,
but the Fèng alone wanders and has no place to alight.
I wish to hold a gag in my mouth and say nothing,
having always received the Lord’s deep kindness.
Tài Gōng reached ninety before he achieved glory;
truly, he had not met his match before.
To where should the Qí jì return?
Where should the Fèng huáng rest?
Changing the old and altering customs, the age decays;
the physiognomists of today choose only the fat.
The Qí jì hides and is not seen;
the Fèng huáng flies high and does not descend.
Even birds and beasts still know to cherish virtue;
why say that a worthy scholar should not dwell here?
The Qí jì does not rush forward to seek service;
the Fèng is not greedy for food to eat recklessly.
Since the Lord casts me far away and does not observe me,
though I wish to be loyal, how can I?
I wish to be silent and break off all connections,
yet I secretly dare not forget the great virtue of the past.
Alone I grieve, and my sorrow harms me;
my bottled-up resentment—where will it end?
Since my youth, I have been pure and incorruptible,
practicing righteousness without ceasing.
Possessing this abundant virtue,
I am dragged down by the vulgar and sullied.
Above, there is no one to examine this abundant virtue,
and I suffer long in parting and misery.
Dì told Wū Yáng:
"There is a man below,
I wish to help him.
His soul is scattered;
divine for him and give it back!"
Wū Yáng replied:
"Lord of Dreams!
The commands of Shàng Dì are hard to follow!
If I must divine and give it back,
I fear that later he will decline,
and will not be able to use Wū Yáng again."
Thereupon he went down and summoned:
O soul, come back!
Leave the Lord's constant frame;
why go to the four quarters?
Abandon the Lord's joyful dwelling
and meet with those ill omens.
O soul, come back!
The East cannot be trusted.
There are giants a thousand fathoms tall
who seek only for souls.
Ten suns come out by turns,
melting metal and stones.
They are all used to it,
but if the soul goes there, it will surely dissolve.
Come back! Come back!
It cannot be trusted.
O soul, come back!
The South cannot be stayed in.
There are people with tattooed foreheads and black teeth
who get human flesh to sacrifice
and make a hash of the bones.
Venomous snakes are thick as grass,
and the giant foxes roam for a thousand miles.
They come and go in a flash,
swallowing men to nourish their hearts.
Come back! Come back!
You cannot linger there long.
O soul, come back!
In the West are dangers:
shifting sands for a thousand miles.
You will be whirled into the Léi Yuān,
shattered and scattered, unable to stop.
If by luck you escape,
beyond is a vast emptiness.
Red ants are like elephants;
black wasps are like gourds.
The five grains do not grow;
only rank weeds are for food.
The soil there rots people;
seek for water and none can be found.
You will wander with nothing to lean on,
a vastness without end.
Come back! Come back!
I fear you will bring harm upon yourself.
O soul, come back!
The North cannot be stayed in.
Layered ice rises high,
and flying snow falls for a thousand miles.
Come back! Come back!
You cannot stay there long.
O soul, come back!
O Lord, do not climb to Heaven.
Tigers and leopards guard the nine gates,
pecking and harming the people from below.
There is a being with nine heads
who uproots nine thousand trees.
Jackals and wolves with vertical eyes
wander to and fro in crowds.
They hang men up for sport
and throw them into deep abysses.
Only after reporting to Dì
can they finally sleep.
Come back! Come back!
If you go, I fear you will peril your body.
O soul, come back!
O Lord, do not go down to this Yōu Dū.
Tǔ Bó has nine coils,
his horns are sharp and menacing.
With a thick back and bloody thumbs,
he chases people swiftly.
He has three eyes and a tiger's head,
his body is like that of a bull.
These all find human flesh sweet.
Come back! Come back!
I fear you will bring disaster upon yourself.
O Soul, come back!
Enter the Xiūmén gate.
The skilled Shaman calls you,
walking backward to lead the way.
With bamboo baskets of Qín and silk threads of Qí,
and netting of fine Zhèng floss.
All the implements for summoning are prepared,
and long cries are made.
O Soul, come back!
Return to your old abode.
In heaven and earth and the four directions,
there are many who are wicked and treacherous.
Your chamber is prepared as in life,
quiet, peaceful, and still.
High halls and deep apartments,
with railings and tiered balconies.
Terraced towers and high pavilions,
overlooking the high mountains.
Latticed doors with red decorations,
carved with interlocking squares.
In winter there is warmth;
in summer the rooms are cool.
River valleys wind and turn,
their waters flowing with a murmur.
The bright wind stirs the Huì orchids,
and wafts over the noble Lán.
Crossing the hall and entering the inner sanctum,
upon red-matted floors.
In the polished stone room are kingfisher ornaments,
hanging on curved jade hooks.
Bedspreads of kingfisher feathers and pearls,
gleaming with uniform brilliance.
Soft silks and fine fabrics brush the walls,
and gauze canopies are spread.
Woven ribbons and patterned silks,
tied with fine Qí and Huáng jades.
Within the rooms, the sights
are full of rare and strange treasures.
Orchis-oil lamps and bright candles,
providing a splendid atmosphere.
Twice eight maidens wait to serve you at night,
taking their turns in succession.
The virtuous daughters of the Jiǔhóu
are many and agile.
Their elaborate hairstyles are of many styles,
filling the entire palace.
Their beauty and grace are peerless,
gentle through the generations.
With delicate faces and firm characters,
they are full of deep feeling.
Beautiful faces and elegant bearing
fill the inner chambers.
With moth-eyebrows and long, glancing eyes,
their gaze flashes with light.
With delicate faces and smooth skin,
they cast lingering looks.
In detached pavilions and behind long curtains,
they wait for you in your leisure.
Kingfisher curtains and emerald canopies
adorn the high hall.
Red walls and cinnabar panels,
with beams of black jade.
Looking up at the carved rafters,
painted with dragons and snakes.
Sitting in the hall or leaning on the railing,
overlooking the winding pond.
The lotuses are just beginning to bloom,
mixed with water-lilies and pads.
Purple-stemmed water-shields
form patterns on the waves.
With robes of patterned leopard skin,
attendants wait by the sloping banks.
The carriages are lowered,
and footmen and horsemen are lined up.
Thick orchids grow by the doors,
and jade trees form the hedges.
O Soul, come back!
Why stay so far away?
Your family and clan are gathered,
and the food is prepared in many ways.
Rice, broomcorn millet, early wheat, and barley,
mixed with yellow millet.
Bitter, salty, and sour flavors,
with pungent and sweet ones added.
Tendons of fat oxen,
tender and fragrant.
Harmonizing the sour and the bitter,
stews of Wú are served.
Stewed turtle and roasted lamb,
with sugar-cane juice.
Sour crane and thick wild duck stew,
fried wild geese and cranes.
Steamed chicken and turtle soup,
strong-tasting but not cloying.
Honeyed cakes and fried rice-balls,
and malt-sugar sweets.
Jade-like wine and honeyed drinks
fill the winged goblets.
Strained of dregs and chilled,
the double-brewed wine is clear and cool.
Flower-decked ladles are laid out,
with jade-like nectar.
Return, return, to your old home,
where you will be honored without harm.
Before the delicacies are finished,
the female musicians are arranged.
They set up the bells and drums
and sing new songs.
"Crossing the River" and "Picking Caltrops,"
and "The Sun-drenched Lotus."
The beauties are now tipsy,
their rosy faces flushed with wine.
With amorous looks and darting eyes,
eyes like rippling waves.
Dressed in patterned silks and fine gauze,
beautiful but not bizarre.
Long hair and flowing tresses,
radiant and dazzling.
Twice eight in similar attire
begin the Zhèng dance.
Their sleeves cross like bamboo poles,
striking the mats as they descend.
Pipes and zithers join in wild harmony,
thundering on the sounding drums.
The palace courtyard shakes
to the Jī Chǔ music.
Songs of Wú and ballads of Cài,
played in the Dàlǚ mode.
Men and women sit together,
mixed without distinction.
They loosen their belts and hat-strings,
mingled in confusion.
Seductive beauties of Zhèng and Wèi
come and are presented together.
The climax of Jī Chǔ
is uniquely outstanding.
Bamboo pieces and ivory chessmen
are used for Liùbó.
Divided into sides, they advance together,
pressing each other hard.
Making an owl and winning the stake,
they shout for the five whites.
In the Jìn style of gambling,
they pass the bright day.
Striking the bells and shaking the jade-stand,
plucking the zithers of catalpa wood.
Wine and pleasure never cease,
sinking into day and night.
Orchis-oil lamps and bright candles,
ornate lamps are arranged.
Composing with deepest thought,
they borrow the fragrance of orchids.
Each person does their utmost
in these poems of one mind.
Having drunk the wine to our hearts' content,
we rejoice with our ancestors.
O Soul, come back!
Return to your old home.
The Envoi says:
As the year begins and spring breaks out,
I went racing on my southern journey.
Green duckweed leaves are level,
and white angelica grows.
The road runs through Lújiāng and to the left are the Chángbó thickets,
resting by the marshes and looking out at the vastness.
Teams of black and grey horses, a thousand chariots in line,
hanging fires blaze up, their dark faces steaming.
Walking or galloping, leading the race,
curbing the horses then turning the carriage to the right,
racing with the King to Mèng marsh, competing to be first,
the King himself shoots, striking the dark rhinoceros.
Bright day follows night, time does not linger,
marsh orchids cover the path, the way is overgrown.
Deep and clear are the waters of the Jiāng, with maples on the banks;
my eyes reach for a thousand miles, and my heart is grieved by spring.
O Soul, come back! Alas for the land of the South!
Cassia trees grow in clusters in the mountain depths,
twisting and winding, their branches intertwined.
The mountain air is heavy and thick, the rocks jagged and towering;
the valleys are steep and craggy, the waters surge with layered waves.
Gibbons and monkeys howl in groups, tigers and leopards roar.
Climbing the cassia branches, one lingers for a while.
The Wángsūn has gone wandering and not returned;
in spring, the grass grows lush and green.
At the year’s end, one is dejected and restless;
the cicadas chirp with a plaintive sound.
Vast and boundless,
the mountain paths are winding and steep.
The heart lingers in the desolate abyss.
Obscure and profound,
sorrowful and chilling.
Tigers and leopards dwell in caves.
In the thickets and deep forests, people shudder with fear.
Craggy peaks and jagged rocks, uneven and piled high.
Tree trunks entwine, forest trees are tangled and dense.
Green sedge mixes with various trees, and fán-grass ripples in the wind.
White deer, roe deer, and stags either leap or lean against one another.
They look towering and lofty,
cold and glistening.
Macaques, bears, and brown bears
yearn for their kind and feel sorrow.
Climbing the cassia branches, one lingers for a while.
Tigers and leopards fight, bears and brown bears roar;
birds and beasts are startled and lose their companions.
Wángsūn, come back!
In the mountains, one cannot stay for long.
The Crown Prince of Chǔ was ill,
and a guest from Wú went to visit him,
saying:
“I have humbly heard that the Prince’s jade-like body is unwell;
is there a slight improvement?”
The Prince said:
“I am exhausted!
I sincerely thank the guest.”
The guest then took the opportunity to say:
“Currently, the world is at peace,
and the four quarters are in harmony.
The Prince is in the prime of his years,
but I suspect he has long indulged in comfort and pleasure,
day and night without limit.
Evil qi has attacked and rebelled within,
becoming knotted and blocked inside.
It is chaotic and turbulent,
sighing with heavy intoxication.
Fearful and apprehensive,
you lie down but cannot close your eyes.
Empty within and hard of hearing,
you loathe the sound of human voices.
Your spirit is scattered and dissipated,
and a hundred illnesses are all arising.
Your sight and hearing are dazed and dazzled,
joy and anger are unbalanced.
If held for a long time without ceasing,
your great life will decline.
Does the Prince have these symptoms?”
The Prince said:
“I sincerely thank the guest.
Thanks to your concern,
it happens from time to time,
but it has not yet reached that point.”
The guest said:
“Now, the sons of the nobility
must reside in palaces and live in inner chambers,
with wet-nurses inside
and tutors outside,
having no place to socialize freely.
Their food and drink are lukewarm, pure, sweet, and crisp,
rich, thick, fatty, and heavy.
Their clothes are layered, fine, and warm,
hot as the summer heat.
Even if one had the hardness of metal or stone,
they would still be melted and dissolved.
How much more so for what lies between the muscles and bones?
Therefore it is said:
Indulging the desires of the eyes and ears
and allowing the limbs to be lazy
harms the harmony of the blood and vessels.
Furthermore, going out in chariots and entering in sedans
is called the machinery of paralysis;
living in secluded rooms and cool palaces
is called the intermediary of chills and fevers;
white teeth and beautiful brows
are called the axe that cuts down one’s nature;
sweet, crisp, fatty, and rich foods
are called medicine that rots the intestines.
Now the Prince’s skin is soft and delicate,
his four limbs are weak and weary,
his muscles and bones are slack,
his blood and vessels are overflowing and thin,
and his hands and feet are limp and useless.
Maidens of Yuè attend in front,
beauties of Qí serve behind.
Coming and going for banquets and strolls,
you indulge yourself in secluded rooms and private spaces.
This is like eating delicious poison
or playing with the claws and teeth of fierce beasts.
The origins of this are very deep and distant,
lingering for a long time without ceasing;
even if you had Biǎn Què to treat the internal
and Wū Xián to treat the external,
how could they reach it?
For one with the Prince’s illness,
it is only suitable to have the gentlemen of the world,
who are widely seen and of strong memory,
to wait for an opening to speak of matters,
to change your measures and alter your intent,
always without leaving your side,
acting as your wings.
Then how could the pleasures of indulgence,
the heart of vast dissipation,
and the will of escapism
ever arrive!”
The Prince said:
“Indeed.
Once the illness is gone,
I shall follow these words.”
The guest said:
“Now, for the Prince’s illness,
one need not use medicines, stones, needles, or moxibustion,
but can be cured by the explanation of essential words and wonderful principles.
Do you not wish to hear them?”
The Prince said:
“I wish to hear them.”
The guest said:
“The paulownia tree of Lóngmén
is a hundred feet high without branches.
Inside, its grain is knotted and coiled,
its roots spread out and separate.
Above are peaks of a thousand fathoms,
below it overlooks a valley of a hundred zhang.
Rushing currents and surging waves
further toss and churn it.
Its roots are half dead and half alive;
in winter, it is struck by fierce winds, sleet, and flying snow;
in summer, it is moved by thunder and lightning.
In the morning, orioles and gàndàn birds sing there;
in the evening, lonely females and lost birds roost there.
A solitary swan cries at dawn above it,
and a kūnjī bird wails and flies below it.
Thus, passing autumn and entering winter,
let the music master Qín Zhì cut and carve it to make a qín-zither,
using the silk of wild cocoons for strings,
the hook of an orphan for the bridge,
and the earrings of nine widows for the tuning pegs.
Let Shī Táng play the ‘Chàng’ melody,
and Bó Zǐyá sing for it.
The song says:
‘The wheat ears are lush and the pheasants fly at dawn,
facing the empty ravine and turning the back to the withered locust tree,
relying on the secluded region and overlooking the winding stream.’
When the flying birds hear it,
they fold their wings and cannot leave;
when the wild beasts hear it,
they droop their ears and cannot walk;
when the crawling insects and ants hear it,
they brace their mouths and cannot move forward.
This is the height of sorrow in the world;
can the Prince force himself to rise and listen to it?”
The Prince said:
“I am ill
and cannot.”
The guest said:
“The tender fat of grass-fed cattle,
seasoned with bamboo shoots and bulrushes.
The savory blend of a fat dog,
covered with mountain mushrooms.
Rice from the sprouts of Chǔ,
grain from Ānhú,
when balled it does not crumble,
but in one sip it dissolves.
Then have Yī Yǐn fry and boil it,
and Yì Yá season it.
Soft paws of the bear,
with a sauce of sháoyào.
Thinly sliced roasted meat,
and sashimi of fresh carp.
Perilla yellowed in autumn,
and vegetables gathered in the white dew.
Wine made from orchid blossoms,
poured to rinse the mouth.
A meal of mountain sorghum,
and the fetus of a farm-raised leopard.
Small bites and large gulps,
like hot water poured on snow.
This is the height of culinary excellence in the world;
can the Prince force himself to rise and taste it?”
The Prince said:
“I am ill
and cannot.”
The Guest said:
"A stallion from Zhōngdài,
harnessed to a carriage of the finest workmanship,
looks like a flying bird in front
and a Jùxū beast behind.
Having fed on young wheat and dwelt in comfort,
it is restless within and spirited without.
Fasten the strong reins
and follow the easy roads.
Then let Bólè judge its form,
Wáng Liáng and Zào Fù act as its drivers,
and Qín Quē and Lóu Jì serve as its attendants.
These two men—
if the horse bolts, they can stop it;
if the carriage overturns, they can right it.
Then, let it carry a weight of a thousand pieces of gold
and compete in a race of a thousand lǐ.
This is the most excellent steed in the world.
Can the Tàizǐ rouse himself to ride it?"
The Tàizǐ said:
"I am ill,
and cannot do so."
The Guest said:
"Having ascended the Jǐngyí Terrace,
looking south toward Jīngshān,
looking north toward Rǔhǎi,
with the River to the left and the Lake to the right,
such joy is unsurpassed.
Then let eloquent and learned scholars
trace the origins of mountains and rivers,
name all the plants and trees,
compare things and categorize matters,
and weave together refined phrases and similar ideas.
Wandering and observing,
then descending to set out wine in the Yúhuái Palace.
Connected corridors spread out in four directions,
the terrace city built in many layers,
a dazzling display of black and green.
Carriage paths cross diagonally,
the Huángchí winds and curves.
Mixed within are snowy egrets,
peacocks, and cranes,
young phoenixes and herons,
with kingfisher crests and purple tassels.
Hornless dragons are virtuously herded,
chirping in harmonious unison.
Sun-fish leap and bound,
spreading their wings and vibrating their scales.
Silent and secluded are the smartweeds and lilies,
with creeping herbs and fragrant licorice.
Young mulberries and river willows,
with white leaves and purple stems.
Seedling pines and camphor trees,
their branches reaching up to the heavens.
Firmiana and palm trees,
forming a forest as far as the eye can see.
All the fragrances are rich and heavy,
scattered by the five winds.
Leisurely and graceful,
waxing and waning with the Yin and Yang.
Seated in rows and drinking freely,
unbounded joy delights the heart.
Jǐng Chūn assists with the wine,
Dù Lián harmonizes the music.
Various flavors are presented together,
meats and delicacies are mixed and complete.
Refined colors delight the eyes,
flowing sounds please the ears.
Then, the surging winds of Jīchǔ are released,
and the bright music of Zhèng and Wèi is performed.
Let Xiān Shī, Zhēng Shū, Yáng Wén, Duàngān, Wú Wá, Lǘ Jū, and Fù Yú,
in mixed skirts and trailing ribbons,
with seductive eyes and hearts in accord,
waving like flowing waves,
mixing with the scent of sweet basil,
veiled in clear dust,
drenched in orchid perfumes,
dressed in beautiful robes to serve.
This is the most elegant, bright, and expansive joy in the world.
Can the Tàizǐ rouse himself to enjoy it?"
The Tàizǐ said:
"I am ill,
and cannot do so."
The Guest said:
"I shall harness Chíjì horses for the Tàizǐ,
hitch them to a carriage with flying bells,
and mount a team of sturdy stallions.
On the right, strong arrows of Xiàfú,
on the left, an engraved bow of Wūhào.
Wandering through the cloud-forests,
racing around the orchid marshes,
slowing the pace by the riverbanks.
Trampling the green duckweed,
riding the clear wind.
Cultivating the solar energy,
stirring the spring heart.
Chasing cunning beasts,
gathering swift birds.
Then, exhausting the talent of hounds and horses,
wearing out the feet of wild beasts,
and using to the full the wisdom and skill of driver and attendant.
Terrifying tigers and leopards,
frightening birds of prey.
Chasing horses with ringing bits,
fish leaping over elk horns.
Trampling through roaming muntjac and hares,
treading upon water deer and stags.
Sweat flows and foam falls,
beasts huddle in fear on the hills,
those that die without a wound,
are surely enough to fill the following carriages.
This is the most magnificent of hunts.
Can the Tàizǐ rouse himself to join it?"
The Tàizǐ said:
"I am ill,
and cannot do so."
Yet a vitality appeared between his eyebrows,
spreading upward,
nearly filling the Great Mansion.
Seeing the Tàizǐ’s pleased expression,
the Guest then pressed forward and said:
"Fires of the hunt approach the sky,
war chariots move like thunder.
Banners and flags wave majestically,
feathers and plumes are solemn and numerous.
Galloping and competing,
yearning for flavor and vying to be first.
The boundaries of the hunting grounds are vast,
their vistas having limits.
Pure and whole sacrificial animals,
are presented at the Duke's gate."
The Tàizǐ said:
"Excellent,
I wish to hear more of this."
The Guest said:
"It is not yet finished.
Then, in the dense forests and deep marshes,
where mist and clouds darken the view,
rhinoceroses and tigers emerge together.
Resolute warriors of great bravery,
strip to the waist to fight them hand-to-hand.
White blades glisten brightly,
spears and halberds interlace.
Catching and capturing to claim credit,
rewarded with gold and silk.
Spreading duckweed and wild grasses,
to make mats for the herdsmen.
Delicious wine and fine meats,
roasted, minced, and grilled delicacies,
are served to the guests.
Spirited feelings arise together,
moving the heart and startling the ears.
Sincerity that will never be regretted,
decisive in giving a promise.
Expressions of loyalty and trust,
carved as if on metal or stone.
Singing loudly and presenting chants,
'Ten thousand years without end!'
This is truly what the Tàizǐ would delight in,
can you rouse yourself to join it?"
The Tàizǐ said:
"I very much wish to follow,
but I only fear being a burden to the various gentlemen."
Yet he had the appearance of rising up.
The guest said:
"On the full moon of the eighth month,
with friends and brothers from the distant lands of the feudal lords,
we shall go together to observe the tidal bore at the Qūjiāng of Guǎnglíng.
Upon arriving, even before seeing the shape of the tide,
merely observing the force of the water’s reach
is enough to inspire a chilling awe.
Observing what it overrides and surpasses,
what it uproots and pulls out,
what it tosses and churns,
what it seethes and swirls,
and what it scours and purges;
though one may possess a clever mind and eloquent speech,
one surely cannot describe in detail how it comes to be so.
Trance-like and fleeting,
vast and trembling,
chaotic and surging,
sudden and bewildering,
abrupt and unconventional,
immense and boundless,
vast and empty.
It fixes its intent on Nánshān
and gazes across to the Dōnghǎi.
It arcs like a rainbow toward the azure sky,
stretching its thoughts to the very edge of the shore.
Its flow encompasses the infinite,
and it returns its spirit to the Mother of the Sun.
It plunges down, riding the current,
sometimes not knowing where it will stop.
Sometimes it turns in a tangled flow,
suddenly winding away and not returning.
Approaching the vermilion banks, it recedes far away,
leaving one's heart hollow and troubled, growing increasingly weary.
After the gathering disperses and dawn breaks,
one maintains one's inner mind and holds oneself firm.
Thereupon, it washes and scours the chest,
rinses and refines the five viscera,
cleanses the hands and feet,
and bathes the hair and teeth.
It casts away indolence and sloth,
pours out filth and turbidity,
resolves doubts and suspicions,
and illuminates the ears and eyes.
At such a time,
even those with long-standing illnesses or lingering maladies
will straighten their hunched backs or rise from lameness,
and the blind will see and the deaf will hear as they gaze upon it.
How much more so for those with mere slight frustrations
or those suffering from a heavy hangover!
Therefore, it is said that opening the eyes of the ignorant or dispelling confusion
are not even worth mentioning."
The Prince said:
"Excellent,
but what is the essence of the tide?"
The guest said:
"I do not recall exactly.
However, I have heard from my teacher
that there are three things which seem divine yet are not:
thunder that is heard for a hundred miles;
the river water flowing backward
as the sea tide rises;
and mountains breathing out clouds,
never ceasing day or night.
Overflowing and surging rapidly,
the waves swell and the tide rises.
When it first begins to rise,
it is vast and drenching,
like white egrets flying downward.
As it advances slightly,
it is immense and white,
like white carriages and white horses with their canopies spread wide.
Its waves surge and clouds scatter in chaos,
bustling like the three armies scrambling to pack their gear.
When it breaks forth from the sides and rushes up,
it is light and swift like light chariots commanding troops.
Six scaly dragons are harnessed,
following behind Tàibái.
Purely galloping like a vast rainbow,
following one after another in succession.
Solemn and dignified,
vigorous and strong,
numerous and orderly.
Formidable as layers of ramparts and fortresses,
it is crowded and chaotic like an army on the march.
With a thunderous roar and crashing sound,
it grinds and swirls, surging forth,
its force impossible to withstand.
Looking at its two flanks,
they are turbulent and roiling,
dark and surging with sudden impact,
striking above and pounding below.
It is like brave and powerful soldiers,
charging in anger without fear.
It tramples the walls and crashes into the fords,
exhausting every bend and following every cove,
leaping over banks to pursue further.
Those who encounter it die;
those who stand against it are destroyed.
It first erupts from the fords and shores of Huòwéi,
where roots and carriages are split as if in a valley.
It hovers and soars over the green bamboo,
biting on gags at Tánhuán.
It rests its whip at Wǔzǐ zhī Shān
and crosses the field of Gǔmǔ.
It surmounts Chì'àn,
sweeps past Fúsāng,
and rushes across like the path of thunder.
Truly exerting its martial prowess,
as if shaking with rage.
Turbid and surging,
its form is like galloping horses.
Roaring and swelling,
its sound is like thunderous drums.
Breaking out in a clattering rage,
it rises clearly and leaps across,
the great waves exerting their might,
engaging in battle at the mouth of the Jìjì.
Birds have no time to fly,
fish have no time to turn,
and beasts have no time to run.
Tangled and orderly,
waves surge and clouds are in chaos.
It washes over and takes Nánshān,
then strikes the northern shore from behind.
It overturns and damages the hills,
and levels the western bank.
Precarious and alarming,
it breaks down embankments and pools,
and only stops after the battle is won.
Then it flows with a gentle murmur,
spreading and scattering its spray.
At the height of its violent tyranny,
fish and turtles lose their footing,
tumbling and lying on their sides,
drifting and floating,
crawling and stretching endlessly.
Its divine and strange wonders
are beyond description.
It makes people fall prostrate,
feeling dizzy, dark, and mournful.
This is the world's most wondrous and bizarre sight;
can the Prince force himself to rise and view it?"
The Prince said:
"I am ill
and cannot."
The guest said:
"I shall present to the Prince men of methods and arts who possess talent and strategy,
such as Zhuāng Zhōu, Wèi Móu, Yáng Zhū, Mò Dí, Biàn Yuān, and Zhān Hé.
I will have them discuss the world's profound subtleties
and the principles of right and wrong for all things.
Kǒng and Lǎo will observe,
and Mèngzǐ will hold the counting rods to calculate it,
without a single error in ten thousand.
These are also the essential words and wonderful paths of the world;
would the Prince like to hear them?"
Thereupon the Prince leaned on his table and rose, saying:
"My doubts dissolve as if I have just heard the words of sages and debaters!"
He broke into a sweat,
and suddenly his illness was cured.
Long ago, Méi Chéng wrote the Qī Fā,
Fù Yì wrote the Qī Jī,
Zhāng Héng wrote the Qī Biàn,
Cuī Yīn wrote the Qī Yī;
each of their compositions was beautiful.
I admired them,
and so I wrote the Qī Qǐ.
I also commanded Wáng Càn to write one."
Xuánwēi Zǐ lived in seclusion at the Dàhuāng zhī Tíng,
fleeing far to distance himself from the vulgar world,
clarifying his spirit and stabilizing his soul.
He disdained official salaries and looked down on the noble,
having no worldly dealings.
He indulged in the void and loved stillness,
admiring this eternal life.
Alone, he let his thoughts gallop between the heavens and the clouds,
where no material object could overthrow him.
Thereupon Jìngjī Zǐ heard of this and went to speak with him.
He drove a team of four horses that could cross the wilderness
and rode a carriage that chased the wind.
Passing through remote deserts
and emerging from dark ruins,
he entered the vast and misty fields
and finally reached the residence of Xuánwēi Zǐ.
As for his residence,
to the left were rushing waters,
and to the right were high peaks.
Behind lay cavernous streams,
and ahead were fragrant forests.
Wearing a Píbìan cap
and covered in a Wénqiú robe,
he emerged from the hidden caves of the mountain slopes
and leaned against steep cliffs to roam.
His spirit was fluttering and soaring,
lofty and towering,
as if the Liùhé were narrow and the Jiǔzhōu were small.
He appeared about to fly but had not yet departed,
as if raising his wings but pausing midway.
Thereupon Jìngjī Zǐ climbed by grasping vines,
stood upon a rock,
and facing the wind, he addressed him:
"I have heard that a gentleman does not hide from the world to abandon his name,
and a wise man does not turn his back on the age to destroy his achievements.
Now you, my master, discard the blossoms of the arts of the Dào
and abandon the excellence of Rényì.
You waste your spirit in the empty void
and neglect the principles of human affairs.
It is like painting a form upon the formless
or creating an echo where there is no sound.
Have you not thought about it?
What plan is it that will not succeed?"
Xuánwēi Zǐ looked down and replied:
"Alas,
are there such words!
In the beginning of the Tàijí,
when Hùndùn was not yet divided,
the myriad things were jumbled and confused,
rising together with the Dào.
Whatever has form must surely decay;
whatever has tracks must surely reach an end.
In the vastness of the Yuánqì,
who knows its conclusion?
Fame defiles my body,
and position burdens my person.
I secretly admire the will of the ancients
and look up to the remaining style of Lǎo-Zhuāng.
Borrowing the divine tortoise as a metaphor,
I would rather wag my tail in the mud."
Jìngjī Zǐ said:
"The beauty of eloquent speech
can make streams flow in dried-up marshes
and make dead wood blossom.
It may move the spirits and stir the soul,
let alone things close to human emotions.
I shall describe for you the supreme pleasure of roaming and sightseeing,
and perform the seductive allure of sound and beauty.
I shall discuss the ultimate subtleties of transformation
and display the grand magnificence of Dàodé.
Do you wish to hear it?"
Xuánwēi Zǐ said:
"You have composed yourself and grown weary of the world,
seeking out the hidden to rescue the sunken.
Not considering the distance of the road,
I am fortunate to have your visit.
I shall respectfully cleanse my ears
to listen to your jade-like voice."
Jìngjī Zǐ said:
"Fragrant wild rice and fine polished grain,
frost-preserved vegetables and dew-drenched mallow.
The white skin of the black bear,
the rich flesh of fattened livestock.
Sliced as thin as cicada wings,
carved delicately and analyzed minutely.
Layered like stacked gauze,
separated like scattered snow.
They lightly fly with the wind,
the blade cutting without needing to be turned.
Mountain sandgrouse and marsh quails,
treasures of pearl and kingfisher green.
Cold tortoises from nests of fragrant licorice,
minced flying scales from the Xīhǎi.
Lean hidden alligators from Jiāngdōng,
stewed singing quails from Hànnán.
Mixed with fragrances and acids,
the sweet harmony is pure.
Xuánmíng adjusts the saltiness,
Rùshōu blends the spiciness.
Purple orchids and cinnabar peppers
are applied with perfect moderation.
The flavors are distinct
and the lingering fragrance spreads far.
Then there is the clear blue wine of spring,
prepared by Kāng and Dí.
It changes in response to transformation,
formed by the feeling of Qi.
Striking the Zhǐ note makes the bitterness emerge,
while tapping the Gōng note makes the sweetness arise.
Then it is served in kingfisher vessels
and poured into carved goblets.
Floating bubbles seethe like ants,
strong and intensely fragrant.
It can harmonize the spirit
and please the intestines.
This is the wonder of delicacies;
can you follow me and eat them?"
Xuánwēi Zǐ said:
"I find goosefoot and pulse sweet
and have no time for such food."
Jìngjī Zǐ said:
"The Bùguāng sword,
its floral patterns are intricate and lush.
Adorned with patterned rhinoceros horn
and carved with kingfisher green.
Decorated with pearls of the Lílóng
and inlaid with jade from Jīngshān.
On land it severs rhinoceros and elephant hides,
yet that is not enough to be called remarkable.
Following the waves it cuts through geese,
and the water does not even wet the blade.
A crown with nine tassels,
scattering brilliance and hanging with patterns.
Chin straps of flowery silk
fluttering in the wind.
Pendants of Jiélǜ and Xuánlí,
treasures of subtle fineness.
Their patterns shine brilliantly,
flowing light and radiating splendor.
Robes of Fǔfú embroidery
and skirts of thin gauze.
Slippers with gold flower patterns
leave behind light with every step.
Numerous ornaments of varying lengths,
delicate and fresh as frost.
Braided pendants intricately tied,
some carved and some inlaid.
Scented with Yōuruò
and spreading fragrance everywhere.
Walking with elegant and leisurely steps,
turning about and displaying radiance.
Nánwēi would break into a smile for it,
and Xīshī would give a clever laugh for it.
This is the wonder of appearance and adornment;
can you follow me and wear them?"
Xuánwēi Zǐ said:
"I prefer coarse fur and hemp
and have no time for such clothing."
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"Galloping and racing are enough to broaden the mind,
and hunting can delight the spirit.
I shall harness for you the flying team of cloud-dragons,
and adorn the many tassels of the jade carriage.
We shall hang the long tassels of the curved rainbow,
and raise the flowery banners of Zhāoyáo.
Take up the arrows of Wàngguī,
and hold the bow of Fánruò.
Suddenly treading on shadows and racing lightly,
outstripping the running steeds and surpassing the lingering wind.
Then the mountain streams are filled and the valleys blocked,
and the thickets and marshes are leveled.
Along the mountains, nets are placed,
and across the fields, snares are spread.
Below, there are no tracks left behind,
and above, there are no escaping birds.
Birds gather and beasts huddle,
and then the encirclement meets.
The hunters spread out like clouds,
and the martial riders scatter like mist.
Red banners shine across the fields,
and halberds and spears gleam brightly.
They drag the patterned foxes,
and capture the wily rabbits.
They strike down the sùshuāng birds,
and brush against the shaking egrets.
Those in the path are crushed by wheels,
and those underfoot are trampled.
The flying carriages pass like lightning,
and the beasts fall beside the turning wheels.
Wings have no time to spread,
and legs have no chance to leap.
Any movement meets a flying point,
and any lift gets caught in a light net.
Searching the forests and seeking out the dangerous spots,
probing the thickets and exhausting the obstructions.
Leaping over mountains and plunging into ravines,
like a fierce wind or a rising flame.
The triggers are not released in vain,
and the hits inevitably bury the feathers.
Then, with people crowded and nets dense,
the terrain is tight and the situation threatening.
Roaring and growling beasts,
baring their teeth and bristling their manes.
Their intent is to butt and charge,
and their fierce spirit is undaunted.
Then, let men like Běigōng and Dōngguō,
pull out leopard tails alive,
and tear apart the shoulders of chū-tigers.
Their forms cannot resist the hands,
and their bones cannot hide from the fists.
They strike bears and shatter their paws,
and they seize tigers and break their striped hides.
The fields have no furred creatures,
and the forests have no feathered flocks.
The accumulated beasts are like hills,
and the flying feathers form clouds.
Then the bells are struck and drums are sounded,
the banners are gathered and the pennons lowered.
The main ropes are set and the nets released,
and the hunters and bears turn to return.
The fine steeds prance together,
shaking their bells and spraying foam.
Leaning down against the golden carriage rails,
and looking up to touch the kingfisher-feather canopy.
Poised and at leisure,
delighting the will beyond the mundane world.
This is the wonder of the feather-hunt;
can you follow me to observe it?"
Xuánwēizǐ said:
"I delight in tranquility,
and have no time for such a spectacle."
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"The secluded palace is spacious and bright,
and the cloud-scraping buildings are radiant.
Built on the high foundations of Jǐngshān,
they face the pure breeze as towers.
Red railings and purple pillars,
carved rafters and flowery beams.
The coffered ceilings hold blossoms,
and golden steps lead to jade side-rooms.
In the warm rooms, one wears fine linen in winter;
in the cool rooms, there is frost in midsummer.
The flowery pavilions reach the clouds,
and the flying staircases scale the void.
Looking down to watch the shooting stars,
and looking up to observe the eight corners of the sky.
Climbing dragons cannot reach them,
and they dwell high on the far horizon of heaven.
Exquisite craftsmanship and wondrous things,
of changing names and unusual forms.
Bān Shū would have no place to apply his axe,
and Lí Lóu would lose his sight because of them.
Beautiful plants are planted together,
of extraordinary species and strange kinds.
Green leaves and vermilion blossoms,
shining toward the sky and reflecting the sun.
Clear water fills the ponds,
and clustered trees form a forest.
Flying birds soar on high,
and scaled creatures hide in the depths.
Thus wandering at ease and leisure,
one suddenly feels as if they have forgotten to return.
Then, let Rènzǐ cast his fishing line,
and Wèi release his mechanism.
Fragrant bait sinks into the water,
and light lines fly to catch birds.
Bringing down the soaring birds that shade the clouds,
and catching the divine turtles from the nine depths.
Then gathering water-chestnut flowers,
and plucking water ferns.
Toying with pearl oysters,
and playing with the mermen.
Reciting what was chanted in the Hànguǎng,
and watching the wandering maidens by the water's edge.
Their divine radiance shines upon the islet,
and they are clad in light gauze and fine silk.
Leaving a lingering fragrance as they walk calmly,
they raise fair hands and sing clear songs.
The song says:
'I look to the edge of the clouds for a good mate,
the road to heaven is long and there is no way to go.
For whom do I adorn myself with orchids and clover?
The gentle company is severed, and my heart is sorrowful.'
This is the wonder of the palaces and halls;
can you follow me to dwell there?"
Xuánwēizǐ said:
"I am devoted to caves and cliffs,
and have no time for such a dwelling."
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"Having wandered and observed the central plains,
and strolled through the secluded palaces,
emotions are let loose and the will is stirred,
but the excessive pleasure is not yet finished.
There will also be talented men and wonderful dancers,
who have left the world behind and transcended the mundane.
They raise the flowing sounds of Běilǐ,
and continue the exquisite melodies of Yáng'ē.
Then, you shall sit in the carved pavilion,
overlooking the Dòngtíng.
Zithers and harps are played together,
with flutes on the left and reed-pipes on the right.
Bells and drums vibrate together,
and vertical flutes and pipes sound in unison.
Then the beautiful people put on flowery robes of patterned gauze,
and shake the fluttering light silks.
Wearing shimmering golden hairpins,
and raising paired plumes of kingfisher feathers.
They scatter flowing fragrances,
and display flying patterns.
Moving across the basins and drums,
they are radiant and dazzling.
Long skirts follow the wind,
and sorrowful songs reach the clouds.
Agile as if flying,
they tread on the void and step far.
Leaping and soaring high,
they move sinuously and swiftly.
Soaring like a swan-goose in flight,
and plunging like a duck into water.
