Giving free rein to their light bodies to rush forward,
their shadows chase their forms but cannot keep up.
Their flying voices stir the dust,
resounding in harmony and intensity.
Their skill is as swift as a god's,
and their forms are difficult to depict.
Then, before the joy has subsided,
the bright sun sinks in the west.
The music disperses and they change their attire,
walking with small steps into the inner chambers.
Black eyebrows are relaxed and the powder falls,
they gather disheveled hair and apply orchid oil,
their forms graceful and their dress elegant, they emanate a subtle beauty.
Their rosy faces are suited for smiles,
and their sidelong glances flow with light.
At times with you,
they walk hand in hand.
Stepping onto the flying steps,
they enter the quiet rooms.
Flowery candles burn brightly,
and curtains and screens are spread out.
Moving vermilion lips,
they sing the pure tones of Shāng.
Raising silk sleeves,
and shaking flowery garments.
On an evening in the ninth month of autumn,
the joy is endless.
This is the wonder of music and beauty;
can you follow me to enjoy it?"
Xuánwēizǐ said:
"I desire purity and void,
and have no time for such enjoyment."
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"I have heard that a superior man delights in exerting his integrity to make righteousness manifest,
and a heroic man willingly risks his body to achieve benevolence.
Therefore, the ranks of the brave and outstanding
form groups and bind themselves to peers.
They value honor and hold life lightly;
moved by duty, they forsake their own persons.
Thus Tián Guāng fell on his sword in Běiyàn,
and Gōngshū met his end in Xīqín.
Firm and resolute, decisive in action,
they stride like tigers, like a valley wind.
Their majesty strikes fear into the lords of ten thousand chariots,
and all of Huáxià acclaims them as heroes."
Before his words were finished,
Xuánwēizǐ said:
"Excellent."
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"These are merely the ranks of wandering knights;
they are not yet worthy of being called marvelous.
As for those like Tián Wén and Wújì,
they were the outstanding young lords of high antiquity.
All of them spread benevolence and raised righteousness,
leaping forth in the Way and the arts.
Their minds roamed without limits,
their aspirations reaching the edge of the clouds.
They overrode the feudal lords
and galloped through their age.
A wave of their sleeves brought wind to the nine wildernesses,
and their passionate fervor turned their spirit into a rainbow.
If you were in those times,
could you follow me and befriend them?"
Xuánwēizǐ said:
"I would indeed desire it.
But compared to the Great Way,
what of the burdens they bring?"
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"In this world, there is a sage minister,
assisting the Emperor to dominate the era.
He measures up to Qiánkūn,
and shines as brightly as the sun and moon.
His profound transformation joins with the divine,
and accords with the spiritual realm.
His benevolent grace spreads to the Límiao,
and his majestic spirit trembles throughout the world.
Surpassing the prosperity and peace of Yīn and Zhōu,
he follows in the footsteps of Xī Huáng and equals Tài.
The court is pure and bright,
and the Kingly Way is universally balanced.
The people's expectations are like the grass,
and our grace is like the spring.
By the riverbanks, there are no scholars washing their ears,
and on the high peaks, there are no people living in nests.
Therefore, men of talent come to serve,
to behold the glory of the state.
In selection, no talent is left behind;
in promotion, each follows their own path.
They assist in ceremonies at the Bìyōng,
and lecture on literary virtue at the Míngtáng;
they correct the flowery talk of the commoners,
and synthesize the old regulations of the house of Kǒng.
The music they perform changes the customs,
the state is wealthy, and the people are healthy.
Divine responses and auspicious signs arrive;
excellent omens are frequently obtained.
Thus the sweet dew falls profusely in the morning,
and auspicious stars spread their light at night.
One observes the swimming dragon in the divine pool,
and hears the singing phoenix on the high ridge.
This is the height of the Hegemon's Way,
and the peak of harmonious prosperity.
Yet the Sovereign still fears his deep grace is not widespread,
and dreads his influence is not vigorous enough;
he gathers the outstanding and exceptional from humble places,
and proclaims imperial brilliance to those in mountain caves.
This is the time of Nìngzǐ’s merchant song,
and the reason why Lǚ Wàng cast aside his fishing line and departed.
You are a citizen of Tàihé;
do you not wish to serve in an age like that of Táo Táng?"
Thereupon Xuánwēizǐ rolled up his sleeves, rose, and said:
"How magnificent are your words!
Just now, what you
described was flowery and excessive;
you wished to encourage me,
but only disturbed my heart.
But having heard of the world's solemn purity,
and the enlightened monarch presiding over the state,
I perceive the true meaning of fullness and emptiness,
and realize the confusion of my stubborn simplicity.
Now I feel expansive,
my body light as if flying.
I wish to return to my original robes,
and follow you back."
Chōngmò Gōngzǐ
contained his brilliance and hid his light.
Finding joy in withdrawal, like a coiled dragon,
he made light of the world and rose above it.
He let his mind roam in the Hàorán,
and delighted his will in the multitude of mysteries.
He cut off his shadow in the remote obstacles of the Dàhuāng,
and swallowed his echoes in the deep recesses of the dark mountains.
Thereupon Xùnhuá Dàfū heard of him and went to visit.
He then ordered his cloud chariot,
with a pair of Fēihuáng horses as outriders.
He crossed the rushing sands,
and rolled over the flowing frost.
Mounting the Fúyáo wind,
he trod upon the ferry of solid ice.
His banners brushed the edge of the sky,
and his carriage tracks left the dark horizon.
The sky was clear and cool, without clouds,
and the wilderness was vast and bright, without dust.
Approaching the layered peaks, he drew the reins;
looking toward the stone chamber, he turned the wheels.
Thus he arrived at the dwelling of Chōngmò.
As for his dwelling,
it was towering, deep, and shadowy,
desolate, empty, and mysterious.
The turbid waters of the Mínghǎi surged behind it,
and the craggy cliffs of Xiègǔ spread out before it.
Tall bamboos with upright stems shaded the ravines,
and the hundred pipes of nature sang together, deafening the mountains.
A sudden gale rose and circled the sun,
and flying gravel rose to sprinkle the sky.
Then, climbing the highest peak
and facing the long wind,
he delivered a speech to resolve confusion,
calling out to the Prince in the midst of the cliffs.
He said:
"I have heard that a sage does not roll up the Way and turn his back on the times,
and a wise man does not abandon his person and hide his tracks.
In life, one must shine with a glorious name on the jade tablets,
and in death, carve great achievements into the golden records.
Now, Prince, you have left the world to sink into the earth,
avoiding the world and hiding alone.
The joys of existence are extinguished,
and the duty of serving one's father is abandoned.
Sorrow permeates a hundred years,
and bitterness overflows a thousand years.
How is this different from a tiny-scaled fish swimming in a puddle,
or a short-feathered bird perching in a dense thicket?
Now I shall honor you with the great treasures of Heaven and Man,
and delight you with the ultimate pleasure of indulging your nature.
You shall roam to the ends of the earth,
and dwell in the center of the heavens.
Exhausting the delights of the Sìhǎi,
and draining the riches of the Jiǔzhōu.
Drilling into the gourd of Qūgǔ,
and loosening the restraints of Shūshǔ,
do you wish for this?"
The Prince said:
"The Grand Master did not leave me behind,
but has come to gather here in the remote wilds.
Although I am not clever,
I shall respectfully listen to your fine words."
The Dàfū said:
"The paulownia of Hánshān
comes from Tàimíng.
It holds the pitch of Huángzhōng to put forth its trunk
and relies on the green peaks to grow in solitude.
Thereupon, the jade precipices are steep and towering,
and the golden banks are craggy and high.
To the left, it faces the Windy Valley;
to the right, it overlooks the Cloud Stream.
Above, there are no nests reaching into the void;
below, there are no paths trodden by feet.
Shaking and steep, it stands loftily,
distant and reaching toward the heights.
It dries in the overflowing dew of the three months of spring
and faces the whistling gales of the nine months of autumn.
Falling snow covers its roots;
drifting frost seals its branches.
Other trees are lush before turning green,
but while the grass is not yet white, this tree withers first.
Thereupon, cloud ladders are constructed
to ascend the towering heights.
They cut the sunny branches of Ruíbīn
and split the shady trunk of Dàlǚ.
The craftsmen carve the raw wood,
and Línglún tunes its sound.
The instrument is raised and music is played;
the melodies are tightened and the pitch is high.
Its sound is as resonant as the Hàozhōng,
and its rhythm as clear as the Ràoliáng.
It seeks the lingering echoes in the Bāfēng
and collects rare melodies in Guīchāng.
It opens the Shǎogōng of Zhònghuáng
and emits the Biànshāng of Rùshōu.
When the Dragon Fire declines in the west
and the warm air first recedes,
flying frost welcomes the season,
and high winds see off the autumn.
Sojourners longing for home
and those wandering with a hundred sorrows,
touching the tightened bridge makes their noses sour with grief,
and plucking the high strings makes their tears flow.
If one pursues the clear sounds
and follows the solemn rhythm,
playing Lǜshuǐ
and emitting Báixuě,
the Stirring Chu melody swirls
and the Flowing Wind gathers.
Mourning the morning fall of the Míngjiá
and grieving the evening waning of Wàngshū,
the lonely and widowed beat their breasts for it,
and the elderly widows choke with sobs.
Wángzǐ brushes his tassels and inclines his ear;
the six horses hiss at heaven and look up with panting breath.
This is the utmost wonder of music.
Can you follow me and listen to it?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"I am ill
and cannot."
The Dàfū said:
"In the orchid palaces and secret halls,
carved halls and silken windows,
cloud-patterned screens are dazzling
and jade walls are lush green.
The main gates are eightfold,
and the Xuán Terrace is nine layers high.
Marked by watchtowers of a hundred *chang*
and enclosed by walls of ten thousand *zhi*,
then the high pavilions catch the wind,
rising prominently into the mid-sky.
Emerald observatories are peak-green;
carved lofts connect to the clouds.
Long eaves overlook the clouds;
flying steps transcend the mountains.
Gazing at the Yùshéng to fix the roof-pole
and receiving the Dàojǐng to open the windows,
red and white shine brightly
and the rafters and brackets are towering.
Shady dragons support the eaves;
sunny horses bear the ridges.
Inlaid with jade blossoms,
carved with golden flowers,
square lattices contain beauty
and circular ceiling-wells spit out petals.
Tiered halls rise one after another;
intersecting silk patterns face the curtains.
Secluded halls are dense by day;
bright rooms are radiant at night.
When a midge flies, a wind is born;
when an inchworm moves, it creates a sound.
If the eyes are weary of familiar sights
and the body is tired of the inner chambers,
I will take Gōngzǐ for a walk
and find joy at times in the forest at the foot of the hills.
Ascending emerald hills,
overlooking cinnabar valleys,
flowery grasses are as dense as brocade
and flying colors are like stars and candles.
Sunny leaves are spring-green;
shady branches are autumn-verdant.
Flowers and fruits take turns being new;
follow your heart and indulge in joy.
Looking up to pluck the Shénxiū;
looking down to gather the morning orchids.
Braving the orchid-scented wind in the thickets;
looking back at the peppered paths on the jade altars.
Then floating the three-winged boats
and playing in the middle of the waters,
submerged gills are startled
and frightened wings take flight.
Sinking lines are cast;
flying arrows are prepared.
Hanging returning wings beyond the red sky;
bringing out magnificent scales from within the purple abyss.
Then letting go of the oars to follow the wind;
resting the paddles to ride the waves.
Blowing the Gūzhú;
plucking the Yúnhé.
The Yuānkè sings the songs of Huáinán;
the boatmen play the 'Gathering Water Chestnuts' song.
The song says:
'Riding the duck-boat for water play,
approaching the fragrant isle to pluck the magic mushrooms.
Joy makes one forget sorrow;
wandering to finish the time.
Exhausting the night to make it day;
completing the year as our term.'
This is the grand beauty of leisure;
can you follow me and live there?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"I am ill
and cannot."
The Dàfū said:
"When the Báishāng and Sùjié seasons arrive,
and the month for distributing winter clothes has passed.
The heavens congeal and the earth closes tight;
the wind is harsh and the frost flies.
Supple branches turn stiff by evening,
and dense leaves become sparse by dawn.
Following the seasonal qi to manifest the power of slaughter,
we approach the Golden Suburbs to drill the troops.
Thereupon, we array the light warriors
and organize the sturdy ranks.
We raise the cloud-like banners
and reveal the heroic blades.
Driving the 'Flying Swallow' of Hóng Yáng,
and teaming with the sùshuāng steeds of the Táng Gōng.
We station the feathered scouts in the outer forests
and release the light cavalry into the central wilds.
Thereupon, we spread the flying nets
and stretch out the long snares.
We ascend the yellow ridges
and hang nets over the green peaks.
We delineate long chasms as boundaries
and use flowing streams as gates.
Thus, inside there are no hidden paths,
and outside there are no escaping tracks.
Striking the gongs to count the catch,
and raising the banners to signal the capture.
Drawing the golden crossbow mechanisms,
and launching the whistling arrows.
We cut down the coarse-haired beasts
and bring down the strong-winged birds.
Chariots and riders compete in speed,
their horses' hooves in step and wheels aligned.
Swiftly and suddenly they move,
like swirling clouds and fierce winds.
Raising halberds like a bristling forest,
and brandishing blades that flash like lightning.
Looking up, we topple the nests in the clouds;
looking down, we exhaust the burrows in the earth.
There are leopards with circular patterns
and tigers with striped foreheads.
Bristling their manes, the wind rises;
glaring their eyes, lightning flashes.
Their mouths bite at frosty blades,
and their feet parry flying points.
Sniffing the forest and stumbling over rocks,
they crash through the deep thickets.
Thereupon, Fēihuáng steeds exert their vigor,
and men like Bèn and Shí display their skills.
They press the giant boars
and fell the rushing swine.
They seize white and black tigers
and subdue the xièzhì.
Hooked claws are crushed,
and serrated teeth are torn apart.
A chaotic abundance of game,
toppling thickets and filling the ravines.
Carcasses hang upon the mountains,
and fallen bodies cover the marshes.
The thickets become a forest of fur,
and the wetlands become a red marsh.
Then we dismantle the enclosure and lower the nets,
roll up the pennants and gather the kites.
The gamekeepers count the beasts,
and the forest wardens calculate the fresh catch.
Merits are weighed to reward the diligent,
and horses are rested as bowstrings are encased.
Chariots of delicacies follow bit by bit,
and wine carriages stand side-by-side.
A thousand cups are drained like lightning,
and ten thousand torches are numerous as stars.
High mounds are soaked with flowing fat,
and mountain valleys are filled with fragrant smoke.
When joy reaches its peak and pleasure is exhausted,
we turn our carriages and return.
This is indeed the grand spectacle of the hunt;
could you join me in doing this?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"I am ill
and cannot."
The Dàfū said:
"The Yáng sword of Chǔ,
crafted by Ōuyě.
Made from the ore of Xiéxī
and the essence of Chìshān.
Smelted more than the Yángtóu ore,
refined from the Púyuè metal.
It is tempered and smelted,
ten thousand times folded and a thousand times quenched.
Fénglóng wields the hammer
and Fēilián fans the coals.
The divine weapon is thus transformed and completed,
with Yang patterns and Yin smoothness.
Its flowing patterns are like connecting stars,
its floating colors brilliantly vivid.
Its light is like scattered lightning,
its substance like shining snow.
Its frosty edges are like congealed water,
its icy blades like pure dew.
Its form surpasses the Háo-Cáo,
its name is more precious than Jùquè.
Point it at Zhèng and the three armies' hair turns white with fear;
brandish it at Jìn and blood flows for a thousand miles.
It is not merely for cutting krakens and swans in the water,
or slaughtering galloping steeds on land,
nor is its skill just in severing floating feathers
or its sharpness just in piercing heavy armor!
As for its spiritual power,
it expands and contracts without limit,
with wondrous points and extraordinary forms.
Its shape shook Xuē and Shǔ,
and its light startled Fēnghú.
Its price is worth three townships,
and its fame is honored in the two capitals.
Some won fame by toppling Qín,
and some flew away at night to Wú.
Thus its merit crowns ten thousand ages,
and its majesty shines without end.
He who wields it has none to stand before him;
he who possesses it is a hero among men.
It can be used to subdue the nine provinces
and to bring the eight barbarian tribes under control.
Generals will follow like shadows,
and all of Huàxià will be moved by its influence.
This is truly a rare divine weapon of the world;
could you join me in wearing it?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"I am ill
and cannot."
The Dàfū said:
"The excellence of a heavenly steed,
its extraordinary posture surpasses all others.
It draws its spirit from the Divine Abyss
and receives its essence from the bright moon.
Its eyes are dark and gleaming,
its black coat shining with deep purple.
Its foam is like scattered red,
its sweat like shaking blood.
Qín Qīng could not judge its many qualities,
and Fāng Yān could not see its fleeting form.
Adorned with cloud-carriages,
it treads upon the morning mist.
It gallops through spring thoroughfares
and is readied for autumn journeys.
It leaps like a hornless dragon and rises like a winged dragon,
it surpasses the qilin and soars like a dragon.
Seeing mountains, it immediately gallops;
seeing forests, it immediately rushes.
Its spirit is full and its fury rises,
moving like flying stars and startling lightning.
Its will surmounts the nine provinces,
and its power crosses the four seas.
Its shadow cannot keep pace with its form,
and the dust has no time to rise.
Before the water clock's arrow moves,
it has already traversed a thousand miles.
Then it crosses the boundaries of heaven
and leaps over the barriers of the earth.
It passes where Hànmàn does not travel
and steps where Zhāng Hài has never left a track.
The Sun Crow pauses its wings for it,
and Kuàfù throws down his staff for it.
This is the most outstanding mount in the world;
could you join me in riding it?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"I am ill
and cannot."
The Dàfū said:
"The millet of Dàliáng,
the grain of Qióngshān,
Táng planted their roots,
and Nóngdì tasted their blossoms.
Then there are the rare treasures among the six kinds of poultry,
and the exotic delicacies of the four types of meals.
Mixed seafood from the farthest seas,
and furred beasts from the remotest lands.
Yī Gōng tended the tripod,
and the Master Chef wielded the knife.
The flavors are refined through nine boilings,
and the harmony is balanced with seasonings.
Morning ducks and dewy swans,
frost-touched sandgrouse and yellow sparrows.
On the round tables, dishes are scattered like stars;
across a fāngzhàng, beauties are intricately arranged.
Fat bear paws,
and the feet of the 'crying-sound' bird.
Swallow thighs and orangutan lips,
the mane-remnants of the yak and the white trunk of the elephant.
Turtles from the Spiritual Depths,
and pufferfish from Láihuáng.
Pipits from the Cinnabar Cave,
and the fetuses of black leopards.
Steamed with autumn oranges,
and seasoned with spring plums.
Picked up with the chopsticks of the Shāng King,
and held in the cups of Dì Xīn.
The fish of Fàn Gōng,
coming from Jiǔxī.
With red tails and cinnabar gills,
purple fins and green dorsal crests.
Then command Zhīlí
to fly the frost-edged blade.
The red flesh scatters like patterned silk,
and the white skin falls like snow.
The fine hair of Lóu Zǐ could not be placed among its thinness,
and the wings of an autumn cicada are not enough to match its translucency.
When the many dishes are finished,
there are also cold appetizers.
Fruits from Shāngshān,
and hazelnuts from Hàngāo.
Peeling the clusters of longans,
and splitting the shells of coconuts.
Fragrant delicacies chosen from ten thousand,
following the heart and presented in turn.
Then there is Wūchéng wine from Jīngnán,
and Zhúyè wine from Yùběi.
Floating yeasts bubble like stars,
and flying blossoms gather like duckweed.
Xuánshí once tasted its flavor,
and Yí Shì presented its method.
Tilting the jars for a single morning,
one can remain intoxicated for a thousand days.
A single flask of wine thrown into a river
can make the three armies proclaim victory.
These are things that both men and spirits admire,
and what the eyes and ears find resplendent.
Can you not rouse yourself to enjoy them?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"To indulge in delicacies that satisfy the mouth,
and to savor the taste of dried meat that is poisonous.
To take medicine that rots the intestines,
and to handle the vessels of a fallen state.
Though these are what you, Dàfū, find glorious,
they are precisely what I fear.
I am ill,
and cannot do so."
The Dàfū said:
"Now, there is the Jìn dynasty which flourishes with imperial wind;
the Golden Brilliance has initiated the omen,
and a Great Man has arisen.
Continuing the brilliance of successive suns,
matching Heaven and illuminating the dwelling.
Its foundational virtue
is more exalted than when Jī Gōng resided in Qí.
Its bestowed benevolence
is more abundant than when the House of Yīn was in Bó.
The winds of the Southern Sieve
cannot fully circulate its transformation.
The clouds of the Net and the Hyades
cannot sufficiently enrich its bounty.
The Imperial Way is brilliant and shining,
and the Emperor's achievements are continuous and bright.
Guiding the vital breath through music,
and proclaiming virtue through poetry.
Its teachings are purer than the age of the Yún Guān,
and its governance is more harmonious than the time of the Niǎo Jì.
The King's Way reaches the four frontiers,
and the land of Xià is tranquil and peaceful.
Cinnabar darkness has discarded the signal fires,
and the green borders have released the alarms.
Turning back the horses to the shafts of the dung carts,
and engraving virtue upon the tripods of Kūnwú.
The common people return to simplicity,
and the culture of the times is flourishing.
Farmers yield their boundaries to others,
and young fishermen yield the land.
Woodcutters are ashamed of the ornaments of high caps,
and servants laugh at the short-backed garments.
The six directions are harmonious in season,
majestic and vast.
Children with black hair sing in the lanes,
and the grey-haired elders beat the ground in joy.
Untying the ropes of Xī Huáng,
and laying aside the images of Táo Táng.
As for the barbarians on the borders,
and the tribes in the distant wilds,
whose languages were not transmitted by the light carriages,
and whose lands were not covered by the official calendar,
none fail to race forward to prostrate themselves,
and offer tribute through multiple translators.
At this time, even insects and ants are moved by grace,
and no mind is left undisturbed by it.
In the gardens play nine-tailed birds,
and in the parks dwell three-footed crows.
Singing phoenixes are in the forests,
more numerous than in the garden of the Yellow Emperor.
There are dragons swimming in the abysses,
filling the ponds of Kǒngjiǎ.
The ten thousand things are in harmonious mist,
and Heaven and Earth are in grand union.
Righteousness is embraced within,
and transformation is felt without.
In the forests, none wear coarse hemp,
and in the mountains, none wear leather belts.
These are all images carved by the many artisans,
and omens revealed through the divine tortoise.
The gentry are numerous and dignified,
and the carriages and caps are abundant.
Their merit competes with the flow of creation,
and their virtue is as great as the two realms of Heaven and Earth."
Before he had finished speaking,
the Gōngzǐ suddenly rose up
and said:
"I am a commoner of meager knowledge,
stubbornly holding to this narrow-mindedness.
Truly, when logic dispels a point,
the lawsuit over a precious treasure is resolved;
when words provoke anger,
the illness of the Qí Wáng is cured.
Previously, you enticed me with music for the deaf,
and housed me in a dwelling of darkness.
Hunting and wandering in dissipation,
with sharp blades and swift steeds.
Since these are what Lǎo Zǐ warned against,
they are not what I desire.
Therefore, I could not respond to you.
But now that I hear the Imperial Wind is praised,
and the Sagely Way of the time is pure.
Gathering the fruits is the autumn,
and spreading the blossoms is the spring.
Below, there are people worthy of being ennobled;
above, there is a great sovereign.
Although I am not clever,
I beg to follow in your footsteps."
The Edict said:
"Truly, for extraordinary achievements,
one must wait for extraordinary people.
Thus, a horse that kicks and bolts might travel a thousand li,
and a man who bears the burden of social disapproval might achieve great fame and merit.
As for the horse that overturns the carriage,
and the man of unrestrained character,
it is simply a matter of how they are managed.
Let the provinces and counties search among the officials and people for those of Màocái and exceptional grade,
who can serve as generals and ministers, or as envoys to distant lands."
I have heard that in the past, under Táng and Yú,
images were drawn as punishments, yet the people did not offend.
Wherever the sun and moon shone,
none failed to follow and submit.
In the reigns of Chéng and Kāng of Zhōu,
punishments were set aside and not used,
and virtue reached even the birds and beasts.
Education reached across the four seas;
overseas, the Sùshèn people were respectful.
To the north, the Qūshōu,
and the Dī and Qiāng came to submit.
The stars did not deviate,
the sun and moon were not eclipsed,
the mountains and hills did not crumble,
and the rivers and valleys were not blocked.
The Lín and Fèng were in the outskirts and marshes;
the Hé and Luò gave forth the Chart and the Book.
Alas!
What was done to reach such a state?
Now that I have attained the honor of serving the Ancestral Temple,
I rise early to seek guidance
and retire late to reflect,
as if crossing deep waters,
not yet knowing how to cross over.
How magnificent! How grand!
What actions can be taken to make manifest the great achievements and excellent virtues of the late Emperor?
Above, to match Yáo and Shùn;
below, to equal the Three Kings.
My own lack of intelligence
means I cannot extend virtue to the distant reaches;
this is what you, Zǐ Dàfū, have seen and heard.
You Worthy and Good men are clear about the essence of royal affairs throughout history;
receive this policy and examine the questions,
and all of you respond in writing.
Set them down in chapters,
and I shall personally review them.
Imperial Decree:
To the Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, Chéngxiàng, Governor of Jìzhōu, and Marquis of Wǔpíng:
Because of my own lack of virtue,
I encountered misfortune and calamity at a young age,
living far away in the western lands,
and moving to the regions of Táng and Wèi.
During that time,
the state was as fragile as a banner hanging by a thread;
the Ancestral Temple lacked sacrifices,
and the Altars of Earth and Grain had no standing.
Myriad villains harbored ambitions,
dividing the various Zhūxià regions;
each person claimed a foot of land,
and I gained nothing.
The mandate of our Gāozǔ
was about to fall to the ground.
I rose early and slept fitfully,
trembling with grief in my heart.
I said: "The ancestors and fathers,
the ministers of the former government—
who among them will take pity on me?"
Then, the heart of Heaven was moved,
and it gave birth to the Chéngxiàng.
You have protected and governed our Imperial House,
and provided great relief during hardships;
I have truly relied upon you.
Now I shall grant you the ritual honors;
listen reverently to my command:
In the past,
when Dǒng Zhuó first incited the national disaster,
the various lords lost their positions
while plotting for the sake of the Royal House.
You then stepped forward,
taking the lead in starting military operations;
this was your loyalty to the Imperial Court.
Later, when it came to the Huángjīn,
who subverted the heavenly constants,
invaded our three provinces,
and reached the common people,
you also suppressed them,
eliminating their traces
to pacify the eastern lands;
this was another of your achievements.
Hán Xián and Yáng Fèng
usurped the authority of the imperial commands;
again relying on your merit,
their troubles were overcome.
Consequently, the capital of Xǔ was established,
building our metropolitan region,
setting up offices and myriad sacrifices,
without losing the old institutions.
Heaven, Earth, and the spirits
thus attained peace;
this was another of your achievements.
Yuán Shù committed treasonous usurpation,
acting recklessly in Huáinán;
fearing your numinous power,
through great and manifest strategy
in the campaign of Qíyáng,
Qiáo Ruí was decapitated.
Your majestic power moved south with severity,
and Shù was thus broken and destroyed;
this was another of your achievements.
Turning your spear to point east,
Lǚ Bù was executed;
while riding a carriage and plotting rebellion,
Zhāng Yáng was thwarted and died,
Suī Gù submitted to his punishment,
and Zhāng Xiù bowed in submission;
this was another of your achievements.
Yuán Shào rebelled against the constants,
plotting to endanger the Altars of Earth and Grain;
relying on his multitudes,
he mobilized troops for internal aggression.
During that time,
the royal army was small and weak,
the world was chilled with fear,
and none had a firm resolve.
You held fast to great integrity,
your essence piercing the bright sun;
unleashing your martial wrath,
you deployed divine strategies,
arrived at Guāndù,
and utterly annihilated the ugly hordes,
causing our state
to be saved from the brink of collapse;
this was another of your achievements.
Crossing the great Hónghé,
you expanded and settled the four provinces;
Yuán Tán and Gāo Gàn
both had their heads exposed.
The pirates of the sea fled and dispersed,
and the Hēishān bandits followed the proper path;
this was another of your achievements.
The three types of Wūwán
had fostered disorder for two generations;
Yuán Shàng relied on them
to forcefully occupy the northern frontier.
Binding horses and hanging carriages,
you destroyed them in a single campaign;
this was another of your achievements.
Liú Biǎo was treacherous and arrogant,
failing to provide tribute and service;
when the royal army first set out,
the wind of your majesty arrived before them,
and a hundred cities in eight commanderies
folded their arms and knelt in submission;
this was another of your achievements.
Mǎ Chāo and Chéng Yí
assisted each other in their shared evil,
occupying the banks of the river at Tóng;
seeking to carry out their desires,
they were exterminated south of the Wèi River,
with tens of thousands of severed heads presented;
thus the border cities were settled,
and the Róng and Dí were pacified;
this was another of your achievements.
The Xiānbēi and Dīnglíng
arrived after multiple translations;
from the Bēiyú down to those in simple dwellings,
they requested officials and followed their duties;
this was another of your achievements.
You have the merit of settling the world,
augmented by your brilliant virtue;
you have established order within the four seas,
proclaimed the beauty of customs,
widely applied diligent teaching,
and been compassionate and cautious in punishments and trials.
Officials have no harsh governance,
and the people harbor no wicked intent.
You have honored and elevated the imperial clan,
and restored extinguished lineages.
For old virtues and former achievements,
none are without their proper rank.
Although Yī Yǐn's greatness reached Sovereign Heaven,
and Zhōu Gōng's glory filled the four seas,
compared to you, they are as nothing.
I have heard that the Former Kings established those of illustrious virtue,
endowed them with land,
and divided the people among them,
exalting their honors and insignia,
and providing them with ritual gifts,
so as to defend the Royal House
and assist their generation.
In the time of Zhōu Chéng,
Guǎn and Cài were not peaceful.
Remembering past hardships and considering merit,
he then sent Shào Kāng Gōng to bestow upon Qí Tài Gōng Lǚ
territory reaching east to the sea,
west to the River,
south to Mù Líng,
and north to Wú Dì.
The Five Lords and Nine Chiefs
were truly under his authority to punish.
For generations, they served as the Grand Preceptor,
representing the Eastern Sea.
Coming to the time of Xiāng Wáng,
there were also the people of Chǔ
who did not perform their royal duties.
He again ordered Jìn Wén,
ascending him to the position of Hegemon,
bestowing two chariots,
the Tiger Warrior guards, the battle-axe and halberd,
the black millet wine and the bow and arrows.
He greatly expanded Nán Yáng
and served as the leader of the alliance for generations.
Therefore, that the Zhōu House did not crumble
was indeed dependent on these two states.
Now, you, My Lord, possess greatly manifest virtue;
you clearly protect My person
and respond to the Mandate of Heaven.
You lead and propagate great achievements,
pacifying the Nine Provinces,
so that none fail to follow and obey.
Your merit is higher than that of Yī and Zhōu,
yet your rewards are lowlier than those of Qí and Jìn.
I am deeply ashamed of this.
I, with my humble person,
am placed above the myriad people.
I perpetually contemplate the difficulties,
as if crossing deep waters.
Without your salvation, My Lord,
I could not bear the responsibility.
Now, taking from Jì Zhōu: Hé Dōng, Hé Nèi, Wèi Jùn, Zhào Guó, Zhōng Shān, Jù Lù, Cháng Shān, Ān Píng, Gān Líng, and Píng Yuán—altogether ten commanderies—
I enfeoff you, My Lord, as the Duke of Wèi.
I send the Envoy holding the Tally, Grandee of Remonstrance Lǜ,
to confer upon you the seals, ribbons, and patent of appointment,
the Golden Tiger Tallies number one through five,
and the Bamboo Envoy Tallies number one through ten.
I bestow upon you the dark soil,
covered with white reeds,
matching your tortoise divinations,
to establish your Great Altar of State.
Formerly in the Zhōu House,
Bì Gōng and Máo Gōng
entered the court as high ministers and assistants.
Zhōu and Shào served as Preceptor and Protector
and went out as the Two Chiefs.
For responsibilities both internal and external,
you, My Lord, are truly suited.
You shall remain Chancellor and Governor of Jì Zhōu as before.
Now I further send down the hereditary seal,
reverently conveying My command
to satisfy the Huá Xià.
You shall return your former seal and ribbon as the Marquis of Wǔ Píng.
Now I also add to you, My Lord, the Nine Bestowals;
listen reverently to the subsequent commands.
Because you, My Lord, have regulated the rituals and laws
to serve as a standard for the people,
enabling them to settle in their professions
without wavering in their intentions,
I hereby bestow upon you one Great Chariot and one War Chariot,
and two teams of four black stallions.
Because you, My Lord, encourage the distribution of resources and focus on agriculture,
working with the people from dawn until dusk,
so that grain and silk have accumulated
and the great enterprise flourishes,
I hereby bestow upon you the Robe and Crown of State,
with Red Shoes as an accompaniment.
Because you, My Lord, value humility and yielding,
leading the people to act with virtue,
so that young and old observe propriety
and those above and below are in harmony,
I hereby bestow upon you the music of the Xuān Xuán [hanging instruments]
and the dance of the Six Rows.
Because you, My Lord, assist in proclaiming cultural transformation,
extending it to the four quarters,
so that distant peoples turn their faces toward us
and the Huá Xià is prosperous and full,
I hereby bestow upon you the Vermilion Door for your residence.
Because you, My Lord, examine with brilliance and wisdom,
contemplating what the Emperor found difficult,
appointing the talented and employing the worthy,
so that every good man is surely recommended,
I hereby bestow upon you the Inward-facing Staircase for ascending.
Because you, My Lord, hold the balance of the state,
maintaining a stern countenance and staying centered,
so that even the slightest evil
is suppressed and retreated,
I hereby bestow upon you three hundred Tiger Warrior guards.
Because you, My Lord, reverently carry out the heavenly punishments,
manifesting the guilt of those who have sinned,
so that those who violate the passes or defy the laws
are all executed,
I hereby bestow upon you one Battle-axe and one Halberd.
Because you, My Lord, advance like a dragon and watch like a tiger,
surveying the eight directions,
suppressing and punishing those with rebellious intent,
and being the bulwark of the four seas,
I hereby bestow upon you one Vermilion Bow,
one hundred Vermilion Arrows,
ten Black Bows,
and one thousand Black Arrows.
Because you, My Lord, take gentleness and respect as your foundation,
and filial piety and friendship as your virtue,
being clear, sincere, and deeply faithful,
which touches My thoughts,
I hereby bestow upon you one flagon of Black Millet Wine,
with the Jade Libation Cup as an accompaniment.
In the State of Wèi, the Chancellor and all other ministers and officials shall be established,
all according to the system of the various kings at the beginning of the Hàn.
Go forth, My Lord, and be diligent!
Reverently obey My command.
Sympathize with and care for your masses,
constantly illuminating all achievements,
thereby completing your manifest virtue
and responding to and promoting the glorious mandate of My Gāo Zǔ.
Empress Xuān Dé respectfully inquires of those in their respective positions:
When merit is so great it cannot be rewarded,
the canon for honoring achievements is therefore incomplete;
when bestowals equal the powers of creation,
the ways to express gratitude for such virtue are indeed few.
Yet one must forcefully give it a name,
so that the administrator of the world has something to rely upon.
The Duke truly was born with virtue from Heaven,
being sage-like, broad, and deep.
Without changing the Shēn and Chén stars, the Nine Stars are looked up to;
without altering the sun and moon, the Two Realms are correctly viewed.
In times past, whether in darkness or light,
you hid your scales and folded your wings.
Broadly conversant in the various classics,
yet yielding in age to a teacher of a single scroll;
your sword-spirit reached the clouds, yet you humbled your tracks beneath ten thousand men.
Your eloquence could match the mouth of Heaven,
yet you seemed as if unable to speak;
your writings were as refined as carving a dragon,
yet once completed, you would always discard the drafts.
When you reached the age of twenty,
you were the first to respond to the summons of the bow and banner.
Traveling as a guest in the Liáng court,
your reputation was exceedingly great;
when your name was recommended to the Chancellor's office,
your spreading fame grew lofty of its own accord.
In the final years of Lóng Chāng,
your diligence in serving the King first became evident;
when Jiàn Wǔ was renewed,
the foundation was built through you.
Your merit was high but rewards were thin,
for such excellent service there was no equal.
Even with the fields of a single horse,
your resolve for Jiè Shān became even more strenuous;
with the rank of six hundred bushels,
the title of the Great Tree was preserved.
When you held the banners in the Sī Bù,
the horses of the Dài dared not graze to the south;
when you pushed the wheel-hubs in Fán and Dèng,
the dust of the Hú rarely rose in the evening.
Only that cunning boy,
who was utterly malevolent and cruel,
caused the destruction of the gentry
and the collapse of ritual and music.
Soon, he marshaled the troops and took an oath before the multitude,
declaring his intent to serve the Royal House.
With one wave of the white-feathered banner,
the Huángniǎo turmoil was settled.
Armor fell away like scales,
and chariots shattered like tiles.
Reaching the limits of Heaven’s mandate,
he bowed with folded hands to the various lords.
Such magnificent merit and abundant benefits
are beyond the power of virtue to describe.
Therefore, auspicious lights arrived together,
and propitious vapors filled the four directions;
the Wǔ Lǎo roamed the Hé,
and a flying star entered Mǎo.
Prime merit and flourishing achievements
are as magnificent as this.
Yet the territory was narrower than the Sì Lǚ,
and the status lower than the Jiǔ Bó.
The Emperor felt ashamed of this,
and the light carriages gathered to a halt.
Now I send certain officials of certain ranks,
leading these many officials,
each to offer his sincerity.
Wishing that the spirit of steadfastness
might return before long.
Directives:
Grand virtue does not perish,
for its righteousness is preserved in the sacrificial rites;
the lament regarding the absence of Guǎn Zhòng
grows deeper as I reflect upon these matters.
Zhāng Zǐfáng’s Way was second only to the Huángzhōng,
and his brilliance was nearly peerless.
With a mysterious resonance like wind and clouds,
he flourished as an Imperial Teacher.
He quelled Xiàng Yǔ and settled the Hàn,
greatly rescuing the world from the overflowing torrents.
He indeed followed the tracks of Yī Wàng,
and his virtue was capped by benevolence.
As for his meeting with the divine on the Yǐ Bridge,
and his Way harmonizing with Shāng Luò,
the boundary between his public life and reclusion
is profound and difficult to investigate;
like a deep current vast and surging,
its source cannot be fathomed.
Passing through the old Pèi,
I stopped the carriage at Liú Chéng.
The ancestral temple was desolate and ruined,
and the remaining portraits were old and dim.
Reflecting on affairs and remembering the man,
my long sighs are truly deep.
Those who pass through Dàliáng
might pause to think of the Yímén;
those who visit Jiǔjīng
also linger in memory of Suí Huì.
Comparing him to such people
is indeed appropriate.
Let the beams and eaves be reconstructed,
and the red and blue paintings be restored.
Let the simple offerings of water-shield and algae
be presented according to the seasons,
to express the feelings of remembering the past
and preserve his unerasable achievements.
Let the responsible officials carry this out.
Directives:
To honor the worthy and exalt virtue
shines ever brighter through a thousand years;
to honor the root and respect the beginning
is a principle that is grand and reaches from afar.
Chǔ Yuán Wáng accumulated benevolence and founded virtue,
opening the vassal state in this region;
his pure style and moral legacy
became a model for descendants.
The blessings of his lineage
truly aggrandized my clan;
the lingering fragrance and remaining achievements
have inspired for a hundred generations.
Yet the burial mounds are overgrown,
and the graves are not tended.
Feeling for the distant past and contemplating what has gone,
I sigh with eternal remembrance.
For one who loves a man, he cares for his tree;
thus the Gāntáng tree was not cut down.
In tracing and honoring the old tombs,
even that of Xìnlíng was not allowed to perish.
How much more so for the place where the dynasty began,
and where the foundation was first established!
Five households near the tomb may be exempted from taxes,
to provide for sweeping and cleaning indefinitely.
This shall be carried out.
Questioning the Xiùcái, Gāodì, and Míngjīng candidates:
I have heard that kings of divine spirit and cultured thought,
and sovereigns of acute hearing and sage virtue,
embody the Way without claiming it
and seek goodness as if they could never reach it.
Thus, at Kōngtóng, there was the request made following the wind;
and at Huáfēng, there was the bow offered while riding the clouds.
Some raised banners to seek scholars,
some set up side-gates to wait for the worthy,
thereby they were able to spread transformation in their time
and leave a legacy for a thousand ages.
I reverently follow the Mandate of Heaven
and respectfully contemplate the eternal plan.
I listen carefully from my high position
and harbor feelings of reverence and fear.
Although every word and deed must be recorded by historians,
the palace gates lack admonitions.
Waking or sleeping, I dream of excellent plans,
and long for those who are loyal and sincere.
You, gentlemen, have been selected for your reputation and promoted in learning;
it is beneficial for you to serve as guests to the King.
Strive to present the essentials of the Three Ways,
to illuminate the head of the Four Categories.
The harmony of the salt and plum
is what I look forward to.
Another question:
Formerly, when Zhōu Xuān neglected the ritual of the Qiānmǔ field,
Guó Gōng offered an admonition.
When Hàn Wén failed in the duty of the three thrusts of the plow,
Jiǎ Shēng presented his words.
Truly, it is because food is the Heaven of the people
and agriculture is the foundation of government.
Even metal walls and boiling moats cannot be defended without grain;
floods and droughts can be prepared for, but not avoided.
I take the former classics as my guide
and treasure this sowing and reaping.
When the signs are right, the green banners solemnize the work;
when the soil is rich, the red tassels signal the rites.
I wish to make it so that when apricot blossoms and calamus leaves appear,
plowing and harvesting are not delayed.
Let the clear irrigation channels and cool breezes
be maintained according to tradition without neglect.
Yet people abandon the plow and wear oxen,
following each other without returning.
The poor are exploited while the rich monopolize,
and this has gradually become the custom.
If the system of Yuánjǐng were opened,
I fear it would alarm and disturb the simple people.
Saline lands could be made fertile,
but I fear the time lacks a Shǐ Bái.
On the methods of promotion and abolition,
set forth your strategies.
Another question:
Discussing litigation and delaying death
is a profound rule of the Dà Yì.
Respecting the law and showing compassion in punishment
is a flourishing principle in the Yú Shū.
Since the common customs have become frivolous and lax,
laws and ordinances have become increasingly numerous.
At the Fèishí, there are few who are not wronged;
in the thorn forests, there are many ghosts crying in the night.
This is why I am moved at dawn
and harbor anxieties even while eating late.
I am pained by the dense net of the autumn reeds
and distressed by the harsh majesty of the summer sun.
I long remember the painted caps
and think back to the time when punishments were put aside.
Merely using the light penalty of a hundred huán
was practiced in the later ages;
while heavy punishments on the four limbs
began in ancient times.
Seeking the wandering bird in the deep valley
established the foundation of the Qín hegemony;
singing of the cockcrow beneath the palace gates
was praised as benevolence in the Hàn records.
If the two paths are different,
then use both to achieve thorough understanding.
Tell me clearly where peace may be found;
I shall personally review it.
Further question:
It is said that gathering people constitutes Wealth;
following this, the administration of government involves Commodities.
The flow of currency manifests its inexhaustibility,
while trade and migration facilitate the exchange between what exists and what is lacking.
Since the use of tortoise shells and cowries has long since ceased,
and strings of coins have been used exclusively,
they have grown more numerous through the generations,
yet losses through melting and leakage have tripled.
The destitute lack the means for two consecutive days of work,
and the middle class lacks capital for successive years.
Thinking of these hidden ailments and distress,
I cannot set aside My pity and lamentation.
Shàngdì looks down broadly,
bestowing upon Me auspicious treasures;
He commanded the valleys of Qióng and Xié
to open and yield copper.
There was also a subsequent command
to engage in the work of melting and casting,
to fill the Dūnèi with gold,
and to continue the duties of the Yuánfǔ.
However, Chìcè coins suffer the malady of clever counterfeiting,
and Yújiá coins make it difficult to balance weight and value.
On what is appropriate for opening or closing,
respond with all your heart.
Further question:
To regulate the calendar and clarify the seasons
is to inherit the cycles of change and reform;
to amend the constitution and order the laws
is to examine the origins of punishment and virtue.
The assignment of duties was manifest among the officials of Táng,
and refined articles were brilliant in the theories of Zōu.
Yet as the office at Yùyí fell into neglect
and the directions at Mèigǔ were lost,
Hàn relied on the signs of Sùzhī,
and Wèi claimed the evidence of the Huángxīng.
Disputes have arisen in vain,
and doubtful theories have no resolution.
Having succeeded to the Great Foundation,
I desire to promote the Ultimate Way.
I hope to make the sun and moon show auspicious signs,
the wind and rain as harmonious as the Jade Candle,
such that the intent of "illustrating virtue" is not far off,
and the meaning of "reverently following" is restored.
What do you, My Great Officers, think of this?
Whether the sacrificial horses change color,
or the months of Yín and Chǒu are differently established,
distinguish and clarify these in your writing.
Questioning the Xiùcái:
I hold the Talisman and govern Heaven,
grasping the Pivot and presiding over the Ultimate.
The Five Heavenly Bodies are watched in vain,
and the Nine Procedures are not yet celebrated in song.
As for contemplating governance at the Míngtái
and seeking the Way at the Xuānshì,
the sorrow as if falling into a pit is ever diligent,
and the concern as if for a wound is constantly grieving.
Therefore, I pity the poor and lighten the taxes,
reducing corvée labor and being cautious in trials.
Fortunately, the four borders are without worry,
and the three autumn harvests are ripe.
Yet though there is much millet and much rice,
the song of the "two-eared grain" has not arisen;
though people are without coarse cloth or clothes,
the lament of the "Seventh Month" must surely abound.
Is it that the administration of policy is not yet excellent,
or that the weary people find it difficult to maintain their livelihoods?
I summon you to the court,
to entrust you with great deliberation.
Let none fail to be of one mind
so as to rectify their Sovereign.
Further question:
When a King establishes a state,
he institutes statutes to appoint officials.
Above, they harmonize with the constellations;
below, they correspond to the rivers and mountains.
One must wait for the Nobility of Heaven to be fully cultivated
and for the Human Bonds to be all in order,
and only then assign duties according to talent
and divide offices by considering affairs.
Therefore, when the Wǔzhèng were established under Zhūxuān,
the common people did not err;
when the Jiǔgōng were inaugurated in the Huángxù,
the various achievements were solidified.
The officials of Zhōu numbered three hundred,
while those of Hàn were double that;
from that time onward,
the idle and lazy have indeed multiplied.
If the idle and redundant are all discarded,
then unruly criticisms will be endless;
if the ranks of those in ceremonial caps and tablets are not clarified,
then idle talk will only accumulate.
What then can be improved?
Give a detailed and proper response.
Further question:
In the past, when the Worthy Pastors divided Shǎn,
and good Governors shared in the rule,
small towns necessarily established their style,
and a single village could be made an achievement.
Some went so far as to pluck the sounding zither in the morning
and set out pure wine during the day,
being refined without being harmful,
and strict without being cruel.
Thus they could lead people out of dangerous realms
and elevate customs to a state of benevolence and longevity.
Therefore Jiǎ Yì said:
"When there is evil in the world,
it is the fault of the officials."
Lately, I have rigorously selected the holders of the jade tallies
and subtly chosen those of the bronze seals and ink;
yet the spring pheasants have not been tamed,
and the autumn borers have not dispersed.
When they are before Me,
they display their wisdom and strategy;
but when they go out to govern the linked cities,
I hear of no achievements from them.
Is it that the way of gathering talent has not been promoted?
Or that the meshes of the net for selection are still too simple?
Devote your thoughts and speak directly,
and do not evade the matter at hand.
Further question:
I have heard that those of superior wisdom benefit the people
and do not merely follow the Rites;
great worthies strengthen the state
and do not only plan according to the old.
Is it not that curing hunger does not require a banquet from tripods,
and saving the drowning does not wait for regulated steps?
Thus the Sānwáng had different ways yet flourished together,
and the Wǔbà had diverse styles yet were ranked together.
Today, farming and warfare are not cultivated,
while literary scholarship is what people compete in,
abandoning the fundamental to pursue the trivial,
the harms of which are manifold.
Long ago, a minister of Sòng considered rites and music to be destructive bandits,
and a ruler of Hàn compared literary works to the music of Zhèng and Wèi;
was it that they wished to defy sages and disregard laws,
or was it to employ expediency once the Way was established?
Now I wish to have men and women specialize in farming and sericulture,
and train the villages in archery and horsemanship;
to return to the Wǔdū and then attend to the schools,
and wait until the Four Classes are wealthy before returning to literature.
How is this way?
Do not just agree to My face.
Further question:
Since the house of Jìn failed to maintain order
and the passes and rivers were divided,
and since the house of Sòng lost its control
and the Huái and Biàn regions collapsed,
I contemplate the former subjects,
always considering how to save them.
Therefore, I select generals and open the borders
to comfort and settle them;
adding to this, I accept sincerity and promote peace,
distributing virtue and cultivating rites,
singing Huánghuá while dispatching envoys,
and composing Gāoyǔ to welcome guests.
This is why the regions of Guān and Luò are moved by the desire to look south,
and the Xūnyí suddenly have thoughts of returning north.
Indeed, a precarious leaf fears the wind,
and a startled bird is easy to bring down.
Without waiting for shields and spears,
one may simply use rhetoric and eloquence
to seek the Sānfǔ with a few words
and settle the Wǔzhōu with a single speech.
To what should this path lead?
Who among people might be capable of this?
Advance your strategies and express your aspirations
to enrich My heart.
Questioning the Xiùcái:
I have driven long distances through Fán and Dèng,
pointing directly toward the outskirts of Shāng,
taking advantage of the coming of the opportune time,
and riding upon this cyclic destiny.
Standing before the screen, I think long and hard;
I still harbor a sense of shame regarding my virtue.
Why is this?
The failings of the hundred kings
were most severe at the end of the Qí dynasty;
the official robes, caps, rituals, and music
were swept away until nothing remained.
I have carved the ornate and rounded the square,
and organized the world in its primordial chaos.
Adopting the rituals of the Sān Wáng,
caps and shoes are roughly distinguished;
following the music of the Liù Dài,
the notes and tones are finally discerned.
However, all systems are in their early stages,
and the granaries are not yet full.
If taxes are not levied on every plot,
then the state's expenditures will lack resources;
if the people do not have enough,
then I feel deep concern and compassion.
Whenever the seasonal fodder and straw are collected,
and the annual land taxes are levied,
my heart feels distressed and pained,
as if pitying my own infants.
Now, I wish to free myself from thoughts of a full hall,
and let the people have the abundance of a self-sufficient home,
gradually achieving a nine-year reserve of grain,
and slowly eliminating the taxes on passes and markets.
You, my scholars, face these three paths;
it is beneficial to serve the King as guests.
Where does the principle for this lie?
I await your excellent discourse.
Question:
I was originally one of the scholars;
from a young age, I had high aspirations.
I shut my doors to refine myself,
and opening scrolls, I gained insights on my own.
The Jiǔ Liú and Qī Lüè,
I have often perused;
the Liù Yì and the hundred schools,
I hope I am not like one facing a wall.
Although I deal with ten thousand affairs a day,
starting the court early and finishing late,
in the leisure between listening and viewing,
the three periods of leisure are never wasted.
The transformation of those below by those above
is like the grass bending when the wind blows;
yet I, in my insignificance,
have been unable to move the customs of the people.
In the past, purple clothing was a lowly garment,
yet it transformed the customs of Qí;
long hat strings were a vulgar preference,
yet they changed the habits of Zōu.
Although my virtue is shameful compared to the worthies of old,
my accomplishments are superior to past deeds.
Furthermore, when the way of the gentry is practiced,
it is because of stipends and benefits.
I devote my heart to finding the bones of a swift steed,
and I do not fear the true dragon.
Carriage canopies and green or purple robes
are like picking up mustard seeds from the ground.
Yet those who wander idly and abandon their studies
make up nine out of ten households;
the sound of singing birds is rarely heard,
and the Blue Collars are no longer composed.
The path of great encouragement
has already been set as such,
yet it remains desolate.
There must be an excellent plan for this.
Question:
I have established the drum for remonstrance
and set up the pillar for criticism;
it has been three years now.
Although many have gathered like spokes at the palace gates,
most do not address the essentials of government.
Daily they prostrate themselves on the green rushes,
but rarely can they be piercingly direct.
Perhaps it is because the late Qí period had many taboos,
and that tradition has persisted.
Or perhaps they think I merely admire antiquity in vain,
and that my receptiveness is not broad.
Yet since I began to rule the ten thousand realms,
and stood above the people,
when have I ever, because a word displeased me,
banished someone to the Northern Regions?
Even if there was a slight disagreement,
or if someone was sentenced to the Zuǒ Xiào,
would that cause upright officials to shut their mouths,
and cut off the path of loyal and straightforward speech?
I fear that the way of expanding and encouraging
may still be incomplete in some other way.
State your thoughts fully,
and speak to the limit without concealment.
Your servant has heard that when the great floods overflowed,
the Emperor sought to bring order,
searching everywhere in the four directions
to recruit the talented and eminent.
In the past, when Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
and intended to expand the ancestral legacy,
he consulted widely to brighten the undertakings,
and a multitude of scholars arrived like an echo.
Your Majesty is wise and sagely,
continuing the foundational line.
Having encountered a period of misfortune,
you work tirelessly and humbly until sunset.
As if the peaks have sent down spirits,
extraordinary men appear together.
I have observed the scholar Nǐ Héng of Píngyuán;
he is twenty-four years old,
and his courtesy name is Zhèngpíng.
He possesses a refined nature and is upright and brilliant,
with heroic talent that is truly outstanding.
When he first delved into arts and literature,
he mastered their inner sanctum;
whatever his eyes see once,
he can immediately recite;
whatever his ears hear for a moment,
he does not forget in his heart.
His nature is in harmony with the Dào,
and his thinking seems divinely inspired.
Sāng Hóngyáng's hidden calculations
and Zhāng Ānshì's silent memory—
if we measure Héng against them,
it truly would not be surprising.
He is loyal, resolute, and upright;
his will harbors the purity of frost and snow.
He regards goodness with awe,
and hates evil like an enemy.
Rèn Zuò's defiant conduct
and Shǐ Yú's rigorous integrity—
they could hardly surpass him.
A hundred birds of prey
are not equal to a single osprey.
If Héng were to stand in court,
he would surely be an impressive sight.
With flying eloquence and galloping rhetoric,
his spirit overflows and surges;
resolving doubts and untying knots,
he would have strength to spare when facing an adversary.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì asked to be tested in a dependent state
to bind the Chányú with a ruse;
Zhōng Jūn wished to use a long tassel
to lead and bring in the powerful Yuè.
Their fervent spirit at the age of twenty
was praised by previous generations.
Recently, Lù Cuì and Yán Xiàng
were also promoted to Tái Láng due to their exceptional talents;
Héng should be compared to them.
If he is allowed to leap like a dragon into the celestial highway,
and flap his wings in the Milky Way,
spreading his fame to the Zǐwēi Palace,
and casting light like a rainbow,
it would be enough to illuminate the many scholars of the inner offices
and increase the solemnity of the four gates.
The Grand Music of the Jūntiān
must have magnificent sights;
the imperial household and the Emperor's dwelling
must store extraordinary treasures.
Men like Héng cannot be found often.
The Jī Chǔ and Yáng Ā melodies,
of the most exquisite form,
are what the masters of music covet;
Fēitù and Yǎoniǎo,
steeds that gallop with incomparable speed,
are what Liáng Lè urgently seeks.
We, your humble servants,
dare not fail to report this.
Your Majesty is earnest and cautious in selecting scholars,
and must subject them to testing.
I beg that Héng be summoned for an audience in his commoner's clothes.
If there is nothing worth observing or selecting,
your servants shall accept the punishment for deceiving the Emperor to his face.
Your servant Liàng says:
The Late Emperor had not yet half-completed his founding enterprise
when he passed away in the middle of his path.
Today the realm is divided into three,
and Yì Zhōu is weary and depleted;
this is truly a critical moment of life or death, survival or ruin.
Yet the officials of the guard do not slacken within the court,
and loyal-hearted soldiers risk their lives on the frontiers,
because they remember the Late Emperor’s exceptional treatment
and desire to repay it to Your Majesty.
It is truly fitting that you broaden your sage hearing,
to glorify the legacy of the Late Emperor’s virtue
and bolster the spirit of your resolute men.
You should not belittle yourself without reason,
or use inappropriate analogies,
so as to block the path of loyal remonstrance.
Whether in the Imperial Palace or the Chancellor's Office,
all are as one body;
in promoting the good and punishing the bad,
there should be no differences.
If there are those who commit crimes or violate the laws, or those who act with loyalty and goodness,
they should be handed over to the proper authorities
to determine their punishment or reward,
to demonstrate Your Majesty’s fair and enlightened governance.
You should not show favoritism,
causing the laws of the palace and the court to differ.
The Palace Attendants and Gentlemen of the Secretariat, Guō Yōuzhī, Fèi Yī, Dǒng Yǔn, and others,
are all honest and upright men,
their thoughts and intentions are loyal and pure;
thus the Late Emperor selected them to be left to Your Majesty.
It is my humble opinion that regarding the affairs of the Palace,
no matter how great or small,
you should consult with them in all matters
before putting them into effect;
this will surely help compensate for deficiencies and leaks,
and provide broader benefit.
General Xiàng Chǒng,
is of virtuous and fair character
and is thoroughly well-versed in military affairs.
Having been tested in the past,
the Late Emperor praised him as capable;
therefore, the consensus has recommended Chǒng to be the Commander.
It is my humble opinion that regarding the affairs of the military camp,
you should consult with him in all matters;
this will surely ensure harmony among the ranks
and that both the strong and the weak find their proper places.
Drawing close to worthy ministers
and distancing oneself from petty men—
this is why the Former Hàn flourished.
Drawing close to petty men
and distancing oneself from worthy scholars—
this is why the Later Hàn declined and fell.
When the Late Emperor was alive,
whenever he discussed this matter with me,
he never failed to sigh with regret and resentment over the reigns of Huán and Líng.
The Palace Attendants, Masters of Writing, Chief Clerks, and Army Counselors—
these are all upright and loyal ministers prepared to die for their integrity.
I hope Your Majesty will draw close to them and trust them;
then the prosperity of the House of Hàn
can be expected in a matter of days.
Your servant was originally a commoner,
personally farming in Nányáng,
seeking only to preserve my life in a chaotic world,
not seeking fame or status among the feudal lords.
The Late Emperor did not consider me base or lowly,
and humbled himself
by visiting me three times in my thatched cottage,
to consult me on the affairs of the age.
Because of this, I was moved with gratitude
and then pledged my service to the Late Emperor.
Later, we met with defeat,
and I accepted my commission at a time of military collapse,
taking up my orders in the midst of peril and difficulty;
since then, twenty-one years have passed.
The Late Emperor knew I was cautious,
and so, when he was about to pass away, he entrusted me with the great task.
Since receiving those orders,
day and night I have worried and sighed,
fearing that the trust placed in me would not be fulfilled,
thereby tarnishing the Late Emperor's discernment.
Therefore, in the fifth month, I crossed the Lú River,
penetrating deep into barren lands.
Now the south has been pacified
and our weaponry and armor are sufficient;
we should encourage and lead the three armies
to pacify the Central Plains in the north.
I hope to exhaust my mediocre abilities to
eliminate the treacherous and evil,
restore the House of Hàn,
and return to the old capital.
This is my duty in repaying the Late Emperor and showing loyalty to Your Majesty.
As for deliberating on what to remove or add
and offering loyal advice to the fullest,
that is the responsibility of Yōuzhī, Yī, and Yǔn.
I hope Your Majesty will entrust me with the task of punishing the rebels and restoring the state;
if I should fail,
then punish my crime
to report it to the spirit of the Late Emperor.
Reprimand Yōuzhī, Yī, Yǔn, and the others for their faults
to highlight their negligence.
Your Majesty should also examine yourself,
to consult and seek the good way,
to examine and accept refined words,
and to deeply reflect upon the Late Emperor's testamentary edict.
Your servant is overwhelmed with gratitude for the favor received!
Now that I am about to depart for a distant place,
as I face this memorial, I shed tears,
and I know not what more to say.
Your servant Zhí says:
I have heard that when a scholar is born into this world,
at home he serves his father,
and abroad he serves his lord.
Serving a father prizes bringing honor to one's parents;
serving a lord values bringing prosperity to the state.
Thus, even a compassionate father cannot love a son who provides no benefit,
and a benevolent lord cannot maintain a servant who is of no use.
He who evaluates virtue to grant office
is a lord who achieves success;
he who weighs his own ability to accept a title
is a servant who will devote his life.
Therefore, the lord does not grant in vain,
and the servant does not receive in vain;
to grant in vain is called a mistaken recommendation,
and to receive in vain is called being a "corpse in office."
The bread of idleness mentioned in the *Shī*,
is the reason those lines were written.
In the past, the two Guó did not decline the responsibility of two states,
for their virtue was profound;
Dàn and Shì did not refuse the enfeoffments of Yān and Lǔ,
for their achievements were great.
Now your servant has received the heavy grace of the state,
for three generations until today.
Precisely at this time of peace under Your Majesty,
bathing in the sage's favor,
and being silently nourished by your virtuous teachings,
I can be said to be deeply fortunate.
Yet I occupy the position of the Eastern March,
and my rank is among the highest,
my body is clad in light and warm garments,
my mouth is satiated with a hundred flavors,
my eyes have seen the height of splendor,
and my ears are weary of the sounds of strings and flutes—
all of which are the result of high rank and thick stipend.
Reflecting in private on those who received rank and stipend in ancient times,
they were different from this:
all of them used their diligent efforts to save the state,
assist the ruler, and benefit the people.
Now your servant has no virtue to speak of,
and no achievements to record;
if I end my years like this,
providing no benefit to the state or the court,
I will be subject to the mockery of "the man and himself" from the poets of the *Shī*.
Therefore, looking up, I am ashamed before my black ceremonial cap,
and looking down, I am embarrassed by my vermilion sash.
Today the realm is unified,
and the Jiǔzhōu are at peace.
Yet looking west, there is still the disobedient Shǔ;
in the east, there is the insubordinate Wú.
This causes the borders to be unable to set aside their armor,
and the strategists to be unable to rest easy.
It is truly desired to unify the entire world
so as to achieve Tàihé.
Thus, when Qǐ destroyed the Yǒuhù, the achievements of Xià became illustrious;
when Chéng conquered Shāng and Yǎn, the virtue of Zhōu became prominent.
Now Your Majesty rules the world with sagely brilliance,
desiring to complete the achievements of Wén and Wǔ
and continue the prosperity of Chéng and Kāng.
You select the virtuous and appoint the capable,
employing ministers like Fāng Shū and Shào Hǔ
to guard the four borders.
For those who serve as the claws and teeth of the state,
this can be called appropriate.
However, the high-flying bird has not yet been caught by the light string-arrow,
and the fish of the deep has not yet been suspended from the hook and bait;
I fear that the techniques of fishing and shooting
might not yet be fully employed.
In the past, Gěng Yǎn did not wait for Guāngwǔ
but swiftly attacked Zhāng Bù,
saying he would not leave rebels as a legacy for his lord and father.
Thus, the attendant on the right died by his sword upon the chariot wheel,
and Yōngmén slit his throat at the border of Qí.
For men such as these two,
how could they hate life and value death?
They were truly indignant that their master was slighted and their lord insulted.
A lord's favor to a minister
is intended to remove harm and promote benefit;
a minister's service to a lord
must involve sacrificing one's life to quell disorder
and repaying the master with merit.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì, at the age of twenty,
sought to be tested in the dependent states,
requesting to bind the neck of the Chányú and control his fate.
Zhōng Jūn, in his youth, went as an envoy to Yuè,
desiring a long rope to bind its king
and bring him captive to the northern palace gate.
Did these two ministers enjoy boasting to their lord or showing off to the world?
Their ambitions were pent up,
and they desired to exert their talents and contribute their abilities to an enlightened lord.
In the past, Hàn Wǔdì built a residence for Huò Qùbìng;
he declined, saying:
"While the Xiōngnú are not yet destroyed,
I have no use for a home!"
Indeed, to worry for the state and forget one's home,
and to sacrifice one's body to relieve difficulties,
is the ambition of a loyal minister.
Now that I reside away from the capital,
it is not that I am not treated generously;
yet I do not sleep peacefully on my mat,
and I have no leisure to savor my food,
for I am constantly concerned that the two regions have not been conquered.
I have observed that the military ministers and veteran soldiers of the late Wǔ Huángdì
who have reached old age and passed away are many;
although the worthy are not lacking in any age,
the veteran generals and old soldiers
are still practiced in warfare.
I venture to not measure my own limitations,
but my ambition is to dedicate my life,
hoping to achieve even a tiny bit of merit
to repay the kindness I have received.
If Your Majesty would issue an extraordinary edict
to employ my meager skills,
allowing me to be subordinate to the Dàjiāngjūn in the west
to command a single regiment,
or to be subordinate to the Dàsīmǎ in the east
to take charge of a secondary force.
I would certainly brave dangers and tread upon perils,
galloping horses and speeding boats,
charging against blades and facing spear-tips,
to be at the forefront of the soldiers.
Although I might not be able to capture Quán or take the head of Liàng,
I hope to capture their heroic leaders
and annihilate their wicked kind.
I would surely achieve a momentary victory
to wipe away a lifetime of shame,
letting my name be recorded by the historian's brush
and my deeds be listed among the honors of the court.
Even if my body is torn apart in the Shǔ territory
or my head is hung at the gates of Wú,
it would still be as if I lived for many years.
If my meager talents are not tested
and I pass from this world without being heard of,
merely bringing honor to my person and abundance to my body,
living without benefiting the state
and dying without affecting the outcome,
vainly holding a high position and shaming a heavy salary,
living like a beast or a bird
until I reach old age,
this is merely the life of an animal in a pen
and is not my ambition.
I have heard rumors that the eastern army was unprepared
and the troops suffered a minor setback;
I stopped eating and abandoned my meals,
flapping my sleeves and rolling up my robes,
clasping my sword and looking eastward,
my heart having already raced to Wúhuì.
In the past, I followed the late Wǔ Huángdì
south to Chìàn,
east to the Cānghǎi,
west to Yùmén,
and north past the Xuánsài.
I observed the methods of moving troops and the maneuvers of warfare,
which can be called divinely subtle.
Therefore, matters of war cannot be predicted;
one must adapt to changes when facing difficulties.
My ambition is to dedicate myself in this enlightened time
and establish merit in this sagely age.
Whenever I read the historical records
and observe the loyal ministers and righteous men of old
who gave up their lives in a single morning
to die for the difficulties of the state,
though their bodies were torn apart,
their merits were inscribed on the Jǐngzhōng bells
and their names were handed down on bamboo and silk,
I never fail to beat my breast and sigh.
I have heard that an enlightened lord employs ministers
without discarding those who have committed crimes.
Thus, generals who fled and lost battles were employed,
and through them, Qín and Lǔ achieved their successes;
ministers who snapped their hat-strings or stole horses were forgiven,
and through them, Chǔ and Zhào overcame their difficulties.
I am privately moved by the early passing of the late Emperor
and the death of Wēi Wáng.
Who am I alone
to be able to endure for long?
I always fear that I will perish before the morning dew
and fill the ravines;
before the soil on my grave is dry,
my person and my name will both be extinguished.
I have heard that when the Qíjì steed neighs long,
Bó Lè recognizes its ability;
when the Lú dog howls mournfully,
Hánguó knows its talent.
Therefore, they are tested on the roads of Qí and Chǔ
to fulfill the task of a thousand lǐ,
and tested against the speed of a wily rabbit
to prove their utility in pouncing and biting.
Now I aspire to the meager merit of a dog or a horse,
yet I privately reflect
that there is ultimately no Bó Lè or Hánguó to recommend me.
This is why I am distressed and privately pained.
Those who stand at a gambling game and lean forward in anticipation,
or who hear music and privately clap their hands,
are perhaps those who appreciate the tone and understand the way.
In the past, Máo Suì,
an attendant in Zhào,
still used the metaphor of the awl in the bag
to awaken his lord and establish merit;
how much more so in the court of the majestic Dà Wèi, filled with many scholars,
could there be no ministers willing to die passionately in times of trouble?
One who advertises and recommends oneself
is an ugly act for a scholar or a woman;
seeking advancement by currying favor with the times
is a clear taboo of the Dàojiā.
Yet the reason I dare to present this to Your Majesty
is truly because I share the same form and breath as the state,
and share in its worries and troubles.
I hope that with the insignificance of dust or dew,
I might supplement the mountains and seas;
and like the faint light of a firefly or a candle,
increase the brilliance of the sun and moon.
Therefore, I dare to risk such ugliness to offer my loyalty,
knowing for certain that I will be laughed at by the court officials.
A sagely ruler does not reject words because of the person;
I humbly pray that Your Majesty might slightly incline your divine hearing,
and I would then be fortunate indeed.
Your servant Zhí says:
Your servant has heard that Heaven is called high
because there is nothing it does not cover;
Earth is called broad
because there is nothing it does not carry;
the sun and moon are called bright
because there is nothing they do not illuminate;
the rivers and seas are called great
because there is nothing they do not contain.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ said:
"Great indeed was Yáo as a ruler!
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yáo modeled himself after it."
Now, the virtue of Heaven toward the myriad things
can indeed be called vast and wide.
In Yáo's establishment of teachings,
he put kin first and the distant last,
extending from the near to the far.
The *Chuán* says:
"He was able to manifest illustrious virtue,
so as to treat the nine branches of the family with affection.
Once the nine branches were in harmony,
he distinguished and honored the hundred surnames."
When it came to Wén Wáng of Zhōu,
he also exalted this transformation.
The *Shī* says:
"He set an example for his wife,
extending it to his brothers,
and thus governed his family and state."
Therefore, all was harmonious and solemn,
and the poets sang of it.
In the past, Zhōu Gōng lamented that Guǎn and Cài were not in accord,
yet he widely enfeoffed his fine kin
to act as a screen and defense for the royal house.
The *Chuán* says:
"In the ancestral alliances of Zhōu,
those of different surnames were placed last."
Truly, the kindness of flesh and blood
may have friction but does not lead to separation;
the principle of loving one's kin
is indeed firm and solid;
