there has never been one who acted with righteousness yet put his lord last,
or one who was benevolent yet abandoned his kin.
I prostrately observe that Your Majesty consults the reverent and brilliant virtue of Dì Táng,
and embodies the cautious benevolence of Wén Wáng.
Your grace reaches the Jiāofáng,
and your kindness illuminates the nine classes of kin.
The various lords and hundred officials
take turns to rest and serve.
Those in power are not neglected in the public court,
and private feelings can be expressed in personal chambers.
The path for family visits is open,
and the sentiments of celebration and condolence are expressed.
This can truly be called measuring oneself to govern others,
and extending kindness to bestow grace.
As for your servant,
the threads of human relations are severed;
I am restricted during this enlightened age,
which your servant secretly grieves over.
I do not dare to hope for interaction with those of my kind,
to cultivate human affairs,
or to arrange human relations.
Recently, marriage ties have been blocked,
brothers have been permanently severed,
inquiries about auspicious or inauspicious events are obstructed,
and the rites of celebration and condolence are abandoned.
The neglect of the bonds of kindness
is worse than that toward strangers on the road;
the difference of our separation
is greater than that between the Hú and the Yuè.
Now, because of certain regulations, your servant
has no hope of ever attending court.
As for focusing my heart on the Huáng Jí
and binding my feelings to the Zǐ Tà,
the divine spirits know it.
Yet if Heaven has truly caused this,
what can be said!
In retirement, I observe that the various princes often have hearts of shared sorrow.
I wish Your Majesty would grandly issue an edict,
allowing the various states to send inquiries of celebration,
and let the four seasons be used for visits,
to narrate the joyful kindness of flesh and blood,
and to complete the sincere righteousness of brotherly harmony.
Let the families of consorts and concubines,
and gifts of cosmetic oils and baths,
be allowed to pass through twice a year,
aligning the principles with the noble clans,
and equaling the grace shown to the hundred departments.
If this is done,
then what the ancients sighed for
and what was sung in the *Fēng* and *Yǎ*
will once again exist in this sagely age.
Your servant prostrately reflects:
how could I be without the use of an awl or a knife?
When I observe those Your Majesty has selected and appointed,
if your servant were of a different surname,
I secretly estimate
that I would not be behind the court officials.
If I could give up my distant travels,
wear the Wǔ Biàn,
untie the red cord,
and wear the green ribbon,
serving as Fùmǎ Fèngchē,
obtaining just one title,
residing in the capital,
holding the whip or sticking a brush in my ear,
following the flowery canopy when going out,
and attending the imperial carriage when coming in,
responding to the Sage's questions,
and correcting omissions by your side—
this is the ultimate wish of your servant's sincere heart,
something I never depart from even in my dreams.
From afar, I admire the banquet of lord and minister in "Lù Míng,"
in between, I recite the warning of "Táng Dì" about having no others,
and below, I think of the righteousness of friends in "Fá Mù,"
and finally, I harbor the endless sorrow of "Liào É."
At every gathering of the four seasons,
I sit alone like a clod of earth;
my attendants are only servants and slaves,
those I face are only my wife and children.
I have no one with whom to share high conversation,
and no one with whom to express principles.
Never do I hear music without clutching my heart,
or face a wine cup without sighing.
Your servant prostrately believes that the sincerity of a dog or horse cannot move a person,
just as the sincerity of a person cannot move Heaven.
Regarding the falling of city walls or the falling of frost,
your servant used to believe in them,
but judging by my own heart,
they are merely empty words.
Like the leaves of the hollyhock or bean plant leaning,
though the sun does not turn its light for them,
the fact that they always turn toward it
is due to sincerity.
Your servant secretly compares himself to the hollyhock and bean plant;
if the bounty of Heaven and Earth is to be lowered,
and the brightness of the three luminaries is to shine down,
it truly rests with Your Majesty.
Your servant heard Wénzǐ say:
"Do not be the first for fortune,
do not be the leader for disaster."
In the current state of separation and obstruction,
brothers share the same sorrow,
yet why is it that your servant alone speaks out?
I secretly do not wish for there to be any being in this sagely age that does not receive your bounty.
If there is a being that does not receive your bounty,
there will surely be a heart of bitter poison;
therefore, in the poem "Bó Zhōu," there is the resentment of "O Heaven!";
in "Gǔ Fēng," there is the sigh of being abandoned.
Yī Yǐn felt it a shame if his lord did not become like Yáo or Shùn.
Mèngzǐ said:
"One who does not serve his lord as Shùn served Yáo
is one who does not respect his lord."
Your servant's ignorance and dullness
are certainly not those of Yú or Yī.
As for wanting Your Majesty to exalt the beauty of "radiance covering the era in harmony"
and to proclaim the virtue of "continuous brightness and illustriousness,"
this is your servant's humble sincerity,
which I secretly hold alone.
Truly harboring a heart of standing like a crane and tiptoeing in anticipation,
I dare to present these words again,
hoping that Your Majesty might perhaps exercise your divine hearing and grant me a spiritual audience.
Servant Hù says:
Yesterday when your servant went out,
I prostrated myself and heard the gracious edict
promoting your servant and causing me to serve among the Tái Sī.
Since your servant began his career
until now, barely more than ten years have passed.
I have held responsibilities both inside and outside the capital,
always in extremely prominent and important positions.
I often think that wisdom and strength cannot be forced forward,
and favor and honor cannot long be misplaced.
Morning and night I tremble with fear,
viewing glory as a cause for anxiety.
Your servant has heard the words of the ancients:
if one's virtue has not yet won the submission of the masses,
yet one receives a high noble rank,
then it causes talented officials not to advance;
if one's merit has not yet won the allegiance of the masses,
yet one bears a generous salary,
then it causes industrious officials not to be encouraged.
Now your servant's person is tied to the Wàiqī,
and my affairs have met with a fortunate turn of fate.
My warning lies in excessive favor,
and I do not worry about being left behind.
Yet suddenly an exceptional edict has been issued from within the palace,
bestowing extraordinary honor.
What merit does your servant have to be able to endure it?
With what heart can I be at peace with it?
To mislead Your Majesty with my person
and disgrace a high position,
ruin would soon follow.
If I wished then to return to guarding the humble cottage of my ancestors,
how could that be possible!
To disobey the command would indeed offend the Heavenly Majesty;
but to comply reluctantly would result in this again.
I have heard that the ancients extended themselves for those who recognized them;
the integrity of a high official
is to stop if it is not appropriate.
Although your servant is a person of low station,
I dare to follow the grace I have received
and keep this principle in mind.
Since the world submitted to your civilizing influence,
eight years have just passed.
Although You lean forward on Your seat seeking the worthy
and do not neglect those in obscure or humble positions,
yet your servant and others cannot recommend those with virtue
or promote those with merit,
to let the Sage's hearing know that those superior to your servant are many,
and those who have not yet attained high office are not few.
If there were neglected virtue among those building walls
or hidden talent among butchers and fishermen,
and yet the court deliberations were to use your servant and not consider it wrong,
and your servant were to occupy the position and not feel ashamed,
how could the loss not be great!
Furthermore, although your servant has occupied positions undeservedly for a long time,
it has never been like today, combining the ultimate favors of civil and military roles
and equaling the high rank of the Zǎifǔ.
Although your servant's view is narrow,
according to what I see, the current Guānglù Dàfū Lǐ Xǐ
holds to his integrity with high brilliance
and conducts himself uprightly in the court.
Guānglù Dàfū Lǔ Zhī
keeps himself pure with few desires,
being harmonious but not conforming blindly.
Guānglù Dàfū Lǐ Yìn
governs with breadth and simplicity,
and maintains a serious countenance in matters of justice.
All have served until their hair turned white,
maintaining ritual propriety from beginning to end.
Although they have passed through favors both internal and external,
they are no different from those in cold and humble families,
yet they have not yet been graced with this selection.
If your servant were to surpass them,
how could I satisfy the expectations of the world
or slightly benefit the sun and moon?
Therefore, I vow in my heart to keep my integrity
and have no ambition for improper advancement.
Now that the roads are not yet opened
and the border regions have many troubles,
I beg You to withhold the previous favor
and allow your servant to return quickly to his garrison.
If I do not, and linger here,
there will surely be deficiencies in external defense.
Your servant cannot overcome his worry and fear,
and respectfully risks offense to present this memorial.
I only hope Your Majesty observes that the will of a common man cannot be taken away.
Servant Mì says:
Because of my ill-fated life and misfortunes,
I early on encountered sorrow and calamity.
When I was a child of six months,
my compassionate father passed away.
When I reached the age of four,
my uncle forced my mother to change her will and remarry.
My grandmother Liú took pity on your servant's loneliness and weakness,
and personally raised me.
When young, your servant had many illnesses,
and at nine years old could not walk.
Forlorn and solitary,
I struggled until I reached adulthood.
Having no paternal uncles,
and in the end having no brothers,
my family line was declining and its blessings were thin.
Only late in life did I have a son.
Outside, there are no close relatives of the Qī or Gōng degrees of mourning;
inside, there is not even a five-foot-tall boy to answer the door.
Solitary and alone I stand,
with only my body and shadow to console each other.
Moreover, Liú has long been entangled in sickness
and is constantly in her bed.
Your servant waits upon her with decoctions and medicine,
never having abandoned or left her.
Coming to serve the Holy Dynasty,
I have been bathed in its pure civilizing influence.
Previously, the Grand Administrator, your servant Kuí, nominated your servant as Xiàolián;
later, the Regional Inspector, your servant Róng, recommended your servant as Xiùcái.
Because your servant had no one else to care for his grandmother,
I declined and did not report for duty.
A special edict was issued
appointing your servant as Lángzhōng;
soon after, I received the state's grace
and was appointed as Xǐmǎ.
Despite being of lowly and humble status,
I was to serve at the Dōnggōng;
this is not something your servant could repay even by laying down his life.
Your servant reported everything in a memorial
and declined to take up the post.
The edict was severe and sharp,
reprimanding your servant for being evasive and slow.
The commanderies and counties pressured me,
urging your servant to take to the road;
the provincial officials came to my door,
more urgent than a shooting star.
Your servant wished to obey the edict and rush to the post,
but Liú's illness became more severe by the day;
I wished to follow my personal feelings for a time,
but my appeals were not granted.
Your servant's dilemma of whether to advance or retreat
is truly a predicament.
I humbly submit that the Holy Dynasty rules the world with filial piety,
and all the elderly
still receive pity and care;
how much more so your servant, who is lonely and suffering,
and whose case is especially extreme.
Furthermore, when young, your servant served the illegitimate dynasty
and held various positions in the Láng offices;
originally I planned to achieve high office
and did not cherish my reputation for integrity.
Now your servant is a lowly captive from a fallen state,
most insignificant and humble,
yet I have been excessively promoted,
and the favored command is generous and rich.
How would I dare to hesitate
or have other expectations!
It is only because Liú is like the sun setting behind the western hills;
her breathing is faint,
her life is in peril and shallow,
and in the morning she cannot be sure of the evening.
If your servant did not have his grandmother,
he would not have reached this day;
if my grandmother did not have your servant,
she would have no way to finish her remaining years.
Grandmother and grandson, these two people,
rely on each other for their lives.
Therefore, because of my small personal concern, I cannot abandon her and go far away.
Your servant Mì is forty-four years old this year;
my grandmother Liú is ninety-six years old this year.
Thus the days your servant can fulfill his loyalty to Your Majesty are long,
while the days to repay and care for Liú are short.
With the private feelings of a young crow,
I beg to be allowed to care for her until her end.
Your servant's hardships
are not only known to the people of Shǔ and the governors and protectors of the two provinces;
Imperial Heaven and Sovereign Earth
truly bear witness to them.
I hope Your Majesty will pity my foolish sincerity
and grant your servant’s humble wish,
so that Liú may be fortunate
and safely finish her remaining years.
In life, your servant shall lay down his head for You;
in death, I shall be like the ghost who knotted grass to repay a debt.
Your servant cannot overcome his feelings of fear, like those of a dog or a horse,
and respectfully presents this memorial to inform You.
Your subordinate official Lù Jī says:
On the ninth day of this month,
the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn sent the Acting Assistant Zhāng Hán
to bring the wooden tablet of the imperial edict and the seal with ribbons,
appointing your servant as the Píngyuán Nèishǐ.
I received the appointment with reverence and trepidation,
not knowing how to compose myself.
Your servant Jī kowtows, kowtows,
a capital offense, a capital offense.
Your servant was originally a man of Wú,
coming from an enemy state.
For generations, my ancestors had no record of exerting effort for this dynasty,
nor was my talent that of a distinguished and upright scholar from the countryside.
The Imperial grace was widely bestowed,
its benevolence reaching far and wide.
I was elevated from among the masses
and repeatedly received honors and promotions.
During my nine years in the court,
I have held six different offices.
I personally ascended to the Three Pavilions
and achieved office in both palaces.
Wearing the ceremonial cap and riding in a carriage,
I was ranked among the noble and prominent.
Rising from obscurity to make my mark,
looking back, I far surpassed my peers.
The kindness shown to me was as heavy as the mountains;
my sense of duty should have led me to sacrifice myself even to ash.
When the state encountered upheaval,
I had no record of integrity to show.
Although I received a broad pardon,
how can I alone show my face?
Bowing my head and dropping to my knees,
my worry and shame are like a pestilence.
Yet I was unjustly framed by the late Qí Wáng Jiǒng,
who falsely accused me of collaborating with others to draft an abdication edict.
I was imprisoned in a dungeon
and was to be the first executed.
My humble sincerity
has not betrayed Heaven or Earth.
In that moment of crisis,
fearing there was coercion,
I, together with my younger brother Yún and the Sànqì Shìláng Yuán Yú,
the Zhōngshū Shìláng Féng Xióng,
the Shàngshū Yòuchéng Cuī Jī,
the Tíngwèizhèng Gù Róng,
and the Rǔyīn Tàishǒu Cáo Wǔ,
considered how to be spared.
Secretly seeking to avoid danger,
we struggled to explain our positions.
Not a single word or character
was involved in the matter.
The traces of the events and the handwriting
could all be cross-examined.
Yet suddenly everything was overturned,
and it was turned into a crime instead.
This tiny life of mine
is not worth pitying,
but my humble original intent
is truly pitiable.
Fearing the pressure of Imperial Majesty,
I accepted the guilt with extreme caution,
remaining silent and tongue-tied,
not daring to appeal to the Heavens.
This greatest of offenses
reaches the Sacred Ears daily,
yet the sincerity of my heart and blood
has never been heard once.
The reason I was fervent in the face of disaster yet cannot help but feel resentment
is this and this alone.
Once again, I received Your Majesty's kind and gentle pardon,
which stayed the frost and withdrew the lightning,
preventing me from perishing.
Once again, I was able to support the elderly and lead the young
as I left the prison gates alive.
Holding the golden seal and trailing the purple ribbon,
I retired to the ranks of lesser officials.
Feeling gratitude while reflecting on my faults,
my emotions were shaken with grief.
I walked as if Heaven were too low and Earth too thin,
as if there were no place for me.
I did not expect the brilliance of the sun and moon
would finally shine upon me,
and the bounty of clouds and rain
would reach even the decayed and exhausted.
Overlooking my weak talent,
and that I have nothing worthy about myself,
you pitied my desolate state,
seeing that my crime was understandable.
If my name were only struck from the criminal records
and I could be restored as a commoner,
then the dust would be washed away by the celestial waves
and slander would cease from the mouths of the people.
This was my initial hope,
yet it had not even reached this far.
Unexpectedly, I was honored with a great command
and publicly granted the tiger-shaped tally.
You allowed the withered branches of spring
to once again emit fragrance alongside autumn orchids,
and the feathers of a sunken bird
to once again flap wings with the soaring swan.
Though Ānguó was released from servitude
and rose to wear the green silk ribbon,
and Zhāng Chǎng was a fugitive
yet eventually sat in a vermilion carriage,
compared to what I bear,
these were not sufficient to be called great.
How could I, who am covered in shame and harboring regret, be worthy of usurping such a position?
It is not something I could repay even if my clan were destroyed and my family exterminated.
Joy and fear are mingled;
sorrow and shame are choked and knotted within me.
Bound by the standard regulations,
I must proceed directly to my post
and cannot hasten myself
to kowtow at the palace gates.
Looking toward the heavenly roads,
my heart races toward the Imperial carriage.
Your servant cannot help but be filled with anxious anticipation.
I respectfully submit this memorial for your information.
On the eighteenth day, Xīnchǒu, of the third month beginning with Guǐwèi, in the fifth year of Jiànxīng,
Envoy with Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Héběi and the three provinces of Bìng, Jì, and Yōu,
Acting Protector-General and General of the Household for the Xiōngnú,
Sīkōng,
Inspector of Bìngzhōu,
and Guǎngwǔ Hóu, your servant Kūn;
Envoy with Credentials, Palace Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Jìzhōu,
General-in-Chief Who Comforts the Army,
Inspector of Jìzhōu,
Worthy King of the Left,
and Bóhǎi Gōng, your servant Dī,
bowing their heads and deserving of death, submit this memorial.
Your servants Kūn and Dī bow their heads, bow their heads;
deserving of death, deserving of death.
Your servants have heard that Heaven brings forth the common people
and establishes rulers for them,
so as to respond to Heaven and Earth
and to shepherd the black-haired masses.
Sage emperors and enlightened kings observe this,
knowing that Heaven and Earth cannot lack offerings,
and thus they humble themselves to serve them;
knowing that the common people cannot be without a master,
and thus they govern them out of necessity.
When the state faces difficulties,
then the imperial kinsmen and feudal lords stabilize its collapse;
when the ancestral temples are neglected,
then the wise of the clan continue the sacrifices.
In this way, they broadly promote the far-reaching customs
and strengthen the dynasty for ten thousand generations.
From the time of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors onwards,
there have been none who did not follow this path.
Your servant Kūn and your servant Pǐdī bow their heads and bow their heads,
a capital offense, a capital offense.
I humbly consider that Gāozǔ Xuān Huángdì laid the foundation of the Great Mandate,
and Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì then unified the realm of Xià.
For three generations, brilliance was renewed,
and four sages followed in their footsteps.
Their benevolent grace equaled that of Yǒuyú,
and their divined years surpassed those of the Zhōu clan.
Since the Yuánkāng era,
hardships and calamities have frequently arisen.
At the time of the Yǒngjiā era,
the pestilential air became ever darker.
The imperial pivot lost its control,
and the Emperor passed away among the base barbarians.
The danger to the state
was like a dangling tassel.
Relying on the virtue of former sovereigns
and the spirits of the ancestral temples,
the Emperor was established as the successor.
The old order was restored;
he was born with reverence and brilliance,
and embraced wisdom and discernment.
His jade-like quality was manifest from his youth,
and his resonant voice echoed early on.
The Grand Regent managed the main principles,
and all the lords assisted in the governance.
All within the four seas longed for the beauty of restoration,
and all living beings cherished the hope of deliverance.
Unexpectedly, Heaven did not relent in its calamities;
great disasters arrived repeatedly.
Before the state could forget its troubles,
bandit harms soon arose.
The rebellious Hú, Liú Yào,
rampaged through the Xīdū,
daring to unleash his dog-and-sheep-like hordes
to violate the celestial city.
When your servants returned from delivering the memorial,
we received word from the Western Court
that in the eleventh month of last year, it could not be held.
The Sovereign was imprisoned and abducted,
again sinking into the barbarian court.
The divine vessels have been scattered,
and were twice humiliated by the wild rebels.
Every time your servants examine the historical records
and observe the writings of former times,
such an extremity of misfortune
has never existed in ancient or modern times.
Even among those who eat the products of the soil
or any living beings that breathe,
none fails to beat their breast and lose their breath,
wailing in the streets and crying in the alleys.
How much more so for your servants, who have enjoyed favor for three generations
and occupy positions among the high ministers?
Receiving the news with shock and fear,
our spirits have flown away.
Both grieving and lamenting,
our five emotions have no master.
We wail at the northern frontier;
high and low weep tears of blood.
Your servant Kūn and your servant Pǐdī bow their heads and bow their heads,
a capital offense, a capital offense.
Your servants have heard that darkness and light alternate,
and misfortune and prosperity succeed each other.
The Mandate of Heaven has not changed,
and the cosmic cycle has its destination.
Sometimes many hardships serve to strengthen the state;
sometimes deep anxiety inspires the sagely and wise.
Qí suffered the calamity of Wúzhī,
yet Xiǎobái became the leader of the Wǔbà.
Jìn suffered the disaster of Lí Jī,
yet Zhòng'ěr presided over the alliance of the lords.
When the altars of state are not at peace,
there must surely be a way to sustain them in danger.
When the common people are nearly extinct,
there must surely be a way to continue their lineage.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty's profound virtue reaches the divine spirits,
and your sagely bearing matches Heaven and Earth.
You respond to the appointed time of the age
and continue the fortune of a thousand years.
As for the signs of auspicious omens,
Heaven and man provide evidence.
The signs of restoration
are recorded in the prophetic charts and texts.
Since the capital region collapsed
and the nine zones fell apart,
the world has been in clamor with nowhere to turn.
Although the Xià encountered Yí Yì
and the royal Jī clan suffered from the Quǎnróng,
nothing could exceed this.
Your Majesty has pacified Jiāngzuǒ
and occupied the old territory of Wú.
You subdue the compliant with virtue
and punish the rebellious with penalties.
You uphold brilliant majesty to awe the unruly
and rely on great obedience to solemnize the realm.
Once pure transformation has spread,
all within the borders fix their hearts on you.
Once the wind of righteousness prevails,
those in distant regions stand on tiptoe in anticipation.
The hundred officials are in order above,
and the four gates are solemn below.
Formerly, the prosperity of Shàokāng
was recorded as a fine story in the teachings of Xià;
the rise of Xuān Wáng
was celebrated in the poems of Zhōu.
How much more so when your great merits reach August Heaven
and your clear radiance shines upon the four seas?
The masses look up with reverence;
none fails to joyfully support you.
Wherever your reputation and teachings reach,
who would not wish to be your subject?
Moreover, of the descendants of Xuān Huáng,
there is only Your Majesty.
To whom the millions turn,
truly there is no other.
Heaven favors the Great Jìn;
there must surely be a sovereign.
He who presides over the sacrifices of Jìn,
who could it be but Your Majesty?
Therefore, those near have no dissenting words,
and those far away have no different hopes.
Those who sing praise all chant of your excellent path,
and those in litigation all think of your sagely virtue.
The boundary of Heaven and Earth has met,
and the feelings of the Huá and the barbarians are in harmony.
The one-horned beast,
the intertwined trees,
and those taken as auspicious signs
number in the hundreds.
Those who wear caps and sashes
and the multitudes of the remote frontiers
who, without consulting, speak with one voice,
number in the tens of thousands.
Therefore, your servants venture to examine the heart of Heaven and Earth
and follow the inclinations of the realm of Xià
to risk death and present this honorable title.
We wish Your Majesty to maintain the selfless spirit of Shùn and Yǔ,
and look down upon the aloof integrity of Cháo and Yóu.
Make the state your primary concern
and do not prioritize minor conduct.
Make the common people your worry
and do not make formal refusal your business.
Above, to comfort the concern of the ancestral temples,
and below, to fulfill the hopes of all under Heaven who look up to you.
Then it will be what is called bringing blossoms to a withered sprout
and growing full flesh on decayed bones.
Both spirits and men will find peace;
there would be no greater fortune.
Your servants Kūn and Dì kowtow, kowtow,
and are guilty of a capital offense, a capital offense.
Your servants have heard that the honored position cannot remain vacant for long,
and the myriad affairs of state cannot be neglected for long.
If left vacant for a single day,
then the honored position is endangered;
if neglected for twelve days,
then the myriad affairs of state fall into chaos.
At present, we meet the end of a hundred dynasties
and face the juncture of the nine calamities.
Cunning invaders peer and pry,
watching for flaws and openings in the state.
The people of Qí are tossed like waves,
with nothing to bind their hearts.
How can the throne be left abandoned without concern!
Even if Your Majesty wishes to hesitate,
what of the Ancestral Temple?
What of the common people?
In the past, when Huì Gōng was captured by Qín,
the state of Jìn was shocked and terrified.
Through the plotting of Lǚ and Xì,
they desired to establish Zǐ Yǔ.
Externally, this was to sever the ambitions of the enemy;
internally, it was to solidify the sentiments within the whole borders.
Therefore it is said, "When a lord is lost, a lord is gained."
The ministers were harmonious and unified;
those who loved us were encouraged,
and those who hated us were afraid.
Not forgetting past events
is the great oracle for later generations.
Your Majesty’s brilliance equals the sun and moon;
there is no darkness you do not illuminate.
Your profound schemes and far-reaching thoughts
come from your own heart.
We cannot overcome our dog-and-horse-like feelings of concern for the state,
and look forward to seeing the path of prosperity opened for gods and men.
Thus we present our sincerity
and declare it to those in charge.
We, your servants, each humbly hold regional responsibilities,
our duties being in distant regions.
We cannot attend the court
to witness the grand ceremony together.
Our hearts are leaping with excitement,
looking south without limit.
Respectfully submitted.
Your servant Kūn respectfully sends the Acting Senior Clerk of the Left and Right Marshal, your servant Wēn Qiào,
and the Registrar, your servant Pìlǘ Xùn.
Your servant Dì sends the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
General of the Vanguard,
Grand Administrator of Qīnghé,
Acting Senior Clerk of the Right,
and Marquis of Gāopíng Pavilion, your servant Róng Shào,
along with the General of Light Chariots and Marquis of Guānnèi, your servant Guō Mù, to present this memorial.
Your servants Kūn and Dì kowtow, kowtow,
and are guilty of a capital offense, a capital offense.
Your servants have heard that Chéng Tāng reformed the Xià and enfeoffed the Qǐ,
and Wǔ Wáng entered the Yīn and established the Sòng.
During the campaigns of the Spring and Autumn period,
Jìn restored the sacrifices of Yú,
and Yàn sacrificed at the temple of Qí.
A state may rise because of one man,
or be abandoned because the predecessor was wise while the successor is foolish;
this is truly something for which a benevolent sage feels grief and cannot bear.
Thus the Three Kings valued the virtue of continuing extinguished lineages,
and the Spring and Autumn period prized the principle of showing leniency to the submissive.
Formerly, when Hàn Gāo received the mandate,
he posthumously preserved the Six States;
all those whose successions were severed
were simultaneously given sacrifices.
He personally competed for survival against Xiàng Yǔ,
yet when Yǔ died,
he went to weep at his funeral.
This was because their positions were once equal in honor
and their power was once matched in strength.
Although he snatched success through merit,
he granted grace in the other's defeat.
Furthermore, for one who rose violently and fell quickly,
he treated him with the rituals of an old friend.
The remains of a mutilated body
were even given a state burial.
If Yǔ had inherited a previous lineage
and his family had wise kings for generations,
and then one morning his strength was exhausted
and he submitted with his life,
then the temple of Chǔ would not have been destroyed,
and there would be hope for an heir.
We humbly submit that the Great Jìn responds to Heaven and accords with the people,
its military achievements ending warfare.
The Western Róng have people following order,
and the capital has opened residences for Wú and Shǔ.
The restoration of the perished is applied to the myriad states,
and the continuation of the severed connects a hundred generations.
Although the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors broadened the Dao,
and Shāng and Zhōu were called benevolent,
their vast principles
are not enough to serve as a comparison.
Therefore, although the Sūn family lost the throne of Wú,
their clan received the glory of Jìn.
Their sons and brothers, measuring their talents,
stood shoulder to shoulder in advancement.
They wore gold seals in the service of marquises
and donned the green ribbons of regional governors.
The grace they received at that time
often exceeded expectations.
Your servants have heard that spring rain nourishes the trees,
flowing from the leaves to the roots;
the owl cares for its work,
loving its young and its nest.
Thus Heaven is said to have limitless grace,
and the sage has the kindness of careful protection.
We look back upon the false Emperor Wǔliè of Wú,
who encountered the weakness of the Hàn house
and the strength of rebellious ministers.
He was the first to lead righteous troops
and face dangers before the multitude.
He defeated Dǒng Zhuó at Yángrén
and rescued the Sacred Treasure at the Zhēn Well.
His majesty shook the various scoundrels,
and his name was prominent in the former court.
Huán Wáng was talented and martial;
at the age of twenty, he inherited the legacy.
He recruited the men of the Bǎiyuè
and exerted a momentum like a soaring hawk.
He rushed west to Xǔdū,
intending to welcome the young lord.
Although his great merit was not completed,
his supreme loyalty was already manifest.
Their family accumulated a foundation of righteousness and courage,
and for generations transmitted the work of supporting the imperiled.
In public life, they were officials devoted to the Hàn;
in retirement, they were rulers who founded Wú.
Yet the seasonal sacrifices have been severed for three generations,
and their park tombs are left to the woodcutters.
Your servant privately mourns this.
We humbly observe that at the beginning of the pacification of Wú,
a brilliant edict was issued to record the former worthies
and to seal their tombs.
I humbly believe these two lords should both be included.
For if we list their labors, their strength surpassed former eras;
if we discuss their virtue, their kindness remains in Jiāngnán.
If we apply the law, their crimes were not against the Jìn invaders;
if we consider collective punishment, they were from a different era and thus the offense is light.
If they are placed among the number of former worthies
and receive the grace of the imperial edict,
granting them a mark of distinction
to honor their departed spirits,
then the people's hopes will be fully satisfied.
Who would not say it is right?
The private slaves of the two lords
mostly remain by the side of the tombs.
Now they are commoners.
I beg to assign five men,
exempting them from corvée labor,
to have them repair and protect the collapsed and ruined parts throughout the four seasons,
and sweep the burial mounds,
making this a permanent practice.
Your servant Liàng speaks:
I am mediocre and stubborn,
and in my youth, I lacked restraint in my conduct.
Formerly, because the Central Province had many troubles
and my old homeland was in chaos,
I followed and served my late father
to take shelter in a place where the Way prevailed.
Thus I lived as a guest to escape hardship,
seeking only enough to eat.
I did not realize I would receive the luck of the times
and encounter a fortunate era.
When the Late Emperor rose like a dragon,
I received extraordinary favor.
He looked upon me as a statesman of the state
and further bonded us through marriage.
Consequently, I ascended through close favor
and repeatedly held positions for which I was not suited.
At twenty, I began my official career,
bathing in the profound influence.
I frequently entered the palace gates
and went out to command the Six Armies.
Within more than ten years,
my position surpassed those of my predecessors.
For being treated with favor without merit,
no one can compare to me.
A man of low character has little fortune;
when blessings are excessive, disasters arise.
Knowing when to stop and being content with my lot
is what I ought to maintain.
Yet I have stolen glory and been obsessed with advancement,
day after day.
Slander and criticism have now gathered,
defiling the Sagely Court above.
At first, I wished to make this known myself,
but the Late Emperor passed away,
and my humble and small sincere feelings
never reached him.
Your Majesty has ascended the throne,
and Your sagely governance is being renewed.
The high ministers are wise and virtuous,
and the various officials are all in accord.
The songs of peace and prosperity
truly reside in the utmost impartiality.
Yet the state’s grace does not cease,
and Your Majesty has again appointed me to lead the Zhōngshū.
For me to lead the Zhōngshū
would be to demonstrate private favoritism to the world.
Why is this?
In relation to Your Majesty,
I am the elder brother of the Empress.
The suspicion regarding relatives by marriage
is indeed different from that concerning blood relations or maternal cousins.
Although the Supreme Sovereign is perfectly impartial
and His sagely virtue is without selfishness,
yet the loss of the Way in the world
has had a long history.
Throughout the vast universe,
everyone favors their marriage relations;
when everyone has private interests,
they then say there is no impartiality in the world.
For this reason, in the Former and Later Hàn,
all were safe when the Empress’s clan was suppressed,
and were endangered when the marriage clan was advanced.
If formerly the seven clans of Xījīng,
and the six clans of Dōngjīng,
had not been marriage factions,
and had each advanced through merit,
even if they did not all remain whole,
they certainly would not have all met with ruin.
Their total ruin today
was further caused by the intimacy of marriage.
I have observed the common surnames in this world:
without a faction at court
and without support from the times,
the foundation of their roots
is light and thin;
provided they have no great flaws,
they may still be tolerated.
As for the external relatives,
they rely on Heaven and Earth,
their power connects to the four seasons,
their roots and support are widespread,
and they are heavy and great.
Yet while they reside in wealth, power, and favor,
the whole world looks askance at them;
if things are not right,
their crimes cannot be pardoned even by death.
Once their persons invite calamity,
the state is harmed by it.
What is the reason for this?
It is simply due to the private nature of marriage ties,
which the feelings of the masses cannot avoid;
thus they take what they suspect and direct that suspicion toward the state.
Therefore, when distant subordinates are attached, there is trust;
when marriage relations are advanced, there is doubt.
When doubt accumulates in the hearts of the common people,
then disaster forms within the multiple gates of the palace.
These are all clear mirrors from past generations,
enough to make one’s heart turn cold!
That which is not permeable to all things,
sages and worthies do not forcibly take.
To risk employing a single talent by relying on kinship
is not as good as preventing suspicion to clarify the public way.
Now, with my talent
combined with such suspicion,
if I am made to be part of the inner core
and externally command military power,
to seek governance by this means
is something I have never heard of;
to invite disaster by this means
is something that can be expected immediately.
Although the two ministers of Your Majesty
understand my humble sincerity,
and the court officials and various officers
somewhat recognize my feelings,
as for the people of the world,
how can one go from door to door to explain,
so as to make them all at ease?
Wealth, honor, favor, and glory
are things I cannot forget;
punishment, poverty, and low status
are things I cannot endure.
Now, to obey the order would be better,
but to defy the order is bitter.
Although I am not wise,
why would I turn against the times and defy my superior,
to bring suffering and blame upon myself?
Truly I look up at the great mirror of the Yīn dynasty,
and weighing myself I know my failings;
my person is not worth regretting,
but I fear bringing regret upon the state.
Therefore, with sincere devotion, I have repeatedly presented my honest feelings,
but my small sincerity is thin and shallow,
and has not yet received Your consideration and understanding.
I am worried and fearful, uneasy and trembling,
not knowing what to do.
Given my current position,
it is clear that I cannot advance;
moreover, having defied the order for a long time,
my crimes have accumulated.
I return my body to my private gate
to await the legal punishment.
I wish Your Majesty would extend the mirror of Heaven and Earth
to examine my foolishness;
then even on the day I die,
it would be like the years of living.
I have heard that once the Tàipǔ is diminished,
the standard of lofty seclusion becomes manifest;
when the Way is lost and the times are dark,
the righteousness of loyalty and integrity is revealed.
Thus there were those who washed their ears or threw themselves into deep waters
to stir the distant wind of profound seclusion;
there were also those who maintained their hearts and corrected their conduct
to strengthen the integrity of the three bonds.
Therefore, the rulers of past ages
all honored and emphasized this path
to enrich customs and instruct the people,
and to quiet the competition for profit.
I humbly reflect that the Great Jìn,
responding to the omens to rule the world,
finds its fortune not always smooth,
and the times have had difficulties.
Shénzhōu is in ruins,
and the three regions are collapsed and split.
The sound of Tùjū has ceased in the forests,
and the Báijū is not heard in the empty valleys.
This is what makes the knowledgeable grieve
and what the refined sigh over.
Your Majesty’s sagely virtue has risen in succession
to restore the Heavenly lineage.
In the past, I served on a mission
to handle affairs in the western lands.
Once the rebels were suppressed,
I thought of spreading the great transformation.
I inquired among the elders
and searched for those in hidden seclusion,
hoping for a Wǔ Luó in the ruins of Yì and Zhuó,
and thinking of a Wáng Zhú in the territory of the fallen Qí.
I have heard that Qiāo Xiù of Bāxī
maintains a firm and upright conduct,
embraces virtue in his fat seclusion,
and raises clear waves in the Wèi River.
At the time when the imperial pole met with the decline of the Way,
the common people trod through the hardships of ruin.
Central China had the sorrow of looking back,
and those in the deep valleys had no hope of moving to tall trees.
Cruel commands repeatedly summoned him,
and treacherous power continued to pressure him.
His person was placed within the tiger’s mouth,
his danger equal to the morning dew.
Yet he was able to maintain his integrity like jade,
vowing not to be humiliated.
He shut his doors and cut off his tracks,
never appearing at the false court.
In advancing, he avoided the calamity of Gōng Shèng’s death,
and in retreating, he lacked the ridicule of Xuē Fāng’s deceptive response.
Although Yuán and Qǐ stayed at Shāng Luò,
and Guǎn Níng remained silent at Liáohǎi,
compared to Xiù,
they probably do not surpass him.
Even now in the western lands,
he is regarded as a topic of high praise.
Honoring virtue and showing respect to the worthy
are the priorities of transformation;
honoring and manifesting extraordinary integrity
are the primary duties of sagely and wise rulers.
Now the world is not yet at peace,
wolves and swine are in the way,
the remaining people are fickle and superficial,
and the voice of righteousness is not heard.
It is even more appropriate to raise up those of the Way and righteousness
to rectify the ills of drifting and fleeing.
If Xiù receives the summons of the cattail-wrapped carriage and silk,
it will be enough to settle the decaying customs
and provide a standard to instruct the clamorous populace.
When those in distant and hidden places look up to the influence,
the nine regions will know transformation.
I, your servant, have heard that when the vast waves shake the ravines,
the rivers have no calm fish;
when the startling gales brush the wilds,
the forests have no quiet branches.
Why is this?
When one's power is weak, one is controlled by a great force;
when one's substance is slight, one has no way to preserve oneself.
Although this may be logically explained,
it is truly what I, your servant, dare to use as an analogy.
In the past, during the era of Huán Xuán,
it is true that many were coerced and pressured;
as for me, your foolish servant,
my crimes are indeed deep.
Advancing, I could not face danger and offer my life,
forgetting myself to die for the state;
retreating, I could not refuse grain at Shǒuyáng,
or shake my robes and bid a lofty farewell.
Instead, I enjoyed the peace of dim-witted favor,
greedily accepting a false title,
and receiving the documents for the usurpation,
never once holding firm alone.
My reputation and righteousness both sank because of this,
and my integrity was compromised from then on;
it is only right that the utmost law be applied,
to distinguish between the loyal and the wicked.
Zhènjūn Chén Yù
restored the altars of soil and grain,
and greatly extended the benevolence of life-giving favor;
he halted the execution of my meager life,
and manifested the great trust of the three drives;
not only favoring me by leaving my head intact,
but also drawing me back into service with the bonds of office.
At that time, the imperial carriage was blocked and separated,
and heaven and man were not yet at peace;
forgetting whether to advance or retreat,
I looked only to where power resided.
Therefore, I diligently carried out my duties,
considering myself a whole person.
Now the celestial pole has returned to its proper place,
and a new beginning has been announced;
the laws and statutes are now clear,
and all things long for the old order.
How thick is the skin on my face,
that I can prominently occupy an honorable position?
I beg to be relieved of my duties,
and await punishment at my private home.
Taking leave of the palace court,
my heart is filled with shame and longing;
I respectfully submit this memorial for your consideration.
Your servant Mǒu says so-and-so.
Chén Yù says:
Recently, having arrayed the troops by the banks of the River,
we raised our banners and marched westward;
we were about to arrive at the old capital,
to overawe and cherish Sī and Yōng.
The river flows swiftly and long,
and the road is obstructed and far;
moreover, the Yī and Luò rivers are overgrown with thickets,
and the ferry routes have long been abandoned;
we had to cut timber to clear paths,
which delayed us for months.
Starting on the twelfth day of this month,
we halted at the old floating bridge of the Luò River.
The mountains and rivers have not changed,
but the city and towers are in ruins;
the palaces and temples have collapsed,
and the bell frames stand empty.
What remains of the halls and houses
has all become fields of grain and millet;
the market streets are desolate,
and the sounds of chickens and dogs are rarely heard.
Moved by the past and filled with eternal yearning,
the pain is visible before my eyes.
On the fifteenth day of that month,
I respectfully visited the Wǔ Líng.
The burial mounds were obscured and sunken,
having been neglected and overgrown for a hundred years.
Now that the heavenly path has opened toward peace,
sentiments and rites can be fulfilled;
the elders wiped away their tears,
and the three armies were moved with sorrow.
On the day of paying respects and bowing,
indignation and grief were intertwined.
Acting Hénán Tàishǒu Máo Xiūzhī and others
have already cleared away the thorns and brambles,
and repaired the ruined walls;
the official duties are now prepared,
and the regional defenses are as they were before.
I prostrate myself and consider your Sacred Heart;
you will feel both distant longing and comfort,
more than my humble feelings can express.
I respectfully send the Chuánzhào Diànzhōng Zhòngláng Chén Mǒu to present this memorial for your consideration.
I have heard that honoring the worthy and signaling the good
are the priorities of royal instruction;
remembering merit and selecting for labor
are the deep meanings of pursuing the distant.
Therefore, the Sīxùn holds the records,
and every instance of diligence must be recorded;
the excellence and brilliance of virtue
become even more manifest after death.
The late Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè
and Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn Chén Mùzhī
rose from a commoner’s status
to assist from the beginning of our righteous cause.
Internally, he exhausted his plans and strategies;
externally, he was diligent in all administrative affairs;
toiling over military and state matters,
he gave his full mental and physical effort.
When he was promoted to the high offices of the court,
and governed the capital region,
he assisted in coordinating the hundred officials,
and helped renew the Great Way.
Recently, while the war chariots were on distant expeditions,
he remained in the center to act as a defense;
his merit in soothing and pacifying
truly permeated the court and the countryside.
His wisdom, capacity, and temperament
were those of a pillar and beam of the state.
He was just about to proclaim and assist in the great transformation,
and to harmonize and uplift this sacred era,
but his ambitions and achievements were not yet completed,
and those near and far are grieved at heart.
Imperial grace has praised and described him,
ranking him with the Sān Shì;
honors for the living and mourning for the dead are both complete,
and the favor and spirit are already great.
I have prostrated myself and reflected:
Since the initial founding in the Yìxī era,
hardships and troubles have not ceased;
external threats were numerous,
and internal difficulties occurred repeatedly.
The times were difficult and the world was in turmoil;
there was not a single year of peace.
I, with my meager and inferior abilities,
bore the heavy weight of the state,
but I truly relied on the merit of Mùzhī’s assistance and support.
It was not only his forthright words and excellent plans
that filled the people's hearing.
As for his loyal regulations and secret stratagems,
his hidden deliberations within the curtains,
and the private conversations where he offered dissenting advice,
no one could see the extent of them.
These matters were hidden from the imperial court,
and his merits were concealed from public sight and hearing;
they are beyond counting.
Thus, for twelve years he exerted his strength,
and finally success was achieved.
Whether I went out on expeditions or stayed in to assist,
I was fortunate not to disgrace my mission.
Without the help of that gentleman,
I could not have successfully settled these affairs.
He practiced humility and lived simply,
holding to it ever more firmly.
Whenever there was discussion of granting him a fief or title,
he would always deeply restrain and refuse it.
Thus, while his merit was high during his time,
the grant of land did not reach him.
Recalling these events and thinking eternally,
how could I let this be overlooked?
I believe it is appropriate to posthumously grant him a formal ministerial rank
and to award him territory,
so that the brilliance of his loyalty and integrity
will not be extinguished after his death;
let the great rewards reach him,
and may he eternally hold the rank of a virtuous man.
I have shared hardships and ease with him;
looking back from beginning to end,
our bond was like gold and orchids,
with deep righteousness and emotional connection.
Therefore, I offer my inner thoughts,
and present them for the court to hear.
What has been submitted
should be forwarded to the outer court for detailed deliberation.
Your servant Luán says:
Having been summoned by the Grand Offices,
they appoint your servant as Shìzhōng,
Zhōngshūjiān,
Piàoqí Dàjiāngjūn,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Lù Shàngshū Shì;
enfeoffing me as the Founding Duke of Xiāochéng Jùn,
with a household stipend of three thousand households,
and adding five thousand soldiers.
Your servant is originally of mediocre talent,
and my intelligence and strength are shallow and brief.
Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì was sincere in his love for me as a nephew,
bestowing the kindness of a family member;
Shìzǔ Wǔ Dì’s affection was like that for a commoner friend,
and his trust was as deep as for one of the same blood.
When Wǔ Huáng was critically ill,
I indeed received his final words.
Although the clarity of self-knowledge
is obscured by my mediocrity,
once a foolish man reaches a certain point,
he may by chance recognize his own limits.
Indeed, I could not bear to persist in refusal during the time of the ritual mourning,
or to disobey beside the jade armrest.
Consequently, I bore the weight of the entrusted care,
and proclaimed the final mandate.
Although the succeeding ruler abandoned the constant virtues
and committed offenses at Xuāndé,
and the royal house was not prosperous,
this was due to your servant’s role.
Why is this?
In kinship, I am like Dōngmóu;
in responsibility, I am like Bólù.
Merely harboring the response of Zǐmèng regarding the state,
how could I escape the ridicule of being the remonstrating official of Chāngyì?
Regarding the opinions within the four seas,
from where can I escape the blame?
Furthermore, the earth of the imperial tomb is not yet dry,
and the instructions and oaths are still in my ears;
the affairs of the family and the state
have come to this point.
If it is not the fault of your servant,
who shall bear the blame?
How shall I solemnly pay respects at the Gāo burial chamber,
or reverently serve at the Wǔ garden?
My grieving heart has lost its plan,
weeping blood as I wait for dawn.
How can I again seek glory from the family’s shame,
or find peaceful leisure amidst the nation’s danger?
The great merit of the Piàoqí Supreme General,
the model for the divine provinces like the Great Peaks—
the Shàngshū was anciently called the Master of Accounts,
and the Zhōngshū indeed manages the royal words.
To merely adorn myself with empty honors
and be entrusted with repelling insults—
I know I am not suitable,
and who would call it appropriate?
But my life is lighter than a swan’s feather,
while my responsibility is heavier than the mountains.
Life and death lead to the same end,
and slander and praise are consistent;
declining one office does not diminish the burden on my person,
and adding one post already defiles the court’s standards.
I should naturally identify myself with the state
and not engage in decorative refusals.
As for merit equal to a great restoration,
and rewards equal to a thousand households,
dwelling brilliantly in the near suburbs,
and possessing an entire state—
even if my death were the deadline,
I dare not accept the command.
I also hope you will graciously grant your inspection,
and immediately grant your permission,
so that the sincere earnestness of Jùpíng will surely remain firm,
and the loyal heart of Yǒngchāng will be expressed.
Then one shall know that the way of ruler and minister
is ample and generous.
If it is said to be easily manifested,
I dare to hold firm to what cannot be taken away.
Therefore, I may hope the heart will expand the discussion,
and measure oneself while being close to others.
Unable to bear my sincerity of gratitude, fear, and hesitation,
I respectfully attach this memorial through Official [Name] to be heard.
Your servant [Name], truly fearful and trembling.
Your servant Yún says:
Having been summoned by the Shàngshū,
they appoint your servant as Sànqì Chángshì
and Lìbù Shàngshū,
enfeoffing me as the Founding Marquis of Xiāochéng Xiàn,
with a household stipend of one thousand households.
Receiving the command, I am shocked;
my heart and face have no place to turn.
Your servant Yún bows his head, bows his head;
it is a capital offense, a capital offense.
Your servant comes from a humble family and an ordinary background,
with no merit in wheel or wing to be chosen.
Advancing, I fail the middle way;
retreating, I am ashamed of being reckless or overly cautious.
Indeed, I once drilled and strove in study,
but did not master even one classic;
I practiced seal-carving and literature,
but accomplished nothing in three winters.
Carrying books to Yān and Wèi,
I only exhausted my beans and grain;
treading in straw sandals through Qí and Chǔ,
I merely lost my way in poverty and lowliness.
Then, having been granted the tiger tally to serve as a governor,
I was ridiculed for my bag and bedding;
holding the axe to serve as a shepherd of the people,
I stirred up slander over Job's tears.
Clad in the reddish-brown clothes of a prisoner,
I saw the majesty of the prison official;
removed from the rolls to be a commoner,
I knew the leisure of the well and the mortar.
A hundred years is the highest age,
and it is said to be in vain.
If that is truly the case,
it is already more than half over.
The distress of chaos and separation—
where can I return to find peace?
Closing my door in the wild outskirts,
I have twice seen the cold and heat pass.
Furthermore, with several mǔ at the eastern bank,
occupying my mornings and evenings,
and one area outside the pass,
I look towards Zhōngfù with regret.
Though there are no girls from Zhào in my house,
there are many busybodies at my door;
though my salary is meager and without bestowed gold,
my joy is equal to that of a happy elder.
Breaking water chestnuts and burning dry wood,
I am sufficient here.
Your Majesty corresponds to the cycle of ten thousand generations,
connecting the succession of a thousand years;
three thousand follow you like shadows,
and eight hundred came without consultation.
Your servant’s offenses and others’ divided hearts—
my merit is ashamed before those of shared virtue;
with mud on my forehead and face,
my coffin carriage is not yet destroyed.
In the formative period of creation,
how dare I claim the merit of Heaven?
The litigations and songs of praise
show the people’s shared will.
Yet high positions and great names
suddenly gather together in one day.
Looking at myself and reflecting,
how could I reach this?
It must be because I am neighbor to Báishuǐ
or have a residence in old Fēng;
forgetting the fault of abandoning the lecture,
retaining the expenses of the various lords,
and picking up the green and purple ribbons as if from the ground—
how could I wait to master the classics?
Your servant Yún bows his head, bows his head;
it is a capital offense, a capital offense.
Now, the weight of the Ministry of Personnel
is related to prosperity and decline;
considering from afar the discernment of the wise,
it was difficult even for the Emperors.
Since the Hàn and Wèi,
men of great insight have followed one another;
to whom both the refined and the common turned,
only Xǔ and Guō were so praised.
Selecting five out of ten
was still considered standing shoulder to shoulder.
As for the rest, their gains and losses are unheard of;
by chance observing the young,
natural intuition momentarily flashes,
but looking back, it is not worth counting.
In Wèi, there was Máo Jiè, who was impartial and upright;
in Jìn, there was Shān Tāo, with insight and capacity.
Comparing your servant to them,
how vastly distant I am!
At the end of Qí, when things declined,
official posts became confused and chaotic;
Hóngdū lost its discipline,
and Xīyuán became a marketplace.
There was talk of golden seals filling chests,
and deep sighs that the flowery marten furs were insufficient.
Now at the very beginning of the new era,
the principle lies in reform and renewal;
You reverently face south,
and the responsibility for results lies here.
How can it be appropriate to recklessly bestow personal favors
and thereby neglect the affairs of the King?
The ornaments of the attached cicada
only become empty signs of favor.
Whether judged by public or private standards,
both the granting and the receiving are failures.
Among the marquises of recent times,
their achievements and lineages vary:
some provided sufficient food in Guānzhōng,
some formed armies in Hénèi,
some achieved victory from within the strategist's tent,
some became close as disciples,
some rose or fell with the times,
some were as powerful as an opposing state,
some determined policy within the forbidden palace,
some achieved success in open battle,
some possessed great virtue like Zhuó Mào,
some were masters of the Way like Huán Róng,
while others of the four noble surnames attended the ancestral sacrifices;
these are no longer worth recording,
and the "Five Marquises" among the imperial relatives
are not according to the old regulations.
However, that to which your servant is attached
lies solely in imperial favor.
Since its meaning is different from rewarding merit,
it truly contradicts the glory of a scholar.
Although a small man might greedily welcome such luck,
how could I alone be without a conscience?
Your servant was originally a mere student,
whose family inherited a simple profession;
my gates knew no wealth or status,
and I left farming to enter officialdom.
My grandfather Xuánpíng
had a character and style that were outstanding in his generation;
during the restoration,
he was a model for the many scholars;
his rank was comparable to the Yuán and Kǎi,
yet his responsibilities were limited to being a provincial governor.
My great-grandfather Shǎolián
early on maintained high principles;
what he was rich in was righteousness,
and what he lacked was the right timing;
he held minor office in the Dōngcháo,
and resigned due to illness in a small district.
Not forgetting the aspirations of my ancestors,
your foolish servant is their successor.
Furthermore, at the beginning of winter last year,
I was merely an old Doctor of the National Academy;
in the first month of summer this year,
I am to be secondary to the Minister of Education.
Although Qiānqiū’s "nine promotions in one day"
or Xún Shuǎng’s "reaching high office within one hundred days"
are compared to your humble servant,
they were not as rapid in their advancement.
Although your servant lacks wisdom
and only looks to what is beneficial,
when it comes to damaging my reputation and diminishing reality,
for the sake of the state and for myself,
I know it is impossible
and dare not recklessly presume to accept.
Your Majesty does not discard the lowly marsh grass,
but loves it as much as silk or hemp.
If the words of my lifetime
are still heard and observed,
my long-held heart and simple will
will never have a second word.
Pity what your servant begs for
and specially withdraw this gracious command;
then the constant laws will be solemn,
and this humble creature will know how to avoid error.
Your servant is currently on leave
and cannot go to the ministry;
unable to bear the weight of my gratitude and fear,
I respectfully offer this memorial for your hearing.
Your servant Yún, with sincere fear, etc.
Your servant Wáng speaks:
Your servant has heard that seeking the worthy is a temporary labor,
but that reigning with folded robes leads to eternal ease;
this is like thinning the soil
or taking the principle of dredging a river.
I prostrate myself before Your Majesty, whose Way is hidden behind the crown’s tassels and ear-plugs,
whose sincerity fills the imperial seals;
your "six dragons" share the dust of the world,
and your "five refusals" of the throne surpass the age.
The white colt is in the empty valley,
the egrets are in the courtyard;
yet you still fear that those with hidden talents might resort to divination,
or that great men might hide as butchers or guards.
You look for talent as far as the mountain passes,
and leave your robes by the river bank;
this is not seeking to make a robe from a single fox's pelt,
but truly seeking flavor by collecting many varieties.
Weary of the five musical sounds,
you consult the various craftsmen;
you deliberate in the ancestral temple
and listen to the common people.
Your servant's position and responsibilities are heavy,
and my duty extends to both family and state;
I truly wish to ensure that name and reality do not conflict
and that the path of opportunism is cut off.
Even those of the high grade from powerful families
should be judged by pure conversation;
talented officials of low rank
should not be limited by status or appearance.
I have observed that the Assistant in the Palace Library, your servant Wáng Jiǎn of Lángyá,
is twenty-one years old,
and has the courtesy name Sīhuì.
For seven generations, his family has shone with repeated glory,
being the crown of all within the seas;
his spirit is clear and his energy is flourishing,
truly following the path of moderation.
He has the detachment of Shūbǎo’s discourse,
and the joy in the teachings of Yànfǔ;
thus he outshines his predecessors
and leads the younger generation.
His dwelling is free from worldly clutter,
his family possesses bestowed books;
his compositions are fresh and pure,
and his speech is profound and distant.
Though his room is near, his mind is vast;
though he is distant from things, he is close to the Way.
He cultivates his character in the hills and gardens,
while the high offices remain vacant for him.
Whether in schools or at court,
ten thousand men look up to him with expectation.
How could it be merely that the spirit of Lord Xún is remembered,
or that Lord Lǐ is not dead!
The former Magistrate of Hòuguān in Jìn'ān Commandery, Wáng Sēngrǔ of Dōnghǎi,
is thirty-five years old,
and has the courtesy name Sēngrǔ.
His principles are simple and restrained,
and his thoughts are calm and quick.
He supported his parents through his writing
and completed his studies by being a scribe.
He went as far as gathering fireflies and using the reflection of snow,
weaving reeds and binding willows.
Regarding the words and deeds of the past,
the character of people and customs,
the inherited rituals of Gānquán,
and the old stories of the Nángōng,
he can draw maps on the ground
and describe them while clapping his hands.
Not only does he have the eloquence to answer regarding the "spotted mouse,"
but his bamboo books are free from the errors of missing slips.
Wáng Jiǎn can stabilize the world with his refinement,
and has already contributed much;
Wáng Sēngrǔ answers inquiries without ceasing,
and is there to resolve any doubts.
Both are secret treasures of the Eastern Gallery,
and magnificent vessels of the ancestral temple.
Truly, though words may be disregarded because of the speaker,
their talent is indeed a resource for the age.
Approaching this memorial with trembling and fear,
I still worry it might not be granted,
unable to bear my humble feelings, etc.
Your servant Zhēn speaks:
Yesterday I received a tally from the Minister of State,
which reverently conveyed the imperial decree,
granting the request of my elder brother Bèn
for your servant to inherit the title of Duke of Nánkāng Commandery.
My family is recorded for its meritorious shade,
and has been brilliantly granted lands.
My brother Bèn has carried on the family line through the generations
and truly possesses great virtue.
Yet he deeply understands when to stop and be content,
casting off the rank of a thousand chariots like a worn shoe.
Consequently, he mistakenly pushed this favor onto me afar,
and it has recently gathered upon my mediocre and thin self.
He is able to yield the state,
and great righteousness finds its place in him.
The will of a common man is hard to change,
and he maintains it without doubt.
In the past, Wǔshǐ was pressured by the plan of a family servant,
and Língyáng was moved by the words of Bǎo Shēng.
Zhāng pleaded with sincerity,
and Dīng was overcome by reason.
Furthermore, my late father, because the main lineage had ended,
ordered your servant to succeed a collateral line;
this was accepted in the past,
and the principle remains unchanged forever.
Eternally thinking of these matters,
everything I see causes me to collapse in grief.
If Bèn is allowed to elevate the style of Yánlíng,
while your servant forgets the integrity of Zǐzāng,
this would be to abandon virtue for the sake of promotion;
how could that be called being worthy?
May Your Majesty examine my sincere feelings
and specially grant a cessation of this command.
Otherwise,
I shall cast myself into the marshes,
merely to fulfill my foolish sincerity.
Unable to bear the height of my sincere desire,
I respectfully go to the palace to offer this memorial for your hearing.
Your servant, with sincere fear and trembling, etc.
Your servant Yún says:
I have observed that to establish and preserve a refined legacy
and to record illustrious achievements after death,
as the accounts of the elders will eventually cease,
one must rely on indelible writings.
If they are stored in famous mountains,
then hills and valleys may shift and change;
if placed in the imperial libraries,
then the green bamboo slips and their cords may fall apart.
However, the traces of matching Heaven
are preserved upon the Sì Shuǐ;
the Way of the Sùwáng
is recorded by the banks of the Yí Chuān.
From this, the principle of honoring the teacher
took its example at Xīhé;
the sentiment of respecting the lord
was directed toward Yáo and Yǔ.
Therefore, when a school is opened,
it must exhaust the magnificence of engraving;
even for the chief of a single city,
the beauty of inscription is fully displayed.
How much more so for one who molded Zhōu Gōng and Shào Gōng
and nurtured Yī Yǐn and Yán Huí?
The late Tàizǎi, Prince Wénxuān of Jìnglíng, your servant [Name],
whether in life or in death,
his righteous examples served as a model for the state;
in venerating Heaven and matching the Emperor,
he was a man like Zhōu Gōng.
He embodied the state and rectified the court,
serving in the provinces and guarding the capital;
when advancing, he thought of the Way that must be reported,
when retreating, he had no selfish desire for personal gain.
The Five Teachings were brought into order,
and the hundred offices were in seasonal harmony.
As for his every word and action,
they were the winds of grand virtue;
his skill in the zither, books, and arts,
and the abundance of his literary works,
though his Way was not limited to universal benefit
and his deeds were centered on delighting in goodness,
they were beyond what words can praise.
Now that he has passed away,
and the years have suddenly shifted,
the owls have migrated east,
and the pines and catalpas have formed rows.
The officials of the Six Offices
and the men and women of the Three Commanderies,
each person keeps silk for writing
and every household holds a lead stylus,
looking toward that Jǐng Shān,
they gaze in vain with longing and admiration.
Formerly, the Jìn dynasty first prohibited the erection of steles;
when Wèi Shū died,
he followed the general ranks.
But since the records of Ruǎn Lüè were lost,
some first braved the strict laws;
those who did so ultimately escaped punishment,
and those who achieved it instead received praise and sighs of admiration.
As for a Way that covers all like benevolence
and merit comparable to that of Guǎn Zhòng,
he should naturally be outside the common rules.
The late Tàizǎi Yuān
and Chancellor Ní,
both kin and worthy, followed the same path,
which serves as an established precedent.
I beg that according to the previous examples of the two lords,
you grant permission to carve and erect a monument.
How can we allow those who long for him at Jiǔyuán,
or the woodcutters and grass-gatherers, to be ignorant of the prohibitions?
Those who stop their carriages at Chánglíng
and the light chariots would not know where to go.
Your servant is of humble and solitary origin from the village,
with no talent to be selected,
yet I encountered the magnanimity of the Qí laws
and the relaxation of the prohibitions on guests;
I registered my name and devoted myself,
and suddenly two decades have passed.
My concerns preceded those of a dog or horse,
but I have not repaid his profound kindness.
While my tattered curtains and broken canopies
have not yet been buried with the mole crickets and ants,
his pearl-sewn robes and jade cases
have already been placed in the dark springs.
Your Majesty promotes and rewards the moral teachings
and does not exclude even the lowly,
enabling your servant to rush to Nánpǔ
and wail long at Běilíng.
Having already received former favors,
I truly look up with hope for future grace.
Perchance to verify Dù Yù’s words on the mountaintop,
and perhaps to preserve the sentiment of Mǎ Jùn who was bound to bow.
Facing this memorial with grief and fear,
my words cannot express themselves.
Your servant is truly fearful and trembling.
Your servant has heard that the officials are discussing the expulsion of guest officials;
I privately consider this a mistake.
Formerly, Mù Gōng sought scholars:
to the west, he obtained Yóu Yú from the Róng;
to the east, he gained Bǎilǐ Xī from Wǎn;
he welcomed Jiǎn Shū from Sòng;
and brought in Pí Bào and Gōngsūn Zhī from Jìn.
These five gentlemen
were not born in Qín,
yet Mù Gōng employed them,
annexed thirty states,
and subsequently became hegemon of the Xīróng.
Xiào Gōng used the laws of Shāng Yāng
to change the customs and transform the traditions;
the people became prosperous and numerous,
the state became wealthy and strong,
the common people were happy to be employed,
and the feudal lords became submissive.
He captured the armies of Chǔ and Wèi,
seized a thousand lǐ of land,
and to this day, the state remains well-governed and strong.
Huì Wáng used the schemes of Zhāng Yí
to seize the territory of Sānchuān;
to the west, he annexed Bā and Shǔ;
to the north, he took Shàngjùn;
to the south, he took Hànzhōng;
he encompassed the Jiǔyí,
controlled Yān and Yǐng;
to the east, he occupied the strategic heights of Chénggāo,
and cut off fertile lands.
He then dispersed the alliance of the six states,
making them face west to serve Qín,
and his merit continues to this day.
Zhāo Wáng obtained Fàn Jū,
deposed the Marquis of Ràng,
expelled Huáyáng,
strengthened the ducal house,
blocked the private gates,
gradually encroached upon the feudal lords,
and enabled Qín to achieve the imperial enterprise.
These four rulers
all relied on the contributions of guest officials.
From this perspective,
how have guest officials failed Qín?
Had these four rulers rejected guests and not admitted them,
or kept scholars at a distance and not employed them,
this would have left the state without the reality of wealth and benefit,
and Qín without the name of strength and greatness.
Now Your Majesty obtains jade from Kūnlún Shān,
possesses the treasures of Hé and Suí,
hangs pearls of the Bright Moon,
wears the sword of Tài'ā,
rides horses like Xiānlí,
displays banners of the kingfisher phoenix,
and sets up drums of the spiritual alligator.
Of these several treasures,
not one is produced in Qín,
yet Your Majesty delights in them—
why is that?
If things must be produced in the state of Qín before they are acceptable,
then the night-shining bi-disks would not decorate the court,
rhinoceros and ivory vessels would not be playthings,
the women of Zhào and Wèi would not fill the rear palaces,
and the fine Jùntí horses would not fill the outer stables.
The gold and tin from Jiāngnán would not be used,
and the cinnabar and green pigments from Xīshǔ would not provide color.
That which is used to decorate the inner palace,
to fill the lower ranks,
to amuse the mind and will,
and to please the ears and eyes,
if it must come from Qín to be acceptable,
then the hairpins with pearls from Wǎn,
the earrings inlaid with gems,
the clothes of Ā silk,
and the ornaments of brocade and embroidery
would not be presented before you;
and the elegant transformations according to custom,
the beautiful and refined women,
the girls of Zhào, would not stand by your side.
Beating on jars and earthen pots,
plucking the zither and slapping the thighs,
and singing "wu-wu" to please the ear—
these are the true sounds of Qín.
The Sāngjiān music of Zhèng and Wèi,
and the Sháo, Yú, Wǔ, and Xiàng,
are the music of foreign states.
Now you cast aside the beating of pots and jars and turn to Zhèng and Wèi;
you set aside the plucking of the zither and adopt Sháo and Yú—
why is this?
It is because what pleases the mind at the moment
is suitable for observation.
Now, in selecting people, it is not so:
without asking whether they are capable,
without discussing whether they are honest,
those who are not of Qín are removed,
and those who are guests are expelled.
This being so, then what you value lies in beauty, music, pearls, and jade,
and what you slight lies in the people.
This is not the technique to stride across the seas and control the feudal lords.
I have heard that when the land is broad, grain is plentiful;
when the state is large, the people are numerous;
and when the army is strong, the soldiers are brave.
Therefore, Tài Shān does not reject soil,
and thus it can achieve its greatness;
the rivers and seas do not pick and choose among small streams,
and thus they can attain their depth;
a king does not reject the common masses,
and thus he can make his virtue shine.
In this way, the land knows no four directions,
the people know no foreign states,
the four seasons are full and beautiful,
and the ghosts and spirits send down blessings;
this is how the Wǔ Dì and Sān Wáng were peerless.
Now you cast away the Qián Shǒu to enrich enemy states,
and reject guest officials to serve the Zhū Hóu,
causing the scholars of the realm to retreat and not dare to face west,
halting their steps and not entering Qín.
This is what is called lending weapons to insurgents and providing grain to bandits.
Indeed, things that are not produced in Qín
but are worth treasuring are many;
scholars who were not born in Qín
but desire to be loyal are numerous.
Now, to expel guest officials is to enrich enemy states,
to diminish your own people to benefit your foes,
to hollow yourself out within while building resentment among the Zhū Hóu without.
To seek to keep the state from peril under such conditions
is impossible.
I have heard that Qín relied on the Qū Tái Palace
to weigh the realm,
drawing a line on the ground that no one dared cross,
and sending its armies against the Hú and Yuè;
but when it reached its late years and final path,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Shèng joined their forces to attack it,
and they occupied positions to strike Hán Gǔ,
so that Xián Yáng was subsequently endangered.
Why was this?
Because the various commanderies were not close to each other,
and ten thousand households would not save one another.
Now the Hú frequently cross beyond the Běi Hé;
above, they overshadow the flying birds,
and below, the crouching hares cannot be seen;
the battles at the cities never cease,
and relief troops do not arrive;
the dead follow one after another,
and the carts for the wounded are connected in a line,
transporting grain in a continuous flow,
unending for a thousand lǐ.
Why is this?
Strong Zhào is blamed for Hé Jiān,
the six Qí look toward Huì Hòu,
Chéng Yáng looks back at Lú Bó,
and the hearts of the people of the three Huái Nán yearn for their ancestral tombs.
If Your Majesty does not worry,
I fear the relief troops will not be concentrated,
and the Hú horses will then advance to peer into Hán Dān,
while the Yuè waters threaten Cháng Shā,
and their boats return to Qīng Yáng.
Even if Liáng were to combine with the troops of Huái Yáng
to go down to Huái Dōng
and cross Guǎng Líng
to cut off the grain of the Yuè people;
and even if Hàn were to turn back from Xī Hé to go down
and defend the Zhāng Shuǐ in the north
so as to assist your great state;
the Hú would still advance further,
and the Yuè would penetrate deeper.
This is what I am concerned about for Your Majesty.
I have heard that when a flood dragon raises its head and ruffles its wings,
then floating clouds emerge and flow,
and mist and rain all gather.
When a sage king establishes his integrity and cultivates his virtue,
then the wandering rhetoricians
return to righteousness and aspire to fame.
