Now if I were to exhaust my knowledge and complete my arguments,
altering my essence and pushing my thoughts to the limit,
then there is no state whose ruler I could not influence;
if I were to adorn a stubborn and narrow mind,
then at which king's gate could I not trail my long robes?
Yet the reason I have passed through the courts of several kings,
traveling a thousand lǐ with my back to the Huái to bring myself here,
was not because I detested my own state or delighted in the people of Wú,
but because I secretly admired your humble conduct,
and was especially pleased by Your Majesty's righteousness.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will not be negligent,
and will examine and listen to my utmost sincerity.
I have heard that a hundred birds of prey
are not as good as a single osprey.
In the time of the whole Zhào state,
there were men of martial strength and great vigor;
those in fine robes beneath the Cóng Tái
once gathered like a market,
yet they could not stop the drowning disaster of Yōu Wáng.
Huái Nán was connected with the knights-errant of Shān Dōng,
and men ready to die filled the court,
yet they could not prevent Lì Wáng from being sent to the west.
Thus, if the plans and deliberations are not successful,
it is clear that even men like Zhū and Bēn could not secure their positions.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will simply be careful in your planning.
Initially, Xiào Wén Huáng Dì relied on the Pass to enter and be established as emperor;
his heart was chilled and his will was melted,
and he would dress before dawn in his diligence.
After he established himself as the Tiān Zǐ,
he had the lords of Dōng Mú and Zhū Xū go east to honor the descendants of Yí Fù,
and carved out deep territories to make kings of infants.
He made his young sons kings of Liáng and Dài,
and added Huái Yáng to them.
But in the end, Jì Běi was overthrown,
and his younger brother was imprisoned in Yōng;
was this not due to people like Xiāng and Xīn Yuán?
Now the Tiān Zǐ has newly taken possession of the late Emperor's legacy;
to the left, he plans for Shān Dōng,
and to the right, he controls Guān Zhōng;
he changes the power and alters the situation,
and his high ministers are hard to understand.
If Your Majesty does not investigate,
I fear the Zhōu Dǐng will rise again in Hàn,
and Xīn Yuán's schemes will prevail at court,
then our remaining descendants in Wú
cannot hope to survive in this world.
Gāo Huáng Dì burned the plank roads
and flooded Zhāng Hán;
his troops never stopped their advance,
gathering the weary of the exhausted people;
he galloped east to Hán Gǔ,
and Xī Chǔ was greatly defeated.
By water attack, Zhāng Hán lost his city;
by land assault, the Jīng Wáng lost his territory.
These were all moments when the state was in critical danger.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
I have heard that loyalty never goes unrewarded,
and that sincerity is never doubted;
I used to think this was true,
but it is merely empty words!
In the past, Jīng Kē admired the righteousness of Yān Dān;
a white rainbow pierced the sun,
but the Prince was afraid of him.
Master Wèi planned the affair of Cháng Píng for Qín;
Venus eclipsed the Pleiades,
but Zhāo Wáng doubted him.
When ultimate sincerity moves heaven and earth,
yet sincerity is not understood by the two rulers,
is it not a tragedy!
Now I have exhausted my loyalty and sincerity,
and completed my arguments wishing to be understood,
yet those around you are not clear-sighted,
and in the end, I am subject to the interrogation of officials,
and doubted by the world.
This is like causing Jīng Kē and Master Wèi to rise again,
only for Yān and Qín to remain unawakened.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
In the past, when the jade-worker offered a treasure,
the King of Chǔ punished him;
when Lǐ Sī exhausted his loyalty,
Hú hài executed him with the extreme penalty.
Therefore, Jī Zǐ feigned madness,
and Jiē Yú escaped the world,
fearing they would encounter such disasters.
I hope Your Majesty will examine the intentions of the jade-worker
and Lǐ Sī,
and then consider the listening of the King of Chǔ and Hú hài,
so that I am not mocked by Jī Zǐ and Jiē Yú.
I have heard that Bǐ Gān had his heart cut out,
and Zǐ Xū was placed in a leather bag;
at first, I did not believe it,
but now I know it is true.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this,
and show a little pity!
The saying goes:
White-headed, yet like strangers;
tilting canopies, yet like old friends.
Why is this?
It is a matter of being known or not being known.
Thus, when Fán Wúqī fled from Qín to Yān,
he offered his head through Jīng Kē to serve the cause of Dān;
when Wáng Shē left Qí for Wèi,
he cut his own throat atop the city wall to repel Qí and preserve Wèi.
Now, it was not that Wáng Shē and Fán Wúqī were new to Qí and Qín while being old friends to Yān and Wèi,
but the reason they left those two states
and died for these two lords
was that their actions harmonized with their wills,
and their longing for righteousness was boundless.
For this reason, Sū Qín was not trusted by the world,
yet for Yān he was a Wěi Shēng;
Bái Guī lost six cities in battle,
yet for Wèi he captured Zhōngshān.
Why was this?
Because there was truly a mutual understanding.
When Sū Qín served as Chancellor of Yān,
people slandered him to the King of Yān;
the King of Yān grasped his sword in anger
and fed him the meat of a fine juétí mule.
When Bái Guī distinguished himself in Zhōngshān,
people slandered him to Marquis Wén of Wèi;
Marquis Wén presented him with a "Glow-of-the-Night" jade disk.
Why?
These two lords and two ministers
trusted each other with opened hearts and split livers;
how could they be swayed by superficial words!
Thus, regardless of a woman's beauty or ugliness,
once she enters the palace she is envied;
regardless of a scholar's worthiness or unworthiness,
once he enters the court he is resented.
Formerly, Sīmǎ Xǐ had his kneecaps removed in Sòng,
yet he finally became Chancellor of Zhōngshān.
Fàn Jū had his ribs crushed and teeth broken in Wèi,
yet he finally became the Marquis of Yìng.
These two men
both believed in inevitable plans,
abandoned the selfishness of factions,
and held to the friendship of the solitary;
therefore, they could not escape the envy and jealousy of others.
For this reason, Shēntú Dí threw himself into the Yellow River at Yōng,
and Xú Yǎn carried a stone into the sea;
finding no place for themselves in the world,
they righteously refused to improperly seek favor or form cliques at court
in order to sway the mind of their sovereign.
Thus, though Bǎilǐ Xī begged for food on the road,
Duke Mù entrusted him with the government.
Níng Qī fed his oxen beneath a cart,
yet Duke Huán assigned him the affairs of the state.
Did these two men previously serve as officials at court
or borrow praise from those around the sovereign
before the two lords employed them?
They were moved in their hearts,
harmonized in their thoughts,
and were as firm as glue and lacquer;
even brothers could not separate them;
how could they be deluded by the talk of the masses?
Therefore, listening to only one side gives rise to villainy;
exclusive reliance on a few leads to chaos.
In the past, Lǔ listened to the words of Jì Sūn and expelled Kǒngzǐ;
Sòng believed the schemes of Zǐ Rǎn and imprisoned Mò Dí.
Now, even with the eloquence of Kǒng and Mò,
they could not escape slander and flattery,
and so the two states fell into peril.
Why?
The mouths of the masses can melt gold;
accumulated slander can dissolve bone.
For this reason, Qín employed the Róng man Yóuyú and achieved hegemony over the Central States;
Qí employed the Yuè man Zǐzāng and became strong under Kings Wēi and Xuān.
Did these two states constrain themselves by customs,
let themselves be pulled by the era,
or be bound by biased and one-sided words?
They listened impartially and observed broadly,
bestowing their brilliance upon the age.
Thus, if intentions harmonize, then the Hú and the Yuè can become brothers,
as was the case with Yóuyú and Zǐzāng;
if they do not harmonize, then even flesh and blood become enemies,
as was the case with Zhū, Xiàng, Guǎn, and Cài.
If the lords of today could truly employ the brilliance of Qí and Qín
and set aside the style of listening found in Sòng and Lǔ,
then the Five Hegemons would not be enough to equal them,
and the Three Kings would be easily compared to them.
For this reason, the sage kings were enlightened;
they discarded the heart of Zǐ Zhī
and did not delight in the "worthiness" of Tián Cháng.
They enfeoffed the descendants of Bǐ Gān
and repaired the tomb of the pregnant woman;
thus their achievements covered the world.
Why?
Because their desire for goodness was never satiated.
Now, Duke Wén of Jìn treated his enemy as kin and became a powerful hegemon over the lords;
Duke Huán of Qí employed his foe and unified and rectified the world.
Why?
Compassion, benevolence, and earnestness
were truly cherished in their hearts;
these cannot be borrowed through empty words.
As for Qín, it used the laws of Shāng Yāng,
weakened Hán and Wèi to the east,
and established its strength over the world,
yet in the end they tore him apart with chariots.
Yuè used the strategies of Grandee Zhòng,
captured the powerful Wú and became hegemon of the Central States,
yet ultimately executed him.
For this reason, Sūnshū Áo thrice left the chancellorship without regret;
Yúlíng Zǐzhòng declined the position of the Three Excellencies
to water gardens for others.
If the lords of today could truly cast off their hearts of pride and arrogance,
harbor the intention to repay service,
lay bare their hearts and bellies,
show their true feelings,
pour out their livers and galls,
bestow thick virtue,
and share in failure or success to the end
without begrudging anything to the scholar,
then even the dog of Jié could be made to bark at Yáo,
and the guest of Zhí could be made to stab Yóu;
how much more so when one relies on the power of ten thousand chariots
and draws upon the resources of a sage king!
In that case, for Jīng Kē to have his seven clans exterminated
or for Yào Lí to have his wife and children burned
—how could these even be worth mentioning to Your Majesty!
I have heard that if a "Bright Moon" pearl
or a "Glow-of-the-Night" jade disk
is thrown at a person in the dark of the road,
there is no one who would not grasp their sword and glare.
Why?
Because it arrived before them without cause.
Coiled wood and deep-set roots,
twisted and strange,
can become vessels for a lord of ten thousand chariots;
why?
Because those around the lord have first groomed their appearance.
Therefore, if one arrives before the lord without cause,
even if they present the pearl of the Marquis of Suí
or a "Glow-of-the-Night" jade disk,
it will only suffice to create resentment rather than being seen as a favor.
Thus, if there is someone to speak for them first,
then even dried wood or a decayed stump
can establish merit and not be forgotten.
Today, the common scholars living in poverty throughout the world
find themselves in humble and lowly positions.
Even if they are steeped in the arts of Yáo and Shùn,
possess the eloquence of Yī and Guǎn,
and harbor the intentions of Lóngféng and Bǐ Gān,
wishing to devote their loyalty to the lords of the current age,
they have no long-standing foundation or recommendation.
Even if they exhaust their spirit,
wishing to open up their loyalty and trustworthiness
to assist the lord in governing,
the lord will surely follow the pattern of grasping his sword and glaring.
This prevents the common scholar
from even having the utility of dried wood or a decayed stump.
For this reason, sage kings control the age and govern customs,
transforming things alone atop the potter's wheel,
not being pulled by the words of the lowly,
nor being swayed by the mouths of the many.
Thus, the First Emperor of Qín relied on the words of the Palace Attendant Méng Jiā
to trust the story of Jīng Kē,
and the dagger was secretly drawn;
King Wén of Zhōu hunted along the Jīng and Wèi rivers,
brought Lǚ Shàng back in his carriage,
and thereby came to rule the world.
Qín trusted those around the throne and perished;
Zhōu employed a chance meeting and became king.
Why?
Because they were able to transcend cramped words,
gallop toward righteousness beyond the ordinary realm,
and observe the bright and vast Way alone.
Today, lords are submerged in the words of flattery
and pulled by the constraints of curtains and walls,
causing unrestrained scholars to share a manger with oxen and thoroughbreds.
This is why Bào Jiāo was indignant with the world and did not remain to enjoy the pleasures of wealth and rank.
I have heard that those who enter the court in full regalia
do not let private matters stain their righteousness;
those who polish their names
do not let profit injure their conduct.
Therefore, because the village name was "Surpassing the Mother,"
Zēngzǐ would not enter;
because the town was called "Morning Song,"
Mòzǐ turned his carriage around.
Now, if one wishes to make the broad-minded scholars of the world
be enticed by the power of authority,
coerced by the nobility of status,
turn their faces and stain their conduct
to serve people of flattery
and seek intimacy with those around the throne,
then scholars will only die in caves and rocky thickets;
how could there be any who would exhaust their loyalty and trustworthiness to hasten to the palace gates!
Your servant has heard that among things of the same kind, there are those with exceptional abilities.
Therefore, for strength, one cites Wū Huò;
for agility, one mentions Qìng Jì;
for courage, one expects Bèn and Yù.
In your servant's foolishness and ignorance,
I privately believe that if humans truly have such individuals,
then animals must also be the same.
Now Your Majesty enjoys traversing rugged and dangerous terrains
to hunt fierce beasts.
Should you suddenly encounter a beast of extraordinary talent
and be startled in a place where safety is not assured,
it might charge at the pure dust of the attendant carriages.
If the imperial carriage does not have time to turn around
and the attendants have no leisure to exert their skill,
then even if one has the techniques of Wū Huò or Féng Méng,
their strength cannot be put to use;
even dry wood or a rotten stump
would all become difficult obstacles.
This would be as if the Hú or Yuè people arose right at the carriage hubs,
or the Qiāng and Yí barbarians were right beside the axle-ends.
Is this not perilous?
Although there might be complete safety without trouble,
yet this is fundamentally not what the Son of Heaven should approach.
Furthermore, even if the road is cleared before traveling
and one gallops down the center of the path,
there are still occasionally accidents involving the bit or the axle-pin.
How much more so when wading through lush grass
and racing across ruins and mounds?
Ahead, there is the pleasure of pursuing a profitable beast,
but within, there is no thought of preparing for sudden change.
As for the harm it could cause,
would it not be difficult to deal with?
To treat the weight of the Ten Thousand Chariots lightly and not consider it as safety,
while delighting in venturing onto a path of ten thousand-to-one danger for the sake of amusement,
your servant privately believes Your Majesty should not choose this.
I have heard that the enlightened see far before things have sprouted,
and the wise avoid danger before it takes shape.
Misfortune is indeed often hidden in subtle and minute things,
and it erupts from what people neglect.
Therefore, a common proverb says:
"A family with a thousand pieces of gold
does not sit beneath the eaves of a hall."
Though these words are minor,
they can be used to illustrate great matters.
Your servant hopes Your Majesty will pay attention and graciously examine this!
Your servant has heard that those who attain completeness will prosper,
and those who lose completeness will perish.
Shùn had not even enough ground to stand a needle,
yet he came to possess all under heaven;
Yǔ did not have a gathering of ten households,
yet he became king over the feudal lords.
The lands of Tāng and Wǔ did not exceed a hundred lǐ,
but above they did not cut off the light of the three luminaries,
and below they did not wound the hearts of the common people,
because they possessed the art of kingship.
Thus, the way of father and son
is human nature.
If loyal ministers do not avoid heavy punishment to give direct admonition,
then in affairs there will be no neglected plans,
and their achievements will flow through ten thousand generations.
Your servant Chéng wishes to open my heart and mind to offer my foolish loyalty;
I only hope the Great King will slightly apply your thoughts and a compassionate heart to the words of your servant Chéng.
Now, to use a single thread of silk to bear
a weight of a thousand jūn,
suspended above an infinite height,
and hanging over an unfathomable abyss—
even a very foolish person would still know to lament that it is about to snap.
When a horse is just becoming startled,
to beat a drum and frighten it;
when the cord is just about to snap,
to further weigh it down—
once the cord snaps from the heavens,
it cannot be tied back together;
once it falls into the deep abyss,
it is difficult to bring it out again.
Whether it can be brought out or not,
the difference is not the width of a hair.
If one can listen to the words of a loyal minister,
one will surely escape danger in a hundred attempts.
If one insists on what you currently wish to do,
it is more precarious than a stack of eggs
and more difficult than ascending to heaven;
but to change what you wish to do
is easier than turning over one's palm
and more secure than Tài Shān.
Now, wanting to reach the ultimate longevity of one's heavenly mandate,
to exhaust endless and ultimate pleasures,
and to fulfill the power of the Ten Thousand Chariots,
requires no more than the ease of turning over a palm
and staying in the security of Tài Shān;
yet you wish to board the danger of stacked eggs
and walk the difficulty of ascending to heaven—
this is what greatly confuses your foolish servant.
In human nature, there are those who fear their shadow and hate their footprints;
they turn their backs and run,
but the more footprints they make,
and the faster the shadow follows.
It would be better to step into the shade and stop,
then the shadow would vanish and the footprints would end.
If you wish for people not to hear,
there is nothing like not speaking;
if you wish for people not to know,
there is nothing like not doing.
If you wish to cool boiling water,
and one person keeps feeding the fire
while a hundred people stir it,
it is of no use;
it is better to cut off the firewood and stop the fire altogether.
If you do not cut it off at that end
but try to save it at this end,
it is like carrying firewood to put out a fire.
Yǎng Yóujī
was a skilled archer of Chǔ;
from a distance of a hundred paces from a willow leaf,
he hit it every time in a hundred shots.
Given the size of a willow leaf,
to hit it a hundred times out of a hundred
can truly be called skilled archery.
Yet where he stopped
was only within a hundred paces;
compared to your servant Chéng,
he did not yet know how to handle the bow and hold the arrow.
Fortune has a foundation where it arises,
and misfortune has a womb where it is born;
accept the foundation
and cut off the womb,
and from where could misfortune come?
Dripping water from Tài Shān can pierce a stone,
and the well-rope of a pulley can cut through a shaft.
Water is not a drill for stone,
nor is a rope a saw for wood,
but gradual friction makes it so.
Now, if one weighs things grain by grain,
by the time it reaches a dàn, there will surely be a discrepancy;
if one measures things inch by inch,
by the time it reaches a zhàng, there will surely be an excess.
But weighing by the dàn and measuring by the zhàng
is direct and has few errors.
A tree of ten spans
begins as a sprout;
one's foot could snap it off,
or one's hand could pull it up and scratch it.
Act while it has not yet grown,
and anticipate it while it has not yet taken shape.
Grinding and whetting on a whetstone—
one does not see the loss,
yet in time it is exhausted.
Planting trees and raising livestock—
one does not see the gain,
yet in time they become large.
Accumulating virtue and building up conduct—
one does not notice the goodness,
yet in time it becomes useful;
abandoning righteousness and turning against reason—
one does not notice the evil,
yet in time one perishes.
Your servant wishes the Great King would maturely consider this and practice it himself;
this is the way that does not change for a hundred generations.
Formerly, in the west, Qín raised defenses against the troubles of the Hú and Róng;
in the north, they prepared the pass at Yúzhōng;
in the south, they resisted the fortresses of the Qiāng and Zuò;
and in the east, they faced the alliance of the Six States.
The Six States relied on the prestige of Xìnlíng,
made clear the treaty of Sū Qín,
and exerted the awe of Jīng Kē,
combining their strength and uniting their hearts to prepare against Qín.
Yet Qín ultimately captured the Six States,
destroyed their altars of soil and grain,
and unified all under heaven.
Why was this?
It was because the geographic advantages were not the same,
and the weight of the people's support was not equal.
Now Hàn occupies all the lands of Qín,
incorporates the populations of the Six States,
practices the righteousness of the Róng and Dí,
and receives the southern court of the Qiāng and Zuò.
In comparison with Qín,
its land is tenfold and its people a hundredfold;
this is what the Great King clearly knows.
Now, those slanderous and flattering ministers who plan for the Great King
do not discuss the righteousness of flesh and blood,
the weight of the people,
or the size of the state,
but instead consider Wú a source of disaster;
this is what your servant considers a worry for the Great King.
To raise the troops of Wú to measure against Hàn
is like gnats or mosquitoes attaching themselves to a herd of cattle,
or rotten meat meeting a sharp sword;
once the blades touch, there will certainly be nothing left.
The world hears that Wú leads the disaffected feudal lords,
wishing to demand the fulfillment of the former Emperor's legacy of treaties.
Now that Hàn has personally executed its Sāngōng
to apologize for previous faults,
this means Your Highness’s majesty is imposed upon the world,
and your merit surpasses that of Tāng and Wǔ.
Now Wú holds the position of a feudal lord,
yet its wealth is more substantial than that of the Son of Heaven;
it has a reputation for seclusion,
yet its residence surpasses that of the Zhōngguó.
Hàn has unified twenty-four commanderies
and seventeen lords;
though local products are sent out in great variety,
and military marches of several thousand lǐ do not end at the outskirts,
its rare treasures are not equal to the storehouses of Shāndōng.
Transporting grain to the west,
land travel never ceasing,
and water travel filling the rivers,
are not as good as the granary of Hǎilíng.
Maintaining the Shànglín Park,
interspersed with detached palaces,
accumulating playthings and curios,
and enclosing birds and beasts,
are not as good as the park of Zhǎngzhōu.
Wandering through the Qǔtái,
or overlooking the Shànglù,
are not as good as the Zhāoxī Pool.
Deep walls and high ramparts,
supplemented by barrier cities,
are not as good as the natural defenses of the Jiāng and Huái.
This is why I rejoice for Your Highness.
If Your Highness now withdraws your troops and returns swiftly,
you may still achieve half of your goals.
Otherwise,
once Hàn knows Wú has the intention of swallowing the world,
it will flare up in rage,
and send the Yǔlín and Huángtóu guards down the river
to attack Your Highness’s capital;
Lǔ and Dōnghǎi will cut off Wú’s supply routes;
the Prince of Liáng will array his chariots and horsemen,
practice feathered warfare and archery,
accumulate grain and maintain a solid defense,
to press upon Xíngyáng,
and wait for Wú to starve.
Even if Your Highness wished to return to your capital,
it would be impossible.
The plan of the three Huáinán states was not to betray the covenant,
yet the Prince of Qí took his own life to erase his tracks;
the four states cannot send troops from their commanderies;
Zhào is confined in Hándān;
these things cannot be concealed,
and are already clear.
Now Your Highness has already left your thousand-lǐ state,
and is restricted within ten lǐ.
Zhāng and Hán command the northern lands;
Gōnggāo is stationed to the left and right;
the soldiers cannot descend from the walls,
and the army cannot even draw a long breath;
I secretly grieve for this.
I hope Your Highness will examine this carefully!
In the past, when a humble official was aggrieved,
flying frost struck the land of Yān;
when a common woman appealed to Heaven,
a violent wind struck the Qí terrace.
Whenever I, your humble official, read of these in books,
I never fail to put down the scroll and weep.
Why?
Men have certain convictions,
and women have unchangeable conduct;
to be faithful yet doubted,
to be upright yet executed—
this is why brave and righteous men
face death without a second thought.
I had heard that benevolence cannot be relied upon
and goodness cannot be leaned on,
and I thought these were just empty words;
but now I know the truth of them.
I prostrate myself and hope Your Highness will temporarily dismiss your attendants,
and grant me a little of your compassionate consideration.
I was originally a man of a thatched door and mulberry pivot,
a scholar in plain cloth and a leather belt;
in retirement, I did not polish the Odes and Documents to dazzle the ignorant,
and in public life, I did not buy fame throughout the world.
Formerly,
I mistakenly obtained the honor of serving in the Chéngmíng Palace,
and entering the Jīnhuá Palace;
when was I not ever shrinking my shadow in solemnity,
or moving cautiously within the forbidden gates?
Secretly admiring Your Highness’s righteousness,
I became a guest under your gate once more,
serving among those with minor skills like mimicking roosters or stealing,
and ranking among the lowest of humble talents.
Your Highness favored me with the light of your grace,
and looked upon me with a kind expression;
I truly wore the golden gift of Jīng Qīng,
and was moved by the duty of a state scholar like Yù Ràng.
I often wished to tighten my hat-strings and fall on my sword,
to repay one ten-thousandth of your kindness,
to cut open my heart or wear down my heels,
to repay the one I regard as Heaven.
I did not expect that I, a lowly man, was so crude,
that I would naturally invite slander and deficiency,
my actions falling under the clear laws,
my body regrettably held in a dark prison;
I walk with my shadow and console my heart,
with a sour nose and aching bones!
I have heard that to damage one’s name is a disgrace,
and to damage one’s body is next.
Therefore, every time the thought arises,
I suddenly feel as if I have lost my soul.
Furthermore, as weeks and months pass,
and late autumn approaches,
the light of heaven becomes gloomy,
and everything around me loses its color.
My body is not wood or stone,
yet I am companions with jailers.
This is why Shàoqīng looked up to heaven and beat his chest,
weeping until his tears were gone and followed by blood.
Although I lack a reputation in my home village,
I have heard of the conduct of a gentleman.
The highest is to live in seclusion in the market stalls,
or lie beneath the cliffs and rocks;
the next is to tie one’s sash in the Court of Jīnmǎ,
and engage in lofty debate upon the Yúntái;
then to retire after capturing the lord of Nányuè,
or tying a rope around the Shányú’s neck.
All are recorded in the vermilion registers,
and together depicted in the green records of history.
Why should one struggle over a fraction of an inch,
or compete for the profit of an awl or a knife?
I have heard that accumulated slander melts gold,
and accumulated defamation wears down bones.
Far in the past, Zhíshēng was suspected of stealing gold;
recently, Bóyú was branded with the name of unrighteousness.
If those two gentlemen
were still treated as such,
how then could I,
escape it?
Formerly, the shame of a great general
was the Marquis of Jiàng in a dark prison;
the shame of a famous official
was Shǐ Qiān in the lower chamber.
As for someone like me,
what is there to say!
The wisdom of Lǔ Lián
was to decline wealth and not return;
the worthiness of Jiēyú
was to sing while walking and forget to return home.
Zǐlíng closed his gates in Dōngyuè;
Zhòngwèi shut his door in Xīqín.
This is indeed easy to understand.
If my deeds were not false,
and my crimes were factual,
I should also clamp my mouth and swallow my tongue,
fall on a dagger to end my life;
how could I then face the men of extraordinary integrity from Qí and Lǔ,
or the scholars of tragic songs from Yān and Zhào?
Now the sacred era is revered and bright,
the world is happy in its work,
blue clouds float over the Luò,
and glorious light fills the Hé.
To the west reaching Líntáo and Dídào,
to the north spanning Fēihú and Yángyuán,
none fail to steep in benevolence and bathe in righteousness,
basking in the sunlight and drinking the sweet dew.
Yet I, a humble official, suffer pain within the round gate of prison,
and harbor resentment at the jail door;
even a creature as small as a single thing
has reason for sadness.
I look up and hope Your Highness will shed a little clarity;
then the soul of Wùqiū
would not be ashamed of its severed head,
and the ghost of Gǔtíng
would have no regrets for its ashen bones.
Unable to bear the intensity of my devotion,
I respectfully present this through your attendants.
Your servant Fǎng submits:
I have received the imperial decree and the gift of the poem for the Qīxī Festival in five rhymes.
I humbly consider that the traces of the Emperor are of many threads,
but your condescension to commonality is unique.
Entrusting your feelings to the poetic style of the Odes,
such rare mastery is seldom seen in this world.
Though the Hàn dynasty spanned four generations,
and the Wèi dynasty boasted its Sānzǔ,
how could they suffice to continue the vision of the Nánfēng,
or harmonize the melody of the Tiáolù?
Your nature and the Way of Heaven
are matters beyond description.
How fortunate I am
to personally encounter them day and night.
In my early days, I served when the dragon was hidden,
entering the inner chamber alongside the likes of Jiǎ and Mǎ;
in later years, I belonged to the time when the dragon flew in the heavens,
awaiting the imperial call like Yán and Xú.
Only the ruler truly knows his servant,
as seen in the intent of your reticent words;
your acceptance without fault
is shown in the play of your eloquent talent.
I have respectfully and crudely followed your lead,
in order to repay the imperial reward;
though I have shown some speed despite my lack of skill,
my vulgarity is already manifest.
As I present this, I am filled with shame and know not where to place myself.
Respectfully submitted.
Your servant Bīn submits:
I have humbly seen the imperial decree and the decree proclaimed by Zhèng Yìtài,
granting the repair of the tomb of my late great-great-grandfather, the former Jìn General of Chariots and Cavalry and Duke of Zhōngzhēn of Jiànxīng, Biàn Hú.
My family line has not flourished,
and the Way of Heaven is obscured;
loyalty met with personal peril,
and filial piety accumulated family disaster;
the teachings of names are equally grieved,
and the secluded are filled with melancholy.
As years and generations have changed,
the orphaned descendants have fallen into obscurity.
Consequently, the steles and markers have been overgrown and obliterated,
the mound and trees ruined and desolate,
foxes and rabbits have made their burrows there,
and young herders sing mournful songs.
Stirred with emotion and mourning for myself,
the passing days and months press upon me.
Your Majesty widely proclaims the teachings of righteousness,
not seeking merit only for the present;
the remaining brilliance of Biàn Hú has not faded,
for he surely exerted his strength for a different age.
Yet such extraordinary grace
was recently lacking in the Jìn records;
the protection from firewood gathering and grazing
extends far into this August dynasty.
What kind of man am I
to dare thank you for such fortune?
I cannot bear the extremity of my sorrowful gratitude!
I respectfully offer this petition for your consideration.
Respectfully submitted.
Fǎng submits:
I recently submitted a petition of appeal,
hoping you would understand my desperate sincerity;
I have received the returned instructions,
but they did not grant me compassionate consideration.
My heart is grieved and my plans are lost;
I weep blood while awaiting the dawn.
Toward the common people,
you show equal care in their molding and creation;
seeking office and praying for glory
is further a means of self-elevation.
To diminish the teachings and abandon the rites,
how could this not concern your sight and hearing?
That which I cannot bear to speak of,
I have fully set forth in this petition.
In the past, I followed a minor official post,
where my salary could not replace farming.
Amidst hunger and cold, I lacked the resources for sweet nourishment;
restricted by duties, I lost half my time for morning and evening care.
The joy at my parents' knees
is already like a passing shadow;
my longing at the mourning table,
how much can I rely upon it?
Furthermore, if I do not personally perform the offerings,
where can their spirits find peace?
Morning and evening are desolate,
as silent as if there were no master.
Since there is no other reason for what I maintain,
how could my desperate choking leave room for many metaphors?
Your Excellency's merit reaches all within the realm;
your resonance with others has a path.
If you would descend like a sudden rain
and grant the suspension of your stern command,
then it will be known that where filial governance reaches,
it even touches those without mind;
where the bestowal of kindness extends,
it is more than just teachings and righteousness.
Unable to bear my collapsing and urgent feelings,
I respectfully offer this petition to be heard.
Respectfully submitted.
Your servant Rèn Fǎng, Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk, bows his head and says:
I have heard that a general should die in his duty,
without retreating a single step;
looking back to avoid the enemy
and hesitating to advance are punishable by law.
Even the Mother of Zhào had such deep insight
that she begged not to be implicated in her son's failure;
the ruler of Wèi established decrees
so that the punishment for those who succumbed was already lightened.
Thus we know that a general of a defeated army
faces death himself and the execution of his family;
since ancient times,
clear punishments have resided here.
Your servant Fǎng knocks his head, knocks his head,
a capital offense, a capital offense.
I have observed that the Xūnxǐan invaded,
temporarily disturbing the borders;
the royal army set out to punish them,
and everything before it crumbled like grass in the wind.
Thus, victory was announced in Huái and Xú,
and the army returned in triumph from the Hé and Yǎn regions.
Dōngguān required not even the effort of a single battle,
and Tǔzhōng saw few expenses of great gold.
However, the Sīzhōu region was distant and isolated,
situated precariously near the enemy's territory;
therefore, the cunning captives were allowed to trample and insult it,
as the months and years passed by.
The late Inspector of Sīzhōu, Cài Dàogōng,
led and encouraged the righteous and brave;
he exerted himself regardless of his life,
defending the city until death.
From winter until autumn,
he still fought endlessly in battle after battle,
repeatedly crushing the ugly captives.
Compared to Jūyán,
Lǐ Lǐng surrendered while Cài Dàogōng held firm;
compared to Shūlè,
Gěng Gōng survived while Cài Dàogōng perished.
If the relief troops from Yǐngzhōu
had provided even a slight amount of support,
then the head of the Shānyú
would long ago have been hung at the northern gate;
how could it have been merely building a surrender mound
or opening the territory of Shè’ān?
It was truly because your servant Cáo Jǐngzōng, the Inspector of Yǐngzhōu,
received the command to punish the enemy
but did not set out at the proper time.
Therefore, he allowed the enemy to cluster like hedgehogs and gather like ants,
having water and grass to rely upon;
he then remained stationary with his armor at rest,
delaying the rescue and thereby aiding the enemy,
so that the isolated city was left to its final defense
and its strength was broken by the fierce power.
Although that is so,
he should have held firm at the Sānguān
and planned further advances,
but instead he withdrew his army and waited,
bringing upon himself loss and defeat;
that the borders were invaded and alarmed
is due to his failures in office.
If there are no severe punishments,
how can execution and reward be properly placed?
Jǐngzōng is the primary culprit.
I respectfully investigate your servant Cáo Jǐngzōng, the Commissioner with Ritual Staff, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yǐngzhōu and Sīzhōu,
General of the Left,
Inspector of Yǐngzhōu,
and Founding Marquis of Xiāngxī County.
He was promoted from the ranks
and encountered such great fortune;
his role in directing the hunt was incomparable,
yet what effort did he exert in capturing the beasts?
His rewards were as abundant as a Marquis of the Realm,
and his honor as high as the ranked generals.
He had barely laid down his burden
when his name was suddenly ranked among the ceremonial vessels.
He achieved nothing in pacifying the Rong,
though the music of the sixteen girls has already been displayed.
From head to heel,
his success is entirely due to the Emperor's creative power;
moistening the grass and coating the plains with blood,
how could he have stopped?
Furthermore, Cài Dàogōng has passed away,
having defended the city for many weeks;
while Jǐngzōng still lives,
having abandoned his armor in a single morning.
The living Cáo and the dead Cài—
such is the difference between their merits.
Only a man such as this
would have the audacity to show his face.
In the past, when Hàn Guāng gave orders to his generals,
he knew the situation a thousand lǐ away while sitting;
when Wèi Wǔ established laws,
cases were handled accordingly.
Therefore, they were able to set out always according to the rules,
without the slightest error.
I humbly consider that your Sacred Martial brilliance is outstanding,
with a strategy that appears once in an age,
calculating the enemy and controlling changes
without error across ten thousand lǐ;
to receive and execute them
indeed expands the temple calculations.
Only this mediocre and stubborn one
is beyond the reach of verbal instruction.
Since the rebellious barbarians have been unrestrained,
they have long been a plague to the Huá lands.
The Sacred Court then looked upon them,
intending to unify the carts and books.
Pitying those common people,
who suffered humiliation where they should not.
Sighing deeply at the early court,
repeatedly harboring compassion and sorrow.
Having led to this loss and ruin,
where can I escape my guilt?
It is proper to apply the penal code
and solemnly clarify the statutes and ordinances.
Your servant humbly submits this impeachment,
requesting that, based on the current facts, Jǐngzōng be dismissed from his current office,
that the Tàicháng be ordered to strip him of his rank and land,
and that he be handed over to the Tíngwèi prison to be tried according to the law.
As for the military aides, staff members,
and subordinate generals involved in the fault,
let the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ separately summon and prosecute them as their violations are determined.
Your servant humbly submits this white memorial to be heard, and so forth.
Rèn Fǎng, the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, bows his head and says:
I have heard that Mǎ Yuán served his sister-in-law,
never entering without his cap;
that Sì Yù raised an orphan,
and there were no favored children in his house.
Thus, righteous men and men of integrity,
hearing of this, are moved to stand firm;
a beautiful tale for a thousand years,
these are the foremost of praise.
Your servant Rèn Fǎng bows his head repeatedly,
a capital offense, a capital offense.
I humbly record that Fàn, the wife of the late Prefect of Xīyáng of the Qí, Liú Yín,
came to the tribunal to petition and state:
She was married into the Liú family
for about twenty years.
After Liú Yín passed away,
she nurtured the orphaned and weak children;
however, her brother-in-law, Liú Zhěng,
constantly desired to harm and seize from them.
Of the previously divided slaves, Jiàozǐ
and Dāngbó,
both have been taken into the common pool.
Furthermore, regarding the purchased maidservant’s sisters and her brother Wēn,
he kept them for his own use;
Liú Zhěng also seized the female slave Lǜcǎo from Liú Yín’s son Liú Qūn,
sold her privately for money,
and did not share it with Liú Qūn.
Liú Yín’s second son by a concubine, Liú Shīlì,
went to Liú Zhěng’s fields in the tenth month of last year;
after twelve days,
Liú Zhěng then demanded six dǒu of rice from Fàn for his meals.
Before the rice could be sent,
he suddenly arrived before her door,
shouting insults with raised fists behind the curtain,
burst into the room,
and took the carriage curtain from the screen as collateral for the rice.
On the night of the ninth day of the second month,
the maid Cǎiyīn stole the carriage railing, the harness, and the dragon-head hitch;
when Fàn asked about the missing items,
Liú Zhěng then beat her son Liú Qūn.
Liú Zhěng, along with his mother and six slaves and maids, came into Fàn’s room,
shouting insults loudly,
and the maid Cǎiyīn raised her hand and struck Fàn’s arm.
She requests an investigation,
as stated in the petition.
I then summoned Hǎigé, an old slave who served Liú Zhěng’s late father, to the tribunal for questioning,
who stated:
Liú Zhěng’s late father, Liú Xīngdào,
previously served as the Prefect of Lǐnglíng
and obtained four slaves.
In dividing the property,
he gave the slave Jiàozǐ to his eldest son Liú Yín.
After Liú Yín died,
the second brother Liú Zhěng seized Jiàozǐ,
claiming he should return to the common pool,
and then Liú Zhěng kept him for his own use;
as for the maid’s sister and brother, each valued at five thousand cash,
he did not share them with Liú Qūn.
The slave Dāngbó
was originally a common slave.
Before Liú Zhěng and his brothers divided the property,
Liú Zhěng’s elder brother Liú Yín used seven thousand cash of his own to pay for Dāngbó
to work the common fields.
When Liú Yín returned from his post in Xīyáng Jùn,
although they had not yet separated their households,
Liú Yín used seven thousand of his private money to redeem Dāngbó
and subsequently sent him to Guǎngzhōu.
After Liú Yín died,
when Liú Zhěng and his brothers later divided the slaves,
only the maid Lǜcǎo remained in the common pool.
Liú Zhěng further claimed that Liú Yín had not yet divided the property when he redeemed Dāngbó,
so he should also belong to the common pool.
Liú Zhěng’s intention was to greedily obtain Dāngbó,
so he pushed Lǜcǎo onto Liú Qūn.
Liú Zhěng planned for Dāngbó’s return,
intending to take him for himself,
but Dāngbó did not return for seven years.
Liú Zhěng suspected he had died and would not return,
so he seized the maid Lǜcǎo instead
and sold her for seven thousand cash.
Liú Zhěng, his brothers, and his sister shared this money,
and again did not share it with Liú Qūn.
Liú Yín’s wife Fàn said
that Dāngbó was redeemed privately by her late husband
and should belong to her son Liú Qūn.
When Dāngbó returned from Guǎngzhōu in the sixth month of the second year of Tiānjiān,
Liú Zhěng again seized him,
claiming he should be part of the common pool,
to compensate for the four years of labor wages while he was in Guǎngzhōu,
and he is now working at Liú Zhěng’s place.
Questioning Liú Zhěng’s maid Cǎiyīn:
Liú Yín’s second son Liú Shīlì
suddenly went to Liú Zhěng’s villa on the twelfth day of the tenth month of last year and stayed for twelve days;
Liú Zhěng asked his brother’s wife Fàn for six dǒu of rice for his meals.
When Fàn had not yet returned it,
Liú Zhěng became angry,
so he entered Fàn’s residence himself
and took a carriage curtain from the screen as collateral.
Fàn sent six dǒu of rice,
and Liú Zhěng then accepted it.
On the night of the ninth day of the second month of this year,
Fàn lost the carriage railing, harness, and dragon-head hitch;
Fàn and her son Liú Qūn said they were stolen by Cǎiyīn.
When Liú Zhěng heard this,
he beat Liú Qūn.
Fàn called out, asking, "Why are you beating my son?"
Liú Zhěng and his mother then went out into the courtyard together,
and insulted Fàn from behind the curtain.
The maid Cǎiyīn and the slaves Jiàozǐ,
Chǔyù,
and Fǎzhì
were then by the side of Liú Zhěng and his mother.
Liú Zhěng said to Cǎiyīn:
"She says you stole the carriage fittings;
why don’t you go inside and curse her?"
Once she entered and began arguing,
she raised her hand and mistakenly struck Fàn’s arm.
The carriage railing, harness, and dragon-head hitch
were indeed not stolen by Cǎiyīn.
Questioning Liú Yín’s wife Fàn’s slave Gǒunú:
He stated that on the night of the ninth day of the past second month,
his mistress lost the carriage railing, harness, and dragon-head hitch,
and suspected they were stolen by Liú Zhěng’s maid Cǎiyīn.
Gǒunú and the young master Liú Qūn went to Jīnyáng Mén to buy rice,
where they happened to see Cǎiyīn at Jīnyáng Mén selling the carriage railing and dragon-head hitch;
Gǒunú immediately wanted to seize them,
but Liú Qūn told Gǒunú it was already done and there was no need to take them back.
Gǒunú hid nearby for a while
and watched a person buy the dragon-head hitch,
which was sold for five thousand cash.
Gǒunú then followed Liú Qūn back to the residence,
but did not see him receive the money.
All these testimonies, such as those from Cǎiyīn
and Jìngnú,
generally correspond with Fàn’s petition.
Re-examining Dāngbó
and Jiàozǐ,
they stated that their mistress was robbed of them
and they are now being used at Liú Zhěng’s place,
which is no different from Hǎigé’s testimony.
Submitting the case to the law,
the Lìngshǐ Pān Sēngshàng deliberated:
If Liú Zhěng did indeed seize and sell the maid from his nephew Liú Qūn’s share
and privately used the slave Jiàozǐ and others,
if there was no official order,
they should be taken and sent to the nearby prison for interrogation.
All those implicated and involved in the source of these wrongs
are to be entrusted to the prison officials,
and all shall be handled according to the legal system.
As the law states,
Liú Zhěng is the primary offender.
Your servant respectfully submits:
The newly appointed Zhōngjūn Cānjūn, your servant Liú Zhěng,
is of low and vulgar origin from the common quarters,
and is ostracized by the teachings of Confucian morality.
Simply because he was a maternal relative of the previous dynasty,
he entered officialdom through the influence of his wealthy youth.
His evils have accumulated and his transgressions are full,
such that his relatives and old friends look at him with resentment.
Reasonably, all communication with him should have been severed,
yet he recklessly vents ugly words;
staying awake all night,
he wrongly inflicts beatings with the heavy staff.
When Xuē Bāo divided property,
he took the old and weak for himself;
Gāo Fèng defiled himself,
by litigating against his widowed sister-in-law.
One does not see the deep concern of Mèngcháng in him,
but only his imitation of the hypocritical traces of Wéntōng.
In the past, when people were harmonious with their kin,
clothes had no fixed owner;
but in Zhěng’s care for his nephew,
he feeds him as if he were a mere acquaintance.
How is it that he cannot forgo debts like Zhōng and Yǔ,
but instead uses curtains and screens as collateral?
Man's heartlessness,
how can it reach such a point!
This is truly intolerable by the moral teachings,
and is abandoned by all the gentry and officials.
Your servants have deliberated
and request that, based on these facts, Zhěng be dismissed from his appointed office,
and be immediately ordered to be handed over to the Tíngwèi to be tried and punished in the legal prison.
As for those implicated who should have their sources cleared,
we leave them to the prison officials,
to handle everything according to the legal system.
The maid Cǎiyīn has not confessed to stealing the cart’s dragon-pull;
we request she be sent to prison to verify the truth.
The clan elders and local officials
initially failed to investigate or report;
regarding them and the others implicated,
we request that this need not be further elaborated.
Your servant Fǎng says so and so,
submitting this with great fear and trepidation.
Your servant Shěn Yuē, Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng, concurrently Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng and the Yì Zhōngzhèng of Wúxīng, prostrates and speaks:
Your servant has heard that "Qí is too great to be a match,"
as recorded in ancient proclamations;
and the refusal of marriage with the Huò family
has left a renowned name among the heroes of the past.
When establishing harmony between two clans
and discerning the righteousness of a marital union,
whether the status is rising or falling, poor or prosperous,
there is indeed no single standard.
It is certainly appropriate to base it on their family background
and not to violate the proper social order,
so that the families of Qín and Jìn are well-matched
and the Jīng and Wèi rivers are not confused.
Since the Sòng clan lost control of the government,
rites and teachings have withered and declined,
and the families of the aristocracy
lose their order day by day.
Marriages have become degraded and mixed,
disregarding whether one is a servant or of common birth;
they sell their ancestors
as a way of trade,
with open eyes and shameless faces,
without any shame or fear.
As for the descendants of great virtue,
whose family legacy is cherished,
such as the families of Luán and Xì,
their past glory is not far off.
When they come of age and marry,
the wealth they illicitly seek is all from lowly servants;
when the marriage knot is tied,
the roles of the wife lose their proper place.
Men of ambition hear of this and feel grieved;
the elders sigh over it.
Since Your Majesty began to govern the world,
greatly reforming the codes and statutes,
although the old is removed and the new is spread,
this custom has not yet been eradicated.
This is why Your Majesty, sitting before the imperial screen, speaks out,
thinking of purifying these corrupt customs.
Your servant is indeed of a scholar's rank
and has been erroneously placed in charge of the Heavenly Statutes;
although I have the ambition of "burying the wheels,"
I will not bow to the influential;
for even small things like foxes and rats
also harm the Great Way.
I have heard by rumor that Wáng Yuán of Dōnghǎi
married his daughter to the Mǎn family of Fùyáng.
Although Yuán’s own character is mediocre and mean,
his ancestry is truly distinguished.
His great-grandfather Yǎ
reached the rank of the Eighth Commandment;
his grandfather Shǎoqīng
served in the inner chambers;
his father Xuán
was promoted to the Crown Prince’s court
and also held prestigious and prominent positions.
Yuán has frequently held military and security posts in various offices
and was included among the ranks of the eminent.
Yet in establishing marriage and friendship,
he seeks only profit;
in bringing disgrace to his peers,
nothing is worse than this.
Since Yuán himself is far away,
I immediately summoned the matchmaker Liú Sìzhī to the tribunal for questioning.
Sìzhī stated:
Mǎn Zhāngzhī of Wújùn
claimed to be of the old Gāopíng clan through hereditary line,
a descendant of Chǒng and Fèn;
his family wealth was sufficient,
and he asked for a marriage to be found for his son Luán.
Wáng Yuán was informed of all the details
and immediately requested Zhāngzhī’s family records;
seeing that Zhāngzhī held the post of Wángguó Shìláng,
and Luán was the Zhènggé Zhǔbù for Wáng Cí in Wújùn,
Yuán and his son then deliberated in detail
and decided to grant the marriage.
Zhāngzhī sent fifty thousand coins
as the betrothal gift.
Yuán had previously lost his wife,
and used the remainder of the betrothal money to take a concubine.
According to what was stated,
it matches the rumors.
Upon investigating Zhāngzhī’s clan,
one cannot distinguish if they are gentry or commoners.
Mǎn Fèn died in the Western Dynasty,
and his descendants were wiped out;
after Wǔqiū,
nothing was heard of them in the Eastern Jìn.
That his claim is false
is obvious without saying.
The marriage between the Wáng and Mǎn families
is truly shocking to public opinion;
the harmony between the Pān and Yáng families
was different from this.
Furthermore, buying concubines and taking handmaids
using the betrothal gift as funds,
the expenses of the betrothal
are turned into filling the bed-chamber;
such base feelings and shameful conduct
were done in haste.
To investigate evil and discipline violations
requires this brief judgment.
Yuán is the principal offender.
Your servant respectfully submits:
Nánjùn Chéng Wáng Yuán
has unworthily relied on his family’s hereditary status
and was able to join the ranks of the officialdom;
he has the appearance of a man,
but a heart different from others;
using a matchmaker for such a purpose
is no different from crude trade.
Moreover, "those who are not of our kind,"
is an aphorism of past sages;
fragrant and stinking herbs should not be mixed,
as heard from ancient texts.
How can a descendant of the Six Ministers
give his daughter to a man of the storehouses;
the Sòngzǐ like the river bream,
sharing a grave with a ghost of the menials.
A high gate lowering itself to a humble one,
although done by himself,
despises his ancestors and disgraces his relatives;
it is most extreme in this matter.
If this custom is not cut short,
its source will then open;
sullying the generations and defiling families,
it will spread to every house.
It is appropriate to place him under clear statutes
and dismiss him from the ranks of his peers.
Let the already stained clan
forever be ashamed before their ancestors;
and let those parties about to form alliances
reform their hearts in the days to come.
Your servants have deliberated
and request that, based on these facts, Yuán be dismissed from his current office
and be barred from office for life;
and immediately issue a prohibition as per custom.
Since Yuán’s official rank requires a decree on yellow paper,
your servant immediately presents this white slip to inform Your Majesty.
Your servant Yuē, with great fear and trepidation,
says so and so.
Yáng Xiū deserves death, deserves death.
I have not attended upon you for several days,
yet it feels like an entire year.
How could this not be because the greatness of your kind regard
has made my feelings of longing and looking up to you so deep?
You have humbled yourself to send a glorious command;
how magnificent is its prose!
I have read it over and over;
even if I were reciting the Yǎ and Sòng sections of the Classic of Poetry,
it would not surpass this.
If Zhòngxuān dominates the region beyond the Hàn River,
the Chén clan spans the territory of Jì,
Xú and Liú distinguish themselves in Qīng and Yù,
and Master Yìng flourishes in the state of Wèiguó,
these are all indeed so.
As for Yáng Xiū,
I only listen for and gather rumors of your fame;
I have no leisure in looking up to your virtue.
Since I was flustered while examining your work,
how could I have time to look down upon others with pride?
I humbly submit that you, My Lord,
grew up in noble prosperity,
possessing the natural talent of Dàn,
and have received sagely and virtuous instruction.
Those observing from near and far
merely said you could proclaim and manifest your excellent virtue
and gloriously support the great enterprise;
they did not think you could also comprehensively examine the commentaries and records
and devote your thoughts to literature.
Now you have surpassed Wáng and exceeded Chén,
outstripping these several gentlemen.
Observers look on in amazement and rub their eyes;
listeners incline their heads and prick up their ears.
If it were not for a comprehensive body and an attained nature
received from the natural world,
who could reach such a level?
Moreover, I have personally seen you, My Lord,
holding the tablets and the brush
to compose something;
it was as if a completed recitation were in your heart,
and you were merely borrowing a book from your hand,
not for a single moment pausing your thoughts.
Zhòngní is like the sun and moon,
which none can surpass;
Yáng Xiū’s looking up to you
is almost like this.
Therefore, I have declined to write about the hé bird,
and having composed the "Rhapsody on Summer" for a whole day, I did not present it;
this is like seeing the beauty of Xīshī
and returning only to feel that one's own appearance is increasingly ugly.
I humbly suppose that you, My Lord,
do not realize this is so,
and having humbly received your kind gift,
you instructed me to edit and finalize it.
When the Chūnqiū was completed,
no one could add or subtract from it;
as for the works of Lord Lǚ and Huáinán,
a single character was worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Yet the disciples kept their mouths shut
and the people in the market folded their arms in respect,
for the excellence of sages and worthies
is truly what distinguishes them from the common and mediocre.
Current rhapsodies and eulogies
are of the same stream as ancient poems;
without being revised by Master Kǒng,
there would be no distinction between the Fēng and the Yǎ.
My ancestor Zǐyún
in his old age did not understand matters;
he forced himself to write a book,
only to regret his youthful works.
If such as Zhòngshān and Zhōu Dàn were like this,
would they all have faults?
You, My Lord, have forgotten the manifest traces of sages and worthies
and repeated the mistaken words of my humble clan;
I privately think you have not considered this.
If you do not forget the great beauty of governing the state
and let your heroic fame flow for a thousand years,
engraving your merits on the Great Bell
and writing your name on bamboo and silk,
this is naturally the refined capacity
you have always cultivated;
how could it conflict with literature?
I have received what you bestowed
and will privately prepare it for the blind musicians to recite and chant,
but how could I dare hope to show kindness like Huì Shī to the disgrace of Zhuāngzhōu?
Jìxù is insignificant;
how is he worth mentioning?
I reply in haste
and cannot express everything fully.
Yáng Xiū deserves death, deserves death.
On the eighth day, Rényín, of the first month,
Acting Master of Records Fán Qīn,
deserves death, deserves death.
Recently I have frequently submitted letters,
which were insufficient to express myself.
Lately, among the musicians,
we have been widely seeking exceptional performers.
At that time, the son of the carriage driver of Commandant Xuē Fǎng,
only fourteen years old,
could warble with his throat and draw out his voice,
matching the sound of the jiā.
I reported this to the superior and presented him;
it was indeed as he said.
That same day, we observed and tested him together;
then I knew that among all things produced by heaven and earth,
there are indeed naturally wondrous things.
His hidden breath turns within,
and his mournful voice resonates without.
At its loudest, it does not become jarring;
at its softest, it does not become faint or scattered.
Its sound is more sorrowful than the old jiā,
and its melody more beautiful than the standard pitch.
When he sang and harmonized alternately
with the Palace Musician Wēn Hú,
the sounds emitted from his throat
all responded like an echo.
In its modulations, sinkings, and floatings,
he followed the changes and entered the rhythm.
From the first trial,
twenty days passed in between;
Wēn Hú wanted to show off what the boy did not know
by challenging him with a song;
but his skill was exhausted and his ideas depleted;
he was unable to do so.
Yet this child’s lingering notes rose and fell
inexhaustibly;
moving through transformations with ease,
his extra flourishes were not yet finished.
When it came to his clear, intense, and mournful singing,
mixed with resentment and longing,
chanting of the far-off expeditions of the northern nomads
or playing the long yearning of the Hu horses,
it pierced the liver and spleen with sadness,
and his sorrow moved even the stubborn and the beautiful.
At that time, the sun was in the western corner,
a cool breeze brushed our robes;
with mountains at our backs and facing a stream,
the flowing springs departed to the east.
Those sitting together looked up and sighed;
those watching bowed their heads to listen.
There was no one who did not shed tears and weep,
their sorrowful hearts filled with noble indignation.
Since the famous singers Zuǒ É and Shǐ Nuà
and the outspoken Jiǎn Jiě
were known,
from what my ears and eyes have seen,
everyone says this is strange and extraordinary,
something never heard before.
I humbly reflect that your Sagely Person
loves everyone and is fond of curiosities;
therefore, taking advantage of this letter,
I first report the details.
I humbly imagine that when you hear of this,
you will certainly feel lingering joy.
I hope that my duties will soon be finished
so I may return to attend your radiant presence,
stay within your courtyard,
and listen to this tune with you;
the joy of the banquet
will surely be boundless.
Fán Qīn deserves death, deserves death.
Chén Lín deserves death, deserves death.
Yesterday you bestowed your favor and humbled yourself to send a command,
together with the "Rhapsody on the Tortoise."
Upon opening and reading it, it was brilliant.
You, My Lord, possess talent that surpasses the world
and hold the instruments of Qīngpíng and Gànjiàng;
when you strike a bell, it is silent,
and you respond to opportunities with immediate decision.
This is indeed a natural and extraordinary endowment,
not something those who study and look up can hope to achieve.
Its tone and meaning are profound,
its clear diction and wondrous phrases
are as brilliant as flashing fire,
comparable to the Fēitù and Liúxīng horses,
leaping over mountains and crossing seas,
whom even the Lóngjì dare not pursue;
how much less could a pack horse
keep pace?
Only after hearing the music of "White Snow"
and seeing the rhythm of "Green Water,"
do the "Rustic of the Eastern Field" and the "Man of Bā"
find their coarseness and meanness even more evident.
I was both joyful and laughing,
wanting to stop but unable to.
I have respectfully stored it in a casket to enjoy and indulge in,
using it for my own chanting and recitation.
Chén Lín deserves death, deserves death.
February 8th, the day of Gēngyín.
Your servant Zhì speaks:
I have respectfully read your handwritten command,
mourning the deceased and showing concern for the living.
The greatness of your grace and sorrow
is expressed within the ink of your writing.
The sun and moon pass slowly,
and the years do not wait for me.
Formerly, when I attended your side,
sitting among the various worthies,
we went out on unofficial excursions,
and came in to the joy of pipes and strings.
Setting out wine and drinking happily,
we composed poems and offered toasts for your longevity.
I thought we could protect one another from beginning to end,
exerting our talents and strength together,
to serve our brilliant lord with loyalty.
Who would have thought that within a few years,
almost everyone would be dead and gone.
What virtue do I alone possess
to endure for so long?
Chén, Xú, Liú, and Yìng—
their talents and learning were manifest.
Truly, as your command stated,
it is a pity they did not fulfill their potential;
it is indeed deeply painful.
All of these several gentlemen,
as refined attendants,
were truly the right men for the task.
But if the borders were in danger,
and the masses were in a state of upheaval,
with military dispatches arriving like spokes to a hub,
and urgent messages racing back and forth,
for those various worthies,
it would not have been their proper role.
In the past, during the era of Xiàowǔ,
literary works flourished.
Men such as Dōngfāng Shuò and Méi Gāo
could not maintain a political discourse;
they were of the same sort as Ruǎn and Chén.
Only Yán Zhù and Shòu Wáng
were consulted on matters of state;
yet neither was careful with his own person,
nor did they plan well for the state.
In the end, they met with ruin and death,
which I secretly find shameful.
As for Sīmǎ Chángqīng, who claimed illness to avoid affairs
and made writing books his primary task,
then Master Xú was close to his likeness.
But now each has passed away,
and they have already become something different.
The gentlemen of later generations
are indeed to be respected.
I prostrate myself before you, who are as my Heaven,
wandering at leisure in the fields of the classics,
and resting in the gardens of literature.
When you speak and raise an argument,
you exhaust all principles and reach every subtlety.
When you spread your floral prose and put brush to paper,
the patterns of phoenixes and dragons soar.
Though your years are equal to those of Xiāo Wáng,
your talent is indeed a hundred times his.
This is why public opinion accords you the highest status,
and why those near and far speak with one voice.
Yet, as the years seem to fall away,
I, Zhì, am already forty-two.
White hair grows at my temples,
and my worries deepen daily;
indeed, I am no longer as I was in ordinary times.
I only wish to preserve my person and discipline my conduct,
not treading upon ground where there are faults,
so as not to become a burden to my confidant.
The joy of excursions and banquets
is difficult to encounter again;
once one’s prime has passed,
it truly cannot be pursued further.
I am fortunate to possess a talent of the lowest stupidity,
yet I have met with this auspicious gathering of wind and clouds.
Though time passes and I grow old,
I still wish to bare my chest and raise my head,
to display my utility in governing.
I cannot overcome my sincerity;
because your command was so detailed,
I have thus briefly set forth my deepest feelings.
Zhì commits a capital offense, a capital offense.
Your servant Zhì speaks:
Previously, I was honored to be invited and received,
attending the banquet all day long.
The Radiant Spirit hid its light,
and we continued by the light of splendid lamps.
Even when Yú Qīng went to Zhào,
or Píngyuán entered Qín,
and received gifts of a thousand pieces of gold,
or floated wine cups for ten days,
they could not have surpassed this.
A small vessel is easily filled;
I was the first to become intoxicated and exhausted.
After waking up,
I did not know what I had said.
I arrived at my office on the fifth day.
Having just arrived and taking over from my predecessor,
I do not yet know the depths or shallows.
However, I observe the terrain
and examine what the soil is suited for.
To the west, it is girded by Chángshān,
with continuous ridges level with Dài.
To the north, it neighbors Bǎirén,
which was the place Gāodì once avoided.
Furthermore, there is the Zhì River,
which moistens the borders.
Sighing deeply,
I think of the clever stratagems of Huáiyīn,
and realize the failed plans of Chéng'ān.
Looking south toward Hándān,
I think of the character of Lián and Lìn.
To the east, it connects to Jùlù,
where the likes of Lǐ Qí remain.
The men and women of the capital
are accustomed to ritual and instruction;
they all possess a fervent integrity
and harbor the stratagems of Zuǒchē.
Yet I, Zhì, am dull and weak,
and have no means to preside over them.
As for extending virtue and planting kindness,
and establishing a reputation,
so that farmers are at ease in the fields,
and women weavers sing at their looms,
this is certainly not within my capability.
As for following the laws and instructions,
and proclaiming clear commands,
so that there are no officials below who abuse their power,
and no overbearing heroes in the towns,
allotting tasks and carrying out punishments
based on precedents—
I also have a trembling heart that hopes to achieve this.
In the past, Yán Zhù left the joy of Chéngmíng Hall
to accept the position in Kuàijī.
Shòu Wáng left the pleasure of being an attendant
to take charge of the duties in Dōngjùn.
Afterward, both were able to return to their former posts
and follow their previous paths.
Now, I alone do not find it so;
is this not strange?
Zhāng Chǎng was away from the capital
and considered himself unremarkable;
Chén Xián's indignation accumulated,
as he longed to enter the capital city.
Did they merely engage in empty talk and boastful discourse
to deceive and dazzle the world?
This was truly because they disdained the glory of being a commandery governor
and valued the service by the lord's side.
Past and present follow one principle;
before and after, they do not differ.
How can one know that those who come later will not be like those of today?
For now, I use this as a meeting with you,
and dare not say more.
Zhì commits a capital offense, a capital offense.
Chōng and the others commit a capital offense.
We humbly see that your excellent command has clearly arrived,
and we have heard that you, Illustrious Lord, firmly decline.
We, Chōng and the others, are deeply concerned;
indeed, we have a humble thought:
we believe that when sage kings established systems,
they were the same throughout a hundred generations.
Praising virtue and rewarding merit
have their origins in antiquity.
Formerly, Yī Yǐn
was merely a servant of the clan of Yǒu Shēn,
but once he assisted Chéng Tāng,
he then bore the title of Āhéng.
Zhōu Gōng relied on a momentum already established
and held onto a legacy already secured,
gloriously dwelling in Qūfù
and possessing Guī and Méng.
Lǚ Shàng was a fisherman of Pánxī,
but with one morning's command,
he was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū.
From then on,
those whose merit was thin but whose rewards were thick
cannot be counted.
Yet, wise and sagacious men
still consider these as fine stories.
How much more so, since the time of the former Chancellor,
your family has possessed brilliant virtue for generations,
assisting and supporting the House of Wèi,
so as to pacify the world.
In the court, there is no deficient governance,
and among the people, there are no words of slander.
Previously,
your Excellency (Míng Gōng) campaigned westward to Líng Zhōu
and approached the desert to the north.
To the west of Yú Zhōng,
the people were awed and submitted at the mere sight of your banners.
The Qiāng and Róng tribes galloped eastward
and turned their heads inward toward the court.
In the east, you punished the rebellious;
your entire army alone was victorious.
You captured the generals of Hélǘ
and decapitated his light and elite troops,
numbering in the tens of millions.
Your prestige reached the Nán Hǎi,
and your name terrified the Sān Yuè.
Within the universe, there is peace and tranquility,
and harsh wickedness does not arise.
Thus, those of exotic customs fear your power,
and the Dōng Yí offer their dances.
Therefore, the Sage Emperor, reviewing the ritual codes and old statutes since ancient times,
has expanded the state and established your residence,
manifesting this in Tài Yuán.
Your Excellency should receive the sacred decree
and accept this great blessing;
it is truly fitting for both Heaven and man.
Your great merit and magnificent achievements
are as brilliant as that;
the nation's land and auspicious mandate
are as lofty as this.
Those within and without are in harmony,
with no error or transgression.
By means of this campaign,
you can cross the river in court robes
and sweep clean Wú Huì;
block the source of the river to the west,
and offer sacrifices to Mín Shān from afar.
Turning your halberds and slowing your pace
to command all under Heaven,
there will be none far away who do not submit
and none near who are not respectful.
Now the virtue of the Great Wèi
is more brilliant than that of Táng Yú;
Your Excellency’s magnificent achievements
surpass those of Huán and Wén.
Then, one may look upon the Cāng Zhōu and take leave of Zhī Bó,
or ascend Jì Shān and bow to Xǔ Yóu;
would that not be magnificent!
Being most just and most fair,
who could be your neighbor?
Why must you diligently make small refusals?
Chōng and the others do not understand the overall situation,
yet we dare to present our observations.
Your former subordinate and scholar, Xiè Tiào, deserves death, deserves death.
This day, I received a summons from the Department of State Affairs,
appointing Tiào as the Record-keeper and Adjutant (Jì Shì Cān Jūn) for the Prince of Xīn Ān.
Tiào has heard that the water of stagnant pools
desires to pay homage to the sea even if it exhausts itself;
a weary and lame horse
hopes to gallop but tires midway.
Why is this?
The marshes and fields are withered and fallen,
and facing them brings melancholy;
the fork in the road leads west and east,
and one may feel stifled with grief.
Moreover, my adherence to righteousness was in vain,
and my desire to return cannot be followed;
it is as distant as falling rain,
as fluttering as an autumn leaf-stalk.
Tiào is truly of an ordinary sort,
with neither conduct nor ability worth calculating.
It happened that the Heaven and Earth are auspicious and bright,
and the mountains and rivers are receptive;
a single person was praised and selected,
and a small virtue was promoted.
Thus, I left the plow in the garden
and took up the brush in the Tù Yuán.
To the east, I crossed the Sān Jiāng;
to the west, I floated on the Qī Zé.
Amidst the hardships of the military banners,
there were leisurely conversations.
My long robes trailed daily,
and my rear carriage was well-oiled;
standing with honor in the government court,
grace was added to my appearance.
Washing my hair and drying it in the sun,
I could not fathom the boundaries of your favor;
clutching my chest and thinking of repayment,
I early on pledged my flesh and bones.
Little did I realize that the vast ocean had not yet turned,
yet the creatures of the waves are tossed about;
just as the Bó Xiě is in spring,
the traveler's feathers are the first to say farewell.
In the clear and secluded princely residence,
my old thatched hut remains lonely.
A light boat sails back against the current,
and I remain alone, mourning my shadow.
White clouds are in the sky,
but the Lóng Mén is no longer seen.
The further I go from your virtue, the more it lasts;
the deeper I think of your virtue, the deeper it becomes.
I only wait for the blue river to be in sight,
watching for the returning ship at the spring islet;
when the red mansion is just opening,
I shall offer my simple heart like autumn fruit.
If my hairpin and shoes still exist
and my robes and mat remain unchanged,
even if my body should fill a ditch or valley,
I would still hope my wife and children would know where to return.
Wiping my tears and saying farewell,
sorrow comes in a sudden rush;
I cannot bear my sincere dog-and-horse-like loyalty.
The Record-keeper and Adjutant Rèn Fǎng deserves death, deserves death.
I humbly acknowledge that on this auspicious day of this month,
you have solemnly received the ceremonial documents.
Your virtue is manifest and your achievements are high,
brilliantly matching the four seas;
all living beings
now have a place of refuge.
Moreover, I, Fǎng, have received the teachings of a gentleman
for nearly twenty years.
Even your casual remarks were seen as grace,
and your glances became my adornment.
A small man cherishes kindness
and looks toward where he should die.
Formerly, I attended a fine banquet,
where there were lingering words;
the intent of your guidance
was expressed in pleasant jests.
How could I have expected such great fortune
that these words would not change.
Although my feelings were mistakenly perceived beforehand,
my traces are immersed in your generous bait.
Bathing and washing are prepared, yet not for mourning;
the great hall is constructed, and I offer my congratulations.
Your Excellency's Way crowns the two realms,
and your achievements surpass those of remote antiquity.
You would have Yī and Zhōu hold the reins,
and Huán and Wén support the wheels.
Your divine merit is beyond record;
how can all creation find a name for it?
As the government court is first established,
the talented and worthy look up in expectation;
only this fish-eye
dares to offend the precious gems.
Looking at myself and following my limits,
I truly know I am as insignificant as dust.
Met once in a thousand years,
such re-creation is difficult to repay;
even if I should perish,
I would still know it is not a sufficient repayment.
I cannot bear my feelings of gratitude and trepidation;
I respectfully go to the hall to present this white letter of thanks.
Fǎng deserves death, deserves death.
Recently, as the court's command contained the appointment documents,
I ventured to present my sincere heart.
Having received the returning command,
I have not yet been granted the favor of your empty reception.
The scholar-officials look up in expectation,
deeply not understanding the situation.
I have heard that receiving gold from the treasury
is the grand aim of an insightful man;
to step high into the corners of the sea
is but the minor integrity of a commoner.
Therefore, when stepping on the mounting stone, Zhōu Gōng did not harbor doubts,
and when presented with the jade ornament, Tài Gōng did not offer refusals.
Moreover, the generations of wise men have followed in succession,
and your ancestral virtue resides with the people.
Governing during the primitive chaos,
the sighs are as deep as those for Wēi Guǎn.
Furthermore, in the campaign of Zhū Fāng,
Jīng Hé was relied upon;
you withdrew the army and inspired the troops,
greatly rebuilding the royal house.
Though one might endure callouses to save Sòng,
or suffer heavy toil to preserve Chǔ.
Looking at the past from the vantage of the present,
what is there worth saying?
Yet the delusion is worse than stealing a bell,
and merit is doubted and goes unrewarded;
Great Heaven and Sovereign Earth
cannot endure such cruelty.
Therefore, the jade horse galloped swiftly,
signaling the departure of Wēizǐ;
the golden tablet emerged from the earth,
proclaiming the resentment of Lóngpáng.
Your Excellency, Mínggōng, leaned on the saddle and ceased weeping,
whetting the will of the three armies;
dwelling alone, you wiped away tears,
arousing the hearts of righteous men.
Thus you were able to make Hǎiruò and the Earth God appear,
offering all maps to bring about good fortune;
the Shānróng and Gūzhú
tethered their horses and followed in your wake.
Punishing the guilty and consoling the people,
you united all and settled the chaos;
not by coveting the credit of Heaven,
but through the true labor of soaking your feet.
Furthermore, Mínggōng, you were originally a scholar
who found joy in the Teachings of Names;
with a refined character and upright reputation,
you presided over the elegant and the common.
Though unpracticed in the ways of Sūn Wǔ,
you encountered such divine martial prowess.
You drove out the masses slated for execution
and saved the customs destined for feudal investiture;
tortoise shells and jade were not destroyed—
whose merit is this?
If you alone act as a superior man,
where would that leave Yī Yǐn and the Duke of Zhōu?
We do not understand flexibility,
but truly possess simple sincerity;
unable to bear our earnestness,
we pay our respects again with all our hearts.
We humbly hope you will accept the ritual scrolls
and fulfill the expectations of the people.
Jí deserves death, deserves death.
I humbly submit to Your Excellency, Mínggōng,
