who, with the virtue of encompassing the One,
occupies the position of the High Minister;
all heroes raise their heads,
and the talented and worthy lift their feet.
On the day you opened your office,
everyone considered themselves your subordinates;
when the summons first arrived,
I, your servant, was the first.
Zǐxià stayed by the Xīhé River,
and Marquis Wénhóu held the broom for him;
Zōuzǐ lived in the shade of Shǔgǔ,
and King Zhāowáng accompanied him in his carriage.
As for those commoners in plain clothes living in poverty with leather belts,
the reason kings, dukes, and great men bow themselves down to them
is because the Way resides within them.
I, Jí, lack the virtue of Zōu or Bǔ but possess their coarseness;
yet I have been unexpectedly selected,
and have no way to match the position.
I was about to farm on the sunny side of Dōnggāo
to pay the taxes of millet and grain,
so as to avoid the path of those in power.
Carrying firewood has left me weary and ill,
and my physical strength is not great.
The summons to fill an official post
is not something I can endure.
I beg you to rescind this misplaced favor
to bring glory to your pure selections.
To my friend Zǐqīng:
You have diligently proclaimed your fine virtue
and recorded your name in these pure times;
your glorious reputation is widely spread,
which is a cause for great fortune!
Being entrusted to a far-off foreign land
is what the ancients grieved over;
looking toward the wind and cherishing thoughts of you,
how can I not be full of lingering regret!
In the past, you did not abandon me,
and you condescended to return a reply from afar;
your diligent consolation and instruction
exceed those of flesh and blood.
Though I, Líng, am not clever,
how can I not be deeply moved!
Since I first surrendered
until today,
my person has been in dire straits;
sitting alone in sorrow and bitterness,
I see nothing all day long
except for foreign tribes.
Leather arm-guards and felt tents
are used to ward off wind and rain;
rank meat and fermented milk
are used to satisfy hunger and thirst.
Looking around to speak and laugh,
with whom can I share joy?
In the lands of the Hú, there is black ice,
and the border lands are harsh and cracked;
one only hears the desolate sound of the mournful wind.
In the cold autumn, the ninth month,
the grass beyond the frontier withers.
At night I cannot sleep,
turning my ear to listen afar;
Hú flutes sound together,
grazing horses neigh mournfully,
howling and whistling in groups,
and border sounds rise from all sides.
Sitting in the morning to listen to them,
unconsciously, my tears fall.
Alas, Zǐqīng!
What kind of heart could I, Líng, have
that I would not be sorrowful?
Since parting with you,
I am even more listless.
Above, I think of my old mother
who was executed in her waning years;
my wife and children were innocent,
yet all were slaughtered like sea monsters.
My person has betrayed the state's grace,
and I am pitied by the world.
You return to receive glory,
while I remain to receive shame;
what can be done about fate!
Born in a land of ritual and righteousness,
I have entered a land of ignorant customs;
betraying the grace of my lord and parents,
I remain forever in the realm of the barbarians.
How tragic!
Causing the descendants of my late father
to instead become a tribe of the Róng and Dí
is another cause for self-sorrow!
My merit was great and my crime small,
yet I did not receive clear scrutiny;
this betrayed my heart, the heart of Líng,
and my humble intentions.
Whenever this thought comes,
I suddenly forget to live.
It would not be difficult for me, Líng, to pierce my heart to prove myself,
or cut my throat to show my will,
but the state is already finished with me.
Killing myself would be of no benefit,
and would only increase my shame.
Therefore, I often roll up my sleeves and endure the shame,
and repeatedly live on in disgrace.
The people around me,
seeing me like this,
think to provide me with unpleasant joys
and come to encourage me.
The music of a foreign land
only makes one sad
and increases one's distress.
Alas, Zǐqīng!
Between those who know each other,
what is valued is knowing each other's hearts.
My previous letter was written in haste
and did not fully express my feelings;
therefore I speak of them briefly again:
In the past, the late Emperor Xiāndì entrusted Líng with five thousand infantry,
to set out on a campaign to the remote regions.
The five generals lost their way,
and Líng alone encountered battle.
Carrying provisions for ten thousand lǐ,
leading a force of foot soldiers,
I went beyond the borders of Tiānhàn
and entered the territory of the powerful Hú.
With a multitude of five thousand,
I faced an army of a hundred thousand.
Spurring on exhausted troops,
we confronted fresh horses.
Yet we still beheaded generals and seized banners,
chasing the fleeing and pursuing the defeated,
wiping out their traces and sweeping away the dust,
and beheaded their formidable leaders.
I made the soldiers of the three armies
view death as a return home.
I, Líng, am without talent
and have seldom held great responsibility;
I thought that at this time,
my achievements would be hard to surpass.
Once the Xiōngnú were defeated,
their whole nation raised an army,
retraining elite troops,
numbering over a hundred thousand.
The Chányú himself arrived at the front
to personally complete the encirclement.
The positions of guest and host
were already unequal;
the relative strength of infantry and cavalry
was also vastly disparate.
Exhausted troops fought again,
one man standing against a thousand;
yet they still supported one another despite their wounds and pain,
risking their lives to be the first in battle.
The dead and wounded piled up in the fields;
those remaining were fewer than a hundred,
and all were burdened with illness,
unable to wield shields and spears.
Yet when Líng raised his arm and gave a shout,
the wounded and sick all rose up;
lifting their blades and pointing at the captives,
the Hú horses fled.
Weapons were exhausted and arrows spent;
men had not a foot of iron,
yet they still bared their heads and shouted vigorously,
competing to be the first to mount the enemy's walls.
At that time,
Heaven and Earth shook with rage for Líng,
and the warriors drank blood for Líng.
The Chányú thought Líng could not be captured again
and was about to lead his troops back.
But a treacherous official instructed him,
so he then resumed the battle.
Therefore, Líng could not escape.
In the past, Gāohuángdì with a multitude of three hundred thousand
was besieged at Píngchéng.
At that time,
fierce generals were like clouds
and strategic ministers like rain,
yet he still went without food for seven days
and only just managed to escape.
How much more so for one in Líng's position;
how could it have been easy to exert one's strength?
But the officials in charge say this and that,
merely resenting Líng for not dying.
That Líng did not die
is indeed a crime;
but when you, Zǐqīng, look at Líng,
am I a man who would steal his life
or one who treasures his own existence?
Could I possibly turn my back on my lord and parents,
abandon my wife and children,
and instead act for personal gain?
That Líng did not die
was because I had something I wished to achieve;
therefore I wished, as I said in my previous letter,
to repay the kindness of the ruler of the state.
Truly, dying in vain is not as good as establishing one's integrity,
and having one's name extinguished is not as good as repaying virtue.
In the past, Fàn Lǐ did not die for the shame of Kuàijī,
and Cáo Mèi did not die for the humiliation of three defeats,
but in the end they avenged the enemy of Gōujiàn
and repaid the shame of the state of Lǔ.
My humble heart
sincerely admires this.
How could I have imagined that before my will was established, resentment had already formed,
and before my plan was followed, my flesh and blood suffered punishment?
This is why Líng looks up to heaven, beats his breast, and weeps tears of blood!
You also say:
"Hàn is not ungenerous to its meritorious officials."
Since you are a minister of Hàn,
how could you not say such a thing?
In the past, Xiāo and Fán were imprisoned;
Hán and Péng were sliced into mincemeat;
Cháo Cuò suffered execution;
Zhōu and Wèi were found guilty.
As for the rest of the officials who assisted the mandate and established merit,
the likes of Jiǎ Yì and Yàfū,
they were all truly the talents of an age,
possessing the qualities of generals and ministers,
yet they suffered the slanders of petty men
and together endured the humiliation of disaster and ruin,
in the end causing those who harbored talent to receive slander
and their abilities could not be displayed.
When those two gentlemen went into distant exile,
who would not feel heartbroken for them!
Líng’s late grandfather, the General,
his military strategy covered Heaven and Earth,
and his righteousness and courage were the foremost of the three armies,
yet he merely lost the favor of an influential official
and cut his own throat beyond the remote regions.
This is why meritorious officials and righteous men carry their halberds and sigh deeply!
How can it be said that Hàn is not ungenerous?
Moreover, in the past, you were an envoy with but a single carriage
going to the captives of ten thousand chariots.
You met with an unfavorable time,
even to the point of falling on your sword without a second thought;
you wandered in hardship and suffering
and nearly died in the wilds of the northern desert.
You undertook your mission in the prime of your life
and returned with a head of white hair.
Your elderly mother passed away in the hall,
and your living wife left your chamber.
This is something seldom heard of in the world
and something that has never occurred from ancient times to the present.
Even the people of the Mán and Mò
still praise your integrity,
how much more should the ruler of the world?
Líng thought that you should enjoy the offering of a fief
and receive the reward of a thousand chariots.
But I hear that upon your return,
your gift did not exceed two million,
and your position was no more than Diǎnshǔguó;
there was not even a foot of land enfeoffed
to acknowledge your diligence.
Yet those officials who obstruct merit and harm the capable
all became Marquises of Ten Thousand Households,
and the relatives and the greedy or fawning types
all became ministers of the imperial court.
If it is even thus for you,
what more can Líng hope for?
Moreover, Hàn punished Líng severely for not dying
but rewarded you meagerly for maintaining your integrity.
To want to make officials who hear of this from afar
hasten to offer their lives upon hearing the news,
this is truly difficult.
This is why, whenever I look back, I do not regret my choice.
Although Líng has forsaken the kindness shown to him,
Hàn has also turned its back on virtue.
Ancient people had a saying:
"Though one be loyal, if they are not fierce,
they view death as a return home."
If Líng could indeed be at peace,
could the ruler still feel any lingering affection?
If a man does not make a name for himself in life,
then in death he shall be buried among the barbarians.
Who could again bow their body and touch their forehead to the ground,
returning toward the Northern Gate,
and let the petty scribes toy with their pens and ink?
I hope you will no longer have expectations for Líng!
Alas, Zǐqīng!
What more is there to say!
We are ten thousand lǐ apart,
our people separated and our paths different.
In life, we belong to different worlds;
in death, we shall be ghosts of different regions.
I take my leave of you forever, in life and in death!
Please convey my thanks to my old friends,
and strive to serve the sage ruler.
Your son is well;
do not worry about him.
Take care of yourself.
From time to time, as the north wind blows,
send me your kind words again.
Lǐ Líng bows his head.
Sīmǎ Qiān, the humble servant of the Tàishǐgōng, bows twice and speaks.
To Shǎoqīng, your excellency:
Formerly, I was honored by your gift of a letter,
instructing me to be smooth in dealing with others
and to make the recommendation of worthies and the advancement of scholars my task.
Your spirit was diligent and sincere,
as if you were disappointed that I did not follow your guidance,
but instead adopted the words of the common crowd.
I would not dare to do such a thing.
Although I am weary and useless,
I have also heard of the legacy of the elders.
However, I consider myself mutilated in body and living in filth;
every move I make brings blame,
and wishing to do good, I only cause harm.
Therefore, I am depressed in solitude, and with whom should I speak?
The proverb says:
“For whom does one act?
To whom does one listen?”
For when Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá never played the zither again for the rest of his life.
Why?
A scholar acts for one who understands him;
a woman beautifies herself for one who takes pleasure in her.
As for me, my physical substance is already flawed and deficient;
even if I possessed talents like those of Suí and Hé
and my conduct was like that of Yóu and Yí,
in the end, it could not be considered an honor,
and would only be enough to cause laughter and bring a stain upon myself.
My reply to your letter was due,
but it happened that I followed the Emperor to the east,
and was further pressured by trivial duties.
Our meetings were brief,
and in such haste, there was not a moment's leisure
to fully express my deepest thoughts.
Now, Shǎoqīng, you face an unfathomable charge.
Within a month,
as the end of winter approaches,
I must soon follow the Emperor to Yōng.
I fear that something sudden and unavoidable might happen,
and I would never be able to unburden my resentment and explain it to you;
then the soul of one long departed would harbor eternal regret.
Please allow me to briefly state my vulgar and humble views.
My long failure to reply,
I hope you will not consider a fault.
I have heard:
Cultivating the self
is the symbol of wisdom;
loving to give
is the beginning of benevolence;
taking and giving
is the manifestation of righteousness;
feeling shame at disgrace
is the determination of courage;
establishing a name
is the ultimate goal of conduct.
If a scholar possesses these five,
then he can find a place in the world
and join the ranks of gentlemen.
Therefore, no disaster is more grievous than craving profit;
no grief is more painful than a wounded heart;
no conduct is more shameful than disgracing one's ancestors;
and no humiliation is greater than gōngxíng.
A man who is a remnant of punishment
cannot be compared or counted among others;
this is not just for one generation,
it has been so since long ago.
In the past, Wèi Líng Gōng rode in the same carriage with Yōng Qú,
and Kǒngzǐ left for Chén;
Shāng Yāng was granted an audience through Jǐng Jiàn,
and Zhào Liáng was dismayed;
Tóngzǐ served as an attendant in the carriage,
and Yuán Sī changed countenance.
Since ancient times, people have been ashamed of such things.
Even for a man of mediocre talent,
if his affairs involve eunuchs,
he is bound to be dejected in spirit.
How much more so for a high-spirited scholar!
Now, even though the court lacks men,
why should a remnant of the knife and saw
recommend the heroes and talents of the world?
I rely on the legacy of my ancestors
and have been allowed to serve near the Emperor's carriage
for more than twenty years.
As I reflect upon myself:
Above, I was unable to offer loyalty and show faith,
or gain a reputation for extraordinary strategy or talent,
to bind myself to the enlightened ruler;
next, I was unable to remedy omissions and supply what was lacking,
recruit the worthy and advance the capable,
or bring to light scholars living in seclusion;
externally, I was unable to join the ranks of the army
to attack cities and fight in the field,
achieving the merit of beheading generals and seizing flags;
below, I could not accumulate days and stack up labors
to attain high office and generous salary,
to bring glory and favor to my clan and friends.
Not one of these four has been accomplished.
I have merely drifted along and sought acceptance,
with no effectiveness in any way;
it can be seen to be thus.
Formerly,
I once stood in the ranks of the Xiàdàfū,
taking part in minor discussions in the Wàitíng.
I did not use that time to uphold the fundamental principles
or exhaust my thoughts.
Now, with a mutilated body, I am a slave who sweeps floors,
among the base and worthless.
If I were now to raise my head and lift my brows
to argue over right and wrong,
would I not be belittling the court and shaming the scholars of this age?
Alas!
Oh!
What more can one like me say!
What more can be said!
Furthermore, the facts of the matter from beginning to end are not easily explained.
In my youth, I was possessed of an unrestrained spirit;
as an adult, I had no reputation in my local district.
Fortunately, because of my ancestors, the Emperor
allowed me to offer my meager skills,
going in and out of the Zhōu Wèi.
I thought: “How can one look at the sky while carrying a basin on his head?”
Therefore, I cut off relations with guests and friends,
neglected my family’s affairs,
and day and night thought only of exhausting my unworthy talents,
striving with a single mind to manage my duties,
seeking to be close to and find favor with the Emperor.
But things turned out quite contrary to my expectations.
I and Lǐ Líng both served at the same court,
and we were not originally close friends.
Our paths and interests were different;
we never shared a cup of wine
or joined in intimate moments of leisure.
However, I observed his character
as an extraordinary and self-disciplined gentleman:
filial in serving his parents,
trustworthy with his peers,
incorruptible in matters of wealth,
and righteous in his dealings.
In matters of protocol, he was deferential;
respectful and frugal, he was humble toward others.
He was always thinking of exerting himself regardless of his own safety
to serve the state in its emergencies.
These qualities he had long cultivated,
and I believed he possessed the spirit of a true national hero.
Now, for a subject to face ten thousand deaths without considering his own life
and rush to meet the hardships of the state
is indeed extraordinary.
Now, because he conducted one undertaking unsuccessfully,
those officials who merely save their own bodies and protect their wives and children
have followed suit by vilifying his shortcomings;
I truly feel pained for him in my heart.
Furthermore, Lǐ Líng led fewer than five thousand infantry
deep into the land of barbarian horses,
treading as far as the Chányú's court.
He was like bait dangled in the tiger's mouth,
boldly challenging the powerful Hú.
Facing a vast army of millions,
he fought the Chányú continuously for over ten days,
and the number of enemies he killed exceeded his own total strength.
The enemy could not keep up with rescuing their dying and supporting their wounded;
the felt-clad rulers and leaders all trembled in fear.
They then summoned all of their Left and Right Xiánwáng
and raised every man capable of drawing a bow,
so that the entire nation together attacked and surrounded him.
Fighting while retreating for a thousand lǐ,
his arrows were exhausted and his path blocked.
Reinforcements did not arrive,
and the dead and wounded among his soldiers were piled high.
Yet, at a single call of encouragement from Líng,
every soldier rose up;
they personally shed tears
and, wiping away blood and swallowing their sobs,
they once more raised their empty fists
to face naked blades,
turning toward the north to vie for a chance to die fighting the enemy.
Before Líng fell,
a messenger came with a report,
and the high officials and nobles of Hàn
all raised their cups to toast the Emperor’s longevity.
A few days later,
when the report of Líng's defeat was heard,
His Majesty found no flavor in his food
and took no pleasure in holding court.
The high ministers were worried and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
I privately did not consider my own lowliness,
and seeing His Majesty so grieved and sorrowful,
I truly wished to offer my sincere and simple view.
I believed that Lǐ Líng always shared hardships and meager rations with his men
and was able to gain their ultimate sacrifice;
even the famous generals of old
could not surpass him.
Although he was trapped and defeated,
observing his intentions,
it seemed he wished to find a proper opportunity to repay his debt to Hàn.
The matter was already beyond help,
but the damage he had inflicted on the enemy
was merit enough to be made known to the world.
I harbored a desire to state this,
but had no way to do so.
It happened that I was summoned and questioned,
and so I followed this line of reasoning to speak of Líng's merit,
wishing to broaden His Majesty's mind
and stop the words of those who held a grudge.
I was unable to make myself fully clear,
and the enlightened Lord did not understand.
He thought I was disparaging Èrshī
and lobbying on behalf of Lǐ Líng;
consequently, I was handed over to the law officials.
My sincere loyalty
could never be fully explained.
Thus, on the charge of deceiving the Emperor,
I finally submitted to the verdict of the officials.
My family was poor,
and my wealth was not enough to redeem myself.
Of my friends and associates, none saved me;
and those close to the Emperor
did not speak a single word on my behalf.
My body is not made of wood or stone,
yet alone I was made the peer of law officials,
confined deep within the prison walls.
To whom could I plead my case?
This is what you, Shàoqīng, personally witnessed.
Was my conduct not truly thus?
Lǐ Líng surrendered alive
and ruined his family's reputation;
and I was then subjected to the silkworm chamber,
becoming a double laughingstock to the world.
How tragic!
How tragic!
These matters are not easily explained to common people.
My ancestors
did not have the merit of split tallies or red-lettered oaths.
Literati, historians, astrologers, and calendar-makers
are close to the status of diviners and priests,
originally kept by the sovereign for amusement,
raised like singers and entertainers,
and held in light regard by common society.
If I were to fall under the law and be executed,
it would be like losing one hair from nine oxen—
how would it differ from the death of a mole cricket or an ant?
Moreover, the world would not credit me with being one who died for a principle,
but would only think that my wisdom was exhausted and my crime extreme,
that I could not save myself,
and thus finally went to my death.
Why is this?
It is because of the position I have established for myself.
A person truly has only one death;
it may be heavier than Mount Tài Shān,
or lighter than a swan's feather,
depending on the purpose for which it is used.
Most supreme is not to bring shame to one's ancestors;
next is not to bring shame to one's person;
next is not to bring shame to one's countenance or expression;
next is not to bring shame to one's speech;
next is to submit one's body to humiliation;
next is to change one's clothes in humiliation;
next is to be bound with wooden stocks and ropes and be flogged in humiliation;
next is to have one's hair shaved and wear iron collars in humiliation;
next is to have one's flesh mutilated and limbs severed in humiliation;
and the lowest is the punishment of castration,
the ultimate extreme.
The *Chuán* says:
"Punishments do not reach the Dàfū."
This says that a scholar's integrity must be encouraged.
When a fierce tiger is in the deep mountains,
all beasts tremble in fear;
but when it is in a cage or pitfall,
it wags its tail to beg for food,
because it has gradually been broken by power and constraint.
Thus, there are those who draw a circle on the ground for a prison,
yet whose dignity makes it impossible to enter;
or carve wood for an official,
yet whose pride makes it impossible to face him;
for they have made their resolve while still pure.
Now with hands and feet crossed,
bound by wood and rope,
with flesh exposed,
receiving the whip and rod,
and confined within circular walls.
At such a time,
seeing a prison guard, one strikes the ground with one's head;
looking at a jailer, one gasps in terror.
Why?
Because of the accumulation of power and constraint.
Having reached this point,
to say one is not humiliated
is merely what is called "brazen-facedness";
how could it be worthy of respect?
Moreover, Xībó,
an Earl,
was imprisoned in Yǒu Lǐ;
Lǐ Sī,
a Chancellor,
underwent all Five Punishments;
Huáiyīn,
a King,
was shackled at Chén;
Péng Yuè and Zhāng Áo,
who faced south and called themselves "Lonely One,"
were bound in prison to pay for their crimes;
the Marquis of Jiàng, who executed the Lǚ clan,
whose power surpassed the Five Hegemons,
was imprisoned in the Qǐng Shì;
Wèiqí,
a Great General,
wore the ochre robes of a convict
and was bound in the three wooden stocks;
Jì Bù became the shaven-headed slave of Zhū Jiā;
Guàn Fū suffered humiliation in the Jū Shì.
These men all reached the rank of Kings, Marquises, Generals, and Chancellors,
and their reputations were known in neighboring states,
yet when their crimes reached the point where the net of law was cast over them,
they could not decide to end their own lives.
Being in the midst of dust and dirt,
the principle is the same in ancient and modern times;
where is their lack of humiliation?
Judging by this,
courage and cowardice
are matters of circumstance;
strength and weakness
are matters of form.
It is clear!
Why should it be surprising?
If a person cannot resolve to take their own life early on when outside the reach of the law,
and gradually declines,
until they are between the whip and the rod,
then wishes to assert their integrity,
is this not too late?
The reason the ancients were careful about inflicting punishment on Dàfū
was probably for this reason.
It is human nature to cherish life and hate death,
to think of parents,
and look after wife and children.
But for those who are stirred by righteousness and principle, it is not so;
they have things they cannot help but do.
Now I am unfortunate;
I lost my parents early,
and have no brothers or close kin;
I stand alone and solitary.
Shǎoqīng, how do you see my relationship with my wife and children?
Furthermore, the brave do not necessarily die for a principle,
and the cowardly admire righteousness;
in what place would they not strive?
Although I am cowardly and weak and wish to survive for a while,
I also somewhat understand the distinction between staying and leaving.
Why would I descend to the humiliation of being bound in ropes?
Even slaves and maidservants
can resolve to end their own lives;
how much more so for someone in my unavoidable situation?
The reason I have endured and lived on,
confined in this filth without refusing,
is that I regret that there is something in my heart I have not fully expressed,
and I am pained that if I died in obscurity,
my literary brilliance would not be manifested to later generations.
In ancient times, those who were wealthy and noble yet whose names vanished
are beyond count;
only the extraordinary and exceptional are praised.
When King Wén was imprisoned, he expanded the *Zhōu Yì*;
when Zhòngní was in distress, he composed the *Chūn Qiū*;
when Qū Yuán was exiled,
he composed the *Lí Sāo*;
when Zuǒ Qiū lost his sight,
he had the *Guó Yǔ*;
when Sūn Zǐ had his kneecaps removed,
the *Bīng Fǎ* was set forth;
when Bùwéi was banished to Shǔ,
the *Lǚ Lǎn* was passed down to the world;
when Hán Fēi was imprisoned in Qín,
he wrote *Shuì Nán* and *Gū Fèn*;
the three hundred poems of the *Shī*
were mostly written by sages and worthies to vent their indignation.
These men all had pent-up frustrations in their hearts
and could not communicate their Way,
so they recounted past events
and thought of those to come.
As for Zuǒ Qiū having no eyes
and Sūn Zǐ having severed feet,
they were ultimately of no use to the world,
so they retired to discuss books and writings
to vent their indignation,
hoping to leave behind empty words to reveal themselves.
I have ventured to be presumptuous,
recently entrusting myself to useless words.
I have gathered the lost and scattered old traditions of the world,
briefly examined their deeds,
synthesized their beginnings and ends,
and investigated the principles of their success and failure, rise and fall.
Starting from Xuānyuán
down to the present day,
I have made ten Tables,
twelve Basic Annals,
eight chapters of Treatises,
thirty Hereditary Houses,
and seventy Biographies,
totaling one hundred and thirty chapters.
I also wish to examine the boundary between heaven and man,
understand the transformations of past and present,
and establish a school of my own.
The draft was not yet finished
when I met with this disaster.
Regretting that it was not complete,
I submitted to the ultimate punishment without a look of resentment.
Truly, if I can finish this book and hide it in the famous mountains,
to be passed to the right person
and circulate in the great cities,
then I shall have repaid the debt of my previous humiliation;
even if I were to be executed ten thousand times,
how could I have any regrets?
However, this can be told to the wise,
but is difficult to speak of to common people.
Moreover, a degraded position is not easy to dwell in;
those in the lower reaches of society suffer much slander and criticism.
I encountered this calamity because of my words,
and I have been laughed at by my village and kin,
thereby defiling my ancestors.
What face do I have to again visit the graves of my parents?
Even after a hundred generations,
the stain will only become more severe!
For this reason, my intestines turn nine times in a single day.
At home, I am dazed as if I have lost something;
when I go out, I do not know where I am going.
Whenever I think of this shame,
sweat never fails to break out on my back and soak my clothes.
Having become merely a servant of the inner chambers,
how could I ever withdraw myself to hide deep in mountain caves?
Therefore, for the time being, I drift with the common customs,
rising and falling with the times,
so as to give vent to my madness and confusion.
Now, Shǎoqīng, you instruct me to recommend the worthy and promote scholars;
is this not quite contradictory to my private feelings?
Even if I wished to polish myself now,
using elegant words to adorn my appearance,
it would be of no use;
the common people would not believe me,
and it would only serve to invite further disgrace.
In short, it is only on the day of death
that right and wrong are finally settled.
This letter cannot fully express my thoughts;
I have briefly laid out my crude and stubborn views.
Respectfully, I bow twice.
Yùn is of decayed talent and defiled conduct;
my substance and refinement have achieved nothing.
Fortunately relying on the legacy of my ancestors,
I was able to serve in the Sùwèi.
Encountering the changes of the times,
I obtained rank and title,
but in the end, I was not equal to the responsibility,
and I finally met with calamity.
You, sir, pitied my ignorance
and bestowed a letter to instruct and correct my shortcomings,
with great kindness and sincerity.
However, I secretly regret that you did not deeply consider the whole matter from beginning to end,
but instead blindly followed the common praise and blame.
If I speak of my lowly and foolish heart,
it might seem like I am being contrary or glossing over my faults;
yet if I remain silent and keep to myself,
I fear I would violate the principle of the Kǒng clan that each should speak his mind.
Therefore, I dare to briefly state my foolish views,
and I only hope that you, a gentleman, will examine them!
When the family of Yáng was at its height,
ten people rode in carriages with red wheels;
their positions were among the Lièqīng,
and their titles were those of Tōnghóu.
They led the secondary officials
and participated in the affairs of state.
Yet I was unable to make any clear contribution at that time
to proclaim virtuous influence.
Nor could I work together with my colleagues
to assist the imperial court in its oversights.
I have long borne the blame for occupying a position without merit.
Cherishing my salary and coveting power,
I could not withdraw myself,
and consequently encountered changes and accidents.
I was unexpectedly accused by words,
confined in the Běiquè,
while my wife and children filled the prison.
At that time,
I felt that even being exterminated would not suffice to answer for my failings;
how then could I keep my head intact
and again attend to the graves of my ancestors?
I humbly reflect that the grace of the Shèngzhǔ
is beyond measure.
The gentleman wanders in the Way,
rejoicing and forgetting his sorrows;
the small man preserves his life,
taking pleasure and forgetting his crimes.
I secretly think that my transgressions are already great,
and my conduct is already flawed;
I shall remain a farmer until the end of my days.
Therefore, I lead my wife and children
to work hard at farming and mulberry cultivation,
watering the garden and managing the estate
to provide for the taxes.
I did not expect that this would again be used as a subject for mockery and criticism.
Those things that human emotions cannot stop,
the Sages did not forbid.
Thus, even for the most honorable and close relationship of a ruler or father,
in seeing them to their end,
there is a time when the mourning concludes.
It has been three years
since I committed my crime.
Farm life is hard work;
during the festivals of Fú and Là,
we boil mutton and roast lamb,
and I console myself with a measure of wine.
My family is originally from Qín,
and we can sing the songs of Qín.
My wife is a woman of Zhào,
and she is naturally skilled at playing the qín.
We have several slaves who are singers.
After drinking, when my ears are warm,
I look up to heaven, strike a ceramic jar, and cry out "wu-wu."
The song says:
"I farm that Nánshān,
but the weeds are overgrown and untended;
I planted a qǐng of beans,
but they fell and became mere stalks."
Life is but for seeking pleasure;
when will one ever attain wealth and honor?
On that day,
I brush off my clothes in joy,
wave my sleeves up and down,
and stamp my feet in dance.
Truly, it is unrestrained and without measure,
and I knew not that it was forbidden.
Yùn fortunately has surplus wealth,
so I buy low and sell high,
seeking a profit of ten percent.
This is the business of common traders,
a place of filth and disgrace,
yet Yùn performs it in person.
A man in the lower reaches of society
is where all slanders converge;
I tremble without being cold.
Even those who have long known me
still follow the wind and fall away;
what praise could there be left for me?
Did Master Dǒng not say?
"Those who clearly seek benevolence and righteousness,
always fearing they cannot transform the people,
are those with the mind of Qīngdàfū;
those who clearly seek wealth and profit,
always fearing poverty and want,
are those engaged in the affairs of Shùrén."
Therefore, those whose ways are different do not plan together.
Now, how can you still use the standards of Qīngdàfū to criticize me?
Xīhé is the land of Wèi,
where Wén Hóu arose;
it retains the legacy of Duàngān Mù and Tián Zǐfāng.
All possess an awe-inspiring integrity
and know the distinction between taking office and retiring.
Recently, you left your old land
and arrived in Āndìng.
Between the mountains and valleys of Āndìng,
in the old territory of the Kūnyí,
the youth are greedy and base.
Could it be that the local customs change a person?
Only now do I see your true intent.
You are in the prime of the Great Hàn;
I hope you will strive forward
and speak no more of this.
Years and months do not stay;
the seasons flow like water.
The age of fifty
has suddenly arrived.
You, Gōng, have just reached fifty;
Róng has passed it by two.
My acquaintances within the four seas
have nearly all withered away;
only Shèng Xiàozhāng of Huìjī still remains.
He is hard-pressed by the Sūn family;
his wife and children are gone,
and he stands alone,
isolated, endangered, and sorrowful.
If sorrow could truly harm a person,
then this man would not live long!
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn says:
"When among the feudal lords some were destroyed,
and Huán Gōng could not save them,
then Huán Gōng felt it as a shame."
Now Shèng Xiàozhāng is truly a hero among men;
the scholars of the world
rely on him to spread their fame,
yet he himself cannot escape imprisonment,
and his life is at risk from dawn to dusk.
My ancestor should no longer have discussed beneficial and harmful friends,
which was why Zhū Mù broke off his friendships.
If you could truly dispatch a single messenger
and send a brief letter,
then Shèng Xiàozhāng could be brought here,
and the way of friendship could be magnified.
Nowadays, young people
enjoy slandering their predecessors,
and some even go so far as to ridicule and criticize Xiào Zhāng.
Xiào Zhāng was originally a man of great fame throughout the world,
whom the people of the Jiǔmù
all praised and admired.
When the Lord of Yān purchased the bones of a fine steed,
it was not because he wanted to ride them for many miles,
but rather to use them to attract legendary horses.
Only you, My Lord, have restored the Hàn imperial house;
when the ancestral shrines were about to be extinguished,
you were able to set them right again.
The method for setting them right
truly requires obtaining worthy men.
Pearls and jade have no legs yet arrive by themselves
because people love them;
how much more so for worthy men who have feet?
Zhāo Wáng built a terrace to honor Guō Wěi;
although Wěi had small talent, he encountered great opportunity
and ultimately was able to reveal the sincere heart of an enlightened ruler.
Consequently, Yuè Yì came from Wèi,
Jù Xīn came from Zhào,
and Zōu Yǎn came from Qí.
If Guō Wěi had been hung upside down and the King did not release him,
or had he faced disaster and the King did not save him,
then scholars would also have soared high and withdrawn far away,
and none would have turned their heads toward the road to Yān.
Everything I have cited
is already known to you,
yet the reason I speak of it again
is that I wish for you to uphold and strengthen this principle.
I conclude this memorial here, unable to express everything.
I have heard that the wise make plans according to the times,
while the foolish act in opposition to reason.
I have often privately grieved for Tàishū of Jīngchéng, who, due to insatiability and lack of worthy advisors,
ended up abandoning himself in Zhèng.
Bótōng, you governed the commandery with your name and reputation
and held the merit of assisting the founding of the mandate;
you oversaw the people and attended to your duties,
cherishing the granaries and treasuries.
Meanwhile, Fú held the responsibility of military campaigns,
wishing to use temporary authority to save a crisis;
both of you were acting for the state.
Even if you suspected that Fú was slandering you,
why did you not go to the palace to explain yourself
instead of making a plan that leads to the extermination of your clan?
The Imperial Court's treatment of you, Bótōng,
has been generous indeed.
You were entrusted with a major commandery
and invested with military power;
in matters of state, you were relied upon as a pillar of support,
and in affection, you were treated with the intimacy of a son or grandson.
Even an ordinary man or a maidservant can sacrifice their life for a single meal;
how can someone who wears three ribbons of office
and governs a great region
disregard kindness and righteousness
and harbor thoughts of rebellion?
Bótōng, when you speak with officials and people,
with what face will you look at them?
When walking, bowing, or rising,
what kind of appearance will you maintain?
When sitting or lying down and thinking of this,
what state will your heart be in?
When you take up a mirror and look at your reflection,
how will you regard your own features?
In your actions and attempts to build merit,
how can you still be considered a human being?
What a pity!
To abandon a fine and beautiful reputation,
to hatch a rebellious plot like an owl,
to cast away the auspicious fortune meant for your descendants,
and to invite the heavy disaster of ruin and defeat.
You speak loftily of the Way of Yáo and Shùn
but cannot restrain a nature like Jié and Zhòu.
To be the laughingstock of the world while alive
and to become a foolish ghost after death—
is this not tragic?
Bótōng, you and Gěng Xiàyóu both rose to assist the mandate
and both received the state's grace.
Xiàyóu is modest and yielding,
often speaking with humility,
but you, Bótōng, boast of yourself,
believing your merit to be the highest in the world.
In the past, there was a pig in Liáodōng
that gave birth to a white-headed piglet.
Thinking it extraordinary, the owner went to present it.
When he reached Hédōng,
he saw that all the pigs there were white,
so he returned home feeling ashamed.
If your merit were discussed at the Imperial Court,
it would be like that pig of Liáodōng.
Now you are so foolish and delusional
as to compare yourself to the Liù Guó.
In the time of the Liù Guó,
each power was flourishing;
their territories spanned thousands of lǐ,
and their armies numbered nearly a million.
Thus, they could hold their lands and contend with one another
for many years.
Today, how vast is the world,
and how many cities are in the various commanderies?
Why would you use the tiny Yúyáng to hold a grudge against the Son of Heaven?
This is like a person on the riverbank
taking a handful of dirt to block Mèngjīn;
it only serves to show a lack of self-awareness.
Just as the world has been settled
and everyone within the four seas desires peace,
scholars, whether worthy or not,
all wish to establish their names in the world.
Yet you alone, Bótōng, have been struck by a fit of madness,
casting yourself away during this flourishing time.
Internally, you listen to the misguided plans of a favored wife;
externally, you believe the flattering words of slandering evildoers.
You will forever be a bad example for all the lords
and a perpetual warning to meritorious ministers.
Is this not a grave mistake?
He who settles the world harbors no private grudges;
do not doubt yourself because of past events.
I hope you will consider your elderly mother and younger brother.
In all your actions, do not do what causes pain to those close to you
and brings joy to your enemies.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month,
Hóng says:
Previously, when the rebels were first defeated,
my spirits were high and my thoughts extravagant;
my description of matters was somewhat beyond the truth.
I received your letter from the twentieth day of the ninth month;
I laughed with joy while reading it
and never tired of appreciating it.
I also wanted to have Chén Lín write a reply.
Chén Lín has been busy lately
and could not do it.
Thinking I would like to provide joy from afar,
I have exhausted my own elderly thoughts.
There is so much to say that I cannot address everything;
I have roughly raised the main points
to serve as a subject for conversation.
The terrain of Hànzhōng
is truly dangerous and solid;
even the Sìyuè and Sāntú
cannot compare to it.
They have tens of thousands of elite armored troops
looking down from heights and guarding the strategic passes.
If one man wields a halberd,
ten thousand men cannot advance.
Yet when our army passed through,
it was like a startled whale tearing through a fine net
or a charging rhinoceros crashing through thin Lǔ silk;
even these are not enough to illustrate the ease of it.
Although it is said that the army of a true King
goes on expeditions without needing to fight,
those who were unrighteous yet strong
were common among the ancients.
Therefore, in the age of Táng and Yú,
the barbarians troubled the Xià;
even in the flourishing time of Zhōu Xuān,
there were great states as enemies.
The Shī and Shū lament and record these events,
speaking of their difficulty.
These all occurred because those enemies relied on natural obstacles and distance.
Therefore, observing this terrain,
I thought that if someone of average talent were to hold it,
it would be almost impossible to take it quickly.
Your letter set forth the crimes of their demonic delusions
and described the broad and magnanimous virtue of the King's army.
How could this not be true!
This is why Xià and Yīn were lost,
and why Miáo and Hù were destroyed;
it is why we were victorious
and why they were defeated.
Otherwise,
how could Shāng and Zhōu have been unmatched?
In the past, the Guǐfāng were ignorant and dim,
Chónghǔ was slanderous and fierce,
and Yīn Xīn was tyrannical;
these three were of the lowest category.
Yet Gāozōng had a three-year campaign,
Wén Wáng had an army that withdrew for cultivation,
and at Méngjīn there was a twice-launched military service;
only after these were the Róng killed and the Yīn defeated,
achieving such military success.
How could there be a movement swift as falling stars and converging shadows,
a seizure like a whirlwind and a strike like thunder,
a long drive across mountains and rivers,
arriving in the morning and gaining victory by evening,
like what has happened now!
Looking at it from this perspective,
they certainly did not even reach the level of the most ignorant,
so the defense of those with mediocre talent
is clearly not so.
If even those with mediocre talent are not like that,
yet your letter suggests that because their evils were full to the brim,
even if there were Sūn, Tián, Mò, and Lí,
they still could not be saved,
I privately have my doubts about this.
Why is this?
In the warfare of old,
even if an enemy state was in chaos,
if there were still worthy men,
then it would not be attacked.
Therefore, as long as the Sān Rén had not left,
Wǔ Wáng withdrew his army;
while Gōng Qí was in Yú,
Jìn did not deploy its troops;
as long as Jì Liáng was still present,
the powerful Chǔ had its schemes thwarted.
But when the various worthy men fled or were dismissed,
the three states became ruins.
This clearly shows that if a state is without the Way but possesses worthy men,
it can still be saved.
Furthermore, regarding the defense of Mò Zǐ,
he used his belt as a wall,
making it too high to scale;
he broke chopsticks to use as weapons,
making them too strong to penetrate.
If one holds Yángpíng,
occupies Shímén,
deploys the Bā Zhèn formation,
and employs the stratagem of the charging bulls,
how could they allow things to crumble like earth or rot like fish!
Suppose defense did not involve skill or clumsiness,
and everything could be scaled and seized,
then Gōngshū would have already overcome the walls of Sòng,
and Yuè Yì would have already captured Jímò.
Why then would the arts of Mò Dí be praised?
Why would the wisdom of Tián Dān be valued?
I, an old man, am not clever,
and have never heard of such a thing.
I have heard that those passing through Gāotáng
imitate the singing of Wáng Bào;
those traveling along the Suī and Huàn Rivers
learn the patterns of refined embroidery.
Since I entered Yì Bù,
I have looked up to the legacy of Sīmǎ, Yáng, and Wáng,
and possessing the elegant aspirations of Zi Shèng,
I have applied myself somewhat to literary composition,
which is different from in the past.
I find it strange that you belittle the Qiū of your own home
and call me a ghostwriter;
what kind of talk is this?
A green steed droops its ears in the forest and fields,
and a wild goose or sparrow folds its wings in a muddy pond;
those who treat them with contempt certainly take them for common birds in a garden
or inferior horses in an outer stable.
But once it braces its powerful muscles
and beats its strong wings,
soaring through the clear air
and gazing over a thousand lǐ,
how could it be said that it borrowed feathers from the Chénfēng bird
or borrowed legs from the Liùbó beast!
I fear you still do not believe my words
and will surely laugh heartily.
Hóng states.
Since our separation and estrangement,
it has been three years until now,
and not a single day has passed that I have forgotten our former friendship.
It is like the bond of marriage;
the affection and kindness are already deep,
while the resentment of discord
is still shallow in comparison.
I cherish this heart;
could you perhaps feel the same!
Whenever I observe the reasons for changes in course throughout history,
arising from slights and insults,
or stemming from flaws and grievances,
hearts become indignant and intentions precarious,
leading to great transformations.
Like Hán Xìn's heartbreak over losing Chǔ,
Péng Chǒng's accumulated resentment over being treated no differently,
Lú Wǎn's suspicion and fear because of an existing rift,
or Yīng Bù's anxiety and pressure when his plot was leaked—
these are the causes of such events.
I and the General share an affection like that of flesh and blood;
I ceded and granted the area south of the river,
which does not belong to the original province;
how could this be like the resentment of Huáiyīn over being discarded?
I restrained Liú Fù
and treated you with increasing generosity;
I would rather set aside the overt memorial of Zhū Fú.
I did not conceal Zhāng Shèng's deceitful betrayal,
nor was there any secret fabrication like the report of Bì Hè;
it was certainly not a grievance like that of the King of Yàn or Huáinán.
Yet you could bear to sever the royal command
and openly abandon our great friendship;
this was truly brought about by the fabrications of sycophants.
Specious words
are always pleasing to the ear;
by shaping appearances and creating images,
they easily change one's perspective.
Presenting one with disasters and hardships,
and provoking one with shame and insults,
a great man's heroic heart
could not help but be stirred with indignation.
Formerly, when Sū Qín persuaded Hán
by shaming them for being a cow's backside,
the King of Hán gripped his sword and flushed with anger;
even though his troops were broken and his lands partitioned,
he still felt no regret;
such is human nature.
You, my kind lord, are in the prime of life and full of vigor,
and influenced by those you trust and favor;
already fearing that disaster was arriving,
and also harboring resentment,
you could no longer consider my heart from a distance
or ponder the current state of affairs nearby,
so you harbored a decisive plan based on feeling slighted
and held a settled resolution to turn away.
In addition, Liú Bèi incited and fanned the flames,
so matters became tangled and grievances linked,
and you proceeded with it.
I imagine that in your original heart,
you did not desire this.
I, with my meager virtue,
hold a high position and heavy responsibilities,
fortunately receiving the destiny of the dynasty's coming prosperity
to pacify the world,
to embrace and gather different peoples,
happily achieving complete success
and long enjoying its blessings.
But our kinship through marriage has been severed while we sat by,
and a rift has grown in our strong alliance;
I always fear that many within the four seas will blame me,
thinking that I, an old man, harbor malicious intentions
and possess the secret trickery of Zhèng Wǔ taking over the Hú,
thereby causing you, my kind lord, to suddenly sever yourself from me.
Because of this, I am filled with indignation,
harboring shame and tossing and turning;
I often think of discarding these small matters
to once again renew our former friendship,
so that both our clans may prosper together
and pass on blessings to our descendants,
to demonstrate the effect of my long-standing inner sincerity.
I have cherished this in my heart for several years,
but have not been able to express my thoughts.
In the campaign of Chìbì,
we encountered a plague,
so I burned the ships and returned on my own
to avoid that ill-fated place;
it was not something the navy of Zhōu Yú could suppress or defeat.
In the defense of Jiānglíng,
supplies were exhausted and grain was gone,
so there was no longer anything to hold onto;
we moved the people and withdrew the army;
again, it was not something Yú could have defeated.
The land of Jīng was originally not my own portion;
I gave it all to you,
hoping to take the rest of the empire;
it was not an encroachment upon your own person,
nor was it any loss through partitioning.
Considering these changes,
they do not harm me;
what mindset leads you to persist in this,
and not return to us?
Gāo Dì established a title to invite Tián Héng,
and Guāng Wǔ pointed to the river and swore an oath to Zhū Wěi;
your burdens of guilt,
how can they compare to those two men?
Therefore, with the utmost sincerity,
I wish to hear your virtuous response.
In past years in Qiáo,
newly built ships
were sufficient for self-transport,
reaching as far as Jiǔjiāng.
The purpose was simply to observe the topography of Lake Hú and Lake Chǎo
and to settle the people along the river banks;
there was no plan for deep invasion or battle.
I fear that the councilors may claim this as a great honor for themselves,
asserting that their strategies were successful
and that there will be no more trouble from the west forever.
Because of this,
they are unwilling to change their minds.
However, the considerations of the wise
are for things before they take shape;
the plans of the accomplished
are for things before they manifest.
Thus, Zǐxū knew that Gūsū would harbor elks,
and Fǔ Guǒ recognized that Zhì Bó would be captured by Zhào.
Mù Shēng excused himself due to illness
to escape the troubles in Chǔ;
Zōu Yáng traveled north
and did not share in the disaster of Wú.
Are these four men
truly sages?
They were simply deeply thoughtful and adaptable,
knowing the manifest through the subtle.
With your intelligence,
observing my methods,
measuring your own position,
and considering the lands,
is it because your power and strength are lacking
and you cannot go far,
that you carve out a piece of Jiāngbiǎo
just to live in peace?
That is certainly not the case!
If you rely on naval battles
and block the key points along the river,
wishing to prevent the royal army from ever crossing,
that is also not necessarily certain.
Naval battles span a thousand lǐ,
and the circumstances are infinitely varied.
Yuè divided into three armies,
and Wú could not resist them;
Hàn crossed secretly at Xiàyáng,
and Wèi Bào did not expect it.
Though the river is wide,
its length makes it hard to defend.
In all things there is what is appropriate,
and I cannot speak of everything.
I intend to restore old friendships and display our power,
but I have no intention of threatening a major enemy again.
Yet I have a fear,
fearing that this letter will be of no benefit.
Why is this?
Previously, when the army approached, I withdrew on my own;
today, from a distance, I offer comfort and reception.
If my words are humble and my intentions narrow,
you might think my strength is exhausted,
which would only increase your arrogance
and fail to move you.
One should just clearly follow the examples of the past
and plan for oneself.
Long ago, Huáinán trusted Zuǒ Wú's plan;
Wěi Xiāo of Hàn accepted Wáng Yuán's words;
Péng Chǒng followed his close officials' schemes.
These three did not wake up
and finally became the laughingstock of the world.
The King of Liáng did not accept Guì Shèng's advice;
Dòu Róng expelled Zhāng Xuán.
These two worthies realized the truth,
and fortune followed them.
I wish you would pay a little attention to this.
If you can internally seize Zǐbù
and externally attack Liú Bèi
to show your sincerity
and restore our former friendship,
then the responsibility of Jiāngbiǎo
will be permanently entrusted to you,
and high positions and heavy titles
will be clearly visible.
Above, let the Sagely Court have no labor of looking east;
below, let the common people have the blessing of safety.
You enjoy the honor,
and I receive the benefit—
would that not be pleasant!
If you neglect sincerity to rely on luck,
treating those two men with kindness
and not bearing to punish them—
this is the so-called "benevolence of a small man,"
the thief of great benevolence.
A man of great character
would not do this.
If you pity Zǐbù
and wish for both to survive,
I can also set aside my heart's resentment,
follow your feelings,
and work with him again
to seek future goodness.
But capturing Liú Bèi alone
would be sufficient as proof.
I have laid out these two options;
carefully choose one.
I hear from the generals in Jīng and Yáng
that they have captured defectors,
who all say Jiāozhōu has been seized by you,
that Yùzhāng resists orders
and does not obey you,
and that epidemics and droughts occur together,
with soldiers and people diminishing.
Each general asks to advance the army,
saying such things.
I heard these words
but did not feel joy.
However, the road is far
and defectors are hard to trust.
Taking pleasure in others' calamities
is not what a gentleman does.
Moreover, the people belong to the state.
I cherish them
and desire to promote harmony.
I hope your brilliant virtue
will come to light,
and peace will be settled without labor,
which is more valuable to me.
Therefore, I hold back the troops
and send this letter to express my intent.
In ancient times, when armies met,
envoys were among them.
I wish for you, kind sir, and me to be open-minded and change our intentions,
to respond to the poet's sigh of "mending the royal robes" in the Shī Jīng and
heed the meaning of "leading back" in the Zhōu Yì.
Wash your scales in the clear stream,
fly your wings in the heavenly path.
A good time is now;
just exert yourself.
May 18th.
Pī says:
Jìzhòng, I hope you are well.
Although the paths are narrow
and my official duties are limited,
my feelings of longing
are truly unbearable.
You govern a remote place,
and letters are few,
which only increases my distress.
Whenever I think of our past outings in Nánpí,
they are truly unforgettable.
Back then, we subtly contemplated the Six Classics
and wandered through the Hundred Schools.
We played Tánqí for leisure
and ended with Liùbó.
High conversation delighted our hearts,
and the mournful zither was pleasant to our ears.
Galloping in the Northern Field,
dining as guests in the Southern Guesthouse,
floating sweet melons in the clear spring,
and submerging red plums in the cold water.
After the bright sun had hidden,
followed by the bright moon,
we rode together in the same carriage
to wander in the Rear Garden.
The wheels moved slowly,
the attendants were silent.
A cool breeze rose at night,
and the mournful reed-pipe sighed softly.
As joy departed, sorrow arrived,
and my heart was filled with melancholy.
I looked back and said,
"This joy is hard to maintain forever."
Your companions
all thought so too.
Now we are indeed separated,
each in a different place.
Yuányú has passed away long ago
and turned into another thing.
Every time the thought occurs,
when can I express it!
Now is the time of the Ruíbīn month;
the scenic breeze fans all things.
The weather is warm and mild,
and various fruits are abundant.
I occasionally ride out to wander,
following the bend of the river to the north.
Attendants sound the reed-pipes to open the way,
and men of letters take seats in the trailing carriages.
The season is the same, but the time is different;
things are the same, but people have changed.
How great is my toil!
Now I am sending a rider to Yè,
so I have him go out of his way to visit you.
Take care of yourself as you go.
Pī says.
February 3rd,
Pī says:
Time passes easily;
since we parted, nearly four years have gone by.
Not seeing each other for three years,
the "Dōng Shān" poem already sighs at the distance;
how much more so when it has exceeded that!
How can such longing be endured?
Although letters go back and forth,
they are not enough to unravel the weary knots of the heart.
In former years there was a plague,
and many relatives and old friends suffered its disaster.
Xú, Chén, Yìng, and Liú
all passed away at once—
can such pain be put into words?
In former days when we traveled and lived together,
when moving, our carriages were connected;
when resting, our mats were joined.
When did we ever lose sight of each other for even a moment?
Whenever the wine cups circulated
and the strings and flutes played together,
flushed with wine and warm in the ears,
we would look up and compose poetry.
At that time,
we were suddenly unaware of our own joy.
We thought a hundred years were our lot
and that we could long protect one another.
Who would have thought that within a few years
they would be scattered and almost all gone?
To speak of it breaks the heart!
Recently I compiled their surviving writings
into a single collection.
Looking at their names,
they are already on the registry of ghosts.
Recalling our former travels,
they are still before my heart and eyes;
but these gentlemen
have turned into dust and soil.
What more can be said?
Looking at literary men of past and present,
they generally do not guard their minor conduct,
and few can establish themselves through reputation and integrity.
But Wěicháng alone embraced both literary talent and inner substance;
tranquil and with few desires,
he possessed the ambition of Jī Shān.
He could be called a refined and cultivated gentleman.
He wrote over twenty chapters of the Zhōng Lùn,
establishing his own school of thought.
Its language and meaning are elegant and classical,
sufficient to be passed to posterity;
this man has become immortal.
Déliǎn often had the brilliant intention of writing;
his talent and learning were sufficient to write books.
That his fine ambitions were not fulfilled
is truly a cause for grief and regret.
Lately, I have looked through the writings of these gentlemen;
facing them, I wipe away tears.
Grieving for those who have passed,
I also think of myself.
Kǒngzhāng’s memorials and petitions are exceptionally vigorous,
though slightly over-elaborate.
Gōnggàn has a lofty spirit,
but it is not yet fully powerful;
among his best five-character poems,
they are incomparably superior to his contemporaries.
Yuányú’s letters and records are elegant,
quite enough to be enjoyed.
Zhòngxuān was naturally gifted at rhapsodies;
regrettably his style was weak
and not enough to elevate his writing.
As for what he was good at,
the ancients could not far surpass him.
In the past, Bó Yá broke his strings upon the death of Zhōng Qī,
and Zhòngní overturned the minced meat upon the death of Zǐlù,
grieving that a soulmate is hard to find
and mourning that no disciple could reach his level.
These gentlemen just did not reach the level of the ancients,
but they were the luminaries of their time.
Of those living now,
none can catch up to them.
The younger generation is to be held in awe,
and those who follow cannot be underestimated;
but I fear you and I will not live to see them.
My years are already advancing,
and my thoughts are ten thousand fold.
Sometimes I have anxieties
to the point of not sleeping all night.
When will my spirits ever be like former days again?
I have already become an old man,
only my hair is not yet white.
Guāngwǔ said that at age thirty-plus,
he had been among the troops for ten years,
and what he experienced was not just one thing.
My virtue does not reach his,
but my age is now equal to his.
With the nature of a dog or sheep,
I wear the patterns of a tiger or leopard.
Without the brightness of the stars,
I borrow the light of the sun and moon.
Every move is watched by all;
when will it ever be easy?
I fear I will never again be able to wander as in the old days.
One should truly work hard while young and strong;
once the years pass,
how can they be pulled back?
The ancients thought of wandering at night with a lit candle;
truly there was a reason for that.
How have you been amusing yourself lately?
Have you written anything more?
Looking east, I am heavy-hearted;
I write this letter to express my heart.
Pī says.
Pī says:
Fine jade is compared to the virtue of a gentleman,
and the Guī and Zhāng jades are praised by poets.
The Chuíjì jade of Jìn,
the Yúfán jade of Lǔ,
the Jiélǜ jade of Sòng,
and the raw jade of Hé from Chǔ
were valued at over ten thousand gold pieces.
Their worth exceeded that of a capital city;
they were praised in the past
and their fame will flow into the future.
Thus when the Chuíjì jade left Jìn,
the states of Yú and Guó were both captured.
When the Jade of Hé entered Qín,
Xiāngrú maintained his integrity.
I have privately seen in books on jade that fine jade is described as
white as cut fat,
black like pure lacquer,
red like a cockscomb,
and yellow like steamed chestnuts.
I have heard these words,
but I have not seen such forms.
Although my virtue is not that of a gentleman
and my righteousness not that of a poet,
the "high mountains and great road"
are what I privately admire.
Yet the four treasures are remote and distant;
in the Qín and Hàn dynasties, I have not heard of anything comparable.
Searching for them for years,
I have not encountered the real ones.
My private wish was not fulfilled,
and my hunger and thirst were not satisfied.
Recently Zōng Huìshū of Nányáng said you once had a beautiful jade ring.
Hearing this, I was surprised and delighted,
laughing and clapping my hands.
I should have written to you myself,
but I feared the rumor was not verified.
So I had my younger brother Zǐjiàn go through Xún Zhòngmào
to leisurely convey my humble intent.
You did not neglect or discard the request,
and showed great generosity and praise.
The rider from Yè having arrived,
the precious jade ring has just come.
Holding the box, I knelt to open it;
my five internal organs were shaken with awe.
The cord was undone and the box opened,
and a brilliant light filled my eyes.
Vulgarly, with my ignorant and lowly appearance,
I was able to see a rare treasure of the world.
Without troubling a single envoy
or losing the price of several cities,
I had the viewing of Qín Zhāo at the Zhāngtái Palace,
without the deception of Lìnshēng’s trickery.
The generous gift is most abundant;
how dare I not receive it with reverence?
I respectfully present one rhapsody
to praise its beautiful quality.
Pī says.
Zhí states:
Having not seen you for several days,
my longing for you has become a toil,
and I imagine it is the same for you.
Since my youth, I have been fond of composing literary works;
continuing until the present,
it has been twenty-five years.
However, regarding the authors of the current age,
they can be discussed briefly.
Formerly, Zhòngxuān stood alone in Hànnán,
Kǒngzhāng soared like an eagle in Héshuò,
Wěicháng held the sole fame in the land of Qīngtǔ,
Gōnggàn displayed his brilliance at the corner of the sea,
Déliǎn rose to prominence here in Wèi,
and you look down from a high position in the capital Shàngjīng.
At that time,
every person claimed to hold the pearl of the numinous snake,
and every family claimed to embrace the jade of Jīngshān.
Thereupon, our King set a celestial net to encompass them
and cast it over the eight directions to capture them;
now they are all gathered here in this state.
Yet these several gentlemen
are still unable to make their carriages fly and leave no trace,
covering a thousand li in a single bound.
With the talent of Kǒngzhāng,
he was not skilled in rhapsodies,
yet he often claimed to share the same style as Sīmǎ Chángqīng.
This is like trying to draw a tiger and failing;
instead, it becomes a dog.
In a previous letter, I mocked him for this,
but in response, he wrote a treatise elaborately stating that I had praised his writing.
Since Zhōng Qī did not fail in his hearing,
he is praised even to this day.
I, too, cannot help but sigh about writing,
for I fear the ridicule of later generations.
In the writings of worldly people,
there cannot be a lack of flaws.
I have always welcomed people's criticism and scrutiny of my writing;
if there is something not good,
I revise and finalize it immediately.
Formerly, Dīng Jìnglǐ often composed small pieces of writing
and had me polish and refine them.
I personally felt my talent did not surpass his,
so I declined and did not do it.
Jìnglǐ said to me:
"Why do you have such doubts and difficulties?
Whether a piece of writing is good or bad,
I will realize it myself.
In later generations, who would be able to know or settle my writing for me?"
I often sighed at these profound words
and considered them a fine sentiment.
Formerly, the literary expressions of Nífù
were shared and flowed with others;
but when it came to composing the Chūnqiū,
even the likes of Yóu and Xià could not add a single word.
Beyond this, to say that one's words have no flaws—
I have never seen such a person.
Only one with the beauty of Nán Wēi
can discuss the elegance of a lady.
Only one with the sharpness of Lóngquán
can deliberate on its cutting and severing.
Liú Jìxù's talent cannot reach that of the authors,
yet he is fond of disparaging and rebuking literature,
picking out merits and flaws.
Formerly, Tián Bā defamed the Five Emperors,
condemned the Three Kings,
and insulted the Five Hegemons at Jìxià;
in a single morning, he overcame a thousand men.
But a single discourse from Lǔ Lián
caused him to shut his mouth for the rest of his life.
Master Liú’s eloquence
is not like that of the Tián family;
a present-day Zhònglián
is not hard to find.
Can he not desist?
Each person has their own preferences.
The fragrance of orchids, angelica, and clover
is what the multitude loves,
yet at the seashore, there is a man who chases stenches.
The music of Xiánchí and Liùjīng
is what the multitude enjoys together,
yet Mò Dí had arguments criticizing it.
How can they be the same!
Now I am sending you a collection of the rhapsodies I have written since my youth.
In street talk and alley gossip,
there must be something worth adopting;
songs sung while striking the shafts of a carriage
may correspond to the Fēng and Yǎ.
The thoughts of an ordinary man
should not be lightly discarded.
Rhapsody is but a minor path;
it is certainly not enough to extol great principles
or to manifest them for future generations.
Formerly, Yáng Zǐyún was merely an official who held a halberd in the previous court,
yet even he claimed that a great man would not practice it.
Though my virtue is thin,
my position is that of a frontier lord;
I still hope to devote my strength to the Shàngguó,
spread blessings to the common people,
establish an undertaking for eternal ages,
and leave behind achievements carved in metal and stone.
How could I merely use brush and ink for my accomplishments,
or consider rhapsody as the mark of a gentleman?
If my ambitions are not fulfilled
and my way is not practiced,
then I shall gather the true records of various officials,
deliberate on the gains and losses of contemporary customs,
determine the heart of benevolence and righteousness,
and establish the teachings of a single school.
Even if I cannot hide them away in famous mountains,
I will transmit them to those of like mind.
This is not to seek recognition only in my old age;
how could it be a matter for today's discussion?
That I speak of this without shame
is because I rely on Huì Zǐ's understanding of me.
Tomorrow morning I shall welcome you.
This letter does not fully express my feelings.
Zhí states this.
Zhí states:
To Jìzhòng.
The other day, although following the regular schedule,
we were able to sit closely together.
Although we feasted and drank for the whole day,
given that partings are far and meetings are rare,
it still did not fully exhaust our pent-up longing.
As for the cups and goblets skimming the ripples in front of us,
and the flutes and pipes sounding behind us,
you soared like an eagle,
sighing like a phoenix and gazing like a tiger.
You said that Xiāo and Cáo were not enough to be your peers,
and Wèi and Huò were not enough to be your equals.
Looking to the left and glancing to the right,
it was as if no one else was there.
Was this not your grand ambition, my friend?
To pass by a butcher's door and chew vigorously—
even if one does not get any meat,
it is still precious and gratifying.
At that moment,
one wished to lift Tàishān to serve as meat,
tilt the Dōnghǎi to serve as wine,
cut the bamboo of Yúnmèng to make flutes,
and fell the catalpa trees of Sìbīn to make zithers.
Eating as if filling a great ravine,
drinking as if pouring into a leaky vessel—
such joy is certainly hard to measure.
Is this not the joy of a great man?
However, the days do not stay for us;
the Sun Yàolíng moves with a hurried rhythm.
In person, there is the speed of fleeting light;
in parting, there is the distance between the stars Shēn and Shāng.
One wishes to restrain the heads of the six dragons,
halt the reins of Xīhé,
pluck the blossoms of the Ruòmù tree,
and close the valley of Méngsì.
But the celestial path is high and remote,
and for a long time there has been no opportunity.
I cherish our bond and toss and turn in bed;
what can be done, what can be done!
I received your recent message;
its literary style is detailed and elaborate,
as brilliant as spring blossoms
and as clear as a fresh breeze.
Reciting it repeatedly,
it is as refreshing as meeting you in person.
Regarding the articles written by the various worthies,
I imagine they have been returned to where you reside.
I have recited them again;
one can have a diligent junior clerk chant and memorize them.
The difficulty of writing
is not unique to the present day.
Even the gentlemen of old
were troubled by it.
If one has a thousand-li horse at home,
a swift steed is not treasured;
if everyone carries a foot-long jade,
the jade of the Héshì family loses its value.
That a gentleman should understand music—
this was a widespread view of old,
yet it was called being "versatile but obscured."
Mò Dí did not like performing arts;
why, then, did he turn his carriage around when passing Zhāogē?
You are fond of performing arts,
and you happen to be in the county where Mò Dí turned his carriage;
I imagine you will help me open my eyes to it.
I have also heard that you are there,
carrying out an excellent administration.
While there are those who seek and do not obtain,
there have never been those who obtain without seeking.
Furthermore, changing one’s course and altering one’s path
is not the driving style of Liáng or Lè;
changing the people to govern them
was not the administration of Chǔ or Zhèng;
I only wish that you exert yourself.
I am just now hosting esteemed guests,
so I dictate this without going into full detail.
Let us often hear from each other through our correspondence.
Cáo Zhí says.
Wú Zhì says:
Your letter has arrived,
and I have received the gift you bestowed.
Opening the envelope and unfolding the paper,
how magnificent and beautiful is the literary style,
and how profound are the words of comfort!
Indeed, only those who climb Dōngyuè
then know how the many mountains wind and stretch away;
only those who serve the Zhìzūn
then know the insignificance of a hundred lǐ.
Since the beginning of my return,
I have been lost in thought for five or six days,
extending even to ten days.
My spirit is scattered and my thoughts wander;
I feel dazed as if I have lost something.
It is not that I dare to envy the excellence of your favored glory,
nor that I long for the wealth of Yī Dùn.
Truly, because my person is as lowly as a dog or a horse,
and my virtue is as light as a swan’s feather,
yet I have passed through the Xuánquè,
pushed through the Jīnmén,
ascended the Yùtáng,
prostrated myself at the open railings of the front palace,
and passed the wine cup by the winding pool.
Having already failed in my dignified bearing,
and having let my words leak out and spill over,
though I rely on the excellence of Píngyuán’s nurturing of scholars,
I am ashamed to lack the talent of Máo Suì who showed his brilliance.
I have deeply received the humble courtesy of Xuē Gōng,
yet I lack the effectiveness of Féng Xuān and his three burrows.
I have repeatedly received the virtue of Xìnlíng who left the left seat vacant,
yet I have none of the praiseworthy beauty of Hóu Shēng.
In all these several matters,
this is the reason why Zhì’s frustration accumulates in my chest,
and why I harbor longing and feel distressed.
If I recall our former banquet,
I would say it was not yet exhausted.
Though we were to tilt the sea for wine,
and combine the mountains for side dishes,
cut bamboo in Yúnmèng,
and chop catalpa trees on the banks of Sìbīn,
only then could we reach the limit of our refined intentions
and exhaust our feelings of joy.
Indeed, the magnificent sight of the Gōngzǐ
is not something a lowly person like me can hope to match.
As for Zhì’s will,
it truly lies with you, my Heaven.
I think of casting aside my seal and releasing my ribbons,
to attend and sit by your side morning and evening,
to delve into the bequeathed teachings of Zhòngfù,
to peruse the essential words of Lǎoshì,
to face the clear wine without drinking,
to restrain from the fine dishes without partaking,
letting Xī Shī emerge from the curtains,
while Mómǔ attends at the side.
This is the path of great virtue,
and what the wise and farsighted preserve.
As for the sights of late,
they truly stirred my lowly heart.
The Qín zither released its fine notes,
and sixteen dancers performed in turns.
The xūn and flutes echoed through the magnificent house,
and the spirit drums vibrated beside the seats.
My ears were so noisy I heard nothing else,
and my spirit leaped like a horse in a saddle.
I thought we could intimidate the Sùshèn to the north,
causing them to offer their thornwood arrows as tribute;
shake the Bǎiyuè to the south,
causing them to present their white pheasants;
how much more so for Quán and Bèi,
how could they be worth looking at?
Returning to my post, I have recited and gathered what you have written,
and observing your brilliant and magnificent works,
they are truly the ancestors of rhapsodies and odes,
and a master for all writers.
What the various worthies have written
each also has its own intent.
In the past, when Zhào Wǔ passed through Zhèng,
seven gentlemen composed poems,
and the Chūnqiū recorded them in order,
regarding it as a fine story.
Zhì is a person of little consequence,
having nothing to offer in response to your command.
Furthermore, what I offer in response to your gift
is ugly in language and shallow in meaning;
even after explaining it several times,
I blush with shame and sweat falls.
The people of this land
are well-versed in rhapsodies and odes;
the Dàfū of the three departments,
none of them fail to recite them.
How could it be limited only to minor officials?
You have again favored me with harsh words,
instructing me on administrative affairs.
Your compassionate kindness
is manifest in your writing.
Mòzǐ turned his carriage around,
but Zhì has been here four years.
Although I have no virtue to give the people,
they sing and dance.
Confucianism and Mohism are different;
this has indeed been so for a long time.
However, a small troop of soldiers
is not enough to spread one’s fame;
within a space of a few paces,
there is not enough room to leave one’s mark.
If I do not change my path and alter my driving,
how then shall I exert my strength?
To remain here and seek great merit
is like fettering the legs of a fine steed
and charging it with a task of a thousand lǐ,
or caging the power of an ape or monkey
and expecting its skill and swiftness.
I cannot bear your showing of sympathy.
I respectfully send this response,
and dare not be wordy.
Wú Zhì says.
Yìng Qú says:
Yesterday, you did not exclude me,
and I was humbly honored by your presence.
Even when in the past Hóu Shēng received a visit at the Yímén,
or Máo Gōng was favored at an inn,
it could not surpass this.
Outwardly, I admire your, the Lángjūn's, virtue of humility;
inwardly, I am fortunate that my dull talent is sincerely recognized as a confidant.
I am full of joy and leaping with excitement;
my feelings are boundless.
Therefore, I hurried my servants and horses,
spreading your orders and seeking all around.
The Yáng Shū was explained to Zhān Hé,
