and Yáng Qiàn spoke to Fàn Wǔ.
Thus, fresh fish were brought from the deep pools,
and fragrant delicacies came from the secluded alleys.
The many platters were beautifully arranged,
and the feathered wine cups flew about.
The high notes of Yá and Kuàng sounded,
and the mournful tunes of Yìqú were stirring.
At that time,
Zhòngrú did not decline his brother’s clothing,
and Mènggōng did not care about the Shàngshū's appointment.
I only regret that just as the banquet’s joy became lively
and the white sun declined into evening,
the black horses were harnessed to the carriage.
My thoughts were not fully expressed,
and I thought back on our integrity,
even until the dawn.
I was just about to send a letter
when I received your command,
knowing that you gentlemen are having another gathering at the Zhāngqú.
To the west of Zhāngqú is the lodge of Bóyáng,
and to the north is the view of the open wilderness.
Tall trees shade the morning clouds,
and patterned birds cover the green water.
The sandy shores are flat and wide,
and the clear breeze is solemn and peaceful.
This is the joy of the Jīngtái terrace;
how can one not wander there and forget to return?
I just happen to have some affairs
that I must attend to myself,
so I cannot attend and sit with you,
which truly increases my distress.
I say this without going into full detail.
Yìng Qú says.
Yìng Qú says:
After you left,
I have missed you very much.
In the poem Shū Tián, there is the song of no one being there;
at the city gate, there is the thought of someone not being present.
The works of the poets in the Airs,
how could they be empty!
Wáng Sù was appointed based on his long-standing virtue;
Hé Zēng was promoted as a later talent.
Both soar like eagles and glare like tigers,
possessing ambitions that span ten thousand lǐ.
Those with meager assistance
cannot pursue or join the heights of the profound;
they fold their wings back on their old branches,
dwelling alone in solitude,
with the intent to leave the flock.
Jí Àn delighted in staying in the Lángshǔ;
Hé Wǔ was ashamed to be a Prime Minister.
Evaluating them across a thousand years,
one knows there were reasons for this.
My virtue is not like that of Chén Píng,
so my gate has no tracks of four-horse carriages;
my learning is not like that of Yáng Xióng,
so my hall has no curious guests;
my talent is inferior to that of Zhòngshū,
so I lack the focus of lowered curtains;
my family is as poor as Mèng Gōng's,
so I lack the joy of setting out wine.
A sorrowful wind rises in the inner doors;
red dust covers the desks and couches.
Fortunately, there is Yuán Shēng,
who occasionally steps with his jade feet here.
We gather firewood and grass but do not cook,
engaging only in pure conversation,
much like Zhōu Dǎng visiting Mǐn Zǐ.
When the skin rots, the hair falls out;
when the river dries up, the fish depart.
What grows in spring flourishes;
what blooms in autumn withers and fades.
These are the cycles of nature;
how could there be any regret!
I merely express my bitter feelings to my elder brother.
I expect your return is near,
so I will not say more.
Qú speaks.
Qú speaks:
Recently there has been a scorching drought,
getting worse day by day.
Sand and pebbles melt and glow;
grass and trees are scorched and curled.
Resting on a cool terrace, there is the distress of stifling steam;
bathing in cold water, there is the misery of burning and scalding.
Though the universe is vast,
there is no shade in which to rest.
Even the poem "Yún Hàn,"
how could it exceed this?
Earth dragons lift their heads in the dark temples;
mud men stand like cranes in Quèlǐ.
This has been practiced for over ten days,
yet there is quietly no sign of effect.
It is clear that these are techniques for encouraging instruction,
not the means to bring about rain.
Knowing you sympathize with the common people,
you personally exposed yourself to the elements,
bowing and rising at the spiritual altar;
your diligence has truly reached its peak.
In the past, Xià Yǔ relieved the drought at Yángxū;
Tāng of Yīn prayed at Sānglín.
Before their words were fully spoken, water began to flow;
before their prayers ended, the bounty was torrential.
Now, the clouds gather heavily but then disperse;
the rain hangs down but then withdraws.
Could it be that the grades of sages and worthies differ,
and their qualities of excellence are distinct,
such that cutting hair should reach the skin,
and trimming nails should penetrate the flesh?
Zhōu campaigned against Yīn and the year was bountiful;
Wèi attacked Xíng and it brought rain.
The response of good or ill
is more immediate than a shadow or an echo;
one cannot believe it to be otherwise.
I imagine your elegant thoughts have not reached this;
I respectfully write this to inspire you.
Yìng Qú speaks.
Qú replies:
During my recent journey to the north,
my joy was boundless.
I climbed Máng Shān and crossed the Hé River;
it was as vast as having one's eyes opened.
Fēngbó swept the path;
Yǔshī sprinkled the road.
Holding the reins on the clear road,
I looked all around at the mountains and fields.
Once I arrived and stopped,
I drank that spring wine.
Walking side by side in a thatched hut,
it was cooler than a great hall;
eating small portions of dried meat,
the flavor surpassed a grand feast.
Wandering leisurely by the embankments and ponds,
chanting poems beneath the dense willows,
I tied spring fragrances to enhance my pendant
and plucked the Ruò flowers to shade the sun.
I shot birds from the high clouds
and baited fish from the deep abysses.
Pú Qiě praised my skill;
Biànhuán called it wonderful.
How joyful it was!
Even Zhòngní forgetting the taste of food because of the Shào music of Yú,
or the people of Chǔ wandering and forgetting to return at Jīngtái,
could not exceed this.
Bān Sì's letter
is truly not false.
Since returning to the capital,
I dwell alone in solitude.
My residence is on the banks of the Luò,
distressed by the noise and dust.
I long for the joy of being on the Wèn River,
even in my dreams.
In the past, Yī Yǔn stopped his plowing,
and Zhì Yǔn threw away his fishing pole,
thinking to bring their lord to the level of Yǒuyú
and save the masses from misery.
But I am about to take up the plow and hoe in Shānyáng,
and sink my hook and line into the Dān River;
I know I am far inferior to the ancients.
Yet Shānfù did not covet the joy of heaven and earth,
and Zēng Shēn did not admire the wealth of Jìn or Chǔ;
this too is their will.
Previously, the people of the district thought of you, my brother, without end,
wanting the province and commandery to honor you with rites,
and the officials to grant you a post;
this is indeed a kind intention.
Looking through history from past to present,
those who enter the military headquarters,
even until their hair turns white,
still may not find their opportunity,
and merely suffer the toil of hunger, cold, and frantic running.
Waiting for the River to turn clear—
how long is a person's life?
Furthermore, in officialdom you lack the support of the Jīn or Zhāng families,
and in your travels you lack the resources of Zǐmèng;
yet to seek the glory of wealth and rank,
or hope for the extraordinary status of a dragon,
would be like traveling to Lóngxī
or the archery of the Yuè people.
Fortunately, relying on the spirit of our late father,
we are exempt from the toil of carrying burdens.
Following the traces of our elders,
we can raise chickens and plant millet,
immerse our minds in the classics,
and establish ourselves to make a name;
this would be acceptable.
Do not let idle talk
increase your anxiety.
The fields in the suburbs and pastures
should be kept in mind;
widely opening up the lands,
I shall grow old there.
As for the two scholars Liú and Dù,
I imagine you visit each other often.
The time of the Bright Summer
has already arrived again.
Our meeting is near,
so I will not write another letter.
Be cautious in the summer and take care of yourself.
Qú speaks.
Kāng speaks:
Formerly, you praised me in Yǐngchuán;
I always considered those the words of one who knows me.
However, I have always wondered about this intention,
as I was not yet well-acquainted with you;
from where did you get it?
The year before last, returning from Hédōng,
Ādū of Xiǎnzhōng said you discussed recommending me to replace you.
Although the matter did not proceed,
I knew you still did not understand me.
You are broad-minded and versatile,
accepting much and finding little strange.
I am of a direct nature and narrow-minded,
unable to endure much.
It is only by chance that you and I became acquaintances.
Recently hearing of your promotion,
I was startled and not pleased,
fearing you would be ashamed to be the only cook carving
and would pull in the master of ceremonies to assist you,
personally presenting the Luándāo
and tainting me with the stench of raw meat.
Therefore, I have fully detailed for you what is possible and what is not.
In the past when I read books,
I encountered people of uncompromising integrity;
some said they did not exist,
but now I believe they truly do.
There are things my nature cannot endure;
one truly cannot force it.
Nowadays, people idly speak of "men of understanding"
who can endure anything,
outwardly not differing from commoners
while inwardly maintaining correctness,
drifting with the current of the age
without regret or error.
Lǎozǐ and Zhuāng Zhōu
are my teachers, yet they
personally held lowly offices;
Liǔxià Huì and Dōngfāng Shuò
were men of understanding,
yet they were content in humble positions.
How could I dare criticize them!
Furthermore, Zhòngní practiced universal love
and was not ashamed to be a groom;
Zǐwén had no desire to be a high minister,
yet he thrice became Lìngyǐn.
This was the intention of a gentleman to help the world.
This is what is called: when successful, one can benefit all without changing;
when in straits, one finds contentment within without distress.
Looking at it from this perspective,
the reigns of Yáo and Shùn,
the cave-dwelling of Xǔ Yóu,
Zǐfáng aiding Hàn,
and Jiēyú singing as he walked—
their guiding principles were the same.
Looking up at these several gentlemen,
one can say they were able to fulfill their own wills.
Thus, there are a hundred ways for a gentleman to act;
though the paths differ, the destination is the same.
Acting according to one's nature,
each finds comfort in their own place.
Therefore, there are theories about remaining at court without leaving
or entering the mountains and forests without returning.
Moreover, Yánlíng admired the style of Gāo Zǐzāng,
and Chángqīng admired the integrity of Xiāngrú.
Where the will and spirit are placed,
they cannot be taken away.
Whenever I read the biographies of Shàng Zǐpíng and Tái Xiàowēi,
I sigh in admiration
and imagine the kind of people they were.
I lost my father early and was raised in isolation;
I was indulged by my mother and elder brother
and did not pursue the classics.
Furthermore, my nature is loose and lazy,
with weak muscles and sluggish flesh.
My head and face often go unwashed for fifteen days or a month;
unless I am in great irritation or itching,
I cannot bring myself to bathe.
Whenever I need to urinate,
I hold it and do not get up,
waiting until my bladder is about to burst before I finally rise.
Moreover, I have been unrestrained for a long time,
and my mind is arrogant and scattered.
Simplicity is contrary to ritual;
laziness and arrogance complement each other.
Yet I have been tolerated by my peers,
who do not attack my faults.
Moreover, reading Zhuāng and Lǎo
has further increased my wildness.
Consequently, my desire for honor and advancement declines daily,
while my feeling for following my true nature becomes increasingly sincere.
This is like a bird or a deer: if caught young and tamed,
it will obey teachings and constraints;
but if caught when grown,
it will stare wildly and break its tether,
rushing into boiling water or fire.
Though adorned with a golden bit
and fed with fine fodder,
it yearns even more for the deep forest
and sets its heart on the lush grass.
Ruǎn Sìzōng never spoke of others' faults;
I always try to emulate him
but cannot reach his level.
His innate nature surpassed others,
he caused no harm to things,
only drinking wine to excess.
When he was censured by the sticklers for ritual law,
who hated him like an enemy,
fortunately, he relied on the Great General to protect him.
I am not as worthy as Sìzōng,
yet I have the defect of being lazy and loose.
Furthermore, I do not understand human feelings
and am ignorant of worldly tactics.
I lack the caution of Wànshí
but have the burden of liking to speak my mind fully.
Staying in contact with affairs for a long time,
flaws and provocations would arise daily;
though I might wish to avoid trouble,
how could I?
Furthermore, human relations have rituals
and the court has laws.
I have reflected on this most thoroughly:
there are seven things I cannot endure
and two things that are absolutely impermissible.
I like to sleep late,
but the gatekeeper would call me incessantly—
this is the first thing I cannot endure.
Holding my zither and singing as I walk,
or shooting arrows and fishing in the wilds,
but having clerks and soldiers guarding me
so I cannot move freely—
this is the second thing I cannot endure.
Sitting upright for a long time
until my legs are numb and I cannot move,
and having many lice on me
so I must scratch without ceasing,
yet having to wrap myself in official robes
and bow to superiors—
this is the third thing I cannot endure.
I have never been good at writing
and do not enjoy doing so,
yet worldly affairs are many
and stacks of documents fill the desk;
if I do not respond,
I violate social norms and damage propriety,
but if I force myself,
I cannot last long—
this is the fourth thing I cannot endure.
I do not like attending funerals,
but the way of the world regards this as important.
I have already been resented by those who are not forgiving,
and even by those who wish to harm me;
though I am startled into self-reproach,
my nature cannot be changed.
If I try to humble my heart to follow custom,
it would be deceptive and insincere,
and in the end, I could not achieve a state of having neither blame nor praise like this—
this is the fifth thing I cannot endure.
I do not like vulgar people,
yet I would have to work with them;
or with guests filling the room,
their voices noisy in my ears
and the air full of dust and stench,
with a hundred tricks and antics
performed before my eyes—
this is the sixth thing I cannot endure.
My heart has no patience for trivialities,
yet official business is overwhelming;
mechanical tasks would entangle my mind
and worldly affairs would burden my thoughts—
this is the seventh thing I cannot endure.
Moreover, I often criticize Tāng and Wǔ and belittle Zhōu and Kǒng;
saying this incessantly in public
would certainly be revealed and is something that worldly teachings cannot tolerate—
this is the first thing that is absolutely impermissible.
I am stubborn and hate evil,
speaking directly and recklessly;
whatever I encounter, I express it immediately—
this is the second thing that is absolutely impermissible.
With a narrow and small-minded nature,
governed by these nine troubles,
if there were no external calamities,
there would surely be internal illness.
How could I stay in the human world for long!
Furthermore, I have heard the bequeathed words of Daoists
that eating zhú and huángjīng
makes one live long,
and I believe in this deeply.
Wandering in mountains and lakes,
watching fish and birds—
my heart finds great joy in this.
Once I become an official,
these things will be abandoned.
How could I give up what I love
to follow what I fear?
When friends understand each other,
it is important to recognize their natural character
and support them accordingly.
Yǔ did not pressure Bó Chéng Zǐ Gāo,
thus preserving his integrity;
Zhòng Ní did not borrow an umbrella from Zǐ Xià,
thus protecting him from his shortcoming;
recently, Zhū Gě Kǒng Míng did not pressure Yuán Zhí to enter Shǔ;
Huá Zǐ Yú did not force Yòu Ān to become a high minister.
These can be said to be people who can maintain a relationship from beginning to end,
truly understanding one another.
You see that straight wood cannot be made into a wheel,
and curved wood cannot be made into a rafter,
because one does not wish to distort its natural talent
but rather allow it to find its proper place.
Therefore, the four classes of people have their occupations,
and each finds joy in achieving their aspirations;
only a man of broad vision can understand this,
which must be within your own consideration.
One cannot, seeing that they look good in a Zhāng Fǔ cap,
force the Yuè people to wear a ceremonial crown;
nor can one, because they themselves crave rotting meat,
feed a Yuān Chú bird with dead rats.
I have recently been studying the arts of nourishing life,
setting aside external glory,
abandoning rich flavors,
letting my mind wander in silence,
and valuing non-action as precious.
Even if I did not have the Jiǔ Huàn,
I would still not care for what you favor,
and I also suffer from a heart affliction,
which has recently become more severe;
privately I have tested myself
and found I cannot endure what I do not enjoy.
I have examined my own destiny clearly;
if the way is exhausted and the path ends, so be it.
You should not needlessly wrong me
and cause me to end up in a ditch or valley.
I have recently lost the joy of my mother and elder brother,
and my heart is constantly filled with grief.
My daughter is thirteen,
and my son is eight;
they have not yet reached adulthood,
and moreover, they are often ill.
Looking at them, my heart is filled with sorrow—
how can words express it!
Now I only wish to stay in a humble alley,
teach and raise my children and grandchildren,
occasionally converse with relatives and old friends,
talk about my life,
drink a cup of cloudy wine,
and play a tune on the qín;
then my aspirations will be fulfilled.
If you continue to pester me without stopping,
it is merely because you wish to find the right person for the government
to benefit the needs of the times.
You have long known that I am careless and coarse,
and do not attend to practical matters,
and I myself realize I am not as virtuous or capable as today's men.
If it is because ordinary people all delight in glory,
yet I alone can distance myself from it,
and you find this admirable,
then this is the closest reason,
and it can be spoken of.
However, if one has great talent and broad capacity,
is proficient in all things,
and yet can refrain from seeking them,
then it is truly valuable.
As for me, I am sickly and weary,
wishing to leave affairs to preserve myself
and safeguard my remaining years;
this is truly because I lack ability.
How could one see a palace eunuch and call him chaste!
If you hasten to have us climb the royal road together,
hoping to bring me there,
thinking it will be for our mutual joy and benefit,
once I am pressured,
it will surely trigger my madness;
unless there is a deep grudge between us,
it should not come to this.
There was a rustic man who enjoyed the warmth of the sun on his back and found celery delicious,
so he wished to offer them to the Emperor;
although he had sincere intentions,
he was nonetheless misguided.
I hope you will not be like him.
My intentions are thus;
I have written this both to explain myself to you
and to bid you farewell.
Jī Kāng writes.
Bāo writes:
I have heard that acting upon seeing the opportunity
is what the Zhōu Yì values;
for the small not to serve the great
is what the Chūn Qiū punishes.
These are the signs of fortune and misfortune,
and the source from which honor and disgrace arise.
Therefore, Xǔ and Zhèng preserved their states by offering ceremonial jade,
while Cáo and Tán brought about their own destruction through lack of propriety.
The records have already noted their success and failure,
and ancient and modern times have manifested their folly or wisdom.
I shall not again cite numerous analogies
or adorn my words with flowery language;
to merely seek a reputation for grandiosity
would instead lose the substance of sincere advice.
Now I shall briefly discuss the situation of the times
to enlighten you.
Formerly, the essence of the Fire became dim and obscured,
and its allotted time was coming to an end.
Huán and Líng lost their virtue,
and disasters and calamities arose together.
Jackals and wolves brandished their poisonous claws and teeth,
and the common people were trapped in the hardships of misery.
Thus the bonds of the Jiǔ Zhōu were severed,
the imperial order unraveled,
the world was desolate,
and it was no longer possessed by the Hàn.
Tài Zǔ received the mandate of fate,
his divine martial prowess met the appointed time;
he campaigned against violence and chaos,
and succeeded in pacifying the realm.
He harmonized and established the sacred omens;
since the Mandate of Heaven had gathered,
he then expanded the great foundation
and took possession of the Wèi territory.
The land is Shén Zhōu and Zhōng Yuè,
and for the ritual vessels, the Jiǔ Dǐng still remain.
Successive generations have displayed virtue and beauty,
and repeated light has followed in succession.
One surely knows that the four borders are unified,
a magnificent sight for the whole world.
Gōng Sūn Yuān inherited his position from his father and brother,
living for generations on the eastern borders.
Controlling the Yàn and the Hú,
relying on the precipitous distance,
he practiced military drills and lingered there,
failing to provide the required tribute.
Internally, he defied the Imperial commands;
externally, he communicated with the Southern State.
Crossing the blue seas by boat,
he exchanged goods and bribes.
Kudzu and hemp were spread in the Shuò Tǔ,
while marten furs and horses reached Wú Kuài;
he believed that with a hundred thousand archers
and sufficient resources to mobilize,
he could indeed break Yàn and Qí to the right,
shake Fú Sāng to the left,
trample over the desert,
and face south to call himself king.
Xuān Wáng led a punitive expedition,
his fierce and sharp forces driving far.
When the army reached Liáo Yáng,
the city walls could not be held;
with a single drumbeat,
the arch-criminal was decapitated.
Then he reached out to the distant borders,
and established commanderies in the vast wilderness.
He gathered the dispersed and the scattered,
and all were settled in their dwellings.
The common people joyfully submitted,
and those of foreign customs sincerely pledged allegiance.
From then on, prosperity flourished,
and the Jiǔ Yě became peaceful and tranquil.
The Dōng Yí offered their musical instruments,
and the Sù Shèn contributed their arrows of thorn wood.
Those who for generations had been untamed
arrived in response to civilization.
How majestic and grand it is!
I imagine you have heard it all in detail.
The former rulers of Wú,
arose from Jīngzhōu;
encountering times of turmoil and unrest,
they took refuge in Jiāngbiǎo.
Liú Bèi, struck with terror,
also fled to Bā and Mín.
They then relied on the natural strength of hills and piled stones,
with the three rivers and five lakes,
vast and boundless.
They drew breath like wandering souls
for a period of forty-eight years.
The two states formed an alliance,
responding to one another from east and west,
mutually inciting each other
to resist the Central Kingdom.
They claimed for themselves the power of a three-legged tripod,
believing they could last as long as Tàishān.
The Chancellor and Prince of Jìn,
assisting the Imperial House,
is valiant in both civil and military arts.
His resolve is as stern as autumn frost;
his plans for victory in the ancestral temple
respond to changes without end.
His singular insight and discernment
surpass the thoughts of the masses.
The Emperor is wise and enlightened,
entrusting him with the myriad affairs of state.
With a long rein he governs from afar,
secretly imparting marvelous strategies.
The secondary armies are of one mind,
and those above and below exert their strength.
With majestic awe they launched a spirited campaign,
penetrating deep into the enemy's obstacles.
Focusing all forces in one direction against the foe,
they stripped them of their courage.
After a minor battle in the river regions,
Chéngdū collapsed of its own accord.
When the army displayed its might at Jiàngé,
Jiāng Wéi surrendered with his hands bound.
Five thousand li of land were opened,
and thirty commanderies were established.
Before the season had even changed,
Liáng and Yì were cleared and pacified.
The hero who had usurped a title
knocked his head at the Crimson Palace.
Jade, gems, and heavy silks
filled the storehouses.
The extinction of Guó led to the fall of Yú;
the annexation of Hán led to the displacement of Wèi.
These are all proofs from past mirrors
and teachers for future affairs.
Furthermore, Lǚ Xìng of Nánzhōng
deeply perceived the Mandate of Heaven;
shedding his old skin to turn inward,
he desired to become a subject.
Externally, you have lost the support of "cheeks and teeth";
internally, there is the gradual shedding of "feathers and down."
Yet you linger in a state of peril,
hoping to prolong your days.
This is like Marquis Wǔ of Wèi pointing back at the rivers and mountains to strengthen himself,
utterly unaware that things have their rise and fall,
and that what he praised was not the land itself.
At present, the hundred officials are numerous and grand;
men of talent fill the court.
Tiger-like ministers and martial generals
overcome enemies ten thousand li away.
The state is wealthy and the soldiers are strong;
the six armies are expertly trained.
They think of soaring like wings
and watering their horses in the Nánhǎi.
Recently, the state
has been refining equipment,
building boats and oars,
and selecting and practicing for naval combat.
Trees are felled in Běishān
until the timber of Tàiháng is exhausted;
the Hé and Luò rivers are dredged
so that all streams flow through.
Ten thousand tower-ships
look upon one another for a thousand li.
Since the time of hollowed logs,
the use of boats and carriages
has never been as flourishing as it is today.
A million valiant soldiers
store their strength and await the moment.
"The labor will not be undertaken twice"—
this refers to today.
However, the Emperor is deeply concerned
and has not yet moved with the speed of lightning
because he believes in loving the people and governing the state,
which are valued by the Daoists.
High walls humiliate themselves;
King Wén withdrew to his quarters.
Therefore, he first displays great good faith,
explaining the choice between survival and ruin.
The purpose of this earnestness
is for the envoy to investigate thoroughly.
If you can discern safety from danger,
and seek much fortune for yourself,
suddenly changing your expression,
reverently accepting the past announcement,
emulating Nányuè
when Yīngqí entered to serve,
facing north to call yourself a subject
and prostrating to hear the imperial decree,
then your lineage shall long rule the Jiāngbiǎo
and forever be a supporting vassal.
Abundant rewards and distinguished honors
will be even greater than today.
But if you are insolent and do not follow the King's command,
then forces will gather like clouds,
and at a single command, they will follow like the wind.
From the two provinces of Yōng and Yì,
they will follow the current and head east.
The warriors of Qīng and Xú
will line the river and head west.
Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù
will compete to drive through the eight thoroughfares.
The armored soldiers of the General Who Conquers the East
will walk like tigers across the hills.
Then the Imperial Carriage will be prepared,
and the six armies will slowly set out.
Feathered dispatches will light up the sun;
banners will be like falling stars.
Swimming dragons will illuminate the road;
songs and pipes will fill the ears.
The soldiers will hasten forward;
they will gather like a forest.
Smoke and dust will rise together,
shaking the heavens and startling the earth.
Soldiers thirsty for rewards
will compete to be at the front of the arrows.
Suddenly, in a single morning, your body and head will be separated,
and your ancestral sacrifices will be slaughtered and overturned,
serving as a warning for ten thousand generations.
Looking south with neck outstretched,
I truly feel a chill in my heart.
He who treats a terminal illness must administer bitter medicine;
he who resolves doubts must speak words that are harsh to the ear.
If you are lost and deluded
and do not know where to turn,
I fear Yú Fù will see you are already exhausted
and Biǎn Què will know his efforts are in vain.
Diligently consider a good plan;
it is for you to choose whether to stay or go.
Shí Bāo speaks.
Ān speaks:
In the past, when Elder Lǐ entered Qín,
he reached the pass and sighed;
when Master Liáng went to Yuè,
he climbed the peak and sang a long song.
Even with the act of a noble withdrawal into seclusion,
they still harbored lingering regrets;
how much more so for one who has no other choice!
Since our parting,
I have wandered alone, away from the crowd.
I have turned my back on glorious banquets
and said farewell to the company of my peers.
I have traveled distant roads
and crossed the desert sands.
When the crowing cock signals the dawn,
I set out fluttering on my morning journey;
when the sun nears the western mountains,
my horse's head has nowhere to rest.
Traveling through winding obstacles,
my deep thoughts become entangled.
Ascending the heights to gaze into the distance,
I see mountains and rivers far apart.
Sometimes the circling winds are fierce and violent,
and the white sun hides its light.
Rugged paths crisscross,
as hills and marshes come into view.
Lingering within the nine marshes,
and feeling stirred atop the heavy ridges,
moving forward I have nothing to rely on,
and retreating I have no ground to stand upon.
I cross marshes to find a path
and part the brambles to seek a way.
Whistling and chanting by the ditches,
it is truly difficult to cross.
These are the hardships of the traveler's road,
but they are not what my heart fears.
As for the orchids and angelica being trampled down,
and the cinnamon groves being transplanted,
their roots and sprouts have not yet taken hold.
The buds are shallow and the strings are tight;
I am constantly afraid that wind and waves will secretly alarm them,
and that hidden crises will burst forth.
This is why I am fearful and cautious on the long road,
pulling on the reins and sighing.
Furthermore, the nature of the northern land
makes it difficult to take root.
To present a night-shining pearl to a person
rarely results in them not clutching their sword in suspicion.
Now, to plant oranges and pomelos in Xuánshuò,
or to make lotuses bloom on Xiūlíng,
to display dragon-patterned garments in a land of nakedness,
or to perform the Sháo dance for a deaf populace—
it is truly difficult to find value there.
If things do not value me,
then no one will assist me;
if no one assists me,
then those who would harm me will arrive.
A wandering scholar drifting far away,
entrusting his person to a land without people,
gathering the reins on a distant road—
then there are the hardships of the aforementioned words.
Hanging the saddle in a humble dwelling,
then there is the warning of later concerns.
When the morning glow begins to shine,
then the body is exhausted from hurried travel;
when the sun hides its light,
then the heart is weary with evening vigilance.
Casting my gaze over the level wetlands,
all is vast and void with nothing to see;
straining my ears toward the long plains,
all is silent and still with nothing to hear.
Alas, how sorrowful!
My heart is wounded and distressed!
Only then does one know that those who rush about
are not worthy of being esteemed.
If one were to look back at one's shadow in the Central Plains,
indignant energy would surge like clouds.
Mourning for all things and grieving for the world,
with passions as fierce as the wind,
gazing like a dragon across the great wilds,
roaring like a tiger throughout the universe,
with fierce spirit in abundance,
and heroic heart occupying the four directions.
Thinking to tread upon the cloud-ladder,
and to strive horizontally across the eight poles,
to cleave through hardships and sweep away filth,
to stir the seas and level the mountains,
kicking Kūnlún so it collapses to the west,
trampling Tàishān so it overturns to the east,
thoroughly cleansing the nine regions,
and expanding the bounds of the universe—
this too is my humble wish.
But time is not on my side;
I droop my wings and depart far away.
Sharp edges cannot be applied,
and the pinions are broken and bent.
Unless one understands fate,
who could not be filled with indignant melancholy?
My friend, you have planted your roots in a fragrant garden,
and raised your excellence in pure streams.
Spreading your leaves on flowery cliffs,
and flying your literary patterns in the cloud-market.
Below, you occupy the abyss of the hidden dragon;
above, you enjoy the shade of the forest where the phoenix perches.
Glorious splendor dazzles before you,
and alluring colors entice behind you.
Good companions associate on your left,
and fame and reputation gallop on your right.
Soaring among your peers,
and showing off your elegance within the inner chambers.
Calmly looking about,
you have ample leisure;
bending and looking up, chanting and whistling,
you think you have achieved your aims.
How could you share with me the joys and sorrows of a great man!
Depart now, Jī Shēng;
we are forever separated!
Alone and drifting,
I approach the desert!
Long and far are the three thousand lǐ,
a road difficult to cross!
The time for holding hands again
is distantly without a day!
The thoughts in my heart become more knotted;
who can say they will be released!
Do not let your voice be like gold and jade
while your heart is far away.
Though our bodies are as far apart as the Hú and Yuè,
let our intentions remain firm enough to cut through gold.
Let each respect your own conduct,
and sincerely practice simplicity and depth.
Flamboyance and drifting vanity
are not what a gentleman admires.
Approaching this letter, I am filled with grief;
I know not what more to say!
Qiú Chí bows his head.
To General Chén, beneath your feet:
I hope you are without ailment,
which would be most fortunate!
General, your courage is the foremost of the three armies,
and your talent is extraordinary for this generation.
You cast aside the small ambitions of swallows and sparrows
and admired the high flight of the great swan.
In the past, you transformed according to the opportunity
and encountered an enlightened lord.
You established merit and affairs,
founded a fief and called yourself "Gū."
With red wheels and ornate hubs,
you held the banner over ten thousand lǐ—
how magnificent that was!
How is it that one day you became a fleeing captive,
your thighs trembling at the sound of a whistling arrow,
and your knees bending before a yurt—
how inferior that is!
Looking into the circumstances of your departure or staying,
there was no other reason
than that you could not examine yourself within,
and externally you were influenced by rumors,
becoming lost and frantic,
and so reaching this point.
The Sage Court pardons crimes and rewards merit,
disregards flaws and employs the capable.
It extends its sincerity to all under heaven
and settles the restless among all things.
This is what the General knows,
and it does not require me to speak of it in detail.
Zhū Wěi shed the blood of the Emperor's brother;
Zhāng Xiù plunged a blade into his beloved son;
yet the Lord of Hàn did not hold suspicion toward them,
and the Ruler of Wèi treated them as old friends.
Moreover, you, General, do not have the crimes of those of old,
and your past merits are heavy in this age.
To know to return when lost on the path
is what the ancient sages approved;
to return before going too far
is what the former classics hold in high esteem.
Our Sovereign bends the law to extend grace;
even a ship-swallowing fish is allowed to slip through the net.
General, your pines and cypresses have not been cut,
your relatives live in peace,
your high terraces have not collapsed,
and your beloved concubines are still there.
Your heart is far-reaching;
what more can be said!
Now the meritorious officials and famous generals
are arranged in order like a flight of wild geese.
They wear purple and carry gold seals,
assisting with plans in the military tent,
or riding light carriages and holding tallies,
taking up duties on the borders.
They have all sworn oaths by sacrificing a horse
to pass these honors to their descendants.
You alone, General, live in shame with a borrowed life,
driven by the leader of those in felt robes—
is this not lamentable?
Consider the power of Mùróng Chāo,
yet his body was sent to the Eastern Market;
consider the prosperity of Yáo Hóng,
yet he was bound and taken to the Western Capital.
Thus we know that where frost and dew fall equally,
different species are not nurtured.
The old lands of Jī and Hàn
do not accept mixed tribes.
The northern captives have usurped the Central Plains
for many years.
Their evil has accumulated and their calamities are full;
by logic, they have reached the point of collapse.
Moreover, their illegitimate scions are dim-witted and cunning,
slaughtering each other.
Their tribes are drifting apart,
and their chieftains are suspicious and divided.
They are about to have their necks bound in the Barbarian Residence
and their heads hung in Gǎojiē.
Yet you, General, are like a fish swimming in a boiling pot,
or a swallow nesting on a tent on fire—
is this not delusion?
In the third month of late spring,
the grass grows long in Jiāngnán,
various flowers bloom on the trees,
and flocks of orioles fly about.
Seeing the flags and drums of your old country,
and being moved by the memories of your past life,
as you touch the strings and mount the parapets, how could you not be filled with grief?
This is why Lord Lián thought of being a general for Zhào,
and Wú Zǐ wept at Xīhé—
it is human nature.
Could it be that only you, General, are without feeling?
I hope you will soon strive for a virtuous course of action
and seek many blessings for yourself.
The current Emperor is grand and enlightened,
and the whole world is at peace and happy.
White jade rings are presented from the west,
and arrows of bitter-wood arrive from the east;
Yèláng and Diānchí
unbraid their hair and request official posts;
Cháoxiǎn and Chānghǎi
bow their heads and receive transformation.
Only the Northern Dí have wild ambitions,
stubbornly resisting amidst the sandy frontiers,
merely wishing to prolong their lives for a few more years.
His Highness the Central Army Prince of Línchuān,
of illustrious virtue and close kinship,
commands these heavy military affairs,
consoling the people at the bend of the Luò River,
and punishing the guilty in Qínzhōng.
If you ultimately do not change,
you will only then reflect upon my words.
I briefly express my past feelings;
may you consider them carefully.
Qiū Chí bows his head.
After Marquis Liú repeatedly raised these difficulties,
it happened that I suffered the mourning of a close relative,
so in the end, I did not deliver the response.
Shortly after, this gentleman passed away forever,
transforming into another form,
and his initial words and remaining discourses
were stored away and not transmitted.
Someone obtained them from his family and showed them to me;
I grieve that his refined tone has not yet faded,
yet the man is already gone;
the green bamboo slips are still fresh,
but the grass over his grave is about to grow thick;
I weep, not knowing from where my tears come.
Though time passes like a horse glimpsed through a crack and does not stay,
and a wave or a flash of lightning vanishes,
yet the autumn chrysanthemums and spring orchids,
their flowery brilliance never ceases;
therefore, I preserve the outline
and further respond to his intentions.
If the words of Mò Dí are not in error,
and the conversation in the Xuānshì Hall has evidence,
I hope the trees of Dōngpíng
will lean westward toward Xiányáng;
and the spring of Gàishān
will flow to the rhythm upon hearing stringed music and song.
But with the sword hanging at the empty tomb,
what can be done about this regret!
Liú Xīn was an intimate attendant;
he wished to establish the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū, the Máo Shī, the Yì Lǐ, and the Gǔwén Shàngshū,
all to be ranked among the official academic positions.
Āidì ordered Liú Xīn to discuss and debate the proposal with the Doctors of the Five Classics,
but some of the Confucian Doctors refused to respond.
Liú Xīn therefore sent a letter to the Doctors of the Tàicháng, rebuking them, saying:
Long ago, after Táng and Yú declined,
the Three Dynasties rose in succession;
sage emperors and enlightened kings
rose repeatedly and followed one another,
and their Way was very prominent.
After the Zhōu house became weak,
rites and music were no longer correct;
such is the difficulty of keeping the Way complete.
For this reason, Kǒngzǐ worried that the Way was not being practiced;
he traveled through various states to accept employment.
After returning to Lǔ from Wèi,
then the music was corrected,
and the Yǎ and Sòng sections found their proper places.
He edited the Yì and arranged the Shū,
and composed the Chūnqiū
to record the Way of emperors and kings.
When the Master passed away, his subtle words ceased;
when the seventy disciples died, the great principles became distorted.
Then came the Warring States period;
the rituals of the sacrificial vessels were discarded,
and military formations were managed instead.
The Way of Kǒng was suppressed,
and the arts of Sūn and Wú flourished.
Decline continued until the tyrannical Qín,
who burned the classics,
killed the Confucian scholars,
established laws against possessing books,
and punished those who "affirmed the past,"
causing the arts of the Way to perish.
When the Hàn rose,
it was far removed from the sage emperors and enlightened kings;
the Way of Zhòngní had been severed,
and there were no laws or regulations to inherit.
At that time, there was only one Shūsūn Tōng,
who briefly established the rituals and ceremonies.
In the world, there were only books on the Yì and divination,
and no other books.
By the reign of Xiàohuì,
the law against possessing books was finally abolished;
however, the high officials and ministers like Jiàng and Guàn
were all armored warriors
and paid no mind to it.
By the time of Emperor Xiàowén,
he first sent the archivist Cháo Cuò
to receive the Shàngshū from Fú Shēng.
The Shàngshū first emerged from the walls of a house,
decayed, broken, and scattered;
the book exists now,
but teachers of the time merely transmit and read it.
The Shī began to sprout,
and various books in the world
frequently appeared,
all being the legends and sayings of the various masters,
yet they were widely established in the academic offices,
and Doctors were appointed for them.
Among the Confucians at court,
there was only Jiǎ Shēng.
By the time of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
then in Zōu, Lǔ, Liáng, and Zhào,
there were several early teachers of the Shī, Lǐ, and Chūnqiū;
they all emerged during the Jiànyuán period.
At this time,
one person could not master the entire classic alone;
some did the Yǎ,
some did the Sòng,
and they were combined to become complete.
The Tàishì was found later,
and the Doctors gathered to praise it.
Therefore, the imperial edict said:
"Rites are ruined and music has collapsed;
the Shū is missing and slips are lost;
I am deeply concerned by this."
At that time, the Hàn had already been established for seventy or eighty years,
and it was certainly far removed from the complete classics.
When Lǔ Gōng Wáng demolished Kǒngzǐ's house
to build a palace,
he found ancient texts within the broken walls.
There were thirty-nine chapters of the Yì Lǐ
and sixteen chapters of the Shū.
After the Tiānhàn period,
Kǒng Ānguó presented them.
Due to the sudden disaster of the witchcraft affair,
they were not yet implemented.
As for the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū compiled by Qiūmíng,
these were all old books in ancient script;
at most, there were over twenty copies,
stored in the secret archives,
hidden and not yet brought forth.
Emperor Xiàochéng, grieved that learning was fragmented and texts were incomplete,
and had gradually moved away from the truth,
so he opened the secret archives
and collated the old texts.
He obtained these three matters
to examine the classics transmitted by the academic offices,
noting where some slips were missing
or some bindings were lost.
When inquiring widely among the people,
it was found that the surviving scholarship of Lǔ Guó Huán Gōng,
Zhào Guó Guàn Gōng, and
Jiāodōng Yōng Shēng was the same as these,
yet it was suppressed and not implemented.
This is what the learned lament
and what the scholar-gentlemen sigh over in pain.
Scholars of the past who pursued learning
did not consider the gaps caused by loss and destruction,
but merely followed crude and meager sources,
dissecting phrases and analyzing characters,
with tedious words and trivial expressions;
scholars grew old and exhausted,
yet could not fully master even one art.
They trusted oral traditions and turned their backs on historical records,
affirming recent teachers and rejecting the ancients.
When it came to the state having major affairs,
such as establishing the rituals for the Bìyōng, the Fēngshàn sacrifices, or the imperial tours of inspection,
they were in the dark and knew not their origins.
Yet they still wish to preserve fragments and guard the incomplete,
harboring the private intention of fearing their views would be refuted,
and lacking the public-mindedness to follow what is good and submit to what is right.
Some harbor jealousy,
not examining the facts,
but blindly echoing one another.
Determining right and wrong based on hearsay,
they suppress these three fields of study,
claiming the Shàngshū is incomplete
and saying the Zuǒshì does not transmit the Chūnqiū.
Is this not lamentable!
Today the Sagely Emperor’s virtue reaches to the divine and bright;
he has succeeded to the lineage and promoted the heritage,
also pitying the confusion and disorder of these cultural teachings
and the state of the scholars being as such.
Although he deeply perceives their sentiments,
he still hesitates in modesty,
delighting in sharing with the scholars and gentlemen.
Therefore he issued a bright decree
to test whether the *Zuǒshì* could be established or not,
sending close ministers to convey the imperial will and carry out the mission,
intending to support the weak and sustain the subtle,
to join intentions and efforts with you gentlemen,
hoping to recover what has been discarded and left behind.
Now it is not so,
as you deeply shut yourselves off and stubbornly resist, refusing to even test it,
abruptly rejecting it on the grounds of not having recited it,
desiring to block other paths
and extinguish subtle learning.
One can enjoy the completion of a task with the masses,
but it is hard to deliberate the beginning with them;
this is the conduct of the common people,
not what is expected of scholars and gentlemen.
Furthermore, the matters of these several houses
were all personally discussed by the Former Emperor
and examined by the current Emperor;
their status as Old Text and ancient books
all have evidence and proof,
corresponding internally and externally;
how could it be just a random matter!
When the rites are lost, one seeks them in the wild;
is not Old Text still better than the wild?
In the past, among the Erudites,
for the *Shū* there was Ōuyáng,
for the *Chūnqiū* there was Gōngyáng,
and for the *Yì* there were Shī and Mèng;
yet Emperor Xiàoxuāndì still further established the Gǔliáng *Chūnqiū*, the Liángqiū *Yì*, and the Dàxiàhòu and Xiǎoxiàhòu *Shàngshū*;
and though their meanings were contradictory,
he still placed them together.
Why?
Rather than the error of discarding them,
it is better to have the error of establishing them.
The *Tradition* says:
"The Way of Wén and Wǔ
has not yet fallen to the ground;
it resides in people;
the worthy remember its great aspects,
and the unworthy remember its minor aspects."
Now the words of these several houses
are that which encompasses the meanings of both the great and the small;
how can they be partially cut off?
If you must be preoccupied with yourselves and guard the broken pieces,
favoring those of the same school,
envying the truth of the Way,
disobeying the bright decree,
and failing the Sagely intent,
thereby falling into the criticism of the legal clerks,
it is something very much not to be taken up by you gentlemen.
The excellence of Zhōngshān,
the spirit of the thatched hall.
Smoke gallops along the courier route;
this proclamation is inscribed in the mountain courtyard.
With the mark of uprightness that rises above the vulgar,
and the thought of elegance that transcends the dust.
Comparing pureness to the white snow,
reaching for the blue clouds to rise straight up.
I have just come to know it.
If he stood tall above all things,
bright and clear beyond the mist,
regarding a thousand pieces of gold as chaff and not looking back,
casting off the position of ten thousand chariots like a worn-out sandal,
hearing the phoenix-flute at Luòpǔ,
or encountering the woodcutter's song at Yánlài—
surely such people existed.
How could one expect the beginning and end to be so disparate,
turning over so rapidly and unpredictably?
Weeping with the sorrow of Zhái Zǐ,
mourning with the cry of Zhū Gōng.
Suddenly turning back his tracks as his heart is tainted;
perhaps first pure and later defiled.
How erroneous!
Alas!
Shàng Shēng is no longer here,
Zhòng Shì has already passed away.
The mountain bend is lonely and desolate;
for a thousand years, who will appreciate it?
In this age, there is a certain Zhōu Zǐ,
a man of outstanding talent among the common.
Being both literary and broad in learning,
versed in both the mysterious and history.
However, his learning was of the recluses of Dōnglǔ,
his practice was the concealment of Nánguō.
Accompanying the flute in the thatched hall,
unjustifiably wearing the scholar's cap in the North Mountain.
He enticed our pines and cassias,
and deceived our cloudy valleys.
Though he borrowed a form on the riverbank,
he bound his heart to fine noble ranks.
When he first arrived,
he wished to push aside Cháofù,
and pull down Xǔ Yóu.
He disdained the Hundred Schools,
and looked down upon kings and lords.
His elegant spirit stretched across the sun,
his frosty vigor spanned the autumn.
Sometimes sighing for the long-gone recluse,
or lamenting that the Prince would not travel.
Discussing the "emptiness of emptiness" in the Buddhist scriptures,
or verifying the "mystery of mysteries" among the Daoist stream.
Wùguāng was not enough to compare with him,
Juānzǐ could not be his peer.
But when the heralds' cries entered the valley,
and the crane-summons arrived at the ridge,
his form raced and his soul scattered,
his will changed and his spirit was moved.
Thereupon his eyebrows lifted at the banquet,
his sleeves rose high above the mat.
He burned his water-chestnut robe and tore his lotus garment,
assuming a dusty face and running with a vulgar appearance.
The wind and clouds are mournful and filled with indignation;
the rocky springs sob and flow down in sorrow.
Gazing at the woods and ridges, they feel a sense of loss;
looking at the grass and trees, they seem in mourning.
When he finally tied on the golden seal
and fastened the black ribbon,
overriding the heroes of the subordinate cities,
and becoming the head of a hundred miles,
spreading his brilliant spirit in the coastal regions
and racing his fine reputation to the west of the Zhè River,
his Daoist scrolls were long buried,
and his Dharma seats long interred.
The clamor of beating and flogging disturbs his thoughts,
and the rush of petitions and lawsuits fills his heart.
The songs of the zither have ceased,
and the rhapsodies of wine have no continuation.
Always preoccupied with taxation and assessments,
constantly entangled in the resolution of legal cases,
trapping Zhāng and Zhào within past records,
and placing Zhuō and Lǔ above former accounts,
he aspires to the traces of the heroes of the Sānfǔ
and spreads his fame as a Shepherd of the Jiǔzhōu.
Leaving our high mists to shine alone,
our bright moon to rise in solitude.
The green pines drop their shadows;
who will be the companion of the white clouds?
The mountain stones are broken and have none to return to;
the stone path is desolate, making us wait in vain.
As for the returning gale entering the curtains,
or the mist flowing out from the pillars—
the orchid-scented curtains are empty, and the night crane laments;
the mountain man has left, and the dawn gibbon is startled.
Formerly we heard of throwing away the hairpin to escape to the seacoast;
now we see the untying of orchids to be bound by the dusty tassels of office.
At this, the Southern Peak offers its mockery,
the Northern Ridge sends forth its laughter.
The various valleys compete in ridicule;
the clustered peaks raise their scorn.
Regretting that the traveler has deceived us,
grieving that no one comes to offer condolences.
Therefore, the forest's shame is endless,
and the stream's embarrassment does not cease.
The autumn cassia abandons its fragrance;
the spring vines stop the moonlight.
Spreading the leisurely criticism of the West Mountain,
carrying the pure visitation of the East Bank.
Now he is again packing his bags in the lower city,
carelessly dragging himself toward the capital.
Although his heart is set on the Wèiquè,
he perhaps takes a detour through the mountain gates.
How can we let the fragrant pollia have such a thick skin,
or the creeping figs be so shameless?
The green ridges are disgraced once more;
the cinnabar cliffs are defiled again.
To let dusty tracks wander on the orchid path,
or to pollute the clear pool to wash his ears?
We should lock the mountain caves
and shut the gates of clouds.
Gather the light mists;
hide the sounding rapids.
Cut off his coming carriage at the mouth of the valley;
block his reckless reins at the edge of the suburbs.
At this, the clusters of branches glare with courage,
and the overlapping ears of grain are angry in spirit.
Some flying branches to break his wheels;
others suddenly lowering boughs to sweep away his tracks.
Please turn back the carriage of this vulgar man;
and for you, I shall decline this runaway guest.
An announcement to the Governors of Bā and Shǔ:
The Mányí have acted willfully,
and it has been a long time since they were last punished.
They frequently invade the borders,
exhausting the scholar-officials.
Since His Majesty ascended the throne,
he has comforted and cared for the world
and brought peace and order to Zhōngguó.
Thereafter, he raised an army and sent forth troops
to the north to campaign against the Xiōngnú.
The Chányú was terrified;
he crossed his arms to receive orders
and knelt on his knees to sue for peace.
From Kāngjū and the Xìyù,
tribute has been brought through multiple translations,
and they have come to offer gifts by kowtowing.
When the army was moved to point toward the east,
the Mín Yuè killed one another.
To the right, he consoled Pānyú,
and the crown prince came to court.
The kings of the Nányí
and the chiefs of the western Bó
have constantly offered tribute and fulfilled their duties,
not daring to be negligent.
They crane their necks and stand on tiptoe in eager anticipation,
all looking toward our influence and admiring our righteousness,
wishing to become subjects.
Because the distances are vast
and the mountains and rivers are treacherous and deep,
they could not come of their own accord.
Those who were disobedient have already been executed,
yet those who act with goodness have not been rewarded.
Therefore, a Zhōnglángjiàng was dispatched to go and treat them as guests,
mobilizing five hundred men each from Bā and Shǔ
to carry silk and cloth as gifts
and to guard the envoy; otherwise,
there would be no military affairs
or the troubles of battle.
Now it is heard that the commanderies have mobilized the army and established regulations,
frightening the younger generations
and worrying the elders.
The commanderies have also arbitrarily engaged in the transport of grain,
none of which was His Majesty's intention.
Some of those who should have gone have fled or even killed themselves;
this is also not the integrity of a subject.
The soldiers of the border commanderies,
upon hearing the beacon fires lit and the signal smoke burning,
all seize their bows and gallop forth,
carrying their weapons and running,
with sweat flowing continuously,
fearing only that they might be left behind.
They face sharp blades
and brave flying arrows,
resolved never to look back,
and determined not to turn on their heels.
Each man harbors anger in his heart
as if to avenge a private feud.
Do they truly love death and hate life?
Are they not registered people,
or do they have a different lord than those of Bā and Shǔ?
It is because they plan deeply and consider the long term,
acting with urgency regarding the state's difficulties
and finding joy in fulfilling the way of a subject.
Therefore, they receive enfeoffments with tally-staves
and titles with jade scepters;
their rank becomes that of a Tōnghóu,
and they reside among the eastern mansions.
Ultimately, they leave an illustrious name to later generations
and pass on lands to their descendants.
Their actions are most loyal and respectful,
their positions are most secure and easy,
their reputation extends to infinity,
and their meritorious achievements are manifest and never extinguished.
This is why worthy men and gentlemen
have their brains smeared on the Central Plains
and their blood and marrow moisten the wild grass without refusal.
Now, when the duty of carrying gifts to the Nányí arrives,
you immediately kill yourselves
or flee and face execution.
You die without a name,
receive the posthumous title of "the most foolish,"
bring shame upon your parents,
and become the laughingstock of the world.
The difference between the capacities of men
is indeed vast!
However, this is not the fault of the travelers alone.
The instruction of fathers and elder brothers did not come first,
and the leadership of the younger generation was not diligent.
They have little sense of integrity or shame,
and the customs are not generous.
Is it not appropriate
that they suffer punishment and execution?
His Majesty is troubled that the envoys and officials are as they are,
and laments that the unworthy and foolish people are like this.
Therefore, he has sent a trusted messenger
to explain the matter of mobilizing troops to the common people,
while also enumerating the crimes of disloyalty and death,
and rebuking the Sānlǎo and the filial and fraternal for the fault of failing to instruct.
It is currently the farming season,
and I am reluctant to trouble the people again.
I have personally seen the nearby counties,
but I fear the people of the distant valleys and mountains have not all heard.
When this notice arrives,
send it down to the counties and districts immediately,
so that all may understand His Majesty's intent.
Do not be negligent.
The Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, concurrently the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, and the Chancellors and Governors of the commanderies and states.
I have heard that an enlightened lord plans for danger to control change,
and a loyal subject considers difficulties to establish authority.
Therefore, there must be extraordinary people
before there can be extraordinary events;
there must be extraordinary events
before extraordinary merit can be established.
That which is "extraordinary"
is truly something that ordinary people cannot fathom.
In the past, when the Qín was strong and the lord was weak,
Zhào Gāo held the handle of power.
He monopolized the authority of the court,
and prestige or blessings came only from himself.
The people of that time were intimidated and coerced,
and none dared to speak uprightly.
This ended in the disaster at Wàngyí,
the destruction of the ancestors,
a disgrace that remains to this day,
and an eternal warning to the world.
Coming to the final years of Empress Lǚ,
[Lǚ] Chǎn and [Lǚ] Lù monopolized the government.
Internally, they controlled the two armies;
externally, they commanded Liáng and Zhào.
They arbitrarily decided the ten thousand affairs of state
and settled matters within the forbidden palace.
The inferiors oppressed and the superiors were displaced;
everyone within the four seas was terrified.
Thereupon, the Marquis of Jiàng and the Marquis of Zhūxū raised troops in anger,
executed the rebellious and violent,
and honorably enthroned Tàizōng.
Thus, the Kingly Way was able to flourish,
and glory was brilliant and manifest.
This is a clear example of great ministers establishing authority.
The grandfather of the Sīkōng Cáo Cāo was the Zhōngchángshì Cáo Téng.
Along with Zuǒ Guàn and Xú Huáng, he acted as a malevolent pestilence.
They were voraciously greedy and acted with unbridled arrogance,
damaging social order and oppressing the people.
His father, Cáo Sōng,
was an adopted son who begged to be taken in.
He obtained his position through bribery,
carrying carriages of gold and carts of jade
to deliver bribes to the gates of the powerful.
He stole the high office of the Three Ducal Ministers
and subverted the sacred vessels of the state.
Cáo Cāo is the foul offspring of a eunuch’s adoption;
he inherently lacks noble virtue.
He is frivolous, cunning, and impulsively aggressive,
delighting in chaos and enjoying calamity.
Our headquarters commanded the brave and soaring troops
to sweep away the wicked rebels.
Later, we encountered Dǒng Zhuó,
who usurped offices and tyrannized the nation.
Thereupon we drew our swords and beat the drums,
issuing commands to the eastern lands.
We gathered heroes together,
overlooking their flaws to employ them.
Thus we consulted and conspired with Cáo Cāo,
entrusting him with an auxiliary force,
considering him to have the talent of a hunting dog or hawk,
whose "claws and teeth" could be put to use.
Yet he was foolish, frivolous, and lacked strategy,
advancing rashly and retreating easily.
Suffering wounds and crushing defeats,
he repeatedly lost his troops.
Our headquarters repeatedly divided our forces and sent elite troops
to mend his losses and replenish his ranks.
We petitioned for him to serve in Dōngjùn
and to act as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
endowing him with the prestige of a tiger's pelt
to bolster his authority,
hoping he would achieve a victory like the Qín army to repay us.
But Cáo Cāo then took advantage of these resources to become overbearing,
giving free rein to his wicked deeds,
exploiting and stripping the common people,
and harming the worthy and the good.
The former Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng, Biān Ràng,
a man of brilliant and extraordinary talent
renowned throughout the world,
spoke directly with a righteous countenance
and his discourse was never sycophantic;
yet his body and head suffered the punishment of execution and public display,
and his wife and children suffered the fate of total annihilation.
Since then, the scholar-officials have been filled with indignation and pain,
and the people’s resentment grew ever more profound.
One man raised his arm in protest,
and the entire province responded with one voice.
Thus he was personally defeated in Xúfāng,
and his territory was seized by Lǚ Bù.
He wandered aimlessly along the eastern borders,
with nowhere to plant his feet.
Our headquarters upheld the principle of strengthening the trunk and weakening the branches,
and would not join the clique of a rebel;
therefore we again raised our banners and donned our armor,
sweeping forward to launch a campaign.
The gongs and drums resounded,
and Lǚ Bù’s masses fled in defeat,
saving Cáo Cāo from the peril of death
and restoring him to his position as a regional governor.
Thus, while our headquarters might not have done a favor for the people of the Yǎnzhōu region,
we certainly bestowed a great blessing upon Cáo Cāo.
Later, when the Imperial Carriage returned
and a multitude of rebels launched attacks,
Jìzhōu was facing an alarm on its northern borders
and there was no time to leave our post.
So we sent the Cóngshì Zhōngláng Xú Xūn to dispatch Cáo Cāo,
ordering him to repair the Imperial Temples
and to guard the young Emperor.
Cáo Cāo then gave free rein to his desires and acted arbitrarily,
coercing the relocation of the Imperial palace.
He belittled and insulted the Royal House,
broke laws and disordered the administrative codes.
He assumed control of the Three Platforms
and monopolized the government of the court.
Titles and rewards were granted according to his own whims,
and punishments and executions depended on his word alone.
Those he favored brought glory to their entire clans,
while those he loathed had their families exterminated to the third degree.
Those who spoke openly were publicly executed,
and those who harbored secret criticisms were covertly slaughtered.
All the officials kept their mouths shut,
and people on the roads communicated only with their eyes.
The Shàngshū merely recorded the court assemblies,
and the Dukes and Ministers merely filled their seats.
The former Grand Commandant Yáng Biāo
had held office in the two supreme departments
and enjoyed the highest positions in the nation.
Cáo Cāo, because of a minor grudge,
accused him of a crime he did not commit,
inflicting beatings and floggings together
until every kind of torture was applied.
He followed his whims and indulged in malice,
disregarding the web of the law.
Furthermore, the Yìláng Zhào Chǎn
offered loyal remonstrance and direct speech;
his righteousness was worthy of being accepted.
Therefore, the Sacred Court listened with tolerance,
showing him respect and granting him honors.
Cáo Cāo wanted to blind the Emperor and seize his clarity
to block the path of free speech,
so he arbitrarily arrested and immediately killed him
without waiting to report the matter to the throne.
Furthermore, King Xiào of Liáng was an elder brother of the former Emperor’s mother;
his tomb was honored and prominent,
and the mulberry, catalpa, pine, and cypress trees surrounding it
should still be treated with solemn respect.
But Cáo Cāo led his generals and soldiers
to personally oversee the excavation,
breaking the coffin and exposing the corpse
to plunder the gold and treasures,
causing the Sacred Court to shed tears
and the officials and people to be heartbroken.
Cáo Cāo even specifically established the Fāqiū Zhōnglángjiàng and the Mòjīn Xiàowèi;
wherever they went, they caused destruction,
and no skeleton was left unexposed.
Personally occupying the position of one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
he behaves like the tyrant Jié and a common rebel,
defiling the nation and oppressing the people,
inflicting suffering on both the living and the dead.
Furthermore, his governance is meticulous and cruelly harsh;
laws and restrictions are set up everywhere,
like fishing nets and tethered arrows filling the paths,
and pits and traps blocking the roads.
Raising a hand, one gets caught in a net;
moving a foot, one triggers a trap.
Therefore, the people of Yǎn and Yù are wretched,
and the Imperial Capital is filled with the resentment of sighs.
Looking through all the historical records,
among wicked ministers
none have been as greedy, cruel, and brutal
as Cáo Cāo.
Our headquarters was then dealing with external traitors
and had not yet had time to rectify him,
so we showed him patience and tolerance
in the hope that he might reform.
But Cáo Cāo has the wild ambition of a wolf,
secretly harboring disastrous plots,
intending to break the pillars of the state
to weaken the House of Hàn,
eliminate the loyal and upright,
and exclusively become a ruthless leader.
In the past, when we launched a northern campaign against Gōngsūn Zàn,
a powerful rebel who was violent and defiant,
he resisted the siege for a year.
Cáo Cāo, because Gōngsūn Zàn was not yet defeated,
secretly exchanged letters with him,
outwardly pretending to assist the Imperial army
but inwardly plotting a surprise attack.
Therefore, he led his troops to the Huáng Hé
and lined up boats to cross to the north.
It so happened that his messenger was discovered,
and Gōngsūn Zàn was also exterminated;
thus his sharp edge was blunted
and his plot did not succeed.
Then, our great army swept through the Xīshān mountains,
and the Túgè and Zuǒxiào tribes
all surrendered and offered hostages,
competing to serve as our vanguard.
The wretched remnants of those dogs and sheep
vanished into the mountains and valleys.
Thereupon, Cáo Cāo’s army was terrified
and fled day and night.
They occupied Áocāng,
using the river as a defensive barrier,
wishing to use the forelegs of a praying mantis
to resist the path of a heavy carriage.
Our headquarters upholds the majestic authority of the Hàn
and overpowers the entire universe,
with a million long halberds
and a thousand troops of Hu cavalry.
Arousing warriors as strong as Zhōnghuáng, Yù, and Huò,
and unleashing the power of fine bows and strong crossbows,
the forces of Bìngzhōu cross the Tàiháng Mountains,
and the forces of Qīngzhōu wade through the Jǐ and Tà Rivers.
The great army crosses the Huáng Hé to confront him in the front,
and the forces of Jīngzhōu descend upon Wǎn and Shè to harass his rear.
With the power of thunder and the stride of a tiger,
they will all gather at the rebel’s court.
It is like using a blazing fire to burn flying tumbleweed,
or overturning the vast sea to extinguish smoldering coals.
How could anything not be destroyed!
Moreover, Cáo's officers and soldiers,
those capable of battle who themselves come from Yōu and Jì,
or who were former followers and units,
all are resentful and long for home,
shedding tears as they look back toward the north.
As for the remaining people of Yǎn and Yù,
and the remnants of the forces of Lǚ Bù and Zhāng Yáng,
they were defeated and coerced,
following only temporarily and opportunistically.
Each has been wounded and mistreated,
and they regard him as a mortal enemy.
If the banners are turned to advance,
and one ascends the high ridges to beat the drums and play the instruments,
waving white banners to open the road for surrender,
they will surely collapse like crumbling earth or breaking tiles,
without waiting for a blade to be bloodied.
At present, the Hàn Imperial House is in decline,
its fundamental principles have slackened and snapped,
the Sacred Court lacks even a single protector,
and the high officials have no power to overcome opposition.
Within the capital region,
the selected and trained ministers
all hang their heads and fold their wings,
having nothing to rely upon.
Though there are loyal and righteous assistants,
they are intimidated by violent and tyrannical ministers—
how can they display their integrity?
Furthermore, Cáo holds seven hundred elite troops of his personal command,
surrounding and guarding the palace gates,
outwardly claiming to be the imperial guard,
but inwardly actually holding the Emperor captive.
It is feared that the seeds of his usurpation and treason
will sprout because of this.
This is the time when loyal ministers would smear their brains and livers upon the earth,
and the opportunity for heroic men to establish their merit—
can one not be encouraged?
Cáo has also forged mandates and claimed the Emperor's authority,
sending envoys to mobilize troops.
It is feared that in distant border provinces and commanderies,
people may listen mistakenly and provide them.
A powerful bandit and a weak lord,
defying the masses and rebelling with his troops;
to support him is to lose one’s reputation
and become the laughingstock of the world,
which a wise and brilliant person would not choose.
On this day, the four provinces of Yōu, Bìng, Qīng, and Jì advance together.
When this letter reaches Jīngzhōu,
immediately muster the available troops
to coordinate your momentum with the General of Jiànzhōng.
Let the provinces and commanderies each prepare their horses and weapons,
patrolling the borders,
raising the army to display its majesty,
and together rectifying the state.
Then extraordinary merit
will thus be manifested.
Whoever obtains Cáo’s head
shall be enfeoffed as a marquis of five thousand households
and rewarded with fifty million coins.
For those subordinates, vice-generals, colonels, and various officers who surrender,
no questions shall be asked of them.
Widely proclaim grace and trustworthiness,
distribute and announce tallies and rewards,
and declare to the whole world,
making everyone know that the Sacred Court is suffering the hardship of coercion.
Let it be as the laws and orders prescribe.
In the [blank] year, month, and day,
Viscount and Prefect of the Masters of Writing Yù,
addresses the various generals, colonels, and units of Jiāngdōng, as well as the relatives and associates of Sūn Quán, both within and without:
I have heard that misfortune and fortune have no gate of their own,
but are summoned only by individuals themselves.
To act upon seeing the opportunity
and not remain in danger and peril
is the brilliance of the highest sage.
To control changes when facing events and to find a way through when cornered
is the deliberation of a wise person.
To be soaked in waste and decadence,
going forward and never returning,
is the blindness of the lowest fool.
Therefore, the noble person of great refinement
thinks of danger while in safety
to stay far from blame and regret;
the petty person harbors thoughts of ease while facing disaster
and waits for death.
The capacity of these two—
are they not truly different?
The young boy Sūn Quán
cannot even distinguish beans from wheat.
His neck and waist are not worth greasing the executioner’s axe,
and his name is not worth defiling the bamboo slips and ink.
He is like a chick in an egg,
just beginning to grow feathers,
yet he already acts with reckless arrogance
and turns back to bark at his master.
He thinks that boats and oars are enough to resist the Imperial majesty,
and that rivers and lakes can allow him to escape divine punishment,
not knowing that the heavenly net is spread wide,
and that he is already within its mesh.
Like a fish in a cooking pot,
its time of dissolution and decay is certain.
If water could be relied upon,
then the Sānmiáo would not have been ruined at Dòngtíng,
Zǐyáng would not have suffered defeat at Jīngmén,
the fortifications of Cháoxiǎn would not have been leveled,
and the banners of Nányuè would not have been uprooted.
In the past, Fūchāi inherited the distant achievements of Hélǘ
and used the military training of Shēnxū;
when he cornered the Yuè at Huìjī,
he could be called powerful indeed.
But when he contended with the great states of the north
and vied for supremacy with Jìn,
his capital was slaughtered by Gōujiàn,
his elite soldiers were scattered at Huángchí,
and he ended in total destruction,
his own person perishing at the hands of the Yuè army.
When Bì, the Prince of Wú, was arrogant and stubborn,
and began his reckless rebellion,
he considered himself to have strong soldiers and a wealthy state,
and his power threatened the capital city.
But as soon as the Grand Commandant led his army
and reached Xíngyáng,
the armies of the seven states
collapsed like tiles and melted like ice.
Before the curses of Bì had even ceased from his mouth,
the blade at Dāntú had already pierced his chest.
Why is this?
Because the Heavenly majesty cannot be withstood,
and the crime of rebellion is grave.
Moreover, the multitudes of the rivers and lakes
are not enough to be relied upon.
Since Dǒng Zhuó caused disorder,
down to the present day,
it has been nearly thirty years.
In the meantime, heroes and tyrants have run rampant,
crouching like bears and squatting like tigers;
those as powerful as the two Yuán,
as brave as Lǚ Bù,
straddling provinces and connecting commanderies,
possessing prestige and fame,
there were more than ten such groups.
The rest, rising up with sharp weapons and defensive strength,
glaring like hawks and looking back like wolves,
contending to be ambitious overlords,
cannot be fully counted.
However, they all fell before the executioner's blade or were entangled by the battle-axe;
their heads and waists were separated,
they dispersed like clouds or were scorched like the plains,
with not a single one remaining.
Recently, the various generals of Guānzhōng
again gathered together
to continue their rebellion,
obstructing the two Huà mountains
and occupying the Hé and Wèi rivers;
they drove and led the Qiāng and Hú,
pointing their weapons eastward in unison,
with high spirits and far-reaching ambitions,
appearing as if they were invincible.
The Chéngxiàng, wielding the battle-axe and soaring like an eagle,
like a fierce fire aided by the wind,
set the grand army in motion,
and before the drums were even beaten, they were crushed;
fallen corpses numbered in the tens of millions,
and the flowing blood floated away shields—
these are all matters known to everyone in the world.
The reason why the great army later reached the river but did not cross
was that Hán Yuē and Mǎ Chāo had escaped and fled,
returning to Liángzhōu,
where they once again wished to howl and bark in rebellion.
The rebel Sòng Jiàn
arrogated a title at Héshǒu;
evil allies came to each other's rescue,
acting as lips and teeth to one another.
Furthermore, Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Zhāng Lǔ,
relying on his strongholds, was disrespectful.
All were those upon whom our King’s punishment should first be inflicted.
Therefore, observing the troops and turning back the banners for a time,
we reorganized the six armies
for a long-distance western campaign
to carry out the world's punishment.
When a lieutenant general crossed Lǒng,
then Sòng Jiàn and Hán Yuē were decapitated and exterminated,
their heads displayed on banners for ten thousand lǐ;
when the army entered Sànguān,
then the various Dī tribes submitted,
and their kings, marquises, and powerful chieftains
hastened to become the vanguard.
Advancing to Hànzhōng,
then Yángpíng could not be defended,
and an army of one hundred thousand
collapsed like earth and rotted like fish;
Zhāng Lǔ fled in hiding,
escaping into Bāzhōng,
but cherishing grace and repenting for his errors,
he offered his allegiance and surrendered.
The Bā Yí King Pǔ Hú and the Cóng Town Marquis Dù Huò,
each leading their tribes,
together surrendered Bājùn
to serve the King's office.
As soon as the gongs and drums sounded,
both regions were settled;
benefits reached as far as the Xīhǎi,
without the weapons' edges becoming dull.
Matters such as these
are all due to the majestic brilliance of Heaven
and the divine martial power of the Altars of Soil and Grain;
they are not merely what human strength can achieve.
The Sagely Court’s broad benevolence covers and carries all,
being truly faithful and truly cultured;
it greatly bestows titles and commands
to show to the four directions.
Zhāng Lǔ as well as Pǔ Hú and Dù Huò all enjoyed enfeoffments of ten thousand households;
Zhāng Lǔ’s five sons
each received estates of a thousand households,
and the sons, brothers, and subordinate officers of Pǔ Hú and Dù Huò who became Lièhóu, Jiāngjūn, and below numbered more than a thousand.
The common people live in peace,
and the four classes of people have returned to their professions.
But as for those of the clique of Sòng Jiàn and Hán Yuē,
they have all become like executed rebels;
the wife and children of Mǎ Chāo
had their heads burned in Jīnchéng,
and his parents and infants
had their corpses exposed in the marketplace of Xǔ.
It is not that the State concentrated misfortune upon them
and sent down blessings upon these others,
but the distinction between rebellion and submission
makes it necessarily so.
