Now, a bird of prey's strike is preceded by flying high—
it is the momentum of the pounce;
the awe-inspiring power at Mùyě
was due to the earlier withdrawal at Mèngjīn.
Now, the thorns and brambles have been cleared away,
the barbarians and the Huáxià are purified,
for ten thousand lǐ all is solemn and orderly,
and the six armies have nothing to do.
Therefore, we are raising a great Celestial Army of a million strong,
together with the Xiōngnú South Chányú Hūwánchú, as well as the Wūhuán of the six commanderies, the Dīnglíng, and the Túgè,
and the Qiāng and Bó of Huángzhōng,
thundering forth and sweeping away all
from Shòuchūn southward.
Furthermore, commanding Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Xiàhóu Yuān and others,
leading fifty thousand elite armored troops,
along with the Dī and Qiāng of Wǔdū
and the sharp soldiers of Bā and Hàn,
to face the Wènjiāng in the south
and choke the routes to Yōng and Shǔ.
The various armies of Jiāngxià and Xiāngyáng
will cross the Xiāng and Yuán rivers
to descend upon Yùzhāng;
the fleet of tower-ships that cross the sea
will point directly at Wúhuì.
Setting a date across ten thousand lǐ,
advancing along five routes simultaneously,
the allotted fate of Quán
has thus arrived.
The Chéngxiàng (Chancellor) bears the majesty of the state,
eliminating harms for the people;
the chief villains and great evildoers
must be executed and exterminated.
As for those who were merely followers,
they are not the specific targets of the imperial decree's wrath.
Therefore, every time a powerful enemy is destroyed,
he never fails to prioritize offering surrender before execution,
selecting generals and recruiting talent,
so that each may fulfill their potential.
Thus, men of merit
all stand on tiptoe and crane their necks,
responding at the first sign of his influence.
In the past, when Yuán Shù committed treason,
and the royal punishment was about to be meted out,
the Tàishǒu (Grand Administrator) of Lújiāng, Liú Xūn, was the first to surrender his commandery
and return to the state.
When Lǚ Bù caused chaos
and the army approached Xiàpī,
Zhāng Liáo and Hóu Chéng
led their troops out to surrender.
During the campaign to suppress Suī Gù,
Xuē Hóng and Jiū Shàng
opened the city gates and submitted to civilization.
At the Battle of Guāndù,
Zhāng Hé and Gāo Huàn took action and established merit.
Later, when Yuán Shàng was attacked,
the Dūdū Jiāngjūn (Commander-General) Mǎ Yán,
the former Cìshǐ (Inspector) of Yùzhōu, Yīn Kuí,
and the Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Archer-at-Call) Guō Zhāo surrendered on the battlefield.
During the siege of Yè Chéng,
Jiāngjūn (General) Sū Yóu acted as an internal ally,
and the nephew of Shěn Pèi opened the gate to let the troops in.
After Yuán Tán was executed,
the Dàjiàng (Great General) of Yōuzhōu, Jiāo Chù, attacked and drove out Yuán Xī,
taking action to submit.
There are hundreds of people of this sort,
all of whom are loyal, brave, decisive, and fierce,
possessing both wisdom and benevolence;
they all participated in planning and strategy with the Chéngxiàng (Chancellor),
thwarting enemies and suppressing troubles,
cutting down foes and capturing banners,
and bringing peace to the land;
how could their actions be taken lightly!
Truly, Heaven enlightened their hearts,
and their planning was deep and far-sighted;
they discerned the path between the heterodox and the orthodox,
and clarified the distinction between what is permissible and what is not;
their bravery was not wasted in empty death,
and their integrity was not established through reckless means;
they adapted to changes,
following wherever the Dào (Way) resided.
Thus they achieved merits as great as mountains
and enjoyed immeasurable emoluments;
in the morning they were enemies and captives,
yet by evening they were top generals.
This is what is meant by knowing how to adapt when facing difficulty
and turning misfortune into blessing.
As for those lured by sweet words,
who cling to small treasures and minor favors,
remaining stagnant and making do,
sinking without realizing it,
drifting with the waves,
and perishing together with the sparks,
they are also very numerous.
Fortune and misfortune, gain and loss—
is it not lamentable!
In past years when the army was in Hànzhōng,
separated by great distances from east to west,
the garrison left at Héféi
was less than five thousand,
yet Sūn Quán personally led a host of tens of thousands,
only to be defeated and flee.
Now he wishes to withstand the thunder of the imperial wrath;
success can hardly be expected.
The Way of Heaven assists the obedient,
and the Way of Man assists the trustworthy.
Serving the superior is called righteousness,
and being close to kin is called benevolence.
Shèng Xiàozhāng
was a lord,
yet Sūn Quán executed him;
Sūn Fǔ
was an elder brother,
yet Sūn Quán killed him.
To betray righteousness and destroy benevolence—
nothing is more extreme than this.
He is a criminal escaping the divine spirits,
and a common enemy of the people below.
A man of such crimes and enmity
is called a vicious bandit.
Therefore, when Yī Zhì left Xià,
it did not damage his virtue;
when Fēi Lián died for Zhòu,
he could not be called worthy.
Why is this?
The way of choosing whether to leave or join
each has its proper fitness.
The Chéngxiàng (Chancellor) deeply considers that the former virtuous and famous ministers of Jiāngdōng
are numerous in the records.
Recently, Wèi Shūyīng stood out like a high peak,
famous throughout the land;
Yú Wénxiù honed his pure integrity,
immersed in learning and fond of antiquity;
Zhōu Tàimíng was a talent of the age,
his virtuous conduct refined and bright.
All should have received much blessing
and protected their descendants.
Yet the households of Zhōu and Shèng were slaughtered without guilt,
and the survivors were scattered,
lost in the forests and wilds.
To speak of it is heartbreaking.
I have heard that Wèi Zhōuróng and Yú Zhòngxiáng each continued their family legacies,
capable of carrying on the family burden.
As well as the elders of the Gù and Lù clans in Wú,
who have held high positions for generations,
they should repay the virtue of Hàn
and bring glory to their ancestors and fame to themselves.
As for the various officers and the relatives by marriage of Sūn Quán,
all are fine treasures and sharp tools of our state,
yet all are being driven and oppressed;
like rain cut off from heaven,
or an axe without a handle,
how can they save themselves?
Falling and perishing together,
is it not sad!
A phoenix sings on a high ridge
to stay far from the nets;
this is the virtue of the worthy and sage.
The shrike bird
nests on the tips of reeds;
the reed breaks and the chicks perish;
this is the delusion of the extremely foolish.
Now the land of Jiāngdōng
is no different from the tips of reeds.
If you worthy men stay there,
it is truly dangerous indeed.
The Holy Court is magnanimous and open,
deeply valuing the lives of the people.
Punishment is aimed at one man alone,
with no ill will toward the masses.
Therefore, extraordinary rewards are established
to await extraordinary merit.
This is the perfect time for heroes and men of character to risk their lives;
how can you not exert yourselves!
If you can suddenly take great action
and establish great merit
to receive illustrious emoluments,
that would be the highest blessing.
If you cannot do so,
then weigh the scale of matters;
to exchange death for survival
is the next best thing.
When a trap catches the foot,
the fierce tiger bites off its paw;
when a viper bites the hand,
the brave man cuts off his wrist.
Why?
Because what he preserves is important,
and what he discards is insignificant.
As for those who enjoy disaster and cling to tranquility,
getting lost and forgetting to return,
obscuring what is preserved in the Dàyǎ (Great Odes),
turning away from the choices of former sages,
neglecting the safety of the morning sun,
and content with the tip of the breaking reed;
forgetting day after day
until reaching complete destruction;
once the great army is unleashed,
jade and stone will both be crushed.
Even if one wishes to save them,
it will be too late.
Therefore, we order the announcement of rewards and ranks;
the articles are listed below.
When this proclamation arrives,
ponder these ultimate words carefully.
Act in accordance with the imperial decree and law.
In the past, when the mandate of the Hàn dynasty declined and grew faint,
the land within the four seas fell into ruin and division.
The lives of the common people
were nearly extinguished.
Our Tàizǔ Wǔ Huángdì,
with divine martiality and sagely wisdom,
quelled the chaos and restored order.
He rescued that which was about to fall
and refounded our Qū Xià.
Gāozǔ Wén Huángdì responded to Heaven and accorded with the people
to receive the mandate and ascend the throne.
Lièzǔ Míng Huángdì continued the brilliant light through successive generations,
expanding and broadening the great undertaking.
However, beyond the rivers and mountains,
there remained different governments and strange customs;
the common people of those lands
had not yet received the kingly transformation.
This is why the Three Ancestors looked back with concern and left behind their unfulfilled will.
Now the current Sovereign’s sagely virtue is reverent and bright,
succeeding and prospering the former lineage.
The high ministers are loyal, solemn, wise, and just,
laboring diligently for the Royal House.
They spread governance and bestow grace so that the ten thousand states are in harmony;
they extend virtue to the hundred barbarian tribes so that the Sùshèn bring tribute.
Lamenting that Bā-Shǔ
alone remains a non-compliant people,
and pitying those commoners
whose labor and military service never cease,
the mandate was therefore given to the Six Armies
to reverently execute the Heavenly punishment.
The various forces of Zhēngxī, Yōngzhōu, and Zhènxī
advanced simultaneously along five routes.
In the military operations of the ancients,
benevolence was the foundation,
and righteousness was used to govern it.
The army of a true King
punishes but does not wage war.
Thus, Yú Shùn danced with the shield and battle-axe and the Yǒumiáo submitted;
Zhōu Wǔ had the righteousness of distributing wealth, opening granaries, and honoring the gates of the virtuous.
Now the Zhènxī General, upholding the proclamation and bearing the mandate,
takes command of the war chariots.
He desires to promote the instruction of civil proclamations
to save the lives of the great masses.
It is not his wish to exhaust military force or push war to its limit
to gratify a temporary ambition.
Therefore, he briefly sets forth the essentials of safety and peril;
may you respectfully listen to his words.
The First Lord of Yìzhōu, being a talent of his age,
raised troops in Xīnyě,
but was cornered and stumbled in the outskirts of Jì and Xú,
his fate controlled by the hands of Shào and Bù.
Tàizǔ rescued and aided him,
and their friendship flourished greatly.
Midway, he turned his back and rebelled,
abandoning the same to join the different.
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng repeatedly planned for Qínchuān,
and Jiāng Bóyuē many times came out from Lǒngyòu,
wearying our borders
and harassing our Dī and Qiāng.
At that time, the state had many troubles,
and had no leisure to carry out the expeditions of the Nine Punishments.
Now the borders are settled and clear,
and there is no trouble within the regions.
We have stored strength to wait for the time,
and combined our armies for a single direction.
But the masses of the single province of Bā-Shǔ,
split and stretched thin in their defenses,
can hardly resist the armies of the whole world.
The demoralized spirit from the defeats at Duàngǔ and Hóuhé
can hardly face a majestic and grand formation.
In recent years,
there has never been a year of peace.
The soldiers are weary and exhausted,
and can hardly withstand the people who come to us like children to a father.
These are things that all you worthies have personally seen.
The Marquis of Shǔ was captured by Qín,
and Gōngsūn Shù lost his head to Hàn.
The natural defenses of the Nine Provinces
do not belong to a single surname forever;
these are things that all of you have heard in detail.
The enlightened see danger before it takes shape;
the wise plan for fortune before it sprouts.
Thus Wēizǐ left Shāng
and became a perpetual guest of Zhōu;
Chén Píng turned his back on Xiàng
and established merit in Hàn.
How could one treat the comfort of the moment like poisoned wine,
clinging to his salary and refusing to change?
Now the Imperial Court bestows the grace of Heaven’s covering,
and the high ministers promote the virtue of broad forgiveness.
They put grace first and punishment last,
loving life and hating killing.
In the past, the Wú general Sūn Yī
brought his followers to submit;
his rank became that of a high official,
and his favors and status were extraordinary.
Wén Qīn and Táng Zī
were great harms to the state,
rebellious subjects and vengeful enemies
who even led the enemy troops.
Táng Zī was cornered and captured,
and Wén Qīn’s two sons returned to surrender;
they were all made generals and enfeoffed as marquises,
and Táng Zī even participated in state affairs.
Sūn Yī and the others returned to their fate when they were in desperate straits,
yet they were still given superior favors;
how much more so for the worthies and the wise of Bā-Shǔ who see the opportunity and act upon it!
If you can truly examine success and failure deeply,
and take a lofty stride from afar,
following the footsteps of Wēizǐ
and the path of Chén Píng,
then your fortune will be the same as the ancients,
and your blessings will flow to your descendants.
The commoners, scholars, and people
will live peacefully and enjoy their work;
the farmers will not change their fields,
and the markets will not close their stalls.
Leaving the peril of piled eggs,
and moving toward a plan for eternal peace—
is this not beautiful?
If you seek the comfort of the moment,
being lost and not returning,
then once the great army is unleashed,
jade and stone will perish together.
Even if you wish to regret it,
it will be too late.
Let each of you announce this
and make it known to all.
Seventy-eight years after the rise of Hàn,
virtue flourished through six generations.
Military power was abundant,
and deep grace was vast as the sea;
all living beings were moistened by it,
and it overflowed to the lands beyond.
Thereupon, an envoy was ordered to go on a western expedition.
Following the currents and sweeping outward,
wherever the wind reached,
none failed to bow down and submit.
Thus he made Rǎn and Máng pay court,
settled Zuǒ and preserved Qióng,
took Sīyú,
and captured Bāopú.
Then, turning his chariot around,
he headed east to report his mission,
arriving at the capital of Shǔ.
Among the elders, officials, and gentry, twenty-seven men
came forward in a solemn manner.
After the ceremonies were finished,
they stepped forward and said:
“We have heard that when the Son of Heaven shepherds the barbarians,
the principle is merely to keep them under loose control and not cut them off.
Now you have exhausted the men of three commanderies
to open the road to Yèláng.
Three years have passed,
yet the work is not finished.
The soldiers are weary and tired,
and the people lack resources.
Now you connect with the Western Barbarians again;
the people’s strength is exhausted,
and we fear they cannot complete the task.
This is also a burden for you, the envoy.
We privately worry for your sakes.
Furthermore, the relationship between Qióng, Zuǒ, and the Western Barbarians with the Central Kingdom
has lasted for many years,
beyond what can be recorded.
The benevolent could not bring them with virtue,
and the strong could not annex them with force.
We suspect that this simply cannot be done!
Now you slice away the common people to attach these barbarians,
exhausting what we rely on to serve what is useless.
We humble people are narrow and ignorant
and do not understand the meaning of this.”
The envoy said:
“Why do you say this?
If it were as you say,
then Shǔ would never have changed its clothing and Bā would never have transformed its customs.
I have always detested hearing such talk.
However, this matter is of great importance
and is certainly not something that mere observers can perceive.
My journey is urgent,
and the details cannot be fully heard.
Allow me to briefly set forth the outline for you, sirs.”
"Indeed, the world must have extraordinary people,
and only then are there extraordinary events;
when there are extraordinary events,
only then are there extraordinary achievements.
As for the extraordinary,
it is naturally regarded as strange by ordinary people.
Therefore it is said:
At the source of the extraordinary,
the common people are afraid;
but when it reaches its completion,
the world is at peace.
In the past, the floodwaters boiled forth,
overflowing and spreading far,
the people moved up and down, migrating,
over rugged terrain and without peace.
Xià Hòu Shì grieved for them,
so he dammed the floods and blocked the sources,
channeled the Jiāng and dredged the Hé,
drained the depths and quelled the disaster,
leading the waters eastward to the sea,
so that the world was forever at peace.
During this toil,
was it only the common people who suffered?
His mind was weary with worry,
and his body personally labored;
his limbs were calloused and hairless,
and his skin grew no hair.
Therefore his great achievements are revealed for eternity,
and his reputation has been widespread until now.
"Furthermore, when a worthy ruler occupies the throne,
how could he merely be trivial and narrow-minded,
bound by texts and constrained by customs,
reciting what he has learned and following tradition,
just to seek the approval of the current generation?
He must put forward profound arguments and grand discussions,
start an enterprise and pass down a legacy,
to be a rule for ten thousand generations.
Thus he strives for comprehensive inclusion,
and diligently thinks of matching Heaven and Earth.
And does the Shī not say?
'Under the vast sky,
there is no land that is not the King's;
to the shores of the land,
there are no people who are not the King's subjects.'
Therefore, within the six directions
and beyond the eight reaches,
where waters spread and overflow,
if there are living things that do not soak in his bounty,
the worthy ruler is ashamed of it.
Now within the borders,
those of the capped and belted class
all receive auspicious blessings,
and none are left out.
But the lands of different customs of the Yí and Dí,
the regions of distant and strange tribes,
where boats and carts do not pass,
and human tracks are rarely seen,
where government and instruction have not yet reached,
and the prevailing influence is still faint.
Internally, they sometimes violate righteousness and encroach on rites at the borders;
externally, they act wickedly and behave lawlessly,
deposing and killing their superiors.
Lords and ministers swap places,
status and order are lost,
the elderly are not spared,
and the young orphans are made into slaves and captives,
bound in chains and crying out,
looking inward with resentment,
saying:
'Indeed we hear that in Zhōngguó there is supreme benevolence,
whose virtue is vast and grace is universal,
and no creature fails to find its place;
why now is only I left out?'
Lifting their heels in longing,
like a parched drought-land waiting for rain.
Even a crude man would shed tears for them,
how much more so the supreme Sage,
and how could he stop?
Therefore, in the north, he sends an army to chastise the strong Hú;
in the south, he dispatches envoys to reprimand the fierce Yuè.
From all four sides they sense his virtue;
the rulers of the two regions
gather like fish scales and look up to his flow;
those wishing to receive titles are counted by the hundreds of millions.
Thus he cleared the gates of Mò and Ruò,
patrolled the borders at Zāngkē,
carved through Língshān,
and bridged Sūnyuán.
He created a path of Way and Virtue,
and handed down a legacy of benevolence and righteousness,
intending to spread grace widely,
to comfort the distant and control the far-off,
so that the remote and isolated are not shut out,
and those in the dark and dim
may obtain the radiance of light,
so as to lay down armor and weapons here,
and cease punitive expeditions there.
Far and near as one body,
internal and external both blessed,
is this not peaceful?
To rescue people from drowning,
to uphold the glorious virtue of the Most Honorable,
to reverse the decline of a decaying age,
to continue the broken legacy of the Zhōu clan—
these are the urgent duties of the Son of Heaven.
Though the common people may labor,
how could it be stopped?
"Furthermore, a King certainly never begins without worry and diligence,
and ends in ease and joy.
Thus the signs of receiving the Mandate
must reside here.
He is about to increase the Shàn at Tàishān,
and add to the rites at Liángfù,
sounding the harmonious bells,
and raising songs of joy and praise,
surpassing the Five above
and ascending over the Three below.
Observers have not yet seen the purpose,
and listeners have not yet heard the sound,
just as the Jiānpéng has already soared into the vast void,
while the netters are still looking
At this, the various grandees were dazed and lost what they had come with,
losing the purpose for which they had advanced.
Sighing, they said together:
"Indeed, the virtue of Hàn!
This is what we humble people wished to hear.
Though the common people may labor,
please let us lead them with our own persons."
They stood back, dazed and unsure,
withdrawing and excusing themselves.
Chǔ Xiāng Wáng asked Sòng Yù:
"Sir, do you perhaps have some flaws in your conduct?
Why do the scholars and common people not praise you so much?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"Yes,
it is so, there is such a thing.
May the Great King pardon my fault
and allow me to finish my words.
A guest once sang in Yǐngzhōng;
at first he sang Xiàlǐ Bārén,
and several thousand people in the capital joined in harmony;
when he sang Yáng'ā and Xièlù,
several hundred people in the capital joined in harmony;
when he sang Yángchūn and Báixuě,
no more than a few dozen people in the capital joined in harmony;
when he drew out the Shāng note and sharpened the Yǔ note,
mixing in the flowing Zhǐ,
no more than a few people in the capital joined in harmony.
Thus, the more refined the melody,
the fewer who join in harmony.
So, among birds there is the Fèng and among fish there is the Kūn.
The Fènghuáng strikes upward for nine thousand lǐ,
cutting through the clouds and rainbows,
bearing the blue sky on its back,
soaring above the deep darkness.
How could a quail in a fence
measure the height of Heaven and Earth with it?
The Kūn fish sets out in the morning from the ruins of Kūnlún,
suns its fins at Jiéshí,
and rests in the evening at Mèngzhū.
How could a salamander in a foot-wide puddle
measure the vastness of the rivers and seas with it?
Therefore, it is not only that among birds there is the Fèng and among fish there is the Kūn;
among scholars there are also such.
The Sage has marvelous thoughts and extraordinary conduct,
standing transcendently alone;
how could the common people of the world understand what I am doing?"
A guest challenged Dōngfāng Shuò, saying:
"Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí once met lords of ten thousand chariots,
and they themselves occupied the positions of chief ministers,
their bounty reaching later generations.
Now you, sir, cultivate the arts of the former kings,
admire the righteousness of the Sages,
and chant the Shī, Shū, and the words of the Hundred Schools
in numbers that cannot be recorded,
writing them on bamboo and silk;
your lips are worn and teeth falling out,
holding them in your heart without letting go.
The effect of being fond of learning and delighting in the Way
is extremely clear,
and you consider your intelligence and ability to be peerless within the seas,
so you can be called wide-learned and eloquent.
Yet you use all your strength and exhaust your loyalty
to serve the Sagely Emperor,
for a long time,
accumulating several decades,
but your office is no more than a Shìláng,
and your position is no more than a Zhíjǐ.
I suspect there are still flaws in your conduct?
Among those of the same generation,
you have no place to reside comfortably.
What is the reason for this?"
Dōngfāng Xiānshēng sighed deeply,
looked up and responded, saying:
"This is therefore not something you can fully grasp.
That was one time,
this is another time;
how could they be considered the same?
In the time of Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
the house of Zhōu had greatly decayed,
and the feudal lords did not attend court.
They relied on power and struggled for authority,
capturing one another with military force,
merging into twelve states.
Without a clear victor yet,
those who gained scholars became strong,
while those who lost scholars perished.
Therefore, their persuasions could be implemented.
They occupied honorable positions,
their interiors were filled with precious treasures,
outside they had granaries and storehouses,
their blessings reached later generations,
and their descendants enjoyed them for a long time.
Today it is not so.
The virtuous influence of the Sage Emperor flows,
and the world is in awe.
The feudal lords submit as guests,
and the lands beyond the four seas are bound like a belt.
It is as secure as an inverted bowl;
the world is balanced and peaceful,
united into one family.
Acts and initiatives
are like moving things in one's palm.
The worthy and the unworthy,
how are they to be distinguished?
Following the Way of Heaven,
and according with the principles of Earth,
nothing fails to find its proper place.
Therefore, if pacified, they are at rest;
if moved, they suffer.
If honored, they become generals;
if humbled, they become captives.
If raised up, they are above the blue clouds;
if suppressed, they are beneath the deep abyss.
If used, they are like tigers;
if not used, they are like mice.
Although one wishes to give full devotion and sincerity,
how can one know what is ahead or behind?
With the vastness of Heaven and Earth,
and the multitude of scholars and people,
those who exhaust their essence and rush to offer persuasions,
advancing together like the spokes of a wheel,
are too numerous to count.
They strive with all their might to emulate them,
yet are distressed by a lack of food and clothing,
and some lose their homes.
Had Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí lived today alongside me,
they would not even have attained the rank of a petty official,
so how could they dare hope to be an Attendant Gentleman!
A tradition says:
'When the world is without harm,
even if there is a sage,
there is no place to exercise talent;
when those above and below are in harmony,
even if there is a worthy man, there is no place to achieve merit.'
Thus it is said that different times bring different circumstances.
"Even so,
how can one not strive to cultivate oneself?
The Shī says:
'Strike the bells in the palace,
the sound is heard outside.'
'The crane cries in the nine marshes,
the sound is heard in the heavens.'
If one can cultivate oneself,
why worry about not being glorious?
Tàigōng embodied and practiced benevolence and righteousness;
at seventy-two,
he was finally employed by Wén and Wǔ.
His persuasions were trusted,
he was enfeoffed in Qí,
and for seven hundred years his line did not end.
This is why scholars are diligent day and night,
cultivating learning and being quick in action, not daring to be idle.
It is like the wagtail,
flying and chirping.
A tradition says:
'Heaven does not stop the winter because people dislike the cold;
Earth does not stop its vastness because people dislike the dangers;
a gentleman does not change his conduct because of the clamor of petty men.'
'Heaven has constant measures,
Earth has constant forms,
and the gentleman has constant conduct;
the gentleman follows what is constant,
while the petty man calculates his achievements.'
The Shī says:
'When there is no error in ritual or righteousness,
why worry about the words of others?'
'When the water is too clear, there are no fish;
when a person is too scrutinizing, there are no followers.'
The strings of pearls hanging from the front of the crown
are used to obscure the vision;
the yellow silk wads filling the ears
are used to block the hearing.
There are things the eyes do not see,
and things the ears do not hear.
Promote great virtue,
and forgive small faults;
do not seek perfection in a single person's righteousness.
Correct what is crooked,
and let them find it for themselves;
be indulgent and gentle,
and let them seek it for themselves;
consider and measure,
and let them search for it for themselves.
For the transformation and teaching of a sage are like this:
wanting them to find it for themselves.
If they find it for themselves,
they will be diligent and broad-minded.
"The retired scholars of today,
though not employed by the times,
standing alone without followers,
living in vast solitude,
looking up to Xǔ Yóu above,
observing Jiē Yú below,
with schemes like Fàn Lǐ
and loyalty matching Zǐxū,
the world being peaceful
and virtue supporting one another,
they have few companions and followers;
this is indeed as it should be.
Why do you doubt me?
As for Yān's use of Yuè Yì,
Qín's appointment of Lǐ Sī,
and Lì Yìqī's bringing down of Qí,
their persuasions flowed like water,
followed as smoothly as a ring;
what they desired they surely attained,
and their merit was like a mountain.
The land was settled,
and the state was at peace;
these are instances of meeting their proper time.
Why should you find this strange?
A proverb says:
'To peek at the heavens through a tube,
to measure the sea with a calabash,
to strike a bell with a stalk of grass'—
how can they grasp the overall connection,
examine the patterns,
or produce its sound?
Looking at it this way,
it is like a shrew attacking a dog,
or a lone piglet biting a tiger;
once they arrive, they are crushed—
what achievement could there be?
Now, to use the lowliest ignorance to criticize a retired scholar,
even if one wishes not to be distressed,
it is simply impossible.
This is just enough to show that they do not understand weighing circumstances
and are ultimately confused about the Great Way."
In the time of Āidì,
Dīng, Fù, and Dǒng Xián were in power.
Those who attached themselves to them
rose from their homes to the rank of two thousand bushels.
At that time, Xióng was just drafting the Tàixuán;
he had that which he maintained within himself,
remaining indifferent.
Someone mocked Xióng for the Xuán's preference for white;
Xióng explained it,
calling it Jiě Cháo.
Its text said:
A guest ridiculed Yáng Zǐ, saying:
“I have heard that for the scholars of antiquity,
who were the bonds and guidelines of humanity,
if they were not born, that was the end of it;
but if they were born, they must above honor their sovereign,
and below bring glory to their parents.
They split the jade tallies of men,
bore the noble ranks of men,
held the tallies of men,
and shared the stipends of men.
They wound green sashes and trailed purple ribbons,
and painted their carriage hubs cinnabar red.
Now you, my sir, are fortunate to encounter an age of bright prosperity,
dwelling in a court where nothing is taboo,
walking together with a host of worthies.
You have passed through the Jīn Mén,
and the day you ascend the Yù Táng is near.
Yet you have never been able to devise a single brilliant scheme,
or offer one plan,
above to persuade the sovereign,
or below to converse with the Gōng and Qīng.
With eyes like shining stars,
and a tongue like a flash of lightning,
whether speaking of the vertical or the horizontal alliances,
no debater could withstand you.
Instead, you look back in silence and compose the five thousand characters of the Tài Xuán;
its branches and leaves are lush and spread wide,
uniquely expounding several hundred thousand words.
Its depths reach down to the Huáng Quán,
its heights reach up to the Cāng Tiān.
In its greatness, it contains the Yuán Qì;
in its fineness, it enters where there is no space.
Yet your rank does not exceed that of a Shìláng,
and you were only promoted to Gěishì Huángmén.
Could it be that your Xuán is too fond of ‘white’?
Why is your official career so desolate?”
Yáng Zǐ smiled and responded, saying:
“You, sir, only see the cinnabar red on my carriage hubs,
not knowing that a single stumble will bring the blood-red execution to my whole clan.
Long ago, when the net of Zhōu was unraveled,
flocks of deer competed to escape.
They separated into twelve,
then merged into six or seven.
Split into four and carved into five,
they became the Zhàn Guó.
Scholars had no permanent sovereign,
and states had no fixed ministers.
Those who gained scholars became wealthy,
those who lost scholars became impoverished.
Scholars trimmed their wings and sharpened their feathers,
following their own whims.
Thus, some scholars filled their own sacks with riches,
while others tunneled through walls to flee.
For this reason, Zōu Yǎn used his soaring rhetoric to seize the world’s wealth;
though Mèng Kē faced difficulties,
he was still a teacher to sovereigns of ten thousand chariots.
“Today, the Great Hàn has the Dōng Hǎi to its left,
Qū Sōu to its right,
Pānyú to its front,
and Jiāo Tú to its rear.
In the southeast is one Wèi,
in the northwest is one Hòu.
The people are bound by ropes and ink lines,
restrained by chopping blocks and axes,
dispersed by rites and music,
refined by the Shī and Shū,
given leisure by years and months,
and bound together by the mourning huts.
The scholars of the realm,
stirring like thunder and gathering like clouds,
overlapping like fish scales,
all occupy the eight regions.
Every household considers itself a Jì or Qiè,
every individual considers himself a Gāo Yáo.
Wearing vertical caps and dangling tassels,
all those who talk compare themselves to Ā Héng;
even a five-foot-tall boy
would be ashamed to be compared to Yàn Yīng or Yí Wú.
Those who find the path ascend to the green clouds,
those who lose their way are cast into the ditches.
In the morning, one who grasps power becomes a Qīng or Xiàng,
in the evening, one who loses influence becomes a commoner.
It is like the shores of rivers and lakes,
or the islands of the Bó Xiè:
if a flock of wild geese gathers, they are not too many,
if a pair of ducks flies away, they are not too few.
Long ago, when the Sān Rén left, the Yīn Xū appeared;
when the Èr Lǎo returned, the fire of Zhōu blazed;
when Zǐ Xū died, Wú perished;
while Zhòng and Lí remained, Yuè became the hegemon;
when Wǔ Gǔ entered, Qín rejoiced;
when Yuè Yì left, Yān trembled;
Fàn Jū, despite being beaten and broken, endangered the Marquis of Ràng;
Cài Zé, with his hesitant chanting, ridiculed Táng Jǔ.
Therefore, when there is trouble,
without the likes of Xiāo, Cáo, Zǐ Fáng, Píng, Bó, Fán, and Huò, there can be no peace.
When there is no trouble,
the followers of chapter and verse sit together to maintain order,
and there is nothing to fear.
Thus, when the world is in chaos, sages and wise men rush about but are still insufficient;
when the world is well-governed, mediocre men sleep soundly on their pillows and have room to spare.
“As for the scholars of antiquity,
some were released from bonds to become prime ministers,
some cast off their coarse clothes to become imperial tutors;
some leaned against the Yí Mén and laughed,
some fished along the riverbanks.
Some spoke for seventy times and did not find favor;
some were enfeoffed as marquises after a single conversation.
Some compelled sovereigns of a thousand chariots to visit their humble alleys,
some held brooms to clear the way ahead.
Therefore, scholars were largely able to stretch their tongues and exert their brushes,
finding gaps and treading on flaws without being bent.
Nowadays, a county magistrate does not invite scholars,
a commandery governor does not welcome teachers,
the various Qīng do not bow to guests,
and generals and ministers do not lower their brows.
Those whose words are unusual are met with suspicion,
those whose conduct is exceptional are punished.
Therefore, those who wish to speak roll back their tongues and make the same sound,
those who wish to walk measure their steps and follow in the tracks of others.
If the scholars of antiquity
were placed in the present age,
if their essays were not in the first rank,
if their conduct were not Xiàolián,
if they were not recommended as Fāngzhèng,
at most they could only submit a memorial,
occasionally discussing right and wrong.
At best, they would wait for an imperial summons;
at worst, they would be dismissed for offending the sovereign.
How then could they attain the green and purple ribbons?
“Furthermore, I have heard
that what blazes brightly will be extinguished,
and what booms loudly will be cut off.
Observe the thunder and observe the fire:
they become full and substantial;
yet Heaven withdraws their sound,
and Earth hides their heat.
In the homes of the high and eminent,
ghosts peer into their rooms.
Those who grab and seize will perish,
those who are silent will survive.
Those in the highest positions are in great danger,
those who keep to themselves preserve their lives.
Thus, knowing the mystery and knowing silence
is the ultimate way of maintaining the Dào;
being pure and being quiet
is the courtyard where the spirit roams;
being solitary and being detached
is the dwelling for maintaining virtue.
Though the ages differ and affairs change,
the way of man is no different.
If I and they were to exchange times,
who knows how it would be?
Now you use the owl to laugh at the phoenix,
and hold a gecko to ridicule the tortoise and dragon;
is that not a sickness?
You laugh at my Xuán being too fond of ‘white,’
but I also laugh at your sickness being so severe
that you have not met Yú Fù or Biǎn Què.
How tragic!”
The guest said:
“In that case, without the Xuán, can one not achieve fame?
For those like Fàn and Cài and below,
why was the Xuán necessary?”
Yáng Zǐ said:
"Fàn Jū
was a fugitive from Wèi.
With broken ribs and crushed hips,
having escaped from bonds,
he hunched his shoulders and treaded submissively,
crawling into a sack to enter Qín.
He inspired the lord of ten thousand chariots,
set aside the Prince of Jìng yáng,
and ousted the Ráng Hóu to take his place;
this was appropriate.
Cài Zé
was a commoner from Shān dōng.
With a sunken jaw and a broken nose,
with tears and saliva flowing,
he bowed westward to the Chancellor of powerful Qín;
he seized his throat and countered his spirit,
patted his back and took his position;
this was the timing.
When the world was already settled
and wars were already pacified,
with the capital at Luò yáng,
Lóu Jìng dropped the carriage-shaft and discarded the pulling-rope,
wagged his three-inch tongue,
and proposed an unshakeable strategy
to uproot the Middle Kingdom and move it to Cháng’ān;
this was suitable.
The Five Emperors handed down the canons,
and the Three Kings passed on the rites,
unchanging for a hundred generations.
Shū sūn Tōng rose from between the drums and drumsticks,
shed his armor and cast aside his spear,
and then established the rituals for monarch and ministers;
this was successful.
The Code of Lǚ was worn out
and the Qín laws were cruel and harsh;
the sagely Hàn used temporary measures,
and Xiāo Hé created the laws;
this was proper.
Thus, if Xiāo Hé's laws were created in the era of Táng and Yú,
it would be an error.
If Shū sūn Tōng's rituals were created during the time of Xià and Yīn,
it would be confusing.
If Lóu Jìng's strategy were proposed in the era of Chéng Zhōu,
it would be contrary.
If the talk of Fàn and Cài were used among the Jīn, Zhāng, Xǔ, and Shǐ families,
it would be madness.
As for Xiāo’s regulations being followed by Cáo,
the Liú Hóu drawing plans,
and Chén Píng devising masterstrokes,
their achievements were like Tài Shān
and their impact like a collapsing mountain.
Though this was due to their courage and wisdom,
it also happened to be a time when such things could be done.
Therefore, doing what can be done when it can be done
leads to success;
doing what cannot be done when it cannot be done
leads to disaster.
As for Lìn Shēng achieving success at Zhāng Tái,
the Sì Hào gathering glory at Nán Shān,
Gōng sūn starting his career at the Jīn Mǎ Gate,
the Cavalry General making his mark at the Qí lián Mountains,
Sī mǎ Zhǎng qīng stealing wealth from the Zhuō family,
and Dōng fāng Shuò cutting meat for his wife Xì Jūn:
I truly cannot be ranked with these several gentlemen.
Therefore, I remain silent and alone, keeping to my Tài Xuán."
During the Yǒng píng era, he served as a Gentleman,
supervising and proofreading the secret library.
He sincerely devoted his will to Confucian learning,
making writing his profession.
Some mocked him for having no achievements,
and he was also moved by the self-analogies of Dōng fāng Shuò and Yáng Xióng,
because they did not encounter the times of Sū, Zhāng, Fàn, and Cài.
Yet they did not refute them with the Right Way
to clarify what a gentleman upholds;
therefore, he briefly replied to them.
The text says:
A guest mocked the host, saying:
"I have heard that sages have fixed theories
and heroic men have unchanging duties;
it is also said to be about reputation alone.
Thus, the highest is to establish virtue,
and next is to establish merit.
Virtue does not become especially grand by being neglected until after one's death,
and merit does not become uniquely manifest by turning its back on the times.
Therefore, in the governance of the sagely and wise,
they were hurried and anxious,
such that Kǒng’s mat did not get warm
and Mò’s chimney did not get black.
Speaking from this,
choosing what to take or leave was the primary task of the men of old,
and writing was merely a side-task for those of the front rank.
Now you, sir, are fortunate to live in the era of emperors,
personally wearing the robes of ribbon and crown.
You float on excellence and splendor,
immerse yourself in virtue and the Way,
and behold the patterns of dragons and tigers;
it has been so for a long time.
Yet in the end, you cannot extend yourself from head to tail,
spread your wings and scales,
shake yourself free from the mire,
or soar across the wind and clouds,
causing those who see you to be startled by your shadow
and those who hear you to be shaken by your sound.
You merely delight in pillowing on classics and books,
bending your body in a humble gate,
with nothing to latch onto above
and no roots below.
Alone, you express your thoughts beyond the universe
and sharpen your thinking within the tip of a hair,
immersing your spirit and silently recording,
continuing through the years.
However, your vessel is not sold in your own time,
and your use is not effective for a single generation.
Though your galloped eloquence is like surging waves
and your spread literary flow is like spring flowers,
it is still of no benefit to the official evaluations.
I suppose
that if you were to employ strategies for morning and evening
and decide on plans for meetings and gatherings,
so that while alive you have a prominent title
and when dead you have a beautiful posthumous name,
would that not be superior?"
The host smiled leisurely and said:
"As for the words of the guest,
they are what is called seeing the flowering of worldly profit
but being blind to the reality of the Way and Virtue,
guarding the flickering candle in a dark corner,
never looking up at the heavenly court to behold the bright sun.
In the past, the royal road was overgrown and neglected,
Zhōu lost its control,
the feudal lords raced side-by-side,
and the Warring States galloped wildly.
Thereupon the Seven Heroes roared like tigers,
partitioning the Zhūxià,
dragons fighting and tigers contending.
Wandering persuaders,
like gusts of wind and flashes of lightning,
rose together to save the situation,
while the rest followed like rushing wind or shadows,
flashing and sparkling among them;
they are truly too many to record.
At that time,
by grasping the decayed and grinding the blunt,
even a leaden knife could make a cut.
Therefore, Lǔ Lián flew a single arrow and caused a thousand gold pieces to fall,
and Yú Qīng with a single glance cast away the prime minister's seal.
Now, chirping sounds and tossed-off tunes,
sounds that affect the ear,
even if they fit the musical scales,
if they are licentious and unfit to hear,
they are not the music of Sháoxià.
Adapting to circumstances and following changes,
assuming a demeanor suited to the times,
if they shift customs and change habits
but are contrary and lack continuity,
they are not the laws of a Jūnzǐ.
When the proponents of Vertical Alliance joined them,
and the proponents of Horizontal Alliance dispersed them,
fugitives drifted about with their persuasions,
and travelers galloped with their rhetoric.
Shāng Yāng held three techniques to bore into Xiàogōng,
Lǐ Sī exerted himself in current affairs to solicit Shǐhuáng.
They all stepped into the convergence of wind and dust,
and walked upon the momentum of ruin and fall,
seizing opportunities and riding on deviance,
to seek the wealth and honor of a single day.
In the morning they were glorious,
by evening they were withered;
their fortune did not fill their eyes,
but their calamities overflowed into the world.
Even an ominous man would regret this for himself,
how much more would a fortunate gentleman rely on it?
Moreover, merit cannot be achieved through emptiness,
and fame cannot be established through falsehood.
Hán used eloquence to provoke his lord,
Lǚ practiced deception to trade for a state.
Once 'The Difficulties of Persuasion' reached its peak,
his person was then imprisoned;
once the Qín merchandise became expensive,
his clan also fell.
Therefore, Zhòngní upheld an ambition as high as floating clouds,
and Mèng Kē nourished his vast, flood-like Qì.
Did they enjoy being impractical and distant?
The Way cannot be of two minds.
Now, the Great Hàn has swept away all filth,
leveled the dangerous and cleared the wild,
broadened the imperial threads,
and expanded the August bond,
its foundation higher than Xī and Nóng,
its scale wider than Huáng and Táng;
its ruling of the world:
warming it like the sun,
overawing it like a god,
encompassing it like the sea,
and nourishing it like the spring.
Thus, within the six directions,
none do not share the same source and flow together,
bathing in Profound Virtue,
and receiving the Great Harmony.
Branches attach and leaves adhere,
just as plants and trees are planted in mountains and forests,
and birds and fish are reared in rivers and marshes.
Those who obtain the Qì flourish,
while those who lose the timing wither.
It matches Heaven and Earth in applying transformation;
how could it be said that human efforts are thin or thick?
Now you, sir, living in an August era, discuss the Warring States;
you show off what you have heard and doubt what you see.
Wanting to measure the height of Tàishān from a molehill,
or to gauge the depth of a deep abyss with a shallow puddle,
you have not yet reached it."
The guest said:
"As for the likes of Yāng and Sī,
those ominous men of the declining Zhōu,
I have heard your instructions.
May I ask about the scholars of high antiquity,
who conducted themselves and practiced the Way,
assisted the world and achieved fame,
and who could be passed down to later generations—
did they merely keep silent?"
The host said:
"How could that be the case!
In the past, Gàoyáo counseled Yú,
Jīzǐ was consulted by Zhōu,
their words reached emperors and kings,
and their plans matched the divine and sagely;
Yīn Yuè's dream originated at Fùyán,
Zhōu Wàng's omen stirred at the banks of the Wèi,
Qí Níng raised his voice on the broad road,
Hàn Liáng received a book at the edge of Pī.
All waited for their destiny and connected with the divine;
it was not through mere words that they were trusted,
therefore, they could establish inevitable strategies
and display inexhaustible merit.
In recent times, Master Lù lived leisurely,
and the Xīnyǔ arose;
Master Dǒng lowered his curtain,
and brilliance bloomed in the forest of scholars;
Liú Xiàng oversaw the records,
distinguishing and clarifying ancient lore;
Yáng Xióng meditated deeply,
writing the Fǎyán and Tàixuán.
All reached the gates of the lords of their time,
and investigated the profound depths of the former sages.
They danced in the fields of arts and techniques,
and rested in the gardens of texts and records,
to preserve their substance and manifest their refinement.
Thereby they were accepted into sagely virtue,
and their brilliance shone for later generations—
is this not being second to the sages!
As for Bóyí upholding his conduct at Shǒuyáng,
Liǔhuì lowering his will in shameful service,
Yán finding hidden joy in a single bowl and gourd,
and Kǒng finishing his book with the hunt in the west—
their voices filled the space between Heaven and the abyss;
they are truly the models and teachers for our kind.
Moreover, I have heard:
one Yīn and one Yáng
are the Way of Heaven and Earth;
refinement and substance
are the bond of the Kingly Way;
to have similarities and differences
is the constant of sages and wise men.
Therefore it is said:
Carefully cultivate your intentions,
and guard your heavenly tally.
Entrust yourself to destiny and provide for yourself,
tasting the richness of the Way.
The spirits will listen to it,
so how could fame ever leave you!
Guest, have you also not heard of the Jade of Hé-shì,
wrapped within the stone of Jīng,
or the Pearl of the Marquis of Suí,
hidden within a clam?
For generations no one looked at them,
not knowing they would contain brilliant light,
and breathe out the essence of blossoms,
shedding light across a thousand years.
The Responding Dragon hides in a puddle,
and fish and turtles treat it with familiarity,
not seeing that it can exert its spiritual virtue,
join with the wind and clouds,
and transcend the vast wilds to reside in the azure sky.
Therefore, that which coils in the mud yet flies in the sky
is the spirit of the Responding Dragon;
that which is first humble and later precious
is the treasure of Hé and Suí;
that which is obscure for a time but long manifest
is the truth of the Jūnzǐ.
As for Yá and Kuàng clearing their ears for wind and string instruments,
Lí Lóu focusing his eyes on the tip of a hair;
Féng Méng's supreme skill with bow and arrow,
Bān and Shū's unmatched craft with axe and hatchet;
Liáng and Lè's extraordinary ability in judging and driving horses,
Wū Huò's strength in lifting a thousand jūn;
Hé and Què's brilliance in acupuncture and stones,
Yán and Sāng's mental calculation without limit—
I, too, am not fit to join the ranks of those with such skills,
and so I quietly amuse myself with these writings."
The Emperor traveled to Hédōng,
sacrificed to Hòutǔ,
and looked back at the imperial capital with joy.
In the middle of the river, he held a banquet with his ministers.
The Emperor was very happy,
and thus he himself composed the Qiūfēng Cí, saying:
The autumn wind rises and white clouds fly,
Grass and trees yellow and fall, the wild geese return south.
The orchids have their beauty and the chrysanthemums their fragrance,
I bring along a fair lady whom I cannot forget.
Floating in a tower-ship, we cross the Fén River,
Crossing the midstream, raising white waves.
Flutes and drums sound, and the oarsmen's song begins.
When joy reaches its peak, many are the feelings of sorrow.
How long is youth and vigor? What can be done about old age!
The preface says:
My family was poor,
and I was wary of distant service.
Péngzé County was a hundred lǐ from my home;
thus, I sought the post there.
After a short while,
I felt a yearning for home
and resigned from office.
Following my heart in these circumstances,
I titled the piece "Guī Qù Lái."
Let me return home!
The fields and gardens will soon be overgrown with weeds; why not return?
Since I have made my heart the slave of my body,
why should I be melancholy and grieve alone?
I realize that the past cannot be mended,
but I know that the future can be pursued.
Indeed, I have not strayed far from the path;
I feel that today is right while yesterday was wrong.
The boat sways lightly as it glides,
and the wind flutters my clothes.
I ask a traveler about the road ahead,
and I regret the dimness of the morning light.
Then I catch sight of my humble home,
and I rejoice and run toward it.
The servants welcome me,
and my young children wait at the gate.
The three paths are becoming overgrown,
but the pines and chrysanthemums still remain.
Leading my children into the house,
I find the wine vessels full.
I take up the jar and cup to pour for myself,
and look at the branches in the courtyard with a happy face.
I lean against the southern window to express my pride,
and realize how easily one can be content in a room that only fits one's knees.
Strolling in the garden daily becomes a delight;
though a gate is set up, it is always closed.
Leaning on my staff, I wander and rest,
occasionally raising my head to gaze into the distance.
Clouds aimlessly emerge from the mountain peaks,
and birds, weary of flying, know to return home.
The light fades as the sun is about to set;
I stroke a solitary pine and linger.
Let me return home!
I shall cut off social ties and end my wanderings.
The world and I are at odds with each other;
why should I harness my carriage to seek anything further?
I enjoy the affectionate talk of my relatives,
and take pleasure in the zither and books to dispel my worries.
The farmers tell me that spring has arrived,
and there will be work to do in the western fields.
Sometimes I call for a covered cart,
and sometimes I row a solitary boat.
I seek out deep valleys through winding paths,
and cross hills via rugged roads.
Trees flourish and bloom,
and springs begin to flow in trickles.
I admire how all things find their season,
but feel that my life is nearing its end.
Let it be!
How much longer can I dwell within this body in the universe?
Why not let my heart take its course, whether to stay or to go?
Why be anxious—where do I wish to go?
Riches and honors are not my desire,
and the celestial realm cannot be expected.
Cherishing a fine day, I go out alone,
or plant my staff to weed and hoe.
I climb the eastern embankment and whistle freely,
and compose poems by the clear stream.
Thus I shall follow the transformation of things until the end,
and rejoice in the mandate of Heaven without further doubt!
Guānjū
reflects the virtue of the queen consort,
and it is the beginning of the Fēng;
it is the means by which the world is influenced and the relationship between husband and wife is rectified.
Therefore, it is used among the local people
and in the feudal states.
Fēng means influence
and instruction.
By influence one moves people;
by instruction one transforms them.
Poetry
is where the intent goes.
In the heart it is intent;
expressed in words, it is poetry.
Emotion moves within and takes form in words.
If words are not enough,
one sighs;
if sighing is not enough,
one prolongs the singing;
if prolonging the singing is not enough,
unconsciously one's hands dance
and feet stomp.
Emotion is expressed in sound,
and when sounds form a pattern, it is called music.
The music of a well-ordered age is peaceful and joyful,
for its governance is harmonious.
The music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
for its governance is perverse.
The music of a dying state is mournful and longing,
for its people are in distress.
Therefore, for correcting successes and failures,
moving Heaven and Earth,
and affecting ghosts and spirits,
nothing is closer than poetry.
The former kings used it to regulate the relationship between husband and wife,
to perfect filial piety and respect,
to deepen human relations,
to beautify instruction and transformation,
and to change customs.
Thus, poetry has six principles:
the first is Fēng,
the second is Fù,
the third is Bǐ,
the fourth is Xìng,
the fifth is Yǎ,
and the sixth is Sòng.
Those above use influence to transform those below;
those below use influence to criticize those above.
By using literary refinement to provide indirect admonition,
the speaker incurs no guilt,
yet the listener receives sufficient warning;
therefore, it is called Fēng.
When the Kingly Way declined,
ritual and righteousness were abandoned,
political instruction was lost,
states followed different policies,
and families had diverse customs;
then the "Changed Airs" and "Changed Odes" were created.
The state historians were clear about the traces of success and failure,
pained by the abandonment of human relations,
and grieved by the harshness of punishments and governance.
They sang of their feelings and nature
to influence those above,
understanding the changes in circumstances
and cherishing the old customs.
Thus, the "Changed Airs" arise from emotion
but stop at ritual and righteousness.
Arising from emotion
is the nature of the people;
stopping at ritual and righteousness
is the grace of the former kings.
Therefore, when the affairs of a single state
are tied to the foundation of a single person,
it is called Fēng;
when speaking of the affairs of the whole world
and describing the airs of the four quarters,
it is called Yǎ.
Yǎ
means correct;
it speaks of the reasons for the decline or rise of kingly governance.
Governance has both small and large aspects;
thus there are the Xiǎoyǎ
and the Dàyǎ.
Sòng
describes the appearance of great virtue
and reports achievements to the spirits.
These are called the Four Beginnings,
the intent of the Shījīng.
Thus, the transformation of Guānjū and Línzhǐ
represents the Airs of the King,
so they are attributed to Zhōugōng.
Nán refers to the transformation spreading from the north to the south.
The virtue of Quècháo and Zōuyú
represents the Airs of the feudal lords,
which the former kings used for instruction,
so they are attributed to Shàogōng.
The Zhōunán and Shàonán
are the way of rectifying the beginning
and the foundation of kingly transformation.
Therefore, Guānjū delights in obtaining a virtuous lady to match a gentleman;
it is concerned with promoting the worthy,
does not indulge in lustful beauty,
laments for the modest and retired,
and longs for the worthy and talented,
without having a heart that harms goodness;
this is the meaning of Guānjū.
In ancient times, when Fú Xī Shì ruled the world,
he first drew the Bāguà,
and created written records
to replace the administration of knotted cords;
from this, written documents arose.
The books of Fú Xī, Shén Nóng, and Huáng Dì
are called the Sānfén,
which speak of the Great Way.
The books of Shǎo Hào, Zhuān Xū, Gāo Xīn, Táng, and Yú
are called the Wǔdiǎn,
which speak of the Constant Way.
As for the books of the Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu,
although the teachings established were not identical,
their elegant proclamations and profound meanings
tend toward a single standard.
Therefore, successive generations have treasured them,
considering them the Great Instructions.
The explanations of the Bāguà
are called the Bāsuǒ,
seeking their meaning.
The records of the Jiǔzhōu
are called the Jiǔqiū.
Qiū means "to gather."
It means that everything within the Jiǔzhōu—
what the land produces
and what is suitable to the local climates—
is all gathered in this book.
The Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn says:
Yǐ Xiàng, the Scribe of the Left in Chǔ,
could read the Sānfén, Wǔdiǎn, Bāsuǒ, and Jiǔqiū.
These are the surviving books of the emperors and kings of high antiquity.
My late ancestor Kǒngzǐ,
born at the end of the Zhōu,
saw the redundant texts of the historical records.
Fearing that those who read them would not find them consistent,
he then settled the rites and music,
clarified the old regulations,
edited the Shī into three hundred poems,
condensed the historical records to compile the Chūnqiū,
praised the way of the Yì to set aside the Bāsuǒ,
and described the regional offices to dispense with the Jiǔqiū.
He examined and discussed the Sānfén and Wǔdiǎn,
beginning his selection from Táng and Yú down to the Zhōu.
He pruned away the redundant and chaotic,
cut out the superficial language,
raised up the grand outlines,
and grasped the essential points,
which were sufficient to leave to the world and establish teachings.
The texts of the canons, counsels, instructions, proclamations, oaths, and charges
numbered one hundred chapters in all,
by which he expanded the Ultimate Way
and showed the lords of men the proper standards.
The systems of the emperors and kings
were made clear and manifest,
ready to be taken up and put into practice.
His three thousand disciples
all received his meanings.
When Qín Shǐ Huáng destroyed the records of the former dynasties,
burning the books and burying the scholars,
the scholars of the world
fled the disaster and dispersed.
My ancestors then hid their family books within the walls of their house.
When the House of Hàn rose like a dragon,
they established schools
and widely sought out the refined Confucians
to clarify the Great Path.
Fú Shēng of Jìnán,
over ninety years of age,
had lost his original scriptures,
but taught them through oral transmission.
There were only twenty-odd chapters;
because they were books of high antiquity,
they were called the Shàngshū.
The meaning of the full hundred chapters
was no longer heard by the world.
When Lǔ Gòng Wáng, who enjoyed building palaces,
demolished the old residence of Kǒngzǐ
to enlarge his dwelling,
he found within the walls the ancient script books of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu hidden by my ancestors,
as well as the Lúnyǔ and Xiàojīng,
all written in tadpole script.
When the King also ascended Kǒngzǐ's hall,
he heard the sounds of bells, stones, strings, and flutes;
whereupon he did not demolish the house
and returned all the books to the Kǒng family.
Tadpole script had long fallen out of use,
and no one at the time could understand it.
Using what had been heard from Fú Shēng's books,
I examined and discussed the text and meaning,
and determined those that could be known
as Lìgǔdìng.
I further transcribed them onto bamboo slips,
adding twenty-five chapters more than Fú Shēng had.
Fú Shēng had also combined the Shùndiǎn with the Yáodiǎn,
the Yìjì with the Gāoyáo Mú,
the three chapters of Pángēng into one,
and the Kāngwáng Zhī Gào with the Gùmìng.
I restored these chapters along with their prefaces,
making fifty-nine chapters in all,
arranged in forty-six volumes.
The rest were disordered or worn away
and could no longer be understood;
I submitted all of them to the officials,
to be stored in the archives
to await those who might be capable of deciphering them.
Receiving an imperial decree to write commentaries for the fifty-nine chapters,
I then researched with precision and deep thought,
extensively consulting the classics and records,
and collecting the words of the rulers
to establish instructions and commentaries.
I condensed the text and explained the meaning,
expounding and clarifying their purpose,
in the hope that it might be of benefit to the future.
The Shù Xù,
being the prefaces that explain the intentions of the authors,
allow the meaning to be clearly seen.
It is appropriate that they be kept near the chapters,
so I have placed each at the beginning of its respective chapter.
Having finished settling the fifty-eight chapters,
it happened that the country was beset by the witchcraft incident,
and the way of the classics was suspended.
Therefore, I did not report it further,
but passed it on to my descendants
to leave it to later generations.
If there be gentlemen who love antiquity and possess broad elegance
and who share my aspirations,
I shall not hide it from them.
The Chūnqiū
is the name of the historical records of Lǔ.
In recording events,
one links the event to the day,
the day to the month,
the month to the season,
and the season to the year,
thereby recording the distance in time
and distinguishing similarities and differences.
Therefore, what the scribe records
must indicate the year to introduce the events;
since a year has four seasons,
it combines them to serve as the name for the records.
In the Zhōulǐ, there were scribal officials
who managed the affairs of the states and the four directions
and communicated the will of the four directions.
The feudal lords also each had their own state scribes.
Major events were written on bamboo bundles,
while minor events were merely on bamboo or wooden slips.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Chǔ called it the Táowù,
Jìn called it the Shèng,
and Lǔ called it the Chūnqiū;
their reality is one and the same."
When Hán Xuānzǐ went to Lǔ,
he saw the Yìxiàng and the Lǔ Chūnqiū,
and said:
"The Zhōulǐ are all in Lǔ!
Only now do I know the virtue of Zhōu Gōng
and the reason why the Zhōu ruled as kings."
What Hánzǐ saw
was likely the old canons and ritual scriptures of the Zhōu.
The virtue of the Zhōu having already declined,
the officials lost their duties,
and those in superior positions were unable to keep the Chūnqiū clear and bright.
Reports of deaths and official announcements,
and all that was recorded and noted,
mostly violated the old regulations.
Zhòngní followed the written records of the Lǔ history to form the text,
examined their authenticity,
and recorded the codes and rituals,
above to follow the legacy of Zhōu Gōng,
and below to clarify the laws for the future.
Where the teachings remained
or where the text was flawed,
he edited and corrected them
to show encouragement and warnings.
For the rest, he used the old history as it was;
since histories have varying styles
and the language varies in detail,
it was not necessary to change them.
Therefore, the Zhuàn says:
“He was good at recording.”
It also says:
“Who but a sage could have revised it?”
Truly, the intentions of Zhōu Gōng
were clarified by Zhòngní.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng received the Jīng from Zhòngní
and believed the Jīng to be an unalterable book.
Thus, the Zhuàn sometimes precedes the Jīng to begin the account of an event,
sometimes follows the Jīng to conclude the meaning,
sometimes relies on the Jīng to distinguish the reasoning,
and sometimes interweaves with the Jīng to reconcile differences,
developing the precedents where they are emphasized according to the meaning.
Fragments of the old history
are not all listed,
because they were not essential to the sage's revisions.
As a national historian himself,
he personally examined the records and books,
and he was certain to record broadly and speak comprehensively.
His writing is relaxed,
his intent is profound,
intending to lead scholars to trace the origins and seek the ends,
to follow the branches and leaves,
and to investigate to the ultimate limit,
immersing themselves in it gently
to make them seek it for themselves;
saturating themselves in it fully
to make them pursue it for themselves.
Like the soaking of rivers and seas
or the moisturizing of rich dew,
doubts dissolve like melting ice,
and principles become smooth and pleasing;
only then is it mastered.
The general rules used to state precedents
are all the constant systems for governing the state,
the laws handed down by Zhōu Gōng,
and the old regulations of historical records,
which Zhòngní followed and revised
to form the unified structure of the Jīng.
As for revealing the subtle and clarifying the obscure,
or determining categories of meaning,
these all state the meaning based on old precedents,
pointing to the events to correct praise and blame.
Various terms like “recorded,”
“not recorded,”
“recorded first,”
“recorded thus,”
“not spoken,”
“not called,”
or “the record says,”
are all used to distinguish the new from the old
and to express grand meanings;
these are called variable precedents.
Yet there are also things the historian did not record
that are taken as having meaning;
these are the new ideas of the Chūnqiū,
so the Zhuàn does not state a general rule
but elaborates on them with nuance.
When the Jīng contains no precedent
but speaks because of the event,
the Zhuàn simply states its ultimate purpose,
which is not a precedent.
Thus, there are three forms of developing the Zhuàn,
and five circumstances for the precedents.
The first is called subtle yet manifest:
the text appears here while the meaning arises there,
such as naming a clan to honor the lord’s command,
omitting the clan to honor the wife,
the destruction of Liáng,
or the walling of Yuánlíng.
The second is called recorded yet obscure:
using concise words to show the system
and deducing from them to know the precedent,
such as not recording the location of a meeting
or using the word jí to indicate participation in a plot.
The third is called evasive yet elegant:
following moral instruction with nuance
to show great compliance,
such as various taboos and avoidances,
or the jade disk used to borrow the fields of Xǔ.
The fourth is called exhaustive but not corrupt:
writing the matter directly
so that the meaning is seen in the complete text,
such as the red-painted pillars,
the carved rafters,
the Tiānwáng seeking carriages,
or the Qí Hóu offering spoils of victory.
The fifth is called punishing evil and encouraging good:
seeking fame but perishing,
or wishing to hide but becoming manifest,
such as recording Qí Bào as a bandit
or naming the three rebels.
By using these five forms to investigate the Jīng and
Zhuàn, and expanding upon them by category,
attaching them to the events of the two hundred and forty-two years,
the correctness of the Kingly Way
and the records of human ethics will be complete.
Someone said:
The Chūnqiū shows meaning through variations in the text;
if it were as you say,
then the Jīng would have instances where the events are the same and the text is different but there is no meaning.
What the former scholars transmitted
was not like this.
I replied:
Although the Chūnqiū uses a single word for praise or blame,
it still requires several sentences to form a statement;
it is not like the lines of the Eight Trigrams,
which can be combined into sixty-four.
One must certainly rely on the Zhuàn to make a judgment.
From ancient times to the present, many have spoken on Zuǒ’s Chūnqiū;
now there are a dozen or so families whose surviving writings can be seen,
but generally they just transmit the teachings of their predecessors.
Advancing, they fail to master the variations of the Jīng text to exhaust its changes;
retreating, they fail to keep to Qiūmíng’s Zhuàn.
Regarding Qiūmíng’s Zhuàn,
where there is something they do not understand,
they all gloss over it without explaining,
and instead superficially cite the Gōngyáng or Gǔliáng,
which is enough to cause self-confusion.
The reason I, Yù, now differ
is that I exclusively follow Qiūmíng’s Zhuàn to explain the Jīng.
The threads of the Jīng
must emerge from the Zhuàn,
and the precedents of the Zhuàn
all return to the general rules.
Deducing variable precedents to correct praise and blame
and setting aside the two other commentaries to remove heterodox views
was truly Qiūmíng’s intention.
Where there are doubts or errors,
I discuss them fully or leave them as gaps
to await future worthies.
However, Liú Zǐjùn first opened the path to the great meaning;
Jiǎ Jǐngbó and his son,
and Xǔ Huìqīng
were all the finest among the former scholars.
Later there was Yǐng Zǐyán,
who, though shallow, was also a famous master.
Therefore, I specifically point out the errors of Liú, Jiǎ, Xǔ, and Yǐng
to show the similarities and differences.
I have aligned the years of the Jīng with the years of the Zhuàn,
compared their categories of meaning,
and explained each accordingly,
titling it Jīngzhuàn Jíjiě.
Furthermore, I have separately collected the various precedents,
along with place names,
genealogies,
and calendrical calculations,
grouping them together
into forty sections
and fifteen volumes,
all clarifying their similarities and differences
and explaining them accordingly,
titling it Shìlì.
This is to allow scholars to observe the collection of differing views;
the Shìlì explains them in detail.
Someone said:
Regarding the composition of the *Chūn Qiū*,
the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* and *Gǔ Liáng* contain no explicit statement.
Commentators believe that when Zhòng Ní returned from Wèi to Lǔ,
he revised the *Chūn Qiū*,
established the *Sù Wáng*,
and that Qiū Míng served as the *Sù Chén*.
Those who speak of the *Gōng Yáng* also say that he demoted Zhōu and treated Lǔ as the royal house,
acting with integrity but speaking with modesty
to avoid the harms of that time,
thus making the text subtle
and its meaning hidden.
The *Gōng Yáng* scripture ends with the capture of the *Lín*,
while the *Zuǒ Shì* scripture ends with the death of Kǒng Qiū;
may I ask which is correct?
I answer:
This is different from what I have heard.
Zhòng Ní said:
"Since King Wén has passed away,
is the *Wén* (culture) not here with me?"
This is the original intent of the composition.
He sighed:
"The *Fèng* bird does not arrive,
the *Hé* brings forth no Chart;
it is over for me!"
This was likely a lament for the governance of the kings of his time.
The *Lín*, the *Fèng*, and the five spiritual creatures
are auspicious omens of a King.
Now the *Lín* has appeared out of its time;
its response is in vain and it has lost its proper place of return.
This is why the Sage was moved to emotion.
Ending the writing with the sentence on the capture of the *Lín*
was prompted by this emotion
and was indeed the reason for its conclusion.
It was asked:
Then why does the *Chūn Qiū* begin with Duke Yǐn of Lǔ?
I answer:
King Píng of Zhōu
was the first king of the Eastern Zhōu;
Duke Yǐn
was a virtuous ruler who yielded his state.
Examined in terms of time, they are contiguous;
spoken of in terms of status, they are of the regional states;
based on their origins, they are the descendants of the Duke of Zhōu.
If King Píng had been able to pray for Heaven's eternal mandate
and initiate a restoration,
and if Duke Yǐn could have broadly proclaimed the ancestral legacy
and brought glory to the Royal House,
then the beauty of the Western Zhōu could have been sought,
and the traces of Wén and Wǔ would not have fallen.
Therefore, following their chronological sequence
and attaching the records of their deeds,
he gathered the old traditions of Zhōu
to assemble and perfect the Kingly Righteousness,
bequeathing laws to the future.
The King recorded
was King Píng;
the calendar used
was the Zhōu calendar;
the Duke referred to
was Yǐn of Lǔ.
Where is there any demoting of Zhōu or treating Lǔ as the royal house?
The Master said:
"If anyone were to use me,
would I not make it an Eastern Zhōu?"
This is its meaning.
As for the text of the composition,
it is used to illuminate the past and examine the future.
Emotions are manifest in the words;
when the language is high, the aim is far-reaching;
when the phrasing is concise, the meaning is subtle.
This is the constant principle of logic,
not an act of concealment.
The Sage encompasses the protection of his whole person;
that after he had finished the work
he would then turn back to hide and conceal things to avoid trouble,
is not something I have heard.
When Zǐ Lù had disciples act as ministers,
Kǒng Zǐ considered it deceiving Heaven;
thus saying Zhòng Ní was a *Sù Wáng*
and Qiū Míng was a *Sù Chén*
is not a sound argument.
Former scholars thought it took three years to compose,
and that once the text was complete, it summoned the *Lín*;
this is already monstrous and absurd.
Furthermore, extending the scripture to the death of Zhòng Ní
is also close to being a fabrication.
Based on the *Gōng Yáng* scripture ending with the capture of the *Lín*,
and the fact that in the *Zuǒ Shì*
"*Xiǎo Zhū Shè*"
is not among the number of the three rebels,
I believe he was moved by the *Lín* to compose it;
the composition began with the capture of the *Lín*,
and thus the text ends where it began,
which reaches the truth of the matter.
As for turning back one's sleeves to wipe one's face
and saying
"My Way is exhausted,"
there is nothing to be taken from that.
Master Xuán Àn said:
The ancients called an unsung praise a *Fù*.
Thus, as for a *Fù*,
it is that which uses objects to initiate a theme,
expanding and magnifying the form and logic
so that people cannot add to it.
Extending and stretching it,
thus the writing must be extremely beautiful;
touching upon categories and expanding them,
thus the phrasing must be fully elegant.
Thus, beautiful and elegant writing
is the creation of the *Fù*.
Those who wrote in the past
did not merely value phrasing for its own sake;
they intended to bind it to the Kingly Teachings,
rooting it in encouragement and admonishment.
From before the Xià and Yīn,
their writings have been lost,
and cannot be known in detail.
The Zhōu looked back upon the two previous dynasties;
the forms of substance and refinement
can be known for a hundred generations.
Therefore, Kǒng Zǐ gathered the airs of the ten thousand states,
corrected the names of the *Yǎ* and *Sòng*,
and collected them into what is called the *Shī*.
Among the works of the poets,
there are miscellaneous *Fù* forms.
Zǐ Xià's preface to the *Shī* says:
the first is called *Fēng*,
and the second is called *Fù*.
Thus we know that the *Fù*
is a stream from ancient poetry.
Regarding the Warring States,
the Kingly Way declined,
and the *Fēng* and *Yǎ* gradually diminished.
Thereupon, worthy men lost their ambitions,
and *Cí Fù* were created.
Because of this, for those of the class of Sūn Qīng and Qū Yuán,
their remaining writings are brilliant,
and their phrasing and meaning are worth observing.
Preserving what they felt,
they all have the intent of ancient poetry.
All used writing to lodge their hearts
and relied on logic to perfect their compositions;
these are the beginnings of the *Fù*.
By the time of Sòng Yù and his kind,
licentious writing spread without restraint,
words exceeded reality,
the rise of competitive boasting occurred,
and the form gradually lost its way.
The standards of the *Fēng* and *Yǎ*
were thus discarded.
Reaching the Hàn, Jiǎ Yì
somewhat tempered it with ritual.
From that time onward,
scholars who composed writing
did not follow the standard words;
they collectively strived for expansion,
and their writings were broad, boastful, and empty in category.
The large ones covered the surface of heaven and earth;
the fine ones entered within a tiny hair.
Even if they filled carts and linked teams of horses,
it would not be enough to carry them;
even if vast halls joined their rafters,
they could not house them.
Among them, the superior ones
were like Xiāngrú's *Shàng lín*,
Yáng Xióng's *Gān quán*,
Bān Gù's *Liǎng dū*,
Zhāng Héng's *Èr jīng*,
Mǎ Róng's *Guǎng chéng*,
and Wáng Shēng's *Líng guāng*.
At first, they reached the peak of grand and extravagant phrasing,
but ended with a concise and simple structure.
Resplendent with literary grace,
dense as gathered scales,
these were all greatness of recent *Cí Fù*.
As for the land, it has its constant products;
for customs, there are old traditions.
Regions are grouped by category;
things are divided by species.
However, the likes of Cháng Qīng
used things not of the region in excess
and situated them in the Central Realm,
falsely boasting of exotic species
and attributing existence to the non-existent.
Scholars who followed their construction
echoed them like thunder or attached to them like shadows,
wandering off and forgetting to return
for more than just one era.
In the past, the Hàn house collapsed from within,
and the four seas were split asunder.
The two families of Sūn and Liú
carved out and possessed Jiāo and Yì;
Wèi Wǔ corrected the chaos
and held possession of Hánxià.
Therefore, the authors first created the two guests of Wú and Shǔ,
extolling the strategic obstacles and magnificent wonders of their home territories,
which could be used to rule as regional kings;
but then for the Lord of Wèi, they described his capital region,
grand, expansive, abundant, and beautiful,
