embodying the intent of possessing all the Huá states.
It treats Wú and Shǔ as comparable to fallen states in their capture and destruction,
while Wèi, through the peaceful abdication, is compared to Táng and Yú.
Having already clarified rebellion and submission,
it also serves as a warning and lesson.
Indeed, Shǔ contained the resources of Liáng and Mín,
Wú carved out the wealth of southern Jīng,
and Wèi bestrode the abundance of the central region.
If one examines the extent of their territories,
calculates the abundance of their products,
compares the purity or corruption of their customs,
and assesses the merits or faults of their scholars,
they cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
The scholars of the two states,
each immersed in what they had heard,
every household thought their own land a delight,
and every person thought their own people excellent;
none of these are comprehensive arguments.
The author, following the dialogue between guests and host,
corrected them with the Capital of Wèi
and subdued them with the Kingly Way.
As for the products of the land,
one can open the maps and verify them.
As for the structures and systems of the state,
one can consult the records and confirm them;
how could this be a fabrication!
In my youth, I had great ambitions,
surpassing the common trends.
At the age of twenty, I entered the court,
and held various positions for twenty-five years.
At fifty, I left office due to circumstances.
In my later years, I took more pleasure in leisure and freedom,
deeply loving the forests and marshes.
So I withdrew to my villa in Héyáng.
In the design of the residence,
behind it was blocked by a long embankment,
and before it faced a clear canal.
The various trees numbered nearly ten thousand,
and flowing water circled beneath the house.
There were towers, pavilions, ponds, and marshes,
where many fish and birds were kept.
My family was traditionally practiced in the arts,
with quite a bit of the music of Qín and Zhào.
When going out, I occupied myself with sightseeing, hunting, and fishing;
when staying in, there was the pleasure of the zither and books.
I also enjoyed dietary alchemy and breath-swallowing,
with my will set on immortality,
proudly possessing an aspiration that reaches the clouds.
Suddenly, I was again pulled by the reins of office,
lingering among the Nine Ranks.
Exhausted by the vexations of the human world,
I often think of returning and sigh longingly.
Searching through the musical scores,
there is the Sī Guī Yǐn.
If the feelings of the ancients
were the same as those of today,
then I have composed this piece.
This piece has strings but no lyrics;
now I have written the lyrics for it,
to express my heart.
I regret there is no connoisseur of music in this age,
to have this new melody composed and spread through strings and bamboo.
The foundation of establishing virtue is constant,
but the paths to achieving merit are many.
Why is this?
He who follows his heart as his measure relies on himself;
he who relies on external things to accomplish tasks depends on others.
That which resides in oneself
increases or decreases only within its own realm;
that which depends on external things
prospers or declines according to what one encounters.
A falling leaf waits for a slight breeze to drop,
yet the power of the wind is actually meager.
Mèng Cháng wept upon meeting Yōng Mén,
yet the stimulus of the zither was secondary.
Why is this?
The leaf that is about to fall
does not need to borrow a gale;
the tears that are about to drop
do not require many mournful sounds.
Therefore, if the time is granted by Heaven
and principles are fully realized among the people,
even an ordinary man can achieve the merits of sages and worthies,
and a man of small capacity can establish the legacy of a hero.
Therefore it is said: his talent is not half that of the ancients,
yet his merit has already doubled theirs;
this is because he has gained the momentum of the times.
Looking through history from ancient to modern times,
those who sought the merit of a single moment
and occupied the positions of Yī and Zhōu have indeed existed.
Now, regarding the self's view of self,
even wise men are still entangled by its burdens;
regarding things' view of other things,
even insects possess this feeling.
With the capacity of one's self,
yet grasping extraordinary merits,
the sacred vessel of the state glows under one's glance,
and the myriad things follow one's every move.
The heart dallies in the peace of habitual status,
and the ears are glutted with flattering words;
how could one recognize that merit lies outside the self,
and that the responsibility exceeds one's own talent!
Furthermore, loving honor and hating disgrace
is the great expectation of all living beings;
to envy fullness and harm those above
even ghosts and spirits cannot avoid.
The ruler wields his constant handle of power,
and all under heaven submit to his great integrity.
Therefore it is said: can one make an enemy of Heaven?
Yet at times there are those in ceremonial robes carrying halberds,
standing beneath the temple gates,
raising banners and swearing to the masses,
aroused upon the paths between fields.
How much more so for those who issue commands on behalf of the ruler,
and personally distribute wealth!
Broadly planting kindness is not enough to counter resentment,
and diligently promoting benefits is not enough to compensate for harm.
Therefore it is said: he who carves on behalf of the master carpenter
will surely injure his own hand.
Furthermore, when the government was run by the Nìng Shì,
loyal ministers were moved to indignation;
when the ruler says "the sacrifice is mine alone,"
the sovereign cannot long endure it.
For this reason, Jūn Shì was dissatisfied,
displeased with the actions of Gōngdàn;
at Gāopíng they marshaled their forces,
looking askance at the power of Bólù.
And Chéng Wáng could not banish suspicion and stinginess from his heart,
while Xuān Dì felt as if he had thorns against his back;
is this not so?
Alas!
Radiating to the four corners,
no virtue is more abundant;
the king calls him "Uncle,"
no relation is closer.
Ascending to the great imperial throne,
no merit is greater;
maintaining integrity until death,
no loyalty is more ultimate.
Yet they tottered and fell,
barely able to preserve themselves.
Thus Yī Shēng embraced clarity and sincerity yet suffered punishment,
and Wénzǐ harbored loyalty and respect yet fell on his sword;
this was indeed their lot.
Judging from this,
even with such profound holiness and close kinship
as magnificent as that,
with great virtue and ultimate loyalty
as flourishing as this,
they still could not gain the trust of the sovereign’s heart
or stop the slander from the mouths of many.
Going beyond this,
how could one see any possibility of success!
The principles of safety and danger
can certainly be recognized.
How much more so for those who hunger for great fame, defying the taboos of the Taoists,
and wielding meager talent while making light of what sages and philosophers found difficult!
Personal danger arises because power is excessive,
and they do not know to relinquish power to seek safety;
calamity accumulates because favor is abundant,
and they do not know to decline favor to invite good fortune.
Seeing the common people plotting against them,
they then increase the palace guards,
to augment a majesty that cannot be sustained.
Fearing that the myriad people will not submit,
they then impose harsh punishments and severe regulations,
thereby inviting heart-wrenching resentment.
Then their majesty reaches the point of intimidating the ruler,
and resentment spreads among both high and low.
The hearts of the masses crumble daily,
the crisis is about to erupt,
yet they are just then lounging back and staring haughtily,
thinking themselves enough to boast to the world,
laughing at the ancients for being unskillful,
forgetting that their own affairs are already clumsy.
They know their past merits are worthy of pride,
but are ignorant that success and failure have their meeting point.
Thus, when affairs are exhausted and luck is spent,
they must surely fall;
when the wind rises and the dust gathers,
the calamity that arrives is always cruel.
The sage avoids merit and fame that exceed his person,
and dislikes favor and salary that go beyond measure;
this is precisely why.
The major ends of aversion and desire
are shared by both the worthy and the foolish,
yet the wandering seeker sacrifices himself for high position during his life,
and the man of ambition thinks of leaving a name behind after death;
the allotted portion of a received life
is merely this.
For an achievement that covers the age,
no name is greater;
for a power that shakes the sovereign,
no position is more flourishing;
to follow one's will without deviation,
no desire is more smoothly fulfilled.
If such a person were to observe the Heavenly Way,
knowing that the limit cannot be increased
and that fullness is hard to maintain for long,
if he were to transcend and withdraw himself,
bowing high and retiring,
then his towering grandeur
would look up to and surpass the former sages,
and his vast influence
would look down and crown the records of the future;
and great desires would not be lacking in his person,
supreme joy would not deviate from the old,
his restraint would be more effective and his virtue more expansive,
his person more at ease and his fame more illustrious.
If one does not do this,
one will surely be blind to that,
and then the traces of rivers and seas will be buried in stagnant streams,
a single basket of offense will accumulate into mountains,
one's name will be recorded in the list of the cruel and obstinate,
and one's person will be weary of the pain of bitter poison;
is this not a great error!
Therefore, I briefly compose this rhapsody,
hoping that for a hundred generations, there may be a few who awaken.
Since tablets and records have been written,
the traces of August Kings have already differed;
bells and stones are all displayed,
yet the sentiments of dance and song are not uniform.
Although the deep streams flow on
and detailed or brief versions are heard differently,
yet those who dwell in the Heavenly Heart
and establish the people's standard,
none fail to revere the Way,
spiritualize their positions,
expand the world and bequeath the succession,
securing ten thousand generations as their measure.
Our Sòng encompasses the realm,
the Imperial plan is grand and far-reaching.
Gāozǔ with sacred martiality fixed the tripod,
his regulations matching the Creator;
His Majesty with sagacious civility succeeded to the succession,
his brilliance belonging to the celestial residence.
The divination for the long-lasting Zhōu is already eternal,
the omen of honoring the Hàn is present here.
The legitimate heir nurtures virtue in the Shàoyáng,
the royal ministers spread wisdom in the supreme chancellery.
The stars and constellations brightly correspond,
mountains and rivers offer their numinous power.
People of the five directions gather in crowds,
from the four corners they come.
Selecting the worthy and establishing kin,
he houses them according to the flourishing statutes;
issuing orders and proclamations,
he must draw from ancient precedents.
The Dàyǔ coordinates the music,
the Shàngxiáng expands the teachings.
Regulations are clear and precise,
the ranks and forms are complete.
National etiquette follows the mandates,
military administration is prepared according to the nature of things.
Officers who admonish faults and record words,
or collate texts and discuss arts,
gather the neglected from within;
light carriages and vermilion chariots,
envoys who cherish the distant and shake the remote,
discuss virtue without.
Red stems and white down,
the auspicious signs of joined branches and shared ears of grain,
the history never ceases to record;
scaling mountains and sailing seas,
tributes crossing sands and surpassing deserts,
the treasury has no empty month.
Signal fires burn in a thousand cities,
courier stations connect ten thousand lǐ.
Lords of the domed dwellings
bow their heads and receive the calendar within;
chieftains in garments of grass
turn their faces and receive officials.
Thus extraordinary people admire the resonance,
and talented men emerge in abundance;
the imperial procession is clear and peaceful,
inside and out are joyful and harmonious.
Soon the capital will be moved to the center of the world,
and music will be performed in the suburbs of Dài.
Increasing the palaces for the Category Sacrifice to the Emperor,
decorating the halls for worshipping the spirits,
songs in the lanes and chants in the towns
have long looked for the dust of the imperial retinue.
The sun resides in the Wèi mansion,
the moon follows the Qīnglù path.
It is the beginning of the Great Earth's generation,
the time when the Sovereign King spreads harmony,
thinking to respond to the heart of the Supreme Numen,
to favor the wishes of the common people.
Furthermore, as the two kings depart,
with a farewell banquet and admonitions,
there is an edict for the Masters of Ritual,
whereupon the Astronomer is ordered
to offer the rite of drinking at the Luò
and prepare the ceremony of Shàngsì.
To the south, they clear the carriage road;
to the north, they purify the forbidden forest;
on the left, they border the rocky cliffs;
on the right, they bridge the source of the tide.
Passing through the riverbanks,
striding across the Zhī fields,
making a park of Tàiyè,
embracing Céngshān.
Pines and stones are steep and craggy,
verdant mists and cloudy vapors,
where those swimming and diving gather,
and those soaring and galloping come and go.
Thereupon, detached palaces are guarded,
separate halls are patrolled,
flag-gates stand open,
curtains extend to the barriers,
flowing water circles the steps,
and the pool is channeled to divide the seating.
The Chūnguān performs his duties,
the Cānglíng serves the path.
Then the Emperor mounts the secret carriage,
followed by the scarlet-clad guards,
shaking the jade bells,
sending forth flowing winds.
The heavens move and the spirits shift,
like a whirlpool or a covering cloud,
descending to the temporary residence,
according to ritual.
Then the Imperial radiance approaches the tent,
all officials take their ranks,
the phoenix carriage soon stops,
and the rainbow banners lower their streamers.
Meats and vegetables are spread in profusion,
wine and ale flow and float.
The appearance of beautiful songs and wonderful dances,
the instruments with silk cords and feathered decorations.
Tunes of three performances and four presentations,
melodies of Liùjīng and Jiǔchéng.
Competing spirits and numerous sounds,
matching transformations and vying for rhythm.
Dragon patterns decorate the reins,
azure-winged boats attend the sovereign.
Those from China and the borders arrive in crowds,
spectators gather in haste.
They wave their sleeves like wind in the mountains,
and raise their robes like shade over the marshes.
Elegant adornment brightens the fields,
fine clothing enriches the river.
Truly it makes the outer regions prosperous,
and the capital interior brilliant.
Above, it receives ten thousand years of life;
below, it brings a hundred blessings.
The entire banquet receives harmony,
the whole hall relies on virtue.
Sentiment lingers while the scene passes quickly,
joy is complete as the sun declines.
The golden carriage gathers the four horses,
the Sage's appearance lingers for a moment.
Regretting that the Jūntái has not been visited,
lamenting that the Fēnggōng is not nearby.
Now he will push open the Phoenix Gate for a high excursion,
and open the Juéyuán Garden for a grand feast.
Ordering all those in office
to present poems and express their will.
Then, in reciting praise with elegance,
and displaying sincerity without shame, would that not be so?
I have heard that "going out for pleasure" forms the hexagram Image,
where the music of Jūntiān is performed;
"riding the seasons" once the position is reached,
where the carriage that drives the winds soars.
Thus, one who attains the One and serves the Celestial,
wanders leisurely in the region of Xiāngchéng;
one who embodies the Primal and models the Great,
gazes longingly at the slopes of Gūshè.
Yet those are distant and lonely,
and he who enjoys them is alone.
As for the two dragons of the Sovereign of Xià,
driving on the Xuántái terrace;
or the eight steeds of Mù of Zhōu,
dancing in the shade of the Yáoshuǐ;
though there were feasts,
they were certainly not shared with the ten thousand people.
Our Great Dà Qí grasped the mechanisms of fate and created the era,
received the mandate and established the House,
accepted the rites at the Èrgōng,
and achieved merits in the Tàishì.
The dark and manifest realms offered their auspicious dates,
and the thunder and wind communicated their offerings.
The treasures of Zhāohuá have been moved hither;
the jade of Yánxǐ has returned there.
Replacing the Sòng and receiving the mandate of Heaven,
protecting and nurturing the ten thousand states,
surveying the capital calmed the sighs of Lùqiū,
and moving the tripods ended the shame of Dàjiōng.
Continuing the pure harmony of the Imperial way,
and linking the manifest virtue of the Royal standard.
Great developments opened distant auspicious omens,
establishing and securing the grand enterprise.
The Huángdì’s person embodies the highest sagehood,
and his destiny focuses on succeeding martial excellence.
He crowns the elegant qi of the Wǔxíng,
and surpasses the heroic spirit of the Sāndài.
Brightly manifest like the Yúnhàn,
glorious as the sun and moon,
encompassing Heaven and Earth,
and governing the mountains and rivers.
He established divine principles to influence customs,
and spread civilizing transformation to pacify the distant.
His bounty is universal and selfless;
his laws are broad and generous without killing.
Yet even so, throughout the night he foregoes sleep,
and by the sun's shadow he forgets his meals.
Mindful of carrying heavy weights over spring ice,
and thinking of driving runaway horses in autumn.
One may call it loftiness unsurpassed
and a vastness that none can name.
Holding the divine charts without being arrogant,
crossing the Mèngmén Pass, how could it be perilous?
The Crown Prince possesses wisdom and sagacity in his person,
with wonderful goodness residing in his nature.
Internally he accumulates harmony and compliance,
and externally he manifests brilliance and elegance.
Refining the ultimate virtue,
and polishing the excellent model.
His words are as bright as cinnabar and azure;
his Way is as lustrous as gold and jade.
He leaves the Lónglóu to consult with his attendants,
and enters the Hǔwéi to associate with the noble heirs.
Love and respect are perfected in his one person,
and his glory reaches to the four seas.
As for the clan, it flourishes like the Línzhǐ,
and the lineage is as firm as a massive rock.
Surpassing the houses of Chāng and Jī,
and overshadowing the Yán Hàn.
The chief ministers are equal to Shàngfù,
and the middle ministers follow the footsteps of Zhōunán.
Dividing Shǎn, they spread the joy of the un-cut pear tree;
entering service, they truly earn the reputation of capability.
All are like guī and zhāng jade,
with fine reputations and high prestige.
Their red knee-covers are grand;
they are the lords and kings of the house.
The prosperity of the root and branches being such,
and the government that examines antiquity being thus,
they were able to rescue all living beings from boiling water and fire,
and lead the hundred surnames into fine harmony.
Commoners in the wilds enjoy their work,
and those guarding the borders fulfill their duties.
Those who look into mirrors all have clear eyes,
and those who come to the ponds have no need to wash their ears.
The resentment of the hidden has vanished,
and the suffering of the recluses has dissipated.
Promoting the incorruptible and recommending the filial
at the appointed times in the outer bureaus;
recording conduct and discussing age
day and night in the central domains.
The offices of Xiélǜ and Zǒngzhāng
deepen relationships and rectify customs;
the roles of Chóngwén and Chéngjūn
guide virtue and standardize rites.
Bearing the clepsydra and declaring the night,
they discern the qi and the new moon at the Língtái;
writing on tablets and using red brushes,
they record words and deeds in the Xiānshì.
Officials who lift their curtains and judge with simple robes,
wearing tall caps and modest shoes;
and valiant warriors
who lift tripods and raise banners.
Diligently they sympathize with the people's hardships,
and investigate and expel the King's evils.
Shooting the falcons gathered on the high wall,
and shooting at the great wind in the long tunnel.
The unkind are far away,
and only the Way is practiced.
Slander and weeds are never heard,
and disputes are silenced.
The sound of drumsticks is rare on the smooth roads,
and lush grass grows at the prison gates.
The aged have no need to wander the markets,
and the young have many chariots and horses to enjoy.
The palace neighbors are bright and peaceful,
and the distant regions are clear and pacified.
Barbarians come to pay homage to the King,
and those with foreign speech enter to serve.
Lords with tattooed bodies and backward heels,
and chiefs with bound hair and pierced chests,
bend their knees and strike their foreheads,
requesting to receive the tether of submission.
Treasures of patterned axes and green stone arrowheads,
tributes of rare woods and fine fragrances,
curiosities like white oxen and dew dogs,
and teams of Chénghuáng and Zībái horses,
overflow in the storehouses
and crowd the suburban preserves.
Tribute boxes and tablets follow one after another,
and the interpreters are never idle.
Unifying the sentries from East to West,
and harmonizing the carriage gauges and scripts from North to South.
Broad hubs bury the rumbling tracks,
and the banners and flags are rolled up.
The four directions have no opposition,
and the five weapons do not resist.
Resting the leather armor and dismissing the chariots,

"Dignified are the numerous scholars,
through whom *Wén Wáng* enjoys peace."
Truly, it is through them that peace is found!
The brilliant spirit is only proclaimed;
among the *Róng* were the *Xiānlíng*.
The *Xiānlíng* were wild and frantic,
invading the western borders of *Hàn*.
*Hàn* commanded its tiger-like ministers,
particularly the *Hòu Jiāngjūn*.
He marshaled our six armies,
to punish and to awe them.
Having reached their territory,
he instructed them with majesty and virtue.
There were those who held to their pride in merit,
saying that he could not overcome them.
They requested to stir up their troops
against the *Qiāng* of *Hǎn*.
The *Tiānzǐ* commanded me
to follow him to *Xiānyáng*.
*Yíngpíng* maintained his integrity,
repeatedly submitting sealed memorials.
Assessing the enemy and securing victory,
his awe-inspiring strategy was unsurpassed.
Consequently, he conquered the western *Róng*,
and returned the army to the capital.
The *Guǐfāng* became submissive,
and there were none who did not come to court.
In the past, during the time of *Xuān* of *Zhōu*,
there were *Fāng* and *Hǔ*.
The poets sang of their merit,
and listed them in the *Yǎ*.
During the restoration of *Hàn*,
*Chōngguó* performed martial deeds.
Valiant and grand,
he also continued the legacy of those before him.
Vast is the high heaven,
descending blessings upon the Hàn.
Establishing the foundation and opening the enterprise,
praised by both humans and spirits.
The five planets shine in the night sky,
and the Sù Líng sighs in the night.
The imperial destiny arrived to be bestowed,
and ten thousand treasures increased in brilliance.
Twelve eras have passed,
and the Mandate of Heaven shifted.
The Xī Líng were not submissive,
and the Dōng Yí encountered rebellion.
Thus the High General was commanded,
and granted a powerful halberd.
Martial was the High General,
truly enlightened by Heaven.
Truly civil and truly martial,
clear in the Odes and delighted in the Rites.
Setting the law for the hundred ministers,
he acted as a model for the age.
Formerly at Mèngjīn,
there was only Teacher Shàngfù.
With one wave of the white yak-tail banner,
he unified the whole realm.
The common people began anew,
and the northern wind transformed the Chǔ.
Slightly attacking the Xiǎnyǔn,
he reached as far as Tàiyuán.
The poets sang of it,
yet still lamented its hardships.
How much more so our General,
at the exhausted cities and the farthest borders.
The drums did not stop sounding,
and the banners were not even briefly lowered.
His grace moistened the distant wilderness,
and his merit is inscribed on the tripod and cauldron.
I set forth my army,
to that western frontier.
The Son of Heaven gave me a farewell feast,
with a state carriage and four yellow horses.
Thinking of the Elder Uncle,
whose kindness was deep at Wèiyáng.
The large jade tablet was already carved,
and ranked lands rewarded his merit.
Now our General
opens the territory of Shàngjùn.
Passed to sons and passed to grandsons,
a brilliant and good reputation.
There is a Dàrén Xiānshēng,
who regards heaven and earth as a single morning,
and ten thousand ages as a brief moment.
The sun and moon are his windows,
and the eight wildernesses are his courtyard and paths.
He travels without wheel tracks,
and dwells without a house or hut.
He uses the sky as a canopy and the earth as a mat,
following his will wherever it leads.
When still, he holds a goblet and grasps a wine cup;
when moving, he carries a flagon and lifts a jug.
His only concern is wine;
how should he know of anything else?
There were noble young scions
and gentry hermits.
Hearing of my reputation,
they debated its reason.
Then, shaking their sleeves and baring their chests,
with glaring eyes and gnashing teeth,
they expounded on rites and laws,
and right and wrong arose like spear points.
The Master then held the jar and received from the vat,
sipped from the cup and rinsed with the unfiltered wine.
Shaking his beard and sitting cross-legged,
he pillowed on yeast and reclined on dregs.
Without thought or worry,
his joy was overflowing.
Suddenly he was drunk,
and clearly he awoke.
Listening quietly, he heard not the sound of thunder;
looking intently, he saw not the form of Mount Tài.
He felt not the cold or heat piercing his skin,
nor the stirrings of profit and desire.
Looking down at the myriad things,
they were as restless as duckweed floating on the Jiāng and Hàn.
The two heroes standing at his side
were like solitary wasps and caterpillars.
Chancellor, Marquis Wénzhōng of Cuán, Xiāo Hé of Pèi;
Chancellor, Marquis Yì of Píngyáng, Cáo Cān of Pèi;
Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince, Marquis Wénchéng of Liú, Zhāng Liáng of Hán;
Chancellor, Marquis Xiàn of Qūnì, Chén Píng of Yángwǔ;
King of Chǔ, Hán Xìn of Huáiyīn;
King of Liáng, Péng Yuè of Chāngyì;
King of Huáinán, Qíng Bù of Lù;
King Jǐng of Zhào, Zhāng Ěr of Dàliáng;
King of Hán, Hán Xìn;
King of Yàn, Lú Wǎn of Fēng;
King Wén of Chángshā, Wú Ruì;
King of Jīng, Liú Jiǎ of Pèi;
Grand Tutor, Marquis Yì of Ānguó, Wáng Líng;
Chancellor of the Left, Marquis Wǔ of Jiàng, Zhōu Bó of Pèi;
Chancellor, Marquis of Wǔyáng, Fán Kuài of Pèi;
Chancellor of the Right, Marquis Jǐng of Qūzhōu, Lì Shāng of Gāoyáng;
Coachman, Marquis Wén of Rǔyīn, Xiàhóu Yīng of Pèi;
Chancellor, Marquis Yì of Yǐngyīn, Guàn Yīng of Suīyáng;
Acting Chancellor of Dài, Marquis Jǐng of Yánglíng, Fù Kuān of Wèi;
General of Chariots and Cavalry, Marquis Sù of Xìnwǔ, Jìn Xī;
Grand Herald, Lord Guǎngyě, Lì Yìjī of Gāoyáng;
Palace Gentleman, Marquis Jiànxìn, Liú Jìng of Qí;
Grand Consultant, Lù Jiǎ of Chǔ;
Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, Lord Jìsì, Shū sūn Tōng of Xuē;
Wèi Wúzhī;
Protector of the Army, Suí Hé;
Elder Dǒng Gōng of Xīnchéng;
Yuán Shēng;
General Jì Xìn;
Imperial Censor, Zhōu Kē of Pèi;
Lord Píngguó, Hóu Gōng;
The above thirty-one men
are those who settled the realm and stabilized the altars of state.
The Eulogy says:
Vast is the universe,
murky above and dark below.
Waves shook the four seas,
and dust flew over the five sacred peaks.
The nine provinces wavered,
and the three spirits changed their divination.
Illustrious was Gāozǔ,
who first received the Heavenly Mandate.
His tracks were hidden in the central lands,
and his name flew into the imperial records.
Auspicious clouds responded with brilliance,
and the imperial steps were granted the wood.
A dragon rising from the banks of the Sì,
a tiger roaring in the valley of Fēng.
Red clouds gathered by day,
and the Sù Líng wailed by night.
The essence of gold then fell,
and the vermilion light became rich.
Ten thousand states settled their hearts,
and the outstanding people offered their service.
Grand was Lord Xiāo,
the royal foundation followed him.
Binding himself to the wise ruler,
none could compete with such a man.
Externally he aided the six armies,
internally he pacified the Sān Qín.
Plucking out the extraordinary and leveling difficulties,
he advanced virtue and relieved the people.
Embodying the state and establishing systems,
harmonious above and affectionate below.
His name covered all other lords;
he was called the pillar of the state.
Píngyáng delighted in the Way;
when things changed, he understood how to pass through.
Being deep and being silent,
he possessed this martial merit.
Driving far into Héshuò,
he struck like lightning east of the soil.
Coordinating strategies with Huáiyīn,
his tracks were second only to Lord Xiāo.
Wénchéng acted as a teacher,
penetrating the profound and piercing the dark.
Ever matching the mandate,
following his heart, he was divine.
Exhausting the spirits to observe transformation,
watching shadows to estimate emotions.
Ghosts had no hidden schemes,
and things had no escaping forms.
Wǔ Guān was thus opened,
and Hóngmén was thus pacified.
Following the difficulties at Yíngyáng,
he immediately planned at Xiàyì.
Melting the seals to advise against waste,
pushing Qí to encourage establishment.
Devising strategies at Gùlíng,
and deciding the plan for the eastern raid.
The three kings followed the wind,
and the five marquises truly gathered.
Overlord Chǔ was truly lost,
and Imperial Hàn entered in triumph.
With a joyful face and high vision,
he folded his wings like a phoenix withdrawing.
Entrusting his traces to Huáng-Lǎo,
renouncing the world and abstaining from grain.
The Marquis of Qūnì was grand and far-reaching,
skilled in deep and profound strategy.
His refined spirit wandered through the vast and distant void,
seeking divine traces.
The double mystery was not obscure to him,
nor the nine depths of the earth too deep.
He foresaw strategies in their earliest signs,
and suppressed the echo within the sound itself.
Six times he put forth marvelous schemes,
and four times his excellent deliberations turned the tide.
He guided his lord by the foot,
and alienated Xiàng Yǔ from his inner circle.
The formidable man then departed in resignation,
and the wings of Chǔ were truly broken.
When the King of Hán was distressed and captured,
the passage through the Hú horses was opened.
He welcomed Emperor Wén with a plan,
and wept for Emperor Gāo with sorrow.
Resplendent was the Marquis of Huáiyīn,
whose spiritual martial prowess surpassed the world.
His tactics emerged without fixed patterns,
his thoughts entered into divine accord.
He raised his arms and clouds arose,
his tracks bounded like a tiger devouring its prey.
Overcoming perils, he surely leveled them;
crushing the rigid, they became brittle.
He began his schemes on the banks of the Hàn River,
and returned to pacify the regions of the Wèi River.
Having seized Jīng and Suǒ,
he led his army north to punish the rebellious.
Crossing the Hé, he subdued Wèi;
climbing the mountains, he destroyed Zhào.
His majesty shone like a fierce fire,
his momentum exceeded a sweeping wind.
He picked up Dài as if finding something lost,
and laid low Qí like mowed grass.
The two provinces were cleared and pacified,
and the four states were all raised.
He turned his attention to northern Yàn,
and then reached as far as the Eastern Sea.
He conquered and killed Lóng Qiě,
and thereupon took his army.
The lives of Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ hung in the balance,
and human strategy sided with him.
Thinking of merit but only of virtue,
his words reached and cut off Chǔ.
Péng Yuè observed the times,
hiding his tracks and concealing his light.
People all looked up to him,
as he spread his wings like a soaring hawk.
His majesty overawed the territory of Chǔ,
while he entrusted himself to the King of Hán.
He pacified troubles between the Hé and Jì rivers,
and took his palace in the old territory of Liáng.
Fierce was Qíng Bù,
with a glaring, tiger-like gaze.
His name was foremost in powerful Chǔ,
his sharp edge was like startling lightning.
Seeing the signs, he shed his skin like a cicada,
realizing his true lord, he changed his countenance.
He took that fierce owl-like wind,
and turned it to fan our side.
Heaven's mandate was just being gathered,
and the King was in the Eastern Xià.
These three valiant heroes
arrived at Gāixià.
Once the arch-criminal was eliminated,
favor and emoluments were bestowed upon them.
To preserve complete and great fortune,
who but the virtuous could do so?
Their schemes were not good,
so they abandoned blessing and chose calamity.
The worthiness of Zhāng Ěr
had a reputation in Liáng and Wèi.
As a gentleman, he was boundless,
yet he brought shame upon himself.
Bowing his head, he thought of old favors;
looking up, he observed the five planets.
He escaped his tracks to avoid disaster,
and clearing the brambles, he arrived here.
He changed his strategy toward western Qín,
and repaid his humiliation in northern Jì.
The withered leaves shone again,
and the dry branches sprouted.
King Xìn was of Hán lineage,
who dwelt in the land and opened the frontiers.
"I plan for your talent,"
so he was moved to Jìnyáng.
Lú Wǎn started from humble origins,
and was affectionately close to our Emperor.
His honors surpassed his merit and virtue,
and fortune bestowed upon him a brilliant chapter.
When men are greedy for disaster,
they would rather face rebellion and death.
The kingship of Wú Ruì
owed its fortune to Méi Juán.
His merit was slight and his power weak,
yet for generations he was recorded as loyal and worthy.
Solemn was the King of Jīng,
who led our three armies.
We planned for the four directions,
and repeatedly recommended his merits.
He served his kinsman with labor,
and the old territory of Chǔ was divided for him.
He went to occupy those lands,
and greatly opened the Huái mounds.
The Marquis of Ānguó turned away from his kin,
and longingly I think of him.
Dear was his wise mother,
both enlightened and compassionate.
She drew her body over a sword,
to eternally solidify his purpose.
This virtuous man and gentleman
was truly the foundation of the state.
Righteousness showed in his expression,
and indignation broke out in his words.
If the lord perished, he would perish with him;
his final command was thus expected.
The Marquis of Jiàng was simple and plain,
of many plans and few words.
Once he showed his loyalty and courage,
the Emperor sighed in admiration.
Like clouds racing over Língqiū,
and shadows flitting over Shànglán.
He pacified Dài and captured Chén Shī,
and suddenly possessed Yàn and Hán.
He settled the chaos with martial force,
and destroyed the Lǚ clan with authority.
He cleansed the filth from the Purple Palace,
and summoned the Emperor from Tàiyuán.
Truly as the Grand Commandant,
the Liú lineage was thereby secured.
Holding merit that overawes the lord
has been difficult since ancient times.
His honors shone in the previous age,
and his life ended in a lower fief.
The Marquis of Wǔyáng met him on the road,
and escorted the Emperor through the deep marshes.
He exerted his strength for the royal house,
not only through his martial prowess.
Grasping his shield at Hóngmén,
he burst through the gates of the Emperor's dwelling.
With a stern face, he rebuked Xiàng Yǔ,
and with hidden tears, he awakened his lord.
The advancement of the Marquis of Qūzhōu
was due to his wise elder brother.
Making you lead your followers,
to follow the King on his campaigns.
He shook his majesty at Lóngtuì,
and exercised his martial skill at Yōngchéng.
Relying on the Six Armies,
he overcame the bitter and captured Qíng Bù.
How admirable was the Marquis of Rǔyīn,
composed and having ample capacity.
Starting his career with the war chariot,
he bore the whip and came to join.
When the horses were exhausted and the reins failed,
he did not let go of the protecting tree.
The imperial heir was then protected,
and at Píngchéng, he had a plan.
The Marquis of Yǐngyīn was sharp and quick,
frequently serving as the vanguard of the army.
Brandishing his halberd at Dōngchéng,
he captured Xiàng Yǔ and established his merit.
Riding the wind and utilizing the sound,
he strode loftily across the Chángjiāng.
He seized Wú and led the Huái,
and brilliantly opened up the east.
The merit of the Marquis of Yánglíng
was in following the Commander-in-Chief.
Trusting in his martial prowess, he went on a punitive expedition,
raising his banners at Jiānglíng.
The barbarian king's state was destroyed,
so that the rebellion was punished.
Across the vast and broad wilderness,
he birthed great plans and excellent schemes.
Coming forward, he offered admirable strategies;
retiring, he guarded famous cities.
To the east, he observed Báimǎ;
to the north, he held Fēihú.
He approached the granaries of Áo and Gēng;
he occupied the strategic Sāntú.
His light carriage trod the east,
and the winds of Hàn were carried forth.
Though he died in Qí,
it was not the fault of his persuasion.
Our Emperor truly remembered him,
and granted favor to his orphaned descendants.
Jiànxìn left his carriage,
clad in coarse cloth to offer treasures of wisdom.
He pointed to the examples of Zhōu and Hàn,
weighing the times and discussing the Way.
He moved the Emperor to the Yī and Luò rivers,
then settled the capital at Fèng and Hào.
To soothe the distant and stabilize the near—
truly, his investigations are to be revered.
How dignified was Lù Shēng,
who knew the consistency of words.
He went to suppress the powerful Yuè,
and returned to visit the Imperial Hàn.
He aligned with Zhōu Bó and Guàn Yīng,
to eliminate the wicked and cut down chaos.
This is the one we call
the eminent talent of the nation.
At the ultimate end of a hundred kings,
the old regulations no longer existed.
Though the virtue of Hàn was bright,
the court rituals were in disorder.
Shūsūn Tōng established the rites;
those below became respectful and those above honored.
Solemn were the imperial ceremonies,
brilliantly filling the gates.
His style looked back to the Three Dynasties,
and his laws flowed down to posterity.
Chén Wúzhī was wise and quick,
alone manifesting extraordinary feats.
His discernment was equal to Chancellor Xiāo Hé,
and his rewards were like the consensus of the multitude.
Suí Hé was eloquent and reaching,
utilizing the resources of the enemy.
Relieving Hàn and splitting Chǔ—
these were the achievements of this scholar alone.
The white-haired Elder Dǒng Sǒu
advised us at Píngyīn.
The three armies donned plain white silk in mourning,
and the hearts of all under heaven returned to Hàn.
Yuán Shēng was elegant and bright,
with a calm mind and good insight.
The flags of Hàn shook the south,
and the prestige of Chǔ was spontaneously thwarted.
His great strategies were deep and revolving,
and his primal merit echoed with effect.
Distant indeed was this man;
how subtle was his knowledge!
Jì Xìn deceived Xiàng Yǔ,
riding in the imperial carriage.
He composed himself and met his fate;
who would not be chastened by such a death?
His body vanished with the smoke,
but his name rose with the wind.
Zhōu Kē was noble and spirited,
his heart as pure as ice.
Punishment may be brutal,
but the will cannot be overcome.
Their loyal paths ended in death together,
but their brilliant traces rose together.
The Emperor rewarded your service,
and your descendants received the honor.
Though Heaven and Earth were in accord,
the King’s heart was troubled.
Longing for his kin and gazing toward Chǔ,
his words were filled with eternal grief.
Hóu Gōng leaned against the carriage bar
and the Imperial Mother returned home.
He was called the Marquis of Píngguó,
and his favored mandate was glorious.
As a mighty wind passes over objects,
the clear and the muddy both sound in response.
When a Great Man rises,
benefit lies in where he goes.
Rivers make the sea vast;
soil makes the mountains lofty.
The Shào and Hù music blend their notes;
the dragon robes match their emblems.
Brilliant were the many sages,
who together assisted the Heavenly Net.
The sword declared its sharpness;
the mirror offered its clarity.
Civil and military virtues filled the four directions;
the mandate of Hàn was able to expand.
Far-reaching is the distant style,
admired for a thousand years.
The Grandee’s taboo name was Shuò,
his style name was Mànqiàn,
and he was a native of Yàncì in Píngyuán.
During the Jiàn’ān period of Wèi,
Yàncì was partitioned to form Lèlíng Commandery;
thus he became a man of that commandery.
He served Hàn Wǔ Dì,
and the Hàn Shū records his deeds in detail.
The Master was extraordinary, vast, and reaching,
his thoughts encompassed change and versatility.
Believing that one should not seek wealth and honor in a corrupt world,
he wandered lightly to attain his position.
Since appearing in public could not be done through an upright path,
he behaved eccentrically to show his disdain for the world.
Since disdain for the world could not serve as a lasting lesson,
he offered direct admonitions to clarify his integrity.
Since clarifying integrity could not ensure long-term safety,
he used humor and wit to gain acceptance.
He kept his path pure while making his traces appear sullied;
he kept his essence clear while making his writings appear muddy.
He relaxed or tightened without becoming deviant,
and advanced or retreated without leaving the crowd.
As for his distant mind and vast tolerance,
his abundant wisdom and grand talent—
he was unconventional and possessed broad knowledge,
capable in many things by categorizing them.
He combined changes to clarify calculations
and offered hidden support to know the future.
From the Sān Fén and Wǔ Diǎn,
the Bā Suǒ and Jiǔ Qiū,
to the study of Yīn and Yáng and apocryphal texts,
the theories of the hundred schools and various flows,
the thorough and swift eloquence of debate,
and the fragmented and complex arts of divination;
from the skills of pulse-reading and medicine
to the arts of archery, charioteering, writing, and arithmetic—
he researched their essence and investigated their principles.
Without practicing, he exhausted their efficacy;
what passed his eyes he chanted with his mouth;
what passed his ears he kept in his heart.
His brilliant aid was open and clear,
containing greatness.
He overrode high ministers
and mocked the bold heroes.
His influence covered everything before him,
and he stepped over those in powerful positions.
In prominence, he did not rest in display;
in lowliness, he did not worry or grieve.
He played with the Emperor as if he were a mere companion,
and looked upon his peers like blades of grass.
His heroic integrity surpassed his generation,
and his high spirit covered the world.
He could be called one who stands out from the crowd,
a traveler beyond the physical world.
Talkers also say that the Master practiced deep breathing to harmonize his spirit,
expelling the old and inhaling the new;
that he shed his skin like a cicada and transformed like a dragon,
abandoning the mundane to ascend to immortality;
that his spirit communed with creation,
and his soul became a star.
These are strange and ethereal matters,
which cannot be fully discussed.
When my father came to govern this land,
I returned from the capital to visit him.
Seeing the Master’s county and town,
I thought of the Master’s high character.
Lingering by the main hall,
I saw the Master’s remaining portrait.
Wandering through the city walls,
I observed the Master’s shrine and temple.
Deeply moved with emotion,
I thus composed this praise.
The text says:
Lofty and resolute was the Gentleman,
living in seclusion while maintaining his constancy.
In retirement, he did not end in stagnation;
in advancement, he also avoided worldly glory.
Coming into the world, he cleansed his feet;
aspiring to the ancients, he shook his hat-strings.
He was like black dye but without stain;
amidst turbid waters, he could remain clear.
What does "without stain" mean?
Being high-minded yet able to be gentle.
What does "remaining clear" mean?
Regarding filth as a floating cloud.
His joy lay in what must be done;
dwelling in sinking depths, he felt no sorrow.
Transcending the generation and surpassing the times,
he stepped far and wandered alone.
Gazing back at past generations,
I think of his distant tracks.
Remote and profound was the Gentleman,
his Way was like that of a dragon.
Immersing his tracks in the court as a recluse,
he was harmonious but not conforming.
He rested in low positions,
merely to be at ease.
I have come from the east,
having arrived at this town.
I respectfully ask about his ruins and tomb,
standing on tiptoe to gaze at the plains and marshes.
The mound and grave exist in vain;
the spirit is forever stilled.
The people long for his example,
and thus this shrine was established.
Wandering about the temple and inner halls,
his lingering image remains in portraits.
Pacing through the shrine,
the courtyards and porticos are overgrown and desolate.
The rafters and pillars are leaning and falling;
the weeds and brambles are not cleared away.
Solemn and respectful was the Gentleman;
how could he still dwell here?
Though he dwells here without form,
my feelings for him are boundless.
For those of virtue in the past,
none failed to leave behind their spirit.
Heaven ordains the rites;
the divine inspection is very bright.
As if amidst the wind and dust,
I leave behind these words of praise.
The common people cannot govern themselves,
therefore a sovereign is established to rule them;
an enlightened sovereign cannot rule alone,
so ministers are appointed to assist him.
Thus, as the Sān Wǔ rose in succession,
through generations inheriting the foundation,
from yielding and abdication to shields and spears,
from civil virtue to military achievement,
all were fashioned by master craftsmen so that various talents might shine,
and the head of state devised strategies while the limbs and torso exerted their strength.
Encountering different circumstances,
their traces were superior or inferior.
As for the deep consolidation of their essence
and the Way's covenant not falling away,
the beauty of their influence fanned out,
and their instruction reformed a thousand years;
their principle is one.
Thus, when the Èr Bā were promoted, the Táng dynasty flourished;
when Yī and Lǚ were employed, Tāng and Wǔ were at peace;
when the three sages advanced, Xiǎobái flourished;
when the five ministers were manifest, Zhòng'ěr became hegemon.
In the middle ages, things declined;
this Way fell into neglect.
Those in high positions did not use ultimate impartiality to manage things;
those below surely used private paths to seek glory.
The one who managed the circle did not lead the masses with sincerity;
those who held the square surely used schemes to distinguish themselves.
Thus, sovereign and minister grew distant, and the moral teachings became thin;
the world was full of chaos, and the times were not governed.
Therefore, Qú and Níng rolled up or unrolled their talents;
Liǔxià was dismissed three times;
Jiéyú went about singing;
Lǔ Lián fled to the sea.
In a declining age,
to maintain one's reputation and integrity,
and for sovereign and minister to sympathize with each other
like the two halves of a tally,
then Yàn Zhāo and Lè Yì
were of that ancient sort.
If one does not encounter Bólè,
then in a thousand years there will not be a single Jì.
When the time met the "Dragon Countenance,"
then in that year he controlled the Sān Jié.
In terms of the Hàn dynasty's acquisition of talent,
it was most precious in this regard.
Although Gāozǔ did not use the Way's supremacy to manage things,
his subordinates were able to exhaust their loyalty;
although Xiāo and Cáo did not serve their lord as in the Sān Dài,
the people did not lose their livelihoods.
Quelling chaos and sheltering the people,
this too was second best.
When the times are in upheaval,
appearing is not as good as hiding;
when all things long for order,
silence is not as good as speaking.
Therefore, the gentlemen of old
did not worry that magnifying the Way was difficult,
but that encountering the right time was difficult.
If encountering the right time was not difficult,
then meeting the right sovereign was difficult.
Therefore, having the Way but no opportunity,
was why Mèngzǐ sighed;
having the opportunity but no sovereign,
was why Jiǎ Shēng wept.
A grand era once in ten thousand years
is the common path for the living;
a meeting once in a thousand years
is the joyful gathering of the wise and virtuous.
Encountering it, one cannot help but be happy;
losing it, how can one not be filled with regret?
The words of the ancients
truly have feeling!
During my leisure days,
I often read the Guó Zhì;
examining its sovereigns and ministers,
and comparing their deeds,
although their Way fell short of previous generations,
they were still the outstanding figures of their time.
Wénruò possessed the foresight of unique insight
and had the heart to save the world.
Assessing the times, the people were suffering in misery;
calculating ability, none surpassed Wèiwǔ.
Therefore, he submitted himself to the hegemon's court
to participate in the deliberation of worldly affairs.
He recommended talent without regard for his own reputation as a judge,
so it was only after a long time that they became prominent;
his planning was not for the sake of seeking credit,
so things were only settled after they reached their conclusion.
Although he lost his life for the sake of clear obedience,
his understanding was high indeed!
During the chaos of Dǒng Zhuó,
the sacred vessels of state were moved by force.
Gōngdá was filled with indignation,
his will set on sacrificing his life.
Speaking from this,
he greatly preserved his reputation and integrity.
As for being a subordinate of Hàn
while his tracks entered the tent of Wèi,
regarding the source and flow of his choices,
it was the same as what was said of Wénruò.
The reason their ends were different
and their beginning and end were not the same—
was it because Wénruò was already enlightened,
and the moral teachings had something to rely upon?
Benevolence and righteousness must be made clear,
so the master of the age raised their essence;
the principle of life must be preserved whole,
so the one of far-reaching insight grasped its key.
Together magnifying the Way,
is it not far-reaching!
Cuī Shēng was lofty and bright,
unbending even when broken.
The reason he pledged his name to Wèiwǔ
and held his tablet in the hegemon's court
was perhaps because the Hàn sovereign was still facing south,
while the Wèi lord was still facing north!
If once the imperial seals were presented
and sovereign and minister swapped places,
then it was something Cuī Zǐ would not go along with,
and Wèiwǔ would not tolerate.
Rivers and lakes are that which carry a boat,
yet also that which overturn a boat;
benevolence and righteousness are that which keep the body whole,
yet also that which destroy the body.
However, former sages were shattered like jade before him,
and coming wise men roll up their sleeves afterward.
Is this not because natural feelings arise from within,
and moral teachings bind all things?
Kǒngmíng lingered,
waiting for the right time to move;
he aspired to the likes of Guǎn and Lè,
and his refined character was clear from afar.
He governed the state with ritual,
so the people had no voice of grievance;
punishments were not excessive,
and there were no remaining tears.
Even compared to the "bequeathed love" of the ancients,
how could they surpass this!
When it came to the deathbed entrustment,
receiving the legacy to serve as Chancellor,
Liú Hòu entrusted him without doubt,
Wǔhóu handled it without fear,
the successor accepted him without duplicity of feeling,
and the common people trusted him without dissenting words;
the relationship between monarch and minister
is truly worthy of praise!
Gōngjǐn was outstanding,
his lofty ambitions were peerless.
Judging his lord from youth,
he had an early bond with Bófú;
in his later years his brilliance shone,
securing the tripartite division at Chìbì.
It is a pity his life was short,
for his ambitions were immeasurable.
Zǐbù assisted Cè,
attaining the beauty of far-reaching reputation;
he ceased the crying and stopped the sorrow,
performing the merit of supporting the leader.
Where his spirit was involved,
was it merely a matter of being outspoken and unyielding?
However, he shut his doors and was not used,
and when the altar was ascended, he faced mockery.
For a single person,
whose brilliance remains unchanged,
yet between being used and being discarded,
there is suddenly a difference;
how much more so for those hidden in ravines,
between those who meet their time and those who do not?
The creation of poems and odes
has its origins.
Some are to sing of emotions and nature,
some to recount virtue and manifest merit;
although the main purpose is the same,
what they rely upon may differ.
As for the path of serving or retiring,
if the name and substance are not stagnant,
then the style and virtuous voice
serve as a model for the world
and cannot be abandoned.
Therefore, I have again composed this preface for my thoughts
to make a eulogy for them.
Nine men from the Wèi Zhì,
four from the Shǔ Zhì,
and seven from the Wú Zhì.
Xún Yù, style name Wènruò;
Zhūgě Liàng, style name Kǒngmíng;
Zhōu Yú, style name Gōngjǐn;
Xún Yōu, style name Gōngdá;
Páng Tǒng, style name Shìyuán;
Zhāng Zhāo, style name Zǐbù;
Yuán Huàn, style name Yàoqīng;
Jiǎng Wǎn, style name Gōngyǎn;
Lǔ Sù, style name Zǐjìng;
Cuī Yǎn, style name Jìguī;
Huáng Quán, style name Gōnghéng;
Zhūgě Jǐn, style name Zǐyú;
Xú Miǎo, style name Jǐngshān;
Lù Xùn, style name Bóyán;
Chén Qún, style name Chángwén;
Gù Yōng, style name Yuántàn;
Xiàhóu Xuán, style name Tàichū;
Yú Fān, style name Zhòngxiáng;
Wáng Jīng, style name Chéngzōng;
Chén Tài, style name Xuánbó.
The Fire Virtue having faded,
destiny was caught in Dàguò.
Great gales fanned the seas,
and the two oceans raised waves.
Though the dragons and tigers were startled,
the wind and clouds were not yet in harmony.
Submerged fish chose their depths,
and high birds waited for branches.
The three magnificent heroes
together turned the celestial axis.
Competing to collect fine timber,
struggling to gather pine and bamboo.
Phoenixes had no time to roost,
and dragons had no leisure to lie hidden.
Valleys had no secluded orchids,
and ridges had no graceful chrysanthemums.
Brilliant Wènruò,
his spiritual insight shone through clearly.
Responding to change, he knew the subtle;
exploring the profound, he appreciated the essential.
Sun and moon were within his person;
the more he was hidden, the more he shone.
Cultural brilliance reflected in his heart;
the more one delved, the more wonderful it became.
While the vast seas overflowed
and jade and stone were crushed together,
this realized man sought the universal good,
setting aside himself to preserve love.
His strategies resolved the troubles of the time,
and his merits aided the entire realm.
At first, he saved the people,
and in the end, he clarified his noble character.
Gōngdá was profound and lucid,
his thoughts matched the milfoil and tortoise.
His applications were without fixed patterns,
and his actions encompassed all gatherings.
From the start of his career,
he encountered these tumultuous times.
His spirit was mysteriously settled;
he handled things with increasing ease.
Quietly within the command tent,
no calculation failed to be thorough.
Diligently reaching the rhythms,
his traces never paused.
Though he held a foot-long jade,
he looked back and smiled at fame and wealth.
Knowing he could save things,
his "foolishness" was enough to preserve his life.
Lángzhōng was warm and elegant,
his capacity and knowledge were pure and simple.
Upright but not stubborn,
versatile but able to remain firm.
A respectful and virtuous heart,
a vast and grand standard of conduct.
His ambitions were established in youth,
and his Way was spread in his later years.
A man of benevolence is surely brave;
virtue also has its expression.
Though he encountered treading on a tiger,
his spirit remained calm.
His conduct was not decorative,
and his reputation and traces had no flaws.
His integrity was not abrasive,
and his simple style became even fresher.
Far-reaching was Cuī Shēng,
his form was upright and his heart was straight.
His natural character was clear and bright,
and his bearing was high and majestic.
Loyalty resided in his tracks,
and righteousness was shaped in his expression.
He thought to plant fragrant orchids
and prune away the thorns and briars.
People detest those above them,
and the times did not tolerate the wise.
Resounding like jade was the gentleman,
elegantly leaning on his reputation and integrity.
Though he met with dust and mist,
he still shook off the frost and snow.
When destiny reached its limit and the Way faded,
this bright moon was shattered.
Jǐngshān was magnanimous and unrestrained,
his rhythm harmonized with the Way.
He did not dwell on physical forms;
his mind was as vast as the sea.
Harmonious but not conformist,
versatile but not confused.
When drunk, he forgot his words;
when sober, he left behind responses.
Chángwén was thorough and elegant,
his righteousness set the standard from beginning to end.
Thinking to support the sovereign,
he would feel the same shame as Yī.
When the people did not yet know virtue,
he feared as if the fault were his own.
Excellent strategies were spread in the court,
and honest words filled the ears.
Although the birth of jade is beautiful,
its light does not exceed a handful.
Although the accumulation of virtue is subtle,
its Way illuminates the world.
Profound was Tàichū,
his capacity and bearing were lofty and elegant.
His character and standard were natural,
a model that required no artifice.
To preserve the self depends on uprightness;
any trace of defilement is surely false.
Facing death was not difficult for him,
for where the Principle resides, it is easy.
All things are tossed by waves;
who can bear their burdens?
The six directions are vast in vain,
for there is no place to house the body.
Devotion to ruler and parents is natural,
not derived from the Teaching of Names.
Since reverence and submission were the same,
both emotion and ritual were fully attained.
Intense was Wáng Shēng,
knowing death, he did not falter.
To seek benevolence was not far;
his aim lay in loyalty and filial piety.
Xuánbó was firm and concise,
greatly upholding reputation and substance.
His will was set on high structures,
adding to the halls and the steps.
Standing upright at the Hǔ Mén,
his direct words were ever enlightening.
Facing danger, he gave his life,
exhausting his heart and ritual.
Imposing was Kǒngmíng,
his foundational bearing was vast and far-reaching.
His talent was equal to the most eminent people,
uniquely endowed with prior awakening.
A standard-bearer of style and grace,
his distant brilliance matched Guǎn and Lè.
At first, like a coiled dragon,
his refined will was ever more firm.
When the Way was lost in the Bǎiliù disaster,
spears and shields were used in succession.
If not for one born to the age,
who could sweep away the mist and miasma?
Thinking of the tranquility of the dynastic house,
he briefly loosened the reins.
Putting off common clothes in the forest,
he became a pillar of the times.
Shìyuán was grand and expansive,
his refined nature inwardly harmonious.
He honored goodness and loved all things,
knowing the end by observing the beginning.
Turmoil and disorder were complete,
and the path to victory had not yet flourished.
The Master signaled it,
raising a clear breeze.
Bound closely to the wise sovereign,
it was a time without falsehood.
Day and night without negligence,
his duty lay in continuous brilliance.
Once the Sān Lüè were presented,
the foundation of hegemony was established.
Gōngyǎn planted his roots,
never forgetting the center and the upright.
Could it be said he was merely imitating?
It truly lay in his refined nature.
Once harnessed and bridled,
he bore the mandate of the times.
Promoting the worthy and humbling himself,
he remained venerable after a long time.
Gōnghéng and Zhòngdá,
held hearts that were deep and solid.
Serving that one man,
they were not confused when facing difficulty.
In the past, when things were not established,
they borrowed wings in a neighboring state.
Advancing, they could spread a fine reputation;
retreating, they did not lose their virtue.
The six directions were in turmoil,
and the people's hearts were about to change.
Birds choose the high paulownia;
a minister must look to where he turns.
Gōngjǐn was heroic and talented,
his bright mind had unique insight.
Parting the grass to seek his lord,
they settled their friendship at one meeting.
Formidable was Wèiwǔ,
outwardly relying on the traces of hegemony.
With a will that overshadowed Héng and Huò,
he relied on battle and forgot the enemy.
Outstanding was that man,
who shone brilliantly at Chìbì.
The three lights were divided into three parts,
and the universe was temporarily separated.
Zǐbù possessed a great name,
meeting the world just as it was in turmoil.
Folding his wings in his home village,
he rested his shoulders in Jiāngbiǎo.
The King's strategy was smooth and easy,
and both Wú and Wèi treasured him.
He then offered grand plans,
to rectify this way of hegemony.
When Huánwáng passed away,
the great enterprise was not yet pure.
Holding the arm and entrusting the orphan,
to only the worthy and the kin.
Stopping the weeping and ending the grief,
he forgot himself when facing difficulty.
That the south-facing position was achieved
was truly due to this old minister.
Talents are born for the age,
and the age also requires talent.
Obtaining them and being able to employ them,
value lies in having no suspicion.
Lofty was Zǐjìng,
rising from the weeds and marshes.
Carrying the load and uttering wonders,
he then constructed the Yún Tái.
Zǐyú was elegant and superior,
his nature pure and excellent.
He admonished without offending,
and was upright without being harsh.
Taking orders in the public court,
he forgot his private position when retiring.
Were there no wagtails?
Yet he was certainly cautious about his reputation and rank.
Bóyán was resolute and upright,
assisting the world with the Dao.
Going out, he could strive for merit;
coming in, he could offer advice and alternatives.
His schemes brought peace to the state,
resolving conflicts and blunting the enemy's edge.
Being upright, he invited suspicion;
being loyal, he suffered punishment.
Yuántàn was solemn and far-reaching,
his spirit harmonious and his form disciplined.
Like that white jade tablet,
his substance had no speck of dust.
He established his superior with constancy,
and rectified his superior gradually.
Clarity did not increase his purity,
and turbidness did not add any stain.
Zhòngxiáng was high-minded and brilliant,
but his nature was not in harmony with others.
He loved being different from the crowd,
and would break rather than bend.
Repeatedly brushing against the inverted scales,
he was dismissed for his straight path.
His lamentations surpassed those of Sūn Yáng;
his exile was like that of Jiǎ and Qū.
Numerous were the many worthies,
a meeting once in a thousand years.
Adjusting their reins on the high thoroughfare,
they raised their heads toward the heavenly path.
Above, they drew from the mysterious flow;
below, they magnified the affairs of the times.
Reputation and integrity took different paths,
but their elegant aims shared the same goal.
The sun and moon are beautiful in the sky;
looking at them, they do not fall.
Benevolence and righteousness were within them;
using them, they were never exhausted.
Thinking still of their double brilliance,
again I draw from and savor it.
Later generations clap their hands in rhythm;
even the cowardly feel their spirit increase.
In the beginning of high antiquity,
the people were born from the vast heavens.
Choosing through the successive rulers
down to the Qín.
Those nearby followed in their footsteps;
those far off heard their reputation.
In great abundance and luxuriance,
those who have vanished without being named
are beyond counting.
Following the Shào and Xià music,
honoring titles and posthumous names,
there are seventy-two lords who can briefly be spoken of.
Is there any who was virtuous and did not prosper?
Is there any who was rebellious and lost who could survive?
Before Xuānyuán,
how distant and remote it was!
Its details cannot be heard.
In the records of the Wǔ Sān and the Liùjīng,
only the general spirit can be observed.
The Shū says:
“The head is enlightened!
The ministers are excellent!”
Speaking from this perspective,
no ruler was more grand than Táng Yáo,
and no minister was more worthy than Hòujì.
Hòujì founded the enterprise under Táng Yáo,
and Gōngliú rose to prominence among the Xīróng.
Wénwáng reformed the systems,
whereupon Zhōu reached its highest peak;
great deeds were completed and surpassed.
Afterward, it gradually declined and weakened,
and for a thousand years its voice was lost.
Was it not a case of starting well but not ending well!
Yet there were no heterodoxies;
they were cautious about the origins in the past
and careful in leaving teachings for the future.
Thus the path was level and easy,
making it easy to follow.
Deep kindness was vast and grand,
making it easy to enrich.
Laws and measures were clear and bright,
making it easy to model.
The lineage was handed down in an orderly way,
making it easy to succeed.
Therefore, the enterprise flourished from its infancy and its loftiness surpassed the two rulers.
Evaluating its beginning
and tracing it to its final end,
nothing exceptionally extraordinary or unique can be verified today.
Yet they still trod upon Liángfù
and ascended Tàishān,
established illustrious titles,
and bestowed honored names.
The virtue of the Great Hàn
gushes like a spring,
surging and overflowing,
spreading to the four boundaries.
Like clouds spreading and mist dispersing,
it reaches up to the nine heavens
and flows down to the eight horizons.
All living things
are soaked and moistened by it.
Harmonious Qi flows everywhere,
and military prestige sweeps like the wind.
Those nearby roam the plains,
and those far away swim in the waters.
The chief evildoers are submerged and gone;
darkness becomes bright and clear.
Even the insects are joyful
and turn their heads toward the interior.
Then, the rare herds of Zhōuyú were enclosed,
and strange beasts like the Milu were captured.
A single stalk with six ears of grain was brought to the kitchen;
beasts with two horns sharing a single base were sacrificed.
The remaining treasures of Zhōu were obtained, and tortoises were released at Qí.
The Cuìhuáng was summoned and dragons were ridden in the ponds.
Ghosts and spirits met at the Língyǔ
and became guests at the secluded guesthouses.
Strange things are mysterious and marvelous,
extraordinary and endlessly changing.
How venerable!
Auspicious omens have reached this point,
yet His Majesty still considers his virtue thin
and dares not speak of the Fēngshàn.
When Zhōu had the omen of the fish leaping into the boat,
they celebrated it with a burnt offering.
If not for such omens,
to ascend the Great Mound
would be cause for shame!
Compared to their way of advancement and humility,
how very different it is!
Then the Dàsīmǎ came forward and said:
“Your Majesty nurtures all living things with benevolence
and subdues the disobedient with righteousness.
The Zhūxià joyfully offer tribute,
and the hundred barbarian tribes bring offerings.
Your virtue equals that of the beginning,
and your merit is second to none.
Your beautiful deeds are pervasive,
and auspicious omens of many kinds
arrive in continuous succession,
not just appearing once.
I believe Tàishān and Liángfù have set up altars awaiting your visit,
to bestow titles to reflect your glory,
but Your Majesty is humble and does not act.
You withhold the joy of the Sānshén
and omit the rituals of the Kingly Way;
the officials are ashamed.
Some say that because Heaven’s essence is obscure,
once it shows precious omens, one cannot refuse them.
If you refuse them,
then Tàishān will have no record and Liángfù no chance.
Though each ruler flourished in his own time,
they all completed their eras and then passed;
what would commentators praise in the future
when speaking of the seventy-two rulers?
Cultivating virtue leads to receiving omens,
and receiving the mandate leads to performing the ceremonies;
this is not overstepping.
Therefore sage kings did not neglect
to perform rituals for the Earth Spirits
and report to the Heaven Spirits.
They carved their merits on the Zhōngyuè
to manifest their supreme status,
spread their grand virtue,
issue glorious titles,
and receive deep blessings
to benefit the common people.
How magnificent is this grand spectacle of the world,
the ultimate achievement of a King;
it cannot be diminished.
I wish Your Majesty to complete it.
Afterward, following the general methods of the scholars,
allow them to receive the faint light and lingering flames of the sun and moon
to display their administrative affairs.
Also, correctly list the meanings
and polish the writings
to create a work like the Chūnqiū.
It will continue the old Six Classics to become Seven,
expressing it without end,
allowing ten thousand generations to be stirred by the clear stream,
raising slight ripples,
flying the heroic fame,
and leaping with lush reality.
This is how former sages preserved their great names forever and were always praised as leaders.
It is fitting to order the Master of Ceremonies to report all the rituals for your review.”
Then the Son of Heaven solemnly changed his expression
and said:
“Indeed!
I shall try it!”
Then he shifted his thoughts and reflections,
summarized the discussions of the high officials,
inquired into the matters of the Fēngshàn,
praised the vastness of the great marshes,
and expanded upon the abundance of auspicious omens.
Finally he composed a hymn, saying:
Since Heaven covers me,
the clouds are thick and lush.
Sweet dew and timely rain fall;
the soil is pleasant to roam.
Moisture seeps and trickles;
what living thing is not nurtured!
Good grain with six ears;
how could our harvest not be stored?
Not only does it rain upon it,
but it also moistens it.
Not only does it cover me,
but it spreads out to protect all.
All things are joyful,
cherishing and longing.
Famous mountains and illustrious positions
await the arrival of the Sovereign.
O Sovereign, O Sovereign,
will you not proceed?
The striped beasts
rejoice in my Sovereign’s garden.
White bodies with black patterns,
their appearance is admirable.
Gentle and solemn,
they have the manner of a gentleman.
One had heard their voice;
now one personally sees them come.
From where do they come?
A sign of Heaven’s omens.
This also happened with Shùn,
when the Clan of Yú arose.
The bright Lín
roams those sacred altars.
In the tenth month of early winter,
the Sovereign goes to the suburban sacrifice.
Galloping to my Sovereign’s carriage,
the Emperor thereby receives blessings.
Before the Three Dynasties,
this has never happened.
The winding Yellow Dragon
ascends with rising virtue.
Its colors are dazzling,
brilliant and radiant.
Manifesting in the pure Yang,
it awakens the common people.
The records carry this,
saying it is what the one who receives the mandate rides.
Its manifestation has patterns;
it need not be repeated tiresomely.
Relying on categories to convey meaning,
it is analogized by the sealing of the peaks.
Opening the literary arts and observing them,
the intersection of Heaven and Man has already joined,
and the high and low mutually inspire and respond in accord.
The virtue of the Sagely King
is cautious and reverent.
Thus it is said: in times of rise, one must consider decline;
in times of peace, one must think of danger.
Therefore, Tāng and Wǔ reached the peak of solemnity
and never lost their respectful reverence;
and when Shùn was within the grand canons,
he looked back and inspected any omissions;
this is what is meant.
To the various officials:
Your servant Xióng, Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
bows his head and prostrates twice to present this memorial to His Majesty the Emperor:
Your servant Xióng's knowledge of the classics is shallow and thin,
and my conduct and abilities are nothing extraordinary.
Having frequently received your profound grace,
and being promoted among my peers,
to stand alongside the many worthies,
I am ashamed to have no way to fulfill my duties.
Your servant humbly reflects that Your Majesty, with the virtue of a supreme Sage,
rose like a dragon to take the throne,
reverent and enlightened, honoring antiquity,
acting as the father and mother of the people,
and serving as the master of all under Heaven.
Holding to the path of pure essence,
like a mirror reflecting the four seas,
listening to the customs and folkways,
surveying broadly and encompassing extensively,
matching Heaven and equaling Earth,
possessing the brilliance of the spirits,
pairing with the Wǔdì,
and surpassing the Sānwáng.
Since the beginning of the world,
nothing like this has ever been heard.
Your servant truly delights in manifesting your new virtue
and illuminating it without limit.
In the past, Sīmǎ Xiāngrú composed the *Fēngshàn* piece
to highlight the beauty of the Hàn dynasty.
Your servant often suffers from dizziness
and fears that one day I will precede the dogs and horses
and fill the ditches and ravines,
with my thoughts left unmanifested
and harboring eternal regret in the Yellow Springs.
I dare to exhaust my heart and soul
to pour out my innermost thoughts
and compose the *Jù Qín Měi Xīn* piece,
and though it does not exhaust one ten-thousandth of the subject,
it represents the limit of your servant’s thoughts.
Your servant Xióng bows his head and prostrates twice to inform you,
saying:
In the beginning, when Heaven and Earth were not yet separated,
all was indistinct and vast.
Some things were dark and sprouted,
some were yellow and budded.
When the Dark and the Yellow were divided,
the upper and lower mutually nurtured each other.
Then, when the people were first born,
Emperors and Kings began to exist.
In those murky and boundless times,
rumors were diffuse and not clearly perceived;
the world could not speak of them.
As for those who could be spoken of:
above, none were more manifest than Xīhuáng;
in the middle, none were more flourishing than Táng and Yú;
recently, none were more illustrious than Chéngzhōu.
Zhòngní did not encounter a time of employment;
thus, the *Chūnqiū* was issued in distress.
Speaking of what the spirits bless
and what the millions of people rely upon,
it never fails to mention Way, Virtue, Benevolence, Righteousness, Ritual, and Wisdom.
Only Qín arose abruptly from the Xīróng,
in the lands of Bīn, Huàng, Qí, and Yōng.
Following the usurped traces of Xiāng, Wén, Xuān, and Líng,
the foundation was established by Xiàogōng,
flourished under Huìwén,
and was energized by Zhāozhuāng.
When it reached Zhèng, he broke the Vertical Alliance and monopolized the Horizontal Alliance,
swallowed the six states,
and finally called himself Shǐhuáng.
He grandly followed the deviant policies of Yāng, Yí, Wěi, and Sī,
and galloped ahead with the military operations of Qǐ, Jiǎn, Tián, and Bèn.
He eradicated ancient texts,
scraped away speech and burned books,
abandoned rituals and ruined music,
and blinded and deafened the ears and eyes of the people.
He then wished to wash away Táng and Yú,
cleanse Yīn and sweep away Zhōu,
burning and removing the records of Zhòngní.
He carved his own achievements,
changed the systems and measurements,
and made everything conform to the records of Qín.
Therefore, elderly scholars and great masters
clutched their books and fled to distant places;
ritual officials and doctors
rolled up their tongues and did not speak.
The bird of good omen
and the beast with fleshy horns
were wild and did not arrive.
Sweet dew and fine wine,
the auspicious signs of brilliant light and soaking pools remained hidden.
Great comets and falling stars,
the anomalies of giant barbarians and ghostly beliefs broke out.
The spirits ceased their guidance,
and the seawater flew in groups.
It perished in its second generation—
how extreme it was!
The Way of the Emperors and Kings
is so cautious that one cannot depart from it.
Those who can be upright and enlightened exhaust auspicious signs;
those who are perverse and deluded reach the limit of disasters and errors.
Looking up at antiquity in the past,
even those with signs to rely on still had deficiencies.
How could one who destroyed and tore down remain whole?
Therefore, those like the ancients praised Yáo and Shùn;
those who were tyrannical and insulting fell like Jié and Zhòu.
How much more so for one who completely swept away the achievements of former sages over thousands of years,
and used only his private will—how could such a one enjoy divine protection?
It happened that the Hàn ancestor rose like a dragon from Féng and Pèi,
swiftly moving from Wǎn and Yè.
From Wǔguān, he exerted joined efforts with Xiàng Yǔ at Xiányáng,
founded the enterprise in Shǔhàn,
began his rise in Sānqín,
defeated Xiàng east of the mountains,
and became Emperor of the world.
He picked out the most cruel and troublesome of the Qín policies
and abolished them according to the time.
Elements like the forest of scholars,
penal laws,
calendar records,
and the use of maps and canons were gradually increased.
The remaining systems of Qín
and the titles and ranks of the Xiàng clan,
though they deviated from antiquity, were still followed.
Thus, the imperial canons were deficient and not repaired;
the royal net was slack and not yet stretched.
The Way reached its limit and the cycle of fate was exhausted;
it became dark and sudden, never to return.
When it came to the Dà Xīn receiving the Mandate,
Shàngdì restored his favor,
Hòutǔ looked back with care,
mysterious tallies and spiritual tokens appeared,
and yellow auspicious omens gushed forth,
bubbling and surging,
flowing like rivers and pooling like the sea,
moving like clouds and bowing like the wind,
gathering like mist and dispersing like rain,
spreading throughout the eight frontiers,
presented above to the Heavenly Court,
with thunderous sounds and the sun's shadow,
fiery light and flying echoes,
filling the space between Heaven and the Deep,
it was truly something that could not be declined.
Thereupon, obeying the Mandate of Heaven,
he reached the peak of favor and the height of honor,
sharing the divine tallies with Heaven
and aligning with the spiritual tokens of Earth,
creating for the millions of people
and planning for ten thousand generations,
extraordinary, magnificent, exceptional, and marvelous
were the sacrifices to Heaven and the services to Earth.
Those rare objects and extraordinary wonders
observed by the Wǔ Wēi Jiàngshuài
and promulgated throughout the world
numbered forty-eight chapters.
They ascended to the Huángqióng
and spread across the lands below;
who else but the Xīn Jiā could have received them?
How lofty and brilliant,
the true marks of the Son of Heaven!
