As for the white dove and the cinnabar crow,
the white fish and the severed snake,
compared to this, they are nothing.
Receiving the Mandate was very easy,
but bringing it to fulfillment required great diligence.
In the past, the Emperors followed the Sovereigns,
and Kings followed the Emperors,
following the footprints of the ancients,
some governing through non-action,
while others perished through additions and subtractions.
How could they know that the Xīn Shì has devoted its heart and concentrated its will,
storing its thoughts and attending to its duties,
working solemnly on all sides,
not sleeping until dawn,
being diligent and earnest—
was it not even more so than that of Qín?
For if one is not diligent,
one cannot match the predecessors;
if one is not earnest,
then the awakening of virtue will not be joyful.
Therefore, he opened the secret storehouses,
perused the forest of books,
gathered from the grove of the refined and elegant,
and soared through the fields of rites and music,
taking up the lost works of Yīn and Zhōu,
and continuing the interrupted traditions of Táng and Yú,
establishing fine laws and excellent measures,
golden codes and jade regulations,
divine hexagrams and spiritual omens,
all the ancient texts were fully revealed,
shining brightly and radiantly,
none failed to be proclaimed and attained.
Carriage bells and banners were used to display them,
the harmony of bells and the Sìxià music were used to pace them,
embroidered robes and caps were used to manifest them,
the correctness of marriage and funerals were used to honor them,
and the kinship of the nine grades of relatives and the virtuous were used to harmonize them.
Now, revising the rituals for the gods and spirits
is the highest ceremony.
Reverently cultivating the hundred sacrifices
is the proper order.
The Míngtáng and the Yōngtái
are magnificent sights.
The Nine Ancestral Temles of longevity
are the ultimate of filial piety.
Formulating the Six Classics
is a grand undertaking.
Winning over the Chányú in the north
is the expansion of virtue.
As for restoring the five ranks of nobility,
measuring the three grades of soil,
managing the jǐngtián system,
exempting people from forced labor,
emulating the Fǔ Xíng,
and correcting the Mǎ Fǎ,
these broaden and exalt the winds of reverence, diligence, brilliant virtue, and beautiful harmony,
and widen the path for the gentry to study, lecture, remonstrate, and recite,
the sounds of vibrant egrets fill the court,
and the ranks of noble swans and phoenixes gradually ascend the steps.
Thus, the legacies of the former sages
are spread and flowed without being hidden or restricted.
How rich and brilliant!
The affairs of Heaven and man are flourishing,
and the expectations of ghosts and spirits are fully met.
Among the various lords and former officials,
none fail to be orderly;
among the wicked and the bandits,
none fail to be shaken by his awe.
Continuing the lineage of Shǎodiǎn,
and manifesting the descendants of Huáng and Yú.
What was missing in the Imperial Canons has been supplemented,
and the kingly bonds that were slack have been tightened,
brilliant and glorious,
is it not beautiful!
Those who were steeped in his influence and transformed
are deep and hidden in the capital,
pervasive within the imperial domain,
diligent in the marches and guards,
and purified in the remote wilderness,
following the former canons,
touring the four classes of people,
reaching the Four Peaks,
adding to the sacrifices at Tài Shān,
and performing the Zen sacrifice at Liángfù,
these are the canonical achievements of one who has received the Mandate.
For one who receives the Mandate, there is never enough time,
and even if one had not received the Mandate,
there would still be things to do.
How much more so for the grand Yǒu Xīn,
appearing exactly at the right time,
the spirits of the lofty peaks, deep seas, and connecting rivers
have all set up altars and fields,
waiting for the arrival of the one who received the Mandate.
In the distant regions beyond the seas,
they truly crane their necks and stand on tiptoe;
turning their faces inward
and looking up with longing.
Though the Emperor is diligent,
how can he stop?
He should command the wise and talented to compose a chapter of the Imperial Canon,
following the tradition of combining the former three into one,
to show to those who come after,
and spread it without limit.
Let ten thousand generations always look up to his loftiness,
walk with trepidation,
smell the sweet fragrance,
taste the sweet fruit,
mirror the utmost essence of purity,
and hear the correct sounds of clear harmony;
then the various officials will be concentrated,
and all achievements will be joyous.
Burdened with the path of Heaven,
and upholding the order of Earth,
this is already the supreme model for the world,
and it can certainly be put to the test!
Your servant Bān Gù says:
In the seventeenth year of Yǒngpíng,
your servant, along with Jiǎ Kuí, Chuán Yì, Dù Jǔ, Zhǎn Lóng, Xī Méng, and others,
was summoned to the Yúnlóng Mén.
The Xiǎo Huángmén Zhào Xuān, holding the *Qín Shǐhuángdì Běnjì*, asked your servants, saying:
"In the concluding appraisal written by Tàishǐ Qiān,
is there anything incorrect?"
Your servant replied:
"This appraisal cites Jiǎ Yì’s *Guò Qín Piān*, saying:
'Had Zǐ Yīng possessed the talent of even a mediocre ruler
and received only moderate assistance,
the altars of the Qín state should not have been extinguished.'
This statement is incorrect."
I was immediately summoned to enter,
and asked:
"Did you originally hear that this argument was wrong?
Or were you enlightened upon seeing the intent of my question?"
Your servant fully replied regarding what I had previously known.
The Imperial Decree then stated:
"Sīmǎ Qiān wrote his book to establish the words of one school of thought
and spread his name to later generations,
but because he himself fell into punishment,
he conversely used subtle writing to sting and satirize,
disparaging his own age;
he was not a righteous scholar.
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú’s conduct was corrupt and lacked moderation,
and he possessed only flowery rhetoric
that was not useful for practical purposes.
Yet, when he was ill, he left behind a loyal testament;
when the Emperor sought his writings,
he eventually obtained a praise of merits and virtues
that spoke of the Fèngshàn sacrifices;
this is the devotion of a loyal minister.
In this regard, he is far superior to Sīmǎ Qiān."
Your servant Gù has often prostrated myself to recite Your Majesty’s sagely discourse,
which clearly distinguishes between likes and dislikes
without omitting the slightest detail,
judging righteousness based on facts,
and acting always within the rules;
even Zhòngní’s expression of intent through history
could not surpass this.
Your servant Gù is among the oldest in learning
and has received deep and increasing favor;
I truly think of exhausting my strength and feelings
for the boundless Hàotiān!
Your servant Gù knocks his head, knocks his head.
I humbly consider that Xiāngrú’s *Fèngshàn*
is extravagant but not canonical;
Yáng Xióng’s *Měi Xīn*
is canonical but lacks substance.
Yet both have spread to later generations
and are handed down as old models.
Your servant Gù’s talent is decayed and cannot reach that of the predecessors;
for those who sing the *Yúnmén* music find it difficult to produce the proper sounds,
and those who look upon the gems of Suí and Hé find it difficult to identify treasures.
Unable to restrain my humble sincerity,
I have privately composed one piece of *Diǎn Yǐn*.
Although it is not sufficient to describe even one ten-thousandth of this grand and prosperous era,
it may still express my indignation and fullness,
enlighten the ignorant children,
glorify the Dà Hàn,
and surpass the reputation of former ages,
after which I may retire into the ravines,
dying yet remaining immortal.
Your servant Gù is ignorant and simple,
knocking his head, knocking his head,
and says:
At the origin of the Tàijí,
the Two Modes first divided;
billowing and swirling,
there was that which was heavy and profound,
and that which was floating and clear.
Heavy and floating intermingled,
and the various species were confusedly formed.
The mandate was first given to the people’s lords,
and the Five Virtues began their cycle,
as in the primal chaos
within the dark confusion.
Transcending knotted cords and surpassing carved tallies,
those who were silent and left no decrees
cannot be connected to a lineage.
Those who had surnames and titles
and continued the unfolding of Heaven
all began their eras with the head of the Tàihào Huángchū;
how lofty and far-reaching!
Their records can still be cultivated.
In the generations following these,
they adapted to changes with divine transformation,
containing light but not yet shining forth.
As for those who examined the laws of Qián above,
descended to receive the dragon’s wings,
and who shone in the *Diǎn* and *Mó*,
crowning virtue with excellence,
none is more venerable than Táo Táng.
Táo Táng set aside his heir and abdicated to Yǒu Yú;
Yǒu Yú also mandated the Xiàhòu.
Jì and Xiè brought brilliance to their duties,
eventually leading to Chéng Tāng and Wǔ.
Once the ministers were complete,
Heaven then attributed the merit to the sovereign
and was about to grant it to the Hàn Liú.
It caused them to inherit the waste and end of the three decadent ages
and encounter the calamities of the overbearing dragon.
The celestial signs were darkened and the constellations were deviant;
the social order was destroyed and the old statutes were missing.
Therefore, Heaven first mandated the Xuánshèng
to compile studies and establish systems,
to magnify the great undertaking,
to manifest and assist the ancestors,
and to praise and guide the wise.
How complete and brilliant,
truly a model for the divine spirits!
Although the diligent assistants like Gāo, Kuí, Héng, and Dàn
were small in comparison to this.
Thus the two sages Gāoguāng
resided in the imperial realm;
when the time arrived and the Qi moved,
they were as dragons appearing and leaping from the abyss.
Even before they flapped their wings to rise,
their majestic spirit was already tumultuous;
within the seas, people rose like clouds,
moving like thunder and flashing like lightning.
The hanging of Hú and the dismemberment of Mǎng
did not even require their personal presence for the execution.
Afterward, they reverently followed the heavens and earth
and courteously bowed to the various lords,
taking their rightful positions in the ancestral temple,
with the profound and modest yielding of one whose virtue is not grand,
and without the appearance of military force or aggressive display.
This was because they received the true succession of Heaven,
accepted the returning fortune of capable yielding,
harbored the intense essence of the rising flame,
and contained the grand displays of Kǒng's assistance.
How vast is such virtue,
the supreme model of emperors,
beyond what proclamations and oaths can reach.
Spreading out to observe the grand and minute measures of the two dynasties,
their depths can be explored.
Both began their traces from a single basket of earth
and both received the submission of the Hóu and Diàn regions.
For generations they labored for the people,
governing as regional lords and overseers.
Taking advantage of the mandate's gift of the majesty of the red bow and yellow battle-axe,
they used them to punish the disrespect of Wéi, Gù, Lí, and Chóng.
Until they united the five regions of Huàxià
and moved their capitals to Hào and Bó,
they then faced south
with their armies like tigers and dragons,
and overthrew the celestial cities.
Therefore, righteous scholars found them flowery but not substantial;
their martial reputation was not perfect,
and their protection had shameful virtues—
was it not so?
Yet like the solemn and beautiful hymns,
the pure and harmonious music,
used to honor the ancestors,
and the sacrifices where the ancestors were paired with God,
they brought forth auspicious omens and flowing blessings
to respond to Heaven and Earth,
shining brilliantly for a thousand years.
Could they not overcome through their own divinity?
Their great outlines followed a constant pattern,
and by examining their words and deeds in the records,
their glorious brilliance is clear and unchanging.
How much more so for the illustrious and sagely Hàn,
with its lofty foundation from Táng!
Tracing its source,
it first conceived Yú and nurtured Xià,
then molded Yīn and fashioned Zhōu,
and afterward proclaimed the double brilliance of the two ancestors,
inheriting the continuous light of the four progenitors.
The divine spirit shines daily,
its light reaching the six dark corners;
the wind of benevolence soars beyond the seas,
and the majestic spirit travels to the regions of ghosts.
No hidden thing is so crooked that it is not straightened,
and no subtle thing is so small that it is not nurtured.
Therefore, in the achievements of manifesting and settling the Three Realms,
without Yáo, they would not have risen;
in spreading the lessons of the remaining strategies among the people,
without Hàn, the Way would not have been magnified.
As for weaving the warp and woof of Heaven and Earth,
going in and out of the three lights,
operating the primal chaos externally,
and soaking into the finest hair internally,
so that all natures follow reason
and all categories of things prosper—
this has already been so for a long time.
How magnificent!
In this imperial era,
the virtuous ministers and various lords
have surpassed the achievements of all previous kings,
their glory mirroring the universe,
with a dignity that has no equal.
At the beginning, they were reverent, firm, diligent, and humble,
cautious and industrious;
they downplayed their successes and restrained their claims of finality,
not daring to discuss the establishment of new systems.
Even when matters such as changing the first month, altering ceremonial colors, and treating former dynasties as guests or models
had spread throughout the world,
the ritual officials and the community of scholars—those diligent and instructive men—
did not pass down even a semblance of the ancestors' achievements.
Although this might be called extreme caution,
is it not actually timidity?
Thereupon, the officials of the Three Excellencies and the Regional Governors
all came forward and said:
"Your Majesty looks up to examine the canons of Táng,
follows the principles of the ancestors within,
and treads the path of the dynastic founders below.
Personally upholding the heavenly laws,
the transformation of sincere harmony and clear distinction is pervasive.
Patrolling and pacifying the common people,
the grace of cherishing and protecting the widowers and widows is thorough.
With the rituals of burning, burying, hanging, and submerging sacrifices,
the ceremonies for reverently serving the various spirits are complete.
Thus, the auspicious phoenixes gather at the palace towers,
the fleshy-horned beasts tame the furred species in the outer parks,
black-patterned and white-bodied creatures are tamed in the suburbs,
and golden-glowing and colorful scales rise in the ponds.
Sweet dew falls at night upon the lush grass,
and three-legged birds soar among the flourishing trees.
As for the auspicious grains and spiritual herbs,
the rare beasts and divine birds,
which match the charts and correspond with the records,
being the ultimate of auspiciousness and omens—
they appear morning and evening in the pastures
and day and night within the capital domains,
surpassing all in the various provinces
and overflowing into the remote and wild regions.
In the past, the Jī family had only the white pheasant,
the vermilion crow,
the black millet,
and the yellow wheat;
yet the lord and ministers were moved,
those on the left and right hastened to one another,
so dignified and reverent,
and so lofty in their bearing.
This was used to manifest brightness and show reverent awe,
to receive the blessings of cherished harmony.
It also glorified Wén and Wǔ,
leaving a legacy of peace to their descendants
and covering them with excellence and brilliance.
How could it be for their own persons that they used such exclusive words?
If it is received in this way,
one should also diligently exert collective strength
to fulfill the Great Way,
opening the 'Golden Coffer' in the respectful hall
and managing the secret treasures of the Eastern Gallery
to spread the prognostications.
The charts and books shine clearly;
this is heavenly wisdom.
The great plan and the prior mandate;
this is sagely sincerity.
Embodying and practicing the root of virtue;
this is the correct nature.
Encountering good fortune and the right time;
this is the great mandate.
Following the mandate to create systems
and relying on established order to harmonize with the spirits
is to respond to the abundant blessings of the Three Spirits
and to expand the brilliant patterns of Táng.
This matter is of great importance,
and it truly occupies the heart whether awake or asleep.
Looking to the past and considering the future,
how could one slight the ancestral temple or fear the command of Heaven?
In examining from the distant past
down to the present day,
there have been seventy-four authors;
some did not receive the mandate but wrote on plain silk,
while others lacked glorious brilliance and left behind incomplete writings.
How can it be that now, in our time, it alone is lacking!"
At that time, the Sage Sovereign had already focused his essence and let his spirit roam,
embracing all the arts and literature.
He repeatedly consulted the various scholars
and questioned the elders,
deliberating with them on the source of the Way and Virtue
and evaluating the depths of benevolence and righteousness,
in the hope that the primal omen would arrive.
Having been moved by the honest words of the various lords,
he also fully grasped the great considerations of the five changes.
He will bind together ten thousand generations,
spread the vast radiance,
arouse the bright flame,
fan the inherited traditions,
and sow the fragrant legacy,
which becomes newer as time passes
and is never exhausted through use.
Vast indeed is the great law of Heaven!
Who could ever encompass it?
How like Táng! How like an Emperor!
How like an Emperor! How like Táng!
The Eulogy says:
Gōngsūn Hóng, Bǔ Shì, and Ní Kuān
all had the wings of a soaring swan,
yet were restricted by swallows and sparrows,
keeping their tracks far away among the sheep and pigs.
Had they not met their time,
how could they have reached such positions?
At that time, the Hàn had been established for over sixty years;
the world was peaceful,
and the treasuries were full,
yet the barbarians of the four directions were not yet submissive
and the systems were largely incomplete.
The Emperor was just then wishing to employ those skilled in civil and military arts,
seeking them as if he could not catch up.
He began by using a carriage with rush-wrapped wheels to welcome Méi Shēng
and sighed with admiration upon meeting Zhǔfù Yǎn.
The various scholars followed the sound like an echo,
and extraordinary men appeared together.
Bǔ Shì was plucked from among the herders,
Sāng Hóngyáng was promoted from among the merchant boys,
Wèi Qīng rose from among the bondservants,
and Jīn Mìdī emerged from among the surrendered captives.
This was as clear as the examples of building walls or feeding oxen in the past.
Hàn’s acquisition of talent
was most flourishing at this time.
In refined Confucianism, there were Gōngsūn Hóng, Dǒng Zhòngshū, and Ní Kuān;
in sincere conduct, Shí Jiàn and Shí Qìng;
in uprightness, Jí Àn and Bǔ Shì;
in recommending the worthy, Hán Ānguó and Zhèng Dāngshí;
in establishing laws, Zhào Yǔ and Zhāng Tāng;
in literary composition, Sīmǎ Qiān and Sīmǎ Xiāngrú;
in wit, Dōngfāng Shuò and Méi Gāo;
in diplomatic response, Yán Zhù and Zhū Mǎichén;
in astronomy, Táng Dū and Luòxià Hóng;
in musical harmony, Lǐ Yánnián;
in strategic planning, Sāng Hóngyáng;
in serving as envoys, Zhāng Qiān and Sū Wǔ;
in generalship, Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbìng;
in receiving final edicts, Huò Guāng and Jīn Mìdī;
the rest cannot be fully recorded.
Therefore, in the building of achievements
and the systems and writings left behind,
no later generation could match them.
Emperor Xiàoxuān succeeded to the throne
and continued the great task.
He also discussed the Six Arts
and selected those of outstanding talent.
Thus, Xiāo Wàngzhī, Liángqiū Hè, Xiàhóu Shèng, Wéi Xuánchéng, Yán Péngzǔ, and Yǐn Gēngshǐ advanced through Confucian learning;
Liú Xiàng and Wáng Bāo became famous for their literary compositions.
In generals and ministers, there were Zhāng Ānshì, Zhào Chōngguó, Wèi Xiàng, Bǐng Jí, Yú Dìngguó, and Dù Yánnián;
in governing the people, there were those such as Huáng Bà, Wáng Chéng, Gōng Suì, Zhèng Hóng, Shào Xìnchén, Hán Yánsòu, Yǐn Wēngguī, Zhào Guǎnghàn, Yán Yánnián, and Zhāng Chǎng,
all of whom had achievements described by later generations.
If one compares their famous ministers,
they were also second only to the previous era.
The Historian-Official says:
The rise of emperors and kings
must await the Mandate of Heaven.
If there is a change of dynasties,
it is not a matter of human effort.
Refinement and simplicity belong to different times,
and what is established differs.
Thus, of those who possessed the world in antiquity,
before the times of Báihuáng and Lìlù,
they acted but did not possess,
they responded but did not seek,
upholding the Great Image.
When the generations of Hóng and Huáng came,
they unified the people.
Yáo and Shùn practiced internal abdication,
embodying refined virtue.
Hàn and Wèi practiced external abdication,
following great reputation.
Tāng and Wǔ carried out revolutions,
responding to Heaven and men.
Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ fought and campaigned,
establishing their achievements.
Each followed their destiny, and the world changed with the times.
How great is the meaning of changing with the times!
In ancient times, they respected a matter and received the mandate at the beginning;
now emperors receive the mandate and use it until the end.
How could this be human effort?
Must it not be the will of Heaven?
The official historian says:
Formerly, Gāozǔ Xuān Huángdì, with his heroic talent and vast capacity,
entered official service in accordance with destiny.
At the time when Wèi Tàizǔ was first establishing the foundation,
he planned for the military and the state.
His excellent strategies were frequently successful,
and he eventually served the carriage of state,
galloping through three generations.
His nature was deep and inscrutable like a fortified city,
yet he was able to be magnanimous and inclusive.
He employed techniques of governance to manage affairs,
and he knew people well and was skilled in selecting and promoting them.
Therefore, both the worthy and the foolish were won over,
and those great and small exerted all their effort.
Thus, he recruited Dèng Ài from the breaks in farming,
and brought forth Zhōu Tài from the labor service,
entrusting them with civil and military duties,
and each excelled in their tasks.
Thus, he was able to capture Mèng Dá in the west,
seize Gōngsūn Yuān in the east,
exterminate Cáo Shuǎng internally,
and surprise Wáng Líng externally.
His divine strategies were his own decisions,
and his four expeditions were all victorious.
He controlled the various lords,
and the great power resided with him.
He repeatedly resisted the disciplined troops of Zhūgě Liàng,
and in the east, he removed the mutually dependent power of the Wú people.
Shìzōng inherited the foundation,
and Tàizǔ continued the work.
The military was frequently mobilized,
yet the borders suffered no loss.
Thereupon the common people supported the capable,
and the Great Image began to take shape.
Xuán and Fēng caused chaos within,
while Qīn and Dàn invaded from without.
Though their secret plots were clandestine,
the signs were inevitably revealed at the critical moment.
The Huái and Pǔ regions were twice disturbed,
yet Xǔ and Luò were not shaken.
All dissident plans were eliminated,
thereby brightening the former achievements.
Afterward, he promoted Zhōng and Dèng,
driving deep into Yōng and Shǔ.
The three passes were swept away like lightning,
and Liú Shán entered as a subject.
Heavenly omens and human affairs
were thus confirmed.
At first, they were accorded extraordinary honors,
and finally, they received the grant of the complete ritual items.
Their prestige and status were higher than those of Zhōu Gōng,
and their authority and control were stricter than those of Yī Yǐn.
Coming to Shìzǔ,
he finally enjoyed the Imperial Ultimate.
He occupied the legitimate position with proper conduct,
valued his words, and was cautious with the law.
He was benevolent to be generous toward subordinates,
and frugal to ensure sufficient resources.
He was harmonious but not lax,
and magnanimous yet capable of decisiveness.
Therefore, the people sang of the new mandate.
All within the four seas were joyful and encouraged.
He diligently pursued the ambitions of his ancestors,
desiring to soothe the suffering of the warring states.
Although his confidants held different views
and the high officials had conflicting opinions,
he alone accepted the strategy of Yáng Hù,
taking the best course despite the many.
Thus, by the end of the Xiánníng era,
he finally pushed aside the various arguments and relied on the resolve of Wáng and Dù.
They sailed boats through the Sānxiá,
and sent armored horses to Guìyáng.
The campaign did not last more than two seasons,
and the Jiāng and Xiāng regions were unified.
He leveled the ramparts of Wú and Shǔ,
opened the dangerous barriers of the two regions,
encompassed the ancient territories of Táng and Yú,
and promulgated the official calendar to the eight wildernesses.
During the Tàikāng era,
all under heaven used the same script
and carriages shared the same gauge.
Cattle and horses covered the fields,
surplus grain rested in the furrows,
travelers stayed in thatched huts,
and the neighborhood gates were not closed.
People met each other like kin,
and those who were in need
obtained resources from the roadside.
Therefore, at that time, there was a proverb: "Under heaven, there are no poor people."
Although the Great Peace was not yet complete,
it was enough to show that the officials followed the laws
and the people delighted in their lives.
It was a unique era in a hundred generations.
After Wǔ Huáng had passed away,
and before the earth on his mountain tomb was dry,
Yáng Jùn was executed,
the Empress Dowager was deposed,
and dozens of clans of court officials and former ministers were exterminated.
Soon, due to the disturbances involving the Two Dukes and Chǔ Wáng,
the imperial clansmen provided no protection as "defensive walls,"
while the conflicts like those of Èbó and Shíchén were fabricated year after year;
the ministers lacked the dignity to be looked up to,
while the calamities of downfall, execution, and humiliation occurred daily.
It even reached the point of exchanging the Son of Heaven for the title of Tàishàng,
and there were rumors of dismissals from office.
The people saw no virtue
and heard only of chaos;
in the morning one was considered a Yī or a Zhōu,
yet by evening one was called a Jié or a Zhí.
Good and evil were submerged in success or failure,
and praise or blame were coerced by power and profit.
Thereupon, frivolous men who violated the laws
employed their treacherous wits to cast themselves into the fray,
like nocturnal insects rushing into a flame.
Internal and external affairs became muddled,
the various officials lost their talent,
names and realities were reversed and confused,
and the knots of the heavenly net were loosened.
The state's administration shifted repeatedly among chaotic men,
the palace guards were dispersed outward to the four directions,
the regional peaks lacked the stability of heavy weights,
and the passes lacked the firmness of "knotted grass."
Lǐ Chén and Shí Bīng
overturned the regions of Jīng and Yáng;
Liú Yuān and Wáng Mí
disturbed the regions of Qīng and Jì;
and within twenty-odd years, Hé and Luò became ruins.
The Róng and Jié tribes declared themselves rulers,
two Emperors lost their dignity,
and the imperial tombs had no place of rest.
Why was this so?
Establishing authority lost its power,
entrustments were given to the untalented,
the four cardinal virtues were not extended,
and policies of expediency were many.
If one establishes laws in a time of order,
their decline may still lead to chaos;
but if laws are established in a time of chaos,
who could save the situation?
Thus, at that time, the world was not just momentarily weak,
and the military was not without foundation.
That Liú Yuān
was merely the General-Military Commandant of Líshí;
Wáng Mí
was a petty official of Qīngzhōu.
They were mostly men of the bow and horse,
people who served as runners,
and talents of common mediocrity,
possessing none of the ability of Wú Xiānzhǔ or Zhūgé Kǒngmíng.
They were newly arisen bandits
and a motley crowd,
no match for the states of Wú and Shǔ.
They discarded plowshares to become soldiers
and tore their clothes to make banners,
not possessing the equipment of the Warring States.
Rebelling from below against the above,
they did not have the power of a neighboring state.
Yet success and failure yielded different results;
they harried the world like driving a flock of sheep,
and seized the two capitals as easily as picking up something lost.
Generals, ministers, marquises, and kings
were executed one after another,
and even those who begged to be slaves could not obtain it.
Empresses, consorts, and princesses
were captured and humiliated by barbarian soldiers;
is this not lamentable!
Now, the world
is a great vessel;
the common people
are precious flocks.
Love and hate attack each other,
and benefit and harm snatch from each other;
this is the constant state of affairs.
It is like accumulated water at a dike,
or a prairie fire on a plain,
never momentarily still.
A great vessel cannot be managed by a small way,
and a moving force cannot be disturbed by petty competition.
The wise kings of old
knew it was so.
Therefore, they warded off great disasters but did not claim the merit;
they resisted great calamities but did not hoard the profits.
The common people all knew that the ruler's supreme virtue gave them life,
and did not say he was exploiting them to sustain his own life.
Therefore, they were moved and responded to him,
rejoiced and turned to him,
like the falcon nesting in the northern woods,
or like dragons and fish hastening to the deep marshes.
He follows Heaven and enjoys its cycle,
responds to men and harmonizes their righteousness;
thereafter, he establishes ritual and culture to govern them,
determines punishments to awe them,
is cautious with likes and dislikes to show them,
carefully weighs fortune and calamity to instruct them,
seeks those with insight to appoint as officials,
and is sincere in compassion and love to solidify them.
Thus the masses know which direction to face,
all delight in their lives and mourn death,
rejoice in his teachings and are at peace with their customs.
Gentlemen are diligent in ritual,
and the common people exert their strength;
integrity and shame are profound in every household and village,
and wickedness is dissolved within the heart.
Thus among the people there are those who would give their lives when seeing danger,
rather than seeking life at the expense of righteousness;
how much less could they be made to raise their arms and shout,
to gather for the purpose of violating laws and creating chaos?
If the foundation is broad, it is hard to overturn;
if the roots are deep, it is hard to uproot;
if principles are regulated, there is no chaos;
if there is cohesion like glue, there is no shifting.
This is why those who possessed the world in the past
were able to endure for a long time.
It was not that there were no deviant rulers,
but they relied on virtue, morality, and legal standards to maintain it.
Thus Yánlíng Jìzǐ listened to music and knew the number of the feudal lords' survival or ruin,
and the length of their terms;
this is because the people's sentiments and the prevailing customs
are the foundation of a state's security or peril.
In ancient times, when the Zhōu rose,
Hòu Jì was born to Jiāng Yuán,
and the Mandate of Heaven was clearly manifested;
the achievements of Wén and Wǔ
originated with Hòu Jì.
Therefore, the poem says:
“How accomplished was Hòu Jì,
who was able to match Heaven.”
It also says:
“He established our many people,
none of whom were not provided with your standard.”
It also says:
“Truly grain-bearing and truly abundant,
residing in the households of Yǒu Tái.”
Until the time when Gōng Liú encountered the chaos of the Dí people,
he left Tái for Bīn,
personally undertaking the labor.
Therefore, the poem says:
“Then they wrapped up dry provisions,
in bags and in sacks.”
“Ascending, he was on the ridges;
then descending, he was on the plains,
in order to settle his people.”
Coming to the time when Tài Wáng was pressured by the Róng and Dí,
because he could not bear the fate of the common people,
he took his staff and left.
Therefore, the poem says:
“In the morning he came, galloping his horse,
along the western riverbanks,
until he reached the foot of Mount Qí.”
The people of Zhōu followed him and thought of him,
saying:
“A benevolent man must not be lost,”
and so they followed him as if returning to a marketplace.
Residing there for one year, it became a village;
in two years, a town;
and in three years, it was five times its original size.
He constantly encouraged and peacefully settled them.
Therefore, the poem says:
“Thus he comforted them and settled them,
thus he placed them on the left and right,
thus he demarcated boundaries and organized the lands,
thus he announced the fields and measured the plots.”
Coming to Wáng Jì,
he was able to spread his virtuous reputation.
Therefore, the poem says:
“He was able to be bright and discerning,
he was able to be a leader and a lord,
bestowing upon him glory.”
Coming to Wén Wáng,
he fully cultivated the ancient virtues
and renewed the Mandate.
Therefore, the poem says:
“Only this Wén Wáng,
was careful and reverent,
clearly serving the High Sovereign,
and thus obtaining many blessings.”
Looking at it from this perspective,
the House of Zhōu accumulated loyalty and generosity for generations;
their benevolence reached even to plants and trees,
internally maintaining harmony among the nine generations of kin,
externally honoring and serving the aged,
caring for the elderly and asking for their wise words,
thereby establishing their blessings and prosperity.
And their consorts and queens personally practiced the four teachings,
respecting their tutors and instructors,
wearing washed clothes,
managing the tedious and humble tasks,
and transforming the world through the Way of women.
Therefore, the poem says:
“He set an example for his wife,
extending to his brothers,
and thus governing the family and the state.”
Thus the women of the banks of the Hàn River
maintained aspirations of purity;
the men in the middle of the forest
possessed the virtue of pure oneness.
Therefore it is said:
“Wén and Wǔ governed the internal from ‘Tiān Bǎo’ and before,
and governed the external from ‘Cǎi Wēi’ and after;
beginning with worry and diligence,
and ending with ease and pleasure.”
Thus, when they possessed two-thirds of the world,
they still served the Yīn with submission;
eight hundred feudal lords met without prior appointment,
yet they still said the Mandate of Heaven had not yet arrived.
With the wisdom of the three sages,
they campaigned against the solitary fellow Zhòu,
yet they still rectified the moral teachings, saying:
“Take by opposition, but keep by compliance;
preserve greatness and establish merit;
tranquilize the people and harmonize the masses.”
They still described the appearance of the Dà Wǔ dance, saying:
“It is not yet perfectly good.”
When Zhōu Gōng encountered changes,
he laid out the origins of the influence and transformation of Hòu Jì and the former lords,
and that which made the royal enterprise difficult,
which were all matters of the labor of farmers and women, and of food and clothing.
Therefore, from Hòu Jì's first foundation of quieting the people,
it took fifteen kings until Wén began to bring peace to it,
sixteen kings until Wǔ began to occupy it,
and eighteen kings until Kāng was able to secure it.
Thus their accumulation of the foundation and planting of the roots,
the weaving of rituals and customs,
the regulation of human emotions,
and the compassion for the hidden affairs of the people
were as interconnected and enduring as this.
Turning to the former generations,
although the refinement and simplicity belonged to different times,
and the achievements and enterprises were not the same,
when it came to settling the people and establishing governance,
their principles were the same.
Now, the rise of Jìn,
its achievements and merits surpassed those of a hundred kings,
and its success was swifter than that of the Sāndài.
Indeed, there was deliberate action in its making.
Xuān and Jǐng encountered times of great hardship;
they strove to strike down heroes
and executed many outstanding men for the sake of expediency,
having no time to cultivate the benevolence of Gōng Liú or Tài Wáng.
Entrusted with the legacy of assisting the government,
they repeatedly encountered depositions and installations of rulers.
Thus the King of Qí was not enlightened
and was not permitted to reflect and reform in Bó;
the Duke of Gāoguì was a youth
and was not allowed to resume his role as an enlightened sovereign.
The two ancestors were pressed by the timing of the dynastic succession
and had no leisure to wait for the juncture of "the three parts" or "the eight hundred."
This was how they established the foundation and set the roots,
differing from previous eras.
Furthermore, the court lacked men of pure virtue,
and the local regions were devoid of steadfast elders.
Customs became dissolute and depraved,
and the sense of shame and what was esteemed lost their proper place.
Scholars took Zhuāng and Lǎo as their masters
while discarding the Liù Jīng.
Talkers took emptiness and shallowness as eloquence
while despising reputation and frugality.
Those conducting themselves took profligacy and impurity as "attainment"
while looking down on integrity and trustworthiness.
Those entering officialdom took opportunistic gain as noble
while disdaining the path of righteousness.
Those holding office took detachment as a sign of loftiness
while mocking diligence and reverence.
Hence, the Sāngōng were viewed with the epithet of "desolate stumps,"
and the highest deliberations were labeled as "empty talk."
Liú Sòng repeatedly spoke of the way of governance
and Fù Xián constantly corrected the corrupt and upright,
but they were both called "vulgar officials."
Those who relied on vacuity and vastness
and who followed others without a mind of their own
all gained great fame within the four seas.
As for Wén Wáng who had no time to eat when the sun was declining,
or Zhòng Shānfǔ who was never idle day or night,
they were collectively mocked and criticized as mere dust
and were reviled and slandered.
Because of this, defamation and praise were confused regarding the reality of good and evil;
hidden wickedness raced along the path of greed and desire.
Those making selections chose officials based on the person,
and those holding office chose benefits for themselves.
The men holding the balance and at the axis of power
personally held offices by the dozens.
The great ones maximized their honor
and the lesser ones recorded the essentials,
yet in the failure of crucial matters,
they failed eight or nine times out of ten.
The sons and brothers of noble families and imperial relatives
leaped ahead and surpassed others,
disregarding qualifications and seniority.
Amidst the drifting dust of the world,
all were men racing and competing;
with officials numbered in the hundreds and thousands,
there was no act of yielding to the worthy.
Zǐzhēn wrote *Exalting Yielding* but no one examined it;
Zǐyǎ established the "Nine Grades" but it was not used;
Chángyú frequently wrote with a direct brush but could not correct the abuses.
Their women's dressing, combing, and weaving
were all completed by maidservants and slaves;
they never knew the labor of women's work with silk and hemp
or the duties of providing wine and food in the household.
Marrying before the proper time
and acting according to their whims,
they were not ashamed of the faults of debauchery and idleness
and were not restrained by the evil of jealousy.
Some were rebellious toward their fathers-in-law and mothers-in-law;
some reversed the roles of firm and yielding;
some slaughtered concubines and handmaidens;
some defiled and disordered the social hierarchy.
Their fathers and brothers did not punish them,
and the world did not condemn them.
How much less could they be expected to have heard the "Four Instructions" of antiquity
or to cultivate chastity and obedience today,
so as to assist their husbands!
Rites, laws, punishments, and administration
were greatly ruined at this point,
like a chamber being built while its joints are removed,
like water being accumulated while its dikes are breached,
or like fire being nurtured while being separated from its fuel.
When a state is about to perish,
its roots must first topple;
is this not what that means?
Therefore, observing the conduct of Ruǎn Jí,
one perceives the source of the collapse of ritual teachings;
examining the matter of Yǔ Chún and Jiǎ Chōng,
one sees the many deviances of the high ministers.
Appraising the merit of pacifying Wú,
one knows that the generals did not yield to one another;
reflecting on the plan of Guō Qīn,
one realizes the brewing conflicts with the Róng and Dí.
Reviewing the words of Fù Xuán and Liú Yì,
one understands the corruption of the hundred officials;
scrutinizing the memorials of Fù Xián
and the *Treatise on the Spirit of Money*,
one witnesses the prominence of favoritism and bribery.
When the customs of the people and the state's momentum were thus,
even if a ruler of mediocre talent
or one who merely maintained the established order were to govern,
Xīn Yǒu would surely have seen it in the sacrifices,
Jì Zhá would surely have perceived it in the music,
Fàn Xiè would surely have asked for death because of it,
and Jiǎ Yì would surely have wept bitterly over it.
How much more so when our Emperor Huì presided over it with his vast and unrestrained virtue!
Thus Empress Jiǎ acted tyrannically within the six palaces,
and Hán Wǔ assisted in the chaos from both without and within;
that which brought this about had developed gradually,
how could it be solely attributed to the evil of one woman?
Emperor Huái obtained the throne after the period of chaos,
but was restrained by powerful ministers.
After Emperor Mǐn was driven into exile,
he merely occupied a hollow title.
The government of the world
had already slipped away,
and unless one was a hero of the age,
it could not be reclaimed.
However, in the first years of Emperor Huái,
auspicious grain grew in Nánchāng.
Those who observe the ethers also said that Yùzhāng possessed the aura of a Son of Heaven.
When the state met with many hardships,
and members of the imperial clan rose in succession,
though [Crown Prince] Mǐnhuái had legitimacy,
the Prince of Huáinán had strength,
the Prince of Chéngdū had merit,
and the Prince of Chángshā had power,
they all ended in ruin and overthrow.
Yet Emperor Huái ascended the heavenly throne as the Prince of Yùzhāng;
the prophecy of Liú Xiàng said:
"After the destruction,
one whose name is like that of water shall obtain it;
those who raise the standard shall occupy the plains of Qín,
and in the southwest they shall find their peers."
Examining Emperor Mǐn,
he was indeed the son of the Prince of Qín,
and obtained the throne in Cháng'ān;
Cháng'ān
is indeed the land of Qín.
In the west, the Prince of Nányáng was made Right Chancellor,
and in the east, the Prince of Lángyé was made Left Chancellor.
The Emperor's personal name was Yè,
so Yè was changed to Línzhāng.
Zhāng is the name of a river.
Inferring from this,
there were indeed omens and signs,
yet the imperial foundation was not established,
and disaster and humiliation befell his person.
Was it that the Lord on High looked upon us but had a divided mind,
or was it because "man can broaden the Way,
but the Way does not broaden man"?
The brilliance of the pure glory had not yet faded,
therefore the Great Mandate gathered once more upon Zhōngzōng, Emperor Yuán.
Before the Xià and Yīn,
the system of empresses and consorts
was brief in its records.
According to the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
when a King established an Empress,
there were three Fūren,
nine Pín,
twenty-seven Shìfù,
and eighty-one Nǚyù,
to fulfill the internal duties.
The Empress held the primary position in the palace,
sharing status with the Celestial King.
The Fūren sat and discussed the rites of women;
the nine Pín managed the instruction of the Four Virtues;
the Shìfù were in charge of funerals,
sacrifices, and guests;
and the Nǚyù were arranged in order for the King's private quarters.
Offices were assigned and duties divided,
each having its own administration.
The female scribes used vermilion brushes
to record merits and write down faults.
In their daily lives, they had the instruction of nursemaids;
when they moved, there was the sound of tinkling jade pendants.
They presented talented women to assist the gentleman,
cherishing the modest and beautiful without being licentious in their lust.
Thus they were able to promote the transformative power of the Yīn
and cultivate the inner regulations;
the inner chambers were solemn and harmonious,
and treacherous flattery did not occur.
Therefore, when Kāng Wáng held audience late,
the "Guān Jū" was composed as a subtle reminder;
when Xuān Hòu rose late,
the Jiāng consort requested punishment for her fault.
When the Zhōu house moved to the east,
the ritual order withered and became deficient.
The feudal lords were arrogant and unrestrained,
and the regulations lacked order.
Qí Huán had six women who were like Fūren;
Jìn Xiàn elevated a Róng woman to be his primary consort,
ultimately leading to the rebellion of the five sons
and the heir apparent encountering hardship.
Down to the Zhànguó period,
discipline and standards grew even thinner;
satisfying whims and indulging desires,
they turned the social order upside down,
leading to the destruction of states and the loss of lives
in numbers too many to be counted.
This was truly a case of slighting rites and relaxing defenses,
placing beauty first and virtue last.
When Qín unified the world,
they were mostly arrogant and self-aggrandizing;
they established offices from all seven states
and divided ranks into eight grades.
When Hàn arose,
it followed those titles,
but the system for women was not regulated.
Gāozǔ did not maintain propriety in the inner chambers;
Xiàowén made no distinction in his sleeping arrangements.
However, selections and inductions were still simple,
and there were few decorative luxuries.
From the reigns of Wǔ and Yuán onwards,
each generation increased excessive expenditures,
even to the point of having three thousand in the Yètíng
and increasing the grades to fourteen.
The signs of seductive favorites destroying the government
and the traces of maternal relatives throwing the state into chaos
have been recorded in detail in previous histories.
When Guāngwǔ achieved the restoration,
he carved away the ornate to return to simplicity.
Regarding the titles of the six palaces,
only the Huánghòu and Guìrén received golden seals and purple ribbons,
and their stipends did not exceed several dozen hú of grain.
He also established three ranks: Měirén, Gōngrén, and Cǎinǚ,
all of whom had no official rank or salary
and were merely provided for with seasonal gifts.
Hàn law usually conducted a census of the population in the eighth month,
sending a Zhōngdàfū with the Yètíngchéng and physiognomists
to inspect the young girls of good families in the districts of Luòyáng.
Those aged thirteen and above
and twenty and below,
whose appearance was beautiful and elegant
and whose features were auspicious,
were taken back to the rear palace.
They were then selected based on suitability
and then introduced to the imperial presence.
This was to ensure clarity and caution in recruitment
and to seek out the virtuous and wise with great detail.
Míng Dì followed the previous emperor's intentions;
the palace education was well-maintained;
when appointing consorts and empresses,
he prioritized virtuous reputation.
Inside, no words crossed the threshold,
and power was not granted through private favoritism;
this can be said to have corrected the previous abuses.
If he had then established prohibitions against maternal relatives,
recorded them in the primary laws,
and reformed the system of empresses and consorts
to pass down to future generations,
would that not have been excellent!
Although he restrained himself with moderation,
his precautions were not thorough.
Therefore, from Xiàozhāng onwards,
appointments were gradually based on beauty;
favor flourished through personal affection,
until the gradual decay was forgotten.
Since ancient times, although there have been young rulers and difficult times
and the royal house faced many troubles,
while relying on the Prime Minister
and seeking out the loyal and upright,
never was there a total reliance on women
to decide the fate of the great vessel of state.
Only Empress Dowager Mǐ of Qín first presided over government affairs;
thus Ráng Hóu’s power was greater than that of Zhāowáng,
and his family was wealthier than the Yíng state.
Hàn continued this error,
knowing the danger but failing to change.
The imperial line of the Eastern Capital was repeatedly interrupted,
and power returned to female rulers.
Four emperors were established from outside,
and six empresses presided over the court.
Every policy was decided behind the curtains,
entrusting affairs to their fathers and brothers.
They coveted child-rulers to prolong their rule
and suppressed the wise and worthy to monopolize their authority.
The responsibility was heavy and the road long;
the benefits were profound but the disasters were swift.
Their persons braved the mists and dew atop the Yúntái,
while their families were bound in shackles within the dungeons.
Destruction followed heel to toe,
and overturned carriages lined the road.
Yet they rushed headlong without ceasing,
even when scorched and ruined was their end.
Finally, the great destiny declined,
and the sacred treasures were lost.
What the *Classic of Poetry* and *Book of Documents* lamented
is largely of the same principle.
Therefore, I have examined and arranged their deeds
to make the *Basic Annals of Empresses*.
Although their successes and failures differed,
those who held the formal title
are all included in this chapter.
Those who were posthumously honored out of private favor
and were not honored during their lifetimes
are appended to other accounts.
Matters concerning their relatives
are according to their respective biographies.
For the rest who do not appear elsewhere,
they are attached to these annals
to continue the record of maternal relatives of the Western Capital.
The commentary says:
Regarding the twenty-eight generals of the Restoration,
previous generations believed they corresponded to the twenty-eight constellations above;
this has not been verified in detail.
However, they were all able to seize the opportune moment,
exert their wisdom and courage,
and be called those who assisted the mandate;
they were all men of ambition and ability.
Many commentators criticize Guāngwǔ for not employing meritorious officials in administrative roles,
even to the point that those of heroic presence and great achievement
were set aside and not utilized.
However, if one considers his deep schemes and far-reaching plans,
there were certainly reasons for this.
When the Kingly Way had already declined
and descended to the virtues of the Hegemons,
they were still able to appoint and receive based only on merit,
giving precedence to both those with military merit and the worthy,
as Guǎn and Xí rose successively during the era of Huán,
and the Xiān and the Zhào shared ranks in the court of Wén;
this can be called a comprehensive approach.
Descending from the Qín and Hàn,
the ages relied on military strength,
and as for those who supported the royal house,
they were all military men who rose from obscurity.
There were also those among the classes of silk-sellers, dog-thieves, and the light and cunning,
some of whom were honored with rewards of contiguous cities,
and some entrusted with the position of Āhéng;
therefore, when power is suspect, rifts are born,
and when strength is equal, rebellion arises.
Xiāo and Fán were even imprisoned in fetters,
and Xìn and Yuè were ultimately executed and minced;
is this not so!
From then on
until the time of Xiào Wǔ,
the prime ministers and assistants of five generations
were all dukes and marquises.
Consequently, the path for the gentry was blocked,
and the worthy and capable were obscured and obstructed;
the court held the selfishness of hereditary succession,
and those below harbored many grievances of gatekeepers.
Those who harbored the Way but were unheard of,
and those who committed themselves to the wilderness,
how can they all be mentioned?
Therefore, Guāngwǔ took warning from the errors of past events
and maintained the intent to rectify wrongs;
although Kòu and Dèng had high merit,
and Gěng and Jiǎ had great achievements,
their allotted lands did not exceed four or five large counties,
and their added titles were merely Tèjìn or Cháoqǐng.
Observing his governance and administration,
assessing duties and assigning blame,
he was perhaps what is called one who leads them by law
and regulates them with punishment!
If judged by the standards for meritorious officials,
the harm was already extreme.
Why is this?
To apply the straight line of law would diminish the grace toward old friends;
to bend one's feelings would violate and discard the prohibitive statutes.
If selecting by virtue, then merit is not necessarily great;
if promoting by labor, then the person might not be worthy.
If many were appointed together, it would be hard to satisfy all hearts;
if they were ranked side-by-side, the potential for harm was not far off.
He could not help but weigh their strengths and weaknesses,
balancing things according to the circumstances.
Therefore, high ranks and generous rituals
were used to appropriately reward great merit,
while stern laws and deep statutes
were used to demand results from administrative officials.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
those made marquises were numbered in the hundreds;
as for those few several lords,
they participated in the state's discussions,
sharing in both prosperity and misfortune,
while the rest were all treated with leniency under relaxed codes,
keeping their fiefs and stipends intact.
None failed to end with their merit and fame preserved,
extending blessings to their descendants.
Formerly, the Marquis of Liú believed that Gāozǔ exclusively employed the old friends of Xiāo and Cáo;
Guō Jí also commented that many from Nányáng were prominent;
and Zhèng Xīng also cautioned against the exclusive appointment of meritorious officials.
To bestow favor excessively on a few
easily leads to the error of personal favoritism;
when ultimate justice is applied equally to all,
it will surely broaden the path for recruiting the worthy.
I suspect this is the case!
During the Yǒngpíng era,
Xiǎn Zōng, recalling the meritorious officials of the previous generation with emotion,
had the portraits of the twenty-eight generals painted in the Yúntái of the Nángōng.
Besides them, there were also Wáng Cháng, Lǐ Tōng, Dòu Róng, and Zhuó Mào,
totaling thirty-two people.
Therefore, following their original order,
I have attached them to the end of this chapter,
in order to record their sequence of merit.
The Yì says:
"Heaven hangs its signs,
and the Sage emulates them."
The four stars of the Eunuchs
are beside the position of the Emperor;
therefore, when the Zhōu Lǐ established offices,
it also provided for their number.
The door-keepers guarded the restrictions of the middle gate;
the eunuch attendants managed the warnings of the women's palace.
It also says:
"Those who manage the King's internal affairs are five people."
The Yuèlìng says:
"In the mid-winter month,
the chief eunuch inspects the gates and doors,
and carefully monitors the rooms."
In the Xiǎoyǎ of the Shī,
there is also the Xiàng Bó chapter criticizing slander.
Thus, the presence of eunuchs in the royal court
has been established for a long time.
Is it because their bodies lack the complete Qi,
their temperaments are focused and mild,
and being common people who pass through the gates,
they are easy to employ and sustain?
However, later generations followed this,
and the scope of their employment gradually widened.
As for the capable among them,
Bó Diāo and Guǎn Sū performed service in Chǔ and Jìn;
Jǐng Jiàn and Miù Xián gained renown in Qín and Zhào.
When it came to their abuses,
Shù Diāo threw Qí into chaos,
and Yī Lì brought disaster to Sòng.
When the Hàn rose,
they followed the Qín system
and established the office of Zhōngchángshì.
However, they also recruited scholars
to participate in the selection;
they all wore silver hat-dangles and the fur of the left-marten,
serving in the palace halls.
When Gāo Hòu took power,
she then appointed Zhāng Qīng as the Dà Yuèzhě,
entering and leaving the inner chambers
to receive and proclaim edicts.
In the time of Wén Dì,
there were Zhào Tán and Běigōng Bózǐ,
who were quite favored.
As for Xiào Wǔ,
he also loved Lǐ Yánnián.
The Emperor often held banquets in the rear gardens,
or traveled secretly to detached villas;
therefore, when requesting or reporting on secret matters of state,
he mostly used eunuchs to manage them.
In the era of Yuán Dì,
Shǐ Yóu served as the Huángménlìng;
he was diligent and offered his loyalty,
providing many benefits.
Later, Hóng Gōng and Shí Xiǎn used flattery and treachery to advance themselves,
eventually leading to the disaster of Xiāo and Zhōu,
which damaged and defiled the Emperor's virtue.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng,
the eunuch offices used castrated men exclusively,
no longer mixing in other scholars for the appointments.
By the Yǒngpíng era,
they first established a fixed number of personnel:
four Zhōngchángshì
and ten Xiǎohuángmén.
When Hé Dì ascended the throne, he was young and weak,
and Dòu Xiàn and his brothers monopolized and gathered power and authority;
the ministers and officials, both internal and external,
had no way to approach the Emperor personally.
Those who resided with him
were only the eunuchs.
Therefore, Zhèng Zhòng was able to exclusively plan within the palace
and ultimately eliminate the great evil;
consequently, he enjoyed the enfeoffment of land
and surpassed others to reach the rank of a palace minister.
From this point, the palace eunuchs began to prosper.
From the time of Míng Dì
until the Yánpíng era,
their appointments became increasingly significant
and their status gradually grew.
There came to be ten Zhōngchángshì,
and twenty Xiǎohuángmén.
They were granted the use of golden ornaments and marten fur on the right
and concurrently held the duties of ministerial offices.
Empress Dèng governed as a female ruler,
but the myriad affairs of state were vast and distant.
When court officials planned and deliberated,
they had no way to participate in decisions within the inner chambers.
Decrees issued in her name
did not leave the inner palace quarters;
thus, she had no choice but to rely on castrated men
and entrust them with the destiny of the state.
Holding royal ranks in their hands
and speaking the laws of Heaven with their mouths,
these were no longer just the duties of the Yèting or Yǒngxiàng,
nor the responsibilities of the inner doors and chambers.
Afterwards, Sūn Chéng secured the merit of establishing Emperor Shùn,
and Cáo Téng participated in the strategy to install Emperor Huán.
This was followed by the Wǔ Hóu plotting together,
and Liáng Jì receiving the ceremonial axe.
Though their actions were framed as public justice,
their favors solidified the favor of the sovereign.
Therefore, those inside and outside the court submitted,
and those above and below held their breath in fear.
Some claimed their achievements equaled those of Yī and Huò,
no less than those recorded in former times;
others said the strategies of Liáng and Píng
were revived in the present day.
Although there were occasionally loyal and public-spirited men,
they were all eventually excluded.
Their movements could shift mountains and seas;
their very breath could change frost and dew.
Those who catered to their whims and sought favor
would bring glory to their three kindred;
those who spoke directly and offended their will
would have their five clans exterminated.
The laws and discipline of Hàn fell into great chaos.
As for those wearing high caps and long swords,
draped in vermilion and clutching gold seals,
they filled the palace gates.
Those who were granted fiefs and tiger tallies
and ruled over subjects while facing south
were numbered in the dozens.
Their offices and mansions
were lined up in the capital and the countryside;
their sons, brothers, and hangers-on
filled more than half of the provinces and kingdoms.
Accumulations of gold from the south,
treasures of Hé,
ice-like silks,
and mist-like gauzes
filled their storehouses to bursting.
Beauties,
maidservants,
singing boys,
and dancing girls
filled their ornate rooms.
Even dogs and horses were adorned with carvings,
and buildings were draped in fine silks.
All this was by flaying and carving the common people
to indulge their competing extravagant desires.
They framed and harmed the wise and virtuous,
and focused solely on planting their own partisans.
There were those who recommended each other
to curry favor with the powerful;
they castrated themselves or their sons
to flaunt their advancement.
Suffering from the same defects and helping one another,
their group became numerous.
Their acts of ruining the state and corrupting the government
cannot be fully recorded.
Because of this, the people within the seas sighed in bitterness;
men of ambition lived in poverty and seclusion.
Rebels and bandits took advantage of the gaps,
shaking and disturbing the land of Xià.
Although loyal and good men harbored indignation
and occasionally took action,
misfortune followed their words,
and they were soon executed along with their families.
Furthermore, they held great trials to hunt down partisans,
with people falsely implicating one another.
Anyone called a virtuous scholar
suffered from this calamity and poison.
Dòu Wǔ and Hé Jìn
held high positions and were close relatives of the throne;
they rode the wave of resentment from the nine regions
and coordinated the power of the heroes,
but because of their hesitation and indecision,
they met with total defeat.
Was this also the ultimate limit of fate?
Although Yuán Shào executed them
until none remained,
he replaced chaos with violence;
what good did that do!
From the time Cáo Téng persuaded Liáng Jì
to finally establish a dim and weak ruler,
Wèi Wǔ took advantage of this
and eventually moved the Nine Tripods.
As it is said:
"If a lord starts with this,
he must end with this."
How true this is!
The Yì says:
"Great indeed is the meaning of the time of Dùn."
It also says:
"He does not serve kings or marquises,
making his own affairs lofty."
Thus, Yáo is praised for modeling himself after Heaven,
yet he did not bend the loftiness of the man of Yǐngyáng;
King Wǔ was perfectly beautiful in virtue,
yet in the end, he preserved the purity of the men of Gūzhú.
From then on,
such noble traditions became more frequent;
the path of permanent withdrawal did not differ,
but the circumstances that moved them to it were not one.
Some lived in seclusion to pursue their will;
some withdrew to preserve their Way;
some quieted themselves to calm their restlessness;
some left danger to seek safety;
some sullied themselves in the world to stir their spirits;
or criticized worldly things to stimulate their purity.
Yet when we see them content in the fields,
or growing haggard by the rivers and seas,
it was not necessarily that they preferred being close to fish and birds or enjoying the forests and grass;
it was simply where their steadfast natures led them.
Thus, the guest who suffered shame
was dismissed repeatedly but did not leave his state;
the integrity of one who would walk into the sea
could not be moved even by a thousand chariots.
If they had been forced to change their choices of whether to serve or leave,
they could not have been themselves.
Though they might seem stubbornly focused on making a name for themselves,
nevertheless, they shed their skins like cicadas amidst the noise and dust,
placing themselves outside the mundane realm.
How different they are from those who polish their cleverness to pursue fleeting profit!
Xún Qīng said:
"When the will is cultivated, one is proud toward wealth and honor;
when the Way and righteousness are heavy, one treats kings and dukes lightly."
When the house of Hàn declined,
and Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
the pent-up righteous indignation of the scholars was extreme.
At that time, those who tore their caps and destroyed their crowns,
holding hands as they departed,
were beyond counting.
Yáng Xióng said:
"The wild swan flies high into the darkness;
how can the hunter reach it?"
This refers to how far they kept from trouble.
Guāngwǔ Dì turned his seat toward recluses,
seeking them as if he could not reach them.
Envoys with banners, silks, and rushes-padded carriages were sent to honor and summon them,
watching one another among the mountain cliffs.
Men like Xuē Fāng and Féng Méng were invited but refused to come;
Yán Guāng, Zhōu Dǎng, and Wáng Bà came but could not be bent.
All sides were satisfied,
and men of purpose cherished benevolence;
is this not what is called "when the recluses are promoted, the hearts of the world turn to the ruler"?
Sùzōng also treated Zhèng Jūn with ritual and summoned Gāo Fèng
to help them fulfill their integrity.
From then on, the virtue of the emperors gradually declined,
and wicked elements controlled the court.
Scholars were upright and resolute,
standing as equals with ministers and high officials,
even to the point of showing defiant indignation without looking back;
many lost the Middle Way.
Here, I have recorded those whose distance from the world cannot be reached
and who are like the original authors of such deeds,
listing them in this chapter.
The Historian says:
People are endowed with the spirit of Heaven and Earth,
and contain the virtue of the Five Constants.
Strength and softness are used alternately,
and joy and anger distinguish their emotions.
When the will is moved within,
then singing and chanting are expressed without.
This is the basis of the Liù Yì
and what the Sì Shǐ are tied to.
Rising and falling in songs and ballads,
they spread through the Fēng sections of the Odes.
Although before the Yú and Xià eras
no surviving texts are seen,
the endowment of qi and the harboring of spirit
were likely no different in principle.
Thus, the rise of singing and chanting
must have begun with the birth of the people.
After the Zhōu House had declined,
the cultural tradition became increasingly prominent.
Qū Píng and Sòng Yù led the way at the clear source in the past,
while Jiǎ Yì and Sīmǎ Xiāngrú stirred the fragrant dust thereafter.
Their heroic words polished metal and stone,
and their lofty righteousness reached the cloudy heavens.
From then onward,
sentiments and aspirations grew ever broader.
Those such as Wáng Bāo, Liú Xiàng, Yáng Xióng, Bān Gù, Cuī Yuán, and Cài Yōng
took different paths but rushed toward the same goal,
successively following one another as masters and ancestors.
Although clear words and beautiful melodies
occasionally burst forth in their writings,
yet overgrown sounds and cumbersome airs
were indeed many.
As for the brilliant flourishing of Píngzǐ,
his writing changed according to emotion;
his peerless songs and lofty traces
for a long time had no echoing successor.
Coming to the Jiàn'ān period,
the Cáo clan established the mandate.
The Sānzǔ and Chén Wáng
all possessed flourishing literary embellishment.
Only then did they use emotion as the warp of writing
and use writing to clothe the substance.
From the Hàn to the Wèi,
a period of over four hundred years,
men of letters and gifted talents
saw the literary style change thrice.
Xiāngrú was skilled in words of formal resemblance;
the two Bāns were adept at discourses on emotion and reason;
Zǐjiàn and Zhòngxuān took vigor and substance as their essence.
Both displayed their abilities and monopolized beauty,
uniquely shining in their own time.
Thus, the scholars of an entire generation
each admired and emulated them.
To trace the origin of this surging current,
none did not take the Fēng and the Sāo as their ancestors.
It was only because their tastes and preferences differed in sentiment
that their intentions and compositions were contrary to one another.
Descending to the Yuánkāng era,
Pān Yuè and Lù Jī were exceptionally outstanding.
Their rules differed from Bān and Jiǎ,
and their style changed from Cáo and Wáng.
Ornate meanings were as dense as stars,
and elaborate patterns met like silk.
They strung together the leisurely echoes of Píngtái
and gathered the lofty rhymes of Nánpí.
Their legacy and remaining influence
reached their peak in Jiāngyòu.
During the restoration of Jìn,
the "Mysterious Style" alone was fanned.
Learning was exhausted in the "Under the Pillar" archive,
and extensive knowledge stopped at the "Seven Chapters."
Galloping through literary expression,
meaning was exhausted in these.
From the Jiànwǔ to the Yìxī eras,
spanning nearly a hundred years,
although comparing sounds and linking words
followed like waves and gathered like clouds,
none did not entrust their words to the "Supreme Virtue"
or lodge their meanings in the "Mysterious Pearl."
Vigorous and beautiful words
were simply not heard of.
Zhòngwén began to reform the style of Sūn Chuò and Xǔ Xún;
Shúyuán greatly changed the air of the Tàiyuán period.
Coming down to the Sòng dynasty,
Yán Yánzhī and Xiè Língyùn rose in fame.
Língyùn's inspired moments were outstandingly displayed,
while Yánnián's stylistic structure was clear and dense.
Together they stood on par with the excellence of the past
and bequeathed a model to posterity.
As for opening one's heart
to evaluate the literary embellishments of the past,
the measures of skill and clumsiness
are perhaps something that can be discussed.
The five colors manifest one another,
and the eight sounds harmonize and flow
because of the black and yellow and the pitch-pipes,
each suiting the fitness of things.
If one wishes to make the Gōng and Yǔ notes alternate
with high and low pitches in varied rhythms,
then if there is a floating sound in front,
there must be a sharp resonance behind.
Within a single slip,
tones and rhymes must be entirely distinct;
within two lines,
light and heavy must be completely different.
Only by subtly mastering this principle
can one begin to speak of literature.
As for the flourishing compositions of earlier scholars,
their chanting is lofty and has been highly praised through the ages:
Zǐjiàn’s work on Hánjīng,
Zhòngxuān’s piece on the banks of the Bà’àn,
Zǐjīng’s chapter on the falling rain,
and Zhèngcháng’s line on the north wind.
All directly express the feelings of the breast
without relying on the Shī or histories;
it is precisely because they used pitch and rhyme to harmonize
that they achieved a height beyond previous models.
Since the time of Língjūn,
many eras have passed.
Although literary styles became somewhat refined,
yet this secret was not perceived.
As for those lofty words and subtle phrases
whose tones and rhymes are naturally formed,
all are secretly in accord with these principles,
yet they were not reached through conscious thought.
Zhāng Héng, Cài Yōng, Cáo Zhí, and Wáng Càn
had no prior awareness of this,
and Pān Yuè, Lù Jī, Yán Yánzhī, and Xiè Língyùn
were even further from it.
Those in the world who understand the subtle tones
have ways of obtaining this,
and these words are not erroneous.
If one says it is not so,
then please await future sages.
The terms "gentleman" and "small man"
are general designations for types of people.
To follow the Way is to be a gentleman;
to violate it is to be a small man.
Butchering and fishing
are lowly occupations;
building walls
is menial labor.
Yet Tàigōng arose to be the Grand Master of Zhōu,
and Fù Yuè left his toil to be the Chancellor of Yīn.
This is not a discussion of noble lineages
or the wealth of prominent families;
it is about highlighting the illustrious and those in obscure places,
selecting only those with talent.
Coming to the two Hàn dynasties,
this Way had not changed.
Hú Guǎng came from generations of farmers,
yet Bóshǐ attained the rank of Chancellor;
Huáng Xiàn was the son of a cattle doctor,
yet Shúdù's name moved the capital.
Moreover, when scholars dwelt at court,
all had specific duties.
Although seven generations of wearing marten furs
was revered in the Western Hàn,
yet the Palace Attendant personally presented memorials
and also managed the imperial robes.
Dōngfāng Shuò was a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate,
holding a halberd below the palace hall.
Commandery and county subordinates and officials
all came from prominent families;
those bearing spears in the night guard
were all from powerful clans.
It was not like later ages where the people were divided into two separate paths.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty during the times of chaos,
Wèi Wǔ began to lay the foundation.
In the haste of military affairs,
the Nine Ranks (Jiǔpǐn) system was provisionally established.
It was originally intended to evaluate the quality of talent,
not to distinguish the high or low status of hereditary families.
Because this was followed over time,
it eventually became an established law.
From Wèi until Jìn,
no one was able to change it.
The Great Rectifiers (Zhōudū) and Commandery Rectifiers (Jùnzhèng)
ranked people based on talent,
yet the talents of the whole world
rarely rose or fell in rank.
They merely relied on their hereditary status
to surpass one another.
The Rectifiers were worldly men
who weighed the circumstances of the times;
their evaluations were many or few,
shifting according to the situation.
This is what Liú Yì meant when he said that in the lower ranks there are no high-born families,
and in the upper ranks there are no lowly clans.
As years passed and changes occurred,
this custom became increasingly ingrained.
All those who wore the official cap and gown
were inevitably in the Second Rank.
From that point downward,
people were deemed lowly commoners.
The way of the Zhōu and Hàn
was to use the wise to employ the ignorant;
palace servants and underlings were varied,
thereby forming a hierarchy.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
the noble have employed the base;
the categories of scholar-official (shì) and commoner (shù)
have been clearly distinguished.
When a sovereign faces south as ruler,
the ninefold depths of the palace are secluded.
Those who attend him morning and night
are rightfully separated from the high officials.
The duties of the gates and thresholds
should be managed by specific officers.
However, favor is born from intimacy,
and trust is solidified through favor.
They do not have an intimidating appearance
but have a countenance that is easy to approach.
During the Xiàojiàn and Tàishǐ eras,
the sovereign's authority was exercised alone.
The various offices were left vacant,
and power was not delegated to outsiders.
Yet the administration and punishments were complex and mixed,
making it difficult for the ruler to understand everything.
Those whom he relied on as his eyes and ears
were his close attendants (jìnxí).
The essentials of rewards and punishments
are what is called national power;
the issuing and receiving of royal commands
fell into their hands.
Consequently, all paths converged
and everyone rushed toward them like spokes to a hub.
The sovereign believed that because their status was base and their positions minor,
their power could not become too great.
He did not realize that "the rat relies on the tutelary shrine for nobility,"
or "the fox borrows the tiger’s majesty."
Outwardly, they lacked the suspicion of threatening the sovereign,
but inwardly, they had the merit of exclusive influence.
Their power overwhelmed the world,
yet it was not realized.
They formed cliques and parties,
and government was conducted through bribery.
Executions and injuries
were plotted in the privacy of the bedchamber.
Attaining high rank and carriage
came from a mere smile or word.
Gold from the south and wool from the north
all arrived by the boatload.
Plain silk and red gems
arrived in double loads.
The Xǔ and Shǐ families of the Western Capital (Xījīng)
are not even worth mentioning,
and the Wáng and Shí families of the Jìn dynasty
could not be compared to them.
By the late years of Tàizōng,
who had experienced both prosperity and decline,
the group of powerful favorites
feared the imperial clansmen and relatives.
They wished to leave the young ruler isolated
to permanently steal the state's power.
They fabricated differences and similarities
to stir up trouble and rifts.
The Emperor's brothers and princes of the imperial clan
were slaughtered one after another.
The people forgot the virtue of the Sòng dynasty;
although there was more than one path to this,
the early fall of the precious throne
was truly due to this.
Alas!
The Hàn Shū has the "Table of Marquises of Grace and Favor,"
and also the "Biographies of Favorites."
I now collect their names
and list them as the Chapter on Favorites (Ēnxìng Piān).
Great was the founder of Hàn,
who continued the lineage of Yáo.
Truly, Heaven bestowed him with virtue;
he was wise, divine, and martially brilliant.
The Qín people lost the guiding thread,
and the net of authority slipped to Chǔ.
Thereupon he began his rise,
slaying the snake and rallying his troops.
The Divine Mother announced the omen,
and the red banners were raised.
He then stepped onto the suburbs of Qín,
where Yīng came to bow his head in submission.
Changing the mandate and creating systems,
he recorded the Three Chapters of Law.
Responding to Heaven and according with the people,
the five stars shared the same path.
The Xiàng clan was rebellious
and banished us to Bā and Hàn.
The hearts of the western lands were settled,
while the soldiers felt indignation and resentment.
Seizing the opportunity to move,
he swept through the Three Qín.
Dividing and occupying the rivers and mountains,
he protected these cherished people.
His legs and arms were Xiāo and Cáo,
who managed the state.
His claws and teeth were Xìn and Bù,
and his core advisors were Liáng and Píng.
Reverently executing Heaven's punishment,
his glory was brilliant and clear.
Xiàochéng was magnificent,
his presence in court was luminous.
His majestic ceremonies were grand,
like fine jade tablets and scepters.
Within the inner chambers, he indulged the Zhào family;
the court administration was in the hands of the Wáng family.
Like a blazing, roaring fire,
its light was truly not auspicious.
Xìn was but a starving servant,
and Bù was truly a tattooed criminal.
Yuè was also a petty thief,
