and Ruì governed the rivers and lakes.
Rising like clouds and soaring like dragons,
they were transformed into marquises and kings.
They were granted the lands of Qí and Chǔ,
and straddled the regions of Huái and Liáng.
Wǎn came from the same village
and guarded our northern borders.
When virtue is thin but the position is high,
it is not a blessing but a disaster.
Only Wú remained loyal and trustworthy,
and so his descendants endured for long.
The Appraisal says:
When the fire-virtue government of Hàn declined,
a great thief usurped the state.
Gale winds swirled through the nine provinces,
and the three luminaries were blocked by fog.
The people were weary of excess and deceit;
divine thoughts returned to virtue.
Shìzǔ received the mandate of birth,
and spiritual omens distinguished him.
His deep insight preceded events,
and his profound strategies regulated civil affairs.
At Xún and Yì, there were a million troops,
like crowds of tigers and leopards.
Long-wheeled chariots thundered through the wilds,
and high banners swept the clouds like comets.
Once his heroic majesty was shaken,
the Xīndū palace was naturally burned.
He suppressed the rebels of Yōng and Dài,
and cleared the chaos in Liáng and Zhào.
The Three Rivers were not yet settled,
and the Four Passes were again disturbed.
The divine banners then looked toward them,
and in turn carried out Heaven's punishment.
Metal walls and boiling moats lost their defenses;
carriages and books shared the same path.
Spiritual blessings having been initiated,
human plans all assisted.
Brilliant were the ancestral temple's plans,
and valiant were his heroic decisions.
How magnificent is the mandate,
continuing our Imperial Hàn.
Duke Xiào of Qín relied on the natural defenses of Yáo and Hán,
and held the lands of Yōng Zhōu.
Lord and ministers maintained a firm defense
to watch the House of Zhōu,
with the intention of rolling up the world like a mat,
wrapping the universe together,
and bagging the four seas,
and the heart to swallow the eight wild lands.
At that time,
Shāng Jūn assisted him,
establishing laws within,
emphasizing farming and weaving,
and preparing the tools for defense and warfare;
while abroad, he formed the Horizontal Alliance to make the feudal lords fight amongst themselves.
Thus, the people of Qín took the lands beyond the Xīhé with their hands folded.
After Duke Xiào passed away,
Huìwén, Wǔ, and Zhāo
followed the established legacy,
and relied on the inherited policies.
To the south, they took Hànzhōng,
to the west, they seized Bā and Shǔ,
to the east, they carved out fertile lands,
and occupied strategic commanderies.
The feudal lords were terrified,
and held meetings to form alliances to weaken Qín.
They did not begrudge precious vessels, heavy treasures, or fertile lands
to attract the talented men of the world,
forming the Vertical Alliance and binding ties,
joining together as one.
At this time,
Qí had Mèngcháng,
Zhào had Píngyuán,
Chǔ had Chūnshēn,
and Wèi had Xìnlíng.
These four lords
were all wise, loyal, and trustworthy,
generous and kind to others,
and honored the worthy and valued the scholars.
They formed the Vertical Alliance to break the Horizontal Alliance,
gathering the multitudes of Hán, Wèi, Yān, Zhào, Sòng, Wèi, and Zhōngshān.
At this point, among the men of the six states,
there were those like Nìng Yuè, Xú Shàng, Sū Qín, and Dù Hè to devise strategies;
those like Qí Míng, Zhōu Zuì, Chén Zhěn, Zhào Huá, Lóu Huǎn, Zhái Jǐng, Sū Lì, and Yuè Yì to communicate their intentions;
and those like Wú Qǐ, Sūn Bìn, Dài Tuó, Ní Liáng, Wáng Liào, Tián Jì, Lián Pō, and Zhào Shē to lead their armies.
Once, with ten times the land
and a million soldiers,
they approached the pass to attack Qín.
The people of Qín opened the pass to welcome the enemy,
but the armies of the nine states fled and dared not advance.
Qín did not spend even a single arrow or a lost arrowhead,
yet the feudal lords of the world were already exhausted.
Thus, the alliance scattered and the agreements dissolved,
as they competed to carve out land to bribe Qín.
Qín had strength to spare to exploit their exhaustion,
chasing the fleeing and pursuing the defeated,
leaving a million corpses
and blood flowing until it could float a shield.
Taking advantage of the circumstances,
they carved up the world,
dividing the rivers and mountains.
Strong states begged to submit,
and weak states came to pay court.
Continuing to Xiàowén Wáng and Zhuāngxiāng Wáng,
the days of their reigns were short,
and the state was without incident.
When it came to Shǐhuáng,
he exerted the remaining glory of the six generations,
brandished his long whip to drive the universe,
swallowed the two Zhōu and annihilated the feudal lords,
ascended the supreme throne and controlled the six directions,
wielding his staff to scourge the world,
and his prestige shook the four seas.
To the south, he took the lands of Bǎiyuè,
turning them into Guìlín and Xiàng Jùn.
The lords of Bǎiyuè
bowed their heads with cords around their necks,
entrusting their lives to the lower officials.
He then sent Méng Tián north to build the Great Wall and guard the borders,
pushing the Xiōngnú back more than seven hundred lǐ.
The Hú people dared not come south to graze their horses,
and the soldiers dared not draw their bows to avenge their grievances.
He then discarded the ways of the former kings,
burned the words of the hundred schools,
to make the black-headed people ignorant.
He destroyed famous cities,
killed heroes and talents,
collected all the weapons of the world and gathered them in Xiányáng,
melting down the blades and arrowheads to cast twelve golden statues,
to weaken the people of the world.
Afterward, he used Mount Huá as a wall,
and the river as a moat,
relying on the walls ten thousand feet high,
looking down into the unfathomable abyss as a defense.
With fine generals and strong crossbows,
guarding the strategic passes,
and with trusted ministers and elite troops,
arrayed with sharp weapons, who would dare do anything?
The world was settled.
In the heart of Shǐhuáng,
he thought the defense of Guānzhōng,
with its thousand-mile golden wall,
would ensure his descendants reigned as emperors and kings,
an enterprise for ten thousand generations.
After Shǐhuáng passed away,
his remaining prestige still shook distant customs.
However, Chén Shè,
a son of a man with windows made of jars and a door pivoted on ropes,
a common laborer
and a conscripted exile,
whose talent did not reach mediocrity,
who lacked the wisdom of Zhòngní or Mò Dí,
and the wealth of Táo Zhū or Yī Dùn,
rose from within the ranks of soldiers
and emerged from the field paths.
Leading exhausted and scattered soldiers,
and commanding a few hundred men,
he turned to attack Qín.
They cut wood for weapons
and raised poles for flags.
The world gathered like clouds and responded like echoes,
carrying grain and following him like shadows.
The heroes and talents east of the mountains
then rose together and annihilated the clan of Qín.
Moreover, the world was not small or weak;
the lands of Yōng Zhōu
and the defenses of Yáo and Hán remained as they were.
The position of Chén Shè
was not more honorable than the lords of Qí, Chǔ, Yān, Zhào, Hán, Wèi, Sòng, Wèi, or Zhōngshān.
Their hoes, plows, and thorn staffs
were not sharper than the hooked halberds and long spears.
The ranks of the exiled garrisons
were not more powerful than the armies of the nine states.
Their deep planning and far-sighted strategy,
and their ways of marching and deploying troops,
did not equal the talented men of former times.
Yet success and failure changed,
and the achievements were opposite.
If one were to make the states east of the mountains compete in length and size with Chén Shè,
and compare their power and measure their strength,
they could not be spoken of in the same year.
Yet Qín, with its small piece of land,
attained the power of ten thousand chariots,
summoned the eight provinces to pay court for
over a hundred years.
Afterward, they took the six directions as their home
and Yáo Hán as their palace.
But when a single man caused trouble, the seven ancestral temples were destroyed,
the ruler died at the hands of others,
and became the laughingstock of the world.
Why?
Because benevolence and righteousness were not practiced,
and the conditions for offense and defense differ.
Fēi Yǒu Xiānshēng served in Wú;
when entering court, he could not cite antiquity to broaden the Ruler’s intentions,
and when retiring, he could not promote the Ruler’s excellence to manifest his achievements.
He remained silent without speaking for three years.
Wú Wáng found this strange and asked him, saying:
“I have inherited the achievements of my predecessors
and been placed above the many worthies.
Rising early and sleeping late,
I have never dared to be idle.
Now you, Sir, have come suddenly from afar
and gathered in the land of Wú,
intending to assist me in governing.
I truly and secretly admired this;
my body was not at ease on the mat,
food did not taste sweet,
my eyes did not look at delicate colors,
and my ears did not listen to the sounds of bells and drums.
Emptying my mind and fixing my will,
I have wished to hear your advice for three years now.
Now you, Sir, enter without assisting my rule
and retire without promoting my reputation;
I privately think this is unacceptable for you.
To harbor ability and not manifest it
is disloyalty;
to manifest it and not have it implemented
is due to the Ruler’s lack of clarity.
Could it be that I am perhaps not clear?”
Fēi Yǒu Xiānshēng prostrated and answered submissively.
Wú Wáng said:
“You may talk now;
I shall listen with focused attention.”
The Master said:
“Alas!
Is it possible?
Is it possible?
How difficult it is to speak!
For there are speeches that offend the eyes and grate on the ears,
confuse the mind but benefit the person.
Or there are speeches that please the eyes,
soothe the ears,
delight the heart but ruin one’s conduct.
Unless there is a bright king or sage ruler,
who can listen to them?”
Wú Wáng said:
“Why should that be so?
‘Those above the average can be told of higher things.’
Try to speak, Sir,
and I shall observe.”
The Master replied:
“In the past, Guān Lóngpáng earnestly remonstrated with Jié,
and Wángzǐ Bǐgān spoke directly to Zhòu.
These two ministers
both exerted their thoughts and exhausted their loyalty,
grieving that the Ruler’s grace did not flow down
and the ten thousand people were in turmoil.
Therefore they spoke directly of his faults
and sharply remonstrated against his wickedness,
intending to bring glory to the lord
and remove calamity from the ruler.
Now it is not so;
instead, it is taken as slandering the lord’s conduct
and lacking the decorum of a subject.
Consequently, they suffered harm to their bodies,
bore the name of the innocent,
punishment reached their ancestors,
and they became the laughingstock of the world.
Therefore I say: how difficult it is to speak!
Thus the ministers who assist and support fell apart,
and wicked, flattering people advanced together,
eventually including Fēi Lián,
È Lái Gé, and others.
These three were all fraudulent and deceitful,
with clever words and sharp tongues
to advance themselves.
They secretly catered to the king’s love for carving and engraving
to win his heart,
striving to satisfy the desires of the ears and eyes
and taking opportunistic accommodation as their measure.
They proceeded without caution
until their bodies were destroyed and executed,
the ancestral temples collapsed,
and the state became a ruin.
They killed and slaughtered worthy ministers
and stayed close to slanderers.
Does the Shī not say:
‘Slanderous people are limitless,
throwing the four states into chaos’?
This is what it means.
Therefore, to lower one’s person and debase one’s body,
using pleasing expressions and subtle words,
being cheerful and sycophantic,
in the end brings no benefit to the governance of the Sovereign;
this is what men of purpose and humanity cannot bear to do.
To take on a solemn and dignified appearance,
to speak deeply and remonstrate directly,
above to correct the ruler’s wickedness,
below to reduce the harm to the common people,
then one opposes the heart of a wicked ruler
and runs afoul of the laws of a decaying age.
Therefore, those who nourish their lives and longevity are unwilling to step forward,
so they dwell among deep mountains,
piling earth to make rooms,
weaving reeds for doors,
playing the qín within,
to sing of the customs of the former kings;
thus they can be happy and forget death.
Thus Bóyí and Shūqí avoided Zhōu,
starving beneath Shǒuyáng;
later generations praised their humanity.
In this way,
the conduct of a wicked ruler is indeed something to be feared.
Therefore I say: how difficult it is to speak!”
Thereupon, Wú Wáng was startled and changed his expression,
discarded the mat and left the table,
and sat upright to listen.
The Master said:
“Jiēyú avoided the world,
Jìzǐ loosened his hair and feigned madness.
These two
both avoided a turbid world to preserve their bodies.
If they had met a bright king or sage ruler,
and were granted the leisure of a pure banquet
and a kind, harmonious countenance,
they would have exerted their indignation and exhausted their sincerity,
planning for safety and danger,
weighing gains and losses,
above to secure the ruler’s person,
below to benefit the ten thousand people;
then the Way of the Wǔ Dì Sān Wáng could almost be seen.
Therefore, Yī Yǐn endured shame and humiliation,
carrying the tripod and cutting board,
blending the five flavors to seek out Tāng.
Tàigōng fished on the north bank of the Wèi River to see Wén Wáng.
Their hearts and intentions coincided;
no plan was unsuccessful,
no strategy was not followed,
for they had truly found their ruler.
Thinking deeply and considering far ahead,
they drew upon righteousness to rectify their persons,
and extended grace to broaden those below.
Basing themselves on humanity and taking righteousness as their ancestor,
they praised the virtuous,
rewarded the worthy and capable,
punished the evil and chaotic,
gathered the distant regions,
unified the various classes,
and beautified the customs;
this is the means by which Emperors and Kings flourished.
Above they did not change natural dispositions,
below they did not deprive people of human relations;
thus Heaven and Earth were in harmony,
and distant regions cherished them.
Therefore they are called Sage Kings.
The duties of ministers and sons having been fulfilled,
then lands were divided and enfeoffments settled,
titles given as Dukes and Marquises,
the state passed to sons and grandsons,
and their names became manifest to later generations.
Even now the people praise them,
because they encountered Tāng and Wén Wáng.
Tàigōng and Yī Yǐn were like this,
while Lóngpáng and Bǐgān alone were like that.
Is it not lamentable!
Therefore I say: how difficult it is to speak!”
At this, the Wú Wáng became solemn,
lowered his head in deep thought,
then looked up with tears streaming down his face,
and said:
"Alas!
That my state did not perish,
and has continued on and on;
how precarious it was,
that our lineage was not cut off!"
Thereupon, he rectified the court in the Míng Táng,
standardized the positions of ruler and ministers,
promoted the virtuous and talented,
distributed kindness and favor,
practiced benevolence and righteousness,
and rewarded those with merit.
He personally practiced frugality,
reduced the expenses of the inner palace,
and diminished the use of chariots and horses.
He banished the music of Zhèng Shēng,
distanced himself from flatterers,
reduced the kitchen staff,
discarded extravagance,
lowered the stature of his palaces and halls,
demolished his private parks and gardens,
and filled in the moats and trenches,
to give them to the landless poor.
He opened the inner treasury,
relieved the impoverished,
cared for the elderly,
showed compassion for the orphaned and widowed,
lightened taxes and levies,
and reduced punishments and penalties.
After practicing this for three years,
all within the seas was peaceful,
the world was in great harmony,
Yīn and Yáng were in balance,
and all things attained their proper state.
The state suffered no disasters or calamities,
the people showed no signs of hunger or cold,
every household was provided for and every person had enough,
savings and stores were in surplus,
and the prisons were empty.
Fènghuáng came to gather,
Qílín appeared in the outskirts,
sweet Gānlù descended,
and Zhūcǎo began to sprout.
People of different customs from distant lands,
drawn by his influence and admiring his righteousness,
each fulfilled their duties and came to pay homage.
Thus, the path of order and chaos,
and the source of survival and ruin,
are as easy to see as this;
yet those who rule over men are unwilling to act.
In my humble opinion, I consider this a mistake.
Therefore, the Shī says:
"The Wángguó was able to flourish,
only because of the integrity of Zhōu;
many and great were the officers,
through whom Wén Wáng found repose."
This is what it means.
After Bào had composed the poem *Zhòng Hé Yuè Zhí Xuān Bù* for the Yì Zhōu Cì Shǐ, Wáng Xiāng,
he also wrote a narrative
titled *Sì Zǐ Jiǎng Dé*
to clarify its meaning.
This Wén Xué questioned Xū Yí Fū Zǐ, saying:
"I have heard that when the Way prevails in a state,
to be poor and lowly
is a cause for shame.
Now, Master, you have closed your doors and avoided the world,
for many days specializing and refining your studies.
Fortunately, you have encountered a sagely ruler and a peaceful era,
yet for a long time you have kept your treasure hidden;
this is like Bó Yá leaving Zhōng Qī,
or Shùn
and Yǔ avoiding Dì Yáo.
In such a case, if you wish to make your name known
and establish great achievements,
is it not difficult?"
Fū Zǐ said:
"Indeed,
there is such a saying.
Now, mosquitoes and gadflies busy themselves all day long,
yet they cannot cross a set of stairs;
but by attaching themselves to the tail of a Jì horse, they can travel a thousand miles,
and by clinging to the wings of a Hóng bird, they can soar across the four seas.
Although I am dull and stubborn,
I wish to follow you.
Nevertheless,
by what means shall I present myself?"
Wén Xué said:
"Declare your sincere devotion before the court,
and engage in discourse at the gates of the high officials."
Fū Zǐ said:
"Without a means of introduction,
how can I walk among the high officials?"
Wén Xué said:
"Why should it be so?
In the past, Nìng Qī sang a merchant’s song to seek an audience with Qí Huán;
Yuè Shí carried fodder and awakened Yàn Yīng.
This was not due to long-standing friendship,
but they met by chance on the road
and became close.
Thus, regarding Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī,
those skilled at slandering cannot hide their beauty;
regarding Mú Mǔ and Wō Kuǐ,
those skilled at praising cannot conceal their ugliness.
If one possesses the ultimate Way,
why must there be an introduction?"
Fū Zǐ said:
"Alas!
To be recognized immediately upon meeting
is an occurrence once in a thousand years.
Seeking the worthy and associating with friends
is the common path for many scholars.
Therefore, if a handle is empty and without a blade,
Gōng Shū cannot use it to carve;
if one only hangs a light string and a tethered arrow,
Pú Jǔ cannot use them to shoot.
Thus, to beat the waves and cross the water with one's own strength
is not as easy as riding in a boat;
to trudge through mist and fields to reach a distant place
is not as swift as following the main road.
Talent is obscured when there is no one to recognize it,
and conduct fails when one has few allies.
This is a problem from ancient times to the present,
and only Wén Xué has considered it."
Wén Xué said:
"Yes, indeed,
I respectfully hear your instruction."
Thereupon, they joined together as companions,
holding hands and traveling together,
seeking the worthy and searching for friends,
passing through Xī Zhōu.
There were two men there,
riding in a chariot and singing.
They leaned against the crossbar and listened:
the sighs and chants were in accord with the *Yǎ*,
and the modulations were in accord with the *Lǜ*.
The tones were relaxed and flowing,
with every turn and cadence never losing the rhythm.
They asked who the singers were:
they were those known as Fú Yóu Xiān Shēng and Chén Qiū Zǐ.
Thereupon, they befriended them according to the etiquette for scholars meeting.
Once the ritual formalities were completed,
Wén Xué
and Fū Zǐ left their mats and said:
"We are rustic people without knowledge,
with limited vision and little hearing.
Just now, while traveling along the road,
we heard your jade-like voices from afar,
and our hearts were secretly moved.
We venture to ask what poem you were singing?
Please let us hear its explanation."
Fú Yóu Xiān Shēng Chén Qiū Zǐ said:
"It is the poem called *Zhòng Hé Yuè Zhí Xuān Bù*,
composed by the Cì Shǐ of Yì Zhōu.
The Cì Shǐ saw that the Supreme Ruler is sagely and brilliant,
his ministers exhaust their efforts,
his virtue and grace are vast and abundant,
the common people are in harmony,
and both Heaven and man respond together,
repeatedly sending down auspicious blessings.
Therefore, he composed this poem in three parts to sing and chant its praise."
Wén Xué said:
"A gentleman’s actions have purpose,
and his composure is measured.
Nán Róng thrice repeated the *Bái Guī* poem,
and Kǒng Zǐ saw in him his cautious warning;
Tài Zǐ Jī recited *Chén Fēng*,
and Wén Hóu understood his underlying intent.
Now, why is it that you, sir, take pleasure in this poem and chant it?"
The Xiānshēng said:
"Music influences people subtly and deeply,
shifting manners and changing customs.
The reason I chant and sing it
is to praise how the ruler's methods are enlightened and the ministers' path is attained.
The ruler is the central heart,
and the ministers are the external limbs.
When the external limbs act,
one then knows the likes and dislikes of the heart;
when the ministers move,
one then knows the principles and directions of the ruler.
If likes and dislikes are not manifested,
then right and wrong are not distinguished;
if principles and directions are not established,
then achievements and fame are not proclaimed.
Thus, beautiful jade is hidden within common wǔfū stones;
ordinary people look at it with indifference.
A skilled craftsman polishes it,
and only then is it known to be the treasure of Hé.
Refined metal is hidden in raw ore;
common people look at it with neglect.
A clever smith casts it,
and only then is its strength known.
How much more so for the towering and vast sagely virtue,
which the common people cannot even name!
Therefore, the Cìshǐ promotes and chants it,
extolling the ruler's virtue and beauty.
It is as deep as the vast ocean,
covering and sustaining all without exception,
abounding throughout heaven and earth,
and filling the silent universe.
The benevolence of the enlightened ruler is revealed,
and the integrity of loyal ministers is fully realized.
In the age of Huáng Táng,
what could be added to this?
Therefore, every time I sing of it,
I do not realize that old age is approaching."
The Wénxué said:
"The Shū says:
'By guiding the One Man, the four quarters are made as sure as divination.'
Loyal and worthy ministers
guide the ruler's will
and receive the ruler's benevolence,
expressing great virtue and transforming the world.
When the world's waters are calm
and every household is worthy of being enfeoffed,
why must one use chants, poems, and rhapsodies to extol the ruler?
I am privately perplexed by this."
Fúyóu Xiānshēng changed his expression as his eyes widened
and said:
"What kind of talk is this!
In the past, Zhōu Gōng chanted the virtue of Wén Wáng and composed 'Qīng Miào,'
establishing it as the lead of the Sòng;
Jí Fǔ sighed that Xuān Wáng was as harmonious as a clear breeze,
and it was listed in the Dàyǎ.
When the age declines and the Way is obscure,
false ministers who give empty praise
are dangerous.
When the age is peaceful and the Way is bright,
ministers and sons who do not proclaim it
are vulgar.
The burdens of vulgarity and danger
harm the Kingly Way.
Therefore, since the Cìshǐ arrived,
he has proclaimed the imperial edicts
and encouraged the people without tiring,
making the common people fully aware of the sagely virtue,
and none have not been moistened by it.
The white-browed elders
all cherish every morning and evening,
wishing to survive for just a little longer
to observe the pure flow of the great transformation.
At this time, the August Grace is abundant
and the ruler's benevolence overflows;
the common people rejoice
and central harmony is felt and expressed.
Therefore, songs were made to chant it.
The Chuán says:
'The poet is moved and then thinks;
thinks and then accumulates;
accumulates and then becomes full;
becomes full and then creates.
When words are not enough,
one then sighs and laments;
when sighing and lamenting are not enough,
one then chants and sings;
when chanting and singing do not suffice,
one does not realize that the hands are dancing and the feet are tapping.'
This is the constant duty of ministers and sons toward their ruler and father;
it is the same from ancient times to the present.
Now you hold onto small measures while ignoring vast estimations,
stay within your own grasp while rejecting the vast cosmos,
and yet you wish to judge the core mechanics of a great man.
To speak of the gains and losses of a Fāngbó,
is that not far-fetched?"
Chén Qiūzǐ saw that the Xiānshēng's words were sharp
and feared the two guests would be ashamed,
so he moved forward on his knees and said:
"Xiānshēng, consider this:
When puddles suddenly gather,
the rivers and seas do not consider them too many;
when loaches and eels flee together,
the nine-mesh net does not consider itself empty.
Therefore, Xǔ Yóu hid from Yáo in deep seclusion,
but the House of Táng did not decline because of it;
Yí and Qí were ashamed of Zhōu and starved in the distance,
but Wén and Wǔ did not become lowly because of it.
Blueflies cannot defile the Chuíjì jade;
perverse theories cannot confuse Kǒng and Mò.
Now the Cìshǐ is naturally keen to spread benevolence
and extend transformation to enhance his reputation,
collecting poems to manifest ultimate virtue
and chanting songs to oversee culture.
Receiving orders as fine as silk,
making them manifest like a thick cord.
The atmosphere of the Gāntáng
can be awaited while leaning back.
Although the two guests have blocked plans and frustrated arguments,
what harm is there?"
He turned to the Wénxué fūzǐ and said:
"The Xiānshēng is slightly boastful when talking about the Way
and does not yield when it comes to benevolence,
but it is not a great fault.
I hope you two will keep this in mind."
The Fūzǐ said:
"No.
When thunder must strike,
what is hidden in the depths vibrates;
when drumsticks and drums resound,
the armored soldiers are roused.
Thus, if things do not vibrate, they do not sprout;
if a scholar is not provoked, he is not brave.
Now the words of the Wénxué
intend to use discussion to move the opponent
and relieve the Xiānshēng's indignation.
I hope you two also have no doubts."
Thereupon, the literary discussions gathered again,
and they began to discourse on virtue.
The Wénxué fūzǐ asked:
"In the ages of Chéng and Kāng long ago,
was it the virtue of the rulers
or the effort of the ministers?"
The Xiānshēng replied:
"Without a sagely and wise ruler,
how could there be Gāntáng ministers?
Thus, when a tiger roars, the wind howls;
when a dragon rises, clouds and mists appear.
Crickets wait for autumn to chirp;
mayflies come out when it is overcast.
The Yì says:
'A flying dragon is in the heavens;
it is beneficial to see the great man.'
Sounds respond to each other;
mates follow one another.
People join together through shared intent;
things group together by their kind.
Thus, the sagely ruler does not look everywhere yet sees clearly;
he does not exhaust his hearing yet hears acutely.
Why is this?
Regarding good people and gentlemen,
those who follow them are many.
Thus, a robe worth a thousand pieces of gold
is not made from the armpit of a single fox;
the timber for a great mansion
is not the wood from a single hill;
the achievement of Tàipíng
is not the strategy of a single person."
For the ruler is the head,
and the ministers are the limbs;
this shows they are of one body,
relying on each other to be complete.
To have a ruler but no ministers—
the *Chūnqiū* criticizes this.
In the era of the Three Dynasties and before,
all had teachers and tutors;
from the Five Hegemons downwards,
each chose friends for themselves.
*Huán* of *Qí* had *Guǎn*, *Bào*, *Xí*, and *Nìng*;
he united the feudal lords nine times
and brought order to the realm.
Duke *Wén* of *Jìn* had *Jiù Fàn* and *Zhào Shuāi*;
he gained prestige and established hegemony
to honor the Son of Heaven.
*Mù* of *Qín* had *Wáng Yóu* and *Wǔ Gǔ*;
he repelled the Western *Róng*
and began the imperial lineage.
*Zhuāng* of *Chǔ* had *Shū Sūn* and *Zǐ Fǎn*;
he pacified the *Jiāng* and *Huái* regions,
his majesty shaking the *Zhù Xià*.
*Gōu Jiàn* had *Zhòng*, *Lǐ*, *Xiè*, and *Yōng*;
he conquered the powerful *Wú*
and washed away the shame of *Kuàijī*.
*Wén* of *Wèi* had *Duàn Gān*, *Tián*, and *Zhái*;
the people of *Qín* ceased their hostilities,
and he repelled enemies ten thousand *lǐ* away.
*Zhāo* of *Yàn* had *Guō Wěi* and *Yuè Yì*;
they crushed the powerful *Qí*
and trapped King *Mǐn* in *Jǔ*.
If even the minor lords of the states
achieved such fame and merit,
how much more so for Emperors and Kings who select from the four seas
and provide wings for the common people!
"Therefore, where there is a sagacious and holy ruler,
there must be wise and intelligent ministers.
If they wish to accumulate virtue,
then the world is easily pacified;
if they wish to establish majesty,
then the hundred barbarian tribes are easily repelled.
Now the Sage Sovereign wears the crown of Way and Virtue,
walks in pure benevolence,
is clad in the Six Arts,
and carries the ornaments of ritual and culture.
He has repeatedly issued bright edicts
to recommend the worthy and good,
seek out men of technique,
summon those of exceptional character,
and promote the outstanding and talented.
Consequently, all within the seas rejoice and admire;
they gather like the wind and collect like rain,
arriving in succession to
fill the courts and overflow the palace gates.
The sounds of cherishing purity and chanting virtue fill the ears;
the rituals of ascending, descending, bowing, and yielding exhaust the sight.
Those who advance delight in the smooth flow of affairs;
those who are weary find themselves unable to stop.
They rest and crawl at the gates of the *Shī* and *Shū*,
and wander within the realm of Way and Virtue.
All purify their bodies and cultivate their thoughts,
expressing their true feelings and laying bare their hearts.
Each exerts their finest efforts to offer loyalty,
sincerely wishing to promote the Sovereign,
broaden the customs, and usher in great peace.
'Numerous are the many officials'—
this was how King *Wén* achieved tranquility.
"As for the implementation of fine governance
and the moistening of great grace,
they cannot be fully detailed.
He promotes the filial to encourage sincere conduct
and honors the capable to attract the worthy.
He removes complexities and abolishes harshness to pacify the common people,
and provides stipends for the industrious while increasing salaries to encourage integrity and incorruptibility.
He reduces his own meals,
keeps his palaces humble,
reduces field officials,
diminishes the imperial parks,
eases corvée labor,
relieves the destitute,
sympathizes with the people in their disasters,
and has no leisure for tours or banquets.
He pities the elderly who encounter misfortune,
sympathizes with those in mourning clothes who must serve,
feels compassion for the castrated people who have died,
and is grieved by the sons and brothers who are imprisoned or hidden.
His grace reaches the flying birds,
and his kindness extends to the walking beasts;
embryos and eggs are allowed to mature and hatch,
and plants and trees flourish in their seasons.
The joyful and easy-going gentleman
is the parent of the people—
is this not so?
"Have you alone not heard of the time of *Qín*?
They turned against the Three Kings,
turned their backs on the Five Emperors,
destroyed the *Shī* and *Shū*,
and ruined ritual and righteousness.
They trusted various petty men
and detested the benevolent and wise.
The deceitful and false were promoted,
and the flattering and sycophantic were admitted.
The Chancellors were harsh and severe,
and the *Dà Lǐ* applied rigorous laws.
Those who held office and administered the government
were all deficient in benevolence and righteousness
but excelled in cruelty and tyranny;
they were like grasping wolves and seizing tigers,
harboring destructiveness and wielding malice.
Wherever they presided,
everyone trembled in fear and submitted;
they blew aside the hair to search for flaws
and applied their stinging venom everywhere.
The common people were terrified and restless,
not knowing where to put their hands or feet.
Their clamorous grievances and sorrows
eventually brought about the destruction of the *Qín* clan.
Therefore, one who raises chickens does not keep wildcats;
one who tends herds does not breed jackals;
one who plants trees worries about woodworms;
and one who protects the people removes those who harm them.
Thus, in the governance of the Great *Hàn*,
simplicity is honored,
leniency and gentleness are valued,
the pure and benevolent are advanced,
and the worthy and talented are recommended.
High and low have no grievances,
and the people are in harmony.
"Now all within the seas enjoy their occupations,
and the court is pure and bright.
Heavenly signs have been manifested,
and human omens are clear.
All things are prosperous,
and mountains and rivers bestow their spirits.
Divine light radiates and glows,
vast and profound, illuminating the heavens.
The *Fènghuáng* has come to perform,
dignified and harmonious.
All manner of birds follow it,
dancing to virtue and showing their forms.
Divine sparrows gather repeatedly,
and the *Qílín* arrives of its own accord.
Sweet dew nourishes the land,
and auspicious grain stands thick as comb-teeth.
The Great Transformation is profound and pervasive;
men and women are flourishing and content.
Every household is provided for, the harvests are bountiful,
and all follow the patterns of the *Sān Rǎng*.
Is this not a grand age!
In the past, King *Wén* responded to the nine-tailed fox and the Eastern *Yí* returned to *Zhōu*;
King *Wǔ* obtained a white fish and the feudal lords spoke with one voice;
the Duke of *Zhōu* received black millet wine and the *Guǐfāng* became subjects;
King *Xuān* captured a white wolf and the *Yí* and *Dí* tribes became guests.
When names are correct, affairs are settled.
Now that a white tiger has been captured in *Nán Jùn*,
it is also an omen for the cessation of military force and the flourishing of culture.
The one who captured it was *Zhāng Wǔ*;
when *Wǔ* is *Zhāng*, the fierce are subdued.
Consequently, the Northern *Dí* are harmoniously submissive;
the borders no longer worry about raiders,
the armored soldiers sleep, and the banners are lowered."
The scholar of letters said:
"I have heard your instruction regarding the signs of Heaven;
may I venture to ask
about the human omens?"
The Master said:
"As for the Xiōngnú,
they are the strongest among the hundred barbarian tribes.
Their nature is arrogant and recalcitrant,
and their customs are fierce and violent.
They despise the old and value the young,
exalting one another for physical strength.
Their industry lies in attacking and conquering,
and their business in hunting and archery.
Their children can ride sheep,
shooting arrows and flying bolts;
they follow water and chase livestock,
having no permanent dwelling.
Like birds gathering and beasts scattering,
they gallop to and fro,
wandering through the vast wilderness
to satisfy their appetites.
Their plows and shares are bows, arrows, saddles, and horses;
their sowing is the drawing of bowstrings and the clapping of hands;
their autumn harvest is the chasing of foxes and galloping after rabbits;
their reaping is the felling and slaughtering of enemies.
Chase them and they flee into hiding;
release them and they act as bandits.
Therefore, the Sān Wáng could not cherish them,
and the Wǔ Bà could not pacify them.
They alarm the borders and harass the soldiers,
repeatedly violating the gatherers of fodder and wood.
Sung of by the poets,
they have been a grievance since antiquity.
Now, sacred virtue is grand and flourishing,
and majestic spirit covers the exterior.
The Rìzhú King and his whole nation have returned to virtue,
and the Chányú calls himself a subject and comes to offer seasonal greetings.
Where the Qián and Kūn open,
where the Yīn and Yáng meet,
countries with braided hair and humble faces,
scorched teeth and owl-like gazes,
shorn hair and tattooed foreheads,
and tattooed bodies and naked chests—
none do not come running to offer tribute,
joyfully coming to attach themselves,
dancing and singing,
drumming their sides and laughing.
In this era of great harmony,
what creature is not joyful?
Flying birds fold their wings;
fish in the springs leap with vigor.
Therefore, the Cìshǐ, moved by their feelings, give voice to their thoughts and chant of the utmost virtue.
I, a person of humble origins and shallow knowledge,
cannot investigate or recognize everything;
I respectfully follow what I have heard,
but have not yet been able to exhaust it all."
Thereupon, the two guests were intoxicated by benevolence and righteousness,
satiated by grand virtue,
sighing in admiration all day long,
and were pleased and submissive with delight.
Formerly, during the abdication of Dì Yáo, he said:
"O Shùn!
The celestial succession rests upon your person."
Shùn also commanded Yǔ in this way.
Down to Jì and Qiè,
all assisted Táng and Yú,
brilliantly aiding the four seas,
their virtue carried through successive generations.
Coming to Tāng and Wǔ,
they possessed the world.
Although they encountered different times
and their successions were not the same,
when it came to responding to Heaven and following the people,
their principles were one and the same.
For this reason, the Liú clan inherited the blessings of Yáo;
their lineage through the generations
is recorded in the Chūnqiū.
Táng occupied the virtue of Fire,
and Hàn succeeded it.
When first rising from the Pèi marshes,
the Divine Mother wailed at night,
to manifest the omen of the Chì Dì.
Speaking from this perspective,
the throne of Emperors and Kings
must have clear, sacred, manifest, and beautiful virtue,
and the industry of accumulated great merit and profound benefit;
only then does their sincerity communicate with the spirits
and their flowing benevolence reach the common people.
Thus, they can be blessed and sacrificed to by ghosts and spirits,
and the world returns to them.
I have never seen a turning era without a root,
or merit and virtue unrecorded,
yet one could rise abruptly to this position.
Common people see that Gāozǔ rose from among the commoners
and do not understand the reason,
thinking that he just happened to encounter violent rebellion,
was able to brandish his sword,
and like the wandering persuaders,
even compare the world to the chasing of a deer,
obtaining it by lucky speed.
They do not know that the Sacred Vessel has a mandate
and cannot be sought by wit or strength.
How tragic!
This is why the world has so many rebellious ministers and treacherous sons.
If it were like that,
how could they only be ignorant of the Way of Heaven?
They also do not see it in human affairs!
As for the starving and destitute vagrants,
hungry and cold on the roads,
who long for a suit of coarse wool
or a storage of a few pecks of grain,
whose wish is no more than a single piece of gold,
but who end up dying in the ditches and valleys.
Why is this?
Poverty and destitution also have their mandate.
How much more so the nobility of the Tiānzǐ,
the wealth of the four seas,
and the succession of the spirits?
Can these be attained by reckless occupation?
Thus, although some may encounter a time of disaster,
and steal the handle of power,
as brave as Xìn and Bù,
as strong as Liáng and Jí,
as successful as Wáng Mǎng,
yet in the end they soak in the cauldron or lie on the execution block,
boiled, minced, or torn apart.
How much more so for those of trivial insignificance who do not even equal these few men,
yet wish to blindly interfere with the heavenly position?
For this reason, a clumsy or lame horse
cannot gallop on a thousand-li road;
the likes of swallows and sparrows
cannot exert the use of the six flight feathers;
materials for rafters and posts cannot bear the responsibility of ridgepoles and beams;
and small men of pecks and hampers
cannot hold the gravity of Emperors and Kings.
The Yì says:
"The legs of the tripod are broken,
spilling the duke's stew."
This means being unable to sustain the responsibility.
At the end of the Qín,
the heroes together urged Chén Yīng to become king.
Yīng's mother stopped him, saying:
"Since I became a daughter-in-law in your family,
we have been poor and lowly for generations.
Suddenly to become rich and noble
is inauspicious.
It is better to attach your troops to someone else;
if the matter succeeds,
you will receive some benefit.
If it does not succeed,
the calamity will have someone to fall upon."
Yīng followed her words,
and the Chén clan was thus at peace.
The mother of Wáng Líng
also saw that the Xiàng clan would surely perish
and that the Liú clan was about to rise.
At that time,
Líng was a general for Hàn,
and his mother was captured by Chǔ.
A messenger from Hàn came;
Líng's mother saw him
and said to him:
"Please tell my son
that the King of Hàn is a man of virtue
and will surely obtain the world.
Let my son serve him diligently
and have no double-heartedness."
Thereupon, facing the Hàn messenger, she fell upon her sword and died
to firmly encourage Líng.
Afterwards,
the world was indeed settled by Hàn.
Líng became the Chancellor
and was enfeoffed as a Marquis.
With the wisdom of an ordinary woman,
she could still deduce the ultimate principles of things
and explore the mechanism of misfortune and fortune,
preserving the ancestral sacrifices for infinity
and leaving her name in the records of the Chūnqiū.
How much more so for the affairs of a great man?
Therefore, poverty or success is determined by fate,
while good or bad fortune depends on the person.
Yīng's mother knew of failure,
and Líng's mother knew of rise.
By examining these two cases,
the lot of Emperors and Kings is decided."
As for Gāozǔ,
his rise was due to five factors:
first, he was a descendant of the Emperor Yáo;
second, his physical appearance was most extraordinary;
third, his divine martial prowess was accompanied by auspicious omens;
fourth, he was broad-minded, enlightened, benevolent, and forgiving;
fifth, he knew people well and was skilled at employing them.
In addition, he was sincere and fond of strategy,
thorough in listening and accepting advice,
pursuing goodness as if he could not reach it,
employing others as if they were himself,
following remonstrance like water flowing downstream,
and seizing opportunities as quickly as an echo.
He would spit out his food while eating to attend to guests,
to adopt the strategies of Zǐfáng;
he would pull out his feet and stop washing them,
to bow to the discourse of Lì Shēng;
he understood the words of a common soldier,
and severed his emotional attachment to his homeland;
he held high the reputation of the Sì Hào,
and sacrificed his personal affection for his own flesh and blood;
he raised Hán Xìn from the ranks of the army,
and recruited Chén Píng while he was a fugitive.
Heroes exerted their efforts,
and all strategies were fully implemented;
this was the grand vision of Gāozǔ,
through which he established the imperial enterprise.
As for the divine omens and auspicious responses,
these may also be briefly heard.
Initially, when Liú Oǔ was pregnant with Gāozǔ,
she dreamed of meeting a god;
there was thunder and lightning in the darkness,
and the strange sight of a dragon and serpent.
As he grew up, he possessed much spiritual power,
and was different from the masses.
Therefore, Wáng Wǔ was moved by his presence and cancelled his debts;
Lǚ Gōng observed his appearance and offered his daughter;
the Qín Emperor traveled east to suppress his auspicious aura;
Lǚ Hòu gazed at the clouds and knew his location;
when he first received the mandate, the white snake was divided;
when he entered the Pass to the west, the five stars gathered.
Thus, the Marquis of Huáiyīn and the Marquis of Liú called it a gift from Heaven,
not something achievable by human effort.
By examining the gains and losses from ancient times to the present,
verifying the success and failure of past events,
investigating the dynastic cycles of emperors and kings,
and considering what these five factors mean,
those who occupy this position without being weary of it,
yet whose omens and signs do not match this standard,
but who blindly pursue power and profit,
and arrogantly seize power out of order,
neither measuring their strength externally
nor knowing their fate internally,
will surely lose their status as masters who protect their families,
forfeit their natural lifespan,
encounter the misfortune of "breaking a leg,"
and suffer the punishment of the axe and halberd.
If heroes truly realize and awaken,
fearing these disasters as warnings,
looking far ahead with a transcendent view,
and possessing deep and profound insight,
they would emulate the clear sense of duty of Wáng Líng and Guàn Yīng,
sever the covetous ambitions of Hán Xìn and Péng Bù,
reject the blind talk of "chasing the deer,"
and examine how the sacred vessels of state are bestowed.
Greed must not lead to vain hopes,
and one should not become the laughingstock of the two mothers,
then blessings and prosperity will flow to one's descendants,
and the heavenly emoluments will last until the very end.
Literary men belittle one another;
this has been so since ancient times.
In the case of Fù Yì and Bān Gù,
they were like elder and younger brothers in talent,
yet Bān Gù looked down upon him.
In a letter to his younger brother Bān Chāo, he said:
"Wǔzhòng became a Clerk of the Orchid Pavilion because of his ability to write,
but once his brush touches paper, he cannot stop."
Men are good at seeing their own merits,
but literature is not of a single form,
and few are able to be good at everything.
Therefore, each person uses their strengths
to belittle the weaknesses of others.
A common proverb says:
"Even if one's house has only a worn-out broom,
one prizes it as if it were worth a thousand pieces of gold."
This is the trouble of not being able to see oneself clearly.
Among the writers of today:
Kǒng Róng, Wénjǔ, of Lǔ;
Chén Lín, Kǒngzhāng, of Guǎnglíng;
Wáng Càn, Zhòngxuān, of Shānyáng;
Xú Gàn, Wěicháng, of Běihǎi;
Ruǎn Yǔ, Yuányú, of Chénliú;
Yìng Yáng, Délián, of Rǔnán;
Liú Zhēn, Gōnggàn, of Dōngpíng.
These seven gentlemen
have left nothing unstudied in learning,
and borrow nothing in their rhetoric.
They all gallop like fine steeds for a thousand miles,
with their heads held high as they run side by side.
To make them submit to one another
is indeed truly difficult.
A gentleman examines himself to judge others,
and thus can avoid this burden
and write this discourse on literature.
Wáng Càn is superior in poetic expositions;
Xú Gàn occasionally has the spirit of Qí,
yet he is a match for Wáng Càn.
As in Wáng Càn's "Initial Expedition," "Climbing the Tower," and "The Pagoda Tree,"
and Xú Gàn's "The Black Ape," "The Leaking Vessel," "The Round Fan," and "The Tangerine,"
even Zhāng Héng and Cài Yōng could not surpass them.
However, in other forms of writing,
they are not quite as good.
The memorials and letters of Chén Lín and Ruǎn Yǔ
are the most outstanding of today.
Yìng Yáng is harmonious but lacks vigor.
Liú Zhēn is vigorous but lacks density.
Kǒng Róng's style and spirit are lofty and wonderful,
surpassing others,
but he cannot sustain an argument,
and his reasoning does not match his words,
to the point of mixing in mockery and playfulness.
As for the things he is good at,
he is the peer of Yáng Xióng and Bān Gù.
Ordinary people value the distant and despise the near;
they follow reputation and turn their backs on reality.
They also suffer from being blind to themselves,
and call themselves wise.
Literature
is the same in its roots but different in its branches.
Memorials and discussions should be elegant;
letters and essays should be logical;
inscriptions and eulogies value facts;
poetry and rhapsodies desire beauty.
These four categories are different,
so those who are capable are usually partial to one;
only a universal talent can be proficient in all styles.
Literature takes "qi" as its primary element.
The clarity or turbidity of "qi" has a fixed form
and cannot be achieved by force.
It is like music:
though the melody and measure are the same,
and the rhythm follows the same rules,
when it comes to the unevenness of the drawing of breath
or the innate skill or clumsiness,
even a father or elder brother
cannot transfer it to a son or younger brother.
Literature is a grand enterprise for the state,
and an immortal achievement.
A man's lifespan has its time to end,
and glory and pleasure stop with his person.
Both of these have a fixed limit,
unlike literature, which is eternal.
Therefore, the authors of old
entrusted themselves to the brush and ink,
and expressed their ideas in books and records.
They did not rely on the words of a good historian,
nor did they depend on the influence of powerful people,
yet their reputations were naturally passed down to posterity.
Thus, Xībó was imprisoned and elaborated on the "Book of Changes,"
and Zhōu Dàn was eminent and established the "Rites."
They did not fail to work because they were in obscurity,
nor did they change their focus because they were in prosperity.
This being so,
the ancients despised a large jade disk but valued an inch of time,
fearing that time would pass them by.
Yet most people do not exert themselves;
when poor and low, they are intimidated by hunger and cold;
when rich and noble, they drift into ease and pleasure.
Consequently, they busy themselves with immediate matters
and neglect the work of a thousand years.
The sun and moon pass above,
and physical appearance withers below;
suddenly they transform and pass away along with all things—
this is the greatest sorrow for a man of ambition!
Kǒng Róng and the others have passed away;
only Xú Gàn has written discourses
that form an independent school of thought.
In the past, the Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu lasted for dozens of generations,
but Qín perished in its second generation.
Why was this?
The rulers of the Sāndài shared the people with the world,
and thus the world shared their worries;
the King of Qín controlled the people alone,
and thus when he faced collapse and danger, no one saved him.
Indeed, he who shares his joy with others,
others will surely worry about his worries;
he who shares his peace with others,
others will surely rescue him from danger.
The former kings knew that solitary rule could not last long,
so they shared the governance with others;
they knew that solitary defense could not be secure,
so they shared the defense with others.
They employed both the kin and the distant,
and advanced both those who were similar and different.
Thus, the heavy and the light were sufficient to stabilize each other,
and the kin and the distant were sufficient to protect each other;
the paths of annexation were blocked,
and rebellious intentions did not arise.
When they declined,
Huán and Wén led with ritual;
when the wrapped couch-grass was not presented as tribute,
the army of Qí attacked Chǔ;
when Sòng did not build walls for Zhōu,
Jìn executed its minister.
The royal authority slackened and then tightened again,
and the feudal lords became arrogant and then respectful again.
After the two hegemons,
the dynasties gradually declined.
Wú and Chǔ relied on the Jiāng
and the fortifications of Fāngchéng;
though their hearts desired the Jiǔdǐng,
they feared and were constrained by the Zōngjī;
treacherous feelings were dissipated in their bosoms,
and rebellious plots vanished from their lips.
Was this not because they trusted and valued their relatives
and appointed the worthy and capable,
so that the branches and leaves were lush and flourishing,
and the roots relied upon them?
After this,
they turned to attacking one another.
Wú was annexed by Yuè,
Jìn was divided into three,
Lǔ was destroyed by Chǔ,
and Zhèng was absorbed by Hán.
By the time of the Zhànguó period,
the various Jī clans were weak,
and only Yān and Wèi remained.
However, they were all weak and small,
threatened by the strong Qín to the west,
and fearing Qí and
Chǔ to the south; barely saving themselves from destruction,
they had no leisure to worry about each other.
By the time of King Nǎn,
he was reduced to a commoner,
yet the branches and trunk still supported each other,
allowing him to occupy a vacant throne.
The realm was without a master
for over forty years.
Qín occupied lands of superior strategic position,
employed tactics of deceit and trickery,
attacked the east of the Pass,
and nibbled away at the nine states like a silkworm.
Coming to Shǐhuáng,
he finally established the imperial throne.
The time taken was as long as that,
and the effort expended was as great as this;
was this not a way of deep roots and a firm base,
an unshakeable path?
The Yì says:
"It is perishing! It is perishing!
Yet it is tied to a cluster of mulberry trees."
The virtue of Zhōu can be said to match this.
Qín observed the flaws of Zhōu
and thought it was seized because of its weakness;
thus they abolished the five ranks of nobility,
established officials for commanderies and counties,
abandoned the teachings of ritual and music,
and employed harsh and severe policies.
The sons and brothers had not an inch of land granted,
and the meritorious ministers had not enough land to stand a needle;
internally, there were no clan heirs to assist and support him,
and externally, there were no feudal lords to act as a protective screen.
Benevolence was not extended to relatives,
and grace did not flow to the branches and leaves;
it was like cutting off one's own limbs
and relying only on the chest and belly;
it was like sailing a boat on rivers and seas
but throwing away the oars and sculls.
Onlookers felt a chill in their hearts because of it,
but Shǐhuáng was at ease,
believing that with the security of Guānzhōng
and a thousand miles of metal walls,
it was an eternal legacy for his descendants to be emperors.
How absurd was that!
At that time,
Chúnyú Yuè remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that the kings of Yīn and
Zhōu
enfeoffed their sons, brothers, and meritorious ministers,
and lasted for over a thousand years.
Now Your Majesty rules over all within the seas,
yet your sons and brothers are commoners;
if there should suddenly be ministers like Tián Cháng or the Liùqīng,
and there are no assistants or supporters,
how will you be saved?
That matters which do not follow antiquity can last long
is something I have never heard of."
Shǐhuáng listened to the biased arguments of Lǐ Sī and rejected his righteousness.
By the day of his death,
there was no one to entrust with his legacy;
he entrusted the weight of the realm to the hands of ordinary men
and placed the command of succession into the mouths of treacherous ministers,
resulting in the likes of Zhào Gāo
exterminating the imperial clan.
Húhài learned harsh and mean teachings in his youth
and followed his cruel father's legacy as an adult;
he could not change the system or alter the laws
to favor and employ his brothers,
but instead modeled his plans after Shēn and Shāng
and consulted with Zhào Gāo;
he secluded himself in the deep palace
and entrusted the government to slandering thieves;
his life ended at Wàngyí,
asking to be a commoner;
could that be possible?
Consequently, the commanderies and states lost their loyalty,
the common people revolted,
Shèng and Guǎng led the cry in front,
and Liú and Xiàng finished it off behind.
Had Shǐhuáng accepted the strategy of Chúnyú,
suppressed the arguments of Lǐ Sī,
divided the provinces and states,
partitioned land for his sons and brothers,
enfeoffed the descendants of the Sāndài,
and rewarded the labor of meritorious ministers,
so that the land had permanent rulers
and the people had fixed masters,
with branches and leaves supporting each other
and the head and tail acting in coordination;
even if his descendants had behaved in ways that strayed from the Way,
and if the people of the time lacked the worthiness of Tāng or Wǔ,
before treacherous plots could even be launched,
the conspirators would have already been slaughtered;
how could the insignificant Chén and Xiàng
have been able to stir a hand or foot?
Therefore, Hànzǔ brandished a three-foot sword,
led a gathered crowd of commoners,
and within five years,
completed the imperial enterprise.
Since the beginning of the world,
in terms of rising to power and establishing achievements,
there has never been one as easy as that of Hànzǔ.
Indeed, it is difficult to succeed when attacking deep roots,
but easy to exert force when destroying what is withered and rotten;
this is the natural logic of circumstances.
Hàn reflected on the failures of Qín,
and enfeoffed its sons and brothers.
When the various Lǚ usurped power,
plotting to endanger the Liú clan,
the reason the empire could not be overturned
and the reason the common people did not change their hearts
was solely because the vassal lords were powerful and great,
as firm as boulders and as solid as glue.
Dōngmóu and Zhūxū received mandates from within,
while Qí, Dài, Wú, and Chǔ acted as guards from without.
Had Gāozǔ followed the methods of the fallen Qín
and neglected the systems of the former kings,
then the empire would have already been passed on
and would not have belonged to the Liú clan.
However, Gāozǔ’s enfeoffments
exceeded the ancient systems in land area;
the large ones spanned provinces and combined territories,
while the small ones joined dozens of cities.
There was no distinction between superior and inferior,
and their power rivaled the imperial house;
therefore, there was the trouble of the seven states including Wú and Chǔ.
Jiǎ Yì said:
“If the vassal lords are powerful and flourishing,
they will breed disorder and give rise to treachery.
To desire the peace and order of the world,
nothing is better than establishing many vassal lords but reducing their power.
Make the situation of the realm
like the body commanding the arm,
and the arm commanding the fingers;
then those below will have no heart for rebellion,
and those above will have no need for executions and punishments.”
Wéndì did not follow this.
When it came to the Filial Jǐngdì,
he rashly used the plan of Cháo Cuò
to reduce and dismiss the vassal lords.
The close relatives harbored resentment,
and the distant ones were struck with terror.
Wú and Chǔ led the conspiracy,
and the five states followed like the wind.
The signs began with Gāozǔ,
and the conflict ripened under Wén and Jǐng;
it was because leniency exceeded the system
and the suddenness of the reduction was not gradual.
As the saying goes: ‘When the branch is too large, it must break;
when the tail is too big, it is hard to wag.’
When the tail is of the same body,
it may still not follow;
how much more so for a tail that is not of the body—
can it be wagged?
Wǔdì followed the strategy of Zhǔfù and
issued the Decree of Extending Favor.
From then on,
Qí was divided into seven,
Zhào was divided into six,
Huáinán was split into three,
and Liáng and Dài were divided into five;
consequently, they gradually declined,
and their descendants became weak and insignificant.
They lived off taxes for clothing and food
and did not participate in political affairs.
Some were reduced or dismissed due to the sacrificial gold issue,
and some had their states abolished for having no heirs.
By the time of Chéngdì,
the Wáng clan usurped the court.
Liú Xiàng remonstrated, saying:
“Your servant has heard that the ducal clan
is the branches and leaves of the state.
If the branches and leaves fall,
then the roots will have nothing to shade them.
Presently, those of the same surname are distant,
while the maternal relatives monopolize the government,
excluding and casting out the imperial clan,
and isolating and weakening the ducal lineage.
This is not the way to preserve the altars of soil and grain
or to secure the succession of the state.”
His words were profound and earnest,
and he cited many examples.
Although Chéngdì sighed in sorrow, he could not make use of them.
By the time of Āidì and Píngdì,
those of different surnames held power,
borrowing the precedents of Zhōu Gōng
while committing the rebellion of Tián Cháng.
With hands folded high, they stole the heavenly throne,
and in a single morning made the four seas their subjects.
The kings and marquises of the Hàn imperial clan
untied their seals and loosened their ribbons,
offering up the state altars.
They still feared they would not even be allowed to be servants or concubines.
Some even fabricated omens for him
and praised the kindness and virtue of Wáng Mǎng.
Is this not lamentable!
Speaking from this perspective,
it was not that the imperial sons were uniquely loyal and filial during the times of Huìdì and Wéndì
and rebellious during the times of Āidì and Píngdì;
it was simply because their power was light and their influence weak,
that they could not maintain stability.
Relying on Emperor Guāngwǔ, who possessed peerless talent,
he captured Wáng Mǎng when his rule was already established
and restored the Hàn sacrifices after they had been severed.
Was this not the strength of an imperial son?
Yet later rulers failed to reflect on the failed policies of Qín,
failed to adopt the old systems of Zhōu,
but instead followed the laws of fallen states,
and gambled on hopes for an eternal reign.
When it came to Huándì and Língdì,
the eunuchs held the scales of power.
The court had no ministers who would die for the cause,
and the periphery had no states that shared the burden.
The sovereign was isolated above,
while ministers manipulated power below.
The root and branch could not control each other,
and the body and hands could not command each other.
As a result, the empire seethed like a boiling cauldron,
and the treacherous and evil struggled together.
The ancestral temples were burned to ashes,
and the palaces turned into overgrown thickets.
Living in the land of the Nine Provinces,
yet finding no place of safety for oneself—
how tragic!
The Grand Ancestor of Wèi, Emperor Wǔdì,
embodied the character of a sage and the enlightened,
and possessed the strategy of divine martiality.
He was ashamed that the royal principles had been abandoned
and lamented the collapse of the Hàn house.
He rose like a dragon from Qiáo and Pèi,
and soared like a phoenix through Gǔn and Yù.
He swept away the wicked and rebellious,
and exterminated the predatory monsters.
He welcomed the Emperor from Xījīng
and established the capital at the city of Yǐng.
His virtue moved Heaven and Earth,
and his righteousness touched men and gods.
The Hàn clan, following Heaven,
abdicated the throne to the Great Wèi.
The rise of the Great Wèi
has now lasted twenty-four years.
Looking at the survival and downfall of the five dynasties,
yet not employing their best strategies;
seeing the overturning of the carts ahead,
yet not changing one's own tracks.
Sons and brothers are kings over empty lands,
and the ruler has subjects he cannot command.
The imperial clan members are hidden away in common alleys,
and do not hear of the government of the state.
Their power is equal to that of commoners,
and their influence is the same as the ordinary masses.
Internally, there is no solid foundation of deep roots that cannot be pulled up;
externally, there is no assistance from a firm alliance of the imperial clan.
This is not the way to secure the state and create an enterprise for ten thousand generations.
Furthermore, today’s Zhōumù
and Jùnshǒu
are the Fāngbó
and Zhūhóu of old;
they all possess territories spanning a thousand lǐ
and hold military responsibilities.
In some cases, several people are in neighboring states,
or brothers occupy positions side by side.
Yet among the sons and brothers of the imperial clan,
there is not even one person placed among them
to maintain mutual support.
This is not the way to ‘strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches’
or to prepare for unforeseen contingencies.
In the current selection of the worthy,
some are promoted beyond their rank to be masters of famous cities,
or commanders of auxiliary armies.
But members of the imperial clan with civil talents are inevitably limited to being magistrates of small counties,
and those with military talents are inevitably placed merely over a hundred men.
This causes scholars of integrity and high character
to confine their ambitions within the yoke and harness,
and people of ability
to feel ashamed at being grouped with those not of their kind.
This is not the way to encourage the advancement of the worthy and capable,
nor is it the ritual for honoring and distinguishing the imperial clan.
When a spring is exhausted, its flow dries up;
when roots rot, the leaves wither.
Those with lush branches shade the roots;
when the twigs fall, the trunk stands alone.
Thus the proverb says:
"A centipede
does not fall over even when dead
because those who support it are many."
Though these words are minor,
they can be used to illustrate great things.
Furthermore, the foundation of a wall cannot be completed in haste,
and a reputation of prestige cannot be established in a single morning.
All are achieved through gradual progress
and built upon a long-standing foundation.
Consider the planting of a tree:
only over a long time do its roots become deep and firm,
and its branches and leaves become lush.
If it is suddenly moved from among the mountains and forests
and planted beneath the palace gates,
even if one banks it with rich black soil
and warms it with the spring sun,
it still cannot be saved from withering;
how could it have leisure to flourish and breed?
Trees are like kinsmen;
the soil is like the gentry and commoners.
If the establishment is not of long duration,
then subordinates will be light toward those above and superiors will be negligent.
If in peaceful times one still fears their desertion and rebellion,
what will be done in times of danger and urgency?
This is why sagely kings are secure but not idle,
so as to consider danger;
they survive and maintain equipment,
so as to fear destruction.
Thus when a sudden gale arrives,
they have no worry of being broken or uprooted;
when there is a change in the world,
they have no affliction of being overthrown or endangered.
For a gentleman is ashamed if his achievements are not established during his prime
and distressed if his name is not praised after his death;
thus it is said,
"Study as if you cannot catch up,
yet still fear losing it."
Therefore the ambitious men of old
mourned the passing of their years
and feared that their reputations would not be established.
They exerted their spirits and sharpened their conduct,
rising at dawn and sleeping at night,
without leisure to rest.
They managed it through months and years
and accumulated it through daily effort.
Like the diligence of Nìng Yuè
or the devotion of Dǒng Shēng,
they immersed themselves in the abyss of virtue and righteousness
and dwelled within the realm of the Way and the arts.
Even with the sagehood of Xībó
and the talent of Jīgōng,
they still had the labor of working until sunset and waiting for dawn;
thus they could greatly elevate the Zhōu Dào
and leave their names for a hundred million years.
How much more for ministers and commoners—
can they afford to stop?
Examining the men of achievement and fame throughout history,
all have traces of extraordinary accumulation:
toiling their spirits and suffering their bodies,
enduring hardships and thinking diligently,
not idling in their profession in peaceful times
and not changing their basic principles in times of poverty.
Thus Bǔ Shì established his ambition in farming and herding,
and Huáng Bà received the Way in prison;
they eventually had the blessing of honor and prominence
to achieve an immortal name.
Thus Shānfǔ was diligent day and night,
and Wú Hàn did not leave the public gates;
how could they have been wandering or idle?
People of the current generation
mostly do not dedicate themselves to the classics and arts,
but enjoy playing bóyì,
neglecting affairs and abandoning their professions,
forgetting sleep and food,
exhausting the day and using up the light,
and continuing with oil lamps and candles.
When they face the board in competition,
with victory or defeat undecided,
they concentrate their spirits and sharpen their will;
their spirits are dazed and their bodies weary.
Human affairs are neglected and not cultivated;
guests and travelers are missed and not received.
Even if there were a feast of the tàiláo
or the music of Sháo and Xià,
they would have no time to attend to them.
It even reaches the point where they gamble their clothes and possessions,
or move pieces and change their moves;
their sense of integrity and shame slackens,
and expressions of resentment and anger break out.
Yet what they aim for does not go beyond a single board,
and what they pursue is no more than the space of the square grid.
Defeating an enemy brings no reward of enfeoffment or title;
capturing territory brings no reality of gaining land.
The skill is not among the Six Arts;
its use is not for governing the state.
Those who establish themselves do not rely on its techniques;
those who are selected for office do not follow its path.
If seeking it in battle formations,
then they are not of the likes of Sūn and Wú;
if examining it in the Way and the arts,
then they are not of the school of Kǒngshì.
If taking deception and fraud as their business,
then it is not a matter of loyalty and trustworthiness;
if taking plunder and killing as their reputation,
then it is not the intention of a benevolent person.
It vainly hinders the day and wastes their profession,
ultimately providing no benefit.
How is this different from setting up wood to strike it
or placing stones to throw them!
Furthermore, when a gentleman is at home,
he toils himself to provide sustenance;
when he is at court,
he exhausts his life to offer loyalty.
When facing affairs, he still eats late;
how can he have leisure to indulge in bóyì?
Because of this,
the conduct of filial piety and fraternal love is established,
and a reputation for chastity and purity is made manifest.
Currently, the Dà Wú has received the Mandate,
and the world within the seas is not yet pacified.
The sagely court is diligent and tireless,
and the focus is on obtaining talent.
Men of brave strategy
receive the responsibilities of bears and tigers;
those of refined Confucian scholarship
occupy the offices of dragons and phoenixes.
A hundred kinds of conduct are all included,
and civil and military matters strive forward together.
They extensively select fine talents
and commend and choose the eminent and outstanding.
They establish subjects for examinations
and bestow rewards of gold and titles.
Truly it is a grand gathering of a thousand years,
a fine encounter of a hundred generations.
The men of this age
should exert themselves to think of the ultimate Way,
cherish their achievements and treasure their strength
to assist this enlightened era.
Let your names be written in the historical records
and your merits be in the Méngfǔ.
This is the supreme task of a gentleman
and the primary urgency of today.
A board made of a single piece of wood—
how can it compare to the enfeoffment of a state?
Three hundred withered game pieces—
how can they compare to leading ten thousand men?
Robes with dragon patterns
and the music of bells and stones
are enough to replace the game board and trade for bóyì.
Suppose the men of this age
shifted the effort used in bóyì and applied it to the Shī and Shū;
they would have the ambition of Yán and Mǐn.
If applied to wisdom and strategy,
they would have the grace of Liáng and Píng.
If applied to resources and goods,
they would have the wealth of Yīdùn.
If applied to archery and charioteering,
they would have the requirements of a general.
In this way,
achievements and fame would be established, and baseness and lowliness would be kept far away.
Some in the world say that immortality can be learned and attained
and that deathlessness can be reached through effort;
others say a long life of one hundred and twenty years
is the same now as in the past,
and anything beyond this
is nothing but delusions and falsehoods.
Both of these miss the true circumstances;
please let me try to discuss this roughly.
Now, although divine immortals are not seen by the eye,
yet they are recorded in the documents and books,
and transmitted in the histories of former times.
If one compares and discusses these accounts,
their existence is certain.
It seems they uniquely receive an extraordinary *qì*,
endowed with it from nature;
it is not something that can be achieved through cumulative learning.
As for conducting nourishment in accordance with principle
so as to exhaust one's natural lifespan—
attaining more than a thousand years at the highest,
and several hundred years at the lowest—
this is indeed possible.
Yet the people of the world are not refined in this,
and therefore no one can attain it.
Why do I say this?
Now, those who take medicine seeking to sweat
sometimes do not succeed;
yet once feelings of shame gather,
perspiration flows profusely.
If one has not eaten by the end of the morning,
one noisily thinks of food;
yet when Zéng Zǐ held grief in his heart,
he was not hungry for seven days.
If one sits up at midnight,
one is dazed and thinks of sleep;
yet when one harbors deep anxiety within,
one does not close one's eyes until dawn.
Vigorous brushing to tidy the hair
and pure ale to redden the face
barely achieve their effects;
yet the rage of a brave warrior
is a startlingly different sight,
as his hair stands erect and pushes against his cap.
Speaking from this,
the relationship of the spirit to the physical frame
is like a state having a ruler.
When the spirit is restless within,
the form perishes without,
just as when a ruler is muddled above,
the state is in chaos below.
Now, for one farming during the era of Tāng,
if there were even just the merit of a single irrigation,
although in the end it would succumb to being scorched and rotted,
the one that received that single irrigation would surely be the last to wither.
Thus, the benefit of a single irrigation
certainly cannot be dismissed as false.
Yet the world usually says that a single fit of anger is not enough to infringe upon one's nature,
and a single instance of grief is not enough to harm the body;
they treat it lightly and indulge in it.
This is like not recognizing the benefit of a single irrigation
yet expecting fine grain from parched sprouts.
Therefore, the gentleman knows that the form relies on the spirit to stand,
and the spirit requires the form to exist.
He realizes that the principle of living is easily lost,
and knows that a single error harms life.
Thus, he cultivates his nature to preserve his spirit,
and calms his mind to keep his body whole.
Love and hatred do not dwell in his emotions;
sorrow and joy do not linger in his thoughts.
He is placid and without affectation,
so his physical *qì* is harmonious and peaceful.
Furthermore, he practices breathing and "exhaling the old and inhaling the new,"
and consumes substances to nourish the body,
causing form and spirit to be intimate with each other,
so that the internal and external both benefit.
Now, regarding those who plant fields,
if one *mǔ* yields ten *hú*,
it is called a good field;
this is the common term used by the world.
They do not know that intensive plot-planting can yield more than a hundred *hú*.
The field and the seed are the same,
but as for the difference in planting and nourishing,
then the results achieved are poles apart.
To say that a merchant cannot have ten times the price
or a farmer cannot have the hope of a hundred *hú*
is to stick to the conventional and not change.
Furthermore, beans make one feel heavy,
elms make one sleepy,
*héhuān* removes anger,
and *xuāngǎo* makes one forget sorrow;
these are known by both the foolish and the wise.
Pungent aromatics harm the eyes,
and pork or fish are not nourishing;
these are recognized by the ordinary world.
Lice living on the head are black;
the musk deer is fragrant because it eats cypress;
necks living in rugged areas develop goiters;
teeth of those dwelling in Jìn are yellow.
Extending this reasoning,
all the *qì* of what is eaten
steams the nature and dyes the body;
none fails to correspond.
How could it only be that "steaming" makes one heavy but not light,
"harming" makes one dim but not bright,
"smoking" makes one yellow but not firm,
and "scenting" makes one fragrant but not prolong life?
Therefore, Shénnóng said,
"Superior medicine nourishes life;
middle medicine nourishes nature."
Truly, he knew the principles of nature and life,
and used support and nourishment to master them.
Yet the people of the world do not observe this;
they only see the five grains
and are addicted to sounds and colors.
Their eyes are deluded by dark and yellow colors;
their ears are occupied with licentious and clamorous sounds.
Rich flavors sear their internal organs;
thick ale boils their intestines and stomach.
Fragrant scents rot their bone marrow;
joy and anger confound their correct *qì*.
Worries and thoughts melt away their spirit;
grief and pleasure injure their peaceful purity.
Now, with such a tiny body,
those who attack it come from more than one path.
With a body so easily exhausted,
yet receiving enemies from without and within,
and the body not being made of wood or stone,
how could it last long?
For those who are extremely willful,
their eating and drinking are without moderation,
thereby producing a hundred diseases;
they pursue lust without tire,
thereby reaching exhaustion.
Calamities from wind and cold,
and injuries from a hundred toxins,
cause them to die prematurely in the midst of many hardships.
The world all knows to mock or lament this,
saying they were not good at maintaining life.
As for placing the body in a way that loses principle,
losing it in the minute details—
accumulated minutes become damage;
accumulated damage becomes decline.
From decline comes white hair;
from white hair comes old age;
from old age comes the end.
It happens as if without a clear beginning.
Those of mediocre intelligence or below
call this natural.
Even if they have a slight realization,
they all sigh and regret at the onset of what they encounter,
yet they do not know to be cautious of many dangers before they manifest.
This is like Huán Hóu harboring a fatal illness
yet being angry at Biǎn Què's foresight,
taking the day the pain was felt
as the beginning of the disease.
Harm forms in the minute but is treated in the obvious;
therefore, there are treatments without success.
Galloping within the realm of ordinary people,
therefore there is only the lifespan of the common lot.
Looking up to observe and down to examine,
it is so in every case.
They use the majority to prove themselves right
and the same to comfort themselves,
saying the principles of Heaven and Earth end here and no more.
