Even if they hear of the matters of nourishing life,
they judge based on what they see
and say it is not so.
Next are those who are suspicious;
although they slightly aspire to it,
they do not know the way.
Next
are those who force themselves to take medicine
for half a year or a year;
they are weary and see no proof,
their will becomes tired and declines,
and they give up halfway.
Some may add to it by the ditch and channel,
yet drain it by the Wěilǘ.
Those who wish to sit and expect clear rewards
might suppress their emotions and endure their desires,
cutting off and discarding glory and aspirations,
yet their cravings are always before their eyes and ears,
while what they hope for is decades away.
Again, they fear losing both,
harboring hesitation within;
the heart battles within,
while things tempt from without.
Immediate and future interests undermine each other;
those like this will fail again.
The ultimate things are subtle and profound;
they can be understood through reason
but are difficult to recognize with the eyes,
just like the Yùzhāng tree,
which grows for seven years before it can be perceived.
Now, with a restless and competitive heart,
one treads the path of seeking stillness;
the intentions are hasty while progress is slow,
the expectations are near while the response is far;
thus, none are able to reach the end.
The aimless do not seek because they see no immediate effect,
while seekers lose their pursuit through a lack of focus;
those who rely on one side fail for lack of comprehensiveness,
and those who chase techniques drown themselves in minor paths.
In all cases such as these,
not one in ten thousand of those who desire it can succeed.
Those who are good at nourishing life are not so.
They are pure, empty, still, and peaceful,
with few private interests and few desires.
Knowing that fame and position harm virtue,
they ignore them and do not strive for them;
it is not that they desire them and then forcibly restrain themselves.
Knowing that rich flavors harm one's nature,
they discard them and do not look back;
it is not that they are greedy and then suppress it.
External things do not exist to burden the heart;
the spiritual essence is uniquely manifest in its purity.
Vast and free from worry or calamity,
silent and free from thought or deliberation.
Furthermore, they guard it with oneness
and nourish it with harmony;
harmony and reason daily improve,
becoming one with the Dàshùn.
Then they are infused with Língzhī,
moistened by the Lǐquán,
dried in the Cháoyáng,
and soothed by the Wǔxián.
In non-action they are self-contented;
the body is subtle and the mind is profound.
Forgetting joy, their happiness is then sufficient;
leaving life behind, their person is then preserved.
Proceeding in this way,
one can perhaps compare longevity with Xiànmén
and rival the years of Wáng Qiáo;
why should it be that such things do not exist?
Order and disorder
are a matter of fortune;
success and failure
are a matter of fate;
nobility and baseness
are a matter of timing.
Therefore, when fortune is about to flourish,
a sagely and enlightened ruler must be born.
A sagely and enlightened ruler
must have loyal and worthy ministers.
The way they meet each other
is a natural joining without seeking;
the way they become close
is a natural intimacy without mediation.
When one sings, the other must harmonize;
when one plans, the other must follow.
Virtue and the Way are profoundly identical,
fitting together like the two halves of a tally.
Gains and losses cannot make them doubt their resolve;
slander and fabrication cannot sever their bond.
Only then can success be achieved.
How they are able to be so,
can it be merely human effort?
That which grants it is Tiān;
that which informs it is the divine;
that which completes it is fortune.
When the Huánghé runs clear, a sage is born;
when the Lǐshè cries out, a sage emerges;
when a group of dragons appears, a sage is employed.
Thus Yī Yǐn
was an escort-servant of the Yǒushēn clan,
yet became Āhéng to the Shāng.
Tàigōng
was a lowly old man on the banks of the Wèi,
yet became Shàngfù to the Zhōu.
Bǎilǐ Xī was in Yú and Yú perished;
he was in Qín and Qín became the hegemon.
It was not that he was untalented in Yú but talented in Qín.
Zhāng Liáng received the tally of Huángshí
and recited the teachings of the Sānlüè;
traveling among the various heroes,
his words were,
like throwing water at a stone,
with no one receiving them.
When he encountered Hànzǔ,
his words were,
like throwing a stone into water,
with no one resisting them.
It was not that Zhāng Liáng spoke clumsily to Chén and Xiàng
but spoke skillfully to Pèigōng.
Thus, Zhāng Liáng's words were the same,
yet one does not know why they joined or separated.
The reason for joining or separating
is the Way of the divine.
Thus those four worthies
have their names recorded in the Lùtú
and their deeds correspond to Tiān and man;
how can they be measured by ordinary worthiness or foolishness?
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When purity and clarity reside in the person,
the spirit and will are like the divine.
When desires are about to arrive,
there must be a prior opening.
Tiān sends down timely rain,
and mountains and rivers produce clouds."
The Shījīng says:
"The Yuè sent down spirits,
which gave birth to Fǔ and Shēn;
Shēn and Fǔ
were the pillars of Zhōu."
This refers to fate and fortune.
It is not only for rising lords;
those who fall into disorder and perish are also like this.
Yōu Wáng's infatuation with Bǎonǚ
was an omen that began in the court of Xià.
Cáo Bóyáng's acquisition of Gōngsūn Qiáng
was signaled at the Shègōng.
Shūsūn Bào's intimacy with Shùniú
led to disaster at Gēngzōng.
Good and bad luck, success and failure,
each arrives according to its predetermined number.
They all join naturally without seeking
and become close naturally without mediation.
In the past,
the Sages received the mandate from the Hé and Luò, which said:
Those who receive the mandate through civil culture
will decline after seven times nine;
those who rise through military power
will be conspired against after six times eight.
When Chéng Wáng settled the tripods at Jiá Rǔ,
he divined thirty generations
and seven hundred years;
this was what Heaven ordained.
Thus, from the time between Yōu and Lì,
the Way of Zhōu was greatly ruined;
after the two hegemons,
ritual and music gradually declined.
The corruption of superficial culture
began under Líng and Jǐng;
the falsehood of sophistry and deception
was completed during the time of the Qī Guó.
The ultimate extreme of cruelty
accumulated in the doomed Qín;
the value of refined culture
was discarded by Hàn Zǔ.
Although Zhòngní was a supreme Sage
and Yán and Rǎn were great worthies,
bowing and yielding within the bounds of rules
and speaking forthrightly along the Zhū and Sì,
they could not stop its source.
Mèng Kē and Sūn Qīng
embodied the two virtues and aspired to sagehood,
following the correct Way with ease,
yet they could not sustain its end;
the world eventually reached a state of drowning from which it could not be rescued.
Now, with the talent of Zhòngní,
yet his capacity was not utilized in Lǔ and Wèi;
with the eloquence of Zhòngní,
yet his words were not put into practice by Dìng and Āi;
with the humility of Zhòngní,
yet he was envied by Zǐxī;
with the benevolence of Zhòngní,
yet he incurred the enmity of Huán Tuí;
with the wisdom of Zhòngní,
yet he was frustrated and distressed in Chén and Cài;
with the conduct of Zhòngní,
yet he invited slander from Shúsūn.
His Way was sufficient to save the world,
yet he could not find honor among men;
his words were sufficient to serve as a guide for ten thousand generations,
yet they were not trusted in his own time;
his conduct was sufficient to resonate with the divine spirits,
yet he could not order the customs of the people.
He accepted invitations from seventy states,
yet not once did he meet his true lord;
he hurried through the lands of the barbarians and the Huáxià,
suffering humiliation at the gates of dukes and ministers—
such was his lack of opportunity.
When it came to his grandson Zǐsī,
he aspired to sagehood and possessed its substance but had not reached the ultimate,
yet he secluded himself and cultivated high standards,
and his influence moved the rulers of men.
In his travels among the feudal lords,
none failed to hitch their four-horse carriages to visit his gate;
even among those who visited his gate, there were some who were not received as guests.
His disciple Zǐxià
was one who had ascended to the hall but not yet entered the inner chamber.
When he retired in old age to his home,
Wèi Wén Hóu took him as a teacher,
and the people of Xīhé solemnly turned to his virtue,
comparing him to the Master and not daring to find fault with his words.
Therefore it is said:
Order and chaos
are a matter of destiny;
failure and success
are a matter of fate;
nobility and meanness
are a matter of the times.
Yet the gentlemen of later ages
obsess over a single ruler
and sigh over a single morning.
Qū Yuán drowned himself in the Xiāng because of this,
and Jiǎ Yì was filled with indignation because of this—
is this not an error?
Thus, that which makes a Sage a Sage
lies perhaps in finding joy in Heaven and knowing his fate.
Therefore, when he encounters adversity, he feels no resentment;
when he dwells in it, he feels no doubt.
His person may be suppressed,
but his Way cannot be bent;
his position may be cast aside,
but his name cannot be taken away.
It is like water:
when allowed to flow, it becomes a river;
when blocked, it becomes an abyss.
Rising into the clouds, it bestows rain;
sinking into the earth, it moistens the soil.
Pure in substance to wash things clean,
it is not muddied by filth;
receiving filth to benefit things,
its purity is not harmed.
Thus, the Sage treats failure and success as one.
That loyalty and uprightness should clash with a ruler,
and independence of character should be at odds with common customs,
is the natural course of principles and circumstances.
Therefore, when a tree stands out in the forest,
the wind will surely break it;
when a mound juts out from the bank,
the current will surely lash against it;
when one's conduct is superior to others,
the multitude will surely criticize it.
The warnings of the past are not far off;
overturned carriages follow one after another.
However, men of purpose and benevolence
still tread this path without regret
and hold to their principles without losing them—
why is this?
It is to fulfill their aspirations and establish their names.
Seeking to fulfill their aspirations,
they brave wind and waves on a dangerous road;
seeking to establish their names,
they endure slander and criticism in their time.
The way they handle this
is surely calculated.
Zǐxià said:
"Life and death are fated;
wealth and honor rest with Heaven."
Thus, when the Way is about to prevail
and fate is about to bring honor,
then Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng rise in Shāng and Zhōu,
and Bǎilǐ and Zǐfáng are employed in Qín and Hàn—
it is obtained without seeking
and met with without striving.
When the Way is about to be discarded
and fate is about to bring lowliness,
is it only that the gentleman is ashamed of it and will not act?
It is also that he knows that even if he acts, he will not succeed.
As for those who seek to please the world and curry favor,
people who are sycophants and flatterers,
looking up and down at the faces of the noble and honorable,
meandering between power and profit,
their minds have no sense of right or wrong;
they offer praise like a flowing stream;
their words have no affirmation or denial;
they respond like an echo.
They take spying and observing as their spirit
and taking sides as their flexibility.
Where power gathers,
they follow it like people flocking to a market;
where power departs,
they abandon it like a discarded garment.
Their words say:
"Which is more intimate, one's name or one's person?
Which is better, gain or loss?
Which is more precious, glory or disgrace?"
Therefore, they make their clothing neat,
show off their carriages and followers,
covet goods and bribes,
and indulge in music and sex,
looking pleased with themselves, thinking they have succeeded.
They see Lóngpáng and Bǐ Gān lose their lives,
but do not consider Fēilián and Èlái whose clans were exterminated.
They know of Wǔ Zǐxū's Zhǔlòu sword in Wú,
but do not take warning from Fèi Wújì's execution in Chǔ.
They mock Jí Àn for growing white-haired in the office of Zhǔjué,
but are not deterred by the disaster of Zhāng Tāng's ox-cart.
They laugh at Xiāo Wàngzhī's stumbling and falling in the past,
but do not fear Shí Xiǎn's hanging later on.
Therefore, in the calculations of those who have attained realization,
each thing has its own limit.
It is said: As for the reason why ordinary people scramble after wealth and honor,
what is it for?
If establishing virtue must require high rank,
then the fact that Yōu and Lì were Sons of Heaven
would not be as good as Zhòng Ní being a minor official.
If it must require power,
then the fact that Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Xián were the Three Ducal Ministers
would not be as good as Yáng Xióng and Dǒng Zhòngshū whose gates were silent.
If it must require wealth,
then the thousand teams of four horses of Qí Jǐng would not be as good as
Yán Huí and Yuán Xiàn who lived in simplicity.
Is it for substance?
Then one who holds a ladle to drink from a river
takes no more than a bellyful;
one who leaves their house to seek the sprinkling rain
gets no more than their body wet;
beyond this and further on,
they cannot receive more.
Is it for fame?
Then good and evil are written in the historical records,
and slander or praise flows for a thousand years;
rewards and punishments hang upon the Way of Heaven,
and fortune or misfortune is illuminated by the ghosts and gods;
this is indeed something to be feared.
Is it to entertain the ears and eyes,
or to delight the heart and mind?
For example, if one orders a carriage to travel through the markets of the Wǔ Dū,
then all the goods of the world are displayed there.
If one hitches up their skirts to wade through the hills of Wèn Yáng,
then the crops of the world are as thick as clouds.
If one binds their hair and guards the granaries of Ào Yǔ and Hǎi Líng,
then the accumulations like mountains and hills are before them.
If one gathers their robes and climbs atop Zhōng Shān or Lán Tián,
then the treasures of night-glowing gems and Yúfán jade are visible.
If it be like this,
the things belonging to the world are many,
but those for oneself are very few;
one does not cherish their own person,
but is stingy with their spirit.
The wind startles and the dust rises;
they scatter without ceasing.
The six illnesses wait before them,
and the five punishments follow behind.
Profit and harm arise to their left,
and assault or seizure comes from their right;
yet do they think themselves to see the closeness or distance between the person and the name,
or distinguish the guest and host of honor and disgrace?
The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life;
the great treasure of the Sage is called position;
that by which one guards position is called Rén;
that by which one rectifies people is called Yì.
Therefore, the kings of old
used one person to govern the world,
and did not use the world to serve one person.
The officials of old
used their office to carry out their sense of duty,
and did not use profit to secure their office.
The gentlemen of old
were ashamed to obtain a position and be unable to govern it,
but were not ashamed to be able to govern and not obtain one.
Tracing back to the nature of Heaven and man,
examining the distinction between the heterodox and the upright,
weighing the gates of calamity and fortune,
and finalizing the calculation of honor and disgrace—
it is manifest.
Therefore, the gentleman rejects the former and takes the latter.
If one’s emergence or retirement does not violate the times,
if one’s silence or speech does not lose the right person,
if when the heavens move and the stars revolve the Celestial Pole still dwells in its place,
and when the armillary rotates and the wheels turn
the axle-beam still maintains the center;
being both enlightened and wise
to preserve one’s person,
handing down plans for their grandsons
to shelter their children—
in the past, my late friend
once devoted himself to this.
Formerly, the House of Hàn lost its grip on governance,
and treacherous ministers usurped authority.
The foundations of calamity were in the Jīng Jì,
and the poison spread throughout the universe.
The imperial bonds were loosened and disordered,
and the royal house became lowly.
Thereupon the various heroes were startled like hornets,
and righteous soldiers gathered from all sides.
Emperor Wǔ Liè of Wú, with a generous heart from the lower states,
rose like lightning from Jīng Nán.
His tactical plans were numerous,
and his loyalty and bravery were unmatched in his age.
His majestic power shook like that of Yí Yì;
in the clash of arms, the ugly captives surrendered their heads.
Thus he swept clean the ancestral shrines
and performed the sacrifices to the imperial ancestors.
At that time, generals rising like clouds held sway over provinces,
and armies rising like storms straddled districts;
roaring packs were driven like the wind,
and multitudes like bears and leopards gathered like mist.
Although the soldiers gathered for a righteous cause,
and the alliance worked with united strength,
yet they all harbored treacherous hearts,
relying on their troops and taking advantage of the chaos.
Some armies lacked discipline and law,
losing their prestige and emboldening the enemy.
But for loyal regulations and martial integrity,
there was none so prominent as his.
After Wǔ Liè passed away,
Huán Wáng of Cháng Shā, an extraordinary talent of his age,
showed his brilliance in his youth.
He recruited the remaining elders
and with them continued the enterprise.
His divine troops drove eastward,
using the few to attack the many.
There were no generals of fortified cities that he did not attack,
and no captives in the clash of blades that he did not defeat.
He punished the rebellious and soothed the submissive,
and thus Jiāng Wài was settled.
He refined the laws and trained the soldiers,
and his majesty and virtue were grandly displayed.
He treated famous worthies with the rites of a guest,
and Zhāng Zhāo was the most eminent among them;
he associated with the heroic and the talented,
and Zhōu Yú was the most outstanding among them.
Those two gentlemen
were both magnanimous, quick-witted, and full of extraordinary ideas,
refined, perceptive, and wise.
Therefore, those of the same way attached themselves by category,
and those of equal temperament gathered by spirit,
and so Jiāng Dōng had many scholars.
He intended to march north against the various Zhūhuá
and eliminate those who violated the principles.
He would return the imperial carriage to the broad path
and restore the imperial seat to the Purple Hall.
He would hold the Son of Heaven to command the lords,
and clear the path of Heaven to return to the old ways.
The war chariots were already stationed
and the various villains looked askance in fear,
but the great enterprise was not yet completed
when he perished in his middle years.
This devolved upon our Great Emperor.
He followed the extraordinary tracks of the previous path
and his sagacious heart relied on the excellent plans.
In governing, he consulted historical precedents;
in spreading laws, he examined the bequeathed customs.
To this he added steadfastness
and applied frugality.
He sought out the talented and eminent,
was fond of planning and good at deciding.
Bundles of silk were sent to the hermitages,
and banners of appointment crossed in the streets and alleys.
Thus the heroes sought the sound and arrived like echoes;
men of purpose looked toward the light and galloped like shadows.
Extraordinary people converged like spokes at a hub,
and fierce warriors were like a forest.
Thereupon Zhāng Zhāo became the Grand Tutor;
the likes of Zhōu Yú, Lù Gōng, Lǔ Sù, and Lǚ Méng
entered to become the heart and mind
and went out to act as the legs and arms.
Those like Gān Níng, Líng Tǒng, Chéng Pǔ, Hè Qí, Zhū Huán, and Zhū Rán exerted their majesty;
those of the group of Hán Dāng, Pān Zhāng, Huáng Gài, Jiǎng Qīn, and Zhōu Tài displayed their strength.
In refinement and elegance, there were Zhūgě Jǐn, Zhāng Chéng, and Bù Zhì,
who brought glory to the state with their reputations.
In administration, there were Gù Yōng, Pān Jùn, Lǚ Fàn, and Lǚ Dài,
who fulfilled their duties with their capacity and responsibility.
In extraordinary greatness, there were Yú Fān, Lù Jì, Zhāng Wēn, and Zhāng Dūn,
who promoted correctness through their criticisms and discussions.
In serving as envoys, there were Zhào Zī and Shěn Héng,
who extended the state’s reputation with their quick-wittedness.
In the arts and calculations, there were Wú Fàn and Zhào Dá,
who aligned virtue with omens of fortune.
Dǒng Xí and Chén Wǔ
sacrificed their lives to protect their lord;
Luò Tǒng and Liú Jī
offered strong remonstrances to mend faults.
Plans left no cleverness behind;
actions did not miss the mark.
Therefore, they finally occupied the mountains and rivers,
straddling and controlling Jīng and Wú,
and vied for power with the world.
The Wèi clan once relied on the prestige of victorious battles,
leading an army of a million,
floating boats from Dèngsài,
and bringing down the multitudes of Hànyīn.
With tens of thousands of feathered oars,
they leaped like dragons with the current,
and with thousands of elite cavalry units,
they stepped like tigers across the plains and marshes.
Strategists filled the chambers,
and military generals were joined in alignment.
With a sigh, they possessed the ambition to swallow the banks of the river
and the spirit to unify the universe.
But Zhōu Yú led our partial army
and repelled them at Chìbì.
Their banners were lost and their tracks thrown into disorder;
they barely managed to escape
and withdrew their traces to flee far away.
The King of Hàn also relied on the imperial title,
leading the people of Bā and Hàn.
Taking advantage of danger and galloping through changes,
he set up fortifications across a thousand lǐ.
His ambition was to avenge the defeat of Guān Yǔ,
and his plan was to reclaim the lands west of the Xiāng River.
But Lord Lù also thwarted him at Xīlíng;
his army was overturned and suffered a crushing defeat.
Only after being cornered did he escape,
and he met his end at Yǒng'ān.
Following this were the invaders at Rúxū,
where their sharp edge was broken at Línchuān;
and in the battle of Pénglóng,
not a single wheel returned.
Because of this, the generals of the two states
lost their spirit and had their blades blunted;
their power was diminished and their wealth exhausted.
Meanwhile, Wú sat smiling, taking advantage of their failures.
Thus, the people of Wèi requested friendly relations,
and the Hàn clan begged for an alliance.
Consequently, Wú ascended to the imperial title,
standing firm like one leg of a tripod.
To the west, they slaughtered in the suburbs of Yōng and Yì;
to the north, they split the banks of the Huái and Hàn;
to the east, they embraced the lands of the Bǎiyuè;
and to the south, they encompassed the regions of the various Mán.
Thereupon, they discussed the rites of the eight generations
and sought out the music of the three kings.
They announced the sacrifices to the Supreme Deity
and bowed to the various lords.
Brave ministers and resolute soldiers
guarded along the river;
long spears and powerful halberds
were brandished upon seeing the storm.
All the officials offered their full counsel above,
and the four classes of people developed their industries below.
Civilization harmonized with distant tribes,
and cultural influence spread to remote borders.
Then, even a single envoy
could pacify and inspect foreign domains.
Great elephants and swift steeds
were tamed in the outer stables;
bright pearls and rare treasures
shone in the inner treasury.
Precious gems arrived in succession,
and rare curiosities came as if responding to a call.
Light carriages galloped through the southern wilderness,
and war chariots rested in the northern plains.
The common people were spared the calamity of war,
and warhorses had no worry of morning harnesses.
Thus, the imperial enterprise was solidified.
After Dàhuáng passed away,
a young lord presided over the court.
Wickedness and treachery ran rampant,
but Jǐnghuáng suddenly arose.
He reverently cultivated the ancestral laws,
and his administration had no major flaws;
he was an excellent ruler who maintained the established order.
Descending to the beginning of the reign of Guīmìng,
the codes and laws had not yet perished,
and the elder statesmen still remained.
Grand Marshal Lord Lù brightened the court with civil and military virtues;
Chancellor of the Left Lù Kǎi offered full counsel with blunt honesty.
Shī Jì and Fàn Shèn were prominent for their prestige and gravity;
Dīng Fèng and Lí Fěi were known for their military prowess.
People like Mèng Zōng and Dīng Gù served as high ministers;
the likes of Lóu Xuán and Hè Shào managed the secretariats.
Although the head was ailing,
the limbs still remained.
Reaching the final years,
the various lords had already passed away;
only then did the common people have the intent to crumble,
and the imperial house had the rift of collapse.
The mandate of heaven diminished according to change,
and the King's army set out, following the turn of fate.
Soldiers scattered in the formations,
and the people fled within the towns.
Cities and moats had no more strength than a fence;
mountains and rivers lacked the strategic advantage of trenches and mounds.
There was no need for Gōng Shū’s cloud-ladder engines,
nor the harm of Zhì Bó’s flooding waters,
nor the siege where the Viscount of Chǔ built houses,
nor the fall of the Yàn people west of the Jì River.
Before the army had spent twelve days,
the state was leveled.
Although loyal ministers felt solitary indignation
and heroic men died for their integrity,
how could it be saved?
Now, the generals of Cáo and Liú
were not chosen in a single generation;
the recent armies
were no more numerous than those of former days.
The methods of warfare and defense
were consistent with previous precedents;
the advantages of rugged terrain
had not suddenly changed.
Yet success and failure traded principles,
and past and present followed divergent paths—
why was this?
The transformations of that time and this were different,
and the talents entrusted with office were of a different caliber.
Formerly, when the three regions were kings:
the people of Wèi occupied Zhōngxià,
the Hàn clan held Mín and Yì,
and Wú controlled Jīng and Yáng while also covering Jiāo and Guǎng.
Although the Cáo clan’s achievements benefited the various Huá,
their tyranny was also deep,
and their people were resentful.
Lord Liú relied on natural barriers to mask his cleverness;
his achievements were already thin,
and his customs were crude.
As for Wú,
Huánwáng founded it with military prowess,
and Tàizǔ completed it with virtue.
Discerning, wise, and far-reaching,
his admirable bearing was grand and profound.
He sought the worthy as if he could not reach them,
and pitied the people as if they were infants.
In receiving scholars, he exhausted the appearance of magnificent virtue;
in befriending the benevolent, he gave all the love of his sincere heart.
He plucked Lǚ Méng from the military ranks,
and recognized Pān Jùn among the captives.
He extended sincerity to trust the scholars,
without worrying that people might deceive him;
he measured ability to bestow office,
without fearing that their power might press upon him.
He held the whip and bowed
to add weight to Lord Lù’s prestige;
he completely entrusted the military guards
to assist the army of Zhōu Yú.
He lived in a humble palace and ate meager food
to enrich the rewards of meritorious ministers;
he opened his heart and humbled himself
to accept the calculations of strategists.
Thus Lǔ Sù entrusted himself upon a single meeting,
and Shì Xiè braved dangers to dedicate his life.
He exalted the virtue of Lord Zhāng,
and reduced the pleasures of excursions and hunting;
he valued the words of Zhūgě,
and cut off the joys of passions and desires.
Moved by the admonitions of Lord Lù,
he removed the complexities of the penal laws;
marveling at the proposals of Liú Jī,
he made the Oath of the Three Cups.
Holding his breath and walking cautiously,
he attended to Zǐmíng’s illness;
sharing delicacies and reducing his own sweets,
he raised the orphans of Líng Tǒng.
Ascending the altar with impassioned spirit,
he attributed the merit to Lǔ Zǐ;
shredding and throwing away malicious words,
he trusted the integrity of Zǐyú.
Therefore, loyal ministers vied to exhaust their strategies,
and men of purpose all were able to exert their strength.
With grand scales and far-reaching plans,
he was certainly not satisfied with merely small matters.
Thus, the hundred officials were united in purpose,
and the various affairs left no room for leisure.
Initially, when the capital was established at Jiànyè,
the various ministers requested that the ritual ranks and honors be fully prepared.
The Emperor declined and did not permit it,
saying:
"What would the world say of me?"
His palace buildings, carriages, and clothing were all quite modest.
When it reached the middle period,
the distinction between Heaven and man had been established,
and the deficiencies in the various regulations were roughly repaired.
Although the rich transformation and beautiful laws
were not yet equal to those of the previous eras,
nevertheless, the instruments for managing the state and governing the country
were sufficient for conducting government.
The territory spanned nearly ten thousand lǐ,
with armored soldiers numbering nearly a million.
Its fields were fertile,
its troops were well-trained,
its weapons were sharp,
and its wealth was abundant.
To the east, it leaned against the vast sea;
to the west, it was obstructed by treacherous passes.
The Cháng Jiāng controlled its domain,
and steep mountains girdled its borders.
Regarding the advantages of a state,
there has never been one greater or more magnificent than this.
If even a ruler of average talent had maintained it with the Way,
and if good men had managed it with proper methods,
following the inherited classics with sincerity,
being diligent toward the people and cautious in administration,
following established strategies,
and guarding the natural hazards,
then they could have lasted for many generations and long years
without the calamity of peril or downfall.
Someone might say:
Wú and Shǔ were states related like lips and teeth;
if Shǔ were destroyed, then Wú would perish.
In principle, this is true.
However, Shǔ
was merely a peripheral buffer and an allied state;
it was not the source of survival or destruction for the people of Wú.
Why is this?
Where their borders met,
there were heavy mountains and accumulated hazards.
On land, there were no paths for long-axled carriages;
on the rivers, the passes were narrow and the currents swift,
with the hardships of alarming waves.
Even with a sharp army of a million,
those who could set out together would not exceed a thousand men;
though ships might stretch for a thousand lǐ,
the vanguard would not exceed a hundred vessels.
Therefore, regarding the campaign of the Liú clan,
Duke Lù compared it to a long snake;
such was the natural momentum.
Formerly, when Shǔ first fell,
the court ministers had different plans.
Some wanted to pile up stones to make the river more treacherous;
some wanted to use mechanical devices to resist changes.
The Emperor gathered the various opinions and consulted the Grand Marshal, Duke Lù.
The Duke believed that the four great rivers are how Heaven and Earth regulate and spread their Qi,
and certainly there is no principle for obstructing them.
As for mechanical devices, they are things shared by both us and the enemy.
"If they were to abandon their superior skills to meet what we are constrained by,
and come to Jīng and Yáng to compete in the use of boats and oars,
that would be Heaven assisting us.
We should simply guard Xiákǒu cautiously
to wait and capture them."
When it came to the rebellion of Bù Chǎn,
who relied on Bǎochéng to invite strong invaders,
and offered heavy wealth and silk to entice the various barbarians.
At that time, the multitudes of the Great State
soared like clouds and struck like lightning,
hanging their banners along the riverbanks,
building ramparts along the shores,
and controlling the strategic points
to stop the Wú people from going west.
Meanwhile, the Bā and Hàn naval forces followed the river downstream to the east.
Duke Lù, with a partial force of thirty thousand,
occupied Dōngkēng in the north,
with deep moats and high ramparts,
resting the troops and nurturing their prestige.
The rebellious captives waited to be executed like trapped animals,
not daring to look north toward a way out.
The strong invaders suffered a crushing defeat and fled by night,
losing more than half their army.
He separately ordered five thousand elite troops
to the west to resist the naval forces.
Victory was achieved in both east and west,
and captives were presented by the tens of thousands.
Truly,
the plans of a worthy man—
how could they deceive us?
From then on, beacon fires rarely signaled alarm,
and the borders had few worries.
But when Duke Lù passed away, hidden schemes began to sprout;
Wú's flaws grew deep, and the Six Armies were terrified.
In the campaign of the Tàikāng era,
the enemy's numbers were not greater than the former armies;
in the rebellion of Guǎngzhōu,
the disaster was more severe than previous difficulties.
Yet the state was overturned,
and the ancestral temples became ruins.
Alas!
When such men are gone,
the state is exhausted and ruined—
is it not so?
The *Yì* says:
"The revolutions of Tāng and Wǔ
were in accord with Heaven."
The *Xuán* says:
"If disorder does not reach its extreme, then order will not take shape."
This speaks of how emperors and kings follow the timing of Heaven.
The ancients had a saying:
"Heavenly timing is not as important as geographical advantage."
The *Yì* says:
"Kings and lords set up hazards
to defend their states."
This speaks of a state's reliance on terrain.
It also says:
"Geographical advantage is not as important as human harmony,"
and "Security lies in virtue, not in hazards."
This speaks of how guarding hazards depends on people.
The rise of Wú
was based on these three factors;
it is what Sūn Qīng called the joining of the three.
When it came to its downfall,
it relied on hazards alone;
this is what Sūn Qīng called the abandonment of the three.
It was not that the people of the four provinces were not numerous,
nor that the lands south of the Great River lacked talented men,
nor that the hazards of mountains and rivers were difficult to defend,
nor that sharp and efficient weapons were difficult to use,
nor that the strategies of former administrations were difficult to follow.
That success did not rise and disaster instead struck—
why was that?
It was because those who used them failed.
Therefore, the former kings understood the long-term regulations for governing a state
and examined the ultimate numbers of survival and ruin.
They humbled themselves to settle the common people,
and were generous with favors to achieve human harmony.
They were broad-minded and modest to invite the plans of the talented,
and were compassionate and harmonious to secure the love of the soldiers and citizens.
Therefore, in times of peace,
the common people shared in their celebration;
and when danger came,
the masses shared in their suffering.
When peace is shared in celebration with the people,
then danger cannot be brought upon them;
when danger is shared in suffering with those below,
then difficulties are not enough to worry about.
Being thus,
they could protect their altars of soil and grain
and solidify their lands and domains.
There would be no sorrow of the "Flowering Wheat" as felt for Yīn,
nor the feeling of the "Drooping Millet" as felt for Zhōu.
Governing the state and managing the countryside
are what the former kings were cautious about;
creating institutions and handing down foundations,
they thought to exalt later generations.
However, the strategic plans were not the same,
and the methods for long-lasting rule varied.
The system of the five ranks
began with Huáng and Táng.
The governance of commanderies and counties
originated with Qín and Hàn.
Gain and loss, success and failure,
are all fully recorded in the Canons and Counsels.
Therefore, their details
can be obtained and discussed.
The former kings knew that the imperial enterprise was of the utmost weight,
and the world was of the utmost vastness.
Vastness cannot be controlled by a partial few,
and weight cannot be borne by one alone;
bearing weight necessitates borrowing strength,
and controlling vastness ultimately depends on employing others.
Therefore, they established offices and divided responsibilities,
as a means to lighten their burden;
they simultaneously established the Wǔzhǎng,
as a means to broaden their system.
Thereupon, they established the canons of boundaries
and regulated the propriety of close and distant relations,
causing the myriad states to uphold one another
to achieve a rock-solid firmness,
and the relatives and commoners to live together
so as to stabilize the enterprise of the Wéichéng.
Furthermore, they saw the long-term governance for pacifying the world
and understood the grand method of human sentiment;
they knew that providing for others is not as good as strengthening oneself,
and benefiting things is not as good as planning for one's own person;
that securing the one above lies in pleasing those below,
and acting for oneself lies in benefiting others.
Thus the *Yì* says:
"Using joy to employ the people,
the people forget their labor."
Sūn Qīng said:
"Benefiting them without prior benefit
is not as good as the benefit of benefiting them after having first provided benefit."
Therefore, by dividing the world to share great joy,
the ruler is then able to share sorrow with them;
by treating the world to abundant profit,
he is then able to share harm with them.
When profit is broad, then grace is deep;
when joy is far-reaching, then concern is profound.
Thus the feudal lords enjoyed the fruits of their land,
and the myriad states received the blessing of hereditary succession.
In this way,
the rulers facing south
each attended to their own governance;
the people of the Jiǔfú
knew they had permanent masters.
The superior's paternal love arose from this,
and the inferior's trust was formed through this.
In times of order, it sufficed to enrich customs;
when the Way decayed, it sufficed to resist violence.
Thus a strong and resolute state
could not monopolize the power of an era;
heroic and talented men
had nowhere to lodge their ambitions of hegemony.
Then the security of the state relied on the myriad nations' desire for order,
and the honor of the lord relied on the various lords planning for their own persons.
It is like many eyes looking in all directions;
thus the heavenly net naturally expands.
The four limbs take on hardships,
and the heart and spine obtain peace.
This is why the Sāndài followed the straight path
and the Sìwáng bequeathed their legacy.
Prosperity and decline, rise and fall,
are inherent in the logic of things;
the abandonment or revival of teachings
depends on the person.
Even good laws are bound to become thin over time,
and the bright Way sometimes becomes dark.
Thus the system of hereditary succession
was marred by the strong and aggressive;
the canons of generosity to those below
leaked through the fractures of later ages.
The rift of encroachment and weakness
began in the Sān Jì;
the disaster of gradual decline
ended with the Qīxióng.
Formerly, Chéng Tāng personally looked into the mirror of the Xià ruler,
and Gōng Dàn personally examined the warning of the Shāng people;
refinement and substance aided each other,
and additions and subtractions had their reasons.
Thus the rites of the Wǔděng
were not changed by the times;
in the system of boundaries,
there was even enhancement.
Could they have been playing with the disaster of the two kings
while being ignorant of the calculations of statecraft?
They certainly knew that a hundred generations cannot be governed from afar,
and even a good system cannot be without flaws;
but the humiliation of encroachment and weakness
is better than the total destruction of ancestral sacrifices,
and the hardship of crumbling earth
is more painful than gradual decline.
Therefore, at the start, they weighed the many blessings;
considering the end, they chose the lesser of evils.
This is not to say that marquises and counts have no signs of potential chaos,
nor that commanderies and counties are not tools for achieving order.
Thus, the state's worries relied on them not abdicating their positions,
and the weak lord relied on their support.
When inheriting weakness and accumulated flaws,
the royal house became lowly;
yet they still preserved their titles and ranks,
and their blessings descended to their successors.
The imperial line was obscure but not interrupted,
and the sacred vessels were in difficulty but necessarily preserved;
was this not caused by the arrangement of power?
Descending to the fallen Qín,
they abandoned the Way and relied on techniques;
punishing the errors of Zhōu,
they were conceited in their own gains.
The destruction began with what it protected;
in regulating the state, they were ignorant in weakening those below.
The state's joy was enjoyed alone,
and no one shared the lord's worries or harms.
Although the rapid fall and rush to chaos
did not follow just one path,
the crack of the collapse
truly resulted from being isolated.
This was because they brooded over the small grudges of the Wǔděng
but forgot the great virtue of the myriad nations;
they knew the gradual decline was a concern,
but were ignorant that the crumbling earth was painful.
The lack of competitiveness of Zhōu
had its origins;
for more than ten generations,
the state lacked an able ruler.
Yet with a single word of "serving the king,"
the feudal lords would surely respond;
whereas once Qín displayed its pride and arrogance,
the distant states were the first to rebel.
Thus, the strong Jìn withdrew its request for the underground passage,
and the violent Chǔ halted its ambition of viewing the cauldrons.
How could Liú and Xiàng have peeked into the pass,
or Shèng and Guǎng dared to cry out in the marshes?
Supposing the Qín people had followed the Zhōu system,
even if they were without the Way,
they would have had others to share the flaws;
how could the disaster of total destruction
have occurred in those former days!
Hàn corrected the Qín's distortions
and greatly established marquises and kings.
Their territories exceeded limits
and did not follow old canons.
Thus Jiǎ Shēng worried about their danger,
and Cháo Cuò was pained by their chaos.
Therefore, the feudal lords relied on the wealth of their states
and the strength of their people;
those with sufficient power rebelled quickly,
while those with narrow lands rebelled late.
Six ministers violated the weak net;
seven sons escaped through the gaps.
The Huángzǔ was leveled by a branded convict,
and the Xījīng was troubled by the "Eastern Emperor."
This was the disaster of over-correction,
not the burden of establishing marquises.
Yet during the crisis of the Lǚ clan,
the court officials looked outward to the princes;
when Sòng Chāng devised a plan for Hàn,
he surely spoke of the feudal lords.
Reaching the middle period,
fearing their loss of restraint,
they carved away the imperial sons;
having titles without reality,
the world was empty,
and they again followed the track of the fallen Qín.
Thus the Wǔhóu exercised their might,
not fearing the myriad nations;
Xīndū usurped Hàn
as easily as picking up something dropped.
Guāngwǔ restored the dynasty
and continued the imperial line,
yet he still followed the ruts of the overturned cart
and nurtured the long-standing ailment of a ruined house.
In only a few generations,
treacherous rebels abounded.
When finally there were powerful ministers monopolizing the court,
then the world fell like grass before the wind;
when a single man acted willfully,
then the city walls leveled themselves.
Was this not dangerous!
In the decline of Zhōu,
troubles arose in the royal house;
seven ministers ignored orders,
and three sons contested the position.
The succeeding kings abandoned the Nine Cauldrons,
and fierce clans occupied the heavenly city;
drums and gongs shook the thresholds,
and blades and arrows flowed into the Crimson Palace.
Yet the disaster was limited to the capital region
and did not spread afar;
the world remained peaceful,
awaiting order from chaos.
Therefore King Xuān rose from Gònghé,
and King Xiāng and King Huì were bolstered by Jìn and Zhèng.
How could it be like the two Hàn?
A brief disturbance in the gates and hallways,
and the four seas were already boiling;
a wicked minister entered the court in the morning,
and the Jiǔfú were in chaos by evening!
Thinking back to the usurpation and rebellion of Wáng Mǎng,
and observing more recently the time when Dǒng Zhuó seized power,
the millions of people felt grief in their hearts,
and the foolish and the wise alike felt the same pain.
Yet the Zhōu dynasty endured because of it,
while the Hàn dynasty perished because of it;
what is the reason for this?
Is it that the world lacked the ministers of former times,
or that scholars lacked the will to rectify and unite?
It is that far-reaching achievements were constrained by different times,
and heroic ambitions were thwarted by a low position.
Therefore, men of heroic spirit wring their hands in frustration,
only to eventually fall into the hands of their enemies;
men of average character change their principles,
to assist the Jié-like tyrants who oppress the nation.
Though at times there were those who gathered like-minded men
to plan for the sake of the imperial house,
yet above there was no wise ruler,
and below there were only commoners from the marketplace;
the armies had no pre-established ranks,
and ruler and minister had no will to protect each other.
Thus, though righteous soldiers gathered like clouds,
they could not save the state from the calamity of abduction and assassination;
before the people’s hopes had changed,
the destruction of the Great Hàn was already seen.
Some believe that because the feudal lords’ positions were hereditary,
they could not always be maintained perfectly;
with muddled rulers and cruel tyrants
following one after another at times,
this is why the five ranks of nobility often led to disorder.
The current provincial governors and prefects
are all appointed to office based on their merit and ability;
though there may be occasional failures,
the successes are certainly many,
and thus commanderies and counties are easier to govern.
When virtue is glorious and bright,
dismissals and promotions are handled daily,
and the leaders of the administrative units
all fulfill their duties;
then even an excessive or muddled ruler
has no room to commit errors;
why then should there not be good governance?
Thus, past generations have prospered by this means.
But if things should decline and decay,
and the hundred regulations themselves become contradictory,
then officials who sell offices,
judging talent by wealth,
will cause the sprouts of greed and cruelty
to be like those of the various feudal lords.
How could there not be disorder?
Thus, later kings have been deposed because of this.
To summarize,
the lords of the five ranks
sought good governance for their own sake;
whereas the heads of commanderies and counties
seek to exploit things for personal profit.
How can this be proven?
Aspiring to advancement and promotion
is the usual ambition of those in service;
while self-cultivation and bringing peace to the people
are things that even good scholars rarely achieve.
The passion for advancement is sharp,
while the reputation for bringing peace to the people comes slowly.
Therefore, those who encroach upon the common people to benefit themselves
are not deterred by their positions;
and those who neglect practical matters to cultivate a reputation
are what officials concern themselves with day and night.
The ruler has no plan that lasts even a full year,
and the minister harbors only the ambitions of the moment.
But the five ranks are not so;
they know the state is their own land,
and the masses are all their people;
when the people are at peace, they receive the benefit,
and when the state is harmed, their own families suffer the affliction.
Therefore, the predecessors wish to leave a legacy for their descendants,
and the descendants think of continuing the ancestral foundation;
those above have no heart for negligence,
and those below know the principle of steadfast loyalty.
If both types were wise and lived in times of order,
then their achievements would differ in degree;
if both were foolish and lived in times of disorder,
then their faults would differ in depth.
Thus, the systems of the eight generations
can almost be unified by a single principle;
while the institutions of Qín and Hàn
can nearly be summarized in a single phrase.
The Emperor once spoke with various eminent worthies about Guǎn Lù,
lamenting that he possessed extraordinary talent but did not attain a high position.
At that time, someone standing below the Vermilion Stairs overheard this discussion,
and returned to tell me.
I said that a scholar’s failure or success
is nothing other than fate.
Therefore, I respectfully record the Emperor’s words,
and accordingly speak of the principles thereof.
I observe that Guǎn Lù
was of a brilliant and magnificent natural talent,
exceptionally refined like fine jade,
truly an eminent hero within the four seas;
how could he be merely of the class of diviners and fortune-tellers?
Yet his office reached only to Assistant of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Shǎofǔ Chéng),
and his life ended at forty-eight;
the rewards and bestowals of Heaven,
how meager they were!
Thus, having high talent but no noble office,
while the gluttonous and greedy occupy great positions,
has been a cause for lamentation since ancient times;
how could it be so for Gōngmíng alone!
Therefore, the way of nature and life,
and the numbers of failure and success,
are confused and obstructed in many ways,
and no one knows how to distinguish them.
Zhòngrèn obscured the source,
and Zǐzhǎng elaborated on the confusion.
As for those in hermit caps and with earthen windows,
they must believe that Heaven has a fixed time for them;
while those of noble families with high status
say that it is only what humans themselves summon.
In the clamor and noisy debate,
divergent views thus arise.
Xiāo Yuǎn discussed the root but did not trace the flow,
while Zǐxuán spoke of the flow but did not clarify the root.
I shall attempt to say of it:
That which brings life to all things
is called the Way (Dào);
to produce without a master
is called Nature (Zìrán).
As for Nature,
things see it as it is,
without knowing why it is so;
they all obtain it together,
without knowing how they obtained it.
It stirs and molds all things without taking credit,
and all species are formed through it, yet not by its conscious effort.
In giving life, it has no heart for nurturing,
and in death, how could it have the intent to kill?
To cast one into the deep spring is not its anger,
and to raise one to the high heavens is not its joy.
Vast and grand,
all treasures are transformed by it;
firm and pure,
once transformed, it does not change.
That which is transformed and does not change
is called Fate (Mìng).
As for Fate,
it is the mandate from Heaven.
Fixed in the preordained signs,
it ultimately never changes.
Neither ghosts nor gods can intervene,
and the sages and wise men cannot plot against it;
the strength to move mountains cannot resist it,
and the sincerity to make the sun reverse its course cannot move it.
If short, it cannot be delayed by even a moment;
if long, it cannot be hurried by the dripping of the clepsydra.
The highest virtue cannot surpass it,
and the highest wisdom cannot avoid it.
Therefore, in the age of Fàngxūn,
the vast floods rose over the hills;
in the time of Tiānyǐ,
the heat scorched gold and melted stone.
Duke Wén trod upon danger,
and Xuānní ran out of food.
Yán Huí’s clump of orchids withered,
and Rǎn Gēng sang while gathering plantains.
Yí and Shú died because of a woman’s words,
and Zǐyú was hindered by Zàng Cāng’s slander.
If even sages and worthies were like this,
then how much more so for the ordinary people?
As for Wǔ Yuán, his corpse floated in the river’s current;
Sān lǘ drowned his body by the banks of the Xiāng River.
Grandee Jiǎ had his spirit dampened in Chángshā;
Commandant Fèng grew white-haired in the officials’ quarters.
Jūnshān ascended like a swan,
only to have his fine feathers clipped amidst the high clouds;
Jìngtōng rose like a phoenix,
only to have his swift wings broken at the wind cave.
Was this because their talent was insufficient or their conduct flawed?
In recent times there was Liú Huǎn of Pèi Guó,
and his younger brother Liú Jìn;
both were outstanding scholars of their age.
Liú Huǎn was known as the Kǒngzǐ of Guānxī;
he was thoroughly versed in the Six Classics,
followed the path of gradual guidance,
and devoted himself to Confucian conduct.
Liú Jìn possessed a will as stern as autumn frost
and a heart as pure as Kūnlún jade;
he stood tall and lofty,
unpolluted by the dust of the world.
Both cultivated their virtue in humble dwellings
and spread their fame throughout heaven and earth.
Yet their offices were lower than that of a Shìláng,
and their positions did not reach that of a Zhíjí.
One after another they passed away,
and their ancestral sacrifices are no longer offered.
Using these two worthies to speak of antiquity,
then those of old who possessed the quality of jade and the appearance of gold,
who were heroic, outstanding, and refined,
were all rejected in their time.
They harbored extraordinary talents but found no use for them;
they withered away with the grass and trees
and died alongside the deer.
Their flesh covered the plains
and their bones filled the valleys;
how can one possibly speak
of all those who were buried and vanished without being heard of!
Thus, the difference between a Zǎihéng and a lowly servant,
between Péngzǔ’s longevity and a child who dies young,
between the wealth of Yī Dùn and the poverty of Qián Lóu,
and between the beauty of Yáng Wén and the ugliness of Dūn Qià—
all are obtained from nature
and do not rely on talent or wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:
"Death and life are determined by fate,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
This is precisely what it means.
However, the substance of fate flows and circulates,
and its transformations are not uniform.
Sometimes there is wailing first and then laughter;
sometimes it begins with good fortune and ends in disaster.
Sometimes it comes without being summoned;
sometimes it is achieved through others.
It is intertwined and complex,
returning and alternating between fortune and misfortune.
It cannot be proven by a single principle
nor verified by a single path.
Yet its way is subtle and profound,
silent, vast, and indistinct.
It has no form that can be seen
and no sound that can be heard.
It must manage things to manifest its spirit
and rely on people to form its images,
much like the tassels on the crown of a Heavenly King
which rely on a hundred officials to manage their duties.
Yet some, seeing the dragon-like leap of Tāng and Wǔ,
believe that the subduing of chaos lay in their divine achievements.
Hearing of the birth of Kǒngzǐ and Mòzǐ,
they believe that their wisdom and brilliance commanded extraordinary renown.
Seeing the leopard-like transformation of Péng and Hán,
they believe that fierce bravery leads to noble ranks.
Observing the crimson robes of Zhāng and Huán,
they believe that understanding the classics allows one to easily attain high office.
How could they know that there is a powerful force driving them?
Therefore, those who speak against fate
suffer from six fallacies.
Allow me to outline their main points.
Now, a delicate face with smooth skin
and a distorted mouth with a collapsed nose
are differences in form.
To bloom in the morning and end by dawn,
or to live for a thousand years like the tortoise and crane,
are differences in years.
To understand words as soon as they are heard
or to be so mentally dim as to not distinguish beans from wheat
are distinctions in spirit.
While all know these three things are determined by creation,
regarding the realm of honor and disgrace, they alone claim it is due to man.
This is like knowing two and five but not recognizing ten.
This is the first fallacy.
The dragon's forehead and the sun-like horn
are the signs of emperors and kings;
eyes like a river and patterns like a tortoise
are the physiognomy of dukes and marquises.
Looking into a mirror, one knows they will be executed;
pressing the seal-cord, it reveals they shall receive the mandate.
Falling stars, rainbows, and the pivot-lightning
are omens of a sage's virtue.
Night wailing and gathering clouds
are the auspicious signs of a rising king.
All these signs appear beforehand
and spread their influence to later generations.
If one claims that driving the fierce beasts
and brandishing a sword
to enter the Zǐwēi palace
and ascend the path of the Emperor
is achieved by man, then they have not reached the truth of the profound mysteries
nor fathomed the calculations of the divine.
This is the second fallacy.
The village of Kōng Sāng
was turned into a great river;
the capital of Lì Yáng
was transformed into fish and turtles.
When the Chǔ army slaughtered the Hàn soldiers,
the Suī Hé river was choked by its flow.
When the Qín people buried the Zhào soldiers alive,
the sound of their boiling cries was like thunder.
When fire blazes on the Kūnlún peaks,
common stones and fine jade are burned together;
when severe frost falls at night,
common weeds and fragrant orchids perish together.
Even the brilliant talents of Yóu and Xià,
or those like Yī and Yán who were nearly perfect,
how could they resist this?
This is the third fallacy.
Some say even the Bright Moon pearl
cannot be without flaws,
and the jade bi of the Sovereign of Xià
cannot be without defects.
Thus Tíngbó died as a county magistrate,
and Xiāngrú ended his life as a garden prefect.
It was not that their talent was not outstanding,
nor that their lords were not enlightened,
yet the great brilliance of the Jié Lǜ jade was shattered,
and the night-light of the Xuán Lí pearl was damaged.
Could it be that the measure of a foot has its shortcomings?
If that were the case,
when Zhǔfù Yǎn and Gōngsūn Hóng failed to pass their examinations with their strategies
and were not accepted after repeatedly offering their counsel,
they herded pigs in the Zī Yuán plains
and were rejected by their provincial offices.
Suppose they had suddenly vanished like a passing shadow
and died suddenly in the frost and dew;
would their disgrace
not have been like that of Cuì and Mǎ?
But when they opened their guest halls
and were served with five bronze tripods,
as swift as lightning and wind,
their fame spread beyond the seas.
Was it because they were foolish before and wise later,
or wrong at first and right at the end?
Rather, prosperity and decline have fixed numbers,
and the Heavenly Mandate has its ultimate limit,
yet people mistakenly produce judgments of beauty and ugliness.
This is the fourth fallacy.
When the tiger roars, the wind rises;
when the dragon emerges, the clouds gather.
Thus when Zhònghuá was established, the Yuán and Kǎi rose to prominence;
when Xīn Shòu was born, Fēi Lián was advanced.
However, in the world, good people are few
and evil people are many;
dark rulers are numerous
and enlightened monarchs are rare.
Fragrant herbs and stinking weeds are not kept in the same vessel;
the owl and the phoenix do not fly wing to wing.
This results in the likes of Hùndùn and Táowù following in the footsteps of those on the Yúntái,
while Zhòngróng and Tíngjiān plow and weed beneath the crags.
To perversely claim that rise and fall depend on oneself
and have no connection to Heaven—
this is the fifth fallacy.
Those Róng Dí
have human faces but animal hearts;
they find comfort in the poison of indulgence
and regard slaughter as morality
and incestuous relations as benevolence and righteousness.
Even if Dàfēng stood at Qīngqiū,
or Záochǐ fought in the Huáyě wilds,
compared to their wolf-like cruelty,
how could those even be a comparison?
Since the virtue of the Metal Power of Jìn failed to compete,
heaven and earth have been in upheaval.
Barbarians with their left-overlapping robes and bubbling lips
took advantage of the gap and struck like lightning,
subsequently overturning Chán and Luò
and toppling the Five Capitals.
They occupy the ancestral lands of former kings
and steal titles within the central counties,
competing with the Three Sovereigns for their subjects
and contending with the Five Emperors for their territories.
Their tribes flourish and multiply,
filling the Shénzhōu.
Alas!
That "blessings come to the good and misfortune to the wicked"
is merely empty words!
Is it not that misfortune and prosperity overturn each other,
and expansion and contraction operate in turn,
yet people confuse it with human effort?
This is the sixth fallacy.
However, that which is called "fate" consists of
death and life,
nobility and meanness,
poverty and wealth,
order and chaos, and
misfortune and blessing.
These ten
are what Heaven bestows.
Stupidity, wisdom, goodness, and evil—
these four
are what humans perform.
If one's spirit is not that of Shùn or Yǔ,
one's heart differs from Zhū or Jūn,
and one's talent is caught within the range of the mediocre,
then it depends on what one practices.
For this reason, plain silk has no constant color;
black and yellow take turns arising.
Abalone or fragrant orchids—
entering their presence, one changes accordingly.
Therefore, Jì Lù studied under Zhòng Ní
and sharpened a character of wind and frost;
Chǔ Mù consulted with Pān Chóng
and brought about the disaster of murderous rebellion.
Yet the evil of Shāngchén
resulted in a flourishing legacy that shined upon his descendants;
the goodness of Zhòng Yóu
could not prevent the ending where he had to tie his hat strings.
Thus, depravity and rectitude depend on the person,
while auspiciousness and ill omen lie in fate.
Some say that ghosts and spirits harm the prideful,
and August Heaven assists the virtuous.
Thus, at a single word from Sòng Gōng,
the Law Star moved three times;
the Yīn emperor cut his own hair,
and clouds came from a thousand lǐ away.
If goodness and evil were without proof,
this principle would not be harmonized.
Furthermore, Yú Gōng built a high gate to await an enfeoffment,
and Mother Yán swept the tomb to anticipate a funeral;
this is why a gentleman exerts himself without ceasing.
If benevolence brought no reward,
why would one cultivate goodness and establish a name?
These are words of straightforwardness.
Now, the words of the sages are manifest yet obscure,
subtle yet gracious,
profound and distant so as to be hard to hear,
vast as the Milky Way and unfathomable.
Sometimes they establish teachings to advance the mediocre and idle;
sometimes they speak of fate to exhaust the nature of the spirit.
"Accumulated goodness leaves a surplus of blessings"
is an established teaching;
"The phoenix does not arrive"
is a statement about fate.
Now, to use a few fragments of their words to debate their essential meaning—
how is that different from a creature that dies in the evening discussing the changes of spring and autumn?
Moreover, despite the virtuous reputation of Jīng Zhāo,
the cinnabar clouds did not disperse;
while Zhōu Xuān prayed for rain,
the jade tablets were exhausted.
Old Man Yú planted virtue,
but did not reach the heights of Xūn and Huá;
Yánnián was cruel and fierce,
but his fate was not as harsh as that of Dōnglíng.
Doing good is the same,
doing evil is equal,
yet misfortune and blessing flow in different directions,
and decline and prosperity leave different traces.
Could the vast High God
be like this?
The Shī says:
"Wind and rain are as dark as night,
yet the cock crows without ceasing."
Therefore, a good person does good.
How could they ever stop?
Eating rice and grain,
consuming fodder-fed livestock,
wearing fox and raccoon fur,
donning fine ice-silk,
watching the marvelous dances of the profound and subtle,
and listening to the qín and sè zithers of Yúnhé—
these are the urgencies of living people,
and are not done because of some external pursuit.
Cultivating the Way and its Virtue,
practicing benevolence and righteousness,
being earnest in filial piety and fraternal love,
establishing loyalty and integrity,
becoming steeped in the richness of ritual and music,
and following the grand models of the former kings—
these are the urgencies of the gentleman,
and are not done because of some external pursuit.
Thus, the gentleman dwells in rectitude and embodies the Way,
rejoices in Heaven and knows fate,
understands that which cannot be helped,
and recognizes that it does not depend on wisdom or strength.
What departs he does not summon back,
what comes he does not resist,
he does not rejoice in life,
and he does not grieve over death.
Jade terraces and grand houses
cannot please his spirit;
earthen rooms and woven reeds
are not enough to cause him worry.
He is not puffed up or humbled by wealth and status,
nor is he restless in his desires.
Could there be any writings of "ill-fated encounters" like those of Shǐ Gōng or Dǒng Xiàng?
A guest asked the host:
"Is Zhū Gōngshū’s Juéjiāo Lùn
right
or wrong?"
The host said:
"Why does the guest ask this?"
The guest said:
"When the grass insects chirp, the grasshoppers leap;
when the carved tiger roars, the clear wind rises.
Therefore, when the generative essences affect each other,
mist surges and clouds steam;
when birds call to each other,
stars flow and lightning strikes.
For this reason, when Wáng Yáng was promoted, Gòng Gōng rejoiced;
when Hǎn Shēng passed away, Guó Zǐ grieved.
Furthermore, their hearts are as harmonious as qín and sè zithers,
and their words are as fragrant as orchids and angelica.
Their Ways are joined like glue and lacquer,
and their wills are as beautifully matched as the xūn and chí flutes.
The sages and worthies used this to engrave on gold plates and carve on basins and bowls,
to write on jade tablets and etch on bells and tripods.
As for the craftsman stopping his wonderful skill of creating a wind,
or Bó Zǐ ceasing his elegant melody of flowing waves.
Fàn and Zhāng were sincere and devoted in the Underworld;
Yǐn and Bān were joyful through the long night.
Coming and going in every direction,
like mist falling and rain dispersing,
what the cleverest calendar-maker does not know
and mental calculation cannot fathom.
Yet Zhū Yìzhōu confused the constant order,
overstepped the plans and instructions,
struck down the direct and blunt,
and severed friendships.
He compared the common people to hawks and kites,
and likened human spirits to jackals and tigers.
I have my doubts
and ask for clarification of this confusion."
The host listened and laughed, saying:
"The guest is like one who plucks the strings for a fine sound
but does not understand how dryness or dampness changes the resonance;
or like one who spreads nets in a marsh
but does not see the wild geese flying in the clouds.
For the sage holds the golden mirror,
and manifests the blast of the wind;
whether soaring like a dragon or curling like a measuring worm,
he follows the rise and fall of the Way.
The sun and moon are like linked jades,
assisting the tireless pursuit of great goals;
clouds fly and lightning flashes,
revealing the subtle meaning of the Dì Huá.
Like the changes of the five notes,
completing the wonderful melody of the nine movements.
This Master Zhū found the dark pearl at the Chìshuǐ,
and spoke by contemplating the divine and sagacious.
As for weaving together benevolence and righteousness,
polishing the Way and its Virtue,
rejoicing in their happiness,
and commiserating in their decline.
To find connection within the Spirit Terrace,
and leave one's traces upon the rivers and lakes;
though the wind and rain are fierce, they do not stop their sound,
though the frost and snow fall, they do not change their color—
this is the pure friendship of the worthy and accomplished,
which occurs but once in ten thousand ages.
When it comes to a decadent age where people are deceptive
and trickery arises like a gale,
mountain valleys cannot surpass their danger
and ghosts and spirits cannot fathom their changes;
they compete for the lightness of feathers
and scramble for the tips of awls and knives.
In such a time, pure friendship ends
and friendship of profit arises.
The world is in a muddle,
like startled birds and crashing thunder.
Thus, friendships of profit share a common source,
but their branches flow differently.
To speak of them in brief,
there are five types:
"If their favor is equal to that of Dǒng and Shí,
and their power weighs as heavily as that of Liáng and Dòu;
if they command all manner of craftsmen
and forge all things in their furnace.
Their breath summons clouds and rain,
and their sighs bring down frost and dew.
The Nine Provinces tremble at their presence,
and the Four Seas are scorched by their brilliance.
Everyone rushes to them like falling stars chasing shadows,
or flows toward them like rivers drawn by a sound.
As soon as the watchmen signal the dawn,
their grand carriages cast broad shadows;
when their high gates open in the morning,
their axles follow one another like a flowing stream.
All are willing to sacrifice themselves from head to heel,
to destroy their courage and tear out their entrails;
they pledge to burn their wives and children like Yào Lí,
and vow to sacrifice their entire clans like Jīng Qīng.
This is called 'Friendship of Power,'
and its current is the first.
"If their wealth equals that of Táo and Bái,
and their assets are as vast as those of Chéng and Luó;
if they possess mountains of copper
and houses filled with gold;
if they ride out from Píngyuán with horses in tandem
and live in neighborhoods where bells chime.
Then there will be guests from the back alleys
and scholars from humble dwellings
who hope for a glimmer of light from their midnight candles
and seek a small measure of the bounty from their luxurious homes.
Like fish in a line or ducks leaping,
they gather in crowds like scales.
They share in the grain intended for geese and mallards
and are moistened by the dregs left in jade cups.
Receiving favors and kindness,
they offer their sincere devotion;
they point to the green pines to show their hearts
and to the clear waters to signal their good faith.
This is called 'Friendship of Wealth,'
and its current is the second.
"When Grandee Lù held banquets in the Western Capital,
and Guō Yǒudào evaluated character in the Eastern Realm,
the high officials valued their immense reputations,
and the gentry envied their status as if they were immortals.
With furrowed brows and wrinkled noses,
and amidst flowing saliva and foam,
they engage in profound debates about the 'yellow horse'
and unleash grand eloquence about the 'green rooster.'
When they speak of warmth, the cold valleys become temperate;
when they discuss severity, the spring thickets lose their leaves.
The rise and fall of others depends on their glance,
and glory or shame is determined by a single word from them.
Thereupon, young noblemen
and pampered sons of the elite,
whose paths are unknown to the wise
and whose names have not reached the lofty halls,
cling to their scales and wings
and beg for their remaining words.
They attach themselves to the tail of a swift steed
and surpass the returning geese at Jiéshí.
This is called 'Friendship of Discourse,'
and its current is the third.
"The expansion of Yáng and the gloom of Yīn
are the great emotions of the people;
union in sorrow and separation in joy
are the constant natures of all things.
Thus, fish moisten each other with foam when the spring dries up,
and birds cry out in sorrow when they are about to die.
Those with the same illness pity one another,
composing mournful songs by the river;
harboring fear in their hearts,
they manifest the grand tradition of the 'East Wind.'
Such 'gold-breaking' bonds arise from narrow and low places,
and 'neck-cutting' friendships start from straw mats.
Thus did Wǔ Yuán wash and bathe with Zǎi Pǐ,
and the Kings Zhāng and Wáng supported each other with Chén Xiāng.
This is called 'Friendship of Adversity,'
and its current is the fourth.
"In these restless times,
among these shallow people,
none do not hold the scales
or grasp the fine silk.
The scales are used to weigh importance,
and the silk is used to detect the breath.
If the scales cannot lift
and the silk cannot fly,
then even if one has the dragon-like talent of Yán or Rǎn,
the fragrance of Zēng or Shǐ,
the jade-like depth of Shū or Xiàng,
or the brilliance of Qīng and Yún that rivals the Milky Way,
they are viewed as floating dust
and treated like clay figures.
No one would spend half a bean on them,
and rarely would anyone pluck a single hair for them.
But if the scales show a heavy weight
and the silk flutters even slightly,
then even if one has the hidden wickedness of Gòng Gōng,
the treachery of Huān Dōu,
the defiance of Nán Jīng,
or the great cunning of Dōng Líng,
everyone will crawl and twist
to flatter them and lick their sores.
Gold paste and kingfisher feathers are sent to express intent,
and flexible, fawning manners are used to convey sincerity.
Thus, where the carriages and canopies travel,
it is never to the houses of Yí or Huì;
where the bribes and gifts enter,
it is always the homes of Zhāng or Huò.
They act only after calculation,
with not even a hair’s breadth of error.
This is called 'Friendship of Calculation,'
and its current is the fifth.
"All these five friendships
are in essence like commerce.
Therefore, Huán Tán compared them to a marketplace,
and Lín Huí likened them to sweet wine.
Cold and heat alternate,
and prosperity and decline follow one another.
Some are glorious at first and withered later;
some are wealthy in the beginning and poor in the end;
some exist at first and perish later;
some are restricted in the past and prosperous now.
Changing and overturning,
swift as the waves.
The desire for profit has never changed,
but the ways of transformation cannot be constant.
From this perspective,
the reason Zhāng and Chén ended in disaster
and Xiāo and Zhū ended in a rift
is clearly understood.
Yet Zhái Gōng was still so meticulous in inscribing his door to warn guests—
why was his realization so late?
"From these five friendships
arise three faults:
corrupting virtue and destroying righteousness,
making men like beasts—
this is the first fault.
Being hard to secure but easy to break,
becoming the gathering place for feuds and lawsuits—
this is the second fault.
Sinking one's reputation into gluttony,
which the upright and pure are ashamed of—
this is the third fault.
The ancients knew that these three faults were obstacles
and feared that the five friendships would bring swift blame.
Thus Wáng Dān disciplined his son with the birch and the whip,
and Zhū Mù spoke out clearly to show his severance.
How meaningful!
How meaningful!
In recent times there was Rèn Fǎng of Lè’ān,
an outstanding talent within the four seas.
Early on he held silver seals and yellow ribbons,
and long since his reputation among the people was clear.
With forceful writing and beautiful compositions,
he was on par with Cáo Zhí and Wáng Càn;
heroic in stature and exceptionally talented,
he was comparable to Xǔ Shào and Guō Tài.
He loved guests in the manner of Tián Wén,
and cherished the worthy like Zhèng Zhuāng.
Seeing a single good deed, he would gaze with intensity and clasp his wrists in admiration;
meeting a single talent, he would raise his brows and clap his hands.
Criticism and praise issued from his lips;
distinction and evaluation were determined by his monthly critiques.
Thereupon officials' carriages converged like spokes,
and robes of scholars gathered like clouds.
Carriages bumped hub to hub,
and his guest seats were always full.
To step across his threshold
was like ascending the hall of Quèlǐ;
to enter his inner chambers
was said to be like climbing the slope of Lóngmén.
As for a single glance from him, it increased one's value manifold;
his grooming and encouragement made one neigh long like a fine steed.
Those with tassels at Yúntái rubbed shoulders,
and those scurrying upon the crimson steps followed in each other's footprints.
None failed to forge ties of kindness and intimacy,
or to form deep and lasting bonds,
longing for the pure renown of Huì Shī and Zhuāng Zhōu,
and aspiring to the glorious deeds of Yáng Jiǎo’ā and Zuǒ Bótáo.
When he closed his eyes in Dōngyuè
and his remains were returned to Luòpǔ,
while the funeral canopy was still hanging,
the gate saw few scholars bringing wine to sacrifice;
before the grass had even grown over his grave,
the fields were devoid of guests in moving carriages.
His young orphans,
unable to plan from one morning to the next,
wandered far to the south of the great sea,
entrusting their lives to lands of mountain pestilence.
Of the heroes who once held his arm,
and the friends as close as gold and orchids,
none possessed the benevolence of Yángshé Shè to shed a tear,
nor did they admire the virtue of Hòu Chéngshū in sharing his home.
"Alas!
The paths of the world are perilous and steep,
even to such an extent as this!
Tàiháng and Mèngmén,
how could they be called precipitous?
Therefore, men of integrity
detest that it is thus;
they tear their robes to wrap their feet,
abandoning the world to flee far away.
Standing alone atop a high mountain,
they joyfully join the company of elk and deer;
brightly distancing themselves from the misty turbidity,
they truly feel shame for it,
and truly they fear it."
Your servant has heard that as the sun sinks and the stars revolve,
it is the means by which the vast heavens record all things.
As mountains are filled and rivers rush,
it is the means by which the sovereign earth spreads its vital breath.
The five elements intermingle to provide utility;
the four seasons alternate to complete the year.
Therefore, when the hundred officials reside in their duties,
they harmonize with the distinct eight tones;
an enlightened ruler holds the tally,
to ensure a gathering of perfect harmony.
Your servant has heard that if a task is heavier than one's strength,
talent will be exhausted and one will be in distress;
if a vessel is used too broadly,
a wide response will bring misfortune.
Thus, when the object outweighs the scale, the balance is endangered;
when the form exceeds the mirror, the reflection is exhausted.
Therefore, an enlightened lord measures talent to assign service,
and a loyal minister exerts his strength while declining excessive rewards.
Your servant has heard that talents of outstanding brilliance
are what the world lacks and finds rare;
excellence from the hills and gardens
rises according to the times.
Thus, when the Great Man founds his mandate,
he does not pluck talent only from the earth below;
when an enlightened lord rises,
he does not receive his assistants only from the azure heavens above.
Your servant has heard that what the world casts aside
is not necessarily without value;
