what a ruler treasures
is not necessarily suited for governance.
Thus, in the thickets where the talented gather,
they rarely receive the summons of the high-wheeled carriage;
yet the crags of gold and jade
are necessarily graced by the messenger of the rising phoenix.
Your servant has heard that granting stipends based on favoritism
is not an act that exalts a family;
granting offices based on kinship
is not the selection to prosper a state.
Therefore, when the three ministers inherit their titles,
the Dōngguó had many policies of decay;
when the five marquises shared power,
the Xījīng faced a fate of decline.
Your servant has heard that when the divine light appears at dawn,
it illuminates all things according to their measure;
when the seasonal wind blows in the evening,
it gives sound according to the form.
Therefore, when the Great Way is practiced,
all species find fulfillment in the world;
when the Great Transformation is pervasive,
the common people lack for nothing in their hearts.
Your servant has heard that casting a net into the deep abyss
cannot summon a dragon;
shaking the net to snare the clouds
does not necessarily summon a phoenix.
Therefore, the elders of Cháo and Jī
did not glance at the gifts from the hills and gardens;
the man who washed his ears in the Wèi River
did not prompt the dream of Fùyán.
Your servant has heard that a mirror’s accumulation has no thickness,
yet its reflection has the depth of layered abysses;
the observation of the eye has its limits,
yet its vision encompasses the boundaries of heaven and earth.
Why is this?
Responding to things is done through the essence, not the form;
creating things is done through the spirit, not the vessel.
Therefore, the joy of the ten thousand states
is not delight in the pleasure of bells and drums;
the world’s return to benevolence
is not out of gratitude for the kindness of jade and silk.
Your servant has heard that although accumulated substance is small,
it must affect things;
although exalted emptiness is vast,
it cannot move the heart.
Therefore, the made-up appearance of city-dwellers
is not pleased by the shadow of Xī Shī;
when riding horses in a hesitant manner,
one does not stop in the shade of Mount Tài.
Your servant has heard that there is a way to respond to things;
if one dwells in difficulty, things become easy.
Keeping one's talent within oneself,
what is lacking is the right time.
Thus, the fragrance that fills the hall
is not difficult for the secluded orchid;
the sound that lingers around the beams
is truly what the winding strings yearn for.
Your servant has heard that when wisdom understands both success and failure,
it is not exhausted by the times;
when talent experiences both peace and peril,
it is not bent by the world.
Therefore, wings that soar through the gale
do not seek a reverse wind;
eyes that shine in the night
do not long for the sun to set in reverse.
Your servant has heard that a loyal minister follows his will
without plotting for reward;
a person of integrity exerts himself
expecting only to make the worthy known.
Therefore, when Liǔ Zhuāng delayed the burial,
it was not out of greed for the reward of Guāyǎn;
when Qín Xī smashed his head,
how could it be to demand the fields of Xiānmáo!
Your servant has heard that even keen eyes looking from the clouds
cannot cast light downward;
when bright jade is covered in grime,
it cannot emit its radiance.
Therefore, even a wise and sagacious ruler
sometimes suffers from being obscured and blocked;
talented and virtuous ministers
often harbor the sorrow of being too late for their time.
Your servant has heard that the most intense fragrance
comes from discarded ashes;
the most complex sounds
arise from broken strings.
Therefore, a virtuous woman seeks her name after her death;
a man of heroic integrity fulfills his principles in his own time.
Your servant has heard that a good official planning for the court
does not need to borrow authority;
a loyal minister defending his lord
needs only to cultivate himself.
Therefore, the power of the Sānjìn
was humbled by the sacrificial vessels in the hall of Qí;
the might of a thousand chariots
was weakened by the weeping at Yángmén.
Your servant has heard that music following a melody
harmonizes the grand and the fine;
the movements of those keeping time in dance
bend and rise according to the song.
Thus, if words are suited to the matter,
both the refined and the coarse can be applied;
if a scholar is suited to the Way,
both a long and short life are a matter of destiny.
Your servant has heard that by relying on clouds to sprinkle moisture,
then fragrant blessings easily flow;
by riding the wind to carry sound,
then the excellence of the music naturally reaches far.
Thus, virtuous instruction waits for things to be fulfilled,
and glorious fame becomes manifest because of the times.
Your servant has heard that looking at a shadow to match the substance
cannot dispel loneliness;
pointing at footprints and yearning for the distant
cannot save one from being late.
Thus, those who follow empty vessels
do not possess the means to respond to things;
those who toy with empty words
do not possess the mechanism for achieving order.
Your servant has heard that drilling wood produces fire
to continue the sunlight of Tānggǔ;
flapping wings generates wind
to follow the achievements of Fēilián.
Thus, a thing may be minute yet assist the prominent;
a matter may be trivial yet aid the great.
Your servant has heard that when the morning sun of the spring breeze shines,
mugwort and wormwood receive its warmth;
when the autumn frost falls at night,
lingzhi and orchids are covered by its cold.
For this reason, majesty is stern by treating all things equally,
and virtue is grand by providing universal salvation.
Your servant has heard that skill is exhausted in tools,
and frequent practice leads to mastery;
the Way is tied to the spirit,
and when the person is gone, it is extinguished.
Thus, while wheelwrights strain their eyes,
there is no shortage of Xīzhòng’s subtlety;
while blind musicians clear their ears,
they lack the discernment of Línglún.
Your servant has heard that in what nature expects,
the noble and the base have the same measure;
at the extremity of principle,
the low and high return to the same point.
Thus, drawing water by aligning with the moon
cannot increase its coolness;
drying in the sun to ignite fire
does not necessarily add to its brilliance.
Your servant has heard that high songs with extraordinary rhythms
are not what ordinary ears find moving;
profound meanings and fragrant tidings
are not what mediocre listeners appreciate.
Thus, Nánjīng has songs that few can harmonize with,
and Dōngyě has arguments that remain unexplained.
Your servant has heard that following smoke to catch a scent,
the fragrance remains even after the incense is spent;
recording the sounds of the Zhēng tone,
the melody ceases once the performance ends.
Why is this?
What is bequeathed to the world can be continued;
what ends with the person is hard to sustain.
Thus, the style of Xuányàn always survives,
but the transformation that moves the spirit has already perished.
Your servant has heard that hiding one's form by relying on darkness
is not considered clever or secret;
concealing feelings by relying on wit
is not enough to hide oneself.
Thus, when double brilliance emits splendor,
seeking the void and capturing shadows;
the great person of upright vision
probes the heart and illuminates errors.
Your servant has heard that parting the clouds to look at the sky,
then the celestial patterns are clear;
calming the wind to look at the water,
then the river currents are level.
Thus, the four clans were banished and Táng was encouraged;
the two ministers were executed and Chǔ was at peace.
Your servant has heard that sound is beautiful when matched to the ear,
and color is joyous when pleasing to the eye.
Thus, what all listeners lean toward
does not rely on the melodies of Bǎilǐ;
what ten thousand men find beautiful
does not wait for the face of Xīzǐ.
Hence, the Sage promotes assistants according to the age,
and the enlightened ruler appoints officials based on the times.
Your servant has heard that what originates from within the self
cannot be enhanced by external things;
what is constrained by the times
cannot be exhorted by self-restraint.
Thus, though profit exhausts all things,
it cannot sharpen the mind of the ignorant child;
though virtue is a model for the people,
it cannot save one from the humiliation of being unsettled.
Your servant has heard that movements following fixed rules
can be observed in the Heavens;
responses without constant rhythms
are perhaps difficult to illuminate in the self.
Thus, by looking at shadows and measuring the sun,
the completion of numbers can be expected;
by placing a hand on the chest and discussing the heart,
one sometimes falls into error.
Your servant has heard that straining the ear to seek sound
results in visual excellence but auditory hardship;
clearing the heart to follow things
makes the body idle but the spirit weary.
Thus, since Heaven differentiates their fates,
even those in the same region cannot share their sorrows;
since principle blocks their passage,
even those of the same substance cannot share their prosperity.
Your servant has heard that the scholar who withdraws from the world
does not possess the nature of a bitter gourd;
the woman living in seclusion
is not without feelings of yearning for spring.
Thus, when fame overcomes desire,
the integrity of being companion to a shadow is held dear;
when poverty is more extreme than success,
the integrity of soaring to the skies becomes stern.
Your servant has heard that when hearing reaches the limit of sound,
one does not yearn for the music of Jūntiān;
when the body has enough shade,
one does not rely on clouds that hang from the sky.
Thus, the people of Púmì
abandoned an era of harmony;
the men of Fēngpèi
forgot the ruler who quelled disorder.
Your servant has heard that when the flying reins halt in the west,
then Lízhū and the blind musicians withdraw their discernment;
when the hanging light rises in the east,
then the Yèguāng pearl and the Wǔfū stone hide their brilliance.
Thus, when talent is out of step with the age, all are distressed;
when achievements match the times, all are encouraged.
Your servant has heard that by showing responses in what is near,
what is distant can be observed;
by placing proof in what is manifest,
what is subtle may be encompassed.
Thus, when the inch-long pitch pipe points downward,
Heaven and Earth cannot deceive with their qi;
when the foot-long gnomon stands upright,
the sun and moon cannot escape with their forms.
Your servant has heard that strings have constant sounds,
hence the tune changes when it ends;
mirrors do not store shadows,
hence they reflect whatever form they encounter.
Thus, by emptying oneself to respond to things,
one must exhaust a thousand changing countenances;
by holding onto feelings while handling affairs,
one cannot observe the wonders of ten thousand differences.
Your servant has heard that the Zhù and Yǔ produce rare sounds
to harmonize the peace of metal and stone instruments;
the small and large drums are struck sparsely
to regulate the rhythm of many strings.
Thus, in governing, one must promote openness,
and in planning for things, always examine their convergence.
Your servant has heard that the eye lacks the discernment to taste sound,
and the ear lacks the spirit to illuminate shadows.
Therefore, regarding what is in me,
I do not punish it in myself;
regarding what exists in things,
I do not demand perfection from others.
Your servant has heard that by living with a relaxed body,
the body is at ease and thus peaceful;
by eating freely,
one is satisfied and thus filled.
Thus, when the royal sturgeon is placed on the sacrificial stand,
it does not rely on fish that swallow waves;
when orchid oil stays in the room,
one does not think of the dragon that holds a candle in its mouth.
I have heard that when surging waves flow calmly,
even a dragon boat cannot be overturned;
but when a tempest bursts forth from a cave,
even a grand mansion may at times collapse.
Why is this?
If one is tethered to movement, then stillness congeals;
if one is bound to stillness, then movement remains upright.
Thus, when lewd winds prevail,
a chaste woman suffers the regret of a seductive appearance;
when pure transformation flows deeply,
Dào Zhí possesses the sentiments of Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú.
I have heard that of the garments worn by the prominent,
some of value may be lost;
but of the items handled by the destitute,
even the lowly must be sought.
Therefore, the Lord of Jiāng Hàn
grieved for his lost shoe;
and the woman of Shǎo Yuán
wept for her missing hairpin.
I have heard that if a stimulus is not of the same kind,
though it be urgent, there is no response;
but if moved by the appropriate means,
though it be subtle, there is compliance.
Therefore, while the Shāng biāo wind may move mountains,
it does not raise a cloud of even a foot;
yet the Gǔ fēng wind, brushing the branches,
must bring down moisture that fills the sky.
Thus, those who are blind to governance
sing complex tunes but find few to harmonize;
while those who examine things clearly
use concise effort yet achieve high success.
I have heard that smoke comes from fire,
but it is not the harmony of fire;
emotions arise from nature,
but they are not the fitness of nature.
Thus, when fire is strong, smoke is thin;
when nature is full, emotions are restrained.
Therefore, at the ruins of Yīn there are sorrows of sensing objects,
while at the capital of Zhōu there are no traces of standing long in wait.
I have heard that in skills for adapting to things,
looking up and looking down have different uses;
in tools for responding to affairs,
opening and closing have different duties.
Thus, while birds perch in the clouds, the tethered arrow flies;
while fish hide in the abyss, the net sinks.
The Bèn gǔ drum is dense and holds its sound;
the Lǎng dí flute is hollow and gives forth its notes.
I have heard that what principle guards,
circumstances often seize;
what the Way closes,
expediency must open.
Thus, life is weightier than profit,
so holding the map involves no pain of wielding a sword;
righteousness is more precious than the self,
so approaching the stream brings the sorrow of casting oneself in.
I have heard that those who understand change
use little but gain much;
those who clarify the essentials
use shallow vessels to respond to the profound.
Thus, the mysteries of Tiān Dì
are encompassed in the six positions;
the melodies of ten thousand variations
are exhausted in five strings.
I have heard that depicting a form from a shadow
does not fully capture a delicate and beautiful countenance;
examining fire from ashes
does not allow one to see the grand and glorious blaze.
Therefore, seeking the Way depends on the person;
observing things must reach their essence.
I have heard that when emotions are seen in objects,
though far, they are still distant;
when the spirit is hidden in the form,
though near, it is intimate.
Thus, by modeling Heaven and pacing the sundial's shadow,
length and shortness can be measured;
but by approaching the abyss to survey the water,
shallow and deep are hard to discern.
I have heard that when cruel heat scorches the heavens,
it does not diminish the cold of solid ice;
when parching darkness congeals the earth,
it does not burden the heat of a soaring fire.
Thus, the strength of those who swallow whole and let go
cannot turn back the will of treading the sea;
the might of those who wash away shields
cannot lower the integrity of the Xī Shān mountain.
I have heard that where principle opens the way,
strength usually reaches;
where fate blocks the path,
might must be exhausted.
Thus, while a fierce fire melts gold,
it cannot burn a shadow;
while deep cold congeals the sea,
it cannot freeze the wind.
I have heard that for those whose nature is sufficient,
heavenly damage cannot enter;
for those whose constancy is fixed in their term,
the burdens of the times cannot corrupt them.
Thus, swift winds and driving rain
do not mislead the perception of the dawn bird;
the harsh cold and killing season
do not wither the heart of the winter tree.
Vast and boundless is creation,
once the two poles were divided.
Dispersing Qi and flowing into forms,
they were both molded and fashioned.
In the time of Emperor Báo Xī,
he first regulated the relations between Heaven and man.
Thus began the roles of husband and wife,
as well as lord and minister.
When the way of the family is correct,
the king's path has order.
A woman's virtue prizes gentleness;
"containing beauty" brings steadfast good fortune.
Gentle, compliant, virtuous, and prudent,
she holds her proper place within the household.
Fastening her sash and tying her matrimonial veil,
she reverently attends to the family meals.
Solemnly maintain your decorum,
and thus look up to pure excellence.
Fán Jī moved King Zhuāng,
so she would not eat the meat of fresh birds.
The lady of Wèi corrected Duke Huán,
so his ears forgot harmonious sounds.
Their wills were stern and their righteousness high,
and thus the two rulers changed their hearts.
When the black bear climbed the enclosure,
Féng Yuàn rushed forward.
How could she have been without fear?
She knew death but did not begrudge it!
Bān Qiè had her words,
declining the joy of sharing the palanquin.
How could she not have cherished it?
She guarded against the subtle and thought of the distant!
There is no Way so exalted that it does not decline;
there is no thing so flourishing that it does not wither.
When the sun reaches its zenith, it sets;
when the moon is full, it wanes.
Honor is like the accumulation of dust;
downfall is like a triggered mechanism.
Everyone knows how to adorn their face,
but no one knows how to adorn their nature.
If the nature is not adorned,
one may fail in ritual and propriety.
Chop it and polish it;
through overcome thoughts, become a sage.
If the words you speak are good,
people a thousand lǐ away will respond.
If you violate this principle,
even those sharing a bed will harbor suspicion.
For words spoken are seemingly subtle,
yet honor and disgrace stem from them.
Do not say it is dark and obscure,
for the Spirit monitors without form.
Do not say it is silent and vast,
for the Divine hears without sound.
Do not boast of your glory,
for the Way of Heaven hates fullness.
Do not rely on your nobility;
those who are high will fall.
Take warning from the Xiǎo Xīng stars;
be cautious of following your own desires.
Match your heart to the Zhōng Sī locusts,
and then your kind shall flourish.
Joy must not be treated with irreverence;
favor must not be monopolized.
Monopolization truly breeds negligence;
when love reaches its extreme, it shifts.
Reaching fullness must lead to loss;
this principle is naturally so.
The beautiful think themselves beautiful,
yet their flightiness brings blame.
A seductive appearance seeking favor
is what a Jūn zǐ loathes.
The breaking of a bond of kindness
stems from this very cause.
Thus it is said:
With caution and reverence,
fortune will arise.
Quietly and respectfully reflect on yourself;
honor and prominence are what you may expect.
The Nǚ Shǐ oversees these admonitions,
and ventures to advise all the Shù Jī.
In the autumn, the seventh month of the first year of the Yǒngyuán era,
there was the Elder Uncle of the Hàn, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Dòu Xiàn.
He reverently assisted the Sage Emperor
and supported the Royal House.
Entrusted with great responsibilities,
his conduct was pure and his radiance illustrious.
Then, with the Zhíjīnwú Gěng Bǐng,
he performed his duties of inspection and defense,
and trained the troops at Shuòfāng.
Officers like soaring eagles,
soldiers like dragons and tigers,
they then mobilized the Six Armies,
along with the Nán Chányú and the various lords and chieftains of the Dōnghú, Wūhuán, Xīróng, Dī, and Qiāng,
numbering one hundred thousand valiant cavalry.
The great war-wagons were light and martial,
the long-axled chariots spread in four directions.
Thunderous supply wagons covered the roads,
more than thirteen thousand in number.
Arranged in the Eight Formations,
and presided over with divine majesty,
dark armor glittered in the sun,
and crimson banners reddened the sky.
They then scaled Gāoquè,
descended through Jīlù,
crossed the stony plains,
and traversed the Great Desert.
They beheaded Wēnyú to consecrate the drums,
and bathed their blades in the blood of Shīzhú.
Then the four divisions advanced horizontally,
like falling stars and sweeping comets,
leaving ten thousand lǐ desolate,
with no remaining enemies in the wilds.
Thereupon the territory was cleared and the regions exhausted.
They reversed their banners and returned.
Consulting records and verifying maps,
they thoroughly surveyed the mountains and rivers.
They then crossed Zhuóxié,
straddled Ānhóu,
and ascended Yānrán Mountain.
They trod upon the settlements of Mòdùn
and burned the Dragon Court of Lǎoshàng.
Above, they vented the long-held indignation of Emperors Gāo and Wén
and glorified the mysterious spirits of the Ancestors.
Below, they secured and fortified later generations,
expanded the borders of the realm,
and shook the heavenly renown of the Great Hàn.
This may be called a single effort for long-lasting ease,
a temporary expense for eternal peace.
They then performed the sacrifice on the mountain and carved the stone,
to brightly record this magnificent virtue.
The inscription says:
Splendid is the Royal Army, campaigning to the wild frontiers!
Exterminating the cruel and violent, cutting off those beyond the seas.
Distant and far-reaching, spanning the boundaries of the earth.
Performing the sacrifice on the sacred mound, erecting this grand stone pillar.
Illustrating the Emperor's deeds, to be broadcast for ten thousand generations!
Do not speak of the shortcomings of others;
do not talk of your own strengths.
When bestowing on others, be careful not to dwell on it;
when receiving from others, be careful not to forget.
Worldly fame is not worth yearning for;
only benevolence is the guiding principle.
Examine your heart and then act;
what harm can slander and criticism do?
Do not let your reputation exceed your reality;
maintaining simplicity is what the Sage praises.
Even in black dye, it is noble not to be stained;
within the dimness, light is contained.
Gentleness and weakness are the companions of life;
Lǎo Shì cautioned against hardness and strength.
A persistent and narrow-minded person is a petty man;
but the far-reaching and composed are difficult to measure.
Be cautious in speech and temperate in food and drink;
knowing contentment overcomes misfortune.
If one practices this with constancy,
over time, one will naturally become fragrant.
Towering is Liáng Shān,
its piled rocks are lofty and steep.
To the south it connects to Jīng and Héng;
to the north it joins Mín and Bō.
Southward it leads to Qióng and Bó;
northward it reaches Bāo and Xié.
Narrower than the passage between Péng and Jié;
higher than the peaks of Sōng and Huá.
It is the gateway to Shǔ,
serving as a stronghold and a protector.
It is called Jiàn Gé,
its walls standing a thousand fathoms high.
It exhausts the perils of the earth;
it reaches the limit of the road's steepness.
When the world is turbid, it is rebellious;
when the Way is clear, it is submissive.
It was closed by the former Hàn;
its opening began with the Jìn.
Qín gained the strength of the "one hundred and twenty,"
and swallowed up the feudal lords.
Qí gained the "twelve,"
as Tián Shēng presented his strategy.
How much more so this narrow pass,
a region outside the central lands!
If one man shoulders a halberd,
ten thousand men will hesitate to advance.
A place of strategic advantage
should not be occupied by anyone but kin.
Long ago, when Wǔ Hóu
was in midstream, he rejoiced.
Yet the strength of mountains and rivers
was disregarded by Wú Qǐ.
Prosperity truly lies in virtue;
peril is also hard to rely upon.
Dòngtíng and Mèngmén—
the two states no longer offer sacrifices.
From ancient times until now,
the Mandate of Heaven is not easily held.
Relying on obstacles to act blindly,
few escape total defeat.
Gōngsūn was destroyed,
and the Liú Shì surrendered with jade in mouth.
The tracks of the overturned cart
should not be followed again.
Carving this inscription on the mountain's edge,
I dare to inform the lands of Liáng and Yì.
Long ago, Shùn reached the Wénzǔ;
Yǔ came to the Shénzōng.
Zhōu changed the customs of Shāng;
Tāng dismissed the administration of Xià.
Although revolution differs from succession,
and yielding the throne differs from war,
the celestial bodies and hidden portents aligned,
and Heaven and man provided guidance.
To illustrate illustrious virtue
and greatly protect the living people—
their principle is one and the same.
At the end of the Qí dynasty,
a dark and cruel ruler reigned.
He defied and insulted the Five Elements,
and lazily abandoned the Three Regulations.
Punishments were as cruel as burning charcoal,
and violence exceeded the greased pillar.
The people resented and the gods were angry;
the masses rebelled and his relatives deserted him.
Treading the earth, they had nowhere to go;
looking at the birds, they had no one to rely on.
Then our Emperor saved them.
He grasped the Northern Dipper,
held the Gōuchén constellation,
was aided by the hundred gods,
and received ten thousand blessings.
Like a dragon flying over the Hēishuǐ,
or a tiger walking through Xīhé.
Moving like thunder and driven like the wind,
acting with the heavens and resting with the earth.
He ordered the troops, and clouds gathered in response;
he ascended the altar, and there was the auspicious omen of descending fire.
The tortoise and yarrow stalks were in agreement;
people and spirits followed like an echo.
Heroes with pierced chests and bare heads,
and chieftains who sat with legs splayed and hair in mallets—
all brandished banners and requested to exert themselves,
holding sharp weapons and vying to be first.
The Xiàshǒu relied on its fortifications;
Yōng and Mín leaned on their obstacles.
They sided with that divided heart,
and opposed this common virtue.
The Emperor blazed with such anger, feeding
his horses and training his troops.
Before the solemn drums had finished beating,
the evil leaders bowed their heads in the mud.
Great ships were linked axle to axle,
massive vessels joined bow to stern.
A thousand groups of iron-clad horses,
ten thousand lǐ of crimson banners.
With a simple note, Lú Jiǔ was captured;
with a proclamation, the Xiāng and Luó regions were surrendered.
The weapons were not stained with blood,
and the soldiers did not lose a single arrowhead.
Thus Fán and Dèng were awed and cherished,
and Bā and Qián were settled and pacified.
Thereupon, the faction of Liú Tāng,
and the followers of Wò Tàn,
held their defenses like frail fences,
and fought like withered wood.
The war chariots approached the encampment,
as the army campaigned in the wilds of Shāng Mù.
Men and women of the Huá and the Yí,
with carriages and hats in continuous line,
supporting the elderly and leading the young,
suddenly gathered like clouds.
Jars of broth filled the fields,
and baskets of food crowded the roads.
It was like the people of the Xià dynasty attaching themselves to Chéng Tāng,
or the men of Shāng looking toward Zhōu Wǔ.
They comforted the elderly and cherished the young,
punishing the guilty and consoling the people;
the farmers did not change their profession,
and the merchants did not alter their prices.
The eight directions submitted their accounts,
and the four corners offered their maps.
Feathered dispatches flew to and fro,
and military documents arrived in rapid succession.
From one day to the next,
it was not merely ten thousand matters of state.
Yet the measure of his dignity
did not falter during military campaigns;
his profound and silent countenance
remained unchanged within the battle formations.
Plans were executed as easily as pouring water,
and thoughts moved like a turning wheel;
strategies were finalized within the curtains of the tent,
and schemes were completed at the desk;
before even twelve days had passed,
the solitary man gave up his head.
Thereupon, the ruler burned those silken mats,
and cast away those precious robes,
returning the pearls of the Xuán Tái,
and restoring the jades to the various lords.
With a wave of his hand, the four seas achieved great peace;
upon alighting from his carriage, the whole world was settled.
Rescuing the people from this mire and charcoal,
saving them from this overflowing flood,
his merit equals Heaven and Earth,
and his brilliance matches the Sun and Moon.
Thereupon, looking up to harmonize with the three spirits,
and looking down to follow the will of the millions,
he received the jade of Zhāo Huá,
and accepted the maps of the Lóng Xù.
He performed sacrifices to the Emperor of Heaven and the ancestors,
illustriously possessing the Great Vessel of State.
He ascended the central peak to sacrifice to the spirits,
and straightened his sleeves to receive the various Huá lords in audience.
He distributed instructions throughout the capital district,
and promulgated governance to the outer regions.
His plans harmonized with the highest strategies,
and his punishments followed moderate laws.
The people of the south with suspended ears,
and the people of the west with backward tongues;
the nations of sword-bearing riders in felt tents,
and people who share the same rivers and caves;
all bent their knees and crossed their arms,
or touched their foreheads to the ground in reverence.
He opened up ten thousand lǐ of empty lands,
and cleared the ground for a thousand cities;
south of the desert, the border defenses were ceased;
west of the river, there were no alarms.
Thereupon, governance was settled and merit achieved;
those nearby were at peace, and those afar were respectful.
They forgot the terror of the startled deer,
and ceased the wary backward glances of the wolf.
He then standardized the six kinds of music,
regulated the five rites,
revised the regulations,
and created the laws.
He established the office of Bó Shì,
and students enrolling were like clouds;
he opened the hall for gathering elegance,
and those coming to study made the gates like a marketplace.
He established schools and academies,
and set up the altars for the suburbs and hills.
Even a single talent was surely recorded,
and rituals without text were all put in order.
Thereupon, the scholars of the world
followed the wind of his influence;
people recognized integrity and honor,
and families knew ritual and yielding.
Instruction reached the attendant sons,
and transformation saturated the Qī Mén guards.
The realm was governed and at peace;
all directions were quiet and still.
Labor was rested and duties simplified,
the years were bountiful and the people harmonious.
Regarding the models of past eras,
and the precedents of former kings,
there was none he did not prune and refine,
truly holding to the Mean.
He considered that the system of ceremonial gate towers, the Xiàng Què,
had its origins in the distant past.
The Chūn Qiū established the teachings of old regulations;
the Jīng Lǐ passed down the text for posting laws;
the Dài Jì revealed words about sightseeing;
and the Zhōu Shǐ recorded the dream of planting towers.
Bright moons of the northern wastes,
and flowing essences of the western extremes;
gold from the seas and mountains,
and purple shells from the river courts;
the designs of the Azure Dragon and Black Tortoise,
and the craftsmanship of the Copper Sparrow and Iron Phoenix;
some were used to hear the grievances of the destitute,
some to display transformations and hang the laws,
some to mark the center of the royal residence,
and some to glorify the imperial capital.
As the Jìn clan grew weak,
and the Sòng dynasty fell into decline,
the ritual classics and old precedents
were desolate with no records,
and their grand designs and glorious achievements
were submerged and rarely mentioned.
They falsely claimed the celestial towers were at Niú Tóu,
and entrusted distant plans to Bó Wàng;
this was a deception to the eyes and ears,
and offered no supplement to the constitutional codes.
Thus, he ordered officials who investigate measurements,
and selected scholars who understand the center,
to set the sun-dial and the gnomon,
to observe the stars and survey the land,
to restore the ceremonial gates,
and to begin the construction of the magnificent Xiàng Què.
It was then the year of the celestial record,
in the month of Tài Cù,
the seventh year of the Emperor's reign over the world.
He constructed this grand model,
and raised this sublime beauty.
People shall hasten past to show respect,
and look upon them to know the law;
all things witness the appearance of the twin stone pillars,
and all people recognize the hundredfold rituals.
It serves as a pattern and a lesson to be passed down;
how illustrious and magnificent!
Thereupon he ordered me, his humble servant,
to engrave this on the rock.
The inscription says:
Only the Emperor establishes the state,
rectifying the position and discerning the directions.
Zhōu planned by the banks of the Luò,
and Hàn opened at Qí and Liáng.
The residence flourished due to his achievements,
and the culture shone through his transformation.
Here stand the Xiàng Què,
which are indeed the old regulations.
The blue canopy reached south,
and the yellow flags pointed east.
Hanging the laws went unheard,
and the stored records were not documented.
The Great Man creates all things,
his dragon-like virtue ends the misfortune.
He builds these hundredfold constants,
and raises these twin structures.
How grand and towering!
How magnificent and lofty!
Flanking the reflections of overlapping layers,
reaching up to the emerald mists.
The spread of education is now manifest,
the first light shines throughout the day.
The hung laws have their place,
and those who submit their writings know where to return.
Towering high with multiple eaves,
the vaulted roof has upturned corners.
The shape soars with flying beams,
and the momentum surpasses floating columns.
The colors follow the roundness of Heaven above,
the design models the squareness of Earth below.
Looking around at the plains and marshes,
looking down upon the mist and rain.
In front, it welcomes the four crossroads;
behind, it backs onto the nine chambers.
To the north, it opens to the two ruts of the road;
to the south, it converges from the five directions.
As summer comes and winter goes,
as long as the earth and as eternal as heaven.
Divine indeed is this magnificent sight!
May it forever accompany the boundless future.
Indeed, when observing the phenomena from the heavens,
the moments of dusk and dawn were not yet clearly distinguished;
in regulating the calendar to clarify the times,
the degrees of expansion and contraction lacked a standard.
The office of *Qièhú* was named,
far-reaching in its righteous utility,
to calculate the shadows and measure the stars,
to watch the *Gōng* and guard the *Jǐng* constellations,
maintaining it with water and fire,
and thus dividing the day and night.
But the calendar officials lost their posts,
and the hereditary specialists abandoned their profession;
the first month of *Mèngzōu* was obliterated,
and the *Shètí* markers had no record.
*Wèi Hóng* recorded the intervals of signal calls,
which were clear but not detailed;
*Huò Róng* described the differences between solstices and equinoxes,
which were detailed but not precise.
In the rhapsody of *Lù Jī*,
he held the "spiritual pearl" in vain;
in the inscription of *Sūn Chuò*,
he pointlessly boasted of the "jade of Kūnlún."
The remaining scrolls of *Hóngdù*,
and the intentions handed down by *Chéngtiān*,
were laid out in books and records,
but did not manifest in the utility of instruments.
They were like those spring blossoms,
or like the dates of the sea.
How could they be used to regulate things and nurture the people,
or serve as a model and instruction to be passed down?
Moreover, the current official clepsydra
comes from *Huìjī*;
the accumulation of water violates the proper method,
and the guided flow deviates from the rules.
The six segments of the day are not distinguished,
and the five watches of the night are not divided.
The year resides in *Yānmào*,
and the month is in the order of *Gūxiǎn*.
In the fifth year of the Emperor's reign over the world,
music shifted from the customs of *Xià*,
and rites changed from the traditions of *Shāng*.
His achievements are like mending the heavens,
and his merits are equal to supporting the earth.
The rivers and seas are calm and peaceful,
and the winds and clouds are in harmony with the pitch-pipes.
Retiring late from the court audience,
and rising early every morning,
he attended to the sound of the passing clepsydra
and listened to the calls of the "Chicken Men."
He believed that the transit of the Fire Star was erroneously centered,
that the use of metal and water was improper,
that the times for opening and closing were mismatched,
and the time-arrows differed by even the slightest weight.
Thereupon he commanded the calendar officials
to draft and create a new instrument.
Then, observing below and gathering from all around,
they ascended the platforms and entered the storehouses.
It was modeled after the "Earthly Four"
and supplemented with the "Heavenly One."
The lingering flaws of *Jiànwǔ*
and the remaining errors of *Xiánhé*,
the designs of the square and round metal tubes,
and the rules for the intake and output of the flowing water—
the changing of the pitch-pipes and the revision of the constants—
all were corrected and reformed.
In the sixth year of *Tiānjiān*,
the year of *Dīnghài*,
on the first day of the tenth month, *Dīnghài*,
the sixteenth day, *Rényín*,
the clepsydra was completed and presented to the Emperor.
It was used to examine the hours and correct the shadows,
to measure the gnomon and observe the dark;
it does not err by the smallest measure
and does not deviate by the weight of a grain.
Furthermore, it can be used to check the alignment and discrepancy of calculations,
to distinguish the rectitude of the heavens,
to observe the fullness and emptiness of the four seasonal breaths,
and to assess the precision of the six calendars.
It shall be an eternal rule for the world,
passed down without end.
How magnificent and brilliant!
It is beyond praise.
In the past, the *Jiāliáng* was a minor object,
and the *Pányú* were small vessels,
yet they still manifested virtue and recorded merit,
preserved in the inscriptions and classics.
How much more so for this divinely inspired design,
which accords with the signs of creation?
Its ability to complete things
is equal to the essence of the Earth.
Its merit is many times that of the inscriptions on pillars and mats,
its significance a hundred times that of those on sashes and stools.
How can we allow it to be more modest than the *Zēngshuǐ*,
or more lowly than *Kūnwú*?
Should the golden characters not be passed down,
and the silver script not be engraved?
Thus he decreed his humble subject to write an inscription for it:
One heat and one cold,
there is light and there is darkness.
The divine way leaves no tracks;
the work of Heaven is rarely replaced.
Thus the *Qièhú* was established,
to glorify the great work.
Its "breath" is balanced like weights and stones,
its shadows are corrected by scales and standards.
When the ways of the world were lost,
and the arts of ritual perished,
they hastily moved the water and fire,
and the order of things was inverted.
The clashing of blades was out of sequence;
the gathered wood deviated from the correct direction.
Investigating and measuring—
it was our Emperor.
The square pot is the outer station;
the circular flow attacks from within.
The magnitude of flow is distinct;
high and low have different levels.
Spiritual *Liángqiú* receive the flow;
*Yīnchóng* spit and suck.
Suddenly going and suddenly coming;
appearing like ghosts and entering like gods.
Minute as drawing silk from a cocoon;
passing like a flash of lightning.
The ear never ceases to hear the sound;
the eye does not linger on the sight.
The *Tóngshǐ* oversees the marks;
the *Jīntú* holds the arrows.
Treading on thin ice without trembling;
facing the deep without shaking.
Granting and receiving without error;
rising and falling without mistake.
Pure and single-minded;
it can be a law and an image.
The moon does not escape in its coming;
the sun has no hidden departure.
Dividing by talismans and contracts;
arriving like a shadow or echo.
The *Héhūn* flower curls at dusk;
the *Míngjié* plant grows at dawn.
Still they distinguish the intent of Heaven
and measure the feelings of Earth.
How much more so our divine creation,
which penetrates the obscure and pierces the spiritual?
It matches the Emperor's limit
and serves as a standard for the world.
On the twenty-fourth day, *Wùshēn*, of the first month of the twenty-second year of *Jiàn'ān*,
the late Attendant Official and Marquis within the Passes of *Wèi*, Lord *Wáng*, passed away.
Alas!
The divine Heaven observes,
and wise men rely on it.
Why did the spiritual deities
destroy our auspicious gentleman?
Who says he was not used?
He entered the darkness at an early age.
Who says there is no grief?
The flowers were numerous but fell in their prime.
The living and the dead flow in separate streams;
the young and the old meet the same end.
To hear the Way in the morning and die in the evening—
this was what the people of old contemplated.
How shall we eulogize his virtue?
Represent it on a plain banner.
How shall we gift him at the end?
Send him off with sorrow.
Thus the eulogy says:
Oh, how grand is the Shìzhōng!
Your distant ancestors were exceedingly fragrant.
Gōng Gāo established great achievements,
assisting Wǔ in the conquest of Shāng.
His rank was equal to those of Qí and Lǔ,
but the state sacrifices eventually ceased.
His descendant Bì Wàn
had meritorious deeds that were truly brilliant.
Jìn Xiàn bestowed a fief upon him
within the borders of Wèi.
Heaven opened up their mandate,
and the later descendants claimed the title of King.
This then became the clan surname,
branching out into various lineages.
For generations, their fragrant excellence flourished,
spreading their renown through the Qín and Hàn.
Then came the times of calamity,
and the fiery light was clouded in the middle.
Shìzǔ quelled the chaos
and then established a time of peace.
The positions of the Sāntái were established,
where those who followed the Path gathered.
The bestowing of favored ranks
was not mere kindness, but a mark of respect.
Starting from your two ancestors,
they were as light and as dragons.
All said, "How magnificent!"
They were fit to assist the Hàn state.
One commanded as Tàiwèi,
another managed as Sīkōng.
The hundred officials were in order,
and the Five Teachings were followed.
Heaven was still and people were in harmony;
the imperial teachings spread afar.
As for your illustrious father,
generations assisted the times.
Internally he managed confidential matters,
and the court administration was well-governed.
Externally he oversaw Shuò and Dài;
all the various achievements were made brilliant.
You, with your pure virtue,
succeeded this grand foundation.
Having fine virtue already,
your talents and skills were widely known.
With a powerful memory and extensive knowledge,
you deeply praised subtle words.
Your writing was like spring blossoms;
your thoughts were like a gushing spring.
Your spoken words were worthy of song;
your pen produced finished compositions.
What Way did you not master?
What art were you not skilled in?
At the chessboard you displayed cleverness;
in games of strategy you were eminent.
The Imperial House met with misfortune;
the capital was overturned.
A regent official seized power,
and the Emperor moved to the west.
You then became a traveler,
leaving these hardships behind.
Suddenly rising like a phoenix,
you took refuge far away in Jīngmán.
Though your circumstances were poor, your will was reached;
living in a rustic place, your conduct remained pure.
Shaking your cap at Nányuè;
washing your hat-strings in clear rivers.
Living hidden in a thatched hut,
you did not seek power or influence.
Our Duke wielded the battle-axe,
displaying his majesty in Nánchǔ.
The people of Jīng were sometimes defiant,
so troops were arrayed and martial arts practiced.
You were then moved by righteousness,
planning for our army.
You esteemed the achievements of a hegemon
and committed yourself to the Imperial House.
Once these words were spoken,
the strategists agreed with you.
What was that agreement?
It was an echo of our bright virtue.
Casting aside weapons at Biān and Ruò,
kowtowing at the north of the Hàn River.
Our Duke truly appreciated this,
praising you before the capital.
He gave you the golden tortoise and purple sash
to manifest your meritorious service.
What was that service?
Toiling with unceasing humility.
Worrying for the world and forgetting home,
with extraordinary strategies standing tall.
He then appointed you as Jìjiǔ,
traveling and staying with you.
Your calculations left out no plan;
your designs never lost their reason.
Our King established the state;
the various officials were talented and wise.
You were prominently raised
to hold authority in the Palace Secretariat.
Wearing the cicada-wing cap and marten fur,
in red robes and white belts.
Entering to attend in the inner tent;
exiting surrounded by an ornate canopy.
Your glory shone in this world;
your fragrant influence was vast.
Alas, those Dōngyí,
relying on rivers and obstructed by lakes.
They troubled the borders,
exhausting our soldiers.
The grand military carriages
moved like thunder and wind.
You attended the ornate wheels,
shining on the King's path.
Thinking of glory and winning over the hearts of others,
hoping for them to be awed by your arrival.
How could it be that it was not to be?
Luck ran out and life waned.
Bedridden with a lingering illness,
you set out in health but returned in tragedy.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The young orphan heir
wails in heart-breaking grief.
Setting off from Northern Wèi,
reaching as far as Southern Huái.
Passing through mountains and rivers,
tears falling like a landslide.
The sorrowful wind stirs deep feelings;
the drifting clouds linger in the air.
The swimming fish lose their waves;
the returning birds forget their roosts.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Between me and you, master,
our friendship was as firm as red and green paint.
In harmony like the zither and lute,
our bond exceeded that of common friends.
I hoped for many long years ahead,
to walk hand in hand together.
How could you so suddenly
leave me and wither early!
Remembering past banquets,
our spirits were both high and lofty.
I joked with you, master,
that metal and stone are hard to wear out.
Human life is inconstant;
fortune and misfortune follow different rules.
Among us joyful people,
who would be the first to fall?
How could I have known, master,
that you would indeed be the first to pass away!
We also discussed life and death,
the cycles of existence and non-existence.
You still harbored doubts,
seeking clear evidence.
If indeed there is a spirit,
your soul wanders in the Great Simplicity.
I shall borrow wings
and soar high in the wind.
Ascending above the auspicious clouds,
to meet you on the celestial path.
Now that the coffin has arrived,
it shall return to the capital of Wèi.
The hearse turns its wheels;
the white horses neigh in sorrow.
An empty expanse where nothing is seen;
your light is hidden and your form obscured.
Who can say Zhòngxuān is here,
when his voice is no longer heard?
Stretching my neck and sighing,
tears falling like rain as we part.
Alas, master!
May you find eternal peace in the dark realm.
Who among men does not perish?
But a wise man dies for his name.
Glory in life and sorrow in death;
this is indeed a great honor.
Alas, how sorrowful!
In the first year of Xiánníng,
in the fourth month of summer, on the day of Yǐchǒu,
the late General of Attacking and Rushing of Jìn, Regional Governor of Jīngzhōu, Marquis Dài of Dōngwǔ, Lord Yáng Shǐ of Xíngyáng, passed away.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Son of Heaven establishes states;
the feudal lords establish houses.
Selecting the worthy and employing the capable,
the government is thus harmonious.
Zhōu relied on Shàngfù;
Yīn leaned on Tàiā.
Vigorous and valiant was Marquis Yáng,
the claws and teeth of Jìn.
His loyalty and integrity were clearly manifested;
his splendid achievements were truly excellent.
He was about to broaden the King's strategies
and clear the remote wilderness.
His allotted years were not long;
his black hair had not yet turned gray.
Carrying regret, he left the world;
such is fate, what can be done?
Alas, how sorrowful!
From ancient times of old,
all who have life must die.
The body perishes but the name remains;
this is what the former sages approved.
Conduct is made known through titles;
virtue is praised through narrations.
Daring to entrust this to the banners,
I here compose this eulogy.
The words say:
Remote indeed were the distant ancestors,
whose lineage originates from Zhōu.
The ancestral lines were prosperous;
branches and descendants diverged.
The clan began with Bóqiáo;
the surname came from the Marquis of Yáng.
For generations, they were greatly illustrious,
truly following the great path.
Heaven grew weary of Hàn's virtue;
the dragons fought with no winner yet.
Your ancestors
were in the midst of many affairs.
A bird chooses its tree;
a minister also selects his lord.
Devoting his heart to the Wèi court,
recording his name and committing his person.
Leaping from the abyss and mud,
rising upon the wind and clouds.
Some commanded the Valiant Cavalry;
some held the post of Army Commander.
Truly, Marquis Dài was born,
his flourishing virtue meeting the times.
Succeeding to the great legacy of his ancestors,
he was able to build upon the foundation.
At the age of twenty, he sought the Way;
he was unrivaled in his time.
His filial piety was truly earnest;
his brotherly love was joyful and harmonious.
Endowed with many talents and abundant arts,
with a strong memory and extensive knowledge.
His eyes could see the tip of a hair;
his mind could calculate without limit.
Skilled in both cursive and clerical scripts,
his letters were surely treasures.
His feet never stopped walking;
his hands never put down a text.
His brush moved as if flying;
papers fell like clouds.
Excelling in studies, he entered officialdom,
thus following the royal administration.
Like unpolished jade revealing its brilliance,
he arrived at Zhǐ to serve as Magistrate.
Transformation spread through the towns;
benevolence reached the common people.
Promoted to high office,
solemnly carrying out the court's commands.
As for the High Justice,
it is the constitution of the state.
You presided over that post,
looking upon the people as if they were wounded.
Litigations were handled clearly and cautiously;
punishments were precise and detailed.
In hearing cases, you joined the ranks of Gāo and Lǚ;
your reputation was equal to that of Zhāng.
Transferred to agricultural administration,
there in Yěwáng.
Granaries were full and stores numbered in the millions;
the state was wealthy and the army strong.
Brilliant was Empress Wén,
gradually rising to the Jìn house.
You, with your dual talents,
joined the military as an assistant.
Thus you were granted lands and dwellings,
receiving this illustrious rank.
The green soil and white thatch;
also the vermilion sash.
The Wèi clan followed Heaven;
the Saintly Emperor received the abdication.
Resplendent Marquis Yáng
truly commanded the imperial guards.
Governing the palace gates,
keeping our imperial palace pure.
Harshness and evil did not arise;
it was as solemn as a gentle breeze.
Considering your meritorious labors,
the bestowed orders became even more exalted.
Vast were the regions of Hǎi and Dài;
the profound transformation was not yet complete.
Rushing were the rivers Jiāng and Hàn;
the borders were divided.
Upholding both civil and military virtues,
at that time there was only Marquis Yáng.
Having guarded Dōngguǎn,
you then governed Jīngzhōu.
Repelling enemies across ten thousand lǐ,
responding to and spreading the King's excellence.
Hearing of good as if startled;
hating evil as if it were an enemy.
Showing both majesty and virtue;
using both force and gentleness.
The Wú barbarians were fierce and extravagant;
their false army feared the pressure.
About to take advantage of the enemy's rift,
to sweep across the southern regions.
Though setbacks followed and food ran out,
his divine plans were unerring.
The fault of a gentleman
is to take the blame and yield the credit.
Like the sun and the moon,
which at times have eclipses.
He bore the blame himself
and yielded the merit of his efforts.
Having returned the banners,
he was dismissed according to the law.
He retired to guard the ancestral graves,
shutting his doors and not going out.
Letting his eyes wander over the ancient classics,
and his heart indulge in Confucian arts.
Many scholars and officials came,
entering his hall and room.
There was no matter they did not consult him on,
no doubt they did not ask him to clarify.
Though his position was lowered, the Way was practiced;
though his circumstances were constrained, his will was untrammeled.
Without worry or plan,
he fell ill and was bedridden.
Great Heaven was not compassionate;
his great life came to an end.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Zǐnáng assisted Chǔ
and his last words were to fortify Yǐng.
Shǐ Yú remonstrated with Wèi
using his corpse to clarify the government.
As you approached your end,
you did not forget loyalty and respect.
Prostrate upon your sickbed,
your thoughts were on the imperial court.
In the morning his words were delivered;
in the evening his life was lost.
The Saintly King sighed in grief,
bestowing favor with burial clothes and shrouds.
Eulogizing his virtue and recording his merits,
evaluating his life to determine a posthumous title.
The many officials are struck with grief;
the state and clan shed tears.
The orphaned heir is in mourning;
colleagues and subordinates are filled with sorrow.
Those attending the funeral share the grief;
even passersby on the road sigh more deeply.
Alas, how sorrowful!
I, with my dullness and obscurity,
have been sheltered by your deep protection.
Looking up, I recall my late father
and your heart as his close friend.
Looking down, I feel the depth of our friendship
and your profound understanding.
Receiving the news of your death, I am grieved;
tears soak my lapel.
How could I forget to rush to you?
But I am weighed down by sorrow and illness.
In your illness I did not visit;
at your passing I did not attend.
Raising my voice, the grief surges;
the sorrow has a lingering sound.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Yáng Suí,
courtesy name Zhòngwǔ,
was a native of Wǎnlíng in Xíngyáng.
He was the great-grandson of the Commander of the Central Army, Marquis Sù;
the grandson of the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Marquis Dài;
and the son of the Marquis Kāng of Dōngwǔ.
He lost his father at the age of eight.
His mother, Lady Zhèng,
was the eldest daughter of the Minister of Imperial Entertainments, Marquis Chéng of Mìlíng.
Her conduct was exceptionally noble;
she nurtured and raised the young orphan
to preserve and maintain her husband’s household,
thereby escaping various hardships.
Marquis Dài and Marquis Kāng produced many writings
and were also skilled in the arts of cursive and clerical script.
In his youth, Suí was an outstanding talent;
he was certainly able to synthesize the profound meanings
and follow the established models.
Although his maternal relatives were prosperous and influential,
he remained orphaned and poor, adhering to simplicity.
His heart was at peace in humble alleys,
and his body was clad in plain garments;
I marveled greatly at him.
As for his pure talent and eminent excellence,
his abundant virtue was daily renewed;
I saw his progress
and never saw it cease.
Drawing upon the favor of three generations of family friendship,
and as your aunt
was my wife,
who died last year in Dégōng Lane,
we shared the same place for mourning.
For several months we were closely connected;
if a person must have a heart,
this was the height of pure sincerity.
Unfortunately, his life was short;
at the age of twenty-nine,
he died in the summer of the ninth year of Yuánkāng, in the fifth month, on the day of Jǐhài.
Alas, how sorrowful!
I thus compose this eulogy:
Of your ancestors,
successive generations were glorious and prosperous.
The grandfather and the great-grandfather
continually spread a beautiful reputation.
Your late father, Marquis Kāng,
died early without enjoying his salary.
Though his reputation and rank were bright,
his meritorious deeds were not fully realized.
He gave birth to my child,
born with a flourish of refined appearance.
Gifted and precocious,
you understood the manifest and the subtle.
You delved into the deep and explored the abstruse,
savoring the Way and investigating the fundamental.
You were no ordinary person,
but the glory of the nation.
You encountered misfortune
before you had even lost your milk teeth.
Like those vulnerable roots
facing a sudden gale.
Your virtue was bright and clear;
there was no darkness it did not illuminate.
At twenty, your fragrance spread;
your eminent reputation was pure and noble.
While your maternal uncles flourished,
your own clan was withered.
From youth, you held unique principles,
avoiding abundance and being content with lack.
You compiled the ancestral teachings
so they would not fall into ruin.
Old texts and new arts—
none were left unstudied.
The harmony between the Pān and Yáng families
has a long history.
Moreover, today,
you were careful of the end as you were the beginning.
Your joys and your sorrows
were as if they were my own.
You looked upon me as a father,
yet I could not keep you as a son.
My respect was indeed earnest;
my love was indeed deep.
Though our years were different,
our hearts were truly the same.
As the sun declines in the west,
I looked for you like the morning shade.
Why were you cut short?
Turning your back on the world and sinking into the void.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Lying ill and lingering,
you maintained your filial and fraternal piety.
Facing death, you forgot yourself,
looking back with longing for your loving mother.
Oh, the grieving mother!
Her heart is pained, her head aches.
The siblings wail loudly,
and the uncles are filled with sorrow.
The spring orchid puts forth its stem,
just about to bloom in full.
The treasure of Jīng produced unpolished jade,
about to be carved by Hé.
You contained your fragrance and let your light fade,
a broken gem and a snapped branch.
Alas, Zhòngwǔ,
what pain, what can be done!
During the hardship at Dégōng,
we shared the same quarters in the outer chamber.
Only I and you
were on adjacent mats and touching pillows.
From that time until now,
not even a full year has passed.
Aunt and nephew died in succession;
what pain could be greater than this?
Alas, how sorrowful!
Opening cases and spreading books,
I repeatedly see your remaining writings.
Some are drafts, some are copies,
some in cursive, some in standard script.
Holding and admiring them repeatedly,
I seem to see the person.
The paper is worn by my hands;
tears soak my kerchief.
The tortoise and yarrow divinations are completed,
the tomb tunnel is opened.
How painful, Master Yáng!
Forever parted from the world.
In the morning, crossing the Luò River,
in the evening, halting at the mountain bend.
Returning birds soar up and down,
drifting clouds hover.
At the grave, a final farewell;
touching the coffin, I exhaust my grief.
Your physical form has no successor,
increasing the sorrow in my heart.
Your soul has departed!
The bridge timber has indeed collapsed.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Xiàhóu Zhàn,
courtesy name Xiàoruò,
was a native of Qiáo.
He became known at a young age.
At twenty, he was summoned to the office of the Grand Commandant.
Recommended as Worthy and Philanthropic, Upright and Square,
he then became a Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince,
a Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
Magistrate of Yěwáng,
a Drafter in the Central Secretariat,
and Chancellor of Nányáng.
Due to family mourning, he requested to return home.
Shortly after,
he was selected as the Servant to the Crown Prince,
but before he could take up the post, the Emperor Shìzǔ passed away.
The Emperor appointed him as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
following the ranks of the court.
At the age of forty-nine,
in the summer of the first year of Yuánkāng, in the fifth month, on the day of Rénchén,
he lay ill
and died at his residence in Yánxǐ Lane.
Alas, how sorrowful!
I thus compose this eulogy:
Yǔ was bestowed the dark jade tablet,
Truly, he was called Wénmìng.
Able to be enlightened and sage-like,
He gloriously initiated the governance of Xià.
In the era of the Hàn,
Surpassing merit belonged to the Yīng family alone.
Thinking to broaden the Confucian enterprise,
In matters small and great, both generations were famous.
Illustrious ancestors displayed their virtue,
Governing Yǎn and Jīng.
His father guarded the Huái and Dài,
His rule was also renowned.
Radiant was the Master,
Brilliant was his excellence.
Flourishing eloquence and spreading literary patterns,
Like abundant flowers and the resonance of jade.
Like the treasures of Suí and Hé,
Emitting brilliance and flowing with luster.
Like that embroidered brocade,
Arrayed on white silk, dotted with splendor.
People saw his exterior,
But none could fathom his interior.
They merely said of my friend,
"When literary style exceeds substance, one becomes a scribe."
With luminous minds and spiritual communion,
There was only I and you.
Having passed through youth and adulthood,
Until witnessing the end from the beginning.
Your devotion to your parents,
Was as filial as Mǐn and Shēn.
Your brotherly affection,
Was as harmonious as the zither and lute.
Serving the lord with the straight path,
Dealing with friends with a trustworthy heart.
Though your song was indeed lofty,
I still appreciated your melody.
At the age of twenty, you sharpened your wings,
Your official dignity first arose.
The Duke's bow having summoned you,
The imperial carriage then recruited you.
Internally assisting the two palaces,
Externally governing the common people.
Your loyal integrity was truly manifest,
A pure breeze was then raised.
In that vast and joyful capital,
You were favored by the King.
Setting up offices and establishing assistants,
He excellently selected the state's finest.
Appointing you as his "throat and tongue,"
You assisted him in Nányáng.
Your kind instructions were tireless,
You regarded the people as if they were wounded.
Looking back north with affection,
You resigned your salary to prolong joy.
I also rested in retirement,
Doing nothing in this bright era.
Our travels of former days—
Two cycles of twelve years have passed since then.
With grey hair, we held hands;
What joy could compare to that!
Sit, and let me speak to you:
The many truly overcome the few.
People loathe the talented and extraordinary,
The vulgar find fault with the refined.
Holding a halberd, Yáng was exhausted;
To Chángshā, Jiǎ was cast.
Do not say you are high,
Or feel ashamed to be beneath others.
You then looked enlightened,
Changing your expression and countenance.
With a sigh of emotion, you said:
"The Ways are indeed different.
Practicing benevolence depends on oneself;
It is not I who seek the ignorant.
Who slanders and who praises?
Where to go and what to follow?
No dye can make it black;
No grinding can make it thin.
I alone maintain a stern countenance;
Though in a humble position, my will expands.
Although I am not employed by you,
I still devote my person."
Offering advice and correction with full regulation,
You served this one man.
Straightforward words and loyal schemes—
Shìzǔ appreciated these.
About to serve the Crown Prince,
Holding the reins at the Chénghuá Gate.
By the final command of the previous reign,
Sage-like honors were illustriously added.
Entering to serve at the imperial gates,
Going out to bring glory to your house.
I have heard that for those who accumulate good,
The spirits bestow auspiciousness.
You should have enjoyed a long life,
And long preserved the heavenly order.
How is it that such a man,
Should have such an illness?
Before even knowing the Mandate of Heaven,
In middle age, you suddenly passed away.
Alas, how sorrowful!
While you were alive,
You were noble not because of rank.
Sweet food and fine clothes,
Rare treasures and multiple flavors.
At the end, you left a testament,
To forever grant to your kind.
Shrouded in the clothes of the season,
The funeral did not use elaborate vessels.
Who can rise above the vulgar?
To nourish life to the fullest,
Yet while nourishing life,
To have such a meager burial?
Profound was such a man!
Letting his heart flow with ease.
Heroic conduct, clear and reaching,
In hardship, even more bright.
The hearse having performed the ancestral rite,
Your physical form returns forever.
Life and death's eternal parting—
The departed cannot be pursued.
Looking at your old carriage,
Beholding your left-behind clothes,
I am choked with emotion and lose my voice,
Tears burst forth and fall together.
If I do not wail for you,
For whom would I wail?
Alas, how sorrowful!
Days go and months come,
Summer retreats and cold attacks.
Falling dew soaks and congeals,
Strong winds are piercing and swift.
Miserable is the pain,
Thinking of my good friend.
Going to your plain mourning hall,
I comfort the orphans and we weep together.
Former thoughts have not ceased,
Later feelings continue to gather.
Accumulated sorrow fills my heart,
You are gone, how can I reach you!
Alas, how sorrowful!
In the autumn of the seventh year of Yuánkāng, on the fifteenth day of the ninth month,
the late Commander and Marquis of Guānzhōng of Jìn, Lord Mǎ of Fùfēng, passed away.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Initially, when the Yōng region became an internal dependency,
the rebellion of the Qiāng had not yet been suppressed,
and the registered households of the Dī also acted out in rebellion.
Although the royal armies were sent to punish them,
and eventually they were exterminated,
yet the bees and scorpions possessed venom.
Having suddenly lost minor advantages,
they caused the common people to become displaced,
frequently cast into extreme misery.
The Jiànwēi General lost his life at Hǎozhǐ,
and the Provincial Governor fled by night at Dàxī.
As for the subordinate officers and deputy generals who lost their lives or saw their armies destroyed,
they could be counted by the tens.
Those who held the tally of office and governed cities,
officials who wore green sashes and black seals,
who fled and abandoned their posts,
were visible throughout the borders.
Among the usurpers in Qín Lǒng,
Gǒng Gèng was the leader;
he had already attacked Qiān and made its county seat his lodging.
You, with your slender person,
were situated within a heavy siege.
Leading a small and weak force,
you held a city of ten zhì.
The various Dī rose like the bristles of a hedgehog,
and from all four sides, arrows fell into the city like rain.
Those in the city dug tunnels to live in
and carried doors on their backs to fetch water.
Wood and stones were nearly exhausted,
firewood and fodder were depleted,
and grass and fuel were completely gone.
Thereupon, the beams and pillars were removed to be used, and
with iron chains and mechanisms,
boulders were released and then raised back up.
Parched wheat was used for cooking,
and the pine wood of the eaves and rafters was shaved for fuel.
Thus, firewood and fodder were not lacking,
humans and livestock were supplied,
blue smoke rose on all sides,
and the horses neighed long.
The heinous villains were shocked and filled with suspicion;
they then dug into the ground to attack.
You ordered that tunnels be dug and trenches deepened,
and placed jars, pitchers, and bottles to detect them.
As they were about to break through,
the sound echoed,
and you burned chaff fire within to smoke them out;
the hidden Dī were annihilated.
After a long time,
the reinforcements of the General of Ānxī arrived,
and you finally escaped the peril of the tiger's mouth,
preserving millions of dàn of stored grain,
and your deeds were recorded in the headquarters.
The Sage Court consulted,
promoting you with an honorable rank,
and distinguishing you with the system of banners and canopies.
But the officials of the province,
on account of a few private servants
and ten bushels of grain,
interrogated the officers and soldiers,
using testimony obtained by the rod to implicate you.
The Great General repeatedly submitted memorials of protest,
saying:
"Dūn firmly held the isolated city,
alone facing the various rebels.
With few, he resisted the many,
passing through winter and summer.
Facing danger, he exerted his integrity,
protecting the grain and preserving the city.
Yet the attendants of Yōngzhōu,
jealous of Dūn’s meritorious service,
have pushed small flaws to the extreme.
This is not the way to reward great merit.
It is appropriate to release Dūn from imprisonment and investigation and grant him his appointment."
The imperial edict quickly granted this,
but you had already died in prison from indignation.
The court heard of this and was grieved.
The mandate read:
"The Emperor consults concerning the late Commander and Marquis of Guānzhōng, Mǎ Dūn.
Loyal, courageous, resolute, and firm,
he led with proper method.
He firmly held the isolated city,
and the critical situation was saved.
Before honors could be bestowed,
he unfortunately passed away;
We are deeply saddened.
We now posthumously grant the seal and ribbon of General of Yámén,
and he shall be sacrificed to with the lesser animal offering."
If your soul has spirit,
may it appreciate this honor and glory.
Yet when a pure gentleman hears of defilement,
how can he easily set it aside?
As for the lower officials who indulge in their stifling harm,
they are all of a jealous sort.
Alas!
Jealousy deceiving the good
is also a blood feud of traded heads.
As the saying goes:
"Someone cautioned his son,
'Be careful not to do good.'"
Words can indeed be like this;
how tragic!
In the past during the battle of Chéngqiū,
Xiàn Bènfù drove the chariot for Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng;
the horses were startled and the battle was lost.
Bènfù said:
"In other days, I never lost a battle,
but today we lost;
this shows a lack of courage."
Thereupon, he died for it.
A groom was washing a horse,
and a stray arrow was found in its flesh.
The Duke said:
"It was not his fault,"
and thus he composed a eulogy for him.
In the time of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
there was one Sīmǎ Shūchí,
who in broad daylight in the city market took a sword to his father's enemy,
viewing death as coming home.
The Emperor also ordered the historian Bān Gù to write a eulogy for him.
Thus, for those of the sort of loyalty, filial piety, righteousness, and heroism,
who die passionately and not by their fate,
the writers of words
have never neglected them.
Since the Son of Heaven has already issued a mandate and granted gifts,
how can a humble official like myself, attached to the end of the old histories,
dare to omit his record?
Thus, I compose this eulogy:
Knowing men is not easy,
and men are not easily known.
Alas for this student Mǎ,
whose rank was low and name was humble.
The Western Róng disturbed China,
and he exerted his extraordinary talent.
He preserved this city of Qiān,
and saved our borders from danger.
How were those borders in danger?
The city was small but the grain was rich.
You, with your slender person,
oversaw its defense.
No guards were added to the soldiers,
and the walls were not further built up.
The various Dī tribes were ravenous,
like wolves and tigers competing in the chase.
Gǒng Gèng acted willfully and arrogantly,
lurking in the government offices.
Qí Wàn roared like a tiger,
shocking the high ministers.
Their power and influence seethed,
and the tribes were fanned into a blaze.
Banners spread like lightning,
and spears and halberds were planted like a forest.
Red beads flowed like stars,
and flying arrows gathered like rain.
Fearful were the men and women,
calling to heaven with tears.
They parched wheat to cook,
and carried doors to fetch water.
A danger like a pile of eggs,
an emergency like being hung upside down.
Mǎ Shēng stood forth,
his brilliance shining more brightly in danger.
His spirit surpassed the white sun;
his ferocity was like autumn frost.
His majestic power could be sharpened;
even cowards were made strong.
He bestowed kindness and nurtured others,
so that poor scholars felt as if they were wrapped in fine wool.
The swarming dogs and sheep
relied on their numbers to oppress the few.
They dug secret tunnels for a hidden attack,
from beneath the nine levels of the earth.
In the anxious, exhausted city,
it seemed as if breath itself could no longer be drawn.
Formerly, life hung from the heavens;
now, it rested solely on Mǎ.
Only this Mǎ Shēng
possessed broad talent and abundant wisdom.
He conducted reconnaissance with jars and jugs,
and arrayed long trenches.
Before the spade could show its tip,
the fire had already burst into flames.
The smoke from corpses filled the caves,
and the holes were blocked by clubs.
Wood and stone were depleted,
stalks and straw were empty.
Master Mǎ remained composed,
proud as if he had more than enough.
Beams were used as rollers,
pine shavings were used as fodder.
The defense did not lack equipment,
and the sound of neighing horses echoed throughout.
Alas, the General of Jiànwēi
lay prostrate before the executioner’s block.
The many brave generals
saw their armies crushed and their equipment lost.
The barbarians released our followers
but publicly executed our commander.
To exchange life for death—
who could remain of one mind?
The Sage Court looked toward the west,
and the region of Guānyòu trembled in fear.
Our granaries in Qiān were divided,
turning into provisions for the bandits.
In truth, we relied on you, Sir,
whose strategies were ever more profound.
You made everyone brave
and taught them to sacrifice their lives for the right way.
Though I am but a minor scholar,
I have heard from the ancient classics:
For ten generations, the capable are forgiven;
tombs are marked to signal the virtuous.
Thinking of a person, one loves their tree;
the sweet pear tree was never cut down.
How much more so for you, my friend,
whose merit is deep while suspicion is shallow?
Before both sides of the case were prepared,
the evidence of your servants was sparse.
Who could have such great achievements
yet not be granted a pardon?
How cunning were the departmental officials,
their hearts shifting and turning!
They carved away at the good and harmed the capable;
they detested the upright and hated the honest.
The shepherd of people moves with ease,
retiring from public service to eat.
Hearing of filth, he soars like an eagle,
never folding his wings.
They forgot your great labors
and suspected you over small profits.
If one does not open one's heart,
to what lengths will one not go?
How resolute was Mǎ Shēng,
with his resonant and high character!
He gave vent to his indignation in the prison;
though dead, his eyes still seemed to watch.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Ānpíng devised extraordinary plans
and defeated the enemy to keep Qí whole.
Zhāng Mèng devised strategies,
so that the endangered Zhào gained peace.
The people of Qiān relied on you,
just as they did on those two.
How could there be such stinginess and jealousy
as to shake you with the tip of a pen?
To empty the granaries for reward would be fitting,
how much more so for private grain?
Barbarian slaves could be bestowed,
how much more so one's own family servants?
They stripped you of your pair of tortoise seals
and bound you in the three woods.
Your merit remained in Qiān City,
but your body died in Qiān Prison.
All those who were besieged with you
felt their hearts broken and torn.
Supporting the elderly and leading the young,
they wailed in the streets and wept in the alleys.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The brilliant Son of Heaven
honored you with exceptional grace.
With radiant and favored posthumous gifts,
the banners are raised at your gate.
The Minister of Merit bestows nobility,
which will also extend to your descendants.
If there is a spirit after death,
may it bring comfort to your wronged soul.
Alas, how sorrowful!
On the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the third year of Yǒngchū,
the Sòng Níngyuǎn Sīmǎ
and Púyáng Tàishǒu, Yáng Jǔn of Péngchéng, passed away.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Zǎn from a young age possessed high principles and integrity;

The officers and soldiers fled in confusion,
