Like the "Ten Ministers" awaited,
the four teachings were without error.
Thinking of pleasing the aunts,
she bequeathed to us the rules for a consort.
Her transformation began in the Duke's Palace,
and reached far into the Southern State (Nánguó).
The brilliance of the Xuān star embraced light,
the White Moon (Sùshū) awaited her virtue.
Alas that I was not blessed,
her compassionate instruction was early lost.
In those years, I was young and small,
with nowhere to lean within her sleeves.
The family has attained the precious legacy,
my person has succeeded the prosperous brilliance.
But the Hall of Longevity (Shòugōng) is silent and distant,
the Pure Temple (Qīngmiào) returns to emptiness.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Emperor moved according to the bright mandate,
people and gods were both pleased.
The celestial light shone without,
but the Yin principle was missing within.
Vainly grieving for the "old sword,"
in vain sighing over the "golden tomb."
How can the jade vessels be offered?
The ceremonial robes are no longer set.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The astrologer announced the omen,
the celestial dwelling is gone forever.
Bequeathing her far-reaching plans,
her final commands are encouraged.
Remembering the close ties of Fēng and Pèi,
leaving behind the vastness of the Divine Capital.
Regretting that she does not follow to Cāngwú,
but follows to Fùyú to share the same earth.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Displaying the images at the park and tomb,
reflecting the carriage bells among the pines and catalpas.
Looking toward Chéngmíng Palace but not entering,
crossing the clear Luò River to travel south.
Connecting the funeral ropes on the thoroughfare,
joining the dragon curtains at the pontoon bridge.
The winding pond is silent in the evening,
the Eastern Stream is calm and does not flow.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Relying on the distant brilliance of the Secret Palace (Bìmì Gōng),
hearing of the far-reaching blessings of the successive women.
Initially harmonizing virtue with the sacrificial plants,
finally matching the Earth to manifest the mandate.
Longing is entwined in the bestowed robes,
sorrow increases daily while touching the mirror.
Thinking of the infinite love like the Cold Spring,
entrusting her legacy to the Red Brush (Tóngguǎn).
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Master’s taboo name was Tài,
and his courtesy name was Línzōng.
He was a native of Jièxiū in Tàiyuán.
His ancestors originated from the lineage of King Jì of the great Zhōu.
There was Guó Shú,
who truly possessed admirable virtue,
and King Wén consulted him.
He was enfeoffed and given a clan name;
some called it Guō,
and the Master was his descendant.
The Master was born in response to the heart of Heaven;
he was intelligent, perceptive, bright, and wise;
filial, brotherly, gentle, and respectful;
benevolent, sincere, kind, and gracious.
As for his capacity, it was vast and deep;
his bearing was grand and extensive,
boundless
and profound,
so deep that he was unfathomable.
He tempered his integrity and disciplined his conduct,
following the straight path and using upright speech.
His steadfastness was sufficient to manage affairs,
and his self-restraint was sufficient to correct the times.
Consequently, he examined and studied the Six Classics
and explored the prognostications and charts.
He traveled throughout Huàxià
and subsequently attended the Imperial Academy.
He gathered the crumbling traditions of the civil and military
and rescued the subtle words that were not yet extinguished.
At that time, those who wore official tassels and ribbons,
and the scholars with sashes and pendants,
looked to his appearance and followed him like shadows,
listening to his fine reputation and responding like echoes,
just as the hundred rivers return to the great sea
or the scaled and shelled creatures honor the tortoise and dragon.
Thus he lived in seclusion within his humble gate,
gathering friends and teaching diligently;
the ignorant relied on him
to remove their blindness.
When the provinces and commanderies heard of his virtue,
they humbled themselves and prepared gifts,
but none could bring him to office.
The various lords admired him,
and he was subsequently summoned as a Sītú Clerk,
and also recommended as Yǒudào,
but he declined all due to illness.
He intended to follow the far-off traces of Hóngyá,
to continue the abandoned paths of Cháo and Xǔ,
to soar beyond the mundane world and spread his wings,
and to stand high above the celestial roads.
His endowed life was not long,
and he lived for forty-two years.
He died in the first month of the second year of Jiànníng, on the day of Yǐhài.
All of us, like-minded people from the four directions,
cherish eternal sorrow and mourning,
with nowhere to place our thoughts.
We then reflected together on the Master’s virtue
to plan for his immortality.
All agreed that although the former people have passed away,
their virtuous voices still remain,
also relying on being narrated by others.
How could we now lack this ritual!
Thereupon we erected a stele and marked his grave,
illuminating the inscription of his great conduct,
so that his fragrant brilliance may strive through a hundred generations
and his good reputation may be manifest for eternity.
The eulogy says:
Oh, the admirable Master!
His bright virtue reached the mysterious.
Pure, beautiful, virtuous, and spiritual,
he received it from Heaven.
Lofty, grand, deep, and remote,
like a mountain, like an abyss.
Ritual and music he delighted in,
the Odes and Documents he esteemed.
Not only did he pick the flowers,
but he also sought the roots.
The palace walls were many fathoms high,
and he truly found the gate.
How admirable was his purity,
how firm was his integrity.
The vast throng of officials
looked up to his height.
He dwelled in seclusion by the river and hill,
good at guiding and able to teach.
The illustrious Sānshì
nearly several times sent their summons.
He declined the calls and recommendations,
preserving this pure subtlety.
His granted years were not long,
and the people thus grieve and mourn.
Here we carve this inscription
to spread his radiance.
Alas, you future generations,
take this as your model and imitation.
The Master’s taboo name was Shí,
and his courtesy name was Zhònggōng.
He was a native of Xǔ in Yǐngchuān.
He contained the harmony of the primal essence
and responded to the cycles of time.
He possessed all the nine virtues
and cultivated all the hundred conducts.
Among his village kinsmen, he was respectful
and refined.
He was good at guiding and leading,
benevolent and loving toward others,
so that the young and old all felt at ease with him.
In his practice of the Way,
he acted when employed and hid when dismissed;
his advancement and retreat followed a standard.
He did not seek fame by attacking others to court the times,
nor did he change his heart when facing subordinates.
Four times he served as the commandery Gōngcáo,
five times he was summoned by Yùzhōu,
six times by the Sānfǔ,
and twice by the General-in-Chief.
He was the Magistrate of Wénxǐ for half a year
and of Tàiqiū for one year.
In virtue, he strove for the Golden Mean;
in teaching, he was earnest without being stern.
Governance was completed through ritual,
and transformation proceeded with tranquility.
He then encountered the Dàngshì,
and was proscribed for twenty years.
He delighted in Heaven and knew his fate,
remaining placid and self-composed.
In social relations, he did not flatter superiors;
in affection, he did not treat subordinates with disrespect.
He saw the signs and acted,
not waiting for the day to end.
When the amnesty arrived via official documents,
he was already seventy years old.
He then retired to the hills and mountains,
hanging up his carriage to announce his retirement.
The four gates prepared the rituals,
and he lived in leisure with a quiet heart.
General-in-Chief Lord Hé
and Sītú Lord Yuán
repeatedly summoned and invited him,
sending people to explain and persuade,
saying they wished to specially recommend him,
so that he could immediately enter and serve as a Chángbó,
be promoted to the Sānshì,
wear the gold and purple ribbons,
and bring glory to the state and leave a legacy.
The Master said:
"I have long given up hope;
I only wait for the end in my simple cap."
In the end, he did not go to any of them.
Lord Yáng of Hóngnóng
and Lord Chén of Dōnghǎi, whenever they held ministerial office,
and the various officials congratulated them,
they would all raise their hands and say:
"Lord Chén of Yǐngchuān
is peerless and surpasses all.
He has not reached a high position,
and I am ashamed of the burden of stealing a position like Zāng Wén."
Therefore, the people of the time held his virtue in high regard,
valuing it more than the positions of the Sānshì or Ministers.
At the age of eighty-three,
in the eighth month of the third year of Zhōngpíng, on the day of bǐngwǔ,
he passed away due to illness.
Facing death, he gave his final instructions,
requesting to be buried where he died.
He wore ordinary clothes and was placed in a plain coffin;
the funds for the outer coffin were just enough for the inner one.
The funeral rites were simple,
surpassing even frugality.
Among the various lords and officials,
there was none who did not sigh in lamentation;
the famous scholars of the mountains and forests
lost their voices and shed tears.
The Grand General sent condolences and offerings,
bestowing an honorable posthumous title,
saying:
"The summoned scholar Master Chén
was endowed with the essence of the sacred peaks and rivers,
and embodied the purity of the spiritual luminaries.
Heaven was reluctant to leave the elder behind,
who served as a shield for our King.
Now the beam has collapsed and the wise man has withered;
at this time, there is no law to follow.
The gentry and the Confucian scholars,
discussing his virtue and deliberating on his traces,
bestow the posthumous title of Master Wénfàn."
The Commentary says:
"How splendid is his culture!"
The Book of Documents says:
"The Nine Categories of the Great Plan,
through which the constant relations are regulated."
'Wén' (Culture) serves as the outward manifestation of virtue,
and 'Fàn' (Exemplar) serves as the standard for scholars.
To have taught while alive and to receive a title when gone—
is this not fitting?
The Three Excellencies sent clerks to offer sacrifices with the middle animal offering.
The Inspector paid his respectful condolences.
The Governor of Nányáng, Lord Cáo, ordered an official to compose a eulogy, which said:
"How glorious was Master Chén,
born to meet the needs of the age!
Containing light and pure virtue,
he served as a model for scholars.
His beginnings were upright,
and his end was also fine.
Following the rites until his death,
how magnificent is his pure reputation!"
Subordinate officials and clerks were sent
to attend the gathering in succession,
and a stone was carved to make an inscription.
The Commandery Vice-Governor and officials from neighboring counties attended the funeral.
Xún Címíng, Hán Yuánzhǎng, and more than five hundred others,
wearing hemp mourning clothes and taking their positions,
escorted him in sorrow.
Those from near and far who gathered for the funeral
numbered more than a thousand.
Lord Zhǒng, the Governor of Hénán, visited the commandery,
where he looked back and sighed at the merits and virtues,
recording the high conduct,
believing that few from near or far could equal him.
He tasked a high-ranking clerk
to complete an inscription in a timely manner.
This can be called having glory in life and sorrow in death,
one who has died but is immortal.
Thus, the inscription was made, saying:
Towering is the lofty peak,
which brought forth the omens and sent down the spirit;
O, the August Master,
who held treasures and embraced rarities.
Why did the Vast Heaven
let this man of culture perish?
His subtle words are cut off and lost;
how shall those who come later hear them?
Chirp, chirp, go the yellow birds,
as they gather on the thorny bushes.
A life cannot be ransomed;
what end is there to this grief!
The highest achievement is to establish virtue;
the next is to establish merit;
this is what is meant by immortality.
Thus, when Zǐchǎn died,
Xuānní wept for the love he left behind;
when Suí Wǔ passed away,
Zhào Wén cherished his remaining influence.
In Lord Wénjiǎn, we see this again.
The Lord's taboo name was Yuān,
his courtesy name was Yànhuí,
and he was a native of Yángdí in Hénán.
Wēizǐ laid the foundation with supreme benevolence,
and Sòng Duàn was given a lineage name for his great merit.
Reaching the two Hàn dynasties,
refined Confucianism continued through the generations;
from the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onward,
successive generations added to the brilliance.
His ancestor was the Grand Tutor, Lord Yuánmù,
whose virtue matched the age
and whose conduct was a model for the region.
Deeply discerning of good and bad,
he did not let criticism or praise show in his words;
shining in his service to the royal house,
he always embraced the Way of modesty and emptiness.
He could be described as one whose gentleness became refined,
and whose will remained obscure.
Since then,
there has been no deviation from the former rules;
officials were appointed based on worthiness,
and high ranks followed one after another.
The Lord was endowed with the spiritual brilliance of rivers and mountains,
and held the radiance of jade ritual vessels;
harmony and submissiveness were condensed within,
while excellence and splendor were manifested without.
His spirit flourished from his early studies,
and his achievements grew great by the time he reached adulthood.
Thus, with benevolence as the warp and righteousness as the woof,
he was kind and harmonious within the family gates;
his voice was like the sound of gold and jade,
resonating clearly throughout the land.
His filial piety and respect were pure and deep,
reaching the utmost level naturally;
he exhausted himself in providing joy day and night,
and people found no fault in him.
He wandered leisurely in the garden of culture and elegance,
and soared in the field of rites and music.
His demeanor was as bright as the autumn moon,
and his reputation as moist as the spring clouds.
His temperament was grand and deep;
neither joy nor anger could be seen in its depths.
His mind was clear and penetrating;
when employing others, his words always originated from himself.
How vast!
How expansive!
It could be said that he was like water that does not become clear when settled,
nor turbid when stirred.
Yuán Yángyuán's talent and spirit were lofty and unique,
and his evaluations were precise and refined;
Sòng Wéntì was upright and wise in presiding over the court,
and his appreciation was never mistaken.
While Yuán spread his reputation far and wide,
the Emperor also settled a marriage with the imperial family.
He was chosen to marry Princess Yúyáo
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Compared to Shūgāo of the Hàn
or the marriage of Wǔzǐ of the Jìn,
they were nothing in comparison.
He began his career as an Assistant Gentleman of the Editorial Service,
and was transferred to become a Special Drafter for the Crown Prince.
Taking office and entering the court,
he was a prominent figure of the age;
rising and falling within the two palaces,
he was truly a treasure of the times.
As his role as a model for all was established,
the hope for him to become a high minister gathered.
He went out to participate in the military affairs of the Grand Chancellor,
and entered to serve as the Crown Prince's Companion,
soon after being promoted to Assistant Director of the Palace Library.
Assisting the Way in the court of the high ministers,
and overseeing literature in the heavenly pavilion;
he shone among the feudal lords,
and his refined reputation was exceptionally great.
He left office due to mourning for his father,
and his mourning exceeded even the deepest grief,
nearly leading to his physical destruction.
Those with knowledge were moved by his feelings,
and even passersby were saddened by his state.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
The King's words are like silk threads;
when they issue forth, they are like silken cords.
He diligently occupied his official post,
and his wisdom was applied with harmony.
At that time, the Prince of Xīn'ān's favor was the greatest among the various domains;
as he spread the state's teachings abroad,
the selection of his assistants
exquisitely exhausted the nation's brilliance.
He went out to serve as Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ
and transferred to become Shàngshū Lìbù Láng.
He wielded the power of selection with fairness
and managed complexities with simplicity.
Péi Kǎi's clarity and permeability
and Wáng Róng's conciseness
were once again found in him.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era,
he entered the court as Shìzhōng.
Before a month had passed,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
At this time, the heavenly path was newly pacified,
but the royal road was still obstructed.
The great army set out,
and the ranks of officials were not yet unified.
Internally, he assisted with strategies and plans;
externally, he stabilized the social hierarchy.
His victories were achieved from afar,
and the distinction between right and wrong became clear.
Rewards did not overlook merit,
and appointments did not overlook virtue.
His achievements were clear to the Emperor's heart,
and his reputation reached the ears of all.
When affairs were settled,
he was to assume the post of Tàizǐ Yòuwèishuài,
but he firmly declined and did not accept.
Soon after, he took the post of Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
For his merit in the inner councils,
he received a rank of respectful service
and was enfeoffed as the Founding Count of Yúdū Xiàn
with a household fief of five hundred.
Having held the principle of declining honors
and cherishing the modest ambition of Qǐnqiū,
the lands and towns he received
did not exceed a hundred jǐng.
After a long time,
he again became Shìzhōng
and assumed the post of Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
He exerted every effort in offering advice and correcting faults,
equal to the merit of Shānfǔ;
he harmonized the King's troops,
combining the prestige of Fāng Shū.
Dānyáng, the capital's auxiliary,
was a standard for far and near;
Wúxīng, the strategic gateway,
was truly a vital limb.
He twice served as Governor,
both times awarded the cicada-adorned crown.
Governance was perfected through ritual,
and the people thereby found rest.
When Emperor Míng was unwell,
and the heir was young and tender,
the legacy entrusted to him
truly belonged to the hope of the times.
He was summoned as Lìbù Shàngshū
to lead the Wèiwèi,
but he firmly declined and did not accept.
He was alternatively appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
He straightened the flow and maintained balance,
being externally lenient and internally upright.
He promoted the high plans of the sixteen virtuous ones
and proclaimed the "Yóu Gēng," leaving behind songs.
When Tàizōng passed away,
his last will appointed the Duke as Sǎnqì Chángshì,
Zhōngshū Lìng,
and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Bidding farewell to the deceased and serving the living,
his loyalty and integrity were truly luminous.
Holding the balance of the state,
he maintained the four directions.
The hundred officials moved according to principles,
and military administration was prepared without warning.
The Duke's ascent to the high steps to govern the world
was considered a beautiful tale by gentlemen,
just as Mèng Kē took delight in Yuèzhèng
and Yáng Zhí took pleasure in Shìbó.
When he entered mourning for his biological mother,
he resigned from his posts.
The severity of his emaciation and illness
reached the utmost due to his sincere heart.
The court discussion was that he should continue his duties,
as the Duke of Lǔ had set a precedent;
preserving the public and forgetting the private,
he provided a clear standard.
Thus an imperial edict was issued
to urgently recall him to his duties.
He firmly requested to wait for a year,
with petitions following one after another.
But time did not wait,
and he humbled himself to promote transformation.
It happened to be a time of dynastic decline,
and the imperial relatives rebelled from within;
the Prince of Guìyáng lost his way
and coveted the throne.
When he beat the oars, the dark waves were shaken;
when he raised the banners, the sun and moon were eclipsed.
Coming out of the Yangtze branches like the wind,
he entered the capital like thunder.
Bowstrings sounded at the ancestral temple,
and arrows flew at the palace gates.
Although heroic ministers faced the battle
and the main rebel was then destroyed,
the remaining party was truly numerous,
and the palaces and temples were anxiously pressed.
The Duke then gathered soldiers as brave as bears
and ministers with no double-heartedness;
they united their strength and exhausted their plans,
overcoming and pacifying the calamity.
He stabilized the state's fate when it hung by a thread
and saved the royal bond from collapse.
This was truly due to the majestic wind of Tàizǔ,
but also the Duke's benevolent assistance.
It can be said his virtue and punishment were detailed,
and his ritual and righteousness were trustworthy;
he was an instrument of war.
For his merit in pacifying the disaster,
he was advanced to the rank of Hóu
and concurrently appointed Shàngshū Lìng
and Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
granted twenty ceremonial sword-bearers.
Having achieved success, he did not claim it,
firmly holding to modesty.
He was alternatively appointed Shìzhōng
and Zhōngshū Jiān,
while remaining Hùjūn as before.
Again, he left office to observe mourning for his mother.
Although the matter arose from ritual duty,
his feelings were equal to natural kinship.
Yán Dīng's compliance with ritual
and the two Liáns' excellence in mourning—
how could they surpass this!
Heaven was weary of Sòng's virtue,
and the Water cycle reached its end.
The succeeding king was reckless and negligent on the throne,
and powerful ministers overran Jīngchǔ.
Regarding the merit of deposing the muddled and continuing the lineage,
and the virtue of quelling chaos and pacifying the people,
the Duke truly assisted the grand design
and participated in the divine calculations.
Although he lacked the merit of direct military command,
he also had the achievements of civilian governance.
He thus became Sīkōng,
and the mountains and rivers were thereby ordered;
concurrently appointed Wèijūn,
the military administration was harmonious and peaceful.
Soon after the virtue of Qí rose like a dragon,
Shùn Huáng loftily abdicated the throne.
Having deeply understood the movements of the Mandate of Heaven,
he assisted and praised the enterprise of following the seasons.
His assistance was balanced and correct;
his excellent principles were grand and far-reaching.
He established a noble reputation
and left behind words of wisdom,
just as Jì and Qiè served the Yú and Xià,
or Xún and Péi served the Wèi and Jìn.
Unless one has a heart of absolute public spirit
and long observes the principles of rise and fall,
who could illustriously assist five emperors
and reverently brighten two dynasties?
He was greatly enfeoffed in Nánkāng
and then ascended to the position of the Three Excellencies;
though offered land and territory,
he firmly declined the governance of a feudal state.
The Shàngshū Lìng of today
is the Zhǒngzǎi of old;
although its rank is lighter than the Gǔnsī,
its responsibility is more profound than that of all other officials.
Briefly following his humble intentions,
he was reassigned to lead the court.
Those nearby had no dissenting words,
and those far away had no different expectations.
The Emperor praised his magnificent merits
and reiterated the previous patent of appointment.
He upheld the Five Rites to rectify the people
and simplified the Eight Punishments so they were rarely used.
Thus he could gallop in achievement along the broad road
and extend the kindness of the wise ruler.
In righteousness, he provided respect;
in sentiment, he was like a friend in plain clothes.
He went out to accompany the imperial carriage
and entered to serve in the curtained palace.
He looked up at the high chants of the Nánfēng
and partook of the secret treasures of the Dōngyě.
There were refined discussions on mornings of governance
and the unfolding of texts on evenings of private banquets.
Mingled with the virtue of wine,
and interspersed with the heart of the zither.
A faint lingering glow remains,
leaving thoughts in the distance.
The lord showed the warmth of a winter sun;
the minister fulfilled the warnings of autumn frost.
Solemn and reverent,
dignified and harmonious.
Thus one sees that the ruler and parent are of the same essence
and knows that the three objects of devotion are as one.
When Tàizǔ ascended to the heavens,
he solicitously entrusted the Duke with his final wishes.
He served as Shìzhōng
and Sītú, overseeing the Lù Shàngshū Shì.
He received the instructions from the jade table
and performed the rites of the imperial mourning clothes.
Selecting the fine codes of the August Qí,
he brought about a reputation and transformation of peaceful harmony.
Peace within and completion without
truly illustrated his former duties.
He was granted an additional thirty Bānjiàn;
the ritual objects had their proper appearance,
and the insignia were appropriate.
His position was noble yet his etiquette was humble;
he dwelt on high but thought of descending.
From summer into autumn,
he requested retirement due to illness.
The court was reluctant to go against his modest wishes,
and to manifest his transcendent loftiness,
he was reassigned as Sīkōng
and Piàoqì Dàjiāngjūn,
while remaining Shìzhōng and Lù Shàngshū as before.
His great fate was not long;
his grave illness lingered.
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán, on the twenty-first day of the eighth month, he died at his private residence,
at the age of forty-eight.
Anciently, when Liǔ Zhuāng was critically ill,
the Lord of Wèi halted the rites when he should have sacrificed;
when Yàn Yīng passed away,
the Lord of Qí rushed his carriage and wept while walking.
Upon the Duke’s passing,
the Sage Court above was shaken with grief,
and the various lords below were moved with fear.
How could it be that sorrow entwined only one country,
or that the pain was deep for the sovereign alone!
He was posthumously promoted to Tàizǎi,
remaining Shìzhōng and Lù Shàngshū as before.
He was granted the Jié, Yǔbǎo, Gǔchuī, and sixty Bānjiàn,
and given the posthumous title Wénjiǎn,
according to the rites.
He who dwells in virtue
cannot have his purity harmed by the myriad things.
He who travels with an empty self
cannot have his bearing disturbed by the current age.
He equated the noble and the low like a gentle breeze
and forgot glory and disgrace between himself and others.
Only then can one benefit the whole world
and end one's years in peace.
Planning the beginning and the end,
he thus avoided regret.
Who can say they are fully prepared?
The Duke truly was.
Therefore, his righteousness bound the gentlemen,
and his kindness moistened the common people.
What words and images cannot form,
and descriptions and songs cannot exhaust.
His former subordinates, such-and-such,
moved by the ceaseless flow of the passing river
and mourning the fading of the clear light,
heard the praises in the villages
and beheld the elegant songs in the capital.
Thinking of the inscriptions on the Wèi tripod
and the legacy of the Jìn bell,
they look up at the high mountain
and carve this dark stone to display his virtue.
The eulogy says:
The essence of the stars responded to the turn of fate;
the spirit of the Àng constellation sent down good fortune.
The Sovereign was enlightened;
the ministers were virtuous.
Heaven scrutinized the revolving stars;
he followed the footsteps of former kings.
Respectful to the Great Minister,
who embodied the subtle and knew the manifest.
Always filial in speech;
friendly by nature.
Benevolence permeated and saved all;
love was deep and he was good at guidance.
Observing the sea, he matched its capacity;
ascending the peak, he equaled its mass.
Of the five ministers, he was the sixth;
of the eight paragons, he was the ninth.
Planning within the curtains,
he shone upon the steps of the Three Excellencies.
None afar were not respectful;
none nearby were not cherished.
Like the wind bending the grass;
like music in harmony.
Illustrating our imperial codes;
harmonizing the common people.
Following the rites and treading in humility;
truly he was the mainstay of the state.
His tracks were constrained in the red carriage;
his will was high in the humble hut.
Far-reaching was the profound mystery;
lush was his literary output.
His righteousness flowed like a river;
his writing dispersed like mist.
The lofty structure has collapsed;
the shade of the bridge is now missing.
His virtuous principles have no successor;
his appearance has long departed.
Sorrowful are the remaining traces;
resonant is the legacy.
Long-lasting and ever-new;
used and never exhausted.

the five planets entered the Mansion constellation.
Also making their horses white,
they served the Zhōu King as vassals.
The main branch and its various lineages,
took their surname from the fief of Cài.
They traveled from Xú to the east;
their righteousness was equal to the migration to Liáng.
From that time onward,
they held high offices, wearing the green and purple.
Their lofty foundation was like towering cliffs;
their long ripples were vast and overflowing.
Only the Sage creates the world,
flying like a dragon with heavenly strides.
Establishing the tripods and enacting changes,
removing the old and spreading the new.
Gāo Huáng was most illustrious,
looking up to receive the gaze of Heaven.
Jǐng Huáng was truly magnificent,
initiating the grand destiny.
Like a high mountain towering steeply,
a hero of the age rose as a worthy man.
Receiving the timely birth of virtue,
surpassing the past and illuminating the future.
Attentive in accomplishing affairs,
he awakened before the people.
Though his position was not the Great Treasure of the throne,
his nobility was granted by High Heaven.
When he first began his career,
his pure reputation spread far.
Ascending and descending the ornate palace steps,
moving gracefully at the gates of the Wèi Palace.
Benevolent dew moistened Wú;
a kindly breeze fanned the land of Yuè.
Crossing the Xià and passing the Hàn,
governance was perfected within a month.
Simplicity was surely followed,
and daily renewal became his greatness.
Toward those above, he was compassionate;
toward those below, he was solemn and respectful.
The plants and trees did not wither prematurely;
the insects followed their nature.
I have fragrant orchids,
which the people sing of in unison.
The various barbarian tribes were restless,
divided by cliffs and separated by peaks.
They poured down the mountains,
following him like clouds.
Leading wives and carrying children,
they formed crowds with burdens on their backs.
Turning their heads to request officials,
what more needs to be said!
In the past, we heard of the Way of Heaven,
where benevolence fails none.
Why is that azure sky so,
to stop the mountain at the last basket of earth?
The four horses were just galloping,
when the six dragons suddenly halted their reins.
To whom shall the people look up?
The state is exhausted and distressed.
When Yàn Píng died in Qí,
people wept on the roads to pay their respects.
When the Prince of Chāng Guó went to Zhào,
all the states shed tears.
How much more so for our lord,
the younger brother of the Emperor.
Grief is felt by the common people;
wailing rises from the palace steps.
The steps are destroyed while the coffin remains;
the river flows while the funeral carriage returns.
Competing to offer rustic sacrifices,
struggling to cling to the departing wheels.
Following the shore and calling out in pursuit,
overlooking the waves and weeping in sight.
Never ending through all eternity,
only the orchids and chrysanthemums remain.
The road leads from the Emperor’s Isle,
but the red carriage is no longer driven.
Facing east toward the graveyard,
entering the palace of the long night.
The flowing river does not wait,
and pure gold is hard to transform.
Bells and stones are carved in vain,
for his fragrant reputation has departed forever.
Having been called the one who returned to Lài,
and also the wife of Hóng;
possessing such excellent virtue,
she was equal to him in every way.
Truly assisting her gentleman,
with a hairpin of wormwood and a staff of goosefoot;
joyfully carrying burdens,
in the fields of Jì.
In her domestic life, she followed the proper way,
and was often heard to be righteous and yielding.
Receiving instruction in Dānyáng,
she spread the influence of the Chancellor.
Her reputation was great in both families;
her refined character was long admired.
Manifesting talent and virtue from the start,
the virtue of the inner chambers was indeed sincere.
Overgrown is the village of Zhèng;
lonely is the tomb of Yáng.
Uneven are the trees of Kǒng,
which have grown from saplings to the size of a hug.
Briefly opening the desolate path,
then long closing the dark mound.
Husband noble and wife honored,
not just by rank, but by their dignity.
An Account of the Conduct of Xiāo Gōng of Zhōng Dū Lǐ, Dū Xiāng, Nán Lánlíng Jùn, Nán Xú Zhōu, at Age Thirty-five.
The Lord’s Way was secondary only to innate knowledge,
illuminating those around him and approaching the level of the sages.
Filial piety is the beginning of human relations,
and loyalty is a fine virtue;
the Lord truly embodied these,
which were not attained through mere praise or blame.
His natural talent was broad and abundant;
his learning was comprehensive and clear.
As for the Rites of Qūtái,
and the Classic of Changes of the Nine Masters,
the division of Music by Lóng and Zhào,
and the analysis of Poetry by Qí and Hán—
what Chén Nóng had not fully investigated,
and what the Prince of Héjiān had not compiled—
if there were any of these,
was there any he did not master!
In the past, Prince Xiàn of Pèi was consulted at the Yúntái,
the Prince of Dōngpíng shared fame with Yáng Shǐ,
the Prince of Huáinán gained honor within the time of a meal,
and Chénsī was praised for his seven steps;
compared to the Lord, they are inferior.
Initially,
Shěn Yōuzhī acted overbearingly in the upper reaches of the river,
claiming rebellion in the Shǎnfú region.
The Sòng General of Zhènxī, the Prince of Jìnxī,
and the General of Nánzhōngláng, the Prince of Shàolíng,
both were stationed at Pénkǒu.
Shìzǔ assisted the two principalities,
and was in general charge of the western campaign.
The Lord was serving in the army at that time,
as the provisional General of Níngshuò and Military Commander of the Zhènxī Headquarters,
and as the provisional Acting Adjutant and Legal Officer of the Nánzhōngláng Headquarters.
At that time, signal fires lit up the clouds,
and urgent messages flew like the wind;
plans emerged from his inner circle,
and the responsibility for records was critical.
He was promoted to Aide and Secretary of the Left Guard for the Prince of Shàolíng.
Having fulfilled the search for talent,
he truly took on the responsibility of being an exemplar.
The brush and knife were not enough to declare his merit,
but his character and bearing brought great benefit.
He was appointed as a Friend to the Prince of Shàolíng,
and later as the Chief Administrator for the Prince of Shàolíng in Ānnán.
Dōngxià is a place of strategic importance,
where the passes and rivers are layered;
he was selected from among many and appointed,
for his diligence and excellence lay there.
He was appointed Commissioner with a Tally,
Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Five Commanderies of Huìjī, Dōngyáng, Línhǎi, Yǒngjiā, and Xīn’ān,
General of Fǔguó,
and Governor of Huìjī.
Tàizǔ received the mandate,
and widely established protective screens for the throne.
The Duke, by virtue of being a son of Gāozhāo and Wǔmù,
was both a close relative and an exceptionally virtuous man.
He was enfeoffed as the Wénxǐ Xiàn Kāiguó Gōng [Founding Duke of Wenxi County],
with a fief of one thousand households.
His administrative performance was consistently rated the best,
and he was promoted to the rank of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn [General of the Champion Army].
The shamans of the Yuè people
observed his upright influence and transformed their customs;
the chieftains of the bamboo forests
were moved by his righteousness and humility, abandoning their fortified strongholds.
The old man of Xié forgot his sunset years,
and Lóngqiū found his eastern marshes too narrow.
It happened that Empress Wǔmù passed away,
and the Duke traveled by starlight in great haste,
weeping tears of blood over a thousand lǐ.
Not a drop of water or broth entered his mouth
as he arrived from Yǔxué.
When the period for removing the external mourning garments arrived,
his heart remained filled with grief and internal sorrow.
Although the rites were constrained by the rules of rank reduction
and he was pressed by the exigencies of official duties,
he harbored deep grief within his very flesh,
and his profound pain was like a lingering wound.
Thus we know that bells and drums are not the essence of music,
and coarse hemp garments are not the vital part of the intensity of mourning.
He was reassigned as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn [General Who Conquers Barbarians]
and Dānyáng Yǐn [Governor of Danyang].
Families of good standing migrated in,
and the imperial relatives' quarters were brought under his administration.
Governance did not follow a single track,
as customs from the five directions were all present.
Internally, the Duke established leniency and clarity;
externally, he applied simplicity and kindness.
The sacred capital became harmonious,
and the area under the imperial carriage became pure.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to the title of Jìnglíng Jùnwáng [Prince of Jingling Commandery],
and one thousand households were added to his fief.
He was further appointed Shǐchíjié [Commissioner with Ritual Staff],
Dūdū Nán-Xú-Yǎn Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì [Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Nan-Xu and Nan-Yan Provinces],
Zhènběi Jiāngjūn [General Who Guards the North],
and Nán-Xú Zhōu Cìshǐ [Governor of Nan-Xu Province].
He was then promoted to Shǐchíjié Shìzhōng [Commissioner with Ritual Staff and Palace Attendant],
Dūdū Nán-Yǎn-Xú-Běi-Yǎn-Qīng-Jì Wǔzhōu Zhūjūnshì [Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for the Five Provinces of Nan-Yan, Xu, Bei-Yan, Qing, and Ji],
Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn [General Who Conquers the North],
and Nán-Yǎn Zhōu Cìshǐ [Governor of Nan-Yan Province].
The Yan and Xu regions shared a border
and had long been moistened by the river's grace.
Even before he alighted from his carriage,
his reputation for benevolence had already spread.
The watchman’s clappers at the Jade Pass were silent,
and the northern gates remained unbolted.
The imperial decree held that while supervising the regional governors
and promoting the state’s education
are important provincial responsibilities,
they are light compared to central duties.
He was summoned as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn [General of the Central Army]
and concurrently appointed Sītú [Minister of Education],
remaining Shìzhōng as before.
Again he was appointed Chēqì Jiāngjūn [General of Chariots and Cavalry],
concurrently Sītú,
and Shìzhōng as before.
Then he was formally appointed Sītú,
with Shìzhōng again as before.
Above, he harmonized the Three Stars;
below, he spread the Five Canons.
He opened the gate of profound mysteries to manifest transformation,
and silenced the ringing bells to embody the state.
He assisted in the governance of filial piety
and refined the central teachings.
To seize gold was considered a shame in litigation,
and even when his fields were trampled, he remained silent.
He did not carve away his natural simplicity,
and used reserve to shroud his brilliance.
That the reputation and transformation of the age were so orderly
was entirely due to the Duke.
When schools were first established,
he was the model for the noble youths;
in the selection of masters,
he truly served as a paragon for the people.
With his current office, he oversaw the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ [Chancellor of the National Academy],
but he firmly declined and did not accept.
When the Eight Offices were first opened,
the Duke was appointed Shàngshū Lìng [President of the Department of State Affairs].
In this manner, he presented his memorials,
and the hundred officials were in proper order.
Now, the way of the state
involves a mutual relationship between the public and the private;
the righteousness between sovereign and kin
alternates between concealment and frankness.
The Duke was consistent in both these extremes,
and love and respect converged in him.
His sincerity was bright and he fully observed all regulations,
and his plans and strategies were grand and far-reaching.
He was further appointed Shǐchíjié Dūdū Yángzhōu Zhūjūnshì [Commissioner with Ritual Staff and Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Yangzhou],
and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ [Governor of Yangzhou],
with all his previous offices remaining as before.
Formerly it was just the region of the Huái and the sea,
but now it was a divinely governed province.
Registered households were prosperous and numerous,
and the customs of the people flourished.
His transformation through non-action
was as effective as if he had gone door-to-door to persuade everyone.
After a short while,
he was relieved of the post of Shàngshū Lìng
and reassigned as Zhōngshū Jiān [Director of the Secretariat],
with all other posts remaining as before.
He offered advice at the pivot of government,
and the imperial edicts were properly harmonized.
When Emperor Wǔ passed away,
the trust placed in him was as deep as bearing the weight of the imperial map.
The Duke looked up to the state statutes
and bowed down to follow the final entrustment.
He beat his breast in mourning for his close kin
and leaped in grief until he fell to the ground.
His conduct during the mourning period
was once again as it had been during the mourning for Empress Wǔmù.
The sagely sovereign has risen to succeed the throne,
and you occupy a position like that of Dàn Shì.
An edict was issued to appoint you as Tài Fù,
concurrently holding the post of Sī Tú,
with all other titles remaining as before.
You sit to deliberate upon the Way,
and your every action demonstrates virtue;
your status is supreme and the honors paid to you are peerless,
for among the imperial kin and the virtuous, none is your equal.
Another edict granted the Duke the privilege of entering the court without hurried steps,
being announced without his personal name,
and wearing his sword and shoes into the palace hall.
The virtue of Xiāo Fù
and the kinship of Cáo Mǎ
are both possessed by the Duke.
Furthermore, to extend prestige and honor the Way,
and to exalt the lineage of virtue,
he was promoted to Overseer of Military Affairs of Nán Xú Zhōu,
with all other titles remaining as before.
He repeatedly submitted memorials
declining honors even until his death.
Heaven was not kind enough to spare him;
the lofty peaks of Liáng Yuè have collapsed.
On a certain day of a certain month in a certain year, he passed away
at the age of thirty-five.
An edict granted him a Wēn Míng coffin and inner casket,
to be shrouded in the Gǔn Zhāng robes,
with the full rites of the Nine Honors.
The Dà Hóng Lú was dispatched to oversee the funeral,
with offerings made morning and evening
supplied by the Tài Guān,
according to the rites.
Thus, grief reached its peak at Jīn Mén,
and sorrow filled Cháng Lè.
It was not merely that the grain-pounders ceased their songs
or the workshops closed their gates!
Then an edict was issued, saying:
"To extol and exalt great virtue
is a fine precedent of former kings;
to honor the deceased and respect kin
is the height of following one's feelings.
Therefore, the former Envoy with Patent, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yáng Zhōu,
Zhōng Shū Jiān,
Tài Fù,
concurrently Sī Tú,
Cì Shǐ of Yáng Zhōu,
and Jìng Líng Wáng,
who was newly appointed as Overseer of Nán Xú Zhōu,
embodied sagacity and walked in righteousness;
his spiritual insight was deep and far-reaching.
His Way was the pinnacle of the people's respect,
and all looked up to him as the standard of truth.
Since his youth,
his filial piety and brotherly love were fully manifest.
When he came to assist in the imperial mission,
he cooperated in elevating the great enterprise.
He harmonized the ministerial stars
and successfully promulgated the Five Teachings.
Reporting at the head of the court,
all administrative affairs were in harmony.
Entrusted with the heavy duty of the former Emperor's dying wish,
his responsibility was like that of a regent.
Truly, his excellence matched the Èr Nán,
and his conduct followed the pattern of past sages.
Just as we relied on his protection and support
to forever assist in the era of peace and harmony,
Heaven was not kind enough to spare him,
and suddenly he passed away.
Sorrow and longing pierce the heart
and tremble within my soul.
Now, as the distant date of the burial approaches,
the tortoise shell divination has shown auspicious signs.
To grandly exalt the glorious regulations
and thus spread his noble influence,
he is posthumously granted the Golden Battle-axe,
Shì Zhōng,
Commander-in-Chief of All Internal and External Military Affairs,
Tài Zǎi,
Acting Grand General,
and Mù of Yáng Zhōu,
with the green and dark-blue ribbons,
and the full rites and regalia of the Jiǔ Xī.
He remains Envoy with Patent,
Zhōng Shū Jiān,
and Prince as before.
He is granted a carriage with nine tassels,
a yellow canopy with a phoenix pennant on the left,
a funerary carriage,
drum and wind ensembles with feather canopies for the front and rear sections,
two troupes for funeral songs,
and one hundred Tiger Warriors with ceremonial swords.
The funeral rites shall entirely follow the precedent of Jìn Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng Fú."
The Duke’s path and knowledge were profound and distant,
and his inner and outer nature were harmoniously integrated;
he was deep like ten thousand acres of water
and towering like a thousand fathoms.
Servants and concubines never saw his joy or anger,
and close attendants never saw him lax or negligent.
The virtues of others
he regarded as if they were his own.
When the people were not good,
the Duke truly felt it as his own shame.
He guided and received others with gentle courtesy,
treating them with a kind expression.
In serving his superiors,
he was fond of seeking criticism to correct himself.
He was scrupulous regarding the accumulation of wealth
and tireless in giving to others.
As the Emperor's son and the youngest heir,
his orders were followed and his prohibitions obeyed;
the laws of the state and the celestial statutes
were held within his grasp.
He never prosecuted anyone with light penalties,
or barred people from office based on severe accusations.
When others were lacking,
he inwardly forgave them as he would himself.
When offended unintentionally,
he would always yield for the sake of reason.
Bearing the weight of the world,
he embodied the excellence of the people.
Flowery robes and coarse hemp were the same to him;
the mountain-patterned garments and thatched huts shared the same leisure.
Fertile fields and spacious houses
accorded with the words of Zhòngcháng;
Máng Shān and Luò Shuǐ
corresponded with the will of Yìng Sǒu.
His gardens in the eastern lands
treated high office as a mere trifle.
Thus, he built halls nestled in the forest
and extended structures beside the cliffs.
The clear cries of gibbons competed with the water-clock keepers at dawn,
while red curtains and white rapids shimmered together.
Placed in an empty chamber,
how could one distinguish between the city and the wilderness?
The eminent Hé Diǎn
walked in straw sandals at the slope of Zhōng Ā;
the summoned scholar Liú Qiú
presented books at Wèi Yuè.
He gifted them with the robes of ancients,
treated them with extraordinary courtesy,
and humbled himself with his love for virtue,
expressing his intention to attract the noble-minded.
Thus one knows that Dàchūn humbled himself before the five princes,
and Jūndà lowered his integrity before the Empress.
There were indeed reasons for this.
As for the rarity of the plants and trees
and the beauty of the springs and rocks,
the Duke’s own Shānjū Sìshí Xù
has described them in detail.
Wén Huángdì cultivated virtue in the Eastern Palace,
matching the path of the creators of old.
Thereupon he composed the "Nine Words,"
which truly encompassed all the hundred types of conduct.
They guide matrimonial bonds before they have even sprouted,
and extend bright warnings to this day.
This is not merely for the mornings and evenings of a thousand years,
but rather for ten thousand generations as one.
He ordered the Duke to provide annotations and explanations,
and General of the Guard Wáng Jiǎn compiled them and wrote a preface.
When the mountain dwelling was first constructed,
he went there alone in transcendence,
looked around and said:
"The dead can return,
but who shall enter the chamber with me?"
Thinking back on former worthies,
it was as if he were facing their spirits.
Thus he ordered painters
to depict them on the porches and windows.
Soon after, while reflecting on the wise and heroic,
he also thought of the talented and virtuous women;
even the integrity of an ordinary woman
was found worthy of inclusion.
There was a guest traveling in the Liáng court
who stepped forward composedly and said:
"I have yet to see one who truly loves virtue;
I am secretly perplexed by this."
Immediately, the Duke ordered deletions and revisions,
not even pausing to put down his staff.
The Duke believed that once words leave the mouth,
even the swiftest horses like Jì and Lù cannot catch them;
if listening and receiving are once mistaken,
the error will lead a thousand miles astray.
The admonitions and inscriptions he composed
accumulated into scrolls;
on gates, steps, doors, and mats,
he placed objects to convey lessons.
Before this, lightning struck the outer sleeping quarters;
the craftsmen considered it inauspicious
and were about to repair it.
The Duke said:
"This is a heavenly reprimand;
do not modify or repair it,
so it may record my faults
and cause me to be cautious and fearful without negligence."
He followed advice like water flowing downstream,
and emptied himself as if he were insufficient.
As for words as piercing as medicine,
he found them as flavorful as fine food;
his sincerity necessarily came from within,
and his countenance showed no outward pretense of joy.
Noble yet fond of ritual,
he found joy and refuge in the classics.
Though pulled by worldly affairs,
he was diligent without rest.
Thus he compiled the *Sìbù Yàolüè*
and *Jìngzhùzǐ*,
establishing them as a singular school
to be suspended alongside the sun and moon.
He broadened the style of Zhū and Sì,
and expanded the transformation of Jiāwéi.
When his illness became critical and he lingered,
his parting words filled the ears;
his request to forgo a formal burial
was of the utmost sincerity and distress.
Is this not what the ancients meant by "establishing words in the world
and not decaying after death"?
Regarding the ritual for a posthumous name,
please follow the precedents of former luminaries.
Respectfully submitted.
Jiǎ Yì served as the Grand Tutor to the King of Chángshā.
After being exiled,
he was dissatisfied in his mind.
When crossing the Xiāng River,
he composed a rhapsody to lament Qū Yuán.
Qū Yuán
was a worthy minister of Chǔ,
but was slandered and banished;
he composed the *Lísāo* rhapsody.
Its final lines say:
"It is over!
The state has no one,
and no one knows me!"
He then threw himself into the Mìluó and died.
Jiǎ Yì felt a lingering sorrow for him
and used him as a self-metaphor.
The lyrics say:
Respectfully receiving your gracious kindness,
I await my punishment in Chángshā.
I have heard of Qū Yuán
drowning himself in the Mìluó.
Entrusting my words to the Xiāng currents,
I respectfully lament you, sir.
Having encountered a world without limits,
you thus destroyed your own body.
Alas, how sorrowful!
You met with inauspicious times!
The phoenixes hide in seclusion,
while the owls soar high.
The lowly and worthless are honored and prominent,
while the slandering and flattering achieve their aims.
The worthy and sage are dragged backward,
while the upright are planted upside down.
The world calls Suí and Yí filthy,
and calls Zhí and Qiào incorruptible.
Mòyé is called blunt,
and a lead knife is called sharp.
Alas, in silence,
life is without cause!
They cast away the Zhōu tripods
and treasure the cracked earthenware gourds.
They hitch tired oxen to chariots
and use lame donkeys as side-horses.
The fine steed Jì droops its ears
and pulls a salt cart.
The Zhāngfǔ ceremonial cap is used as a shoe—
this degradation cannot last long!
Alas, how bitter it is, sir,
that you alone suffered this calamity!
The envoi says:
It is finished!
The state does not know me;
alone and depressed, to whom can I speak?
The phoenix drifts and ascends high;
it surely withdraws and goes far away.
Like the divine dragon in the nine-layered abyss,
it hides deep and cherishes itself.
Forsaking otters and beavers to live in hiding,
how could it follow shrimp, leeches, and worms?
What is valued in the sage's divine virtue
is to keep far from the turbid world and hide oneself.
If a fine steed could be bound and bridled,
how would it differ from a dog or a sheep?
That you, Bān, in confusion met with this fault,
was also because of your own ways, Master!
You traveled the nine provinces to seek a lord;
why must you cherish this particular capital?
The phoenix flies at a thousand fathoms;
seeing the radiance of virtue, it descends.
Seeing the treacherous signs of meager virtue,
it beats its wings and flies far away.
How could those ordinary muddy ditches
accommodate a giant fish that can swallow a boat?
The sturgeons and whales of rivers and lakes
will surely be controlled by mole crickets and ants.
In the eighth year of Yuánkāng,
Lù Jī began his service as a Departmental Gentleman and was appointed to the Palace Library.
While wandering through the Secret Pavilion,
he saw the testamentary edict of Wèi Wǔdì.
He sighed deeply with emotion
and was moved for a long time.
A guest said:
Beginning and ending
are the ultimate return for all things;
death and life
are the boundaries of fate.
Thus one feels sorrow only when attending a funeral
and ceases weeping upon seeing the withered roots.
Now you are grieving at the span of a hundred years,
and raising sorrow in a place without emotion;
I wonder if you only know that sorrow can exist,
but do not yet realize that emotion can be absent?
Jī answered him, saying:
Now, a solar eclipse arises from the intersection of paths;
a mountain collapse starts from decaying soil;
these are simply matters of natural fate.
However, the reason the common people find it strange
is perhaps because one endowed with such high and brilliant character
cannot escape the burden of the low and turbid,
or because one occupying a position of perpetual security
eventually suffers the calamity of collapse and departure.
With the power to turn back heaven and topple the sun,
he could not preserve what was within his own physical frame.
With the wisdom to save the world and pacify difficulties,
he suffered distress beneath the Wèi Què.
Thus, one whose influence reached above and below
is now hidden within a small piece of wood;
one whose light shone to the four corners of the world
is now obscured by a tiny patch of earth.
His heroic heart was broken by tender emotions;
his grand designs ended in mournful intentions.
Long-term calculations yielded to short days;
far-reaching tracks were halted on a truncated road.
Alas!
Is it only the blind musicians and official historians who find the eclipsing sun unusual,
or the common folk who wonder at the crumbling cliff?
Observing how he left his final commands to his eldest heir
and bequeathed his plans to his four sons,
his strategy for governing the state was indeed far-reaching,
and his instructions for exalting his house were also grand.
He also said:
“While I was in the army,
I upheld the law.
As for minor fits of anger
or major faults,
you should not imitate them.”
How excellent are the upright words of a man of realization!
Holding his concubine's hand and pointing at Jì Bào to show his four sons, he said:
“I leave him to your care!”
Then his tears fell.
How tragic!
Formerly he took the whole world as his responsibility;
now he entrusts his beloved son to others.
That which is shared by all who perish leaves nothing behind;
that which is gained by those who are gone does not remain.
However, his tender affections within the inner chambers
and his meticulous concern for domestic affairs
were almost too detailed!
He also said:
“My Jié Yú and dancing girls
shall all be stationed at the Tóng Jué Tái.
In the hall of the terrace, set an eight-foot bed
with fine hemp curtains,
and at morning and evening offer dried meat, cooked grain, and the like.
On the first and fifteenth of each month,
they shall perform dances and music toward the curtains.
You all should occasionally ascend the Tóng Jué Tái
to look upon my Xī Líng tomb fields.”
He also said:
“The remaining incense may be distributed among the various ladies.
If the women in the various quarters have nothing to do,
let them learn to make shoe cords for sale.
The ribbons I received through my various offices
are all stored in the treasury.
My surplus clothes and furs
can be placed in a separate storage.
If that is not possible,
the brothers can divide them among themselves.”
Eventually, they were indeed divided.
What is gone need not be sought;
what remains need not be violated;
do not seeking and violating both cause harm?
How sorrowful!
There are great loves that must be lost,
and extreme dislikes that must be encountered;
wisdom cannot remove what is disliked,
and power cannot preserve what is loved.
Therefore, those with foreknowledge do not trouble their minds with such things,
and sages rarely speak of them.
As for tying one's emotions to external objects
and leaving lingering thoughts in the ladies’ chambers,
should these not be abandoned by the worthy and the talented?
Thereupon, filled with indignation and grief, I offer this lament:
He connected with the final threads of the Great Hàn,
and encountered many deviations in the Kingly Way.
He waited in the deep abyss to nurture the scales of the dragon;
he brushed the auspicious clouds and flew far away.
He wielded the divine way to carry his virtue;
he rode the spiritual wind to spread his majesty.
He crushed the various heroes like a lightning strike;
he swept away powerful enemies as if they were nothing.
He pointed to the eight directions with far-reaching strategy;
he surely pruned them before pacifying them.
He regulated the missing canons of the Three Powers;
he opened the forbidden gates of Heaven and Earth.
He lifted the broken strands of the great net;
he retied the loosened strings of the Great Sound.
He swept away the clouds to bring a righteous vision;
he gathered the myriad paths to return to the center.
His great virtue provided wide protection;
drawing upon the sun and moon, he matched their brilliance.
He accomplished great merit across the Nine Provinces;
he was surely esteemed by the whole world.
With such great achievements in human affairs,
where could he go and not reach his goal?
Yet he was about to overturn his basket in a deep valley
and push a mountain into the Nine Heavens.
If principles are exhausted and nature reaches its end,
how can long-term calculations investigate it?
He realized the sorrow of looking upon the river;
surely the great beam must collapse.
In the twenty-third year of Jiàn’ān,
it was truly a difficult time for the Great Mandate.
Though his glory shone in former years,
he would unyoke his carriage in this year.
The descent of the spirit was remote and distant,
a far-reaching hope spanning a thousand years.
Truly this martial spirit was not lost;
he received the spiritual tally and it resided here.
Although the dragon flew to Wén Chāng,
it was not what the King's heart found pleasing.
Indignant at the western Xià, he gathered his troops;
going up the Qín Chuān, he raised his banners.
Passing through Hào Jīng, he felt unwell;
arriving at the banks of the Wèi River, he had doubts.
He hoped to recover on the following day,
but after forty days it became a disaster.
Chanting of the return path, he turned back his banners;
ascending Xiáo and Miǎn, he came back.
Arriving at the banks of the Luò River, his illness became grave;
he pointed to the six armies and said, “Remember this!”
The brilliance of the King
was truly a rarity throughout antiquity.
His majesty preceded heaven and covered the world;
his strength churned the seas and uprooted mountains.
What danger was so treacherous that he could not cross?
What enemy so strong that he could not destroy?
He always turned calamity into fortune
and walked through danger into certain safety.
Yet arriving at this point, all was obscured;
his concerns were locked away without a cause.
He surrendered his life to await the end;
painful was the eternal word as he departed the world.
Caressing his four sons with deep thoughts,
he looked at his own body and sighed in decline.
While his soul had not yet departed,
he borrowed his remaining breath for his final letters.
Holding his concubine with a distressed face,
he pointed to Jì Bào and wept.
His breath surged in his breast with sobs;
tears hung from his lashes and flowed like a flood.
He left the whole land to sleep in peace;
he confined the vastness of heaven within a single coffin.
How lofty and remote was his great magnanimity;
how truly prosperous was his grand legacy.
He thought of the end while caring for the beginning;
he gave his commands as he faced death to begin their proclamation.
He drew upon signs of misfortune to warn against regret;
though it was within him, it was not good.
Pity the lingering attachment of his inner concerns;
regret the trivial details of his final testament.
He bent his grand thoughts toward making shoe cords;
he dusted his pure reflections with leftover incense.
Binding his remaining affections in tender intimacy—
how short was his life, yet how long were his intentions!
Ceremonial robes were displayed by the curtained seat;
fair ladies accompanied him in the jade chambers.
Providing all necessities for the empty vessels;
mournful sounds were emitted by the former singers.
Forcing a sad countenance to follow the rhythm,
hiding falling tears while offering the wine cup.
Nothing, however small, did not remain;
no body, however blessed, did not perish.
One hopes for the resonance of the sage spirit;
one imagines the dark spirit's return to light.
But if form and sound are obscured and gone,
then even the voice and image must be hidden.
The clear strings are tuned for a solo performance;
but when the dried meat and grain are served, who will taste them?
Mourn the darkness of the hemp curtains;
resent the vastness of the Xī Líng.
Ascending the Tóng Jué Tái, all are in sorrow;
gazing with beautiful eyes—what is there to see?
Since he emulated the ancients to leave behind burdens,
he truly simplified the rites and had a modest burial.
But why were the furs and robes kept?
Leaving behind the dust of criticism for later kings.
Alas, where great love resides,
even the wise cannot forget.
Reading his final writings with deep emotion,
I offer this text with sorrow and grief.
The Dōngfǔ was digging a moat north of the city.
Having descended over ten feet,
they discovered an ancient tomb.
There was no mound or boundary above it,
nor were any bricks used.
The outer coffin was made of wood,
and inside were two coffins,
perfectly square,
with no seams at either end.
As for the funerary objects,
made of wood, pottery, bronze, and lacquer,
there were dozens of varieties,
many of strange shapes,
which could not all be identified.
Human figures were carved from wood,
three feet in height,
numbering about twenty.
When first opened and seen,
they all had human forms,
but when poked with an object,
they crumbled into ash at the touch.
On the coffin were over a hundred wǔzhū coins.
In the water were sections of sugarcane, plum and prune pits, and melon seeds,
all of which floated to the surface, not significantly decayed.
No inscription remained,
so the era could not be known.
The official in charge of the city walls ordered them to be reburied at Dōnggāng,
and sacrificed to them with pork and wine.
Since neither their names nor their dates were known,
they were provisionally given the title of Lord Míngmò.
On the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Yuánjiā era,
the Attendant to the Sītú and Concurrent Commander of the Direct Guard,
Supervisor of City Construction and Record Keeper,
Magistrate of Línzhāng and Marquis of Tíng, Zhū Lín,
having prepared a sacrifice of pork and wine,
respectfully offers it to the spirit of Lord Míngmò:
Unworthily leading the labor gangs,
I was in charge of the pounding and building.
Reaching the deep springs to make a moat,
piling up earth to form a foundation.
One outer coffin was opened,
and a pair of coffins was found here.
Casting aside the baskets in sorrow,
letting fall the shovels with tears.
The straw figures are already destroyed,
the clay carriages are broken.
Table and mats are rotted,
ritual vessels have toppled.
The plates still hold plums,
the jars still hold meat and vinegar.
The sugarcane passed down remaining joints,
the melons show their left-over seeds.
Remembering you, sir,
in what era were you born?
How many years did your physical form shine?
How many years has your spirit been hidden?
Did you live long or die young?
Were you prominent or obscure?
The inscriptions have vanished,
your name is not passed down.
Who are your descendants now?
Who were your ancestors then?
Whether your deeds were noble or base,
how can they be so forgotten?
A hundred walls are all rising,
seventy feet high they stand even.
The walls cannot be moved,
the moat cannot be diverted.
The cedar timbers are destroyed,
the side chambers have collapsed.
Gazing at the front of the coffin, thoughts arise;
touching the figurines, grief increases.
The Archer-Spirit showed benevolence,
the Governor of Guǎnghàn spread kindness.
Sacrificing to the remains by the prefecture bend,
covering the bones at the city corner.
Looking up in admiration of ancient ways,
I chose a new burial site for you.
The wheels move to the northern moat,
the tomb is at the eastern foot.
The vault is newly constructed,
the coffin remains the old wood.
Joint burial was not the ancient custom,
but it was what Zhōugōng preserved.
Respectfully following the ancient meaning,
I reunite the two souls.
Wine in two jars,
a single pig for sacrifice.
Your dark spirit seems to be present,
enjoy my sacrificial vessel.
Alas, how sorrowful!
On the [...] day of the [...] month of the fifth year of the Sòng era,
Zhāng Shào, Inspector of Xiāngzhōu and native of Wújùn,
respectfully receiving the Imperial command,
set up banners in the old land of Chǔ.
Seeking the depths where the sand was embraced,
finding the shore where the jade pendant was cast.
Restraining the carriage at Luó Lake,
mooring the boat at the Mì islet.
I then sent a certain Assistant of the Household Department,
to respectfully sacrifice to the spirit of the late Grand Master of the Three Gates of Chǔ, Lord Qū:
The orchid is fragrant but destroyed,
the jade is fine but broken.
Things are envied for their hardness and fragrance,
people are shunned for their brilliance and purity.
As for you, sir,
you met with a flawed time.
Warm winds were idle then,
flying frost came in an urgent season.
Yíng and Mié met in conflict,
Zhāo and Huái were not upright;
Plans were broken by Yí and Shàng,
integrity was slighted by Jiāo and Lán.
Your person was severed from the gates of Yǐng,
your tracks were everywhere along the banks of the Xiāng.
Comparing yourself to the fragrant grasses,
associating yourself with dragons and phoenixes.
Your voice resonates like metal and stone,
your will is as radiant as the sun and moon.
Like that fragrant tree,
truly flourishing and truly blooming.
Looking at the Mì River, my heart sighs;
gazing at Luó Lake, my thoughts wander.
The offerings used may be but dust,
but your manifest loyalty can never be lacking.
In the third year of the Xiàojiàn era of Sòng.
On the nineteenth day, Xīnwèi, of the ninth month starting with Guǐchǒu,
Lord Wáng, with mountain delicacies and rustic wine,
respectfully sacrifices to the spirit of Lord Yán:
Alas, how sorrowful!
Virtue is established through the Way,
rites are purified through benevolence.
Only your excellence, sir,
spread its fame in your early years.
Your righteousness exhausted the subtleties of the machine and the symbols,
your writings eclipsed Bān and Yáng.
Your nature was stubborn, upright, and pure,
your mind and depth were deep and heroic.
Entering the court to bring light to the state,
you were truly the flower of Sòng.
Your talent spanned across the Hàn and Wèi eras,
your reputation reached as far as Guīshā.
You held rank according to the Imperial statutes,
yet set your heart on the cloudy ridges.
In pure companionship with plain friends,
sharing the same ripples of light.
Your spirit was as high as Shūyè,
your sternness as upright as Zhòngjǔ.
With leisurely wings, you soared alone,
a solitary style without peer.
Lingering in the virtue of wine,
whistling and singing to the threads of the zither.
Wandering and looking for years,
together in hardship and ease.
When the spring breeze led the season,
we would talk and compose.
Before the autumn dew had condensed,
your spirit returned to the Great Primordial.
Setting out at dawn in my carriage,
I look at your cottage and watch the road.
My heart is pained and my eyes are wet,
my feelings are tangled like drifting clouds.
Cold shadows cover the porch,
the bright moon's radiance sleeps.
The faint lamp flickers its light,
whom do the table and scrolls now illuminate?
Dust has long settled on the bedding,
the strings and woodwinds have ceased their tune.
Gripped by grief in the orchid hall,
shedding tears on the pine ridge.
Since ancient times all reach their end,
even at Mount Niú there were tears.
It is not only Great Heaven
that has destroyed my brilliant and excellent friend.
With this I restrain my grief,
and respectfully lay out these offerings.
Offering wine with long-lasting memory,
I look back and sigh.
Alas, how sorrowful!
